And [it is forbidden] in connection with the discharge of urine, feces, or semen, and with the consumption of food. 1.50 — 1.47.
[The letter H represents the sound *sneh* for *srehu*.]

The particle *ca* serves to carry forward the requirement for sipping water (*ācamana*). "Discharging" (*visraṃsana*) means casting out; this is connected individually with urine, feces, and oily substances. "Contact with food" (*abhyavahārasaṃyoga*) is the consumption of edible substances. This statement is made for the purpose of removing stains and odors because such contact is impure; since the requirement for sipping water is already established by the rule "having slept or having eaten," one should effect the removal of stains and odors by washing with earth and water. Thus, in the case of the statement "that [removal] first with water," what was said regarding the removal of food-stains with powder and so forth should be understood as applicable here when that [washing] is impossible.

Alternatively, the mention of the connection with eating is intended solely for the purpose of *ācamana* (ritual rinsing). That which is already established by the phrase "having slept and having eaten" is restated here for the sake of establishing the proper order. How so? By the inclusion of that [eating], the removal of food-residues is indicated; the meaning is that one should rinse after first performing that removal. Otherwise, there would be doubt. Thus says Āpastamba: "Having voided urine or feces, having washed away the residues of urine and feces, the residues of food, the residues of impure remains, and whatever residues of semen there may be, and having washed his feet and performed *ācamana*, he becomes pure" (*ĀpDh* 1.15.23). "Urine" and "feces" are well known. "Sneha" means semen. The mention of urine and the others is for the purpose of *ācamana*, since the removal of stains and odors is already established by the rule: "Purity consists in the removal of stains and odors. (1.50)

The word "ca" (and) serves to include what was previously mentioned. "Sneha" means semen. "Visraṃsana" means the discharge or removal of urine, feces, and oily secretions. "Abhyavahāra" refers to an inedible substance; contact with such a substance is what is meant here. On account of these causes, purification is to be performed as before with earth and water. 1.47.
And where the sacred tradition (āmnāya) would enjoin [a rule]. 1.51 — 1.48.

In this context, the remainder of the sentence is "that very thing [remains]. The *āmnāya* is the Veda; where, in the domain of sacrifice, it prescribes purification by mere washing for objects such as the wooden sword (*sphya*), there that very thing [applies], and not [purification] such as carving on the basis of the commonality of being wood. If it is argued that this is established simply because [the Vedic rule and the worldly practice] possess unequal authority, [we reply: this statement is made for the purpose of preventing what is declared in the *Śruti* from entering into the worldly domain. Just as, in the context of sacrifice, purification by washing is prescribed for the ladle (*darvī*) by the *Śruti*, so that when that same ladle is employed in a worldly activity, purification based on the commonality of being a ladle as declared by the *Śruti* should not apply; rather, one should perform only that which is prescribed by *Smṛti*. It is for this purpose that the statement is made.

Alternatively—the word *āmnāya* refers to Manu. Wherever he prescribes purification, that alone applies, as in the passage beginning, "But for ascetics, fourfold" (MDh 5.137). If it is argued that there is no doubt precisely because it has been stated by him, we reply: in a matter where nothing at all is stated, that which is stated in another *smṛti* applies. However, in a case where something such as the removal of stains and odors is mentioned, a suspicion arises regarding an option (*vikalpa*) with another *smṛti*; therefore, it is said, "and wherever the *āmnāya* prescribes. And thus, even when the removal of stains and odors has been performed, one must still resort to rules such as, "twofold for a student" (MDh 5.137). || 1.51 ||

In whatever matter a particular purification the tradition (āmnāya) may prescribe, that alone shall be the rule for it; as, for example, the cleansing with water at the Mārjālīya fire of the *camasa* cups that have been smeared with remnants. 1.48.
Now he describes the rule for approaching the teacher for the purpose of study by the student who has performed his purification:
"Next is the rule for approaching the teacher:
having grasped the left hand [of the teacher], excluding the thumb, he should address the teacher, saying, 'Recite, sir! (1.52).

Having grasped the teacher’s left hand with his own, excluding the thumb, he should address the teacher, saying, "Recite, sir! Thereupon, with his eyes and mind fixed on the teacher, he should touch his vital breaths with *darbha* grass. 1.49.

Having grasped with his right hand the left hand—excluding the thumb, that is, devoid of the thumb—he should request the teacher, the instructor, saying, "Recite, sir! The mention of the "hand" is for the purpose of excluding the feet. Because the context concerns the hand, it is understood that "the left hand" refers specifically to the hand. It is understood that the grasping occurs at the region of the fingers, since it is stated to be "devoid of the thumb. (1.52)

With his own right hand—since the word "left" is used as a qualification, it is understood that [the student uses] the right—he should grasp the left foot of the teacher, excluding the big toe (that is, with the exception of the big toe). Having done so, he should address the teacher, saying, "Recite, sir! In this regard, having fixed his mind and eyes upon the teacher, he should remain attentive. His vital breaths are the sense organs located in the head; the young student must perform the ritual rinsing (*upasparśana*) of those [organs] with *darbha* grass according to the sequence prescribed for the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*). 1.49.
Furthermore:
therein, the eye and the mind [are faculties]. 1.53.
The meaning is that one should fix the eyes and the mind upon the guru there. || 1.53 ||
Furthermore: the touching of the vital breaths with *darbha* grass. 1.54.

The word "should be done" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Since direct contact with the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) is impossible, the term "vital breaths" refers here to the sense organs located in the head, such as the eyes and so forth. One should touch them with *darbha* grass according to the sequence prescribed for the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*). 1.54.
Furthermore: "The three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) consist of fifteen measures (mātrās). [1.55] — [1.50]

The word "should be performed" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. *Prāṇāyāma* is the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is remaining in a state of suspended breathing; these three [breaths] should be performed. Each consists of fifteen *mātrās*. A *mātrā* is what is commonly known in the world by the term "the sound of the middle finger and thumb. (1.55)

The word "should be performed" (*kāryā*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Having rubbed [the hands] along the sides of the knees, one should make a single snap; that constitutes one *mātrā*. One should hold the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*) for as long a time as it takes to complete those fifteen [snap-sounds]; that is one *prāṇāyāma*. Three of these should be performed. As Manu says:
"One should recite the Gāyatrī together with the *Vyāhṛtis*, the *Praṇava*, and the *Śiras* three times while the breath is restrained; that is called *prāṇāyāma*."
Furthermore:
"And the seat [should be] on grass blades pointing eastward. (1.56) — || 1.51 ||

"On blades of *darbha* grass with their tips pointing eastward"—this follows from the context; "seating" means sitting down; "should be performed" is the ellipsis. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that he should also have *darbha* strainers in his hands.
He made his seat upon darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward; "it should be done" is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 1.51 ||
Furthermore: "The five *vyāhṛtis* preceded by *oṃ* and ending with *satya*. (1.57)—[this was stated in] 1.52.

The word "should be recited" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Each [of these] begins with the *praṇava* (OM), consists of the three worlds starting with *bhūr*, has *puruṣa* in the middle, and ends with *satya*. This is well known thus in the *Jābāli-śruti*. 1.57.

The *vyāhṛtis* are five: *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, *svaḥ*, *satyam*, and *puruṣaḥ*. Here, however, the fourth should be called the *puruṣa-vyāhṛti* and the fifth the *satya-vyāhṛti*. Furthermore, each of these should be preceded by the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*). || 1.52 ||
Furthermore: "In the morning, there is the clasping of the feet of the teacher. (1.58) — (1.53)

The word "to be done" (*kāryam*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. Although one might have said "clasping the feet" (*upasaṃgrahaṇam*), the use of the term "feet" (*pāda*) is intended to include the rules taught in other *smṛtis*. As Manu says: "The clasping of the teacher's feet should be performed with crossed hands; the left foot is to be touched with the left hand, and the right foot with the right hand. (MDh 2.72). "Every day," meaning rising again and again in the morning. The mention of the "teacher" is so that this rule does not apply to oneself. Prior to that, there is the touching of the vital breaths (*prāṇopasparśana*) by oneself. (1.58)
Every day at dawn, one must perform the clasping of the teacher’s feet. Manu says:
"The clasping of the teacher’s feet should be performed with crossed hands;
the left foot is to be touched with the left hand, and the right foot with the right hand" (MDh 2.72). 1.53.
Furthermore:
"And at the beginning and end of the recitation of the Brahman [text]. (1.59) — (1.54)
"At the beginning and end of the Veda-recitation" means at its commencement and conclusion. The word "and" (ca) serves to include the clasping of the teacher's feet. || 1.59 ||
"Brahman" means the Veda; "recitation" means teaching it. In that regard, the clasping of the teacher's feet must be performed at both the beginning and the end. 1.54.
Furthermore: Having been permitted, the disciple should sit to the south, facing either east or north. 1.60–1.55.

Instructed by the teacher, he should sit to the south of him, facing either east or north; this option is possible depending on the circumstances. The meaning is that he should sit facing either east or north in such a way that he is directly opposite the seated teacher. How so? Because it has been stated: "There, his eye and mind [should be fixed]" (GDh 1.53). The mention of the "pupil" (śiṣya) is for the purpose of making known that this same rule applies to anyone else who has approached for instruction. And the phrase "permitted, to the south" is a restrictive rule, meaning that one should not sit down without permission, nor anywhere other than to the south. 1.60.
Permitted by the teacher, he should sit to the teacher's right, facing either east or north; the choice depends on the requirements of the task at hand. 1.55.
Moreover:
"The Sāvitrī and the recitation [of the Veda] must be performed at the beginning when undertaking the study of the Brahman. 1.61.
And the recitation of the Sāvitrī. 1.56.
The *sāvitrī* is the verse beginning with "tat savituḥ," etc. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), the *vyāhṛtis* preceded by the syllable *oṃ* are also included. Thus says Manu:

"The three imperishable *mahāvyāhṛtis* preceded by the syllable *oṃ*, and the three-footed *gāyatrī*, should be known as the mouth of Brahman. [MDh 2.81] It is to be recited (*anuvacana*) at the taking up of Brahman—that is, at the commencement of the Veda; the meaning is: at the time of beginning the study. This is to be done first, at the outset. 1.61
"This [verse], 'tat savitur vareṇyam,' is the one belonging to the deity Savitṛ, and no other; it must be recited at every study session as part of the *anuvacana*. || 1.56 ||
At the beginning, [the word] "brahman" is used in the sense of taking up. 1.57.

“Having grasped the left foot with the hand,” and so forth—whatever has been stated ending with the recitation of the Sāvitrī must be performed at the very beginning, at the time of receiving the Veda (brahman) from the teacher (guru). This applies immediately after the initiation (upanayana) and at the time of the instruction of the Sāvitrī; however, on subsequent days, one should simply direct one’s eyes and mind toward him. Furthermore, at the beginning and end of the morning study, one must grasp the feet of the teacher and sit down only when permitted. || 1.57 ||
Furthermore: "The syllable *oṃ* [is used] elsewhere as well. (1.62) — (1.58)

Immediately after the recitation, the syllable *oṃ* should also be uttered elsewhere. Herein is the sequence: having risen in the morning, one should perform the clasping of the teacher’s feet; then, being called by him, one should sit upon *darbha* grass. Then, touching the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) with *darbha* blades, and having performed breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), one should utter the five Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*). Having addressed the teacher with joined palms, saying “Recite, sir,” and having uttered the *vyāhṛtis* preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and the *Sāvitrī*, one should study, beginning with the *praṇava*. This rule applies only to the first study. Why? Because, although it would have been sufficient to say “and the *Sāvitrī*, then he should study,” the text begins with the phrase “the taking up of the Veda from the beginning. On every subsequent day, one should simply utter the syllable *oṃ*. Why? Because it was stated that the syllable *oṃ* is for “elsewhere. “Elsewhere” means other than the first study. The word “also” (*api*) is intended to include the *praṇava* even in the first study. Some, by the phrase “also elsewhere,” maintain that the *praṇava* should be used at the beginning of the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) and so forth. (1.62)
The syllable *oṃ* should be uttered even on occasions other than the recitation of the *Sāvitrī*; the meaning is that it should be done every day at the time of study. (1.58)
But if he goes in between, there must be a renewed initiation. 1.63. — 1.59.

If someone should pass between [the teacher and student] while they are studying, then for the sake of expiation, one must again perform the entire procedure beginning with the clasping of the feet and ending with the utterance of the *praṇava*. Even though this is not part of the formal context (*aprakaraṇa*), the expiation is performed immediately following [the interruption] so that the study may proceed. This applies to the passage of humans; for others, it is mentioned later. Since no mention of a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) is heard here, one should study immediately after the expiation. The mention of "again" is in reference to the first commencement of study, because there is no formal sitting down (*upasadana*) elsewhere. Therefore, in other cases, the sitting down must be performed solely for the purpose of expiation, and study must be undertaken immediately thereafter. Thus says Āpastamba: “Having said, ‘Recite, sir! one should either study or teach” (ĀpDh 1.10.15–16). || 1.63 ||

Going between the teacher and the pupil is "interfering" (antarāgamana). Upon anyone interfering, the formal sitting down (upasadana) must be performed again. The upasadana consists of the rites beginning with "with the left hand" [GDh 1.49] and ending with "the syllable Om even elsewhere" [GDh 1.58]. 1.59.
Furthermore:
for dogs, mongooses, snakes, frogs, and cats, there shall be a fast and a period of separation from the community for three days. 1.64 — 1.60.

These [animals] are well known. For dogs and the others, if any one of them passes between [the teacher and student], the penance is the abandonment of food for three days; "separation from the teacher" (*vipravāsaḥ*) means staying apart from the teacher for one day. And thus, precisely because of the instruction regarding separation from the teacher, the non-study (*anadhyāya*) for one day is established. If it is asked why the duration is understood as one day, it is because of the lack of a compound (i.e., *tryaham* and *vipravāsaḥ* are not compounded). Otherwise, he would have said, "three days of fasting and separation. Therefore, the non-study lasts for exactly one day. And so says Manu: "In the case of cattle, frogs, cats, dogs, snakes, and mongooses..."

"One should know that there is no study for a day and a night during the passage [of such animals]" (MDh 4.126). Thus, here too, the mention of the "dog" is an *upalakṣaṇa* (inclusive indicator) for four-footed domestic animals (*catuṣpada-paśu*), since the cat is included within the category of four-footed animals. Its separate mention, however, is for the purpose of increasing the severity of the penance (*prāyaścitta*). As Uśanas says: "Upon the passage of a cat between [the teacher and pupil], one should consume clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and fast for three days. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to draw in the requirement of sitting near the teacher (*upasadana*). Therefore, having performed that [penance] at the time of study, one should then proceed with the recitation. Some say that fasting implies the abandonment of study; whether this is correct or not should be deliberated upon. (1.64)

If dogs and other such animals pass between [the teacher and the student], a three-day fast and a stay away from home must be observed; "stay away from home" means dwelling elsewhere than at the teacher’s family residence. However, Manu states: "In the case of cattle, frogs, cats, dogs, snakes, and mongooses passing between [the teacher and the student], one should know that there is no study for a day and a night" (MDh 4.126). That rule refers to the period after the Veda has been mastered (*dhāraṇādhyayana*). The rule of Gautama, however, refers to the period of learning for the purpose of acquisition (*grahaṇādhyayana*). 1.60.
Furthermore:
"For others, there shall be breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and the consumption of clarified butter. (1.65) — (1.61)

For others, such as crows and the like, there are three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), because of the hearing of the plural number. The consumption of ghee (*ghṛtaprāśana*) is merely a bathing of the body. The word "and" (*ca*) is for the purpose of drawing in the act of approaching the teacher (*upasadana*). Therefore, having performed three breath-restraints, consumed ghee, and performed the approaching, one should study, since no prohibition of study (*anadhyāya*) is heard in this case. 1.65.

In the case of other animals, excluding dogs and the like, if they enter between [the teacher and the disciple], three *prāṇāyāmas* should be performed and the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśana*) should also be performed. All of this is an expiation for the disciple, not for the teacher; others, however, maintain that it applies to both. 1.61.
And likewise when studying near a cremation ground. 1.66 — 1.62.

Āpastamba has stated: “One should not study within the range of a *śamyā*-throw from any direction” (ĀpDh 1.9.6). Therefore, studying in the vicinity of that [cremation ground] constitutes "studying at a cremation ground" (*śmaśānādhyayana*). The prefix *abhi-* is intended to indicate that the act was intentional. Consequently, for an unintentional act, another, lighter expiation (*prāyaścitta*) should be understood as applicable. Thus Uśanas says: “If one studies at a cremation ground unintentionally, one should recite, ‘Recite, sir! and then continue the study. By the word *ca* (“and”), there is the application of everything mentioned immediately prior, such as the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and so forth; however, by the word *evam* (“thus”), the application is restricted specifically to the *upasadana* (approaching the teacher) mentioned immediately before. If it is argued that the word *evam* alone should have been used, we say no; for this specific meaning is obtained only when both [words] are present. How so? When either the word *evam* or the word *ca* should have been used, it is proper to assume a different purpose for the reading of both, rather than for only one. Therefore, the *upasadana* itself must be performed. Accordingly, another *smṛti* states: “Having studied near a cremation ground, one should restrain the breath, perform the ritual touching of water (*prāṇopasparśana*), offer salutation (*abhivādana*), and recite the *Sāvitrī*,” and so forth. The repetition [of the concluding phrase] marks the end of the chapter. All this aforementioned expiation applies only to the student, because the study and other related acts are for his sake. Furthermore, in all cases, the expiation consists precisely of the *upasadana*; and since *upasadana* involves salutation and the like, such salutation is not possible toward the teacher himself. 1.66.

Regarding *abhi* in the sense of "above," such as over a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*) or during the study [of the Veda], the penance is likewise breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśana*). The repetition [of the rule] is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the section on teaching. 1.62.
Now begins the second chapter.

The initiation (*upanayana*) of the twice-born has been described; however, since some maintain that they possess entitlement to certain duties of their respective classes even prior to initiation, he speaks for that purpose. In connection with the initiated, the duties of the uninitiated are now stated.
Before initiation, one may act, speak, and eat according to one's desire.
Before initiation, there is freedom of action, freedom of speech, and freedom of eating. 2.1.
But surely this should have been stated even before the initiation ceremony; therefore, the phrase "prior to initiation" need not be mentioned there.

It is said: This is true; however, the purpose for stating the initiation (*upanayana*) at the beginning has already been explained. It is not enjoined by this [sūtra], because it is already established by the sense of the matter. Nor is it restricted, because there is no necessity for its performance, given that it will be stated later that "the initiation and so forth constitute the restriction" (GDh 2.10), and because there is an absence of optionality. Nor is it an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*), because there is nothing to be excluded; for the state of acting without desire and so forth has not been previously established for this [act]. Therefore, this sūtra is merely a restatement (*anuvādaka*), intended to make known the absence of penance and royal punishment, since those two have been taught in a general manner.

But surely, royal punishments and penances are prescribed for the non-performance of what is enjoined or the performance of what is prohibited; yet this person has no entitlement (*adhikāra*) with respect to injunctions or prohibitions, nor is any injunction or prohibition heard regarding him. It might be argued that his status as one who has not offered the *āhuti* and so forth will either be enjoined or prohibited, such that both [punishment and penance] would apply upon its transgression, because of the instruction concerning the father and others. Therefore, this sūtra is useless.

To this it is replied: whatever expiation has been prescribed for the non-performance of what is enjoined or the practice of what is prohibited, or whatever royal punishment [is ordained], both of these certainly apply to him as well. Even though no specific injunction or prohibition is heard with reference to him alone, nevertheless, that which is stated in general terms—such as "non-violence, truthfulness, and non-stealing" (MDh 10.63)—applies to him too because it constitutes the duty (*dharma*) of his social class (*varṇa*). Upon its transgression, both royal punishment and expiation occur. Therefore, this aphorism (*sūtra*) is commenced in the form of a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the purpose of precluding those [penalties].

By the sūtra, “The rule begins with the initiation ceremony” (GDh 2.10), it will be stated that expiation applies only to the transgression of those injunctions prescribed starting from the initiation ceremony, and not to the transgression of others. By that very principle, one can understand that there is no expiation for the transgression of the duties of the social classes (*varṇadharma*), nor even a royal punishment. Nevertheless, this sūtra has been commenced for the following purposes: to introduce half of the expiation for one who has passed the fixed time for initiation due to negligence but remains capable; to introduce the full expiation for his parents and others if he dies before the age of five; and to indicate the absence of any offense if he dies before that. Thus says the Bhārgavīya:
A child who is less than sixteen years old, or one who is eighty years of age,
as well as women and those who are afflicted by disease, deserve only half of the prescribed penance.
For one who is less than eleven years of age but more than five years old,
a friend or a teacher should perform the penance for the sake of purification.
"Therefore, for one who is even more ignorant [than that], no offense exists anywhere;

consequently, neither royal punishment nor penance is prescribed for him. Thus, although it has been stated in general that before initiation (*upanayana*) there is freedom of action (*kāmacāritva*), nevertheless, absolute freedom of action applies only until the age of five. After that, he must be enjoined to the duties of his caste (*varṇadharma*) by his father and others, because a penance for the parents and others is heard of in the scriptures when the child transgresses them. Enough of this digression.

Now the Sūtra is being explained: before initiation (*upanayana*), there is freedom of action (*kāmacāra*) and freedom of movement according to one’s will. Therefore, regarding the touching of a *caṇḍāla* and similar acts, he will state that mere sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) suffices, as in the rule: "except for [the cases requiring] sprinkling" (GDh 2.6). That too is said to apply only prior to the fifth year. After that age, upon touching a *caṇḍāla* or others, he must be made to bathe; after the eleventh year, he should bathe by himself. This applies everywhere. Freedom of speech (*kāmavāda*) means he may speak even vulgarities and the like. Freedom of eating (*kāmabhakṣa*) means he may eat even stale food and the like. After the fifth year, however, he should be made to perform actions that do not conflict with the duties of his social class (*varṇadharma*). The phrase "before initiation" includes even the initiation performed in times of distress (*āpadkalpa*). Why? Because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) "a religious student" (*brahmacārī*). Since it is already established that lapses in celibacy (*brahmacarya*) are impossible prior to the regular time for initiation, an instruction on the preservation of celibacy would otherwise be purposeless. He himself will give an example of freedom of action: "He becomes one who voids urine and excrement wherever he happens to be" (GDh 2.4). Therefore, even during the stage of extreme childhood, one must take care to prevent him from committing such acts as killing a Brahmin. Even in the stage of extreme childhood, he must be carefully prevented from false accusations and the like under the heading of "freedom of speech," and from drinking liquor and the like under "freedom of eating"; for although these are already covered by the term "freedom of action," they are mentioned again specifically. The inclusion of the word "prior to" (*prāk*) when "before initiation" (*upanayanāt*) could have sufficed is for the sake of restriction, meaning that freedom of action exists only prior to initiation. If this restriction were absent, then by the rule "and for the subsequent [stages], this is not inconsistent" (GDh 3.10), practices such as eating the remnants of sacrificial offerings would apply even to ascetics (*yatis*). 2.1.

The phrase "until the sixteenth year for a Brāhmaṇa" refers to the subject of the *upanayana* performed in times of distress (*āpad-kalpa*). "Acting according to one's will" means acting as one pleases. "He may sell even things that should not be sold; he may live even by the 'dog's livelihood'"—this is the statement regarding acting according to one's will. "Speaking according to one's will" refers to the utterance of vulgar, untruthful, and other such speech. "Eating according to one's will" refers to eating garlic, stale food, and so forth, or eating four or five times a day—one who does this is described in that way. However, there is no over-extension to include such acts as killing a Brāhmaṇa or drinking liquor. (2.1)
Now he states the exception regarding the consumption of meat obtained through desire: "Except for what is offered. (2.2)

The term *hutam* refers to what has been offered, such as the *caru* and *puroḍāśa* that remain after the oblation, but not the remnants of the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, because the latter is intended for all purposes. Thus says Āpastamba: “In the *vaiśvadeva*, one should make all [deities] sharers” [ĀpDh 2.9.5]. The phrase “it should be done from the *ahuta*” (what is not offered) is the understood remainder. This prohibition of what is naturally implied is an instruction specifically for the ancestors and others, since a child lacks discernment; it is stated that after the eleventh year, the rule applies to the child himself. 2.2.

The *huta-śeṣa* is the remains of the sacrificial oblation, such as the *puroḍāśa* cake. One who eats that is *hutāt*; one who is the opposite of that is *ahutāt*. For it is said: "One who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*) should not eat the *huta*. (2.2)
A celibate student. || 2.3 ||
One must practice the preservation of celibacy. 2.3.

This is an exception to the rule regarding acting according to one's desires and so forth. Since it has been stated [that this applies] "until the sixteenth year," there is the possibility of attachment to women; therefore, a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) should be one who has conquered his senses. And likewise, in another Smṛti: "The penance for one who has violated the vow is purified by the *avakīrṇi*-vow; one should initiate him, but not after that time, because of both the *vrātya* and the *avakīrṇi* vows. (2.3)
Now he states an illustration of acting according to one's own will: "He passes urine and excrement wherever it may happen. (2.4)
The meaning is that just as urine and feces are produced even when one is pulled by the hair or while standing, if one’s head is wrapped [in cloth], one should do so right there.

He is described as such because he discharges urine and feces according to what is available; even one facing east or another direction may do so. Furthermore, there is no restriction regarding location, such as the rule "not on the bare ground" (GDh 9.38). 2.4.
Moreover:
"No rule for sipping water (ācamana) applies to him. (2.5)

From the age of five upwards until before the eleventh year, the ritual rule for sipping water (*ācamana*), that is, the procedure for *ācamana*, does not exist. Because of the prohibition of the ritual rule, it is understood that there is merely the act of sipping water itself. In this regard, since another Smṛti states, "For he is equal to a Śūdra as long as he is not born through the Veda" (MDh 2.172cd), and because his duties are heard to be identical to those of a Śūdra, his *ācamana* should be regarded as being like that of a Śūdra. Why is it said "of one less than eleven years"? Because of the commencement with the word "of him" (*asya*), because the absence of fault is heard prior to the fifth year, and because from the eleventh year onwards he is entitled to the duties of his own caste (*varṇadharma*). It is thus understood that even the ritual rule for *ācamana* exists for him after the eleventh year. || 2.5 ||
Because mental construction is prohibited, sipping water (ācamana) is permitted [for him], just as it is for women and Śūdras.
Now, regarding the very young child, [the rule] says:
except for wiping, rubbing, and sprinkling. (2.6)

The phrase "is not found for him" continues [from the previous rule]. The meaning is that for this child under five years of age, no method of purification other than wiping and so forth exists. "Wiping" (*apamārjana*) refers to the removal of food remnants from the mouth with the hand moistened with water. "Rinsing" (*pradhāvana*) refers to washing after urination, defecation, and the like. "Sprinkling" (*avokṣaṇa*) refers to sprinkling water upon contact with a *caṇḍāla* or similar person. If it is argued that since there is no possibility of [the application of] the rule for sipping water (*ācamana*), the two prohibitions—"no rule for sipping water exists for him"—and "except for wiping, rinsing, and sprinkling"—would be redundant, this is not a fault. By the statement "no rule for sipping water exists for him," the rule for sipping water is prescribed for those under sixteen years of age by means of a prohibition for those under eleven. Furthermore, by the statement "except for wiping, rinsing, and sprinkling," the acts of wiping and so forth are prescribed for the child under five years of age by means of a prohibition against other methods of purification. (2.6)

Excluding the wiping (*apamārjana*) and other such acts, there is no ritual for sipping water (*ācamana-kalpa*). This means that the wiping and so forth do exist. Although the wiping and other acts are not included within the ritual for sipping water, they are nevertheless prescribed by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*). Here, "wiping" (*apamārjana*) refers to rubbing with a hand containing water that which is smeared with food remnants and the like. "Washing" (*pradhāvana*) refers to cleansing with water and clay that which is smeared with impure substances and the like. "Sprinkling" (*avokṣaṇa*) refers to [cleansing] that which has been touched by a woman in her courses and so forth; this applies to very young children. For those over six years of age, they require bathing. For an uninitiated child (*anupanīta*) of this description, this much is the penance (*prāyaścitta*) in the event of transgressing the rules regarding acting according to one's own will and so forth. Regarding this, another Smṛti states:
A child under sixteen years of age, as well as one who is eighty years old,
women, and those who are afflicted by disease, deserve only half of the prescribed penance.
For one who is less than eleven years of age but more than five years old,
the teacher and likewise a friend shall perform the penance for the sake of purification.
Therefore, for this most ignorant one, there is neither offense nor sin;
consequently, neither royal punishment nor penance is prescribed for him.
Thus [ends the section]. 2.6.
Moreover: "There is no impurity resulting from touching that [corpse]. (2.7)

By the mention of "that," one who has not yet performed purification is meant. Due to touching such a person, or being touched by him, impurity does not arise; this applies specifically to very young children.

In that case, the prescription for its purification would be useless. Why? Because only two purposes for the prescription of purification are observed: to make it fit for contact with others, and for the sake of ritual performance (*anuṣṭhāna*). However, this [purification] does not serve to make it fit for contact with others, because even one who has not undergone purification is fit for contact, as stated in the rule: “There is no impurity from touching it. Nor does it serve for the sake of ritual performance, because there is no performance of this [purification].

It is not purposeless, because the prescription for purification is for the sake of protection. And so says another Smṛti: "One should perform purification for the sake of protecting a child until the fifth year. The use of the prefix *upa-* is intended to indicate the absence of fault upon touching this very person when he has not yet performed purification. Thus, in the case of touching others who have produced impurity through food remnants, urine, or feces, sipping water (*ācamana*) must be performed. There is no fault in touching them, because they are included among those touched by a corpse in the relevant Sūtra. Likewise, another Smṛti states: "He who touches one who is impure is indeed defiled alone."
"Having touched that, another shall not become defiled; this is the rule regarding all substances.

Regarding the touch of a *caṇḍāla*, however, he will state in the Sūtra on touching a corpse (GDh 14.22): "One should touch water. While it would have been sufficient to say "one should touch water," the author has composed the weighty sūtra "there is no impurity from touching that" in order to override even the restriction found in the rule "before initiation" (GDh 2.1). Consequently, even after initiation, one must perform *ācamana* upon touching food-leavings, urine, or feces. 2.7.

Because of that contact—due to touching him even though he has not yet performed his initiation (*upanayana*) and has been touched by a woman in her courses (*udakyā*) and so forth—there shall be no impurity (*aśauca*). "Contact" (*upasparśana*) means the touching of one who has been touched. Because of that, bathing is not to be performed. Even from touching one who has eaten leftovers or has voided urine or feces, there is no requirement for sipping water (*ācamana*). This too applies only before the age of six. For what purpose, then, is purification prescribed for him? It is certainly not for the sake of performing religious rites, nor for the sake of fitness for touch, since he is fit for touch even when his purification has not been performed. We say it is for the sake of protection. And thus says another *Smṛti*:
"For the sake of protection, one should practice purification for a child from the fifth year onwards. (2.7)
Furthermore:
"But one should certainly not employ him for the Agnihotra oblation or for the receiving of sacrificial offerings. (2.8)
H reads "haraṇayoḥ" for "grahaṇayoḥ."

The word *enam* (him) is used for the purpose of including everyone who has not yet been initiated (*anupanīta*). That which is performed in the fire, such as the *agnihotra* oblation and so forth, is called *agnihavana*. The *baliharaṇa* is the offering of food (*bali*) given to the deities of the quarters after the *vaiśvadeva* rite. The particle *tu* expresses a distinction: one should not employ him even for tasks such as washing the feet of Brahmins during the *aṣṭakā* rites and others, let alone for the specific acts of *agnihavana* and *baliharaṇa*. Because there is no restriction [on his activities] otherwise, if he were to study a mantra somewhere and proceed on his own accord in the *agnihotra* or similar rites, then even the one who permitted it would not be considered a consenter; it is for this very reason that the word *eva* (only/alone) is used. This statement is intended to enjoin the initiation (*upanīta*), since there is no other basis for its application. Thus, although the injunction "the learned man should offer the *agnihotra*" implies—according to the Vedic text—that only one with extensive learning is qualified, nevertheless, in the absence of such a person, one should employ even a boy of little knowledge who has been initiated. And so says Manu:

“Neither a maiden, nor a young woman, nor one of little learning, nor a fool, nor one who is afflicted, nor likewise one who is uninitiated, shall be the *hotṛ* priest for the *agnihotra*. (MDh 11.36) In this regard, since the prohibition is already established by the very prohibition of one of little learning (*alpavidya*), the further prohibition of the “uninitiated” (*asaṃskṛta*) is explained as being intended to permit even one of little learning provided he has been initiated, in the absence of another who is learned. As for that which was stated beginning with “prior to initiation” (GDh 2.1), it should be understood to apply to women also until their marriage. Why?

"The rite of marriage for women is declared to be their initiation (upanayana)," according to the observation of another Smṛti. Thus, the prohibition of the appointment (niyoga) for a maiden regarding the Agnihotra and Bali offerings is established. Therefore, the appointment must be performed after the time of marriage. In that regard, because it is prohibited for a woman by the Vedic text "A woman shall not offer oblations," this [prohibition] should be understood to apply to the *aupāsana* fire and similar rites. And so says another Smṛti: "The wife shall offer oblations in the *aupāsana* fire and perform the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice," and so forth. Furthermore, the prohibition "not a young woman" involves no fault, as it refers to the wives of others (*paradāra*). (2.8)

One should not employ this [boy] who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*) in the *agnihotra*, the *aupāsana-homa*, the *bali-haraṇa*, the *vaiśvadeva*, and so forth; that is to say, one should not employ him. By the word "but" (*tu*), it is implied that he should not be employed even in other rites accompanied by mantras. The particle "only" (*eva*) is used for emphasis. Now, Āśvalāyana says: "From the taking of the hand [of the bride] onwards, one should perform the domestic rites (*gṛhya*) oneself, or the wife, or the son, or the daughter, or the pupil. And the followers of the Sāmaveda (*chandoga*) state that the wife may offer the oblation. Thus, in this alternative permitted for the wife, daughter, and others, the meaning is: "But certainly not him [the uninitiated boy]. (2.8)
Moreover:
"One should not utter the word 'brahman' except when offering the *svadhā* libation. (2.9)

The word "thus" (*evam*) is understood to carry over. By the word *brahman*, the Vedas are meant. Therefore, one should not teach him [the Veda]. Since the study of the Veda is already established for one who has been initiated (*upanīta*) by the rule, "After the introductory ceremony (*upākaraṇa*), he should study the meters," the prohibition regarding the uninitiated is already accomplished; however, the specific prohibition of the Veda is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), meaning that the Veda alone must not be taught. Consequently, there is no fault in teaching the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*). Because of the principle of acting according to one's own will, one should not even utter a mantra acquired by any other means. Why? Because the rule "one should cause to teach" is introduced without a specific context as "one should utter [it]," whereas the phrase "except at the pouring of the *svadhā*"—meaning, excluding the pouring of the *svadhā*—is introduced with a specific context. The "pouring of the *svadhā*" refers to what is given to the deceased, such as the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and water, after saying, "Svadhā to so-and-so. This also serves as an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the entire ritual for the deceased. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "Except at the water-rites connected with the *svadhā* and the ancestors" (VaDh 2.7). And in this way, even when a son is uninitiated, the funeral rites for the deceased must not be performed by the *sapiṇḍa* relatives and others, lest there be the undesirable consequence of the scriptural injunction becoming meaningless. 2.9.

"Brahman" means the Veda. One should not cause him who has not been initiated to recite, nor should one make him utter it. Is this without exception? No, he says: "except for the pouring of the *svadhā*. This is an elliptical expression for all ancestral (*pitrya*) rites; for we see in the *Vasiṣṭha-dharma-sūtra*: "Except for water-rites and those connected with the *svadhā* and the ancestors" (VaDh 2.7). And there are such texts as: "A son who has not yet mastered the syllables is worthy of the sacraments of his parents," and so forth. If no other [person] is available, then at that time, having caused him to learn the mantras, he should be made to perform the entire ancestral rite. 2.9.
Having now stated [the rules] for one who has not been initiated, he speaks regarding one who has been initiated:
"The rule begins with the initiation ceremony" (2.10).

The rule that has been stated beginning from the initiation ceremony (upanayana) is designated as "observance" (niyama). Thus, in the case of its non-performance, there is an expiation for this [subsequent rule], but not for the former. Or rather, starting from this point, the observance—the maintenance of vows which will be described as the kindling of the fire and so forth—is the "observance"; it must be performed beginning with the initiation ceremony.

The rule concerning fire, fuel, and so forth that will be stated hereafter refers precisely to those who have undergone initiation (*upanayana*) and the like; since [the rules] pertaining to those not initiated are interrupted, this [present section] is for the purpose of establishing the authority of those who have been initiated. (2.10)
Furthermore, celibacy has been explained. 2.11.

The inclusion of the word "stated" [in the rule] indicates that this restriction applies even prior to the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). Consequently, in the event of a transgression of that [rule], it should be understood that even for one who has not been initiated, eligibility [for the rite] is restored solely through the penance for a *avakīrṇin*. To this effect, another Smṛti states: "One who has become defiled [by emission] should be purified by the vow of an *avakīrṇin* and initiated if he is under seventeen years of age; beyond that, by both the vow of a *vrātya* and the vow of an *avakīrṇin*. If it is argued that for a religious student (*brahmacārin*), this is already established by implication because of the prohibition against looking at women and so forth, we say no, because such an act is possible even with animals and the like. (2.11)

The celibacy (brahmacarya) prescribed for one who has not been initiated is the same for one who has been initiated as well. Now, it may be objected that a prohibition will be stated later regarding "gazing at and touching women" [GDh 2.16]; nevertheless, this [present rule] is intended to prohibit recollection, praising, and so forth. 2.11.
Moreover:
[The refutation of] fire and fuel, and the practice of begging for alms. (2.12)

The kindling of the fire, the fuel, and the oblation—these are well known. These two must be performed daily. Their mention together is for the purpose of ensuring their immediate performance. Thus says Manu:
"Having taken up the desired staff and having worshipped the Sun..."

"Having circumambulated the fire from left to right, he should go about for alms according to the rule. (MDh 2.48). It has been stated there as well that by the phrase "having circumambulated the fire from left to right," the offering of fuel-sticks (*samidh-homa*) is intended. Since the twice-daily meal is prescribed in the text, "In the evening and in the morning, however, he should eat food with reverence, without disparaging it" (GDh 9.59), it should be understood that the kindling of the fire also occurs twice—in the evening and in the morning. And so says another Smṛti: "Having brought fuel-sticks from afar, he should place them in the open air."

"Unwearied, he should offer oblations into the fire with those [verses] both in the evening and in the morning. [MDh 2.186]. Some, however, desire that the offering of fuel-sticks (samid-ādhāna) take place only in the evening.

The fuel for the fire, its kindling, and the oblation; the collection of alms is *bhaikṣa*; wandering from house to house for that purpose is *bhaikṣacaraṇa*. These two must be performed every day. Regarding this, Manu says:
"Having fetched fuel from afar, he should place it in the open air;
evening and morning, he should offer oblations into the fire with that fuel, remaining unwearied."
"Having failed to go out for alms and having failed to kindle the fire, one who is not ill shall perform the vow of an *avakīrṇin* for seven nights. [MDh 2.186–87].
Āpastamba, however, states: "Some say that the worship of the fire should take place only in the evening. [ĀpDh 1.4.17]. 2.12.
Furthermore:
speaking the truth. 2.13.

The phrase "that which ought to be done" (*kartavyakriyā*) is to be supplied everywhere. The explicit mention of the word "speech" (*vacana*) is for the sake of removing doubt; otherwise, there might be the doubt that it refers merely to "touching water" (*upasparsanam*). The separate mention [of speech] is so that it may be performed even by one who is ill. Consequently, that [rule] does not apply to the two preceding cases. And thus says Manu:
"Without having gone for alms and without having kindled the fire, one who is not ill shall perform the vow of the *avakīrṇin* for seven nights. (MDh 2.187) || 2.13 ||
One who has been initiated must speak only the truth. 2.13.
Furthermore: touching water. 2.14.
The mention of "ashes" (abgrahaṇa) is an elliptical expression for ashes and the other [means of purification]. Thus says Bhṛgu:
"Five meritorious baths have been proclaimed by the great seers:
the fiery, the watery, the Brāhma, the windy, and the celestial."
Bathing with ashes is said to be Āgneya; immersion in water is Vāruṇa; that performed with the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā" is Brāhma; and bathing in the dust raised by cows is remembered as Vāyavya.
"That which is a divine year of heat is called a bath [in the sun].
If one is unable to perform the Varuṇa bath, one should perform the Āgneya or other [substitutes]. Thus it is said.

Although it should have been stated simply as "bathing" (*snānam*), this specific designation is intended to include the rules for bathing mentioned in other *smṛtis*. And thus, what is stated in other *smṛtis* should be understood [as applicable here]. The prefix *upa-* is for the purpose of excluding water that is not well-known [or impure]. The separate mention of "kindling the fire" and "begging for alms" is for the purpose of prohibiting the daily bath for one who has already eaten, but not for the occasional (*naimittika*) bath; therefore, the occasional bath must be performed. The separate mention of "speaking the truth" is for the purpose of prohibiting even the occasional bath for one who is ill. Some say that the prefix *upa-* is for the purpose of prohibiting bathing at midnight. Whatever has been stated here has all been stated by Manu as well.
"One should not perform a bath after eating, nor when ill, nor at midnight, nor with one's clothes on, nor constantly, nor in an unknown body of water" (MDh 4.129). Thus [ends the section]. 2.14.
"Upasparśana" means bathing; that too must be performed day after day. 2.14.
Some [say it consists of] the gift of a cow and so forth. 2.15.

The *godāna* is the second vow (*vrata*) for the *chandoga*s; it should also be observed by others in the sixteenth year. Some desire that even for them the *godāna* be performed in the sixteenth year. From that point on, some desire the ritual bath (*snāna*). Before the *godāna*, one should not perform the daily bath (*nityasnāna*); only the occasional bath (*naimittika*) should be performed. After that, some teachers desire that the daily bath also be performed. Because of the use of the word "some," however, Gautama does not hold this view. (2.15)

The vow called *godāna* is to be performed in the sixteenth year; it is the second among the vows. Some teachers of the *Chandoga* school maintain that the ritual bathing (*snāna*) begins with the *godāna*, because even this [period] is subject to the rules of the initiation into celibacy (*brahmacarya-dīkṣā*), just like one who has been initiated previously. This is a prohibition against the daily bath (*nityasnāna*); however, the occasional bath (*naimittika*) must be performed. In that case, the immersion is to be done like [holding] a staff, according to the traditional teaching of Āpastamba: "One should not bathe in water while boasting" (ĀpDh 1.2.30). 2.15.
And there is the state of being outside the twilight [periods]. 2.16.

The word "and" (ca) is for the purpose of following the opinion of some [teachers]. Some desire that the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) be performed outside the village; however, Gautama does not [hold this view]. This is what is meant: the opinion of some is that the twilight worship must be performed only outside the village, whereas the opinion of Gautama is that it should be performed anywhere in a pure place, whether outside or inside [the village]. 2.16.

He for whom the two twilights—morning and evening—occur outside the village is one who has his twilights outside (*bahiḥsaṃdhya*); that is his state. Thus, the twilight worship must be performed only outside the village. (2.16)

Now, as an incidental discussion, [the author] states when and how that twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana) should be performed; thus he says: "One should stand during the former [twilight] and sit during the latter, while the light still remains, or until the light is seen, remaining silent. (2.17)

The term *vāgyataḥ* (restrained in speech) is connected with both standing and sitting. That time at which the sun rises is the morning twilight (*pūrvā saṃdhyā*). The word *saṃdhyā* is carried over from the preceding portion of the sūtra. That time at which the sun sets is the later twilight (*uttarā saṃdhyā*). Here, standing and sitting are subordinate; the primary ritual act is the worship (*upāsana*). Therefore, although it is stated that "he should stand," it should nevertheless be understood as "standing he should worship" and "sitting he should worship. Thus says Manu: "Reciting [the Gāyatrī] while standing during the morning twilight, one removes the sin of the night."

"Sitting facing the west, however, he destroys the impurity committed during the day" (MDh 2.101). "Sajyotis" refers to the period of light: in the east, it is the light of the stars; that time which exists together with the light of the stars is "sajyotis. The commencement [of the rite] should be made during that "sajyotis" period. In the other direction (the west), it is likewise the light of the sun. Therefore, "until the appearance of light"—meaning until the sun is seen in the east or until the stars are seen in the west. Although one could have simply said "until light," the inclusion of the word "darśana" (appearance) is for the sake of clarity. And so says Manu:

"One should stand reciting the Sāvitrī during the morning twilight until the appearance of the sun; but one should sit during the evening twilight until the stars are clearly visible" (MDh 2.102). The meaning is that the recitation should be discontinued at that point. Here, the prefix *ā-* has the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*), because the practice of "long twilight" (*dīrghasaṃdhyā*) is intended. And so Manu says:
"The seers attained long life through the practice of long twilight."
“Wisdom, fame, renown, and indeed the splendor of sacred knowledge.

[MDh 4.94] Now, one might object: by the rule “and this applies to the subsequent ones provided it does not conflict with them” [GDh 3.10], this [period] is not obtained for a *snātaka* who maintains the sacred fires (*agnimān*), because that time is already occupied by the fire-oblation (*agnihavana*).

It is said: First, regarding the *smārta* (tradition-based) morning and evening *homa*, there is no contradiction whatsoever due to the difference in time. How so? By the word "evening" (*sāyam*), night is meant, and by the word "morning" (*prātaḥ*), day is meant. Since there is no such rule here as in the scriptural injunctions concerning the *udita-homa* (offering after sunrise), the *homa* should be performed immediately following the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*). Furthermore, even for those for whom the *homa* is prescribed specifically at the time of twilight, since a long duration for the twilight is desired, there remains ample opportunity for the twilight worship even after the *homa*. Thus, even in the case of the *śrauta* (Vedic) *udita-homa* and other such rites, there is indeed no contradiction.

Although it should have been stated simply as "one should attend to the morning twilight while standing and the evening twilight while seated," the phrasing used here is intended to include the injunctions mentioned in other Smṛtis. Thus Uśanas says:

Having gone to water in the evening and in the morning, having become pure and having purified himself with a strainer (*pavitra*), he should recite the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, those without specific markers (*abliṅga*), and the *vāmadevya* hymn. Then, seated on *darbha* grass in a clean place upon more *darbha* grass, holding *darbha* blades, facing west, and restraining his speech, he should meditate upon the Self. Then, having performed three breath-control exercises (*prāṇāyāma*) consisting of exhalation (*recaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*), he should repeat the *Sāvitrī* verse beginning with *bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ*—preceded by meditation on the seer (*ṛṣi*), the meter (*chandas*), and the deity (*devatā*)—one thousand times, or one hundred times, or at least ten times. Then, rising and bowing toward the west, south, and north to Agni, Yama, and Brahmā respectively, and having circumambulated three times clockwise, he should again bow toward the western direction. In this very same manner in the morning, standing and facing east, he should bow to Mitra and the other deities.
Thus [ends verse] 2.17.

One should stand during the morning twilight and sit during the evening twilight. The accusative case is used here to denote duration (*atyantasaṃyoga*). He explains the commencement and conclusion of standing and sitting: beginning at a time when light is still present, until another light appears. In the morning, this means beginning with the light of the stars until the appearance of the sun's light; in the evening, beginning with the light of the sun until the appearance of the stars. During that entire time, one should remain restrained in speech. And so says Manu:
"One should stand reciting the *Sāvitrī* during the morning twilight until the sun is seen."
"But one should sit facing the west when the stars have clearly appeared," thus [Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.101]. 2.17.
One should not look at the sun. 2.18.

If this prohibition applied only during the two twilight periods (*saṃdhyā*), then a single sūtra would have been composed as follows: “One should stand during the morning twilight and sit during the evening; while the stars are visible, or until the stars appear, one should remain silent and not look at the sun. If it were intended to apply at all times, then the author would have mentioned looking at the sun even in the context of the rule “one should avoid honey and meat” (GDh 2.19). Since he has not done so in either case, it can be understood that this was stated with another intention in mind. That intention should be seen as expressed in other Smṛtis. As Uśanas says: “One should not look at the sun when it has reached the twilight, when it is at midday, when it is eclipsed by Rāhu, or when it is reflected in water. (2.18)
This prohibition regarding the constant looking at the sun applies to the *brahmacārin*; however, for the *snātaka*, there is this [rule]:
"He should never look at the rising sun, nor the setting sun; not when it is eclipsed, nor when reflected in water, nor when it has reached the middle of the sky" (MDh 4.37). || 2.18 ||

One should avoid honey, meat, perfumes, garlands, sleeping during the day, collyrium, ointments, vehicles, shoes, umbrellas, lust, anger, greed, delusion, speaking, playing musical instruments, bathing, cleaning the teeth, exhilaration, dancing, singing, slander, and fear.

One should avoid honey, meat, perfumes, garlands, sleeping during the day, anointing the body, vehicles, shoes, umbrellas, sensual desire, anger, greed, delusion, speaking, playing musical instruments, bathing, cleaning the teeth, exhilaration, dancing, singing, slander, and fear. 2.19.

The word "one should avoid" (*varjayet*) is connected to each item individually. *Madhu* refers to honey. There is no fault in consuming it unintentionally, as another *smṛti* states: "Honey that comes to one unintentionally does not cause defilement, according to the Vājasaneyaka" (VaDh 23.13). As for meat, although it is not prohibited for a householder, even in that case there is no fault in consuming the meat of the guru’s leftovers when one is ill for the sake of medicine, as another *smṛti* states: "If he should become ill, he may at will eat everything that is the guru’s leftover for the purpose of medicine" (VaDh 23.9). Thus, for one who is not ill, it must be avoided even at a *śrāddha*. And so says Manu:
One should act like one observing a vow in rites dedicated to the gods, and like a seer in rites dedicated to the ancestors.

“If invited, he may eat at will; his vow is not thereby violated” (MDh 2.189), and so forth. *Gandha* refers to sandalwood and the like. This prohibition applies even to that which is for the sake of pleasure, but not to that which is consecrated by the deities (*devatāśiṣṭa*), because another Smṛti text is seen stating: “A student (*brahmacārī*) should accept only that which is consecrated by the deities. The same applies to garlands (*mālā*). *Divāsvapna* is sleeping during the day; this also is not a fault for one who is ill. *Añjana* is collyrium for the eyes; here too, the prohibition applies to that used for enjoyment, not to that used for medicinal purposes. *Abhyañjana* is the anointing of the limbs with oil. Some say this is a prohibition against scented oil; in that view, there is no fault regarding other types of oil. If it is argued that this prohibition is already established by the prohibition of *gandha* (fragrance) itself, we say no; because it is specifically well-known in common usage, it does not refer to fragrance in general. *Yāna* refers to palanquins and the like; this also applies only to one who is not ill. *Upānah* (shoes) and *chattra* (umbrella) are well known. There is no fault in using one made of peacock feathers. *Kāma* is the desire for sexual enjoyment. *Krodha* is the thinking of harm toward others. *Lobha* is the seizing of another’s property and such by unjust means. *Moha* is ignorance. *Vāda* is excessive chatter. *Vādana* is the beating of drums and the like. *Snāna* refers to bathing the head and so forth, provided it is for enjoyment; other forms are permitted because they are prescribed. *Dantadhāvana* (cleaning the teeth) is well known. That must not be done even with a betel leaf, because another Smṛti text is seen stating: “The observer of the vow should have teeth free from dirt. *Harṣa* is joy. Thus, the prohibition of witnessing plays (*nāṭaka*) and the like, which cause that joy, is also established, since it is impossible to prevent the arising of joy upon seeing them. *Nṛtta* is the movement of the limbs. *Gīta* is the utterance of words related to music (*gāndharva*). *Parivāda* is the proclaiming of another’s faults. *Bhaya* is the frightening of others, as the other types of fear cannot be avoided. 2.19.

One should avoid honey and the rest. Honey is that produced by bees. Meat is that of deer and other animals. Fragrance refers to sandalwood and the like. Garlands are flowers. Day-sleep is sleeping during the day. Eye-ointment is for the eyes. Anointing is the rubbing of oil on the body. A vehicle is a cart and so forth. An umbrella and a sandal are well known. Desire is sexual union with women. Anger is wrath. Greed is the longing for material objects. Delusion is the absence of discernment. Excessive talk is idle chatter. Playing is the playing of lutes and other instruments. Bathing for pleasure is the washing of the body from the neck downwards with warm water and the like. Cleaning the teeth is the removal of dental impurities. Joy is the exaltation of the mind resulting from the attainment of what is desired. Dancing and singing are well known. Slander is the speaking of others' faults. Fear is the cause of fear, such as entering a wilderness; this [category] should also be understood to include joy. (2.19)
Furthermore:
upon seeing one's teacher, one must avoid covering the neck, using a cloth sling across the shoulders, leaning against a support, or stretching out the feet. 2.20.

"Guru" refers to the teacher (*ācārya*) and others. Why? If only the teacher were intended, then one should have said "seeing the teacher. The mention of "guru" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all those who occupy the position of a guru. Accordingly, another *smṛti* states: "One should stand with limbs drawn together in the presence of all those worthy of respect. "Covering the neck" means throwing a cloth over the neck. "Tying the knees" (*avasakthikā*) means binding the girdle above the knees. The rest is well known. Since these acts are performed under the influence of others, they are prohibited [when one is alone]. (2.20)

"Gurus" refers to parents, teachers, and so forth. In a place suitable for seeing them, one should avoid such things as covering the neck with a cloth and the like. "Covering the neck" (*kaṇṭhaprāvṛta*) means wrapping the neck with a garment or similar item. "Squatting on the thighs" (*avasakthikā*) means remaining in a position with one foot placed upon the thigh. "Leaning against a support" (*apāśrayaṇa*) means sitting while leaning against a wall, pillar, or the like. "Stretching out the feet" (*pādaprasāraṇa*) is well known. The meaning is that one should remain in the presence of elders with the restraint of modesty. (2.20)
Furthermore:
spitting, laughing, yawning, and cracking the knuckles. (2.21)

The separate mention [of these acts] is for the purpose of avoiding them both in the presence of the guru and in the presence of others. Spitting is well known. Laughter, even when under the influence of another, must be restrained with effort; and thus Āpastamba says: "One should not smile; if one should smile, one should smile after covering [the mouth]," as stated in the Brāhmaṇa (ĀpDh 2.7.6–7). Yawning is well known. Cracking the knuckles is the making of a sound by releasing a joint. 2.21.

"One should avoid" means: spitting is the noisy expulsion of phlegm from the throat; laughing is laughter; yawning is a yawn; cracking the knuckles is the noisy rubbing together of the fingers. (2.21)
Furthermore:
"In the case of looking at or touching a woman, when there is suspicion of sexual intercourse. (2.22)

The word "should avoid" (*varjayet*) carries over from the previous context. "Beholding" (*prekṣaṇa*) means looking intently, that is, the examination of individual parts; it does not mean merely seeing the form, for it is impossible to prevent that by closing one's eyes. "Touching" (*ālambana*) means physical contact. Although one could have simply said "touching," this specific term is used to exclude intentional touching. Thus, there is no fault if [touching] occurs through inadvertence. However, with intention, one must not touch her even in darkness and similar circumstances. One should not perform either of these two acts toward a woman. This applies only to her regarding whom others might suspect sexual intercourse, and not toward any other woman. (2.22)

"Beholding women" means examining them part by part, not merely looking at them casually. "Touching" means physical contact. He should avoid these as well. Because of the statement "when there is suspicion of sexual intercourse," there is no fault in the case of young girls, the elderly, or those who are ill, nor for one who himself is in such a state [of incapacity].
Gambling, service to the low, taking what is not given, and violence. || 2.23 ||

"He should avoid" means exactly that. Gambling is [playing] with dice and so forth. Service to the base is service such as cleaning away urine and excrement; and thus, even for a teacher, one should not perform unsuitable service. Taking what is not given is the seizing of anything not permitted, even if it has been discarded. Violence is the killing of living beings or the harming of living beings. He should neither cause nor even permit uneven seats. (2.23)

"One should avoid gambling. Gambling is of two kinds, distinguished by whether it involves living beings (*prāṇin*) or non-living things (*aprāṇin*). Gambling with living beings includes ram-fights and the like; gambling with non-living things includes games of dice and the like. "Service to the base" means service to those of low birth and so forth; it is both base and a form of service, such as carrying water for cleaning purposes and the like. "Taking what is not given" is the taking of that which has not been given by anyone, even if it is discarded or ownerless. "Violence" is the infliction of pain upon living beings. (2.23)
Furthermore: [One should avoid] the names of the teacher, his son, women, and initiated persons. 2.24.
"One should avoid" is the subject under discussion. One should not utter the names of one's teacher, his son, his wife, or one who has been initiated, as assigned by the father and others. (2.24)

One should avoid using the names of one's teacher, his son, or his wife, as well as the name of one who has been initiated. Even in their absence, one should employ only their descriptive titles. 2.24.
Furthermore, the syntactical connection of this sūtra is also with the verb "one should avoid," extending from honey and meat up to this point. [Corrupt] words are like vinegar. 2.25.
A Brahmin must always abstain from intoxicating liquor. || 2.25 ||
One should avoid all speech that is harsh, cruel, and causes distress to others. (2.25)

A Brāhmaṇa should always avoid white [liquors], those that are foul-smelling, and those that cause distress to others; likewise, he should avoid intoxicating substances and liquor. Because of the specific mention of "always" regarding the Brāhmaṇa, there is no sin for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya householder in the consumption of liquor other than that made from flour (paiṣṭī). || 2.25 ||
A Brāhmaṇa must always avoid intoxicants. || 2.26 ||

"One should avoid"—this is the subject under discussion. A Brāhmaṇa should always avoid liquor made from molasses, honey, or flour, as well as anything else that causes intoxication, even prior to his initiation (*upanayana*). In the case of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, there is no prohibition against *surā*—provided it is not that made from flour—from before initiation until after the period of studentship (*brahmacarya*), as seen in other Smṛtis. As Manu says:
"Liquor made from molasses, honey, and flour should be known as the three kinds of *surā*.
Just as one is so, so are all; they must not be drunk by the best of the twice-born" (MDh 11.94). 2.26.
Now, for the purpose of explaining what ought to be done, he says:
"Sleeping on a low bed or seat, rising before [others], and retiring last. (2.27) — [2.26]

In the presence of his guru, he should occupy a lower bed and seat. He should rise before him and go to rest after him. As Manu says: "In the presence of his guru, his bed and seat must always be lower;
he should rise before him and be the last to lie down" (MDh 2.198). || 2.27 ||
The meaning of this is clear in the *Mānava* (Manusmṛti):
"In the presence of his guru, his bed and seat should always be low;
he should rise before him and go to rest after him" (MDh 2.194). || 2.23 ||
Furthermore:
"Restrained in speech, arms, and belly. — || 2.28 || — || 2.27 ||

The word "syāt" (should be) is to be understood as the ellipsis [at the end]. "Restrained in speech" means one who has desisted from idle chatter. "Restrained in arms" means one who avoids crushing clods of earth and similar acts. "Restrained in belly" means one who eats what is wholesome and in moderation. Some read the text as "vāgbāhūdarakarmasaṃyataḥ" (restrained in the actions of speech, arms, and belly); however, since this is already established by the term "restrained in arms," it must be considered whether that reading is appropriate or not. (2.28)
Restraint of speech is the avoidance of excessive chatter; restraint of the arms is the absence of crushing clods of earth and the like; restraint of the belly is moderation in eating. || 2.27 ||
Furthermore:
One should mention the name and lineage of the teacher with respect. (2.29) — (2.28)

The mention of the *guru* is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the *ācārya* and others. "From the *samāna*" means properly bowed down, i.e., humble; the meaning is that having meditated upon him, one should perform a salutation. And thus, in that same context, the mention of the *ācārya* in the rule "the *ācārya* and his son" [GDh 2.24] is also an elliptical indication for the *guru* and others, because the utterance of their names is likewise prohibited. Accordingly, another *Smṛti* states:
"The *ācārya*, his son, his wife, the initiated *guru*, the father, the paternal uncle, the mother, and likewise the maternal uncle."
A wise man should not mention by name his father-in-law, his husband, or his mother’s sister, even if they are well-disposed toward him.
But if he should speak, one should meditate upon him, pay homage, and then address him. (2.29)

One should indicate one’s own name and lineage while bowing to the teacher. "While bowing" means properly inclined, that is, free from concealment. Another says: one should indicate the teacher’s name and lineage while bowing—that is, being correctly bowed down, having become humble. (2.28)
And likewise when worshipping the supreme good. || 2.30 || — || 2.29 ||

"Venerable" means one who is worthy of honor and learned; "superior" should be understood as one who desires one's welfare and is advanced in age. Since this is already established by the word "and" (*ca*), the word "thus" (*evaṃ*) serves to extend [the rules] in their entirety to this case. Consequently, whatever [rites] such as salutation (*abhivādana*) and so forth are prescribed upon seeing a teacher, those should also be observed here. (2.30)

"Honored" means worshipped in the world; "superior" means excelling through knowledge and other qualities. "In the same way, he is properly bowed down to by both of them. Regarding this, there is another Smṛti text:
"The teacher, his son, his wife, one initiated for a rite, a guru, a father, a paternal uncle, a maternal uncle, and likewise a mother."
A wise man should not speak harshly even when bowed down to by his well-wishing father-in-law, his husband, his mother, or his sister.

The word "and" (ca) in the phrase "and [in the case of] the worshipful and the superior" extends by analogy everything that was said regarding the teacher—both what [was said] and how much. Therefore, even the bed, seat, and so forth, must be low when in their presence. (2.29)
Leaving behind his bed, seat, and place of stay, he gave his assent. || 2.31 || — || 2.30 ||

When the guru gives a command, then—having abandoned and left behind the bed such as a couch, the seat such as a plank, and the place where he is standing—the meaning is that he should give a response or reply. (2.31)
When the teacher issues a command, he should respond with an affirmative answer, rising from his bed, seat, or standing place, and approaching him. (2.30)
Approaching [the teacher] is [required] because of the verbal instruction, even when [the teacher] is not seen. 2.32 — 2.31.
The meaning is that when an instruction is being given by an invisible teacher, one should perform *abhikramaṇa*, which is to go toward him. || 2.32 ||
If the teacher, standing outside, speaks without having seen the student, then the student must approach and draw near; he must not show disrespect by thinking, "I am not seen. || 2.31 ||
One should rise when the wind from below, the seat, or from the side blows, and also upon seeing one's teacher. || 2.33 ||
One should remain in a lower position while seated, rise when attending to lateral winds, and rise upon seeing one's teacher. 2.32.

When the teacher stands or sits below or at a lower level, or when one is attending to a side wind (tiryagvāta) or performing the voiding of urine and feces, upon seeing the teacher therein, one should stand up; the word "and" (*ca*) implies that one should also turn one's face away from him. Thus, another Smṛti states:
"Upon seeing the teacher standing in a well, or likewise standing on the bank of a pond, the disciple and the servant should likewise stand, having turned their faces away."

Alternatively—the word "and" (ca) indicates departure. In that case, the meaning of the Sūtra should be understood as follows: "In the case of [the wind] staying below, sitting, or moving crosswise, one should rise up and depart in sequence. Therein, the sequence is: upon seeing [the wind] staying below or sitting, one should rise up; in the case of its moving crosswise, one should depart. (2.33)

When the teacher occupies a lower place or seat while one is oneself situated on a high place or seat, then, upon seeing the teacher, one should rise. One should also rise upon seeing the teacher when attending to lateral winds (tiryagvāta) or during the voiding of urine and feces. The word "ca" (and) serves to include these cases in conjunction with the preceding rule. 2.32.
One should follow him as he goes. || 2.34 || — || 2.33 ||

"Having seen him going, one should follow after him. The word "and" (ca) carries over; by it, even what is not explicitly stated is included: having seen him sitting, one should stand up; having seen him lying down, one should sit. And so another Smṛti states: "One should follow him when he goes, stand up when he sits, and sit near him when he lies down" (VaDh 7.12). || 2.34 ||
One should follow after the teacher when he is walking. 2.33.
Karma is explained by means of what is made known. 2.35 — || 2.34 ||

Having informed the teacher, "I shall perform whatever task is to be done by him," and having performed it, he should stand by having reported, "It is done. Because the sentence is incomplete, the word *kṛtvā* (having done) must be supplied after *vijñāpya* (having informed), and the verb *tiṣṭhet* (he should stand) must also be supplied after *ākhyāya* (having reported), just as in the example, "Enter, [eat] the cake" (*praviśa piṇḍīm*). (2.35)

The meaning is that, having informed the teacher, "I shall perform this expiation for whatever needs to be done by this pupil," he should understand and carry out whatever is required of the teacher, such as fetching water-jars and so forth, and then report to him, "It has been done. Thus should he conduct himself. (2.34)
He should study when called upon. 2.36.
When summoned, he should meditate. || 2.35 ||
Only when he is summoned by the teacher should he study; the meaning is that he should not prompt the teacher himself. 2.36.
"Being summoned by the teacher, one should study, but one should not initiate the lesson oneself. (2.35)
He is intent on what is pleasant and beneficial. (2.37) — (2.36)

The word "should be" (*syāt*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the verse].
