He is "properly intent" (*tatparaḥ*) upon both the pleasant and the beneficial taken together; for that which is beneficial but unpleasant ought not to be done. "Pleasant" (*priya*) means that which causes delight, and "beneficial" (*hita*) means that which is suitable for the future. The meaning is that one should do only that which is both pleasant and suitable for the future. (2.37)

One should be devoted and intent upon that which is both pleasing and beneficial to the teacher. "Pleasing" means that which causes satisfaction at that very moment; "beneficial" means that which produces [satisfaction] at a later time. || 2.36 ||
And likewise with regard to his wife’s sons. 2.38 — 2.37.

He should also be intent upon the welfare and benefit of those two who are his wife and son, provided they are of the same caste (*savarṇa*) and similar to him; the word "and" (*ca*) implies that he should also provide for their clothing, covering of the neck, and so forth. If it is asked why only those of the same caste are mentioned, it is because the plural number is used for the sake of honor. (2.38)
Toward the wife and sons of that teacher, one should behave in the same manner as toward the teacher himself. || 2.37 ||
Now he states the exception to that:
the exception to this is that there shall be no eating of leftovers, bathing, adorning, washing of the feet, massaging, or clasping [the feet].

One should not perform these [services] for his wife or son; since they are naturally expected to act out of affection and a desire for his welfare, they are here specifically prohibited. Because of this prohibition regarding these two alone, it follows that these services must indeed be performed for the teacher (*guru*). Thus says Āpastamba: “When he has gone abroad, he should eat after having offered the alms-food into the fire; alms-food is praised as being equivalent to an oblation (*havis*). In that regard, the teacher serves the purpose of a deity and the purpose of the *āhavanīya* fire; having fed him, whatever remains as leavings (*ucchiṣṭa*) he eats—that is indeed the leavings of the oblation. Likewise, Vasiṣṭha also says: “The leavings of one who is not a teacher are not to be eaten,” and so forth. *Prasādhana* means ornamentation. The rest is well known. (2.39)

"Eating the remnants" means eating what remains after [the teacher] has eaten. "Bathing" is an ablution preceded by the massaging of the head and limbs with bathing powders and other such substances. "Adorning" means decorating. "Washing the feet" is well known. "Massaging" refers to anointing with oil, rubbing the body, and so forth. "Greeting" (upasaṃgrahaṇa) is as previously described in [MDh 2.72]: "with crossed hands," and so on. These acts should not be performed for the teacher's wife or sons; therefore, it is established that they are to be performed only for the teacher himself. (2.38)
Now he states the exception to the rule regarding salutation: "Next is the exception to the rule regarding salutation:
one should salute the wives of one's gurus after returning from a journey. (2.40) — (2.39)
One who has returned from living abroad must perform the formal salutation (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*) to the wives of his teachers; not at any other time, nor toward any other woman. (2.40)
Having returned from a journey after having gone abroad, one should perform the salutation by clasping the feet of the wives of one's teachers. (2.39)
But even there, it is not [the case] for many [who have attained] the conduct of young women. 2.41 — 2.40.

The meaning is: "by one who is capable of legal transactions" (vyavahārasamarthena), that is, by one who has reached the full age of sixteen years. Some maintain that one should not have sexual intercourse even with young women (yuvatī) after returning from travel, but Gautama does not hold this view. This should be understood in consideration of whether the women are suspicious or not suspicious. 2.41.

However, some teachers maintain that for young wives of gurus, even when they have returned from a journey, a disciple who has reached the age of sixteen and is engaged in formal conduct should not perform the salutation by clasping the feet. 2.40.

It has been stated: "The kindling of the fire and the practice of begging for alms" (GDh 2.12). Regarding that, since the kindling of the fire is obtained separately from each household, he now states the rule for the practice of begging for alms.

It was said: "the kindling of the fire and the practice of begging for alms. Since the kindling of the fire is established according to each individual household, he states the rule for the common practice of begging for alms:
"The practice of begging for alms is from all castes, excluding those who are accused of crimes and those who have fallen [from their status]. (2.42)
He shall go for alms among all castes, with the exception of those accused of crimes and those who have fallen from their caste. 2.41.

For what purpose is this Sūtra commenced? First of all, the practice of begging for alms is not enjoined by this [text], because it has already been enjoined by the rule: "The fire, fuel, and begging for alms" (GDh 2.12). Furthermore, the exclusion of those accused of crimes has already been stated by the rule: "Among those praised for their own duties" (GDh 17.1). Regarding this, some say: "This commencement is for the sake of including the Śūdra, because he is not included by the rule 'among those praised for their own duties'."

And this is not tenable, because the permission for a Śūdra woman in times of distress is already established by the rule: "If there is no subsistence without a Śūdra woman" (GDh 17.5). Nor is it proper to infer from this a permission for a religious student (brahmacārin) even when not in distress, since it is absolutely prohibited in another Smṛti:
"He whose limbs are nourished by the essence of a Śūdra's food, even though he studies constantly..."

"Even though he offers oblations or recites prayers, he does not attain the higher state. [VaDh 6.28] Therefore, this undertaking is intended for the purpose of reaching even those twice-born castes who are unworthy, specifically in cases other than times of distress (*anāpadi*). Since all unworthy persons would otherwise be reached without distinction, the prohibition "excepting those accused of grave sins and the outcastes" (*abhiśastapatitavarjam*) is appropriate. Otherwise, if only the Śūdra were reached, a prohibition for those accused of grave sins and others would be illogical, as they would not have been reached in the first place; thus, one cannot claim that this exception applies solely to the case of the Śūdra. For where the twice-born are authorized as worthy recipients, the Śūdra is likewise worthy; therefore, there is no possibility at all for the other [unworthy] to be reached.

Therefore, it is established that for one in the first stage of life (*brahmacārin*), the practice of begging for alms should first be from those who are praiseworthy; in their absence, from those who are not praiseworthy; in their absence, from the teacher (*ācārya*) and others; and in the total absence of all these, during times of distress, even from a *śūdra*.

It is called *sārvavarṇika* because it is fit for all castes (*sarvavarṇa*); the meaning is that it belongs to everyone. The inclusion of the word "all" (*sarva*) is for the purpose of including the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya; otherwise, since only a Brāhmaṇa has the entitlement to receive gifts (*pratigraha*), it would belong to him alone. The inclusion of the word "caste" (*varṇa*) is for the purpose of including the Śūdra as well; for if the word "caste" were not used, the term "all" would apply only to those two (the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya). Therefore, the word "caste" is employed so that it may apply even to the Śūdra who was not previously included. Consequently, there is no fault in a Śūdra who is destitute of a livelihood wandering for alms. The word *bhaikṣa* means a collection of alms; therefore, it should be gathered from many houses. An "accused person" (*abhiśasta*) is understood to be one accused of a minor offense (*upapātaka*), because one accused of a major sin (*pātaka*) is already covered by the mention of the "outcast" (*patita*). Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "Having falsely accused a Brāhmaṇa of a crime causing loss of caste (*patanīya*) or a crime not causing loss of caste (*upapatanīya*)" [VaDh 23.39].

Some perform the grammatical analysis as *sārvavarṇika*, meaning "belonging to all castes" (*sarveṣu varṇeṣu bhavam*). For them, we do not see the purpose of the word *sarva* (all). If it is for the sake of including those of inferior twice-born status, that cannot be so, because that very purpose is already served by the commencement of the Sūtra itself. Even if it were for the sake of including Śūdras, the refutation has already been stated. Therefore, this matter should be investigated by the Brahmins (*bhūsura*s). 2.42.

"Sārvavarṇika" means occurring among all castes. Having excluded those who are accused of crimes and those who have fallen from their caste, alms should be sought among all castes. "Accused" refers to those guilty of minor offenses (upapātaka). 2.41.
The word *bhava* (existence) should be employed at the beginning, middle, and end [of the discourse], according to the sequence of the syllables. 2.43 — || 2.42 ||

Regarding the two-footed [request], when the word "give alms" (*bhikṣāṃ dehi*) is used in a request, the word *bhavat* (sir) must be employed by a Brāhmaṇa at the beginning, by a Kṣatriya in the middle, and by a Vaiśya at the end—this being understood through the inherent power (*sāmarthya*) of even the word *dehi*. Since *bhavat* is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and cannot be used in isolation, it must be used in the vocative case-ending in the presence of women, as in: "O Lady, give alms" (*bhavati bhikṣāṃ dehi*). In the presence of men, it is: "O Sir, give alms" (*bhavan bhikṣāṃ dehi*). Because of the prefix *pra-*, one should also observe what is stated in another Smṛti: "The letters *kṣa* and *hi* should not be pronounced loudly. As the Gṛhya-smṛti says:

A Brāhmaṇa should beg, saying, "Lady, give alms"; a Rājanya, using the word *bhavat* in the middle, saying, "Lady, give alms"; and a Vaiśya, using the word *bhavat* at the end, saying, "Give alms, lady. Furthermore, he should not increase the words *kṣāṃ* and *hiṃ*. Thus it is said.

The mention of the *varṇa* (caste) is for the purpose of providing the mantra to the Śūdra; consequently, one of the mantras belonging to the three [upper] castes alone should be seen as applicable, or else another specific composition should be made. This is because another Smṛti states, "The livelihood of a Śūdra is like that of a Vaiśya," and thus the mantra prescribed for a Vaiśya should be seen as applicable. The mantra was not stated directly in order to indicate that his livelihood is unrestricted. And so Vasiṣṭha says: "And his livelihood is unrestricted, and his hair and dress are unrestricted," and so forth. The inclusion of the word "successive" (*anupūrva*) is so that there may be no option regarding only a single [mantra]. (2.43)

The word *bhavat* (vocative singular) should be employed at the beginning, middle, and end of the two-word phrase "give alms" (*bhikṣāṃ dehi*) according to the sequence of syllables. For women, it should take the feminine gender. For a Brāhmaṇa: *brāhmaṇasya bhavan bhikṣāṃ dehi* (O sir, give alms to the Brāhmaṇa). For a Brāhmaṇī: *brahmaṇyāṃ bhavati bhikṣāṃ dehi* (O lady, give alms to the Brāhmaṇī). For a Kṣatriya: *kṣatriyasya bhikṣāṃ bhavan dehi* (O sir, give alms to the Kṣatriya), or *bhikṣāṃ bhavati dehi*. For a Vaiśya: *vaiśyasya bhikṣāṃ dehi bhavan* (O sir, give alms to the Vaiśya), or *bhikṣāṃ dehi bhavati*. 2.42
If [the aforementioned] teachers, kinsmen, or gurus are unavailable, one may do so elsewhere. 2.44 — [End of] 2.43.

The teacher has stated: "kinsman" refers to a sapinda; "teacher" refers to a maternal uncle and others; "one's own" refers to what belongs to oneself. If [alms] cannot be obtained elsewhere, one should request alms from these [categories]. The sequence, however, has already been established. (2.44)

The teacher says: "Relatives" refers to paternal uncles and others who are *sapiṇḍas*; "elders" refers to maternal uncles and others; "one's own" means belonging to oneself. "Except for alms" means that in the absence of [other] alms, one should go for alms to the houses of the teacher and others. 2.43.
In this case as well:
one should avoid each preceding one among them. 2.45 — 2.44.

Whichever among them is mentioned first in each respective case, from that one he should avoid [the others]. If [alms] cannot be obtained elsewhere, even after avoiding the preceding ones, he should continue to seek alms from those very same persons. The mention of them is for the purpose of this restriction—that [he should not seek alms] from the house of his preceptor (upādhyāya) alone. Consequently, it should be understood that when nothing is obtained anywhere else, he may indeed go to the house of his preceptor. And so says another Smṛti: "If there is no gain elsewhere, even from the house of the preceptor. (2.45)

Among those, such as the teacher and others, he should avoid each one that was mentioned first. If [a preceptor] is not found elsewhere, [he may stay] in his own house; if not there, among his gurus; if not there, among his kinsmen; and if not even there, in the house of the teacher. 2.44.
Having offered [the food] to the teacher, he should eat when permitted by him. 2.46 — 2.45.

Having announced to the teacher, "This is alms-food," he should eat it only after being permitted by him with the words, "Eat. Thus, this announcement is for the purpose of consecrating the alms-food, as indicated by the expression "being permitted. If the teacher should take [some] for himself, then more must be brought. (2.46)
Having announced to the teacher, "This alms-food has been brought," he should eat it when permitted by him; if the teacher should take it himself, then he should bring something else. 2.45.
In his absence, [the debt shall be paid] by his wife, son, fellow student, or a virtuous person. 2.47 — 2.46.
In some manuscripts, the reading is *sabrahmacāribhyaḥ*.

This is for the purpose of indicating that the wife and son belong to the same caste (*samānajātīya*). A *sabrahmacārī* is one who practices the same Vedic course (*samānacaraṇa*); "san" means excellent, possessing preeminent qualities. (2.47)
In the absence of the teacher, having informed the teacher’s wife or others as appropriate, he should eat with their permission. 2.46.
To the question "How then should he eat?", it is said: "Restraining his speech, eating until satisfied, not being greedy, and having water close at hand. (2.48) — [This concludes] 2.47.

"Restrained in speech" means silently; "being satisfied" means practicing contentment—the sense being that even if one was previously dissatisfied, one should rejoice at the mere sight of food. And so another Smṛti says:

"Upon seeing [the food], one should rejoice, become serene, and welcome it in every way" (MDh 2.54). "Not being greedy" means avoiding excessive eating by abandoning specific cravings; and so another Smṛti says:
"Excessive eating is detrimental to longevity, detrimental to health, and detrimental to strength."
"It is demeritorious and loathed by the world; therefore, one should avoid it.

(MDh 2.57) Alternatively, the meaning is "without omitting the rules for eating. Accordingly, the rules for eating should be observed as stated in another *smṛti*: "having properly set down water, one should sip it. The prefix *sam-* is intended to include the procedure mentioned in other *smṛtis*. Thus Uśanas says: "Having sprinkled water with the mantra beginning 'Truth, do not deceive,' and so forth, one should cause [the guest] to sip [water] with the mantra beginning 'The under-layer of nectar' (*amṛtopastaraṇam*)."

Alternatively, "water" (udaka) refers to a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu). Having placed that [nearby], it follows that the student (brahmacārin) must also carry a water-pot; for Manu likewise indicates the carrying of a water-pot by the student through its prescription as a rite of acquisition along with the girdle and other items:
"The girdle, the deerskin, the staff, the sacred thread, and the water-pot..."

"Having thrown those that have become spoiled into the water, one should take others accompanied by the sacred formulas" (MDh 2.64). And thus, the sipping of water (*ācamana*) must be performed from that very source, by the force of the scriptural statement. There is no fault in touching what has been defiled by food remnants (*ucchiṣṭa*). Or rather, that which is stated in another *Smṛti* should be observed. As Vasiṣṭha says:
"Fire is considered pure when placed upon water, in the hand, or on wood;
therefore, one should wipe the water-pot with both hands and water" (VaDh 12.15). Some justify this meaning based on the prefix *sam-* itself. 2.48.

He remains silent for as long as he eats; satisfied by the mere sight of the food, rejoicing, and not being distracted, he does not harbor excessive longing. The term *saṃnidhāya* has the causative sense internalized, meaning "having caused [the water] to be placed near. Thus, *udaka* refers to the vessel of water. (2.47)
Now, if a religious student (*brahmacārī*) does not properly abide in the discipline of his teacher, what should then be done? To this he says;
he states the method for instructing the student:
"Instruction of the student is by means of non-corporeal punishment" (2.49).—[End of] 2.48.

"Discipline of the pupil" (*śiṣyāśiṣṭiḥ*) means the instruction of the pupil; the meaning is that it should be carried out through censure and so forth, excluding "killing," which is killing without [just] cause. Although this is established by the context itself, the mention of the "pupil" is for the purpose of making known that this same duty applies to anyone else who is to be disciplined, such as a wife, a son, and so on. (2.49)
"Killing" means striking. A disciple should be disciplined by the teacher through means such as verbal reprimands, provided he is not struck. (2.48)
If one is unable [to do so], [one may strike] with a thin rope or a split bamboo cane. 2.50 — 2.49.

If he cannot be disciplined by means of reprimand and so forth, he should be punished with a rope or a split bamboo cane; since these two, when prescribed together, serve the same purpose, there is an option between them. Even with that [punishment], he should be corrected only mildly. (2.50)

If he cannot be restrained by means of threats and the like, then he should be disciplined even by striking him with a thin rope or with a split bamboo cane—there being an option between these two items listed as a copulative compound (dvandva), as seen in the *Mānava Dharma Śāstra* (8.229): "with a rope or with a split bamboo cane. Having struck him with those two weak instruments, he should thus be disciplined. 2.49.
One who kills with another [weapon] shall be punished by the king. || 2.51 || — || 2.50 ||
One who strikes with anything other than the hand or foot out of anger should be punished by the king; the mention of the "king" is for the sake of showing respect. 2.51.
If he strikes [the teacher] with his hand or other limbs out of anger, the teacher is to be punished by the king; thus has the residence of the disciple in the teacher’s family been described. 2.50.
Now, he states for how long a time one should conduct oneself in this manner;
and as to what the limit of that time is, he says:
"One should observe the life of a student (*brahmacarya*) for twelve years with respect to a single Veda. (2.52) — [This concludes] 2.51.

One who is about to study a single Veda shall observe, that is, practice, the student's life (*brahmacarya*) for twelve years in the manner previously described. By the word *brahmacarya*, the entire collection of restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) is meant, because it is for the sake of Brahman. 2.52.

Although each Veda has many branches—namely, the Ṛgveda is divided twenty-one ways, there are one hundred branches of the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda has a thousand paths, and the Atharvaveda is ninefold—nevertheless, in this context, by the word "Veda" is intended only as many branches of each respective Veda as were adopted by former teachers through study and ritual practice. He who studies one Veda shall observe the vow of studentship (brahmacarya) for twelve years in the teacher's house. (2.51)
Or twelve times each. 2.53.
Or, in all cases, twelve each. 2.52.
Or he should observe the vow of celibacy for twelve years for each Veda.

But he who is capable of studying the four Vedas—meaning twelve years for each Veda, totaling forty-eight years—as Āpastamba says: "For one who has been initiated, the period of residence as a student in the teacher’s household is forty-eight years" (ĀpDh 1.2.11–12).
Or, [the practice] may extend up to the point of grasping in all cases. 2.54.
Or [the rule applies] up to the point of grasping. 2.53.

One should observe the life of a religious student (brahmacarya) for exactly as long as it takes to complete the study of all the Vedas, because that is the purpose of it. The inclusion of the word "all" is for the sake of indicating whether one studies one, two, or all of them. And so says Manu: "Having studied the Vedas, or two Vedas, or even one Veda, in due order" (MDh 3.2). This is an exception (apavāda) to the previously stated limit, whether it be exceeded or fallen short; the statement regarding the rule is that "study performed according to the rule becomes powerful. (2.54)
For as long a time as it takes to be able to master one, two, three, or four Vedas—such is the duration. || 2.53 ||
At the conclusion of the Vidyā, the teacher is to be invited with a gift. || 2.55 || — || 2.54 ||

Upon the completion of his studies, but not necessarily upon the completion of his vows, the student should invite the teacher—the *ācārya*—for a purpose or need, asking: "What may I do for the sake of my teacher? (2.55)
Upon the completion of his studies, the teacher is to be invited with wealth as the purpose—that is, he is to be asked: "O Teacher, please accept this wealth. (2.54)
Then, having performed the bath, or [the bath] permitted [by the teacher]. 2.56 — || 2.55 ||

"Having performed" means having given; that is, the purpose instructed by the teacher. Or, for one who has been permitted with the words, "Enough with the teacher's fee," the ritual bath is the *samāvartana* (the rite of returning home). 2.56.

Then, having performed what was commanded by the teacher with the words "Bring [the materials]," he should perform his bath. Or, when permitted by him with the words, "My dear boy, I am satisfied by your very virtues; enough with wealth," he should perform the bath, which is the *samāvartana* ceremony. (2.55)
Now, since there are many gurus such as one's father and others present together, [the author] states which one is to be honored first:
"The teacher is the most excellent among gurus. (2.57)
"The teacher is the best of gurus; some say the mother, others say the mother. (2.56)

The teacher (ācārya) is defined by the characteristics already mentioned; he is the most excellent and the foremost among all gurus, such as one's father and others. Consequently, in the rule "in the case of a conflict, [the injunction of] the other" (GDh 6.4), it is this very person who is referred to by the word "other. || 2.57 ||

Among gurus such as one's father and others, the teacher (*ācārya*) defined by the aforementioned characteristics is the most excellent. For he indeed produces that [person] through knowledge; that is the superior birth. Therefore, when there is a gathering of many gurus, he alone is to be honored first. However, some teachers consider the mother to be the most excellent. And so says Vasiṣṭha:
"The teacher of the Vedas (*upādhyāya*) is ten times more venerable than the [biological] teacher (*ācārya*); a hundred teachers are equal to the father."

"The mother exceeds the father tenfold in terms of reverence. Āpastamba also states: "The mother undertakes many tasks for the sake of her son's birth; therefore, service toward her is perpetual, even if she has fallen from her status. The repetition [of the concluding verse] is intended to mark the completion of the chapter.
"Mother," say some; "mother," say others. 2.58.

Some consider the mother to be superior; others [consider] the father, because of the use of the particle *iti* [to indicate an alternative view]; otherwise, the form "the mother alone" (*mātaika*) would have sufficed. The teacher is more important than the father alone. And so Manu says:
"That which the mother and father produce from one another out of desire, one should know that to be his mere physical birth (*saṃbhūti*), which occurs when he is born from the womb."

"But that birth which the teacher, having mastered the Vedas, produces for him according to the rule by means of the Sāvitrī—that is true, that is ageless and immortal" (MDh 2.147–48). If the father himself is the teacher, then the father is distinguished; yet the mother is the best of all. And so Vasiṣṭha says:
"The teacher is ten times superior to the sub-teacher, but the father is a hundred times superior to the teacher."
"But a mother exceeds a thousand fathers in respect. [VaDh 13.48]. Here, by the word "father," it is understood that only one who is both a father and a teacher is intended. 2.58.
Now begins the third chapter: Regarding one who has thus fulfilled his vows and completed his studies, some authorities declare that there is an option concerning his stage of life (āśrama). 3.1.
Of him who has maintained his vow of celibacy without interruption; and so Manu says:
"Having studied the Vedas, or two Vedas, or even one Veda, in due order..."

"One who has not violated his vow of celibacy (*avipluta-brahmacarya*) shall dwell in the stage of the householder" (MDh 3.2). And thus, for one who has violated it, an expiation for a minor offense (*upapātaka*) is to be observed. Alternatively, that mention [of the stages] is for the purpose of excluding the Śūdra, lest the duties of the stages of life apply to him as well. Or else, the repetition "of each and each" (*tasya tasya*) is for the sake of distributive iteration, meaning "of the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya. If it is argued that this is already established by the very fact of eligibility even without that specific mention, we say no; for its purpose is to dispel the suspicion that there might be some other apparent Smṛti text [to the contrary]. For such an apparent Smṛti text appears as follows:

“This fourfold duty of a Brahmin has been declared to you” (MDh 6.97). Regarding this, one might suspect that this fourfold duty belongs to the Brahmin alone, while for the other two [castes] it is of only one kind. If that is so, how is it to be understood? In that regard, the mention of the "Brahmin" is for the sake of illustration (*pradarśanārtha*). How is this known? Because of the observation of another Smṛti text stating, “The four stages of life (*āśrama*) belong to all three castes. And likewise Āpastamba says: “For all [castes], residence in the teacher’s family begins from the initiation (*upanayana*). For all, there is no cessation until the completion of sacred learning. Having mastered the duties, one may undertake whatever one desires” (ĀpDh 2.21.3–5).

Some say: "Because the fruits are equal, there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the stages of life (*āśrama*). For the fruit is twofold—consisting of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and consisting of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*)—and either one of these is obtained. Thus says the Śruti: "There are three branches of dharma: sacrifice, study, and charity—this is the first; austerity alone is the second; and dwelling in the teacher’s family is the third. Having ascended these, one goes to the world of Brahman; established in Brahman, one attains immortality" (ChU 2.23.1). The meaning is as follows: there are three supports of dharma. "Sacrifice, study, and charity" is the designation for the householder; "torture alone" is the dharma of the forest-dweller and the wandering mendicant; "dwelling in the teacher’s family" is that of the student. "Having ascended these" means having properly undertaken the stage of the student, the stage of the householder, the stage of the forest-dweller, or the stage of the wandering mendicant. "He who among them is established in Brahman"—meaning the knower intent on Brahman—"attains immortality," that is, he goes to liberation (*mokṣa*). And since this establishes the attainment of the world of Brahman for all of them, it is stated that the fruits are indeed equal. Likewise, in the Jābāla-Śruti, the equality of the fruits is also heard: "Having completed his studentship, he should become a householder; having been a householder, he should become a forest-dweller; having been a forest-dweller, he should renounce. Or otherwise, he may renounce directly from studentship, or from the household, or from the forest; he goes to the world of Brahman" (JābUp 4). Manu also says:

"All these, when practiced in succession according to the scriptures, lead a Brahmin who acts as prescribed to the supreme goal" (MDh 6.88). Here, by the use of the word "all" (*api*), it should be understood that even a single one [of them] is intended. Āpastamba also says: "There are four stages of life (*āśrama*): the householder’s stage, dwelling in the teacher’s family, the life of a silent sage (*mauna*), and forest-dwelling (*vānaprasthya*). One who conducts himself without distraction in all of these according to the instruction attains security" (ĀpDh 2.21.1–2). Therefore, because they yield equal results, there is an option (*vikalpa*) among them.

But surely, if they were equal, since both kinds of fruit would be attained through celibacy alone, there would be the undesirable consequence that the injunctions for the other stages of life are purposeless.

It is said: the injunction for other stages of life (*āśrama*) is intended for one who is capable of practicing a particular stage, so that he may enter that specific stage; or else, it is for the sake of entering a desired stage through the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of previous births. Scripture also states: "Knowledge and action, as well as prior wisdom, accompany him" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2). Furthermore, the scriptural injunction regarding lifelong duties (*yāvajjīva-śruti*) should be understood as applying to a householder who possesses the requisite capacity and desire. When this is accepted, the scriptural text concerning renunciation (*vyutthāna-śruti*) also becomes consistent: "Having known this very Self, they rise above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, and then lead the life of a mendicant" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.5.1). Otherwise, the instruction to "lead the life of a mendicant" would not logically constitute an injunction for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*). The scriptural passage concerning "one being born" (*jāyamāna-śruti*) establishes the necessity of performing sacrifices and other duties for the householder, but not for every person merely by virtue of being born, because the connection with the three debts (*ṛṇatraya*) is absolutely impossible for everyone, and because such an interpretation would contradict the scripture stating, "One should renounce even from the stage of studentship" (Jābāla Upaniṣad 4), while remaining consistent with Smṛti texts such as, "From that very stage of studentship he renounces," and "He may dwell in whichever [stage] he desires" (Vasiṣṭha Dharma Sūtra 7.3). Moreover, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) exist for the sake of completing the ritual action. Therefore, the meaning of the words should be understood as follows: "Being born" refers to a householder who has entered the state of householdership due to previous latent impressions. The mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya as well. He becomes indebted to the gods by sacrifice; therefore, sacrifice must be performed. He becomes indebted to the ancestors by progeny; therefore, the procreation of offspring must be performed. He becomes indebted to the seers (*ṛṣi*) by studentship; therefore, the observance of celibacy on festival days and the like must be maintained. When understood in this way, there is no contradiction between the Śruti and Smṛti anywhere. Regarding the use of the singular "some" (*eke*), it does not refer to Gautama, for his view is that all stages are to be combined (*samuccaya*). How is this known? Because the position of the "single stage" (*aikāśramya*)—as in "But the teachers [hold] to a single stage" (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 3.36)—is presented as the opinion of others (*paramata*) as a counter-position, and because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in "There are three stages of life before the last" (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 28.49), since the triad of stages cannot exist before the final one. Gautama maintains the position of option (*vikalpa*) in this manner.
Through sacrifice one attains the gods; through austerity, the realm of Virāj;
through renunciation, the station of Brahman; and through dispassion, dissolution into Prakṛti.

Because they are taught as having distinct results; because even in the *Jābāla-śruti*, instead of saying "having ascended any one of them," it says "having ascended these," thus expressing the intention of their combination (*samuccaya*); because the attainment of the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*) is also taught as the result of their combination; because in the *Jābāla-śruti* as well, the position of combination is stated first as the primary view; because in the verse of Manu, "All of them in succession" (MDh 6.88), the word "api" has the sense of combination; because in the statement of Āpastamba, "in all of them" (ĀpDh 2.21.2), the plural number indicates that one does not abide in just one, but rather in all of them; because the scriptural teaching of the three debts (*ṛṇatraya*) is also logically consistent only in this sense; because the scriptural passage "and former knowledge" (*pūrvaprajñā ca*) is also consistent with the intention of referring to spiritual knowledge (*vidyā*); because even the lifelong injunction (*yāvajjīva-śruti*) shows its non-permanence in the *Jābāla-śruti* passage: "If a householder should enter the forest, and if he should desire the household state alone, then he should perform the *agnihotra* for as long as he lives"; because in this view, the scriptural teaching on renunciation (*vyutthāna-śruti*) is all the more consistent; and because by the verse "the fourth part of life" (MDh 4.1), Manu also speaks while relying precisely on the position of combination. Therefore, the position of option (*vikalpa*) and the position of sublation (*bādha*) are presented merely as the views of others. Thus, statements such as "he may dwell in whichever he desires" (VaDh 7.3) should be understood as being spoken from the perspective of teachers who advocate option. This mention is made even though the meaning is already established, with the intention of stating that one who is incapable of performing the combined practice—due to defects such as blindness or lameness, or due to poverty and so forth—should resort to the position of option.

Alternatively, he who possesses knowledge of the inner self (adhyātmajñānin) should resort to the path of discriminative discernment (vikalpapakṣa), while the other should follow the path of synthesis (samuccayapakṣa). Why? Because the purpose of ritual performance is the arising of higher realization (vijñāna). Once that has arisen, the goal of human life (puruṣārtha) is accomplished for a person regardless of which stage of life (āśrama) they inhabit. The mention of "stages of life" is for the sake of conventional usage, as in such passages as “the castes and the stages of life” (GDh 11.9). 3.1.

Regarding such a student who has thus studied the Vedas, some teachers say that the four stages of life (*āśrama*) to be described hereafter are to be chosen optionally; others, however, maintain that they are to be practiced cumulatively. On this point, Āpastamba says: "Among all of these, one who conducts himself according to the instructions without distraction attains security" (ĀpDh 2.21.2), and also: "Having understood the ritual actions, he may undertake whichever he desires" (ĀpDh 2.21.5). Likewise, Baudhāyana, after describing the stage of studentship, states: "From this very stage, one who remains a student goes forth into the wandering life" (ĀpDh 2.21.8). By Manu, however, their cumulative practice is shown.
Having discharged the three debts, one should fix the mind on liberation;
but he who seeks liberation without having discharged them falls downward. All these stages, moreover, when entered upon in due order according to the scriptures, [lead to the goal].
"They lead the Brahmin who acts according to what has been taught to the supreme goal. (MDh 6.88) Thus [ends the section]. 3.1.
What, then, are those stages of life? To this he says: What, then, are those stages of life? The student, the householder, the mendicant, and the forest-dweller. 3.2.

One who practices *brahmacarya* (the life of celibacy), or one who moves about free from desire regarding the domain of *Brahman* itself, is a *brahmacārī*. A *gṛha* is a wife; because of union with her, one is a *gṛhastha* (householder). One whose nature is to subsist on alms is a *bhikṣu* (mendicant). The *vaikhānasa* is the scripture proclaimed by Vikhanas; one who conducts himself according to its rules is a *vaikhānasa* (forest-dweller). This non-compound form [of these terms] is for the purpose of indicating their distinctness. As Uśanas said: "There are two types of *brahmacārīs*: the *upakurvāṇa* and the *naiṣṭhika*; two types of *vaikhānasas*: those with a wife and those without a wife; two types of *saṃnyāsins*: the *bhikṣu-saṃnyāsī* and the *veda-saṃnyāsī*; and the householder is of many kinds, through the divisions of *śālīna*, *yāyāvara*, and so forth. And so on.

But surely, in another *smṛti*, after mentioning the *vaikhānasa*, the term *bhikṣu* is used; for what purpose, then, is there a change in the order here? It is said: the change in the order in the passage, "The first three are those belonging to the stages of life" (GDh 28.49), is for the purpose of excluding the *vaikhānasa*. If it is argued that this is already established by the very prohibition of his entering a village, we say no; for it is possible that seekers might go to the forest as well. And so says another *smṛti*:
"One learned in the four Vedas, a ritualist, an etymologist, and a reciter of the Dharma..."
"The student, the householder, and the mendicant—this assembly consists of at least ten members.
However, some say:
"Having performed the Prajāpatya sacrifice, in which all one's possessions are given as the sacrificial fee..."

Relying on another Smṛti text which states, "Having internalized the sacred fires within himself, a Brāhmaṇa should renounce from his home," they explain that this difference in sequence means that renunciation (saṃnyāsa) must be performed directly from the state of a householder. The learned among the twice-born (bhūsura) should investigate whether this has already been established by the preceding Sūtra or not. 3.2.120.

Although this stage was previously mentioned as the *brahmacarya-āśrama*, what is intended here is the status of the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārin*) who desires to enter it. A *bhikṣu* is a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*); a *vaikhānasa* is a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*). Because he conducts himself according to the path proclaimed by the *Vaikhānasa*s, that stage of life is indicated here as the primary one. In other scriptures, the *vaikhānasa* is the third and the *bhikṣu* is the fourth stage; however, there is a change in the sequence here for the purpose of excluding the *vaikhānasa* from the reference in the rule: "The three aforementioned stages of life" (GDh 28.49). 3.2.
Among them, the householder is the source of the others, because they do not produce offspring on their own. 3.3.

Among all four stages of life (*āśrama*), the householder is the cause [of their existence], because the others—the student (*brahmacārin*) and so forth—lack progeny. The mention of the forest-dweller (*vaikhānasa*) is for the sake of providing a reason; for the student is already established by the very preservation of his vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and the mendicant (*bhikṣu*) is likewise ordained to be one whose semen is drawn upward (*ūrdhvaretas*). Thus, even in the case of the forest-dweller who maintains a wife, the preservation of celibacy must be practiced. Although their eligibility is already established by implication, the explicit mention of them is for the purpose of showing that their entitlement to these duties belongs only to those who have been born as householders. And so says Śātātapa:
"Cāṇḍālas, those who have fallen from their caste, wandering mendicants, and ascetics—the offspring born of them should be made to dwell together with the Cāṇḍālas. Thus it is said.

When it is stated, “the householder alone is their source,” the use of the restrictive particle *eva* (alone) already establishes that others must observe the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*). Nevertheless, this specific mention is made so that there may be no turning back for them [from the householder stage]. If they were to turn back toward the state of householdership, then they become outcasts (*caṇḍāla*). Why? Because of the cited statement of Śātātapa. In that regard: “They become outcasts. This refers to those wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*), ascetics (*tāpasa*), lifelong students (*naiṣṭhika*), and forest-dwellers (*vaikhānasa*) who have fallen away or turned back. Therefore, the meaning is that the king or a village community should cause the offspring born of them to dwell together with outcasts. 3.3.103–104.

Among those residing in all four stages of life (*āśrama*), the householder is the source and the place of origin. It is only through the householder that those belonging to the four stages of life are produced; for the procreation of offspring is forbidden for those residing in stages of life other than the householder’s. Regarding this, Śātātapa says:
"Caṇḍālas, outcasts, wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*), and ascetics (*tāpasa*)—one should cause their offspring to live together with the Caṇḍālas."
Thus [ends section] 3.3.

Now, since the duties of the stages of life (āśramadharma) are to be explained in their proper sequence, and having first described those of the student (upakurvāṇa) because of his commonality with all stages, the author speaks in order to describe those of the lifelong student (naiṣṭhika) which follows in sequence.
Now, intending to declare the duties of the stages of life, he speaks first of the student (brahmacārin), who was mentioned at the outset. Regarding that, it has been said: "Of the student... (3.4).

In this regard, the extension (*atideśa*) is that whatever has been stated concerning the kindling of the sacred fires and so forth by way of the *upanayana* ceremony applies to him as well. Now, one might ask: how is it known that this applies only to the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*) and not to the temporary student (*upakurvāṇa*)? It is said: because [the duties] have already been stated for the temporary student; because the householder, the mendicant, and the forest-dweller are yet to be described; therefore, it applies only to the lifelong student.

If it is asked, "Then for what purpose is the mention of the *brahmacārin*?"—it is for this purpose: that only one who has performed the vows of the *upakurvāṇa* [householder-bound student] has the qualification for being a *naiṣṭhika* [lifelong celibate]. 3.4.

In that regard, among those [types of students], it is stated that for the lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika) as well, the very same rule that was prescribed for the temporary student (upakurvāṇa)—beginning with the words "the discipline beginning with the initiation ceremony" (GDh 2.10)—applies to him too. 3.4.
Having stated that, by virtue of this extension, the very same vow of the *upakurvāṇa* student must be observed by the *naiṣṭhika* ascetic as well, he now states its specific rule:
"In this regard, the specific rule is:
dependence upon the teacher until the end. (3.5)
Dependence upon the teacher—that is, following his will—must be maintained until death. 3.5
Until the end, until the falling away of the body, he should remain in the teacher’s family itself, engaged in service to him. 3.5.
Furthermore: he should mutter [the mantra] with the remainder of the teacher's ritual duties. 3.6.

At times other than those spent in service to the guru, one should perform *japa*. Thus, *japa* alone is his distinguished means for accomplishing dharma. Although "teacher" (*ācārya*) was the subject under discussion, the use of the term "guru" is intended to include the service of both mother and father as well. Accordingly, Manu says: "Service to these three is declared to be the highest austerity;
without being authorized by them, one should not practice any other dharma" (MDh 2.229). 3.6.

Since the teacher (*ācārya*) has been the subject of discussion, the word "guru" is intended to include the parents as well. Therefore, while serving the teacher and his parents, he should recite the Veda at times other than those occupied by that service; he must not remain under their exclusive control.
In the absence of the guru, one's conduct [toward him] is the same toward his offspring. 3.7.
In the absence of the guru, the livelihood of his offspring; in his absence, that of an aged fellow-student, or [the maintenance] in the sacred fire. || 3.7 ||

In his absence, [one should serve] the son of the guru; in his absence, one who is advanced in knowledge and so forth; in his absence, a fellow student (*sabrahmacārin*) who practices the same observance (*samānacaraṇa*); in his absence, in the fire. Service to the fire means meditation upon the fire in its form as light. 3.8.

The conduct that has been prescribed toward the teacher is to be observed toward his son in his absence; in the absence of his son, toward an elder who is superior in learning or age; in the absence of an elder, toward a fellow student (sabrahmacārin); and in the absence of a fellow student, it is to be performed toward the sacred fire. Toward the fire, the conduct is to be observed through the offering of fuel-sticks and other such rites. 3.7.
In the absence of these, [the offering should be made] to an elderly fellow-student or into the fire. || 3.8 ||

In the absence of that [the teacher], [one should serve] the son of the teacher; in the absence of him, one who is advanced in learning and so forth; in the absence of him, a fellow-student (*sabrahmacārin*) who has practiced the same course of study; in the absence of him, the fire. Service to the fire means meditation upon the fire in its form as light. 3.8.
What, then, is the fruit of this stage of life? To this he says: "One who conducts himself thus, having conquered his senses, attains the world of Brahman. (3.9) — [End of] 3.8.

Thus, acting according to the instruction, one attains the world of Brahmā, the abode of Brahmā, provided that he has conquered his senses. Since the organ of generation has been mentioned due to the instruction on the preservation of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), this [conquest of the senses] should be understood as referring to the objects of the eyes and the other organs. As Manu says: "That man who, having heard, touched, seen, tasted, or smelled, neither rejoices nor desponds—he is to be known as one who has conquered his senses" (MDh 2.98). This injunction at the conclusion of the results is for the purpose of showing that this very [mastery of the senses] is the primary requirement even for those who follow the subsequent stages of life. 3.9.
The meaning is clear. The state of having conquered the senses (*jitendriyatva*) has been shown by Manu:
"That man who, having heard, touched, seen, tasted, or smelled, neither rejoices nor desponds—he is to be known as one who has conquered his senses" (MDh 2.98). || 3.8 ||
Now he states the common characteristic of the others as well: "And this is not incompatible with the subsequent ones. (3.10) — [End of] 3.9.

Whatever has been prescribed for the student (brahmacārin) applies also to those who follow him, provided it is not contradictory—such as the avoidance of gambling and similar acts. That which is contradictory is excluded; for example, the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) is excluded for the renunciant (*pravrajita*), residence in the teacher’s house for the forest-dweller (*vaikhānasa*), and the observance of celibacy for the householder. The word "and" (*ca*) indicates that whatever is about to be stated for the subsequent stage also applies to the preceding ones if it is not contradictory, such as: "One should not converse with barbarians, the impure, or the unrighteous" (GDh 9.17), and so forth. 3.10.

For the subsequent stages of life (*āśrama*), whatever is not in conflict with this [householder’s] conduct is common to them. For example, the avoidance of gambling and similar activities. That which is in conflict is as follows: the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) for the renunciant (*pravrajita*), residence in the teacher’s house (*gurukulavāsa*) for the forest-dweller (*vaikhānasa*), and celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for the householder; such is another mode of conduct. Furthermore, the entire collection of duties (*dharmajāta*) belonging to the subsequent stages of life should be understood as applying to this [stage]. Is this without distinction? No; it is that which is non-conflicting. This means that which does not conflict with the duties of the [respective] stage of life; thus, rules such as “one should not converse with barbarians (*mleccha*), the impure, or the unrighteous” [GDh 9.16] apply to him as well. (3.9)
Because there is much to be said, [the author] bypasses the householder, even though he comes next in order, and speaks of the duties of the mendicant:
"A mendicant is one who has no accumulation" (3.11).—[End of 3.10]

Now, it might be asked: "The duties of the householder, whose turn has come in the sequence, ought to be stated; why are they being set aside to speak instead of those of the mendicant? To this it is replied: The householder has much to be said about him. Some of his duties, being non-conflicting with others, are stated out of order for the purpose of ensuring that they may be known by the ancients. If it is then asked, "In that case, the duties of the forest-dweller (*vaikhānasa*) should be stated," there is no fault, because they have already been mentioned according to the order of their introduction.

Therefore, it is said first regarding the monk: by the word "non-accumulation" (anicaya), the relinquishing of material objects that are subject to increase is meant, not the relinquishing of permanent objects such as the topknot or the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*).
But is it not more logical to relinquish only what is permanent? By the word "sacrificial thread," a specific manner of wearing is designated:
"When the right arm is raised, one is called 'sacrificing' (*upavītin*) by the wise. [MDh 2.63]
The *upavīta* is the *yajñopavīta* (sacrificial thread) intended for sacrifice; however, this is not applicable here because he lacks the qualification for performing sacrifices.

This is because the abandonment of the sacrificial thread and other such items is taught in the following passage: "He who has no attachment to a water-pot, nor to water, nor to clothing, nor to the three *puṣkara* [vessels], nor to a house, nor to a seat, nor to food—he is indeed a knower of liberation" (*VaDh* 10.23). Furthermore, even in the *Jābāla-śruti*, the abandonment of the *yajñopavīta* is taught: "Having clipped his nails, he should cast away the *yajñopavīta*. Thus it is said.

It is said in reply: First, regarding what was stated—that there is no qualification for sacrifice (*yajña*)—the word *yāga* (sacrifice) also applies to the worship of the gods and similar acts. For this [ascetic], the worship of the gods indeed exists in the form of the worship of the Supreme Self through meditation. Why?
Because he is constantly in the forest, has conquered his senses, and brings about the cessation of attachment to all things.
For one whose mind has entered into internal reflection.

For it is seen in another Smṛti: "For the one who maintains equanimity (*upekṣaka*), non-return is indeed certain" (VaDh 10.17). Furthermore, because the qualification for this is the sacrifice of the self (*ātmayāga*) alone, it is heard in the Śruti: "Righteousness and unrighteousness are the oblation; the mind is the sacrificial ladle; the vital breath is the Adhvaryu priest; the senses are the Udgātṛ priests; and sound and the other objects are the Hotṛ priests. With these officiating priests and with that ladle, the ascetic (*yati*) must offer that oblation day after day into the fire of the Supreme Self. Therefore, since there exists the qualification for this sacrifice, there is no fault. As for what was said—"There is no attachment to a water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*) nor to water" (VaDh 10.23)—even there, the abandonment of attachment itself is intended for the sake of avoiding the diversity of things such as the water-pot, not the abandonment of the water-pot and so forth. Why? Because it will be stated in that very same context: "Wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavītin*) with a water-pot in hand" (VaDh 10.31). If it is argued that—since the phrase "the most righteous of all stages of life" (VaDh 10.30) applies to all stages of life by virtue of its general nature—it is therefore sublated by the specific rule—this is not so, provided that the qualification for all stages of life is accepted therein. In that context, for the purpose of constructing the meaning of the sentence and the utterance of the words, the author would have used an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) to express "the state of wearing the sacred thread and having a water-pot in hand. Having first stated, "The avoidance of backbiting, envy, pride, egoism, dishonesty, self-praise, reviling others, hypocrisy, greed, anger, and delusion is the most righteous of all stages of life" (VaDh 10.30), the subsequent mention using a negative suffix (*abhāvapratyaya*) with a specific reference—"wearing the sacred thread with a water-pot in hand" (VaDh 10.31)—can be understood as being for the purpose of excluding the qualification for all stages of life. Therefore, since there is no qualification for all stages of life in that instance, one can certainly conclude that the statement "no attachment to a water-pot or water" (VaDh 10.23) intends the abandonment of attachment alone, so that there may be no contradiction between the preceding and following passages. That is precisely the reason for the use of the word "attachment" (*saṅga*). Consequently, even by that [rule], there is no abandonment of the water-pot and the rest. And as for what was said—"having clipped his nails and cast off the sacred thread"—even there, at the time of first entering the stage of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), only the casting off of the old sacred thread is performed; it is not a prohibition of the one being taken up at that time. Why? Because another Smṛti states: "Having clipped his nails and having discarded his old garment, sacred thread, and water-pot, he should enter the stage of life after taking up new ones. Therefore, the abandonment refers to those items belonging to the previous stage.

Furthermore—by abandoning the permanent wearing of the substance (the sacred thread), a monk would also incur the absence of ritual sipping (*ācamana*), because of the rule beginning with, "One should sip water while wearing the sacrificial thread" (*ācamane yajñopavītī*, ĀpDh 1.15.1); in its absence, even the act of sipping itself would become impossible.

If you argue that, just as in the case of the rule "He may be shaven-headed or wear a topknot" (*muṇḍaḥ śikhī vā*, GDh 3.22), you accept that sipping is permissible even for one who is devoid of the topknot which is an auxiliary part of the sipping when following the shaven-headed option, we too maintain the same position.

No; there is no fault in that case because of the specific scriptural statement: "He may be shaven-headed or wear a topknot" (GDh 3.22). However, for you, since there is no such statement that the sacred thread (yajñopavīta) must be discarded, the fault remains exactly as it is.

While it should have been stated as "a monk who is without accumulation," the mention of "dharma" at the beginning is for the purpose of including the renunciation even of those things considered permanent, such as the *agnihotra* fire and one's wife. Thus, he who goes forth from the state of a householder must renounce the *śrauta* and *smārta* fires, along with the expansion of a wife, sons, sacrifices, and so forth. Likewise, he who goes forth from the state of a forest-dweller (*vaikhānasa*)—in that case as well, whether he has a wife or not—must renounce his wife (if applicable) and the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*) and other prescribed duties associated with the *śrāmaṇaka* fire.
Some explain that the mention at the beginning is for the purpose of prescribing the state of non-accumulation even for the *naiṣṭhika* (lifelong student).

That is incorrect, because in the rule, "He should mutter [the Veda] with the remainder of his duties toward the teacher" (GDh 3.6), it is the muttering itself that is taught as the primary element; by that alone, the absence of the formal taking up of the sacred fires and other such rites can certainly be understood. 3.11.
A store is a collection of substances; it would be devoid of that [if such a substance did not exist]. || 3.10 ||
One whose semen is drawn upward. 3.12 — 3.11.

By the statement, "And this is not inconsistent with the subsequent [stages]" (GDh 3.10), since the preservation of celibacy already established for the *brahmacārin* is also accomplished for him, the mention of "one whose semen is drawn up" (*ūrdhvaretas*) is for the purpose of indicating that one should employ means such that the depletion of semen does not occur; and the means consist of consuming small amounts of food and so forth. As the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva has said:
"The objects of the senses turn away from the embodied one who abstains from food."

"Except for taste; even his taste for it ceases upon seeing the Supreme" (BhG 2.59). Likewise, with the intention of advocating the consumption of little food, it is stated in another Smṛti: "Eight mouthfuls are the meal of a sage," and so forth. And thus, there is no fault in a student (*brahmacārin*) eating a full meal. Accordingly, another Smṛti states:
"The ox, the student, and the one who has established the sacred fires—these three succeed only while eating; for them, there is no success through fasting" (VaDh 6.21). || 3.12 ||

Regarding the rule "and this is not inconsistent with the following [stages]" (GDh 3.9), although mastery over the senses has already been established, the further statement "one whose semen is drawn up" (ūrdhvaretas) is intended to mean that one should strive so that the flow of the seminal fluid is brought to a halt. 3.11.
He should remain fixed in one place during the rainy season. 3.13—3.12.

Because of the plural number in the word *varṣāsu* (in the rains), the meaning is that one should not travel from village to village during the four months of the rainy season. The mention of *śīla* (conduct) implies that even while staying in one place, there should be no exertion such as wandering about. By this very rule, his state of being homeless (*aniketana*) is established. And so says another Smṛti: "At the edge of a village, in a temple, in an empty house, or at the root of a tree" (VaDh 10.13). Furthermore, by employing the term *śīla*, he makes it known that this is not necessarily an absolute requirement; therefore, in cases such as famine or the collapse of a kingdom, one may indeed travel. 3.13.
The word *varṣā* is always used in the plural; it means that when the rainy season has arrived, one should be steadfast in conduct and remain in one place. (3.12)
One seeking alms should go to the village. 3.14 — || 3.13 ||

"Bhikṣā" refers to alms-food because it is begged for; "vāsa" refers to clothing, a water-pot, and so forth. For the sake of these, he should go to the village. By implication, it is established that during the remaining time he should stay in the forest, in a temple, or similar places. (3.14)
One should enter the village only at the time for alms; at all other times, one should dwell in a temple or at the roots of trees. (3.13)
When the time for alms has arrived, the student says:
"One should go for alms at the last [hour], before [the meal] is finished. (3.15) — (3.14)

"Jaghanyam" means after the act of eating; that is the sense. And so Manu says: "When the smoke has ceased, when the pestle has been laid aside, when the embers have vanished, when the people have finished their meal, and when the removal of the dishes has taken place, the ascetic should always go for alms" (MDh 6.56). "Anivṛttam" means that he should not enter again on that same day a house in which he was refused on that occasion. The word "caret" is used for the purpose of including other Smṛti texts. As Vasiṣṭha says: "When the smoke has ceased and the pestle has been laid aside, wearing a single garment or an antelope skin... (VaDh 10.8). || 3.15 ||

If, at the time for alms-gathering, one has been delayed by failing to reach a house, he should not enter that same house again on that day. Regarding this, Manu says: "When the smoke has ceased, when the pestle is laid aside, when the embers are extinguished, when the people have finished eating, and when the removal of the dishes has been completed—at these times the ascetic should always go for alms" (MDh 6.56). 3.14.
One whose desires have ceased. || 3.16 || — || 3.15 ||

The meaning is that he does not offer blessings in response to alms-giving, salutations, and the like. If it is argued that this is already established by the rule "he does not undertake acts of injury or favor" (GDh 3.25), we say no; for while favor (*anugraha*) consists of an action, a blessing (*āśis*) consists of speech. 3.16.
One should not be intent on pronouncing blessings in the houses of others for the sake of obtaining excessive alms. || 3.15 ||
Restrained in speech, sight, and action. || 3.17 || — || 3.16 ||

In the section on the religious student (*brahmacārin*), although this is already established by the rule, "Restrained in speech, arms, and belly" (GDh 2.28), it is stated again for the sake of emphasis. Therefore, restraint of speech is silence (*mauna*), except for Vedic study, recitation, inquiries on the road, and inquiries regarding dharma and yoga; for even for an ascetic, speaking the words "give, please," for the sake of alms, is not censured. Furthermore: "Dharma-yoga, inquiry on the road, Vedic study, and likewise, speaking the words 'give, please' for the sake of alms—even for an ascetic, these do not incur blame. (YDh 3.54) Thus, silence is prescribed as a specific form of restraint for the student. However, this does not mean that one must remain silent at all times. For it is said: "One should always speak the truth, and that which is pleasant; one should speak what is true and pleasant, or even what is true if it is unpleasant. One should never speak what is pleasant if it is false. This is the eternal dharma of the twice-born. (MBh 12.168.29–30) And: "One should always speak the truth, and one should speak what is pleasant. Truth and pleasantness are the highest dharma. What is both true and pleasant is indeed difficult to find. One may speak what is true even if it is unpleasant, or what is pleasant even if it is untrue. But one should never speak what is both untrue and unpleasant. One should speak what is true and pleasant, or even what is true if it is unpleasant, for the welfare of all beings. One should never speak what is pleasant if it is false. This is the eternal dharma of the twice-born. (MBh 12.168.29–30) Therefore, while silence is prescribed as a particular practice for the student, it is not intended to be an absolute rule. Rather, one should always speak the truth and what is pleasant, and avoid falsehood and unpleasantness. Thus, silence is a specific observance within the broader context of truthful and agreeable speech. It is not meant to imply that one should remain mute at all times. As it is said: "One should always speak the truth, and one should speak what is pleasant. Truth and pleasantness are the highest dharma. What is both true and pleasant is indeed difficult to find. (MBh 12.168.29) Consequently, silence is a specific form of restraint for the student, but it is not an absolute requirement. It

This is because of the statement in another Smṛti: "Restraint of the eyes" means that one should not even look at the ailments of oneself. And so says Vasiṣṭha: "One who is indifferent toward all beings" (VaDh 10.29). "Restraint of action" means performing only what is prescribed, so that there may be no engagement in actions for the sake of desired results. 3.17

Restraint of speech is silence. Restraint of the eyes is not directing the gaze toward any place other than where one is stepping. Restraint of action is for a mendicant not to transgress the prescribed duties. Regarding this, there is another Smṛti text concerning the contradiction of restraint of speech: "One does not censure even an ascetic who speaks for the sake of dharma, for inquiry about the path, for Vedic study, or for the words 'give, O people,' when seeking alms. (3.16)
Now, by the rule "a monk is one who has no accumulation" (GDh 3.11), once all accumulated property has been renounced, an exception is made:
he may wear a garment for the purpose of covering his private parts. 3.18.
Or he may wear a garment for the purpose of covering his private parts. 3.17.

"Kaupīna" refers to nakedness. One should wear only such clothing as serves to cover that [nakedness]. And thus, there is no fault in accepting just that much from praiseworthy members of the twice-born. Furthermore: "He who, having granted safety to all beings, turns back from his vow, and he who always accepts gifts—[he] destroys both those born and those unborn."
Thus, the enumeration of faults found in another Smṛti should be understood as referring to cases other than this one. 3.18.
*Kaupīna* is the name for the private parts; he should wear only as much clothing as is required to cover them. However, he should not wear anything more, such as upper garments or the like. (3.17)
Some say it is discarded after being washed. 3.19 — || 3.18 ||

Some think that for the sake of avoiding the fault of accepting [garments], one should wash and then wear what has been discarded on the road or elsewhere; the term "having washed" (*nirṇijya*) is used for the purpose of attaining personal purity. (3.19)
Some think that even that loincloth, if it has been discarded, worn out, or abandoned by others, may be washed and worn. (3.18)
One should not take a limb of plants or trees that has not been separated [from the main body]. 3.20 — 3.19.

Herbs (oṣadhayaḥ) are those whose life ends with the ripening of their fruit. Those that bear fruit without flowers are forest trees (vanaspatayaḥ). By the inclusion of both categories, all stationary beings (sthāvarāḥ) are also included. One should not take from them what is inseparable from them and not detached, such as branches, leaves, and so forth. If it is argued that this is already established by the rule, "One who does not undertake violence or favor" (GDh 3.25), [the response is: some say that in that context, "violence" (hiṃsā) refers only to the killing of mobile beings; since [the present rule] was stated with that intention, there is no fault. Because of the prefix *upa-*, even the one who causes another to do it (the instigator) would not be exempt. 3.20.

One should not take—that is, one should not accept—the limb of trees, creepers, and so forth that is not separated from its fruit, leaves, and so on, nor has it fallen from them; however, one may accept what has fallen of its own accord. || 3.19 ||
Since it has been taught that his conduct must be constant, and since one might otherwise act according to one's own will outside of the rainy season, he says:
"He shall not stay in a village for a second night during the non-rainy season. (3.21) — [End of] 3.20.

By the word *ṛtu*, the rainy season alone is meant. When the rainy season has passed, he should not stay for a second night in a village; the meaning is that he should not stay in a single village for two days. Because of the mention of "village," there is no fault in staying in the forest. Because of the mention of "when the season has passed," there is no fault even if he stays for a second [night] during the rains. By the word *varṣā* (the rains), the winter and summer seasons are also implied. Consequently, it follows as a matter of course that during that time of the rains, he may stay in one place alone and should not stay elsewhere. (3.21)

Except for that season in which a fixed residence has been prescribed—namely the rainy season—one should not stay a second night in any village where one has stayed for one night during other seasons; thus it is said, "one should stay only one night in a village. (3.20)
Shaven-headed or with a topknot. 3.22 — 3.21.
This undertaking is for the purpose of prohibiting the matted-hair ascetic; there is an option according to one's desire.

One should have all the hair shaved together with the top-knot (*śikhā*), or one may shave it except for the top-knot. By stating the option "either shaven-headed or wearing a top-knot," the alternative between adopting a single staff (*ekadaṇḍa*) or three staffs (*tridaṇḍa*) is also indicated. Regarding this, there are the following *Śruti* and *Smṛti* texts:

"He whose top-knot consists of knowledge, and no other, like the crest of fire—he, the wise man, is called 'one who possesses the top-knot' (*śikhin*), and not others who merely wear their hair. [Brahma Upaniṣad 87]
Having shaved his head including the top-knot (*śikhā*), the wise man should discard the sacred thread (*bahiḥsūtra*).
Then, taking up the single staff (*ekadaṇḍa*), he should practice the dharma of a mendicant (*bhikṣu*).
Alternatively, one who possesses the top-knot and the sacred thread may do so if he is fully awakened to the truth.
Having taken up the triple staff, one should practice the dharma of a mendicant.
One should avoid the destruction of seeds. 3.23 — 3.22.
One should not perform the destruction of seeds, such as rice and other grains, by means of threshing and similar processes.

Seeds are rice and so forth; their destruction is threshing with a pestle and the like. One should not perform that. By this, even the preparation of rice into cooked grain is implied, because he has ownership only over food that has been prepared. (3.22)
He is equal toward all beings. 3.24.
For he is equal toward all beings in both harming and favoring them. 3.23.
He should remain impartial toward all living beings; the meaning is that he should avoid making a distinction between his own side and the side of others. 3.24.
He who is the same toward injury and favor regarding living beings—remaining unchanged whether one harms or another shows favor—is [the yogin]. (3.23)
One who does not undertake acts of injury or favor. 3.25.
One who does not undertake [new actions]. || 3.24 ||

Since this is already established by the rule "violence" (hiṃsām) [GDh 2.23] within the section on the religious student (brahmacārin), this repetition is for the sake of emphasizing its gravity. Consequently, even when the killing of a living being is unintentional, an expiation must be performed day after day to avoid that [sin]. Thus Uśanas says: "For the purification of an unintentional killing, one should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) during the night and during the day. By the word "favor" (anugraha), affection (sneha) is meant; the meaning is that he should not even show such affection [toward forbidden things]. 3.25.

One should not undertake any undertaking pertaining either to this world or the next. As Āpastamba has said: "One should live without desire for this world and without desire for the next" (ĀpDh 2.21.10). || 3.24 ||

Having spoken concerning the monk, he now states the dharma of the forest-dweller (*vaikhānasa*): "Now [the author] speaks of the forest-dweller: 'The forest-dweller, subsisting on roots and fruits in the forest, is devoted to austerity. (3.26) — [End of] 3.25.

The term *vaikhānasa* has already been etymologically explained. Living in the forest, he should be one whose habit is eating roots and the like; the meaning is that he should not eat prepared food. He should be devoted to austerity, meaning he should be intent on the emaciation of the body. And thus, even of roots, fruits, and so forth, he should eat only a very small amount, as seen in another Smṛti text which states, "For the forest-dweller, sixteen [mouthfuls]" (VaDh 6.20). || 3.26 ||

A *vaikhānasa* is a forest-dweller who, living in the forest, should eat roots and fruits, whether raw or ripe, but not cooked rice. Asceticism (*tapas*) is the emaciation of the body; therefore, he should consume even roots and fruits only in very small quantities. (3.25)
Having established the sacred fire according to the Śrāmaṇaka rite. 3.27 — || 3.26 ||
The *śrāmaṇaka* is the manual of the *vaikhānasas*. Having established the sacred fires according to that, he should perform the evening and morning oblations; this is the remainder [of the sense].

The *Vaikhānasa-śāstra* is called the *Śrāvaṇaka*. The remainder of the sense is that, having established the sacred fire according to the method prescribed therein, one should offer oblations in the evening and in the morning.
He should not eat vulgar food. 3.28 — 3.27.
One should not eat even wild roots and fruits that have been cultivated in a village. 3.28.
He should not eat even fruits or roots that grow in cultivated areas. 3.27.
He is a worshiper of the gods, ancestors, humans, spirits, and sages. || 3.29 || — || 3.28 ||

The five great sacrifices (*pañca mahāyajñāḥ*) of the householder are accomplished with village-grown food. This section is commenced so that there might not be an exclusion of them due to the prohibition against non-village-grown food for him. And so Manu says:
"With various pure forest products, or with vegetables, roots, and fruits, he should perform these very same great sacrifices according to the prescribed rule" (MDh 6.5). 3.29.
Day after day, he should perform the five great sacrifices with wild fruits and roots alone. Regarding this, Manu says:
"With various pure forest products, or with vegetables, roots, and fruits, he should offer these very same great sacrifices according to the prescribed rule" (MDh 6.5). 3.28.
He should be hospitable to all guests, with the exception of those who are prohibited. 3.30 — 3.29.

Everything that goes to his hermitage is indeed his guest. The meaning is that there is no restriction of caste, such as "a non-Brahmin is not a guest of a Brahmin" (GDh 5.43), nor is there any restriction of number; however, those who are prohibited—thieves and the like—and those born of inverse unions (pratiloma) are excluded from this.

All those who approach him are his guests; however, there is no such restrictive rule as that "for a Brahmin, one who is not a Brahmin is not a guest" (GDh 5.39). Even in that case, he should avoid thieves, outcasts, and the like, with the exception of those whose exclusion is specifically forbidden. (3.29)
One may also consume meat from a sacrificial animal. 3.31 — 3.30.

The meat of an animal killed by predators such as tigers is *vaiṣka*; one may consume that. The word "api" (even/also) is used here in a sense of censure; therefore, one should consume it only in times of distress (*āpad*). 3.31.

*Vaiṣka* refers to the meat of wild beasts such as tigers and the like; he may consume even that. The word *api* (even) has a figurative sense, meaning that even in the absence of fruits, roots, and so forth, that [meat] is also edible. In that case as well, one must exclude anything other than what is prescribed by the rule: "Five five-toed animals are edible. The phrase "excluding what is forbidden" (*pratiṣiddhavarjam*) is connected to both parts of the sentence according to the maxim of the crow’s eye (*kākākṣinyāya*). (3.30)
He should not stand upon ground that has been ploughed by a plow. 3.32 — 3.31.

"Even in the forest, he should not step upon ground that has been ploughed; the meaning is that he should not make his dwelling there. Although "should step upon" (*ākrāmet*) would have sufficed, the use of the term "should occupy" (*adhitiṣṭhet*) is intended to indicate that there is no fault in stepping upon such ground inadvertently. Although "ploughed" (*kṛṣṭam*) would have sufficed, the inclusion of the word "plough" (*phāla*) is for the purpose of prohibiting a dwelling in the immediate vicinity of a field. (3.32)
Dwelling in the forest, he should not occupy a place that has been ploughed by a plow. || 3.31 ||
And he should not enter a village. 3.33—3.32.
One should not enter a human habitation even by a path that has not been ploughed; because of the word "and," this applies to entering another village as well. 3.33.
Even for one dwelling in the forest, entering a nearby village at will is forbidden. (3.32)
With matted hair, clothed in rags and skins. || 3.34 || — || 3.33 ||

*Jaṭilaḥ* means one with matted hair (*keśī*). This rule is undertaken for the purpose of restriction, so that he must indeed be one with matted hair. *Cīra* is made of *darbha* grass and similar materials; this is to be understood as his lower garment. *Ajina* is a skin; this is his upper garment. And thus another *Smṛti* states: "Clad in rags and having a skin as an upper garment. (3.34)

The *jaṭila* is one who maintains his matted hair, beard, body hair, and nails; he wears a garment made of bark or *darbha* grass and so forth, with a deerskin as an upper garment, as is seen in the established rules of other *smṛtis*. (3.33)
One should not eat more than once a year. 3.35 — 3.34.

One should not consume even roots and fruits that are more than a year old. Thus says Manu: "In the month of Āśvayuja, one should abandon [stored food]," and so forth. In this way, the rule of storing for only one year is established. (3.35)
When a year has passed, or even more than a year, he should not eat even forest-grown food. On this point, Manu says:
"In the month of Āśvayuja, he should discard what was previously collected and produced, as well as worn-out garments, flowers, roots, and fruits" (MDh 6.15). 3.34.
