Having spoken regarding the Vaikhānasa, he now says, desiring to state the view of certain authorities (ekīya) that the stages of life (āśrama) may be sublated [by one another]: "The stages of life have been stated, and their optionality (vikalpa) as well as their cumulative nature (samuccaya) have also been shown. He demonstrates their primary status: 'But the teachers maintain the single stage of life (aikāśramya), because of the direct injunction for the householder's life. Regarding the householder's life...

*Aikāśramyam* means "that which exists in a single stage of life" (*ekāśrama*). The word *tu* is used for emphasis. The genitive case in *gārhasthyasya* denotes the object of the action. The teachers maintain that only the householder’s stage (*gārhasthya*) is [the one stage]. Why? Because of its direct injunction; the meaning is: because of the injunction found in the revealed scripture (*śruti*). Even though it is not enjoined in the form "one should be a householder," nevertheless, since the performance of rites such as the *agnihotra*—which are to be accomplished by a householder—is enjoined, the injunction must be understood as pertaining to that very stage. (3.36)

The word *tu* expresses a distinction. In all the Vedic scriptures, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas, the duties of the householder—namely the Agnihotra and so forth—are prescribed most extensively. Therefore, all teachers consider the state of the householder to be the single stage of life (*ekāśramya*) and the primary one. For those who are incapable in that regard, the duties of the other stages of life are prescribed; for the other stages are directly enjoined and because they depend directly upon the householder. The repetition [of the verse] has been explained. (3.35)
Now begins the fourth chapter.
The duties of the religious student (*brahmacārin*) and others have been stated; now the duties of the householder (*gṛhastha*) must be explained. Therefore, he says:
"The duties of the householder are being declared."
A householder should marry a wife who is of equal status, who has belonged to no other man before, and who is younger than himself.

The designation "householder" is used here as a future title, intended for the student (*snātaka*) to enter the duties of a householder—which are not yet forbidden—until he takes a wife. A suitable woman is one by birth, not by family; for learning, once lost, can be regained, but upon the loss of caste, there is total ruin in this world.
Since she is to be honored according to the reputation of her family,
one should therefore marry a woman of noble birth.

For it is heard in another Smṛti that [a wife] must be obtained from a superior family. "A wife" means one who is to be supported and endowed with auspicious marks; "he should obtain" means he should seek her; "one who has not belonged to another" means she who has not been given away even by word of mouth to anyone else; "younger" means of lower age than himself. (4.1)

"Householder" (*gṛhastha*) is a designation based on a future status. Alternatively, it is for the purpose of showing that those duties which belong to a householder are the same even for a *snātaka* prior to marriage. He should take—that is, marry—as his wife one who is equal to him in birth and family, who has not been promised to another even by word of mouth, and who is of younger age. || 4.1 ||
The exception to this is marriage with those who do not share the same *pravara*. 4.2.

"Having the same *pravara*" means having the same *ṛṣi* lineage; the absence of that is "not having the same *pravara*. Marriage should be performed with those who do not have the same *pravara*. Although one could simply say "those who do not have the same *pravara*," the expression used here is intended to indicate that even if there is a common *gotra* on the mother’s side, there is no fault. Thus, the prohibition against a common *gotra* applies only to the father’s side. And so says Manu:
"She who is not a *sapinda* of the mother and she who is not of the same *gotra* as the father...
(MDh 3.5), and so forth. 4.2.

There is no marriage with those who share a common *pravara*. For example, among the descendants of Aṅgiras—namely Harita, Kutsa, Piṅga, Śaṅkha, Darbha, Haimaka, and Bhava—the *pravaras* are Āṅgirasa, Ambarīṣa, and Yauvanāśva. The detailed expansion of such *pravaras*, including the rule that "one should not marry a woman of the Hārīta or Kautsa lineage," is to be found in the *Āpastamba-dharmasūtra*. 4.2.
Beyond the seventh generation on the paternal side, [there is no relationship]. 4.3.
Beyond the seventh degree from paternal relatives and beyond the fifth degree from maternal relatives on the side of the progenitor. 4.3.

"Paternal kinsmen" refers to the father's maternal uncles, sisters, and so forth; marriage may take place beyond the seventh generation from them, or rather, marriage should be performed starting from the eighth generation—this is the meaning. (4.3)

When counting the circle of paternal relatives starting from the father, one may marry a girl born beyond the seventh degree; when counting the circle of maternal relatives starting from the mother, one may marry a girl born beyond the fifth degree. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "beyond the seventh from the progenitor" (*bījinaś ca saptamād ūrdhvam*), this is established. For example, a husband who is barren or diseased may request his brother-in-law, saying, "Procreate a son in my field. Or, when the lineage is in danger of extinction, elders may appoint a widow; as was seen when Vyāsa procreated Dhṛtarāṣṭra and others in the field of Vicitravīrya at the word of Satyavatī. As Yājñavalkya has said:

"A son begotten by appointment (niyoga) in the field of another by a man who has no son is, according to dharma, the heir to the estate and the giver of the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to both. This refers to that case [in Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.127], namely, "and of the seed-owner. 4.3.
And [the same applies] to one who possesses the seed. 4.4.120.

The word "ca" (and) serves to draw forward [the rule] from above the seventh [generation]. Regarding the seed that has been sown in another's field, [the prohibition applies] from the very moment it is born. This is a prohibition [of marriage] which would otherwise have been applicable due to the lack of a common *pravara*. (4.4)
From the fifth [generation] on the mother's side. || 4.5 ||

The phrase "one should find [a bride] above" continues [from the previous rule]. "Maternal relatives" refers to the maternal uncle, the mother's sister, and so forth. In that regard, marriage should be performed with someone beyond the fifth degree [of kinship]. 4.5.
Now he states the rules for marriage. Next, the varieties of marriage:
In the *brāhma* rite, one should give a girl, having clothed and adorned her, to a man endowed with learning, good conduct, kinship, and character. (4.6) — (4.4)

"Brahma" is the designation for this form of marriage. "Vidyā" refers to the three Vedas; "cāritra" is the performance of enjoined duties; "bandhu" is a noble lineage; and "śīla" is the very orientation toward righteousness (*dharma*). The word "endowed with" (*saṃpanna*) is to be connected with each [of these qualities]. Having clothed the bridegroom with a pair of garments and having adorned her with ornaments and the like, he should give her away preceded by the pouring of water. The phrases "having clothed" and "having adorned" are to be understood as applying to the other three forms of marriage as well. (4.6)

Knowledge (*vidyā*) is the knowledge of the Vedas; conduct (*cāritra*) is the performance of enjoined duties; kinsmen (*bandhu*) are relatives such as maternal uncles and others; and character (*śīla*) is faith in what is prescribed. To one endowed with these qualities, having clothed him in a pair of garments and adorned him according to his means, one should give a daughter. This type of marriage is designated as *brāhma*. (4.4)
The mantra for the union in the Prājāpatya rite is: "Let dharma be practiced together. (4.7) — [End of] 4.5.

*Prājāpatya* is the designation for a form of marriage. In that *prājāpatya* marriage, the mantra intended for the purpose of union is the "union-mantra"; having recited it at the time of giving her away, he should give her. What is that mantra? "Let dharma be practiced together. (4.7)

In the marriage known as Prājāpatya, the mantra for the giving [of the bride] is: "Let dharma be practiced together. Although the practice of dharma together occurs in the Brāhma and other forms of marriage as well, nevertheless, by this mantra, a covenant is made that dharma must be practiced with her alone until the end; one must not enter another stage of life (āśrama), nor should another woman be taken as a wife. This is the distinction of the Prājāpatya from the Brāhma and others. "Having clothed and adorned her" is the same [as in the previous rule]. (4.5)
In the Ārṣa form of marriage, he should give a pair of cattle to the bridegroom along with the girl. 4.8–4.9.
The term *ārṣa* refers to a form of marriage. In that rite, after the groom has first given a cow and a bull, he should subsequently give the bride, having clothed and adorned her. (4.8)

In the marriage known as the Ārṣa, one should give a pair of cattle, consisting of a male and a female, to the father of the girl; this may be done by the groom himself or by some relative of his. "Having clothed her and adorned her" is the same [as in the preceding rule]. (4.6)
The giving of a gift to a priest within the sacrificial altar is the divine [marriage rite]. 4.9.
Giving to a priest within the sacrificial altar is the divine rite; [it is performed] after having adorned [the bride]. 4.7.

The term *antarvedī* is used for the purpose of referring to the sacrifice that has been commenced; this is because, as seen in such rules as “the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) and the father-in-law” (GDh 5.28), the designation *ṛtvij* is applied even after the performance of the ritual act is completed. The mention of *dāna* (giving) is intended to indicate that this exceeds the regular obligatory sacrificial fee (*nityadakṣiṇā*). The term *daiva* is a technical name for the marriage rite. 4.9.

Within the sacrificial altar (antarvedi), at the time of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇākāla), the giving of a girl, having adorned her, to a priest who is performing the ritual—that is the Daiva marriage. Regarding the phrase "having clothed and adorned her," the explicit mention of "having adorned her" in this context is for the purpose of adorning the groom as well with rings and other ornaments. (4.7)
The Gāndharva form consists of a union initiated by the woman herself when she desires it after having adorned herself. 4.10.
The Gāndharva marriage is the union of two who desire each other of their own accord.

Having adorned herself by her own hand, she will say: "Having cast off the ornaments of my father" (GDh 18.21); this refers to that case. Desiring [him], she should unite with the groom of her own accord; that is the Gāndharva marriage. 4.10.
The Gāndharva marriage is the union of a willing bride and a willing groom; from the word "herself," the desire of the groom is understood. (4.8)
The *āsura* [form of marriage] consists of the non-bending [of the bride] by means of wealth for those who possess women. 4.11. — 4.9.

That marriage in which the bending down [of the bridegroom] is performed by the giving of wealth to the bride's guardians is called the Āsura form. Although it should have been stated as "to the bride's guardians" (*kanyāvatām*), the inclusion of the word "women" (*strī*) is for the purpose of precluding the fruit that would otherwise accrue from the gift of a maiden. (4.11)

The Āsura marriage is that in which the father or other relatives of the girl—who possesses sons—acquire honor by means of the payment of wealth, that is, the giving of riches. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states: "The Āsura [arises] from the taking of wealth" (YDh 1.61). And Manu says:
"Having given wealth to the kinsmen and to the girl according to one's ability, the giving away of the girl out of one's own free will is called the Āsura dharma" (MDh 3.31).
Because of the expression "of those who have [already] wives," the giving of wealth to a maiden alone is not the basis for the Āsura form of marriage. And so says another Smṛti:
"That the kinsmen do not take a bride-price (śulka) from those [maidens] is not a sale;
it is merely an honorarium for the maidens, out of kindness, and not solely [for the purpose of purchase]. (4.9)
The Rākṣasa [form of marriage] results from taking [the bride] by force. 4.12. — 4.10.
That [form of marriage] in which there is taking [of the bride] by force is the Rākṣasa. || 4.12 ||
The taking of a maiden by force after defeating her kinsmen is the Rākṣasa form of marriage. 4.10.
Because it is performed without the woman's consent, that is the Paiśāca rite. 4.13. — || 4.11 ||

When one approaches a girl who is unknown to him—whether she is asleep, intoxicated, or heedless, or occupied with another task—that is the marriage called *paiśāca*. The term "approaching" (*upagamana*) should be understood here as referring to acts such as embracing and the like, because for a girl whose virginity has been violated, there is no [requirement for] the sacramental rite. Thus says Manu:
"The mantras pertaining to the taking of the hand are established only for virgins" (MDh 8.226). || 4.13 ||
When one approaches a woman while she is asleep, intoxicated, or mentally deranged, without her conscious knowledge, that is the Paiśāca form of marriage. 4.11.
Thus the eight forms of marriage have been described; among them, the first four are lawful. 4.14—4.12.

Only the first four are not devoid of the Dharma. Although one could simply say "the first," the term "initial" (*prathama*) is used for the purpose of indicating that whatever is first is also excellent. Consequently, each subsequent [quality] should be understood as existing only in the absence of each preceding one. (4.14)
From the beginning, the four forms of marriage are lawful for all castes; they do not deviate from dharma and are praised. (4.12)
"Some say there are six. 4.15 — || 4.13 ||

Some, however, consider even the Gāndharva and Āsura forms to be lawful. Thus Vasiṣṭha says: "There are six forms of marriage: Brāhma, Daiva, Ārṣa, Gāndharva, Kṣatra, and Mānuṣa" (VaDh 1.28). And so, the Rākṣasa and Paiśāca forms, though extremely base, are to be understood as permissible by the force of the injunction when the preceding ones are not possible. 4.15.
Some legal scholars say that six [forms of marriage] are lawful; they maintain that even the Gāndharva and Āsura forms do not deviate from dharma. 4.13.

Now, for the sake of specifying those sons born of them, he states the distinct designations designated in the scriptures for the sons born from Brāhmaṇas and others by women of the Kṣatriya and other castes in the context of the *kraya-vivāha* (purchase-marriage): "Those born in the direct order (*anuloma*) from women one degree, two degrees, or three degrees lower are the Savarṇa, Ambaṣṭha, Ugra, Niṣāda, Dauṣyanta, and Pāraśava. (4.16)
Those born from women of the same caste, or from those one, two, or three degrees lower, are respectively known as Savarṇa, Ambaṣṭha, Ugra, Niṣāda, Dauṣmanta, and Pāraśava. (4.14)

The *anuloma* [progeny] are those born in the direct order of the castes (*varṇa*). For a Brāhmaṇa, the woman immediately following him is a Kṣatriyā; one separated by one intermediate caste is a Vaiśyā; and one separated by two intermediate castes is a Śūdrā. For a Kṣatriya, the woman immediately following him is a Vaiśyā; one separated by one intermediate caste is a Śūdrā; for him, there is no woman separated by two intermediate castes. For a Vaiśya, the woman immediately following him is a Śūdrā; for him, there is no woman separated by one intermediate caste. Consequently, one born from a Brāhmaṇa and a woman immediately following him is of the same caste (*savarṇa*). One born from a Kṣatriya and a woman immediately following him is an Ambaṣṭha. One born from a Vaiśya and a woman immediately following him is an Ugra. One born from a Brāhmaṇa and a woman separated by one intermediate caste is a Niṣāda. One born from a Kṣatriya and a woman separated by one intermediate caste is a Dauṣyanta. One born from a Brāhmaṇa and a woman separated by two intermediate castes is a Pāraśava. (4.16)

From a Brāhmaṇa, by a Kṣatriya woman who is next in rank, one born is a Savarṇa. From a Kṣatriya, by a Vaiśya woman, from her [is born] an Ambaṣṭha. From a Vaiśya, by a Śūdra woman who is next in rank, from her [is born] an Ugra. From a Brāhmaṇa, by a Vaiśya woman separated by one degree, from her [is born] a Niṣāda. From a Kṣatriya, by a Śūdra woman separated by one degree, from her [is born] a Dauṣmanta. From a Brāhmaṇa, by a Śūdra woman separated by two degrees, from her [is born] a Pāraśava. The detailed exposition regarding the determination of castes is to be found in another Smṛti. 4.14.
He speaks of those born in the inverse order:
"The inverse-born are the Sūta, Māgadha, Āyogava, Kṣattṛ, Vaidehaka, and Caṇḍāla. (4.17)
But those born in the inverse order are the Sūta, Māgadha, Āyogava, Kṣattṛ, Vaidehaka, and Caṇḍāla. || 4.15 ||

Those born in the reverse order (*prātilomya*) are the *pratiloma* castes; they are produced only from women who are immediate, one-removed, or two-removed [in rank]. For a Kṣatriya, the immediate woman is a Brāhmaṇī; for a Vaiśya, the immediate woman is a Kṣatriyā; for a Śūdra, the immediate woman is a Vaiśyā. For a Vaiśya, the one-removed woman is a Brāhmaṇī; for a Śūdra, she is a Kṣatriyā. For a Śūdra, the two-removed woman is a Brāhmaṇī. A son born to a Kṣatriya from an immediate woman is a Sūta; born to a Vaiśya from an immediate woman, he is a Māgadha; born to a Śūdra from an immediate woman, he is an Āyogava. Born to a Vaiśya from a one-removed woman, he is a Kṣattṛ; born to a Śūdra from a one-removed woman, he is a Vaidehaka. Born to a Śūdra from a two-removed woman, he is a Caṇḍāla. Such, then, is the opinion of Gautama (4.17).

The phrase "born from those separated by one, two, or three [classes]" is understood to carry over. From a Kṣatriya, a Brāhmaṇī woman who is one class below is his *anantarā*; from him and her is born a Sūta. From a Vaiśya, a Kṣatriyā woman who is one class below is his *anantarā*; from him and her is born a Māgadha. From a Śūdra, a Vaiśyā woman who is one class below is his *anantarā*; from him and her is born an Āyogava. From a Vaiśya, a Brāhmaṇī woman who is two classes below is his *ekāntarā*; from him and her is born a Kṛta. From a Śūdra, a Kṣatriyā woman who is two classes below is his *ekāntarā*; from him and her is born a Vaidehaka. From a Śūdra, a Brāhmaṇī woman who is three classes below is his *dvyantarā*; from him and her is born a Caṇḍāla. (4.15)
Now, according to the opinion of others, he states the distinction of designations.
According to the opinion of others, having grouped those very [sons] by each caste, he states the distinctions of their designations:
"The Brāhmaṇī gave birth to sons from the castes in due order."
The Brāhmaṇa, Sūta, Māgadha, and Caṇḍāla. || 4.18 || — || 4.16 ||

The Brāhmaṇī gave birth [to these] from the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa in their respective order: from the Brāhmaṇa a Brāhmaṇa, from the Kṣatriya a Sūta, from the Vaiśya a Māgadha, and from the Śūdra a Caṇḍāla. The use of the past tense "gave birth" (ajījanat) is for the purpose of demonstrating the beginninglessness of saṃsāra. (4.18)
The meaning is clear. Here, the mention of "succession" (anupūrvya) refers to the intended sequence of phonemes, but not to a forward order (anuloma). 4.16.
From those very [Kṣatriyas] were born the Mūrdhāvasiktas, Kṣatriyas, Dhīvaras, and Pulkasas. (4.19)

From those very [Kṣatriyas] come the Mūrdhāvasikta, Kṣattṛ, and Dhīvara-Pulkasa; from those very [Vaiśyas] come the Bhṛjjakaṇṭha, Māhiṣya, Vaiśya, and Vaideha; and from those [Śūdras] come the Pāraśava, Yavana, Karaṇa, and Śūdra—some say these are all Śūdras. (4.17)

The phrase "she gave birth in due order" also applies here. From those very same [classes], the Brāhmaṇa and so forth, she (the Kṣatriya woman) gave birth in sequence: from a Brāhmaṇa, a son born of a Kṣatriya woman is a Mūrdhāvasikta; from a Kṣatriya, a son born of a Kṣatriya woman is a Kṣatriya; from a Vaiśya, a son born of a Kṣatriya woman is a Dhīvara; and from a Śūdra, a son born of a Kṣatriya woman is a Pulkasa. (4.19)

Some traditionalists (smartas), according to the sequence already stated—beginning with "the Brāhmaṇa woman gave birth"—maintain that there are distinct designations for those born in order from Brāhmaṇas and the other castes upon Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra women. (4.17)
From those very same [Kṣatriyas], Vaiśya women give birth to the Bhṛjjakaṇṭha, Māhiṣya, and Vaidehaka.

The phrase "he procreated in due order" continues [from the previous verse]. Thus, one born of a Brāhmaṇa from a Vaiśya woman is a Bhṛjjakaṇṭha; one born of a Kṣatriya from a Vaiśya woman is a Māhiṣya; one born of a Vaiśya from a Vaiśya woman is a Vaiśya; and one born of a Śūdra from a Vaiśya woman is a Vaidehaka. (4.20)
Some say that a Śūdra woman may bear Pāraśava, Yavana, and Karaṇa sons from these [three higher castes]. 4.21.

She gave birth [to these] in this very sequence. From a Brāhmaṇa father on a Śūdra mother is born a Pāraśava; from a Kṣatriya father on a Śūdra mother is born a Yavana; from a Vaiśya father on a Śūdra mother is born a Karaṇa; and from a Śūdra father on a Śūdra mother is born one who is designated simply as a Śūdra. Thus some teachers describe them by means of different names. And the statement of these different names according to the opinion of certain authorities is for the purpose of showing that even if these designations are found in other regions, no difference in caste (jāti) should be inferred. 4.21.
And for these as well, there is entry into another caste through the seventh [birth], by means of either elevation or degradation. (4.22)
The transition to another caste occurs through advancement or degradation in the seventh or fifth generation, according to the teachers. 4.18.

By the word *varṇa*, the generative seed (*utpādakabīja*) is meant; the meaning is that one should become of the same *varṇa* as the generative seed. By the seventh cycle of generations (*yugaparivartana*). By the word *antara*, "field" (*kṣetra*) is meant. And from this, the sequence is to be understood: through excellence (*utkarṣa*), the state of having the *varṇa* of the generative seed, and through deficiency (*apakarṣa*), the *varṇa* of the field. From that, excellence is to be considered in relation to the woman, and deficiency in relation to the man. For example: when a Brāhmaṇa [begets] a Kṣatriya woman, a Mūrdhāvasiktā is born. That Mūrdhāvasiktā, possessing the superior quality of the seed, begets a daughter with the superior quality of the seed by a Brāhmaṇa alone, and she likewise [begets one] by a Brāhmaṇa; thus, in the seventh generation, she becomes a Brāhmaṇī—such is excellence. Likewise, when a Brāhmaṇa [begets] a Kṣatriya woman, a Mūrdhāvasikta is born. When he unites with a Kṣatriya woman, as before, he becomes a Kṣatriya—such is deficiency. In this way, it is to be understood everywhere, even in the case of the offspring of a Śūdra woman and so forth. And so says Manu:
If one born of a Śūdra woman from a Brāhmaṇa father procreates with a superior man,
he attains the higher caste of his superior within the seventh generation.

"A Śūdra attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa, and a Brāhmaṇa goes to the state of a Śūdra; one should know that it is likewise for those born from a Kṣatriya and similarly from a Vaiśya. [MDh 10.64–65] Thus [ends verse 4.22].

The completion of the sentence is "they consider [themselves]. For those very *savarṇa* and other offspring born in the direct order (*anuloma*), through excellence on the father's side, there is the attainment of a higher caste from the seventh generation; through deficiency on the mother's side, there is the attainment of a lower caste from the fifth generation. For example: a daughter born to a Brāhmaṇa from a married Kṣatriya woman is a *savarṇa*; she too, being married by a Brāhmaṇa, gives birth to a child from her, and so on until the seventh. But the child whom the seventh one, married by a Brāhmaṇa, begets—that belongs to the Brāhmaṇa caste itself. Likewise, a son begotten by a Brāhmaṇa on a Kṣatriya woman is a *savarṇa*; he too, having married a Kṣatriya woman, begets a son, and he also [marries] a Kṣatriya woman, and so on until the fifth. But the child whom the fifth one begets from a Kṣatriya woman—that belongs to the Kṣatriya caste itself. Such is the meaning of this alternative rule. Even in that case, regarding the transition to another caste, if there is abundance of conduct and Vedic study, one becomes superior in the fifth generation; but through low conduct, one becomes inferior in the fifth generation. The same should be understood for a Kṣatriya with a Vaiśya woman, and for a Vaiśya with a Śūdra woman. (4.18)
By the fifth [verse], the teachers [are indicated]. 4.23.

Some teachers describe that the transition to another caste occurs through exactly five cycles of the ages; this too should be understood as being in consideration of the general course of events. 4.23
And [the same applies] to those born in other creations. 4.24–19.

The "creation" refers to the four castes (*varṇas*). Following that are the *mūrdhāvasikta* and others. Those born from them are "born from another creation. The phrase "transition to another caste" occurs through both advancement and decline; the word "and" (*ca*) serves to include the teachers' view that this happens by means of the seventh and fifth [generations]. Consequently, even in those cases, one should understand the transition between the caste of the progenitor and the field-born as occurring after conceiving the *anuloma* and *pratiloma* sub-castes. (4.24)

Apart from the four primary castes (*cāturvarṇya*), there also occurs a mutual transition between different castes through the increase or decrease of status among those born in the direct order (*anuloma*), such as the *Savarṇa*, *Ambaṣṭha*, and others. For example: a daughter produced by a man of the same caste on an *Ambaṣṭhī* woman is again married by a man of the same caste; the daughter produced by him on her in turn is likewise married by a man of the same caste. Thus, up to the seventh generation, when a daughter is married by a man of the same caste, the offspring he produces becomes that very caste itself. Similarly, if that same girl is married by an *Ambaṣṭha* and gives birth to a daughter, and she too is married by an *Ambaṣṭha*, then when the seventh-generation girl is married by an *Ambaṣṭha*, the offspring she produces becomes an *Ambaṣṭha* indeed. This should be understood to apply to the case of two *Ambaṣṭhas* as well. (4.19)
But from the reverse order, one is devoid of dharma. 4.25. — 4.20.
H reads: *pratilomāḥ*

The word *tu* (but) serves to indicate a distinction: even among those born from the reverse order (*pratiloma*), such as the *sūta* and others, who are devoid of *dharma*, one born in that interval [the *ambaṣṭha*] is distinguished by being especially so. By the word *dharma*, the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) is to be understood. Thus, the initiation of those born in the natural order (*anuloma*) is established. However, a prohibition regarding Vedic study is to be understood. Why? Because of the observation of other Smṛti texts stating: "For those born in the natural order, there is indeed initiation, but no Vedic study, no five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*), no domestic fire ritual (*aupāsana*), no *agnihotra*, no fuel-offering (*samitkārya*), and no twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*); even the initiation is performed silently (*tūṣṇīm*)," and so forth.

Some do not read the word *ca* (and). For them, the word *ca* must be supplied from the subsequent sūtra, "And in the case of a Śūdra woman" [GDh 4.26], and joined to this sūtra, "Of those born from other castes" [GDh 4.24].
Others explain that this is actually a single sūtra: "Of those born from other castes, but from the reverse order, he is devoid of dharma.
In all cases, the interpretation remains essentially the same. 4.25.

Those born from inverse unions, such as the Sūtas and others, are devoid of dharma; they are devoid of dharma such as the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) and so forth. Among them, in another scripture, the initiation ceremony alone is accepted for the Sūta. (4.20)
And [the same applies] in the case of a Śūdra woman. 4.26 — 4.21.

One born from a Śūdra woman through men of higher castes is likewise excluded from initiation (*upanayana*) and other rites. Among these, initiation is prescribed only for the Savarṇa, Ambaṣṭha, and Niṣāda. Thus, another Smṛti states: "Having initiated a Savarṇa, one should teach him the Veda; having initiated an Ambaṣṭha, the science of medicine; having initiated a Niṣāda, the training in elephant-keeping; for others, there is no initiation. Some explain that one born from a Savarṇa man and an Ambaṣṭha woman should be initiated and taught dancing. The Ugra and others are to be understood by their specific occupations: the Ugra is a slayer of wild beasts and the like; the Dauṣyantha is a fisherman; the Pāraśava is a worshiper of Bhadrakālī; the Sūta is a trainer of horses; the Māgadha is one who follows the trade of commerce; the Āyogava is a weaver of cloth; the Kṣattṛ is a wheelwright (or a charioteer), and he is also a seller of salt; the Vaidehaka is a keeper of goats, and so forth. (4.26)

Even one born from a *śūdra* woman in the direct order (*ānulomya*), such as a *pāraśava*, is devoid of *dharma*. Thus, it is established that those born in the direct order, beginning with those of equal caste (*savarṇa*), are entitled to *dharma*. And so says Manu:
"Six sons—those born of women of their own caste and those born of other castes—possess the *dharma* of the twice-born.
But all those born of *śūdra* women through transgression (*apadhvaṃsa*) are declared to share the *dharma* of *śūdras*. (MDh 10.41) 4.21.
And from a Śūdra woman who is not of equal status, he lives the life of an outcast. || 4.27 ||
H reads "tu" instead of "ca.
The meaning is that one born from a Śūdra woman to a man of a superior caste must be avoided, like an outcaste (patita), in matters such as physical contact or receiving gifts. (4.27)

One born from a Śūdra father and a woman of a different class, such as a Vaiśya or others, is an Āyogava and so forth; he follows the occupation of outcasts and, like an outcast, must be avoided in matters such as being seen, touched, or receiving gifts. Likewise, one born from a Vaiśya father and a Kṣatriya mother, or from a Kṣatriya father and a Brāhmaṇa mother, does not follow the occupation of outcasts. (4.22)
The last [of these] is the most wicked. 4.28 — 4.23.

One born of a Śūdra father and a Brāhmaṇī mother is the most sinful; therefore, he must be avoided at all costs. Accordingly, another Smṛti states: "One should go [beyond] a Caṇḍāla, a cow, or a fly-whisk," and so forth.

In that regard, because the rule for taking a wife applies only to those born in the natural order (*anuloma*), and because those born out of an improper order (*pratiloma*) are unfit for it—even though the injunction "one should take a wife of equal status" (GDh 4.1) prescribes marriage only among those of the same caste—it nevertheless indicates that for one who has already established a lineage, marriage may occur even with women of lower castes in due course. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "A Brāhmaṇa may have three wives according to the sequence of the castes; a Kṣatriya two; and a Vaiśya and a Śūdra each one" (VaDh 1.24). Although it would have been sufficient to say "one born from a woman of the reverse order or a Śūdra is devoid of Dharma," the author of the Sūtra composes a separate rule stating "and from a Śūdra woman" (GDh 4.26); by this, he shows that there is some degree of eligibility even for marrying a Śūdra woman. Consequently, for a lustful man who has already fathered sons with women of higher castes, marriage to a Śūdra woman should be understood as permissible, provided it is performed without the sacred mantras. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "Some [allow] even a Śūdra woman, excluding the mantras" (VaDh 1.25). In this context, the word "even" (*api*) implies censure, and the meaning therein is "for one who has already fathered sons. By the statement "but from the reverse order, one is devoid of Dharma" (GDh 4.25), he shows that a man of lower caste has no right to marry a woman of a higher caste. And so says Vasiṣṭha.

"But whatever [sons] are born from clandestine unions who rely on the qualities of the inverse order, one should recognize them by their actions due to their deviation from virtuous conduct and proper behavior" (VaDh 18.7), and so forth. The meaning therein is that, because they are born from clandestine unions, there is an absence of marriage according to the inverse order. 4.28.

Among those born from a Śūdra of a different class, he who is the last-born—that is, one born of a Brāhmaṇa woman—is a Caṇḍāla; he is the most sinful and must be strictly avoided. And so says another Smṛti: "One should avoid a Caṇḍāla [at a distance] as far as a cow's tail-fan. (4.23)

Having explained the ritual of marriage and the procreation of sons, he now speaks for the purpose of praising marriage. He praises the marriages under discussion: "Virtuous sons purify. (4.29) — [End of] 4.24.
They purify; the meaning is that they protect one from suffering. And so Vyāsa says:
"The word *pud* is a designation for hell, and they know hell to be suffering.
Because he protects (*trāṇa*) from *pud*, therefore they desire a son both in this world and in the next."

The virtuous are born only through lawful marriage; therefore, one should not procreate a son through a paramour, or in a manner contrary to the natural order. Sons must be educated. Why? Because of the Vedic revelation: "Therefore, they say that a son who has been instructed is conducive to the world" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.17). 4.29
Virtuous sons of good conduct, born of us, purify the lineage of their progenitor. 4.24.
In this regard, there is a distinction:
[the lineage] extends three generations beyond the ṛṣi. 4.30–4.25.
The meaning is that one born of a woman wedded by the *ārṣa* rite rescues three generations of ancestors, beginning with the father, from hell. (4.30)
A son born of a woman wedded according to the Ārṣa rite sanctifies three generations; he delivers them from hell. (4.25)
Ten [times] for the gods. 4.31.
Ten from the divine [offering], and ten indeed from the offering to Prajāpati.
One born of the Daiva form of marriage [sanctifies] ten generations of men. || 4.31 ||
In this context, the word *puruṣa*, though forming a compound, is also connected with the word *daśa*. The particle *eva* is intended for the purpose of restriction (*nirdhāraṇa*). 4.26.
From the Prājāpatya penance, it is exactly tenfold.
Lest there be the misconception that [the rule] applies to both cases, the word "also" (*ca*) was not used in the phrase "and from the Prājāpatya"; the word *eva* is for the sake of clarity. 4.32.
A son of Brahmā saves ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself—a son of Brahmā, indeed, a son of Brahmā. (4.33) — (4.27)

H reads: "A son born of the *brāhma* marriage purifies ten descendants; he purifies ten ancestors who have passed away and ten future descendants. By departing from the order of presentation and stating the results out of sequence, it is intended to show that even for the giver of the girl there is an abundance of reward, as the *Jābāla-śruti* states: "He who gives his daughter to a worthy man obtains the fruit of the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice. Likewise, the *Kauṣītaki-brāhmaṇa* also says: "His sons inherit his property; his friends [inherit] his good deeds, and his enemies [his] evil deeds. (4.33)

A daughter wedded by the Brāhma rite is called a Brāhmī; a son born of her purifies ten ancestors—ten preceding generations starting with the father—and ten descendants—starting with the future son—and himself as the twenty-first. Therefore, the Brāhma marriage is most excellent. (4.27)
Now begins the fifth chapter.

The marriage of a wife for the purpose of procreating offspring and for the performance of ritual acts has been described. In that regard, he first states the rule for procreating offspring and introduces the proper time for conception (*garbhādhāna*).
He should approach his wife during her season. 5.1.
The *ṛtu* is the period of sixteen days and nights characterized by the woman’s capacity for conception. Thus says Manu:

"The natural *ṛtu* of women is traditionally held to consist of sixteen nights, together with the other four days which are censured by the virtuous" (MDh 3.46). During that time, he should approach—that is, have intercourse with—his wife, gladdening her and not like a beast, as indicated by the prefix *upa-* in the verb *upeyāt*.

This is not an injunction (*vidhi*), because the matter is already established by natural desire alone. Nor is it a restrictive rule (*niyama*). What, then, is a restrictive rule? A restrictive rule is the restatement of that which is already optionally obtained; it restricts an activity that might otherwise proceed from mere whim. Since both approaching and not approaching one’s wife during her season (*ṛtu*) would otherwise be possible, the rule "one must certainly approach her during her season" serves as a restriction. If this position were accepted, there would be neither an injunction nor a prohibition regarding non-seasonal intercourse (*anṛtau*); thus, activity would simply occur as in the case of *marīca* and similar substances. Nowhere in the Dharmaśāstras is it heard: "One may eat *marīca*, or one may not eat it. Nevertheless, cultured people (*śiṣṭas*) do eat it; likewise, in this case too, activity would simply occur. Consequently, the rule "or everywhere" (GDh 5.2) would become redundant, and there would be no expiation for failing to approach one’s wife.

But surely both cases are accepted; for it is heard that one who acts out of desire falls into hell, as stated: "But where activity proceeds from the perception of pleasure, there the scripture has no authority; he who follows such [impulse] prepares himself for hell. Therefore, the commencement of the rule "or in all cases" (GDh 5.2) is for the purpose of preventing that. Furthermore, in another Smṛti, an expiation is prescribed for non-approach:
"He who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses and is present near him, is joined with the terrible sin of foeticide; of this there is no doubt. (BDh 4.1.18).

This is not so. First, regarding the passage beginning with, “But where there is activity due to the perception of pleasure,” this is its meaning: in whatever performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) there is activity due to the perception of pleasure—that is, activity out of a desire for that pleasure after knowing the fruit—it means activity with an intention toward a result (*phalābhisaṃdhi*). In such activity, scripture does not exist; the meaning is that it does not bear fruit at all. One who follows that, performing the performance with an intention toward a result, prepares for hell—he goes to hell. This statement is intended to ensure the performance of twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and other such rites by abandoning the intention toward a result. And thus the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva said: “Do not let the fruit of action be your motive” (BhG 2.47), and so forth. If there were a prohibition of activity based on pleasure in every case, then scripture would have to be prescribed even for Marīci and others, because without scripture there would be a fall into hell. Therefore, even the rule “or in all cases” (GDh 5.2) need not be stated for the sake of being favored by scripture. Furthermore, as for what was said, “But he who [approaches] his wife who has bathed after her menses” (BDh 4.1.18), etc., that too is a statement for the purpose of the husband seeing himself in his wife who has bathed after her menses. Why? Because of the observation of the Jābāli-Śruti. Thus it is heard: “A wife who has bathed after her menses gives birth to a son like the one whom she first sees. Therefore, the husband himself should first show himself in her presence. Consequently, since there is no penance for approaching her, the absence of fault follows as a matter of necessity (*niyamena*). For those whose position is that a restatement of what is already established constitutes a restrictive rule (*niyama*), even the suspicion of a restrictive rule is not applicable here, because there is no prior establishment of approaching only during the fertile period (*ṛtu*); rather, activity occurs everywhere according to one’s own will.

Therefore, this Sūtra is for the purpose of restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*). What is this restrictive enumeration? It is a statement made when there is a possibility of application both in that case and elsewhere. Since activity occurs according to one's desire, there is a possibility of approaching [one’s wife] both during the fertile period (*ṛtu*) and outside of it; thus, the meaning is that one must engage only during the fertile period. If it is argued that this too is redundant because of the commencement of the rule "or at all times" (*sarvatra vā*), we say no, because it serves the purpose of establishing a regulated option (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*). The regulation should be seen as follows: if the activity is solely for the sake of obtaining a son, then one should approach only during the fertile period. But if it is for the sake of pleasure (*rati*), then "or at all times. If it is argued that the taking of a wife is for the purpose of procreating a son and fulfilling the duty enjoined by the Vedic texts on the three debts (*ṛṇatraya*), and not for the sake of pleasure, we say no, because another Smṛti states: "A woman has pleasure and sons as her fruits" (*ratiputraphalā nārī*). Furthermore, the view of Vasiṣṭha is seen: "That pleasure which exists without transgression is based on Dharma" (*yā syād anaticāreṇa ratiḥ sā dharmasaṃśritā*); the view of Auśanasa is seen: "One should be content with one's own wife"; and the Vājasaneya Śruti is seen: "Even women about to give birth should lie down with their husbands. Moreover, another Smṛti is seen: "The dispassionate man should become a mendicant (*bhikṣu*); the other should enter the householder stage."

"However, for those who proceed out of desire, these [following options] would be inferior in sequence," according to the teaching of Manu (MDh 3.12). Furthermore, because the Vedic injunction regarding the three debts (*ṛṇatraya*) teaches celibacy (*brahmacarya*) even outside the fertile period (*anṛtu*), this supports the view that the teacher’s instruction is optional. For if the view were one of mandatory combination (*samuccaya*), the phrase "by means of sacrifice and progeny" would be logically applicable as a mere illustration; thus, there would be no contradiction with the Smṛti concerning the injunction for the householder stage (*gārhasthya*). Therefore, for one whose passion has not yet subsided, taking a wife even for the sake of sexual pleasure is indeed required. Consequently, if both husband and wife become dispassionate, and their approach is solely for the sake of a son, then they should approach only during the fertile period. But for those who are still passionate, the rule "or at all times" is appropriate. If it is argued that, in that case, there would follow the absence of fault for one who does not approach during the fertile period, and that this constitutes a fault—[we reply: no, for we also desire precisely the absence of fault. If it is further argued that, even so, one who seeks a son and approaches outside the fertile period incurs a penance, and that this constitutes a fault—[we reply: no, because that very [penance] results from the exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*). Even for those who hold that a restatement of what is already established by scripture is an exclusion, this is consistent. For example: "One who has fathered a son should establish the sacred fires," and based on the Vedic text "One is born burdened with three debts," and the Smṛti text "Virtuous sons purify," since approaching only during the fertile period follows from the capacity for conception for the purpose of producing a son, this restatement—"for one who has not yet fathered a son"—is understood to be intended to prohibit approaching at non-fertile times. Therefore, this is indeed an exclusion: "if he should approach, only during the fertile period."
Now, one might object: "If the journey is for the sake of obtaining a son, then it would not apply to one who already has a son.
It is replied: because having many sons is desired. As Śaṅkha says:
"For one who is established in sons and grandsons, who has many offspring, and who is living..."
And so on. Likewise, the Śruti says: "Place ten sons in her; make the husband the eleventh. Therefore, it is established that this Sūtra is for the purpose of exclusion (parisaṃkhyā). 5.1.

The period of sixteen days and nights beginning from the appearance of the menses is the *ṛtu* (fertile season) for women, the time for conception; during that time, one should approach one's wife. Regarding this, there is a specific rule in the *Āpastamba-smṛti*: "They teach that approaching one's wife during the *ṛtu* should be done on even nights starting from the fourth night up to the sixteenth, for the sake of the excellence of progeny. But according to the *Mānava-smṛti*: "The natural *ṛtu* of women is recorded as sixteen nights, together with those four days which are censured by the virtuous."
Of these, the first four are censurable, as is the eleventh; the thirteenth also is censurable, while the remaining ten nights are commended.
[The nights of] the new moon, the eighth, the full moon, and the fourteenth—

"A twice-born man who has taken the ceremonial bath (*snātaka*) should always remain a celibate student (*brahmacārī*), even during the fertile period (*ṛtu*). Thus says Manu (MDh 4.128). Yājñavalkya, however, states:
"Approaching his wife in this manner, he should avoid her when she is emaciated, and should avoid the *maghā* and *mūla* constellations" (YDh 1.80).

"Boys are born on even nights, and girls on uneven nights" (MDh 3.48). Thus, among the sixteen nights, the first three must be avoided by all means. By approaching his wife on the remaining nights—abandoning the prohibitions enjoined in all the *smṛtis*—he begets an excellent son. Conversely, by failing to approach her during her season out of hatred or other such motives, he incurs sin. And so Devala says: "He who, being healthy, does not approach his own wife when she has bathed after her menses..."
"He incurs the sin of killing an embryo by destroying a fetus that has been conceived. And another Smṛti states:
"If a man does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses and is present before him, his ancestors lie within her menstrual flow for that entire month."

But this [duty], although it is obtained through passion (*rāga*), becomes twofold because of the scriptural injunction regarding transgression (*pratyavāya*) for its non-performance. Furthermore, according to the opinion of some, it is also a restrictive rule (*niyama*), as in: "One should approach [one's wife] only during her season (*ṛtu*). (5.1)
But the Teacher establishes an enumeration as well:
"Or everywhere, with the exception of what is forbidden. (5.2)
Festivals and other such occasions are prohibited. As Manu has said:

"A twice-born *snātaka* should always remain celibate on the new moon day, the eighth, the full moon, and the fourteenth, even during the fertile period (*ṛtu*). [MDh 4.128] The word "or" (*vā*) signifies a restricted option (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*).

Others, however, explain: "By the rule 'one should approach her during the season' (GDh 5.1), approaching once specifically during the season is enjoined; by the rule 'or at all times,' approaching once at any time is enjoined. This is incorrect, because we observe the Vedic text: "One should approach her during the season twice or once, or at will outside the season" (ŚB 12.4.1.10). 5.2.

"One may approach [one's wife] at all times—both during the fertile period (*ṛtu*) and outside of it—avoiding the forbidden days; or one may act according to one's desire, keeping in mind the boon granted to women. And the boon is: "May we unite at will until the birth [of a child]. Furthermore, even though one has conquered the senses, it is recorded in the Smṛti: "One's lawful wife must always be protected," and "Guard this lineage with vigilance; let not the seeds of others be sown in your field" (VaDh 17.9). 5.2.
Now follow the five great sacrifices:
he who honors the gods, the ancestors, humans, sages, and elemental spirits. || 5.3 ||

These are the five great sacrifices (*pañca mahāyajñāḥ*). Among them, by the term "worshiper of the gods" (*devapūjaka*), the *vaiśvadeva* offering is meant. By "worshiper of the ancestors" (*pitṛpūjaka*), it is meant that one should daily feed a Brahmin for the sake of the ancestors. Thus says Manu: "One should feed even a single Brahmin for the sake of the ancestors during the fivefold sacrifice; however, one should not feed anyone at all for the sake of the *vaiśvadeva*. [MDh 3.83] In the absence of food, one should give milk; in its absence, roots; in its absence, fruit; and if nothing is available, water. Thus says Manu:
One should offer the śrāddha daily with food, or even with water.

"Or even by means of water, roots, and fruits, he brings satisfaction to the ancestors. (MDh 3.82). In that regard as well, it should be understood that "water" is prescribed when all other things are unavailable. Regarding the phrase "one who honors men," this refers to the honoring of guests. Even there, in the absence of food, one should offer grass for a seat; in its absence, ground for lying down; fire for warding off the cold; water for removing mud; and sweet speech. As Vasiṣṭha says: "Grass, ground, fire, water, kind words, truthfulness, and freedom from envy—these are never lacking in the houses of the virtuous" (VaDh 13.61). He himself will also speak of the honoring of guests later on; what was stated by Vasiṣṭha should be seen as a supplement to that. Regarding "one who honors beings," this refers to the offering of *bali* oblations to the deities of the quarters following the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice. Regarding "one who honors the sages," this refers to the daily recitation of the Vedas (*nitya-svādhyāya*). Their mention prior to the taking up of the sacred fires (*agni-parigrahaṇa*) is for the purpose of ensuring their performance even by one who does not maintain the sacred fires, using a common (*laukika*) fire. Consequently, this should be understood to apply to a Śūdra as well, even in the case of the *pākayajña* sacrifices, using a common fire; the same applies to the *avakīrṇi-homa*. (5.3)

In this context, the word *pūjaka* (worshipper) is connected to each member of the compound beginning with "gods. According to the grammatical rule that "the final member of a *dvandva* compound is heard as being connected to each preceding member," a householder should be a constant worshipper of the gods and the others. Therein, the worship of the gods consists of the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, the *sakala-homa*, and other fire-rituals (*agnikārya*). Regarding the worship of the ancestors, Manu says:
"One should feed even a single Brahmin for the sake of the ancestors during the *pañcayajña*;
however, one should not feed any twice-born person there for the sake of the *vaiśvadeva*. (MDh 3.83)

"And: 'Day after day he should offer the *śrāddha* to the ancestors with food and drink, or even with milk, roots, and fruits, bringing them satisfaction' (MDh 3.82). Worship of humans is the worship of guests; worship of beings is the offering of oblations (*bali*); worship of the *ṛṣis* is the *brahmayajña*; "the sacrifice to the *ṛṣis*" and "*brahmayajña*" are synonyms. (5.3)
And these [duties] are being explained; here, the sequence is not intended to be significant. But as for the *brahmayajña*, it is the daily private recitation (*nityasvādhyāya*). 5.4.

The "constant study" (*nityasvādhyāya*) is designated as the *brahmayajña*. It was already mentioned previously by the term "worshipper of the sages" (*ṛṣipūjaka*); even when one is unable to perform the other [five] sacrifices, this [brahmayajña] must be performed constantly, though perhaps deficient in its details. While it could have been called the "sage-sacrifice" (*ṛṣiyajña*) according to the manner previously stated, it is expressed in this way for the purpose of incorporating the injunction found in another *smṛti*. Thus Uśanas says: "Now, in the *brahmayajña*, sitting upon *darbha* grass, holding *darbha* blades, facing either east or north, one should recite a portion of the Vedas preceded by the *praṇava*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *sāvitrī*; or the beginning of the Vedas; or one verse from the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, or *Sāman* Vedas three times; or the *praṇava*; or a verse from the *Itihāsas*—all with a concentrated mind," and so forth.

This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Its specific procedure is set forth in the *Taittirīyaka*, beginning with the words "about to perform the *brahmayajña*. Here, by the use of the word "regularly" (*nitya*), it is shown that one should study whenever opportunity permits, even at times other than those dedicated specifically to the *brahmayajña*. 5.4.
The sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña), however, consists of the offering of water to the ancestors. 5.5.
And the offering of water to the ancestors, as well as other [rites], according to one's ability. (5.5)

By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), [the offering is extended] to the deities and the sages (*ṛṣis*). Although the term "water" (*udaka*) was sufficient, the inclusion of the word "giving" (*dāna*) is for the purpose of making known that this is preceded by the *tarpaṇa* (libation). Thus, another *smṛti* states:

"Having satiated the deities and the sages with a concentrated mind, one should afterwards give to the ancestors, preceded by the utterance of *svadhā* and accompanied by sesame seeds. By the very injunction to give water daily to the ancestors, daily bathing is also established by implication, since the giving of water is preceded by that [bathing]. And so says Manu:

"Having bathed daily and being pure, one should perform the libations for the gods, sages, and ancestors. [MDh 2.176] The offering of water is of two kinds: that which is offered into the water and that which is offered into the air. Now, an objection is raised: it is prescribed that the offering should be made on the ground alone, not in the water, as Bhṛgu has said:
"Neither in water, nor in vessels, nor when angry, nor with only one hand..."
"That water does not reach [the ancestors] which is not offered upon the ground. Likewise, Bṛhaspati also says:
"One should never offer water for the ancestors while standing in water;
rather, having stepped out onto a clean spot, one should perform the libation of water (udakatarpaṇa)."
This is not so, because it contradicts other Smṛtis and because it explains the distinction between their respective domains. As Uśanas says:
"All the hosts of gods are water, and the hosts of ancestors are remembered as water;
therefore, water should be given in water, for what is given to the ancestors becomes inexhaustible. Regarding this, Kātyāyana states the distinction between their domains:
"One should offer a handful of water (*jalāñjali*) to the gods and the ancestors in the water;

one should offer a handful of water to those who have died without the funeral rites (*asaṃskṛta-pramīta*) on dry land. Thus it is said. The offering of water beginning with the *tarpaṇa* and ending with the pouring of water should be performed with both hands. Regarding the mere pouring of water, there is no fault, because of the specific mention of "a handful of water" (*jalāñjali*). However, in the case of the *tarpaṇa*, this is not appropriate, because one hears a contradictory statement: "not with a single hand. And so says Bhṛgu: "A twice-born man performing the *tarpaṇa* with water using both hands..."
"That fool goes to the Kālasūtra hell with his head hanging downwards.
This is not a fault, because of the hearing of the statement regarding the division [of the water]. Thus Bṛhaspati said:
"If it is the time for pouring at a Śrāddha, one should cause [the water] to be given with a single hand."

"In the libation (tarpaṇa), however, one should perform both; this is the eternal law. Therefore, one [libation] is prescribed in water alone, while that which is prescribed in the air is the other. As Bhṛgu said:
"Standing in water reaching up to the navel, with mind directed upwards and reflecting, [one should say]:
'May my ancestors come; may they accept this handful of water.'"
The wise man, remaining silent and facing south, should cast water three times each into the air with joined palms, raising them higher and higher as he speaks the words aloud again and again.
"Space is the abode of the ancestors, as is the southern direction;

therefore, whatever is given there in that manner shall be inexhaustible for the ancestors. Whatever is offered to the ancestors should be understood to be accompanied by sesame seeds and *darbha* grass, as Bhṛgu has said:
"Water joined with sesame seeds and *darbha* grass, when offered with the *svadhā* exclamation..."
"all that shall become nectar and be inexhaustible for the ancestors. Therefore, the offering of water to the ancestors must be performed. 5.5.

One should always offer water to the ancestors; other items such as food, fruits, and roots should be offered according to one’s enthusiasm and capacity. Here, by the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it is indicated that the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for the gods and the sages must also be performed regularly. Regarding this, Manu, speaking of the religious student (*brahmacārin*), says:

"Having bathed daily and being pure, he should perform the libation for the gods, the sages, and the ancestors. [MDh 2.176] Kātyāyana states: "One should offer handfuls of water in the water for the deities and the ancestors."
"One should offer handfuls of water on the ground for those who have died in the unconditioned state. Thus says Bhṛgu:
"Neither in water, nor in vessels, nor when angry, nor with only one hand [should one offer]."
That water does not reach [the ancestors] which is not offered upon the ground.
Uśanas says:
"The waters are all the hosts of gods; the waters are remembered as the hosts of ancestors.
Therefore, water should be offered into the waters; what is given to the ancestors becomes inexhaustible. Bhṛgu states another method:
Standing in water reaching to his navel, with his mind directed upwards and reflecting, [he says]:
"May my ancestors come; may they accept this handful of water."
"Three times each, the wise man, with speech restrained and facing south, should cast water upward while looking toward the sky, saying it again and again at higher and higher elevations. (5.5)
The rest according to one's enthusiasm. 5.6.

Whatever remains of the duties of a householder other than the *brahmayajña* and the giving of water, he should perform that according to his ability, because of the statement regarding enthusiasm (*utsāha*). Consequently, when the primary means are unavailable, the duty must still be performed by means of secondary ones; as has been cited: "Or even with milk, roots, and fruits" (MDh 3.82), and so forth. 5.6.
Since the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) is the foundation of the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*), he first states the time for the formal adoption of the sacred fires:
"The fire is either that of the wife or that of the inheritance. (5.7) — (5.6)
By the word *bhāryā* (wife), marriage is understood; by the word *agni* (fire), the *aupāsana* fire. The meaning is that one should maintain the nuptial fire in the form of the *aupāsana*.

Some explain it thus: this is a designation for the very fire of birth (*jātakāgni*), which has been handed down through tradition, for the purpose of maintaining it in the form of the *aupāsana* after the time of marriage.

That is incorrect, because of the *Gṛhya-smṛti* which states: "Performing the marriage, having established the worldly fire (*laukika-agni*). If the fire of birth (*jātakāgni*) itself were to come [into the house], then one would not employ the term "worldly" in that context. Consequently, due to its impurity, the fire of birth must indeed be abandoned. Alternatively, one may take possession of the fire at the time of partition with one's brothers or father; even after the marriage, there is an option depending on one's wealth, since rituals are accomplished through material resources. For he who possesses wealth should take possession of it at the time of marriage, while he who is destitute should do so at the time of inheritance.

Some explain that one may take possession of the inheritance and the sacred fire even before marriage; however, that is incorrect, because another Smṛti states: "A man who has lost his wife and marries again should take the fire again, since there is no fire for one who lacks a wife. How is it understood that this refers only to the maintenance of the Smārta fire and not the Śrauta fire? Because of the Vedic injunction, "One who has fathered a son should establish the fires," and because the plural form "fires" (*agnīn*) is used therein. (5.7)

By the word "wife" (*bhāryā*), marriage is indicated. One should tend the sacred fire (*agni*) beginning from the day on which the wife is led to that fire, or beginning from the day on which the partition of the inheritance is made by the father, brothers, or others; this service begins in the evening. There is no transgression for one who, prior to the partition of the inheritance, lives off the ritual work of his father or eldest brother. (5.6)
In that [fire], the domestic rites are performed. 5.8.
In that [fire], the domestic rites are performed. 5.7.

One should perform the domestic rites, such as the *puṃsavana* and others, in that very same *aupāsana* fire. This applies to the case where [the fire] has been formally taken; if it has not been taken, they are to be understood as being performed in the ordinary (*laukika*) fire. 5.8.
When the domestic fire has been thus consecrated, the rites pertaining to human beings, such as the *puṃsavana* and others, are to be performed. 5.7.
The sacrifices to the gods, the ancestors, and humans, as well as the private recitation of the Veda. 5.9.
The sacrifices to the gods, the ancestors, and humans, as well as the private recitation of scripture and the offering of oblations. 5.8.

The *devayajña* is the *vaiśvadeva* offering. The feeding of Brahmins for the sake of the ancestors is the *pitṛyajña*. The *manuṣyayajña* is the honoring of guests. Regarding these, while connection with the sacred fire (*agni*) is well-established for the *vaiśvadeva*, for the *pitṛyajña* it consists of the cooking intended for their feeding, and for the *manuṣyayajña* it consists of the cooking intended for the feeding of guests; the *brahmayajña* is expressed by the term *svādhyāya* (Vedic study). According to the opinion of some, its connection with the fire is also established; thus there is a compound [of all five]. Thus Uśanas says, beginning with "Now the *brahmayajña* near water," and after describing the *brahmayajña*, stating: "Near the fire, according to some. If it is argued that this is already established because these are rites prescribed in the *Gṛhyasūtras*, we say no, because the repetition is for the purpose of removing a doubt. What is the doubt? It might be that since the *devayajña* and the others were previously prescribed in the worldly fire (*laukika-agni*), they belong only to that, not to the *aupāsana* (domestic) fire. Furthermore, by the rule "In that [fire], the *gṛhya* rites [are performed]" [GDh 5.8], someone might suspect that only those *gṛhya* rites excluded from those [five] are meant, because those were previously mentioned separately. Thus, they have competence in both fires. Consequently, there is no fault even if the fire is used in the worldly fire. And so says the *sūtra* of Bādarāyaṇa: "Even for one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), the five sacrifices are prohibited from the worldly fire by this specific statement. (5.9)

The word "in that" (tasmin) is understood to carry over from the previous context. In that regard, the connection of the *devayajña* with fire is well known. As for the sacrifices to the ancestors (*pitṛ*), humans (*manuṣya*), and beings (*bhūta*), however, food for their sake is cooked in this domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*). Regarding the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*), its connection with fire has been shown by Uśanas as an alternative: "Some say [it should be performed] near the fire. Since the performance of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) is prescribed even for one who does not maintain a consecrated fire, these [sacrifices] should be performed in the common worldly fire (*laukikāgni*). 5.8.
The rite for the return [of the deceased]. 5.10.

By this, the *bhūtayajña* (sacrifice to beings) is declared. Its explicit mention is for the purpose of removing any doubt [regarding its necessity]. The word "and" (*ca*) is carried over from the preceding sūtra; its purpose is to draw that [preceding rule] into this one, meaning that it must be performed immediately after the *vaiśvadeva* and not as a separate act. For this reason, it is treated separately again. Thus says the author of the *Gṛhya-sūtra*: "Having first offered to the gods, he should afterwards offer the *bali*. While it could have been stated simply as "the *bhūtayajña* is as before," the present formulation is intended to indicate that the sacrificial material (*havis*) is distinct from that of the *vaiśvadeva*. Consequently, one should take a portion of the prepared food for the sake of both the *vaiśvadeva* and the *bhūtayajña*. Accordingly, Jaimini states: "Having increased the *bali* of the food. The dual number indicates that it is to be performed both evening and morning. The inclusion of the term "rite" (*karman*) implies that the *vaiśvadeva* itself is also to be performed both evening and morning. Thus says the *Gṛhya-smṛti*: "The *vaiśvadeva* and the offering of the *bali* are to be performed evening and morning," and "Then, evening and morning, he should sacrifice of the prepared sacrificial food," and so forth. (5.10)
Now he states the Vaiśvadeva offering for the sake of including even those for whom no *gṛhyakāra* (author of domestic ritual manuals) has been mentioned;
he now states the procedure for the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*) and the Vaiśvadeva:
"Agni in Agni, Dhanvantari, the Viśvedevas, Prajāpati, and Sviṣṭakṛt"—these are the oblations. 5.11 — 5.9.

Although fire is already implied by the mention of *homa* (offering), the phrase "in a well-kindled fire" is stated again for the purpose of specifying the fire used for the offering. The plural form "offerings" (*homāḥ*) is intended to exclude the notion that there is only a single oblation. The mention of *homa* serves to indicate the utterance of *svāhā*. The particle *iti* is for the purpose of including the dative case. The separation of the compound is for the sake of establishing the presence of other mantras. Thus: *agnaye svāhā*, *dhanvantaraye svāhā*, *viśvebhyo devebhyaḥ svāhā*, *prajāpataye svāhā*. The term *sviṣṭakṛt* should be understood as having *agni* as its prefix and ending in the dative case: *agnaye sviṣṭakṛte svāhā*. This much constitutes the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice. 5.11.

In this context, because of the traditional teaching of Āpastamba that “those injunctions involving the *juhoti* [offering] have the utterance of *svāhā* as their primary element,” the word *homa* (oblation) refers here to the utterance of *svāhā*. One should offer [the oblation] into the fire with [mantras] beginning with *agnaye* and ending with *svāhā*. Furthermore, the term *Sviṣṭakṛt* should be understood as having *agni-* as its prefix (*agnisviṣṭakṛt*). Since the fire is already established by the very fact that it is a *homa*, the explicit mention of “into the fire” (*agnau*) is for the purpose of stating that it must not be performed on the ground, as is the case with the *bali* offerings. Therefore, the ritual characteristic of the *homa*, namely the utterance of *svāhā*, also applies to the *bali* offerings. Thus says Āśvalāyana: “Then, ‘*svāhā*’—this is the *bali* offering. For the followers of Āpastamba, the mantras are indeed recited ending with *svāhā*. (5.9)
Now he states the rule for the sacrifice to beings (*bhūtayajña*);
then he describes the offering of the *bali* to beings:
"And to the deities of the directions, each according to their own [quarter]. (5.12)—(5.10)

One should offer the *bali* to the deities of the directions in the east: to Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Soma, and Īśāna, proceeding clockwise from the east; to Viṣṇu above; and then to Ananta. The mantra to be used here is "Obeisance to Indra" (*indrāya namaḥ*). Because of the word "and" (*ca*), one should also include [offerings] to their attendants (*tatpuruṣa*); thus, "Obeisance to the attendants of Indra" (*indrasya puruṣebhyo namaḥ*) and so forth should be understood. The meaning is: according to each [deity], in their respective places. (5.12)

The offering (bali) for each deity should be presented in the direction assigned to that deity. Starting from the east and proceeding clockwise up to the northeast, one should perform the rite with the formula "Svāhā to Indra," and so on. || 5.10 ||
To the Maruts at the doors. || 5.13 ||
To the great ones at the doors. 5.11.

Because of the plural number, [the formula] is to be understood as "Obeisance to the Maruts" (marudbhyo namaḥ) in all cases. In this instance, there is no injunction for a *tatpuruṣa* compound, due to the absence of the particle *ca*. 5.13.
In as many doors as there are in the house, one should offer oblations with the formula, "Svāhā to the great ones."
Having entered for the sake of the household deities. || 5.14 || — || 5.12 ||

Because of the word "having entered," it should first be observed outside the house. Therefore, having made a mandala with cow dung in one place outside the house and offered the *bali* to the deities of the directions, and then having offered the *bali* at the outer and inner doors, one should enter the interior itself and offer the *bali* to the household deities (*gṛhadevatā*). These are Śrī and the others, as Uśanas says: "One should give [the offering] saying 'Salutation to Śrī' in the place of the head of the bed; saying 'Salutation to Bhadrakālī' in the place of the feet; saying 'Salutation to Dhanapati' in the storehouse; saying 'Salutation to Rudra' in the dwelling of the pillar; saying 'Salutation to Mitra' in the cow-pen; saying 'Salutation to Varuṇa' for the mortar and pestle; saying 'Salutation to Ahi Budhnya' for the well; and for the grinding stone and near the fire, one should give [the offering] saying 'Salutation to these deities. (5.14)

Having entered [the house], one should offer the bali-oblation to the household deities with the formula "svāhā. Because of the word "having entered," this must not be performed by one standing outside the door.
To Brahmā, in the center. || 5.15 || — || 5.13 ||
In the middle of the house, one should offer [the portion] with the words, "Salutation to Brahmā. || 5.15 ||

In the middle of the house, an offering (bali) should be presented with the formula "To Brahmā, svāhā. By the word "and" (ca), it is indicated that offerings should also be presented immediately after the one to Brahmā to the deities mentioned by the author of the Sūtra—namely, Earth, Wind, Prajāpati, and the Viśvedevas—as well as to the deities of the directions. 5.13.
From water, into a water-pot. || 5.16 ||
One should offer [water] into the water-pot with the words, "Adoration to the waters. || 5.16 ||
"To space" [he offers] in the intermediate region. || 5.17 ||
Saying "To Ākāśa," an offering should be thrown into the intermediate space.

One should offer [the oblation] to space with the words "Obeisance to Ākāśa" in the open courtyard of the intermediate region. The word *iti* indicates the manner [of the formula]. Consequently, it should be understood that one offers to Death with the words "Obeisance to Mṛtyu" in the kitchen, and to Aja Ekapād with the words "Obeisance to Ajaikapada" upon the threshing floors. 5.17.
And one should cast the bali offering into the air for all the gods, as well as for the spirits that roam by day and those that roam by night; thus says Manu (3.90). 5.14.
And in the evening, [one should offer] to the night-walkers. 5.18–5.15.

If it is evening, after the offering of fruit-slices, he should offer [the remainder] into the air with the words, "Obeisance to the night-walkers. The word "and" (ca) serves to include the previous [offering]; otherwise, it would apply to the night-walkers alone. 5.18.

In the evening bali-offering, this is the distinction: the bali should be offered with the words, "Svāhā to the night-walkers. Because of the word "and," it is also for those previously mentioned. (5.15)
Having recited the blessing of "Svasti," the giving of alms is not preceded by [other formalities]. 5.19 — 5.16.

Having caused the mendicant to say "Svasti," he should then give him almsfood preceded by the offering of water. Since a woman has the authority over the giving of alms and it is she who is requested [for it], the householder should therefore have her perform that very act. Some explain that because this rule is prescribed immediately after the Vaiśvadeva rite, it applies only to the first alms received and not to ordinary alms; according to their view, it should be understood that the recitation of the "Svasti" formula must be performed by a man alone. (5.19)

After the offering of the *bali*, the giving of alms (*bhikṣādāna*) should be performed. Having uttered the words of benediction, "May there be well-being," one should first give water into the hand of the mendicant. There is a specific rule regarding the wandering ascetic (*parivrājaka*):
having given water into the hand of the ascetic (*yati*), one gives the alms, and then water again.

"Alms should be as vast as a mountain, and that water [offered] like the ocean. This giving of alms, in the absence of honoring a guest, shall constitute the sacrifice to humans (*manuṣyayajña*). These five great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*), excluding the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*), must be performed both evening and morning. Why? Because of the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Āśvalāyana: "Then, in the evening and morning, one should offer oblations of prepared sacrificial food (*haviṣya*)," and because of the statement in the *Kātyāyana-sūtra*: "It is said that [the sacrifice] is for beings (*bhūta*) in the evening and morning," and so forth. (5.16)
And likewise regarding righteous acts of giving. 5.20 — 5.17.

By the word *dadāti* (gives), the giving of gold and so forth is meant. Because of the inclusion of the term *dharmya* (righteous/legal), the giving to friends and others for a visible worldly purpose is not intended. In this very manner, one should give preceded by water. Although the sense is already established by the word *ca* (and), the word *evam* (in this manner) is used for the purpose of ensuring that the entire [procedure] applies. Consequently, just as the gift of alms performed by a woman is valid when done with the husband’s permission, so too is the gift of gold and other such things valid. And thus says Nārada: "They say that transactions performed by a woman are invalid in times of non-distress; especially so are the gifts of houses, fields, and religious duties, not their sales."
"These very means of proof [are valid] if the husband permits," and so forth. Even the giving of alms must not be performed without the husband's permission. Likewise, Manu states:
"By a girl, a young woman, or even an aged woman, nothing whatsoever should be done independently, even within the home. (MDh 5.147) || 5.20 ||
Regarding those who give gifts—those gifts which are righteous and not motivated by fear or other such causes—in them there is likewise "unprecedented giving" (appūrvadāna). 5.17.
In connection with the topic of giving, he states the distinction of the fruits:
"The fruits [of giving] to non-Brahmins, Brahmins, learned Śrotriyas, and those who have mastered the Vedas are respectively equal, double, a thousandfold, and infinite. (5.21)

The fruits for those who are not Brahmins, for Brahmins, for learned Vedic scholars, and for those who have mastered the Vedas, increase respectively by two thousandfold, ten thousandfold, a hundred thousandfold, and infinitely. || 5.18 ||

This undertaking is for the purpose of demonstrating that the excellence of the fruit depends upon the excellence of the recipient. "Equal" means yielding only a slight fruit; this refers to gold and the like, or alms-food (*bhikṣā*), given to one who is not a Brāhmaṇa. By the word "non-Brāhmaṇa," one who has merely undergone the initiation (*upanayana*) is meant. Thus Uśanas says: "He by whom the Vedas have not been studied and whose vows have not been observed—he is indeed a non-Brāhmaṇa. It was a Brāhmaṇa himself who employed the term "non-Brāhmaṇa" [in this context]. "Twofold is the gift given to a Brāhmaṇa. By the word "Brāhmaṇa," one who has performed the Vedic vows but has not yet studied the Vedas is meant. As Vasiṣṭha says:
That which is a wooden elephant and that which is a leather deer;

"And the Brahmin who has not studied [the Veda]—these three are merely bearers of the name. (VaDh 3.11) A gift given to a *śrotriya* becomes a thousandfold. By the word *śrotriya*, one who studies a single recension (*śākhā*) is meant. As Baudhāyana says: "Having studied one recension, one becomes a *śrotriya*" (ĀpDh 2.6.4). An infinite reward accrues from what is given to one who has mastered the Veda (*vedapāraga*). By the word *vedapāraga*, one who studies the Veda along with its auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga*) is meant. As Kaṇva says: "He by whom the Veda together with its auxiliaries has been studied becomes a *vedapāraga*. Since the rewards for these have been stated previously, it should be understood that the same applies even based on specific castes (*jāti*). As Prajāpati says:
A gift given to a Śūdra yields an equal reward; to a Vaiśya, it becomes twofold;
they say it is threefold for a Kṣatriya, and it becomes immeasurable when given to a Brāhmaṇa.
Thus [ends verse] 5.21.

A non-Brāhmaṇa is one of the Kṣatriya or other castes; a Brāhmaṇa is one who possesses the mere caste. A *śrotriya* is one who has studied the Veda. One who has studied the Veda along with its auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), its ritual manuals (*kalpa*), and its secret doctrines (*rahasya*) is a master of the Veda (*vedapāraga*).
