A gift given to these [recipients], in their respective order, yields fruit that is equal, double, a thousandfold, and infinite. Thus says Manu: “A gift to a non-Brāhmaṇa yields an equal reward; to one who merely calls himself a Brāhmaṇa, it is double; to a *śrotriya*, it is a hundred-thousandfold; and to a master of the Veda, it is infinite. (MDh 7.85) || 5.18 ||
Having thus explained the fruit of giving with respect to its specific results, he now, in connection with that topic, describes another mode of giving;
and as an extension of the discussion on giving, he describes the domain where something must necessarily be given, and the transgression incurred by failing to give it.

Outside the sacrificial altar, one should share wealth with those who seek it for the sake of their teacher, for a marriage, for medicine, for the maintenance of their livelihood, those who are impoverished, those about to perform a sacrifice, those engaged in Vedic study, those on a journey, and those who have won a universal contest. 5.22. — 5.19.

The mention of the "guru" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for one's mother, father, and dependents. As Manu has said: "One who seeks offspring, one who intends to perform a sacrifice, a traveler, and one who has given away all his wealth..."

“For the sake of the teacher, for the sake of parents or servants, or for one distressed by the pursuit of sacred study” (MDh 11.1), and so forth; as well as “for the sake of marriage. Even after begging in this manner, the marriage must be performed. This should also be understood as applying to the view that these items are to be taken collectively. Regarding the mention of "wealth" (*artha*) when the context was already the taking of wealth for medicinal purposes, the repetition of the word "wealth" is intended to indicate the relative gravity or lightness of the wealth according to the specific knowledge [of the recipient], or rather, to indicate that it should be given only to those who are destitute. As Manu has said:

“Gifts should be given to these indigent persons according to their specific knowledge,” and so forth. One whose means of livelihood are exhausted is one in distress (*āpanna*). The phrase “one who intends to sacrifice” (*yakṣyamāṇaḥ*) refers here to the obligatory (*nitya*) sacrifice; therefore, other Smṛti passages such as, “He is fit for Soma, not one who has not sacrificed with Soma; he is worthy to drink the Soma,” are to be understood as referring to optional (*kāmya*) sacrifices. Even when begging, one may be considered “intending to sacrifice” for the sake of the obligatory sacrifice. “For the sake of study” means for the purpose of Vedic study. “One engaged on a journey” (*adhvasaṃyogaḥ*) means one who is traveling on a road; the inclusion of the word *saṃyoga* (connection) implies that this also includes one who is exhausted and needs food for the journey. “The performer of the Viśvajit” is one by whom the Viśvajit sacrifice has been performed. A distribution (*saṃvibhāga*) must be made to these from gold and other wealth, because of the mention of “substance” (*dravya*). It must be done as a rule (*niyamena*), because of the use of the prefix *sam-*. Since begging is prohibited for the performer of the Viśvajit for up to a year, the gift should be given even to one who does not ask. One may give to others whether they ask or do not ask. Furthermore, the distribution of wealth should be made in such a way that no hardship arises for one’s own family, because of the use of the prefix *vy-*. Consequently, the meaning is that only a portion should be given. Because of the mention of “outside the sacrificial altar” (*bahirvedi*), it follows that outside the altar, gifts may be given to others as well. And since this is a mandatory duty, for one who fails to perform it, there is not merely a lack of reward; rather, there is sin (*pratyavāya*). If it is argued that even for one who performs it, the only purpose is the avoidance of that sin and not the attainment of a reward, we say no; the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the phrase “according to their specific knowledge” indicates that there is a distinction in the reward based on the excellence of the recipient (*pātra*). Thus says Vyāsa: [End of excerpt]
O Bhārata, for the sake of the preceptor’s household, for the sake of medicine, for the sake of Vedic study,
for one set out on a journey, and likewise for the sake of sacrifice;
O King, even one who has performed the Vaiśvajit sacrifice, if his means of subsistence have been exhausted,
is glorified in the heavenly world by giving [to such a person] through the excellence of his knowledge.

And so forth. Therefore, this should be understood as being like the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*). Just as for one who does not perform the twilight worship there is transgression, while for one who performs it there is both the absence of transgression and the attainment of the fruit. || 5.22 ||

That gift which is given to the members of the sacrificial assembly (*sadasyas*) at the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) during a sacrifice is "within the altar" (*antarvedi*). Other than that, it is "outside the altar" (*bahirvedi*). The distribution of goods (*dravyasaṃvibhāga*) refers to the giving of gold and other such items. That must necessarily be performed in the case of one's teacher and others. For one who has studied the Veda, it is for the sake of the sacrificial fee or for the sake of the teacher. "Marriage and medicine": marriage (*niveśa*) means wedding; "for that purpose" means for the sake of the first [marriage]. "For medicine" (*auṣadhārtham*) means for the sake of a remedy for the sick. "Deprived of livelihood" (*vṛttikṣīṇa*) means one who lacks a means of subsistence for that day. "About to sacrifice" (*yakṣyamāṇa*) means one who intends to perform a sacrifice. "Connected with study or travel": he whose connection is with study is "connected with study" (*adhyayanasaṃyoga*); he whose connection is with travel is "connected with travel" (*adhvasaṃyoga*). These are *bahuvrīhi* compounds. "The performer of the Vaiśvajit" (*vaiśvajitaḥ*) means one who has performed the Viśvajit sacrifice and is thus destitute of wealth due to having given away all his possessions. When requested by these [persons], one must certainly give gold and so forth according to one's ability. By not giving, one incurs sin. By specifying "outside the altar," this applies to those initiated for a sacrifice (*saddīkṣita*); within the altar, however, gifts may also be given to others. (5.19)
When others are begging, [he should give] prepared food. 5.23–5.20.
One should give prepared food to those begging who are distinct from those already mentioned. Some read "to others" (*itarebhyaḥ*), for whom this is the very same meaning.
Now, one might object that since this is already established by the rule, "The giving of alms occurs after the *svasti* has been pronounced" (GDh 5.19), this need not be stated.

It is said: that [previous rule] refers merely to the manner of performance (*itikartavyatā*). This one, however, is for the purpose of ensuring that alms must be given as a matter of necessity. If this is so, then this [rule] should also be understood as being like the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and other such duties, because it is stated without distinction. Almsgiving may take place both outside and inside the sacrificial altar (*vedi*). Since there is mention of "cooked food" (*kṛtānna*), there is no restriction regarding rice grains and the like. While it would have been sufficient to say "among others [he may beg]," the statement "among those begging" (*bhikṣamāṇeṣu*) indicates that the restriction applies only when they are actually requesting with such mantras as "Lady, give alms. Alternatively, this restriction applies only to those who are worthy of receiving alms. As Vasiṣṭha has said:

"For that village where twice-born men wander for alms while being without vows and unlearned, the king should punish; for it is a provider of sustenance for thieves. (VaDh 3.4). In that regard, when giving alms, one should also offer water into the hand of the ascetic (*yati*). As Bhṛgu says:
"One should give water into the hand of the ascetic, give the alms, and then give water again."
The alms-food would be as large as a mountain, and that water would be like the ocean. Thus [it is said]. (2.23)

To other mendicants—those distinct from those already mentioned—one must certainly give prepared food, that is, cooked food. There is no fault in not giving money or other such items. Regarding the matter of prepared food, Vasiṣṭha states:

"The king should punish that village where twice-born men who do not observe vows, do not study the Vedas, and wander about for alms reside; for he is bound by the same rule as the punishment for a thief. (VaDh 3.4) || 5.20 ||
The refutation of giving is now stated. Now, as for the refutation of giving:
even after having made a promise, one should not [give] to one associated with unrighteousness.
One should give. || 5.24 ||
Even after having given a promise, one should not give to one who is joined with unrighteousness. || 5.21 ||

One should not give even what has been promised to one who, being joined with unrighteousness, makes a request for the sake of his teacher or others but does not act upon it; by the use of the word "api" (even), it is implied that one should not give even what has already been intended as a gift. (5.24)

Even after having promised "I will give," one need not give in a matter connected with unrighteousness (*adharma*), if one should know that the other person will use that property for unrighteous purposes such as visiting a prostitute and the like. By the expression "connected with unrighteousness," it is shown that one incurs sin by not giving what was promised in any other case [than those involving unrighteousness]. (5.21)
One should not accept that something is connected with unrighteousness merely from the word of anyone at all; thus he says, specifying the exceptions regarding what one should accept:
"The words of those who are angry, delighted, afraid, afflicted, greedy, childish, aged, dull-witted, intoxicated, or insane [are not to be relied upon]."
Falsehoods that do not constitute mortal sins. || 5.25 || — || 5.22 ||

The unreliability of the speech of those possessed by anger, joy, fear, disease, or greed, as well as that of children and the like, should not be concluded merely from their words, because their speech lacks authority. The mention of "speech" (vākya) is intended to establish the lack of authority of their words even in other contexts. 5.25.

Words spoken by one who is angry and so forth—though false and not corresponding to reality—do not produce sin, for they do not constitute a transgression. "Angry" means possessed by anger; "joyful" means possessed by joy; "frightened" means possessed by fear. Because these [states] are permeated by other qualities, the speech is not authoritative. Therefore, there is no fault even in their failure to deliver what was promised. (5.22)
Having spoken incidentally, he now states the subject at hand.
Next, he speaks of those who must be fed first by the householder:
"One should feed first the guest, the child, the sick person, the pregnant woman, the newly married woman, and the elderly."
And those who are inferior. 5.26 — 5.23.

He should feed these first before himself: the guest (to be described below), the youth, the child, the sick person afflicted by disease, the women in their courses who are pregnant daughters, the elderly, and the attendants. By the word "and" (*ca*), the poor, the helpless, and others are included. The irregular arrangement [of the terms] is for the purpose of establishing the sequence; therefore, he should feed them according to their relative need for favor. 5.26.

The guest (atithi) is one who will be described [later]. Children (kumāra) are infants. The sick (vyādhita) are those afflicted with disease. Pregnant women (garbhiṇyaḥ) are well known. Female relatives living in the household (svavāsinyaḥ) are daughters and sisters. The elderly (sthavira) are the aged. The dependents (jaghanya) are servants and the like. One should feed these before oneself and eat afterwards. The separate mention of the dependents is for the purpose of indicating their immediate sequence. 5.23.
But for one's teacher, father, and friends, one must carry out their word after having informed them. (5.27) — (5.24)

For if at this time anyone, such as a teacher or the like, should come to the house, then having offered the prepared food to him, one must carry out what he says; the meaning is that one should do whatever they tell one to do. The word *tu* (but) is for the purpose of restriction, implying that one should do only that and never act independently. Since it has been stated that "one must perform their command," if they say nothing at all, then one may act independently. (5.27)

If the teacher and others should arrive at the time of eating, then, having offered the prepared food to them, the performance of that meal-rite should be carried out according to their wish; the meaning is that while they are present, one should not be independent. 5.24.
The honey-mixture (madhuparka) is offered upon the arrival of a sacrificial priest, a teacher, a father-in-law, a paternal uncle, and a maternal uncle. 5.28—5.25.

But when officiating priests and others come to one's house, worship with the *madhuparka* must first be performed; because of the mention of "approaching," it is not required for a second visit or subsequent ones. The procedure for the *madhuparka* is to be found in the *Gṛhya-sūtra*. (5.28)
When officiating priests and others have arrived at one's house, the honey-mixture (madhuparka) should be offered. || 5.25 ||
Again, after a year. || 5.29 || — || 5.26 ||
If they, having been honored, should return after a year, then the madhuparka must be offered again; not before that. 5.29.
If they, having been honored, should return after a year, the madhuparka must be offered again; not before that. (5.26)
Before [the end of] the sacrifice or the marriage ceremony. 5.30 — 5.27.

Honey-mixture (madhuparka) should be offered even within a year to those who have arrived at a sacrifice or a wedding; since the offering of honey-mixture to officiating priests at a sacrifice is already established by the revealed scripture (śruti), this rule is commenced for the sake of fathers-in-law and others. 5.30.

Even before a year has passed, the madhuparka must be offered to those who have arrived for a sacrifice or a wedding; the procedure for the madhuparka is to be understood as that prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras. 5.27.
And [the same applies] for a king who is a master of the Vedas. 5.31 — 5.28.

And at the reception of a king, the honey-mixture (madhuparka) should be offered if he is a Śrotriya; because of the separate mention [of the king], this applies even before a year has passed. By the use of the word "and" (ca), clothing is also included. 5.31.
In this same manner, the madhuparka should be offered to a king who is also a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya). || 5.28 ||
One should not offer a seat or water to one who is not learned in the Vedas. (5.32) — (5.29)
If the king is not learned in the Vedas (aśrotriya), he should be honored with nothing more than a seat and water. || 5.32 ||
For a king who is not a śrotriya, the honey-mixture (madhuparka) consists merely of a seat and water. 5.29.
But for a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya), he should provide water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), and various kinds of food. (5.33) — (5.30)

[The guest] is a Brāhmaṇa who is a Śrotriya. Why is this so? Because of the repeated mention of the term "Śrotriya. If it were intended for a Vaiśya, it would not be so, because another Smṛti is seen to state: "A Vaiśya is not to be honored with the Madhuparka; therefore, one should simply feed him. The word *tu* (but/however) is for the purpose of specification. If he is endowed with good conduct (*vṛttasaṃpanna*), then upon his arrival, water should be given for the purpose of washing his feet and for the sake of honor. [The terms] *pādya* and *arghya* are used as separate compounds; and the *Madhuparka* consists of specific kinds of food distinguished by varieties such as boiled rice with lentils (*mudga*) and so forth. By the use of the word *ca* (and), specific side dishes (*upadaṃśa*) and the like are also included. Due to the prefix *pra*, there is an abundance of clarified butter (*ghṛta*). And thus says the Śruti: "For a Brāhmaṇa who has arrived as a guest, one cooks food rich in clarified butter. (5.33)

The word "tu" (but) does not exclude the Brāhmaṇa. For a learned Brāhmaṇa guest, one who is capable should provide *pādya*—water for washing the feet—and *arghya*—such as fruit offerings, betel, and so forth—as well as various kinds of food, such as milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and cakes (*apūpa*), in an excellent manner. 5.30.
But when there is incapacity; however, if it is incapable, it is either permanent or distinguished by refinement. 5.34 — 5.31.
Whatever food is always available in his house, that alone, distinguished by abundant side-dishes, is superior to [food obtained from] common sources. 5.34.
Whatever is always available in his house, that very thing he should prepare, distinguished by seasonings such as black pepper and cumin. || 5.31 ||
The gift of food to one who is of good conduct but not a learned scholar is middling. (5.35) — (5.32)

But when a Brāhmaṇa who is not learned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*) is present—one who is of virtuous conduct and established in good behavior—food accompanied by the middle refinement (*saṃskāra*) should be given to him. The mention of "food" is for the sake of restriction: only food is to be given, not water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth. The mention of "giving" is for this purpose: that he should not be deprived of the refinement simply because he is not learned in the Vedas. (5.35)
But when a guest who, though lacking in learning, is of virtuous conduct arrives, food should be given to him with the intermediate preparation. 5.32.
But when it is the opposite, [the requisites are] grass, water, and ground. 5.36.
Even toward those who are hostile, he shows welcome, and ultimately offers them honor, respect, and hope. 5.33.

By the word "tu" (but), the case opposite to both is indicated. Consequently, if even a learned man is of improper conduct, he too should be regarded as one for whom "food is always [to be given], distinguished by refinement" (GDh 5.34); it is not merely grass, water, and ground that should be given. 5.36.

One who is contrary [in conduct] and lacks true knowledge, even if endowed with learning, is not of virtuous character. One should offer him ground, grass, a seat, and water, saying, "Please sit here. One should offer a welcome immediately thereafter, and should extend a greeting of "Welcome" (svāgata). Worship should be performed with hospitable conversation, yet it should not be excessive. "Excessive" (atyāśa) refers to a special sequence of foods such as milk-rice (pāyasa) and cakes; other than that, it should be performed according to the moderate manner. "Āśa" means eating. 5.33.
Welcome, at last! || 5.37 ||

"Welcome" means kind and truthful speech. "In the end," meaning even in times of distress, when the giving of grass and water is impossible, one should utter kind and truthful speech; such is the meaning. || 5.37 ||
And there is also the desire for honor and fame. 5.38.

After speaking pleasant and truthful words, one should offer honor; indeed, the very act of not showing contempt is honor. Therefore, the meaning is that one must not show contempt. Furthermore, "not being overly eager" means that one should not eat oneself even if one has not fed [the guest] even a single mouthful, especially in times of distress. (5.38)
The offering of a bed, a seat, a dwelling, following [the guest], and attendance are the same for both an equal and a superior. (5.39) — (5.34)
H reads "samānāni".

For a guest who is equal to oneself or superior to oneself, bedding and other such items should be provided that are equal to one’s own. "Bedding" refers to couches and the like; "seats" refer to wooden planks and the like; "lodgings" refer to inner rooms and the like; "following" means walking behind; and "waiting upon" means prostrating and so forth. Since it is impossible for following and waiting upon to be exactly equal to oneself, the instruction is intended to mean that following and waiting upon should be performed for one who is equal to or superior to oneself. However, the bedding, seats, and so forth should be provided with equality to one's own. This equality is in relation to oneself and not in relation to each other, because a superior person is to be honored more highly. Thus he will say later: "In the case of equals and unequals, there is inequality based on honor; and [the food] is unhonored... (GDh 17.18–19). Therefore, it should be understood that for a peer or a superior, these items are equal in relation to oneself, but unequal in relation to each other. 5.39.

An *atithi* (guest) is one who is equal to oneself in terms of learning, conduct, and so forth, as well as one who is superior; to both of these, bedding, seats, and other such things should be given that are equal to one's own. An *āvasatha* is a specific place within the house. Since following after (*anuvrajyā*) and attending upon (*upāsanā*) are impossible for oneself, equality in those respects is not possible; however, the meaning is that even those two duties must be performed [for others]. (5.34)
Even to a small extent, [one should not give] to an inferior. || 5.40 || — || 5.35 ||
Even when [the number of syllables] is slightly deficient, they should be made equal. 5.40.

Some say that when a guest arrives who is even slightly inferior to oneself, one should give him bedding and other such things exactly as one would to an equal. We, however, say this: when an inferior guest arrives, bedding and other items should be given in small measure; but one must not, on the grounds that he is inferior, practice total omission. 5.35.
He states the definition of a guest: "A guest is one from a different village, staying for only one night, who waits upon the sun while remaining under a tree. (5.41) — [End of] 5.36.

A guest who has come from another village, whose habit is to stay for only one night, and who presents himself after midday, is to be understood as a *atithi*. To such a person, a gift must be given according to this rule; and in failing to give, there is sin. Even if he lacks a single characteristic due to an irregularity, he does not cease to be so. By the expression "the sun behind the trees," the evening time is meant. And thus Vasiṣṭha says: "One should not offend a guest who arrives in the evening" (VaDh 8.4). 5.41.

"One from a different village" means one who dwells in another village. "Staying for one night" means he stays for a single night; thus, he is "one-night-staying. "When the sun is above the trees" refers to the time when it is midday; or else, it refers to that time when the sun's rays are above the trees, which is evening. A guest who has arrived at such a time is in every way most worthy of honor. (5.36)
Furthermore, what indeed should be said to a guest? To this he says:
"The final inquiry for a Śūdra concerns his welfare, his well-being, and his health. (5.42)
An inquiry after one's welfare, health, and freedom from disease. 5.37.

The guest should be questioned in due order: "Is it well with the Brāhmaṇa? "Is there freedom from disease for the Kṣatriya? "Is there health for the Śūdra? Thereafter, that which is stated in another Smṛti regarding the Vaiśya should be observed. Thus says Manu: "Having met a Brāhmaṇa, one should ask about his welfare (kuśala); a Kṣatriya relative, about his freedom from disease (anāmaya); a Vaiśya, about his security (kṣema); and a Śūdra, about his health (ārogya) alone. (MDh 2.127). || 5.42 ||

Among the three castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, when they are encountered on the road or elsewhere, inquiries regarding their welfare and so forth should be made in the following order: a Brāhmaṇa should be asked, "Is it well with you, venerable sir? (api kuśalaṃ āyuṣman); a Kṣatriya, "Is there freedom from illness for your lordship? (apy anāmayaṃ tatra bhavataḥ); and a Vaiśya, "Are you free from disease? (apy arogo bhavān). (5.37)
The last [is] for the Śūdra. || 5.38 ||
Among the auspicious and other [mantras], that which is last should be employed by a Śūdra, even when he is free from disease. || 5.38 ||
A non-Brāhmaṇa who is not an invited guest at a sacrifice is not a guest for a Brāhmaṇa, provided he is not one of those excluded from the rite. 5.43.
For a Brāhmaṇa, one who is not a Brāhmaṇa is not a guest. 5.39.

Even if a Kṣatriya or others possess the aforementioned characteristics, they are not guests for a Brāhmaṇa. Consequently, [food] must not be given to them as a rule. "In a non-sacrifice" means other than at a sacrifice; however, at a sacrifice, it certainly occurs. If that Brāhmaṇa is well-conducted but poor, [the rule applies]; even outside of a sacrifice, it certainly occurs when there is abundant food. Because of the mention of "Brāhmaṇa," it certainly occurs for a Kṣatriya and others. Since the Brāhmaṇa is excluded from non-Brāhmaṇas, for a Brāhmaṇa, it certainly occurs with a Brāhmaṇa guest. (5.43)

A non-Brāhmaṇa, such as a Kṣatriya or others, does not become a guest of a Brāhmaṇa. The duties of a guest mentioned previously are not to be applied in that case; he is to be received only by providing water, food, and so forth. (5.39)
If he is covered [with a cloth] during a sacrifice. 5.40.
If he is invited at the time of a sacrifice, he should be honored like a guest. 5.40.
In that regard as well: "But the meal for the Kṣatriya is after the Brāhmaṇas. (5.44) — [End of] 5.41.
The word "tu" (but) is intended to indicate an alternative view: according to the view of the guests, one should feed the Kṣatriya after the Brāhmaṇas have eaten. 5.44.
Even when he is acting as a host, he should provide food for the Brāhmaṇas only after they have finished eating. 5.41.
Others [he should support] along with his servants for the sake of compassion—for the sake of compassion. (5.45) — (5.42)

If he has the means, he should feed others—such as Vaiśyas and the like—along with his servants, including slaves, laborers, and workmen; even if they are not guests, he should do so for the sake of non-cruelty and compassion, for there would be cruelty in the world if he were to reject them. (5.45)

Others, such as Śūdras and the like, who have arrived at the time of hospitality, he should feed together with his servants, laborers, and so forth, provided that he has the means to do so. Even though they do not possess the status of guests (*atithi*), he should nevertheless feed them for the sake of compassion (*anṛśaṃsya*). Cruelty (*nṛśaṃsatā*) is manifest harshness; this is done to avoid that. Since it is said, "Compassion is the supreme duty," compassion itself is indeed the highest duty. [The repetition marks the conclusion of the chapter. 5.42.
Now begins the sixth chapter.
Here, in connection with the honoring of guests, he describes another mode of honoring others as well.
The honoring of guests has been described; now he describes the mode of honoring others as well.
In a gathering, one should daily perform the clasping of the feet.

The clasping of the feet must be performed according to the procedure taught in another Smṛti due to the employment of two prefixes. As Manu says: "The grasping [of the feet] should be done with crossed hands" (MDh 2.72), and so forth. "In a gathering" means in a meeting. "Daily" means every day; the word "must be performed" is to be supplied. It should be understood as referring to the meeting of those who will be mentioned hereafter. 6.1.

In the presence—that is, the assembly—of the mother and others who are about to be mentioned, one must perform the clasping of their feet every day, according to the previously described method: "It should be done with crossed hands" (MDh 2.72). 6.1.
But having approached [a guest] after he has been away for a long time. || 6.2 ||

Having returned from a distant foreign land, he should go to that house facing him; the word "tu" (but) is intended to include this with respect. Consequently, one should not expect a casual or accidental meeting. 6.2.

The word *tu* (but) serves to exclude the previously mentioned case. Having gone abroad oneself—that is, having undertaken a journey—or upon their going abroad, one should go to where those [elders], such as mother and father, are staying, and perform the clasping of their feet (*pādopasaṃgrahaṇa*). Thus ends verse 6.2.
To whom, then, should this be performed? To this he says:
"To them, [namely] mother, father, and so forth.
[This refers to] the mother, the father, their relatives, ancestors, teachers of knowledge, and the teachers of those teachers. (6.3)

The mother and father are well known. Their kinsmen are the maternal uncle, the maternal grandfather, the paternal uncle, the paternal grandfather, and so forth. "Elder kin" (pūrvaja) refers to one's own elder brothers, since the teacher of the Vedas was mentioned previously. "Their teachers" (tad-guru) are those who are the teachers of learning for the fathers and others. By the use of the word "and" (ca), friends of the teacher and others are also included. In the case of the assembly of these [relatives], one should approach them daily; and after having stayed away from home, one should likewise visit them. The non-compounding of the term *pūrvaja* and the others is intended to include the teacher’s father-in-law and other such elders. (6.3)

Mother and father are well known. Their kinsmen include maternal uncles, maternal aunts, paternal uncles, paternal aunts, and so forth. Elder siblings are one's older brothers. Teachers of learning include preceptors (ācāryas), instructors (upādhyāyas), and others. Their teachers include [the aforementioned] preceptors and so forth. The two preceding sūtras concern these [categories]. || 6.3 ||
In the presence of another. 6.4.
In the case of a combination, [the accent belongs] to the subsequent [element]. 6.4.62.

When many people are gathered in one place, then that which belongs to the most eminent person should be performed first. And he has been described [by the author] with the words: "The teacher is the best among gurus," and so forth (GDh 2.57). 6.4.

When one’s mother and others meet or come together simultaneously, the salutation (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*) of the most eminent person must be performed first. Regarding this eminence, it was previously stated: “The teacher (*ācārya*) is the best among gurus; some say the mother” (GDh 2.56). Āpastamba, however, has prescribed the salutation as follows: “In the case of a meeting between the teacher and the sub-teacher (*prācārya*), having saluted the sub-teacher, one should desire to salute the teacher,” and so forth (ĀpDh 1.8.19). || 6.4 ||
He states the rule for salutation:
"In an assembly of knowledgeable persons, a salutation consists in announcing one's own name with the words 'I am so-and-so'. (6.5)

One's own name is that which was given by one's father and others. Having pronounced that with excellence, and immediately thereafter having uttered the word *aham* (I), there is the direct instruction "this" (*ayam*); for its purpose, the word *asmin* (in this) should be employed. The word *iti* expresses a manner. At the end, the word *bhoḥ* is used because it takes the place of the teacher's name due to the context. Thus, it should be employed as: "I am the one named Devadatta, sir. This is the salutation at the time of clasping the feet. The meaning is that it must be uttered while facing [the teacher]. "In the presence of those who know" means in the assembly of those who know the rule for returning a salutation. And the rule for returning a salutation is to be seen in another Smṛti. As Manu says:
When greeting a Brahmin, one should say, "May you be long-lived, O gentle one."

"And the letter *a* should be pronounced at the end of this name, with the preceding vowel protracted (*pluta*). [MDh 2.125] Likewise, Vasiṣṭha also says: "In a vocative, the final vowel is protracted; a non-pragṛhya diphthong undergoes the state of *āy* or *āv*, as does the word *bho-bhava*. [VaDh 13.46] Examples of such usage in the rule for returning a greeting should be understood as: *āyuṣmān bhava saumya Viṣṇumitra-a* (O gentle Viṣṇumitra, may you be long-lived), *āyuṣmān bhava saumya Dāśaratha-aya* (O gentle Dāśaratha, may you be long-lived), and so forth. However, when one is among those who are ignorant [of the rules], one should not perform the formal clasping of the feet (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*). The same applies to the greeting itself. If it is asked what should be done in that case, one should simply say, "I greet you" (*abhivādaye*). One should perform the mere act of greeting, as Āpastamba states: "A Brāhmaṇa should greet by extending his right arm level with his ear; a Kṣatriya level with his chest; a Vaiśya level with his waist; and a Śūdra with his hands joined in reverence and his head lowered. [ĀpDh 1.5.16–17] Thus, it should be understood that the rule for clasping the feet, beginning with "with crossed hands," [MDh 2.72], is the rule for the formal salutation (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*), while the rule cited from Āpastamba is the rule for the verbal greeting (*abhivādana*). || 6.5 ||

When meeting someone who is capable of returning a greeting, one should perform the salutation by first stating one's own name—that which is used in common practice and well-known—then saying "I am [Name]" with great clarity and loudness. The term *abhivāda* means "salutation"; it is derived from the root *vad* with the prefix *abhi* and the causative suffix (*ṇic*), followed by the suffix *ac*. Thus, for those who understand the meaning, when there is a gathering of elders whose excellence is known, one should perform the salutation by stating one's own secret name according to the order of salutation, saying "I am [Name]. This refers to cases where the person being saluted is not inferior. For example: "I salute you; I am Haradattaśarman by name, sir. Regarding this, the rule for the return greeting has been shown by Manu: [The text continues with the rules for the return greeting.]
When greeting a Brahmin, one should say, "May you be long-lived, O gentle one."

"And the letter *a* should be uttered at the end of this name, with the preceding vowel being protracted (*pluta*). [MDh 2.125] The meaning of this is as follows: by the word "vipra," this refers specifically to a Brāhmaṇa. The one who offers salutation should be addressed as: "O gentle one, may you be long-lived (*āyuṣmān bhava saumya*). At the end of his name, the letter *a* should be uttered with the preceding vowel protracted. The phrase "with the preceding vowel protracted" is an adjective qualifying the letter *a*. Because that which precedes the final [consonant] is the one to be protracted, this applies even when there is an intervening consonant. For example: "May you be long-lived, O gentle Haradatta3a. With an intervening consonant, for instance: "May you be long-lived, O gentle Agnida3. Such is the usage. Vasiṣṭha, however, states a specific rule regarding diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*): "In an address, the final vowel is protracted; they say that a diphthong is not subject to the *pragṛhya* rule. [VaDh 13.46] This means that it undergoes the change into *ā* and *u*. According to the grammarians: "When a non-*pragṛhya* diphthong is called from a distance, the first half becomes *ā* and the second half becomes *i* or *u*. In that case, when the letter *a* is employed at the end, *y* and *v* are substituted for those two [diphthongs] before a vowel in *saṃhitā*: thus the usage is "May you be long-lived, O gentle Pinākapāṇā3ya" and "O Viṣṇā3va. However, according to the view that this applies only in the presence of ignorant people (*ajñasamavāya*), this method of salutation does not apply. Regarding that, there is another Smṛti text:
Those ignorant persons who do not know the prolation of the name in returning a greeting, [should be treated as Śūdras].

"But having lived abroad among them, he might as well address them as he would women. Just as with women, there is an addressing by some word whatsoever—without the aforementioned specific form, but by means of local dialects or the like—even so it is with them. The term "addressing" (*abhivādana*) is a general indicator, since it includes even those forms employed for women and others that are devoid of the prescribed specific manner. Regarding the manner of addressing, Āpastamba states: "A Brāhmaṇa should address [his teacher] while extending his right arm to the level of the ear; a Rājanya [should extend it] to the level of the chest; a Vaiśya, to the middle [of the body]; and a Śūdra, with palms joined, below that. (ĀpDh 1.5.16) || 6.5 ||
Some maintain that there is no fixed rule regarding salutation when a man and a woman meet. 6.6.

Regarding the matter of husband and wife, the meaning is that when the wife has arrived at the point where she ought to perform a salutation to her husband, even though the husband may be knowledgeable in returning a salutation, some authorities maintain that there is no fixed rule. They hold that there is no restriction such as "I am so-and-so," and that it may be done in any manner whatsoever. Gautama, however, maintains that it must be performed according to the specific rule beginning with "I am so-and-so. This option depends upon one's proficiency. 6.6.

In the context of the union of a woman and a man—that is, in the meeting of wife and husband—the suffix *tasi* has the sense of all case endings (*sārvavibhaktika*). Regarding the occasion of salutation, some maintain that there is no fixed rule. Even though the husband knows how to return a salutation, they do not require a formal rule for the wife’s salutation to him. They do not accept a fixed procedure such as "I, so-and-so, salute you"; rather, there is merely a general salutation. And thus, the wife must perform a daily prostration to her husband. Because of the word "some" (*eke*), according to the view of Gautama, there is indeed a fixed rule. (6.6)
One should not kiss women other than one's mother, paternal uncle’s wife, or sister after returning from a journey abroad. 6.7.

One should not perform the salutation (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*) of women when away from home. The mother is well known. The paternal uncle’s wife is the wife of the father’s younger brother. The sister is one’s own uterine elder sister. Having excluded these, one should perform the salutation of these [other women] every day. And so it is stated in another *Smṛti*: "One should perform the salutation of one's mother and likewise of one's sister."

"And likewise, having approached the wife of his paternal uncle every day... [so it is said]. For other women who occupy the position of a guru, a student who has returned from a journey away must perform either a salutation (*abhivādana*) or a formal clasping of the feet (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*). In this regard, it should be understood that for those who occupy the status of an absolute guru, such as the wives of maternal uncles and others, one must perform *upasaṃgrahaṇa*, whereas for others, a simple *abhivādana* is required. (6.7)

This is an exception to the rule "every day" regarding social gatherings (*samavāya*). For women other than one's mother, paternal uncle’s wife, and sister, one should not perform the clasping of the feet (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*) or salutation (*abhivādana*) unless one has been away from home; rather, these should be performed only upon returning from a journey. However, for one's mother and the others [the aforementioned], they should be performed every day even without having been away. Thus, another *Smṛti* states:
"A twice-born man should perform the clasping of the feet every day during a social gathering for his sister, his mother, and likewise for the wives of his paternal uncles. (6.7)
One should not engage in sexual intercourse with the wives of one's brothers or with one's mother-in-law. (6.8)
H reads "svasṝṇām" (of sisters).

Even for one who has returned from abroad, [the greeting] obtained through the mediation of someone standing in the position of an absolute elder is prohibited; thus, the requirement of salutation (*abhivādana*) is established. The compound is analyzed as a *viṣamāsa* (irregular compound) for the purpose of including the clasping of friends' feet. And the word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of including the clasping of the feet of the wife of one's father-in-law's friend. 6.8.

Upon returning from a journey abroad, one should not perform the formal clasping of the feet (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*) for these women; however, the salutation (*abhivādana*) must certainly be performed. In this regard, for those who occupy the position of supreme elders, such as maternal uncles' wives and others, the clasping of the feet is required, while for other women, the salutation alone suffices. (6.8)
But one must rise for officiating priests, fathers-in-law, paternal uncles, and maternal uncles who are younger; they are not to be saluted [by lying prostrate]. 6.9.

H reads: “They are to be saluted. When officiating priests and others who are younger than oneself are present, honor should be shown by merely rising from one’s seat. Since they are not to be saluted, they are therefore also not to be clasped by the feet. The word *tu* (but/however) expresses a distinction. Furthermore, those of equal age are not to be saluted, especially those who are younger. 6.9.
One should perform the worship of officiating priests and others who are younger than oneself by merely rising from one's seat; however, they are not to be saluted with the formal greeting. 6.9.
Likewise, another man who is at least eighty years older, even if he is a Śūdra, [may be honored] as if he were one's own son.

Just as these [categories] are not to be saluted and must be stood up for, so too is this other person who is older in age than the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and others: a fellow citizen (*paura*), a resident of the same place, who is at least eighty years old—the meaning being that he is firmly established at eighty years of age. And therefore, from that point on, even a Śūdra is to be so regarded; by the use of the word "even" (*api*), Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas are also included. By a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya who is equal to his own offspring—even if he is of a different caste. One might have the doubt that, despite the presence of the word "other" (*anya*), the term "equal to one's offspring" refers only to those of the same caste; hence [the author] states this. (6.10)

Just as officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and others are to be saluted by rising but are not to be formally greeted with a prostration (*abhivādya*), so too is this person. He is "other than them" (*anyas tebhyo ’nyaḥ*). "Earlier" (*pūrvaḥ*) means superior in age. "A townsman" (*pauraḥ*) means a resident of the city. Even though he is superior in age, his inferiority due to being a townsman is stated. "Eighty" (*aśīti*) refers to one who is eighty years old; "inferior to that" (*aśītikāvaraḥ*) means less than eighty years of age. Such a Śūdra, even if equal to one's own offspring, is to be saluted by rising but not to be formally greeted. By the phrase "equal to one's offspring," his relative youthfulness is indicated. The mention of the "Śūdra" is an illustration for those of the lower castes (*avaravarṇa*). Consequently, it is established that the Śūdra must be saluted by rising by all three castes, the Vaiśya by two, and the Kṣatriya by the Brāhmaṇa alone. (6.10)
Even a lower noble may [be honored] by a Śūdra. 6.11.

Even one who is lower—that is, even one of extremely inferior age—a noble twice-born man (ārya dvijāti) must rise to meet a Śūdra. The mention of the Śūdra is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) for Vaiśyas and others as well; therefore, it should be understood that a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, and a Vaiśya must be met by rising by a Śūdra, a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya by a Vaiśya, and a Brāhmaṇa by a Kṣatriya. The word "even" (api) serves to include the act of salutation. (6.11)

Even by a Śūdra who is less than eighty years old, a member of the three higher castes (traivarṇika) who is an Ārya—be he younger or even junior in age—must rise to meet him, though he need not be saluted with formal prostration (*abhivādya*). Here too, the mention of the "Śūdra" is an illustration for any person of a lower caste. Consequently, it is established that the three castes must be met by a Śūdra, two by a Vaiśya, and one—the Brāhmaṇa—by a Kṣatriya; those who are younger in age must be met by rising, but need not be formally saluted. (6.11)
And he should avoid using his name. 6.12.

H reads: "The repetition of the word 'asya' (of him) is for the sake of distributive emphasis, meaning 'of this one and that one. One should not utter the name of a superior person, nor of an inferior person. The phrase 'without qualification' is to be supplied. And because of the word 'ca' (and), there is also the prohibition of derision. Consequently, a superior person may indeed utter the name of an inferior person. (6.12)

Regarding the phrase "asya," there is an elision of repetition (*vīpsā*); that is, one should not utter the actual name of this person, who is superior to the most superior, but rather one should utter a figurative name. (6.12)
And the king’s messenger shall not be liable for the recitation [of the mantra]. 6.13.

A Brahmin who is a servant performing menial tasks should avoid addressing a king by name; this is a prohibition against what would otherwise be expected due to his low status. This applies provided he is "ajapa," meaning one who has not studied the Vedas (an *aśrotriya*). By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), this also includes a Vaiśya. However, there is no fault in the case of a Śūdra. (6.13)
One who does not recite [the Veda] is unlearned; one who performs menial service is a servant. Even a Brahmin of superior caste should avoid pronouncing the name of an anointed king. 6.13.
"Bho bhavān" is used for a friend born on the same day. 6.14.

He should be addressed as "bho bhavān. The words *bho* and *bhavān* are to be employed with reference to the specific action at hand; this much alone constitutes honor. As for the one who is a *vayasya* (companion) or *sakhi* (friend), his defining characteristic is that he was born on the same *ahaḥ*. Here, the word *ahaḥ* is a synonym for *saṃvatsara* (year), because the *Naighaṇṭuka* records it as a synonym for *saṃvatsara* in the passage: "abdaḥ, saṃvatsaram, ahar, jalam. Consequently, [the term refers to] one born in the same year. In common worldly usage as well, those born in the same year are known to be of equal age. Therefore, after a year has passed, one becomes older. (6.14)

A *vayasya* is one who is equal in age. One born on the same day—here the word "day" signifies a year—is one born in the same year; such a person is to be addressed with either of these two terms, "bho" or "bhavan. (6.14)
A citizen ten years older [is to be honored]. || 6.15 ||
A citizen ten years older [is fined] five *kalās*; a Vedic scholar and a bard three each. || 6.15 ||

The term "bho bhavan" (O, sir) continues [from the previous rule]. The meaning is that one should address [an equal] with "bho bhavan," as if speaking to a friend. Even a citizen ten years older [is addressed thus], provided he is a resident of the same place. 6.15.

A man who is pure but devoid of qualities, even if he is ten years older, is to be addressed as "bho bhavan" (sir), provided he is adorned with at least one of the sixty-four arts and has become ten years older by practicing them for five years. A *śrotriya* is one who has studied the Veda. A *cāraṇa* is a fellow student. All of these are to be addressed as "bho bhavan. However, Āpastamba maintains that salutation (*abhivādana*) is required in all such cases:
"Friendship based on city-dwelling lasts ten years; that with a fellow student lasts five years;
a *śrotriya* who is three years senior deserves salutation" (ĀpDh 1.14.13). 6.15.
The ornament of the five arts. || 6.16 ||

Even one who resides in the same place as oneself, if he lives by means of artistic skills—such as music, painting, leaf-cutting, and other arts and sciences—he may be addressed like a peer, even if he is five years older. 6.16.
A learned Vedic scholar who is also a wandering minstrel [is purified] by three [days and nights].
A *śrotriya* is one who has studied the *mantras* and *brāhmaṇas*. A *cāraṇa* is one who follows the same *caraṇa* (Vedic school).
Some describe him as being characterized by dance, song, and so forth; that is incorrect, because such qualities are already included under the term *kalābhara*. (6.17)
One who performs the duties of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya but is devoid of learning [is a Śūdra]. 6.18 — 6.16.

Whether one subsists by the occupation of a Kṣatriya or the occupation of a Vaiśya, even if he is superior in action, as long as he remains in that state—that is, until he ceases from that work—he is not [superior] even if he is extremely aged; and he who is devoid of learning is likewise inferior to one who is superior in learning. (6.18)

The word *karma* (action/occupation) is connected with each [term]: "one whose occupation is that of a Kṣatriya" (*rājanyakarmā*) and "one whose occupation is that of a Vaiśya" (*vaiśyakarmā*). Even a Brāhmaṇa, if he lives by the occupation of a Kṣatriya or the occupation of a Vaiśya, must be addressed as "Sir" (*bho bhavān*), even if he is extremely old. And one who is devoid of learning, though old, must be addressed in that same way by one who possesses superior learning. (6.16)
And [the sacrificer] is consecrated prior to the purchase [of the Soma]. 6.19 — || 6.17 ||

Even one who is of equal age, if he has been initiated, is already an elder prior to the sale of the Soma; after that point, he is to be honored—this is the purpose of the instruction. By virtue of the word "and" (ca), it should be understood by implication that even one established in a higher stage of life (āśrama) is [to be honored] prior to the consumption of the *trivṛt* [oblation]. Thus Uśanas says: "He by whom the *trivṛt* has been consumed becomes the teacher of all. (6.19)

This refers to a *vayasya* (a fellow student). A *vayasya* who has been initiated may be addressed as such before the purchase of the *soma*; thereafter, he is to be honored like an elder. Regarding those in the highest stage of life (*uttamāśrama*), Uśanas states: "One who has studied the Vedas (*śrotriya*) becomes a teacher to all, even when eating. (6.17)
Wealth, kinship, occupation, birth, knowledge, and age are grounds for respect. 6.20.
Wealth, kinship, occupation, birth, learning, and age are grounds for respect, provided they are more powerful than those of the other person. (6.18)

Since it is impossible for wealth and the other qualities to be objects of respect in themselves, it should be understood that those who possess them are to be respected. One who possesses wealth is wealthy; one who possesses kin is one who has many distinguished brothers and so forth; one who possesses action is one who performs what has been prescribed; one who possesses birth is one endowed with noble lineage; one who possesses learning is one who has studied the Vedas and the Shastras; one who possesses age is one of advanced years. (6.20)

Since it is impossible for wealth and the other qualities to be honored directly, those who possess them are indicated by these terms as being worthy of honor: one who possesses wealth is "wealthy" (*āḍhya*); one who possesses kin is "endowed with distinguished siblings and others"; one who possesses action is "one who performs the prescribed duties"; one who possesses birth is "endowed with noble lineage"; one who possesses knowledge is "one who has studied the Vedas and the Shastras"; one who possesses age is "advanced in years. Such persons are to be honored by those who do not possess these qualities. However, when they occur together, each subsequent quality is more powerful than the preceding one, and thus that which follows is to be honored first. Honor consists of salutation and other forms of respect toward one who is worthy of honor. (6.18)
The stronger [rules] prevail over others. 6.21.

Whatever is subsequent should be understood as more venerable than each preceding one. Consequently, one who possesses wealth is more honorable than one who merely has kinsmen; one who performs ritual action is more honorable than both, and so forth—this should be applied accordingly. "Honor" refers to salutation and other such marks of respect. (6.21)
But learning is more important than all [these]. 6.22 — 6.19.

*Śruta* is the thorough comprehension of the meaning of the Vedas. But surely this should have been taught at the end of the previous *sūtra*; since that would be established by the very fact of the subsequent rule being stronger, a separate teaching here is purposeless. It is said in reply: this separate undertaking is for the sake of specification. What is intended here by *śruta* is a specific kind of learning, namely the thorough comprehension of the meaning of the Vedas. Previously, it was merely the recitation of the Veda itself. The word *tu* (but/then) also serves to express this distinction. Consequently, this [learning] is to be honored by all. (6.22)

The thorough comprehension of the meaning of the Vedas through the division into *mantra* and *brāhmaṇa* is more important, indeed much more important, than all [other things] such as wealth. This is a separate aphorism intended to exclude the notion that what was previously stated—that "the subsequent is stronger"—might apply here. 6.19.
Why?
And why again is sacred revelation (*śruta*) more venerable than all else? To this he says: "Because dharma has that as its root" (6.23).
Because dharma and sacred revelation have that as their root. 6.20.

That which one who has heard [the Veda] practices is also established as a root of Dharma, as previously explained: "And the tradition and conduct of those who know it" (GDh 1.2). Likewise, Manu says:
"The entire Veda is the root of Dharma, as well as the tradition and conduct of those who know it, the practice of the virtuous, and also self-satisfaction" (MDh 2.6).
Alternatively, because Smṛti is preceded by a thorough comprehension of the meaning of the Veda—as Manu has said:
"The sages perceive the Śruti; they likewise remember the Smṛti. (6.23)

Practice has its root in sacred learning (*śruta*), and Dharma has its root in practice; thus, according to the scripture, the unbroken tradition is also the root. Therefore, sacred learning is of greater importance. The superior importance of sacred learning is established in the *Chāndogya*: "The Brāhmaṇa is called 'Śaiśava'; indeed, Śiśu Āṅgirasa was a composer of mantras among the composers of mantras. Manu also says: "The wise Śiśu Āṅgirasa taught his ancestors; having embraced them with knowledge, he said, 'O my sons'. (MDh 2.151). 6.20.
And because of scripture. 6.2.24.

He alone is more venerable even than Śruti. Śruti, moreover, should be understood as the *Śaiśava-Brāhmaṇa* spoken by Manu: "The infant Kavi, son of Aṅgiras, taught his ancestors; having encompassed them with knowledge, he said to them, 'O little sons'! (MDh 2.151), and so forth. The citation of this example from Śruti is for the purpose of making known the superior authority of that which has been heard when it is accompanied by excellence in study. 6.24.
Way must be yielded to a wheel-turning monarch, one who stands at the tenth stage, a bridegroom, a bride, a student who has completed his studies, and a king. 6.25. — || 6/21 ||

One should assist others on the road by giving way to those who do not possess such [high] qualities, such as the wheel-bearer (cakrī) and so forth. A "wheel-bearer" refers to one with a cart; that is, a *cakrī*. One "standing in the tenth stage" (*daśamīstha*) means one who is in the tenth state of life, i.e., one who is extremely aged. One "to be favored" (*anugrāhya*) is one afflicted by disease. A "bride" (*vadhū*) is a pregnant woman and so forth. A "snātaka" is one who has completed his studies and vows. A "king" (*rājā*) is one who has been consecrated. (6.25)

A *cakrin* is one who possesses a wheel, such as a cart and the like; one situated upon that is a *cakristha*. One situated in the tenth stage, the tenth decade of life, is a *daśamīstha*, meaning an elderly person. One worthy of favor is one afflicted by disease. A *vadhū* is a pregnant woman. A *snātaka* is one who has performed the ceremonial bath following the completion of his studies and vows. A king is one who has been consecrated. On the road, the way must be yielded to these and others [who are encountered]. (6.21)
When a king and a Brāhmaṇa meet, there is a specific rule regarding that: [the gift] from the king, however, is for a Śrotriya, and [the gift] from the Śrotriya is for a Śrotriya. 6.26 — 6.22.

The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of specification. If the king should be of lesser [merit] and the Śrotriya more highly endowed with excellence—provided he is indeed a Snātaka—then the path must be yielded to him by the king. In this same manner, it must be yielded to others by the king alone. Regarding the former [categories] as well, the mutual proximity [of their qualities] should be understood according to what requires favor. 6.26.
In an assembly of those learned in the Vedas, the king himself must yield the path. The repetition [of the word "path"] is for the purpose of indicating the end of the chapter. 6.22.

Now begins the seventh chapter. It has been stated that "learning is indeed weightier than all [other duties]" (GDh 6.22), thus establishing the primacy of knowledge (*vidyā*). Furthermore, its acquisition must be obtained from a Brāhmaṇa, because only he possesses the authority for instruction (*pravacana*). But when there is an absence of a Brāhmaṇa capable of instructing, how should one proceed? To this he says: "Learning is indeed weightier than all," thus stating the primacy of knowledge. That knowledge is to be acquired from a Brāhmaṇa; this is the primary rule (*kalpa*). In the absence of such a person, since knowledge must necessarily be acquired, he states the rule for times of distress (*āpad-kalpa*).
In times of distress, it is permissible for a Brāhmaṇa to acquire knowledge from one who is not a Brāhmaṇa. 7.1.

The heading "the rule for times of distress" (*āpatkalpa*) is maintained until the end of this chapter. "Distress" (*āpad*) refers to the absence of Brāhmaṇas capable of expounding the sacred teachings; the "rule" (*kalpa*) or procedure applicable therein is the "rule for times of distress. Even in times of distress, the mention of "Brāhmaṇa" is for the purpose of ensuring that the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas acquire knowledge from a Brāhmaṇa alone. Non-Brāhmaṇas here refer to Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, because the others lack the qualification for Vedic study. Furthermore, it should be understood that among them, [knowledge is first acquired] from a Kṣatriya and then from a Vaiśya, as seen in the statement: "In the absence of that, the occupation of a Vaiśya" (GDh 7.7). The branches of knowledge (*vidyā*) are fourteen; thus says another Smṛti.

"The limbs [of the Veda] are four: Mīmāṃsā, Nyāyavistara, Purāṇa, and Dharmaśāstra; these are the fourteen sciences (*vidyā*). Here, "application" (*upayoga*) means acceptance, because the root *yuj* denotes a relationship. By this very principle of "otherwise inexplicability" (*anyathānupapatti*), the teaching of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas is inferred. That too is solely for the sake of invisible merit (*adṛṣṭa*), for it is said: "Of his six duties, three are his means of livelihood."

"From officiating at sacrifices, from teaching, and from receiving gifts from a pure person"—thus [Manu 10.76]. Since Manu has prohibited these for anyone other than a Brāhmaṇa on the grounds that they serve a visible purpose (dṛṣṭārtha) for him alone, [the rule] "study from a non-Brāhmaṇa" should have been stated; however, the commencement with the phrase "application of knowledge" (vidyopayoga) is for the purpose of a restrictive rule (niyamārtha), meaning that in times of distress, one must study specifically from a non-Brāhmaṇa. Consequently, even when there is an injunction to give away one's entire property in cases such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa (brahmahatyā), a Kṣatriya or other [caste] should not give it if a Brāhmaṇa capable of receiving it is absent. 7.1.

The limbs [of the Veda] are four: Mīmāṃsā, Nyāyavistara, Purāṇa, and Dharmaśāstra; for these are indeed the fourteen branches of knowledge (*vidyā*). "Utilization" (*upayoga*) means acquisition preceded by formal rules. A non-Brāhmaṇa refers to a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya; therefore, a Brāhmaṇa must utilize knowledge [from others], and that constitutes a rule for times of distress (*āpadkalpa*). The phrase "the rule for times of distress applies to the Brāhmaṇa" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*); by this, it is established that even a Kṣatriya may utilize knowledge from a Vaiśya. This rule for times of distress remains in force until the end of the chapter. (7.1)
Now, since the entirety of service is obtained by means of study, he says:
"Following after is service" (7.2).

Service consists merely in following behind him as he walks; nothing else, such as salutation and so forth, need be performed. This is stated for a time other than that of formal study, because [those acts] are already implied during that period. (7.2)
In that regard, service consists solely in following [the teacher] for as long as the period of study lasts, and nothing else such as massaging his feet. 7.2.
When it is completed, the Brāhmaṇa is the teacher. || 7.3 ||

When the study is completed, not even the mere act of following [the teacher] should be performed. That [following] must be performed by the Brāhmaṇa alone, because of the statement "the Brāhmaṇa is the guru," which is made despite the fact that it should have been stated as "following and service until completion. (7.3)
But when the study is completed, the Brāhmaṇa alone is the teacher. || 7.3 ||
Now, another rule for times of distress is stated: sacrificing for others, teaching, and accepting gifts are permitted for all [twice-born classes]. (7.4)

By the term "all," only the three [upper] castes that are not commended are understood, because the prescribed rules for those who are commended apply except in times of distress (*anāpadi*). This is because of the commencement [of the rule] regarding the Śūdra: "If there is no means of livelihood other than from a Śūdra" (GDh 17.5). If it is argued that the word "all" must be taken in the ablative case (sarvasmāt), there is no fault, as the word "from" (*sakāśāt*) is supplied by ellipsis. The plural number in "of all" (*sarveṣām*) is intended to include those born in the direct order (*anuloma*). This is stated with reference to the Brāhmaṇa, because of his specific qualification and because of the indicative mark: "In the absence of that, the occupation of a Kṣatriya. Consequently, in this state, there is no fault in performing censurable acts such as officiating at sacrifices, due to the force of the scriptural injunction. Thus says Manu:

"No fault attaches to Brahmins from teaching, from officiating at sacrifices, or from accepting gifts—even from those that are censured—for they are like fire and water" (MDh 10.103). "A Brahmin who has fallen into distress may accept gifts from anyone" (MDh 10.102), and so forth. Likewise, the Śruti says: "Therefore, by whatever means possible, one should obtain abundant food" (TaitUp 3.10.1). 7.4.

Sacrificing for others and so forth are the livelihoods of a Brāhmaṇa; these are permitted for all [castes] in times of distress, not for the Brāhmaṇa alone. Another says: "In times of distress, everyone should be made to sacrifice, everyone should be taught, and one may accept gifts from anyone; there is no fault in this. And so Manu says: "By teaching, by sacrificing, or by accepting gifts—even from censurable persons—no fault accrues to Brāhmaṇas, for such a person is like fire and water. (MDh 10.103) || 7.4 ||
Each preceding one is more venerable than the following.

Among these, such as officiating at sacrifices and so forth, whichever has been mentioned earlier is to be understood as more weighty than the one following it. Therefore, the mention of the "former" is intended to establish the sequence: that if livelihood cannot be obtained by each subsequent means, one should live by each preceding one. A penance should be observed for violating this order, since the word "weightier" (*guru*) is used where "each preceding one is better" (*pūrvaḥ pūrvaḥ san*) would otherwise have sufficed. (7.5)

Among these, such as officiating at sacrifices and the rest, whichever has been mentioned earlier is to be understood as more weighty than the one following it. In times of distress, one may live by accepting gifts; if that is not possible, by teaching; and if that is not possible, by officiating at sacrifices. (7.5)
In the absence of that, the livelihood of a Kṣatriya [is permitted]. || 7.6 ||

The word "syāt" (might be) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. In the event that the previously mentioned mode of livelihood for a Brāhmaṇa cannot be obtained, the livelihood of a Kṣatriya consists of subsisting by means of [the recitation of] the *Sāvitrī* and so forth, or by means of protection and the like. The mention of that [Kṣatriya livelihood] is for the purpose of making it known that even a Brāhmaṇa's livelihood, though utterly devoid of merit, is better. And thus says Manu:
"One’s own duty, though deficient, is better than the duty of another well-performed."

"For one who lives by the dharma of another indeed falls immediately from his caste" (MDh 10.97). When it is said, "or likewise the occupation of a Kṣatriya," since the word *vā* (or) implies an alternative, it is understood that in the absence of a Brāhmaṇa's occupation, the occupation of a Kṣatriya may be adopted. However, the inclusion of the term *alābhe* (in the absence/unavailability) indicates that even for one living by the occupation of a Kṣatriya, when a Brāhmaṇa's occupation becomes sufficient for livelihood, then he must abandon the Kṣatriya occupation and resort only to the Brāhmaṇa occupation. And so says Nārada:
"When people have been supported by a Brāhmaṇa through the occupation of a Kṣatriya after he has crossed over a time of distress..."
Having performed that purification for himself, he should abandon that occupation of a Kṣatriya. [NSm 1.55] 7.6.

This refers to the case of a Brāhmaṇa. If even the occupation of officiating at sacrifices for those who are censured is unavailable, he may adopt the livelihood of a Kṣatriya; that is, a Brāhmaṇa may live by service and the like. When the time of distress has passed, Nārada says:

"Having crossed over the distress while his people are supported by the Kṣatriya livelihood, the Brāhmaṇa should abandon that Kṣatriya livelihood after performing purification for himself" (NSm 1.55). 7.6.
In the absence of that, he may follow the occupation of a Vaiśya. || 7.7 ||

The mention of "not taking" (alābhagrahaṇa) is intended so that there may be no confusion of livelihoods (*vṛttisaṃkara*). And thus, even in the case of such confusion, an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is to be observed. That [mention of] "taking" has already been explained. However, because there is no injunction here [regarding the lower modes], the possibility of resorting to a superior livelihood simply does not arise. As Vasiṣṭha says: "But never [should one resort to] a higher [livelihood]. (VaDh 2.23) || 7.7 ||

Even when the occupation of a Kṣatriya is unavailable, a Brāhmaṇa may live by the occupation of a Vaiśya. The mention of "unavailability" is intended so that there may be no confusion of occupations. That a Kṣatriya may subsist by the occupation of a Vaiśya is established by the logic of the "stick and the cake" (daṇḍāpūpanyāya). 7.7.
That is his merchandise. 7.8.

That acceptance [of gifts] applies only to a Brāhmaṇa, not to a Kṣatriya who subsists by the occupation of a Vaiśya. And thus, for a Vaiśya, the saleability of wealth—which is established by implication—is prohibited; having abandoned that, he may take what is prohibited or what is not prohibited after giving [in exchange]. In the absence of that, even what is not normally for sale may be sold. (7.8)

The items that must not be sold by that Brāhmaṇa who follows the occupation of a Vaiśya will now be stated. By the use of the word "his" (tasya), it is indicated that for a Kṣatriya who subsists on the occupation of a Vaiśya, the items about to be mentioned do not constitute forbidden merchandise (apaṇya). (7.8)
What is that which is not to be sold? To this he says:
"Scent, liquids, prepared food, sesame, hemp, linen, and skins. (7.9)

Fragrance and ointment; liquids such as oil and the like; prepared food such as sweetmeats (*modaka*) and the like; sesame seeds, which are well known; hemp, a product of the *śaṇa* plant; linen, a product of *kṣumā* (flax or *atasī*); since the prohibition applies to the derivative product, the raw material is not prohibited; and antelope skin, that is, leather. 7.9.

Fragrance refers to sandalwood and the like; flavor refers to oil, ghee, salt, molasses, and so forth; prepared food refers to sweetmeats, cakes, and the like; sesame seeds are well known; hemp refers to products made from *śaṇa*, such as sacks and the like; linen refers to a specific type of fine cloth produced from flax; and hide refers to skins such as those used for mats and the like. These are not to be sold. Since the prohibition regarding hemp and linen applies to their manufactured forms, there is no prohibition against their raw materials. (7.9)
Two garments dyed with red ochre. || 7.10 ||
"Red" refers to that which is dyed with lac and similar substances; "washed" means cleansed. || 7.10 ||
"Red" means dyed with lac or other dyes; "washed" means laundered by a washerman or the like. Even such garments as these are not for sale. (7.10)
Milk and its derivatives. 7.11.

"Milk" (*kṣīram*) means *payaḥ* (the liquid); [it includes] its derivatives (*vikāraiḥ*), such as curds (*dadhi*) and so forth. Here, because of the mention of "derivatives," it is understood that there is no prohibition regarding the derivatives of sesame. Alternatively, the mention of "derivatives" is for the purpose of including even the derivatives where there is a reference to milk alone. Regarding the former position, it must be stated that the mention of the derivatives of hemp and linen is for the purpose of prohibiting the primary substances themselves. (7.11)
Milk together with its derivatives, such as curd and the like, is not for sale. 7.11.
Roots, fruits, flowers, herbs, honey, meat, grass, water, and unwholesome things [are not to be accepted]. 7.12.

Roots include turmeric and the like; fruits include betel nut and the like; flowers include *damanaka* and the like; medicinal herbs include lentils and the like; honey includes that of bees and the like. Although the prohibition of honey is already established by the mention of "flavors" (*rasa*), it is stated again for the purpose of prohibiting it even under the alternative rule: "But in case of inability, one may subsist on anything" (GDh 7.22). Meat and water are well known. Grass is well known. Poison is unwholesome. 7.12.

Roots are ginger, turmeric, and so forth; fruits are betel nut and so forth; flowers are *cambaka* and so forth; medicinal herbs are long pepper and so forth; honey is that produced by bees; meat, grass, and water are well known; and unwholesome things are poison and the like—these are items that must not be sold. Although liquids (*rasa*) were already prohibited previously, the specific mention of honey here is for the purpose of prohibiting it even under those alternative positions where one’s livelihood is otherwise impossible. (7.12)
And animals [are the objects] when there is a connection with injury. 7.13.

Domestic animals, such as cows and the like, are not to be sold when associated with violence (*hiṃsā*). Although the term *yoga* (connection) would have sufficed, the prefix (*upa-sarga*) is employed to indicate that they are also not to be sold even when in the hand of a sacrificer (*yajamāna*). If it is argued that there is no association with violence because there is no fault in the act of killing in that context, that is true; however, that [permission] applies only to the sacrificer and not to anyone else. By the word "and" (*ca*), peacocks and other such creatures are also included. (7.13)
Domestic animals such as goats and others must not be sold for the purpose of slaughter to butchers and the like when such a connection with violence exists. (7.13)
And [the meat] of a human, a bull, a young girl, and a castrated animal is always [forbidden]. 7.14.

A "man" (*puruṣa*) means a human being; the mention of him includes women as well, because the term denotes the genus. Thus says the Śruti: "He places the head of a man, not that of a woman. A "barren cow" (*vaśā*) is a cow that does not bear calves. A "maiden" (*kumārī*) is also a cow; since a human maiden is female, she is already included by the mention of "man. A "barren cow" (*vehat*) is one that destroys its own fetus; she too is a cow, according to the same reasoning stated previously. The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to include the "crow-barren" cow (*kākavandhyā*) and others. Some say the word "always" (*nityam*) implies that this applies even in cases other than those involving injury (*hiṃsā*). That is incorrect, because in the case of injury, the prohibition is already established by the fact that they are animals; it is only by the force of the renewed commencement [of the rule] that the application to other cases can be understood. Others qualify the substance with the word "always," meaning "these are always of such a nature. That too is incorrect, for humans and the like might at some time not be of such a nature. Therefore, the word "always" is intended to indicate the non-permanent nature of other items such as sesame seeds. Consequently, it should be understood that sesame seeds and the like produced by one's own cultivation may be sold, whereas those produced otherwise (by others) must not be sold. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "Or, at will, they may sell sesame seeds produced by their own cultivation" (VaDh 2.31). The meaning there is: "If they may even sell sesame seeds, how much more so other things? (7.14)

"Men" refers to slaves and the like. A "vaśā" is a barren cow; a "kumārī" is a heifer; a "vehad" is a cow that destroys the embryo. These are never to be sold. Because the word "always" (nityam) is used here, the prohibition applies even in cases other than those involving injury. Another teacher says: because of the inclusion of the word "always" here, the prohibition regarding the previously mentioned items such as sesame seeds is not absolute. Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha states: "Or they may sell sesame seeds at their own will, provided they have produced them themselves. (GDh 7.14)
According to some, [the gifts] are land, rice, barley, goats, sheep, horses, bulls, milch-cows, and oxen. 7.15.

"Land" (*bhūmi*) means "house" (*gṛha*), for in the *Naighaṇṭuka* lexicon we hear it as a synonym for house in such passages as "the dwelling is the house; the house is the land, the abode. "Rice" (*vrīhi*) is well known, as is "barley" (*yava*); the mention of these two serves as an illustration for all grains. "Goat" (*aja*) is a he-goat. "Sheep" (*avi*) is well known. "Horse" (*aśva*) is a steed. "Bull" (*ṛṣabha*) is a male ox. "Milch-cow" (*dhenu*) is a cow that gives milk. "Ox" (*anaḍvān*) is a draft-ox capable of pulling a cart. These are not to be sold. Some teachers maintain that this prohibition applies even in cases other than when connected with violence, but Gautama does not hold this view. The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to include the camel, as Uśanas says: "Camels, bulls, and horses are not to be sold. Others say it is intended to draw in the notion of their being permanent (essential) property.

Land is real estate. Rice, barley, goats, sheep, and horses are well known. A bull is a cow capable of breeding. A milch-cow is one that has calved once. An ox is a draft animal fit for pulling a cart. Some maintain that these also are not for sale; however, because of the word "one" (*eka*), we permit it. Even here, the mention of goats and sheep refers specifically to cases involving the act of killing. (7.15)
But as for the exchange: 7.16.

The word "should be performed" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. *Nimaya* is the exchange of two prohibited articles. The word "tu" (but/however) indicates a distinction: the exchange may be performed whether the items are equal or inferior [in value]. And so says Vasiṣṭha: "It should be exchanged whether [the items] are equal or even inferior. (7.16)
"Restriction" (niyama) means exchange; however, by the word "but" (tu), restriction is authorized. Thus ends [the commentary on] 7.16.
By means of the flavors of flavors. || 7.17 ||

The commencement of this sūtra is for the purpose of establishing a rule: that when an exchange must be made, the exchange of liquids such as oils and the like must be made only with liquids such as molasses and so forth.

An exchange must be made using only liquids such as oil, ghee, molasses, and so forth; for example, by giving oil, one may receive ghee. Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha states: "By means of liquids, it may be equal or less" (VaDh 2.37). || 7.17 ||
And [the same applies] to animals. 7.18.

The word "ca" (and) is intended to bring in the word "paśu" (animals) as that which ends in the third case, [meaning] "with animals for animals. This should be understood as referring to animals whose sale is prohibited; for the sale of those not prohibited is already established by the very fact that they are not forbidden. (7.18)
An exchange of four-footed animals for other animals should be performed.
Nor [should one eat] salt and cooked food together. 7.19.

Salt must not be bartered for another substance that possesses flavor. This prohibition sets aside what would otherwise be obtained by the rule "substances with flavor for substances with flavor. Prepared food may be exchanged for any other substance whatsoever, as there is no such restrictive rule regarding it. (7.19)
Even the exchange of salt for cooked food is forbidden.
And [the same applies] to sesame seeds. 7.20.

The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to carry forward the prohibition of exchange; the meaning is that there is no exchange of sesame seeds for anything whatsoever. Their separate mention is for the purpose of permitting exchange with an equal amount of grain in times of distress. Thus Manu says: "Sesame seeds may be exchanged for an equal amount of grain" (MDh 10.94).
