And an exchange of sesame seeds must not be performed. The giving of salt, prepared food, or sesame seeds by receiving another substance in return is forbidden, because such an exchange is possible when the substances are of equal value. (7.20)
Now, for the purpose of providing an exception regarding cooked food, he says:
"But with equal raw meat, [one may eat] cooked [food] when there is immediate need. (7.21)

An exchange is made with that which is equal, equivalent, and unblemished; the word "now" (*samprati*) indicates that if the prepared food is consumed at that very time, the particle *tu* expresses a specific qualification, and therefore it should be understood as "with rice.
Some say that the particle *tu* serves a restrictive purpose, meaning that the exchange must be performed in that very manner and not otherwise.

That is incorrect, because the restriction is established by the very force of the commencement of the Sūtra itself. If the exchange were permitted with anything whatsoever, then, since it would already be established by the general rule "But [exchange] may be made," the commencement [of this specific rule] would be redundant. Consequently, those substances which are flavors and so forth must be exchanged only for specific substances; for the remaining three [categories], it should be understood that they may be exchanged for anything whatsoever. The meaning is that an exchange of cooked food must be made only with an equal measure of rice measured by *prastha* and other such units. And thus, the word "cooked food" (*kṛtānna*) in the phrase "scent, flavor, and cooked food" indicates that it applies to rice as well; otherwise, since there would be no prohibition against selling it, the commencement of the rule regarding exchange would not apply, because the commencement of exchange pertains only to those things that are prohibited [from being sold]. (7.21)

In the present context, a restriction regarding cooked food must be made with an equal measure—that is, with an equal quantity—of uncooked rice, for the purpose of its direct consumption. Manu, however, permits a restriction of sesame seeds by means of an equal quantity of grain, stating: "Sesame seeds are equal to grain" (MDh 10.94). Because of the prohibition against selling what is "not for sale," there would otherwise be no prohibition on purchasing as much as might be required for consumption. Furthermore, by the word "restriction" (*niyama*), only the giving away of liquids and so forth is intended; otherwise, it would be impossible to substitute other substances for liquids and the like when they are not available. (7.21)
In every way, however, one who is unable [to follow the primary rule] may subsist by means other than that of a Śūdra. 7.22.

He may also live by selling forbidden items, by bartering, by engaging in the occupations of other castes, or by combining these means. In the event of incapacity during an extreme emergency, he may even adopt the occupation of a Śūdra, provided it is not that of a Śūdra who follows the *aśaudra* (non-Śūdra) path; however, he must avoid eating the remnants of food (*ucchiṣṭa*), manual crafts for hire, and similar activities. The particle *tu* is used to indicate that there is some degree of sin in what is prescribed for times of distress. As another Smṛti has stated: "Having purified himself... (7.22).

In the manner described, the impossibility of maintaining one’s family is "incapacity. When that exists, there is "subsistence in every way. The suffix *thāl* is used here in the sense of "manner"; thus, he may live by every possible means, even those that are prohibited. Even in that case, however, he must not live by the work of a Śūdra. (7.22)
Some say that even this [is permissible] when there is a danger to life. 7.23.
Some maintain that even the work of a Śūdra is permissible when the risk of death has arisen, because life must necessarily be preserved. And so Vyāsa says:
"Life is the foundation for the existence of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa."

“By killing them, what is not killed? By protecting them, what is not protected? (MDh 10.105). Furthermore, by the mention of "life" (*prāṇa*), one's sons, wife, and so forth, whose livelihoods depend upon it, are also included, based on the observation that "these [dependents] are indeed the external breaths" (MDh 1.29). Because of the use of the word "some" (*eke*), this is not the view of Gautama, since even in such a state [of distress], it is censurable according to him. Here, because of the mention of a "danger to life," it is understood that there is also another kind of calamity (*āpad*). Consequently, that state in which the instruction for the aforementioned alternative course applies should be understood as characterized by the lack of capacity to perform the obligatory rites (*nityakarman*). As Manu says: [MDh 11.30].
"He who does not offer [oblations] to these five—the deities, guests, dependents, ancestors, and himself—does not truly live, even though he breathes. [MDh 3.72] Thus [ends verse 7.23].
However, some teachers maintain that when there is a threat to life, even that work belonging to a Śūdra is permitted. As Vyāsa has said:
"Life is the foundation for the establishment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
By killing it, what is not killed? By protecting it, what is not protected? (7.23)
But there is a restriction regarding the mixing of castes and the consumption of forbidden food. || 7.24 ||

By the term *tad* (that), the Śūdra is meant. *Saṃkara* refers to sharing a seat and so forth with him. *Abhakṣya* (unfit food) refers to his leavings and the like, or garlic and such which are unfit for him; *niyama* is the avoidance of these two. The word *tu* (but/and) expresses a distinction: that in this state, the rule applies specifically to the Brāhmaṇa. (7.24)

The rule is avoidance. Even for a Brāhmaṇa who subsists by the occupation of a Śūdra, there must be avoidance of both: *saṃkara* (mixture), such as sitting together on the same seat or physical contact with one of the Śūdra caste; and *abhakṣya* (unfit food), such as garlic and the like. He must practice this avoidance and not act according to his own whims, thinking, "I am following the occupation of a Śūdra.
Even a Brāhmaṇa may take up arms when his life is in danger. (7.25)

By the mention of "life-breaths" (*prāṇa*), sons, wife, gold, and so forth are also included, according to the scriptural insight: "For these external things are indeed life-breaths. By the word "also," Vaiśyas and Śūdras are likewise included; for a Kṣatriya, this is already established by his duty, since he is engaged in protection and other such tasks. Or else, it may apply even to a Kṣatriya. (7.25)

When there is a danger to life, even a Brāhmaṇa may take up arms for the sake of self-protection. Since taking up arms is already established by the rule that in the absence of such [weapons] one may follow the occupation of a Kṣatriya, this restatement is made to show that it does not prohibit the Brāhmaṇa from his own [peaceful] occupation even while he is in such a situation. By the use of the word "even" (api), it is implied: how much more so for a Vaiśya or a Śūdra! (7.25)
The duty of a Vaiśya belongs to a Rājanya; the duty of a Vaiśya belongs to a Vaiśya. 7.26.

If even a Kṣatriya, being unable to subsist by his own duty, should adopt the occupation of a Vaiśya, it has been stated that for him, too, there is no prohibition against forbidden goods (*apaṇya*). The commencement of this Sūtra is intended to make known that one should not conceive such a notion as: "Just as a Brāhmaṇa may follow the occupation of a Kṣatriya, so a Kṣatriya may follow the occupation of a Vaiśya; and just as a Brāhmaṇa may follow the occupation of a Vaiśya, so a Kṣatriya may follow the occupation of a Śūdra. Why? If it were intended for others [the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya] as it is for the Brāhmaṇa, then he would have said that all [castes] may adopt the occupation of the one immediately following or the one separated by one degree. Since he did not say that, but rather began with "The Rājanya [Kṣatriya] the occupation of a Vaiśya," it makes known that the occupation prescribed for a Kṣatriya in times of distress applies only to him, and not to the Vaiśya or the Śūdra; furthermore, it indicates that even for a Kṣatriya, there is no occupation of a Śūdra. Consequently, a Kṣatriya may indeed adopt the occupation of a Vaiśya in times of distress. And so says Manu: [Manu 10.97].
"A Kṣatriya who has fallen into distress may live by all of this," [Manu Dharma Śāstra 10.95]. Thus ends section 7.26.
In a life-threatening crisis, a Kṣatriya may take up the occupation of a Vaiśya; by that means he should protect himself. (The repetition indicates the end of the chapter. 7.26
Now begins the eighth chapter.

Now, if someone should become involved in an action prescribed for times of distress (*āpad*) out of ignorance of its defects or out of greed, by whom is he to be restrained? By the king and the Brahmin, through instruction and punishment respectively. For it is they alone who [restrain him].
To the question, "If one who has resorted to a livelihood in times of distress should take pleasure in that very same [action], by whom is he to be restrained?", the author says:
In this world, two are firm in their vows: the king and the learned Brāhmaṇa. || 8.1 ||

The word "two" (*dvau*) expresses excellence and is not intended as a numerical designation, since duality is already established by the dual number itself. There are indeed instances where a numerical designation serves to indicate excellence, such as: "In this village, there are only two Brāhmaṇas. In that case, it is understood that while there are other Brāhmaṇas as well, these two alone are devoted to the performance of religious duties (*anuṣṭhāna*). Here too, the purpose is to show that the King and the Brāhmaṇa possess vows with particular excellence, not to exclude others. The inclusion of the word "world" (*loka*) is for the sake of distributive repetition (*vipsā*); the meaning is "in every world," that is, in every kingdom. Otherwise, since all activities fall within the domain of the world, this [specification] would be redundant. Thus, it is understood that just as one must be a king in every kingdom, so too must one be deeply learned (*bahuśruta*). They are "upholders of vows" (*dhṛtavratau*), meaning they are the sustainers of religious observances and rites. The "king" (*rājā*) is a Kṣatriya, and he is endowed with qualities such as consecration (*abhiṣeka*), according to the statement of Śaṅkha: "He becomes a king when consecrated on the head. And the Brāhmaṇa is "deeply learned. Although the Brāhmaṇa holds primacy, the mention of the king first is for the purpose of qualifying him as being deeply learned. The particle *ca* (and) is used to draw in the quality of deep learning for the king as well. Therefore, it should be understood that the king too must be deeply learned, though the Brāhmaṇa is especially so. "Deeply learned" (*bahuśruta*) means one by whom much has been heard. While one might have said "the king and Brāhmaṇa are deeply learned," the use of a non-compound construction (*visamāsa*) is for the purpose of showing that the king also possesses qualities such as valor in an eminent degree. Consequently, the ellipsis is to be supplied: "those two should be upholders of vows. (8.1)

The world is the kingdom; here, the repetition [of the word] should be understood as being elided. In every world, there are two who uphold the vows—that is, the sustainers of vows, which are actions: the king and the highly learned Brāhmaṇa. These two are the preventers of all calamities for everyone, by means of punishment and instruction. 8.1.

For: "The life of those two [the gods and the ancestors], as well as that of the fourfold class of humans and of those possessing internal consciousness—namely, those that move, fall, and crawl—is dependent upon them. (8.2)

Because these two are mentioned together with a common designation, the meaning is "of the fourfold human race," that is, the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*). "Those with internal consciousness" refers to those born in the natural and inverse orders (*anuloma-pratiloma*), as well as the gods, according to the Vedic revelation: "For from this [human] offering, the gods subsist. "The moving" are the stationary beings such as trees; "the flying" are the birds; and "the crawling" are the insects and so forth. Their life—the maintenance of vital breath—is dependent upon these [Brāhmaṇas]. How so? Those belonging to the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramiṇaḥ*), when favored by the Brāhmaṇa, engage in activities for visible and invisible purposes; through the performance of these rites, they contribute to the welfare of the world by means of rain and other effects. Thus, their existence is dependent on the Brāhmaṇa. And so says Manu: [Manu 1.97–98] "Just as all living beings exist by depending on the air, so do all orders and castes exist by depending on the Brāhmaṇa. Just as all sacrifices, rituals, and works, as well as the three Vedas, depend on the Brāhmaṇa, so does everything depend on him. And likewise: [Manu 1.100] "Upon the Brāhmaṇa depends the protection of this whole world, both seen and unseen; therefore, the entire world rests upon the Brāhmaṇa. And: [Manu 1.102] "From the Brāhmaṇa arose the Brahman-knowledge, from the Brāhmaṇa arose the Kṣatra, and from the Brāhmaṇa arose the Vaiśya; from the Brāhmaṇa alone arose the Śūdra. And: [Manu 1.93] "Whatever exists in this world, whether moving or unmoving, has its root in the Brāhmaṇa; know that to be the fruit of the Brāhmaṇa's power. And: [Manu 1.99] "The Brāhmaṇa is the root of this whole world, the source of the Kṣatriya, and the origin of the Vaiśya and the Śūdra. And: [Manu 1.101] "When the Brāhmaṇa is satisfied, his satisfaction nourishes the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra; therefore, one should always satisfy the Brāhmaṇa. And: [Manu 1.103] "The Brāhmaṇa is the highest among beings; he is the first-born and the eldest. He was created for the protection of this whole world. And: [Manu 1.104] "The Brāhmaṇa is the lord of all beings, the protector of the world, and the guardian of the treasury of the sacred law (*dharma*). And: [Manu 1.105] "The Brāhmaṇa is the father, the teacher, and the ruler of all people; there is no one equal to him, much less anyone superior. And: [Manu 1.106] "The Brāhmaṇa is the root of the sacred law, the source of the Kṣatriya, and the progenitor of the Vaiśya and the Śūdra. And: [Manu 1.107] "The Brāhmaṇa is the highest among bipeds, the middlemost among quadrupeds, and the foremost among those who possess internal consciousness. And: [Manu 1.131] "The Brāhmaṇa is the highest among bipeds, the middlemost among quadrupeds, and the foremost among those who possess internal consciousness. And

"A libation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun," and so forth. Furthermore, the king is a direct cause of livelihood by means of suppressing highway robbers and by means of restraining violence. (8.2)

The intermediate origins of the fourfold human race—the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*)—such as those born in the natural order (*anuloma*) and so forth, are not mentioned separately because they are rooted in those [four]. "Those with internal consciousness" refers to immobile beings such as trees, which possess growth and decay; they are so called because their consciousness is internal and not external. And thus says Manu:
"Driven by manifold darkness, caused by karma..."

"These possess internal consciousness and are endowed with both pleasure and pain" (MDh 1.49). "Moving" refers to animals and the like; "flying" refers to birds; "creeping" refers to reptiles, such as snakes and the like. The livelihood of these beings, beginning with humans, is dependent upon those two—the king and the Brahmin—and subject to them. The king, moreover, is the cause of their livelihood by means of suppressing adversaries and other such duties. But how is the other [the Brahmin] "highly learned"? To this he says: "The oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun."
"From the sun rain is born; from rain, food; from that, living beings"—by such reasoning, this is the cause of life. (8.2)
And not merely their livelihood depends on them; what then? "Their duty consists in procreation, protection, and the prevention of intermixture. (8.3)

H reads: "The protection of progeny. Progeny means growth, and that [growth] depends upon him; for through his instruction on the wielding of punishment toward kings and Brahmins, they act as prescribed, and because of the absence of calamities such as disease by way of rain and so forth, growth occurs. Furthermore, protection from thieves and others results from the wielding of punishment and the instruction on expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*); and the absence of social confusion (*saṃkara*) results from the instruction on restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*). Since punishment is wielded against the non-performance of what is enjoined and the practice of what is forbidden, even *dharma* itself depends entirely upon him. (8.3)

"Procreation" means growth. Growth occurs through punishment and instruction by way of causing people to act as prescribed, through rain and other such means, and by the pacification of afflictions such as disease. Protection also results from the suppression of thieves. Furthermore, the non-confusion—that is, the non-mixture—of the social classes (varṇas) arises through the application of punishment and the prescription of penances. Dharma also comes about through instruction on what is enjoined and the imposition of punishment for the practice of what is forbidden. All of this depends upon those two [punishment and instruction]. (8.3)
Now, by how much learning does one become "one who has heard much"?
To this he says: he demonstrates what is meant by "one who has heard much":
"He is such a one who has heard much. (8.4)

“This is that” is an instruction combining the indirect and the direct. Regarding the statement, “But what has been heard is weightier than all [other virtues]” (GDh 6.22), it is this very same kind [of learning] that is intended there as well. The meaning of “he becomes one who has heard much” (bahuśruta) is that he attains such a state. The inclusion of the verb *bhavati* (“becomes”) is for the purpose of indicating that even if one possesses only a slight understanding of these [subjects] such as the worlds, or has heard something else besides, one nevertheless truly “becomes” a learned man; otherwise, the status of being a *bahuśruta* would already be established by the mere fact of having heard much. (8.4)
"This very one" is the reference to what will be stated hereafter. 8.4.
One who knows the worlds, the Vedas, and the Vedāṅgas. || 8.5 ||

By the word *loka*, worldly conventions such as village boundaries and the like are expressed. By the first word *veda*, the *upavedas* such as Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, and so forth are expressed. By the second word *veda*, the four Vedas are expressed. By the word *aṅga*, grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), phonetics (*śikṣā*), prosody (*chandas*), ritual manuals (*kalpasūtra*), astronomy (*jyotiṣa*), and etymology (*nirukta*) are expressed. The word *vi* (in *vicchabdaḥ*) is connected with each [of the preceding terms]. By the phrase "one who knows the Vedas" (*vedavit*), the recitation of the Vedas (*vedapāṭha*) should also be understood, because another Smṛti prohibits other branches of knowledge for one who has not studied the Veda. As Manu says:

"A twice-born man who, without having studied the Vedas, exerts himself in other pursuits, quickly falls to the status of a Śūdra while still alive, along with his lineage. [MDh 2.168] Thus [ends verse 8.5].

By the word "world" (loka), the customs of regions and so forth established by worldly convention are meant. Of these, the Vedas are four: the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharvaṇa. The auxiliary sciences (aṅgas) are six: grammar, phonetics, prosody, astronomy, the ritual manuals (kalpasūtras), and etymology as well. One who knows these, both in their recitation and in their meaning, is [a knower of the world]. (8.5)
He is skilled in dialogues, discourses, histories, and ancient lore.
"Vākovākya" means a treatise on logic (*tarkaśāstra*) consisting of statements and counter-statements; thus says Manu:

"He who investigates by means of reasoning knows Dharma, and no other" (MDh 12.106). Itihāsa refers to the *Mahābhārata* and the *Rāmāyaṇa*. Purāṇa is that wherein the creation, maintenance, and dissolution [of the world] are described; such is the *Purāṇa*, beginning with the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*. One should be proficient (*nipuṇa*) in these as well, but only in their meanings, not as in the case of the former [Vedas], where proficiency pertained to both the text and the meaning, because here a different type of verbal action is commenced. And thus, one should study not only the Veda alone, but also its auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*). Accordingly, another Smṛti states: "The Veda, together with its auxiliaries, is to be studied. (8.6)

Sentences consisting of arguments and counter-arguments useful for the Vedic scriptures; for example, in the *Mahābhārata*, such as "Who indeed wanders alone? The sun wanders alone," and so forth—this is *vākovākya*. The *itihāsa* consists of the *Mahābhārata*, the *Rāmāyaṇa*, and others. The *purāṇa* is of eighteen kinds, such as the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* and the *Śivapurāṇa*. One who is skilled in these is *samartha* (competent). 8.6.
Depending on that, it functions therein. || 8.7 ||

Dependent upon that [the Veda], he is one whose habit is the recitation of the meanings established by the Veda; his livelihood consists of being intent on the performance of the rituals prescribed therein. 8.7
"Regarding those [worlds] beginning with 'the world' which have been mentioned, he 'looks toward' them; that is, he is the performer of the rites prescribed therein. (8.7)
It is conditioned by forty formative factors. || 8.8 ||
He was consecrated with forty purificatory rites. || 8.8 ||

And these are the rites to be described hereafter, beginning with *garbhādhāna* (conception); he is one who is endowed with them. Since their nature is already established by the fact that they will be described, the specific mention of their number is intended to preclude the sense of mere conjunction (*samuccaya*). Because of the use of the plural number, the requirement is fulfilled by three or more. If it is argued that even in the passage, “But for whom even a single portion of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*)... (GDh 8.25), the word “even” (*api*) implies conjunction, we say no; for the word “portion” (*ekadeśa*) would then redundantly imply a part of the rites themselves. Therefore, because conjunction is explicitly stated here, it follows that in other cases where the term “portion” is used, it serves to include only a few of the purificatory rites. 8.8.
Forty sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*), beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*) and so forth, will be described; he is consecrated by these. 8.8.
One who delights in the three types of action. || 8.9 ||

These—characterized by Vedic study together with its ancillaries (aṅga), giving, and sacrifice—are those mentioned here in the rule: "Vedic study for the twice-born" (GDh 10.1). One who is devoted to them is one whose habit is their constant performance. Although the performance is already established by the rule "subsisting by that" (GDh 8.7), this is commenced again for the sake of specification. The specification consists either in the practice of these with excellence or in making known that they serve a transcendental purpose (adṛṣṭārtha). 8.9.

Sacrifice, study, and giving are the three activities; he is devoted to them, a performer of them continuously. Although this is already established by the phrase "one whose livelihood is that," the repetition is for the sake of extreme firmness. (8.9)
Or in six [fingers]. 8.10.

Together with officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and receiving gifts, there are six [occupations]. This is restated again for the purpose of making it known that these also have an invisible (adṛṣṭa) purpose. 8.10.

Together with officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and receiving gifts, there are six duties; he is devoted to these. By the word "or" (vā), there is a restriction to those previously mentioned. 8.10.
He is thoroughly trained in the rules of customary conduct. || 8.11 ||

The *sāmayika* (conventional) rules are those recorded in the *Smṛtis*; the *ācārika* (customary) matters are those practiced by the learned (*śiṣṭa*) which are not so recorded. He is thoroughly trained in both these types of rites, knowing them and being devoted to their performance. (8.11)

"Conventional rule" (*samaya*) refers to human-established ordinance. The practices rooted in that are "conventional practices" (*samayācāra*); those duties pertaining to them are "conventional-observance duties" (*sāmayācārika*), namely the duties prescribed by tradition (*smārta*). One who is "thoroughly disciplined" (*abhivinīta*) in these is one who has been properly instructed by his father and others. (8.11)
Such is the brahmin;
such indeed is the brahmin.
He is one who must be exempted by the king—neither to be killed, nor to be bound, nor to be punished with fines, nor to be banished, nor to be censured, nor to be avoided. (8.12)
A king should avoid [these] six things. 8.12.

Even if an offense occurs unintentionally that would otherwise merit execution or similar punishment, because there is no possibility of such an act occurring intentionally—since [the rule] applies to intentional acts—he should be exempted from the six [punishments]. The mention of "six" implies this even when the offenses are cumulative. "Execution" (*vadha*) means repeated beating; since that is not applicable here, it is excluded. "Imprisonment" (*bandha*) is the binding with shackles and the like. "Fine" (*daṇḍa*) is the confiscation of wealth. "Exile" (*bahiṣkaraṇa*) is banishment from the village or other settlements. "Censure" (*parivāda*) is the public proclamation of one's faults. "Abandonment" (*parihāra*) is the act of renouncing [him]. The word "and" (*ca*) has the purpose of indicating that he should not be a consenter nor an instigator. The particle "iti" indicates a manner; consequently, one should not engage in conversation or other forms of interaction with him. (8.12)
He is to be avoided by the king through the six [punishments], beginning with execution, which will be described hereafter. "Avoidance" (parihāra) means exclusion. 8.12.
He states those [qualities], beginning with non-killing:
"He is not to be killed, nor to be imprisoned, nor to be punished, nor to be banished, nor to be censured, nor to be avoided" (8.13).

Killing is beating; binding is fettering; punishment is the confiscation of wealth; banishment is expulsion from the village and so forth; reviling is the proclamation of faults; and exclusion is abandonment. These six—beginning with killing—are to be avoided by the king when committed unintentionally against a learned Brāhmaṇa, because there is no possibility of repetition in the case of intentional acts. The word "iti" indicates manner; thus, whatever else is of this kind, such as censuring [his character], that too is to be avoided. (8.13)
It has been stated, “by means of forty sacraments” (GDh 8.8). As to what these are, he states them:

“The forty sacraments have been mentioned; he states them: conception, the rite for a male child, parting the hair, birth-rite, naming, the first feeding of solid food, the tonsure, and initiation. (8.13–8.14)

The *garbhādhāna* (conception) and other rites are prescribed in the *Pratigṛhya* texts; however, their mention here is for the purpose of making known their status as *saṃskāras* (purificatory rites). Their status as *saṃskāras* has also been stated by Manu: "From conception (*niṣeka*) until the end at the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*)" (MDh 2.16), and so forth. The *garbhādhāna* occurs precisely during the menstrual period; one should look to the *Pratigṛhya* texts for the details, such as "having offered oblations at the time of cohabitation" (*saṃveśane hutvā*). The *puṃsavana* (rite for ensuring a male child) is enjoined for the third month, but only in the first pregnancy and not otherwise; furthermore, it must be performed when the fetus is manifest. Some authorities maintain that it should be performed for every pregnancy, while others hold that it is done only once. The same applies to the *sīmantonnayana* (parting of the hair); it is enjoined for the fourth, sixth, or eighth month. The *jātakarma* (birth rite) should also be understood as occurring before the infant's tasting of breast milk, the eating of solid food, or the cutting of the umbilical cord. The naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*) takes place on the tenth or twelfth day, or under an auspicious lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). The *annaprāśana* (first feeding of solid food) occurs in the sixth month or after one year, as Śaṅkha says: "The *annaprāśana* is performed after one year or in the sixth month. The *caula* (tonsure) occurs in the first year or the third. The *upanayana* (initiation) has already been discussed. The *upaniṣkramaṇa* (taking out of the house) is not mentioned here because it is included within the *annaprāśana*; this was stated by Manu.
"In the fourth month, the infant's first exit from the house should be performed" (MDh 2.34). Thus [ends verse 8.13].

This is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāradvandva*). *Garbhādhāna* (conception) refers to the *niṣeka* (impregnation) performed according to the procedure prescribed by the authors of the Sūtras, such as the rule for the timing: "One should approach [the wife] during her season" (*ṛtāv upeyāt*, GDh 5.1). The sacraments beginning with *garbhādhāna* are described in their respective Gṛhya-sūtras; however, here, only a mere definition of their essential nature has been provided for the purpose of enumerating the sacraments. (8.14)
Furthermore: there are four Vedic vows. 8.14–8.15.
The separate instruction is for the purpose of grasping the Veda; the mention of "Veda" is for the sake of indicating that four [verses] are to be learned from each Veda. (8.14)
These [rites] are prescribed in the Gṛhyasūtras for each Veda and for each branch [of the Veda]. 8.15.
Furthermore: bathing; union with one’s partner in dharma; and the performance of the five sacrifices toward the gods, ancestors, humans, spirits, and Brahman—these [are the duties]. 8.15.
Bathing and union with the partner in dharma. 8.16.

Bathing refers to the completion of Vedic studies (*samāvartana*). Marriage is the union with a partner in the practice of dharma (*sahadharmacāriṇī-saṃyoga*). The term *visamāsa* (separation) is intended to indicate that marriage does not necessarily follow immediately after bathing. While one could have simply said "marriage," the inclusion of the term *sahadharmacāriṇī* is for the purpose of indicating that taking a wife is for the sake of performing ritual acts (*karma*). Consequently, there is no fault in the case of one who has not taken a wife or one who is widowed, provided there is an absence of the five sacrifices and so forth. The performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) means the carrying out of the five sacrifices, beginning with the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*). The use of the genitive case (*pañcānāṃ yajñānām*) is for the purpose of connecting them with the act of performance. The inclusion of the word "performance" is not to imply that they occur only occasionally like the *agniṣṭoma* and other such rites; rather, it is for the purpose of showing that they must be performed "day after day. Although the five great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*) are indeed the sacrifices to the gods and so on, the explicit mention of the gods and others is for the purpose of indicating that there are five distinct sacraments (*saṃskāras*); otherwise, there might be the suspicion that the performance of the five sacrifices constitutes only a single sacrament. The gods and the others have already been explained. The particle *ca* (and) in the phrase "of these" (*eteṣāṃ ca*) is for the purpose of aggregating the personal qualities (*ātmaguṇa*). Thus, it is established that the five sacrifices, when accompanied by personal qualities, alone lead to the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), and not when they exist separately. The term "of these" (*eteṣām*) is an elliptical reference (*upalakṣaṇa*) to those [qualities] that will be mentioned later, and not merely to the five sacrifices already stated. Why? If it were intended that only the five sacrifices were to be accompanied by personal qualities, then he would have said, "the performance of the five sacrifices together with their qualities. Therefore, it should be understood that even the qualities to be mentioned later, when accompanied by personal qualities, lead to union with Brahman (*brahmasāyujya*). (8.15)
The ritual bath is the ceremony of returning home; marriage is the union with a partner for the practice of dharma. 8.16.
The performance of the five sacrifices is for the sake of the gods, the ancestors, humans, spirits, and Brahman. 8.17.

The sacrifices of the five classes of gods constitute their performance; this performance of the five great sacrifices (pañcamahāyajña) must be carried out day by day. However, the purification (saṃskāra) is not accomplished by performing them only once. Because of the mention of "five," these five are distinct purifications and do not, when combined, constitute a single purification.
And of these [eighteen], || 8.18 ||
The performance of the pākayajñas, such as the aṣṭakās and others that will be described hereafter, constitutes a saṃskāra. (8.18)
He said to them:
"The Aṣṭakā, the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha, the Śrāvaṇī, the Āgrahāyaṇī, the Caitrī, and the Āśvayujī—these are the seven forms of the Pākayajña. (8.16–8.19)

“The three dark fortnights following the full moon of Āgrahāyaṇī—in each of these, one [rite] occurs; these are called the Aṣṭakās. The *pārvaṇa* is the *sthālīpāka*; it is called *pārvaṇa* because it takes place on a *parvan* (a festival day). The *śrāddha* is called the *māsi-śrāddha*. By the word *śrāvaṇī*, the *upākaraṇa* is meant, because it is connected with the full moon of the month of Śrāvaṇa. By the word *āgrahāyaṇī*, the *āgrahāyaṇa* is meant. By the word *caitrī*, the *śūlagava* is meant. By *āśvayujī*, the *indradhvaja-homa* is meant. The mention of the number “seven” is for the purpose of counting each one individually. The mention of *pāka* is for the purpose of connecting them with the *sthālīpāka*. The mention of *yajña* is for the purpose of connecting them with the sacred fire (*agni*). The term *saṃsthāḥ* means they are properly established; the meaning is that they have been fully described in the *Gṛhyasūtra* itself. (8.16)

The Chandogas maintain that there are three dark fortnights following the Āgrahāyaṇī full moon, and in each of these there is one Ekāṣṭakā. Āśvalāyana says that there is an Aṣṭakā on the eighth day of each of the four dark fortnights of the winter and cool seasons. Āpastamba states: "That which occurs after the middle full moon of the winter season is the Madhyāṣṭakā; the eighth day of that [fortnight] coincides with the Jyeṣṭhā nakṣatra, and they call that the Ekāṣṭakā. Such is the Aṣṭakā. A *sthālīpāka* (cooked offering) performed on a *parvan* (festival day) is called *pārvaṇa*. The *māsi-śrāddha* is the monthly ancestral rite. The *Śrāvaṇī* is the universal offering (*sarvabali*). Regarding this, the Chandogas state: "On the full moon of Śrāvaṇa, having brought forward the domestic fire," and so forth. Āpastamba says: "On the full moon of Śrāvaṇa, when the sun has set, the *sthālīpāka* [is offered]. The *Āgrahāyaṇī* is the snake-offering (*sarpabali*) and the *utsargahoma* performed on the full moon of Mārgaśīrṣa. The rite known as *pratyavarohaṇa* (the descent) in the winter is also designated by the term *Āgrahāyaṇī*. The *Caitrī* is the *śūlagava* (the spit-ox sacrifice), well-known among the followers of Āpastamba; it takes place on the full moon of Caitra. However, Āśvalāyana says the *śūlagava* occurs in autumn or spring. The Chandogas say: "For Rudra, on the full moon of Āśvayuja. Āśvalāyana prescribes the performance of that rite on the full moon of Āśvayuja: "Having adorned themselves, bathed, and put on clean clothes, they should offer a *sthālīpāka* to Paśupati and sacrifice it. For one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice also takes place at that very time. These two rites are intended here by the term *Āśvayujī*. "Pākayajña" is the name for the group of rites according to Gārya. As Āpastamba says: "The term *pākayajña* applies to worldly (domestic) rites. This means there are seven types of *pākayajña* rites, categorized by their specific forms. 8.19.

The establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), the fire-oblation (agnihotra), the new- and full-moon sacrifices (darśapaurṇamāsa), the first-fruits sacrifice (āgrayaṇa), the four-monthly sacrifices (cāturmāsya), the independent animal sacrifice (nirūḍhapaśubandha), and the Sautrāmaṇī—these are the seven forms of the haviryajña. (8.17–8.20)

H reads: "The mention of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices is a restatement of rites well-known from the Śruti, intended to show that they are purificatory (*saṃskāra*) acts. Here, by the word *āgrayaṇa*, the *āgrahāyaṇī-ṣṭi* is meant, because the other [sacrifice] has already been mentioned previously. By *agnyādheya*, the *ādhāna* (the laying of the fires) is meant. The *agnihotra* is a *haviḥ-yajña* (oblation sacrifice) well known in the Śruti. However, among the purificatory acts, the *darśapūrṇamāsa* constitutes only one [single composite rite]. The others are well known [as individual acts]. The purpose of mentioning the number 'seven' has already been stated; the same applies to the remainder. (8.17)

The *agnyādheya* and other rites established by Śruti are enumerated among the purificatory ceremonies (*saṃskāras*). Because of the mention of "seven," the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) constitute a single purificatory ceremony as a collective unit. They are called "sacrifices of cooked offerings" (*haviryajña*) because they lack a connection with the Soma.
The Agniṣṭoma, the Atyagniṣṭoma, the Ukthya, the Ṣoḍaśī, the Vājapeya, the Atirātra, and the Aptoryāma—these are the seven forms of the Soma sacrifice. 8.18–21.

The Sūtra is to be explained by the very same principle already stated. The separate mention of the *pākayajña*s and so forth is for the purpose of making known that they have distinct results. (8.18)

The Agniṣṭoma belongs to a Kṣatriya. That sacrifice where the Ṣoḍaśin cup is drawn is the Atirātra-agniṣṭoma. It must be considered how this [Atyagniṣṭoma] can be a purificatory rite for a Brāhmaṇa; the others are well known. 8.21.
Thus, these are the forty formative forces (saṃskāra). || 8.19 || — 8.22 ||

"Thus these"—this is the conclusion of what has been stated. "Forty" is for the purpose of restriction, meaning that there are exactly this many purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*). Consequently, one becomes endowed with the complete accomplishment of all Smārta and Śrauta rituals. 8.20.

This concludes the summary. Because forty [items] are mentioned, there are exactly that many purificatory rites (saṃskāras). The others are the Smārta rituals, such as those performed for specific desires (kāmya) and so forth.
Now, the eight qualities of the self: 8.20–8.23.

The word "will be stated" (*vakṣyanti*) is the ellipsis to be supplied. The word *atha* signifies "immediately following"; thus, the meaning is that the qualities of the self (*ātmaguṇāḥ*) will be stated immediately after the [eight] purificatory rites (*saṃskārāḥ*). Some hold that the mention of "eight" is for the purpose of indicating that all these [qualities] are to be combined with the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna*, and not taken according to their availability. That is incorrect, because it would result in the redundancy of the mention of "eight" in the passage: "But he who has even a portion of the purificatory rites, [namely] the eight qualities of the self. Therefore, the statement is for the sake of a technical designation (*saṃjñā*), so that wherever the "eight qualities of the self" are mentioned, it may be understood that compassion (*dayā*) and the others alone are intended. The creation of this heavy technical term is for the purpose that only those [qualities] taken together should be included.
The word "will speak" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The word "atha" (now/then) is used in the sense of possibility or introduction.
Compassion toward all beings, patience, freedom from envy, purity, lack of weariness, auspiciousness, lack of miserliness, and lack of possessiveness. (8.21–8.24)
Compassion (*dayā*) is the thought of the welfare [of others]. Thus it is stated in the Purāṇa:
"He who always acts for the sake of the auspicious and the welfare of all beings as if they were himself, being ever joyful—this indeed is remembered as complete compassion."
Because of the inclusion of the term "all," this applies even to stationary beings (*sthāvara*). Patience (*kṣānti*) is the endurance of both external and internal dualities. As Vyāsa said:
"Whether reviled or even struck, one should neither revile nor strike back;
being free from malice in speech, mind, and body—that is remembered as *titikṣā*, which is forbearance (*kṣamā*)."

Anasūyā is the absence of malice toward those possessed of virtues. As it has been said: "The wise person who never feels hatred toward one who attains dharma, artha, kāma, or even mokṣa—that is remembered as anasūyā."
Purity (*śauca*) refers to the purity of objects and so forth. As Vyāsa has said:

"The seers who perceive reality have declared that purity is fourfold: purity of objects, purity of mind, purity of speech, and likewise purity of body. Effortlessness (*anāyāsa*) is the non-commencement of self-inflicted suffering. As Vyāsa has said:

"That which causes constant and extreme distress to oneself at its very commencement should be avoided, even if it be righteous; that is called 'effortlessness' (anāyāsa). Thus, auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) is indeed praiseworthy. As Vyāsa said:

"The constant practice of what is praiseworthy and the avoidance of what is blameworthy—this indeed is declared to be auspiciousness by the sages who perceive the truth. [And] lack of miserliness even in adversity, absence of dejection, and a delight in sharing. As Vyāsa said:
"Even in the midst of terrible adversity, one should not become dejected toward anyone."
And one should have a delight in sharing; that is called non-miserliness.

Freedom from longing (*aspṛhā*) is contentment with one's own objects and the absence of desire for the property of others. As Vyāsa said: "A man should always avoid longing for sense-objects and desire for the property of others;

this is called 'freedom from longing' by the wise. The use of the particle *iti* is for the purpose of concluding [the definition], signifying that such is the refinement (*saṃskāra*) to be performed by a person. The use of a compound (*visamāsa*) is for the purpose of indicating the distinctness of the results. As Vyāsa said:
The patient man conquers the earth; the compassionate man enjoys happiness;
the man free from envy attains heaven, and through purity, he attains the supreme self.
He is to be honored even more than the auspicious deities in this world and the next;
through effortless means, he attains equality with the gods, and through lack of miserliness, he achieves dissolution into the primordial nature.

"One who is free from desire always obtains infinite bliss, as well as the station of Brahman through all purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) and likewise [other means]. Thus, even when nothing at all is obtained, one should accept whatever may be obtained, because the scripture declares that there is a distinct fruit even for such [limited] acceptance. (8.21)
That which proceeds constantly with joy for the welfare and the auspiciousness of all beings as if they were oneself—this indeed is remembered as universal compassion. (1)
Whether reviled or even struck, one should neither revile nor strike in return;
being free from malice in speech, mind, and body—that is remembered as endurance and patience. (2)
The wise man who never feels resentment toward one who attains virtue, wealth, pleasure, and even liberation— that, according to the learned, is remembered as freedom from envy.
Purity of substance, purity of mind, as well as purity of speech and purity of body—thus has fourfold purity been proclaimed by the seers who perceive the truth. (4)
If, at the outset, there should be constant and extreme suffering for oneself, one should avoid that even if it is consistent with dharma; that is proclaimed as being without exertion.
The constant practice of what is praiseworthy and the avoidance of what is blameworthy—this indeed is declared as auspiciousness by the sages who perceive reality. (6)
Even in the midst of dire adversity, he should not become dejected toward anyone;
rather, he should take delight in sharing [his resources]—this is called "freedom from wretchedness. (7)

A man should always avoid discontent regarding sense objects and the longing for the wealth of others; this is what is called "freedom from desire" by the wise. (8) Thus, in the manner described, there are eight qualities of the self. (8.24)
He states their excellence:
"He who possesses these forty purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) but lacks the eight qualities of the self does not attain union with or residence in the same world as Brahman. (8.22–8.25)

The phrase "of which man" (*yasya tu puruṣasya*) refers to the person; the reference to these [qualities] by the term *ete* (these) is for the sake of honoring the virtues. The number "forty" is intended to indicate that even when combined, they lack independent efficacy. Furthermore, the eight qualities of the self are both taken collectively and individually, as indicated by the word "and" (*ca*). This too is a praise of the qualities. "He does not go to union with or residence in the same world as Brahman": *Brahmā* here refers to a specific deity. *Sāyujya* is oneness of essence; *sālokya* is dwelling in the same realm. And this censure is solely for the purpose of praising the qualities. Because of its preeminence, *sāyujya* is mentioned first. (8.22)
Sālokya is the state of residing in the same world. Sālokya arises from conjunction with one part [of the deity], while sāyujya arises from complete union. || 8.25 ||

But indeed, he for whom even a single portion of these conditioned factors consists of the eight qualities of the self, goes to, goes to union with and residence in the same world as Brahman. 8.23–8.26.

The word *tu* expresses a distinction, meaning that by the mention of a single part, only the *upanayana* (initiation) is intended. The word *khalu* is used for emphasis, meaning "he alone goes. From the word *api*, it follows that even all [the rites] together [lead there]. From the word *atha*, it is understood that he goes immediately after [the initiation]. It should be understood that through connection with a single part one attains *sālokya* (residing in the same world), while through connection with all [the parts] one attains *sāyujya* (union). This, too, is a praise of the qualities [of the rite]. 8.23.

The word *tu* expresses a distinction. The word *khalu* indicates well-known fact. He for whom there exists even a connection with only a few of the forty purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) rooted in the status of the twice-born, yet who possesses the eight qualities of the self—he indeed attains union with and residence in the same world as Brahman; this is the meaning of the word *atha*, which serves here to specify. [The repetition marks the end of the chapter. 8.26
Now begins the ninth chapter.
The superior observance of vows by the king and the Brahmin has been stated. Now, for the purpose of describing the nature of those vows and for determining their duration, he says:

"Having bathed according to the prescribed rule and having taken a wife, the Snātaka, while practicing the duties of a householder as they have been declared, should observe these following vows. (9.1)
While practicing the duties of a householder, he should observe these vows. 9.1.

The word "he" (*saḥ*) is used to refer individually to both the king and the Brahmin. "According to rule" (*vidhipūrvam*) means by means of the scriptural injunction; because of the inclusion of the word "preceded by," this implies that it may be by means of knowledge, by means of a vow, or by both. Otherwise, one would have simply said "according to rule" (*vidhivat*). The mention of "having bathed" (*snātvā*), although already implied by the statement regarding the acquisition of a wife, is stated for the purpose of making it known that the "bath" (*snāna*) refers specifically to the formal entry into the householder stage of life (*gṛhasthāśrama*), and not to the undertaking of any other stage of life. "Having acquired a wife" (*bhāryām adhigamya*) means having taken a spouse.

Regarding this, some explain that after bathing, one must take a wife, because of the use of the suffix *ktvā* [indicating immediate sequence], and because it is improper for one to remain without belonging to an āśrama.

That is incorrect, because immediate succession (*ānantarya*) is impossible; for the acquisition of a maiden depends on others, and because other *smṛtis* prescribe a fixed time for marriage. As Uśanas says: “A thirty-year-old man should marry a maiden. Even in that case, since the matter is already established by the very injunction regarding the time for the ceremonial bath (*snāna*), it need not be stated again, both because of established custom and because no one is observed to perform an expiation after the bath without first performing the marriage, nor is such a person censured by the learned (*śiṣṭas*). Furthermore, there is the instruction to wait for the northern solstice (*udagayana*), the waxing fortnight, and an auspicious day; and in the *Mānava Dharma Śāstra*, there is the instruction regarding the state of one who has not yet married: “one who seeks offspring, one who is about to sacrifice” (MDh 11.1). Moreover, even in that context, it is stated: “for the sake of his teacher, or for entering a household” (GDh 5.22). Grammarians maintain that the suffix *-ktvā* merely denotes priority in time. Even the mention of immediate succession is intended to prohibit the householder’s life for one who has not performed the bath; thus, marriage must be performed immediately after bathing.

As for what was said—that it is improper for one who does not belong to an āśrama to remain [without one]—to that it is replied: he is certainly not such a person (anāśramin). How so? Having completed his student life (brahmacarya) and bathed according to the permission of his teacher, for as long a time as he remains engaged in effort until he obtains a wife, during that period he is one who has undertaken the vows of a *snātaka* and whose student life is unimpaired; thus, he is indeed included within the householder stage (*gṛhastha*). For this very reason, in the rule "A householder [should marry] a suitable [woman]" [GDh 4.1], the term "householder" is employed even with respect to one who has not yet performed the marriage ceremony.

Nor is this state of residence indefinite in duration, because other Smṛtis prescribe the undertaking of the stages of life (*āśrama*) within a division of the lifespan. As Manu says: "The fourth part of one's lifespan... (MDh 4.1), and so forth. Furthermore, according to the aforementioned statement of Uśanas: "One should become a householder at forty years of age"; the statement of Vyāghra: "A *snātaka* should not remain [without marrying] for three years"; and the statement of Kaṇva: "He should not remain [unmarried] for three years. Since the division of the lifespan is difficult to determine, the fourth part of a hundred-year lifespan is taken as the standard. That too applies to one who studies a single Veda. As for what was said regarding "forty years," that refers to one who studies the three Vedas, provided he has already completed his learning. If he has not completed his learning, then for as long as it takes to complete it and perform the ceremonial bath (*snāna*), after that time he should not remain without having taken a wife; thus, his residence is indeed of fixed duration. Therefore, this [stage] is included within the householder stage itself. And consequently, [the following applies]:

"A twice-born man who does not belong to any stage of life (anāśramī) should not remain so even for a single day"—this statement by Dakṣa should be understood as referring to one who is widowed (*vidhura*). In that context, the phrase "even for a single day" implies "if it is possible," because the acquisition of a maiden depends on others. Alternatively, [the rule] may be:
"One who does not belong to any stage of life should not remain so even for a single day."

The phrase "without making an effort" is to be understood as the ellipsis. In that regard, according to the former position, there is fault for one who does not act when it is possible; there is no fault when it is impossible. According to the latter position, there is fault for one who does not make an effort.

One who practices the duties of a householder as they have been described should observe these vows as well. Although this is already established because they are mentioned in that very same context, their instruction here is for the purpose of including them within the *snātaka-vratas* (vows of the bath-graduate), even though they were previously stated in the rule: "A householder [should marry] a suitable [woman]" [GDh 4.1]. Therefore, even upon the transgression of those, the penance for the omission of the *snātaka-vratas* mentioned in other *smṛtis* should be observed. As Manu says:

"In the world of the *snātaka* vows, however, the penance is fasting. [MDh 11.203] The inclusion of the phrase "as stated" (*yathokta*) is intended to remove any suspicion that there might be duties of a householder not explicitly mentioned here. Although those duties of a student (*brahmacārin*) which are applicable to the subsequent stages by the rule, "And this applies to the others provided it is not inconsistent," are already established by the very mention of what was stated, they are included here again so that even upon their transgression, the penance for the breach of a *snātaka* vow shall apply.

But surely it should be stated that "having obtained a wife, he should practice the duties as described," because one is entitled to the duties of a householder only after the time of obtaining a wife.

It is said: the mention of the "householder" (*gṛhastha*) is for the purpose of making known the distinctness between the duties of the householder and those of the *snātaka*. The duties of the householder have already been stated; the *snātaka* duties, which are yet to be described, are distinct from them. Furthermore, this is for the purpose of establishing that the observance of the *snātaka* vows and the performance of penance for their transgression apply as a rule only to kings and Brahmins, whereas for others, there is spiritual merit (*abhyudaya*) in performing them, but no sin (*pratyavāya*) or requirement for penance in not doing so. Thus, another *smṛti* states:
"But an expiation is prescribed for the violation of the *snātaka* vows;
however, this applies only to kings and Brahmins, never to others.
Here too, the intended meaning is precisely this, because of the specific statement regarding the maintenance of vows: "In this world, two are holders of vows" (GDh 8.1).

One should draw forth these vows that are about to be described; one should perform them for as long as one lives. The term "vows" (*vrata*) is used for the purpose of indicating that these are duties to be performed out of necessity and not for the sake of specific rewards. Furthermore, the instruction regarding the reward—namely, that "the *snātaka* never falls from the worlds of Brahman"—should be understood as being like the instruction regarding rewards in the passage, "One desiring heaven should conquer by means of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*. The inclusion of the word "these" (*imāni*) is intended to dispel the doubt that the following might be different types of vows rather than the very ones to be described. Once their performance as vows is established, the phrase "one should draw forth" (*anukarṣet*) is used to signify that they must be observed for the duration of one's life. The inclusion of the term "*snātaka*" is for the sake of providing a designation: a householder who performs the vows about to be described is called a *snātaka*. Otherwise, since this would already be established by the statement, "Having bathed according to the rule," it would not need to be stated here. (9.1)

By the word "that" (tat), the king and the Brāhmaṇa mentioned in the preceding chapter are referred to. However, he will state a specific rule for the Vaiśya regarding the Snātaka. Having performed the bath according to the rule—that is, having placed the rule before him, having brought the Vedic vows to completion, and having performed the *samāvartana*—and having obtained a wife, that is, having performed the marriage, thereafter, while practicing the duties of a householder such as the honoring of guests as previously described, he should also carry out these vows which are about to be stated; that is, he should cause them to reach himself, or he should practice them. 9.1.
The Snātaka. || 9.2 ||

The *calopa* is to be observed. A *snātaka* should likewise observe these vows of a householder. Because he has returned from the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*) and because there is no other stage of life (*āśrama*) apart from that of the householder, the preceding rule was commenced with the words "after obtaining a wife. However, since it may be impossible for a *snātaka* to obtain a wife, another rule was commenced stating that the duties of a householder must be performed for as long as one lives. Furthermore, this performance of the *snātaka* vows and the penance for their transgression are prescribed specifically for kings and Brahmins; thus, another *smṛti* states: "Only for kings and Brahmins, and not for others under any circumstances. (9.2)
What, then, are those? To this he says:
"What, then, are those vows?
One should be constantly pure, habitually bathing with fragrant substances. (9.2)
He should be constantly pure, fragrant, and habituated to bathing. || 9.3 ||

The word "should be" (*syāt*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. "Constantly pure" means pure through ritual sipping (*ācamana*) and so forth; because of the inclusion of the word "constant," this applies even in a state of illness. "One whose habit is bathing with fragrant substances" refers to one whose nature it is to bathe with fragrant items such as *āmalaka* and the like. This is a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) to what was prohibited in the section on the religious student (*brahmacārin*) by the rule: "Bathing, cleaning the teeth... (GDh 2.19). Because of the inclusion of the word "habit," there is no fault if he cannot do so and merely bathes. The compound is a non-coordinative (*visamāsa*) intended to include those items which a *snātaka* must always wear. As Vasiṣṭha says:

"For those who have completed their Vedic studies (snātakas), however, there are the following obligatory items: an inner garment as well as an upper garment, two sacred threads, a staff, and a water-pot with water. [VaDh 12.14] Because of the inclusion of the word "well" (*su*) in the phrase "one whose habit is bathing with fragrant substances," it follows that anointing with ointments must also be performed after the bath. 9.2.

He should always be pure through acts such as sipping water (*ācamana*) and so forth; when capable, he should not remain impure even for a moment. He should be fragrant, his limbs scented by being anointed with sandalwood and similar substances; or alternatively, "fragrance" refers to good character (*śīla*), meaning he should be well-conducted. He should be habituated to bathing, that is, he should bathe daily. Regarding this matter concerning the *snātaka*, Vasiṣṭha says:
"For *snātakas*, there should always be an inner garment as well as an upper one, two sacred threads (*yajñopavīta*), a staff, and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) containing water. (VaDh 12.14). Manu says:

"One should carry a bamboo staff, a water-pot with water, the sacred thread, a bundle of *darbha* grass, and two auspicious golden earrings. (MDh 4.36). "Veda" refers to a handful of *darbha* grass. 9.3.
If he possesses wealth, he should not wear clothes like those who are worn out and filthy. || 9.3 || — || 9.4 ||
If another is available, one should not wear a worn garment, just like a soiled one. (9.3)
When another is available for his use, he should not wear a garment that is worn out, like a soiled cloth. || 9.4 ||
One should not wear clothing that is dyed red, gaudy, or worn by another. 9.4–9.5.

"Red" means dyed with safflower and the like; "vivid" (ulbaṇa) means excessively bright or not dyed at all; "worn by another" refers to anything except that which belongs to one's teacher, because the latter is permitted as his leavings. Because of the force of beginning the compound separately, one should not wear it even in times of distress. The use of the non-compound form (*visamāsa*) is for the purpose of excluding each [of these items] individually. 9.4.

One should not wear garments dyed with safflower and the like, nor those that are gaudy, nor those of great value, nor those previously worn by others—provided they have not been worn by one's teacher—with the exception of those worn by one's preceptor. The phrase "if one has the means" is understood to apply here as well. (9.5)
Nor [should he wear] a garland or sandals. 9.5–9.6.

The garland (*sraj*) is one characterized by the previously mentioned qualifications; the sandals (*upānahau*) are dyed with lac and the like, but not with a decoction (*kaṣāya*). The commencement of two rules is for the purpose of avoiding their application according to numerical order. 9.5.
One should not wear a garland or sandals that have been worn by another. || 9.6 ||
If he is unable [to perform the full penance], he shall wash it. 9.6–9.7.
But in the absence of others, he should wear clothing and such items that have been purified; "absence of others" refers to a lack of capability [to obtain them]. (9.6)

The inability to obtain another [garment] constitutes incapacity. In the event of incapacity, he should wash and wear a garment, a garland, and sandals belonging to another. In that regard, the washing of the garment should be performed by boiling it in saline water. 9.7.
One who has not grown a beard does not [do so] all at once. 9.7–9.8.

The mention of the beard is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) of the nails and other parts as well. Because of the use of the term "grown" (rūḍha), there is no shaving; rather, there is merely the trimming [of them] to an even state. Thus says Manu: "With his hair, nails, and beard trimmed" (MDh 6.52). In that context, the trimming of the hair consists of removing impurities and making it smooth. As Uśanas says: "A Snātaka should wear hair and so forth that are clean, smooth, and exceedingly fragrant. (9.7)

The mention of "beard" (*śmaśru*) is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the nails and other parts of the body as well. One should not let the beard grow when there is no valid reason; however, one may let it grow when a reason exists. That reason is stated in another *Smṛti*:
"One should avoid the act of shaving in the sixth year, the sixteenth year, and likewise in the year of marriage, as well as while one's wife is pregnant."

Thus [it is said]. Since shaving (*vapanam*) also has its time prescribed by such rules as “at the Gaṅgā, in the field of the Sun,” how then should it be performed? On this point, Manu says: “With his hair, nails, and beard trimmed” (MDh 4.35). *Klpti* means making even by cutting. And Yājñavalkya says:
“Wearing white garments, with his hair, beard, and nails short, being pure” (YDh 1.131). || 9.8 ||
One should not carry fire and water at the same time. || 9.8 || — || 9.9 ||

“Simultaneously” means at one and the same time. The irregular compound (*visamāsa*) is for the purpose of connecting with the subsequent sūtra. The particle *ca* (and) is for the purpose of including food. As Vyāghra has said: “A *snātaka* and likewise his wife should never carry water, fire, and food simultaneously. (9.8)

One should not hold fire in one hand and water in the other simultaneously. Regarding this, Vyāghra states a specific rule: "A Snātaka, as well as his wife, should never hold water and fire, nor water and food, at the same time. (9.9)
One should not drink from joined palms. 9.9–10.

Water [is intended] because it is the subject under discussion. *Añjali* is the joining of two hands; therefore, there is no fault in using one hand. However, there is no prohibition regarding milk and the like. Some say that, since there is no specific distinction made, one should not drink anything at all; for them, the purpose of the composition of the preceding sūtra must be sought. 9.9.
Whatever drinkable liquid, such as milk or water, one should not drink from the cupped hands; the *añjali* consists of two hands joined together. (9.10)
Nor while standing. || 9.10 ||
One should not sip water for ritual purification while standing with water drawn up [in a vessel]. 9.11.

"And one should not drink while standing. Although the prohibition "while standing" was already established, this repetition is for the purpose of including milk and other such liquids as well. (9.10)

One should not perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) while standing with water that has been drawn up; one should sip only while seated. Because of the specific mention of "with water that has been drawn up," the ritual sipping is not prohibited for one who is standing even knee-deep in water at a pond or similar body of water, provided the bank area is impure. Such is also the practice of the learned (śiṣṭas). 9.11.
One should sip water from which the impurities have been removed. 9.11.
By the word *uddhṛtodaka* ("with water drawn out"), a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) is meant; with that, he should sip water for purification (*ācamet*). 9.11.
Nor with food offered by a Śūdra, nor that which is impure, nor that which is offered with only one hand. || 9.12 ||

One should not sip water using a *śūdra* caste person, nor even with an impure person who is not of the *śūdra* caste, nor with only one hand, even if that person is pure and not of the *śūdra* caste. By this prohibition of what would otherwise be permissible, [the author] indicates that there is no restrictive rule (*niyama*) from the preceding sūtra. Consequently, an option (*vikalpa*) is to be understood: one may sip water using a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), or with a non-śūdra who is pure and whose hands are both employed. And thus, since there is no restrictive rule for sipping water by means of the water-pot alone, it indicates that the carrying of it is also not mandatory, because the carrying of it is solely for the purpose of sipping water. (9.12)

One should not perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) with water that has been drawn out by a *śūdra*, even if he is pure, or by a twice-born person who is defiled by contact with the untouchable, or with water drawn by only one hand. If it is argued that this is because the state of being drawn by one hand is the same in the case of water drawn by one's own left hand for the purpose of *ācamana*, [the answer is] no; for both hands are connected to the act of *ācamana*, and such is observed in the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭas*). (9.12)
Nor should he discard urine, feces, or other impurities while looking toward the wind, fire, Brahmins, the sun, water, deities, or cows. 9.13.

One should not discharge urine or the like while facing the wind and so forth; nor should one do so even when not facing them, provided one is looking at them. By the word "deities," their images in the form of paintings and the like are meant. Although the mention of "deities" alone would suffice to include the wind and other such elements, their explicit inclusion is for the purpose of further specification. Consequently, there is no fault in seeing the moon, planets, stars, and so on. From the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it follows that one should not perform these acts even while recollecting them. Because urine and feces are impure (*amedhya*), the term "impure" is repeated for the sake of specifying particular types of impurity. Therefore, it should be understood that one must also avoid spitting and similar acts. (9.13)

The *dvandva* compound ending with the word *ap* (water) does not take a *samāsānta* suffix because of its archaic (*ārṣa*) nature; according to some, the *samāsānta* suffixes are non-obligatory. "Deities" refers to images. The meaning is that one should not discharge urine and so forth toward the wind and other such directions, whether intentionally avoiding them or even while looking at them. "Not toward" (*prati*) means avoidance by facing [them]. "While looking" (*paśyan*) means that due to the restrictive rule, one should not look [at them] even though one is facing them. Because urine and feces are mentioned separately, the term "impure" (*amedhya*) is intended to include spittle, food remnants, and the like. If that were so, the term "impure" alone would suffice; however, the specific mention of urine and feces is for the purpose of emphasizing their extreme avoidance. (9.13)
One should not stretch out one's feet toward these deities. || 9.14 ||

The mention of "deity" again is for the purpose of indicating that cows and Brahmins are deities. Regarding the dual number in the word "pādau" (feet), it is not intended to be restrictive; one should not extend even a single foot, let alone both. 9.14.

One should not stretch out one's feet toward these deities, beginning with Vāyu. The mention of "feet" is an elliptical expression; one should not stretch out even a single foot. The application of the term "deity" to cows and Brahmins is likewise intended as a figurative designation. (9.14)
One should not remove urine or feces with leaves, clods of earth, or stones. 9.15.
By the word "loṣṭa," clay is meant; from that, one should effect the removal by other means. 9.15.
One should not perform the scraping or wiping away of urine and feces with leaves and such; however, one may do so with other materials. 9.15.
One should not stand upon ashes, hair, husks, potsherds, or impure things. 9.16
One should not stand upon ashes, hair, nails, husks, potsherds, or heaps of grain.
One should not step upon ashes and the like; nor human hair; nor potsherds, which are fragments of broken vessels; nor impure substances, such as urine and so forth. (9.16)

One should not step upon ashes and the like. *Tuṣas* are the husks of rice and other grains; the others are well known. One should not stand upon them. By the term "stand upon" (*adhitiṣṭhet*), it is implied that there is no fault in a mere accidental touch. 9.16
One should not converse with barbarians, the impure, or those who are unrighteous. 9.17

"Mlecchas" refers to the Persians and others; "impure ones" refers even to Āryas who are so; "unrighteous ones" refers to those who have fallen from their status and the like. One should not consult with them. Although the sense of "together" is already established by the use of the third case ending (*saha*), the word *saha* is employed for the sake of emphasis. Consequently, one should not converse with such a person after having entered into a common purpose with him; however, there is no fault in [consulting] regarding matters such as asking the way. (9.17)

Those who dwell in regions such as Siṃhaladvīpa that are devoid of the duties of the castes and stages of life (varṇāśramadharma) are Mlecchas. Even those Āryas who are impure and do not perform the prescribed rites such as the twilight prayers (saṃdhyāvandana) are likewise described [as Mlecchas]. Those who are unrighteous include the fallen (patita) and others. One should not converse with them. Although the meaning is already established by the use of the prefix *sam-* in "converse" (*saṃbhāṣeta*), the inclusion of the word *saha* ("with") is for the purpose of indicating that one should not converse even while being engaged in a common task with them; therefore, there is no fault in asking for directions on the road and similar instances. (9.17)
Having conversed with those who have performed meritorious deeds, one should meditate upon them in the mind.

If, however, he should converse out of ignorance or due to necessity, then he should mentally contemplate many virtuous doers of meritorious deeds—many being indicated by the use of the plural number. The mention of "mind" (*manas*) is for the purpose of recollection through the visualization of their individual features. (9.18)

If, due to some necessity, he should converse with them, then he should mentally meditate upon Vasiṣṭha and other performers of meritorious deeds. The word "mentally" (manasā) is a restatement of the inherent nature of meditation. 9.18.
Or he may converse with a Brahmin. 9.19.

Only one who has performed meritorious deeds is a true Brāhmaṇa. Because of the inclusion of the word "together," this refers to what the Brāhmaṇa might say; it is a prescription for penance outside of the specific context [of the preceding rules] for the purpose of immediate performance, or for the sake of brevity. (9.19)
From the context, it follows that even a Brahmin must be a performer of meritorious deeds. 9.19.
One should say of a non-cow, "She is one that shall become a cow. || 9.20 ||

A "non-cow" (*adhenu*) is a barren cow; one might refer to her as "one who is to become a cow" (*dhenubhavyā*). The particle *iti* is used for the purpose of excluding other such forms, so that there may be no naming of other things of this kind. This same purpose applies to the uses of the particle *iti* that will be discussed hereafter. (9.20)
A milch cow is a *dhenu*; a non-milch cow is the opposite. One should call even the latter a "cow that is to become a milch cow" (*dhenubhavyā*), but not a "non-cow" (*adhenu*). (9.20)
"An ill omen as a good omen. || 9.21 ||

"Unfortunate" means not to be approached because of being devoid of splendor or because of being inauspicious; one would call that "fortunate," just as one might call the unfortunate "fortunate. 9.21.
One should speak of even an inauspicious thing as being auspicious. 9.21.
"The skull is the vulva. || 9.22 ||
One should call a skull a fragment of a broken vessel, or a "bhagāla.
When saying "skull," one should say "cranium. || 9.22 ||
"Maṇidhanus" refers to Indra's bow (the rainbow). || 9.23 ||
One should say "rainbow" or "jewel-bow"; by the authority of the scriptural statement, these alone are the designations. 9.23.
One who says "Indra’s bow" should rather say "the jewel-bow. 9.23.
One should not point out to another a cow that is suckling. 9.24.
One should not point out to another a cow that is suckling; because of the mention of "another," one may point out one's own. 9.24.

“*dheṭ pāne*” [Dhātu-pāṭha 902]. This [verb] is used in the passive sense with an active suffix by way of transposition. One should not tell another, one’s own master, that a cow is suckling [her calf]; however, it must certainly be told when there is a specific occasion such as, “the calves have been driven away for the sake of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) and they might suckle,” according to the specific rule in the *Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra*: “and [if she is] joined with her calf” [ĀpDh 1.31.10]. || 9.24 ||
And one should not prevent her. || 9.25 ||
The word "enām" (her) refers specifically to one who belongs to another; by the use of the particle "ca," it is also understood to include those who are surrounded and so forth. 9.25.
And he should not himself attempt to stop her either. 9.25.
Having united with his wife, he should not delay in performing the purification rites. 9.26.

Having united with a woman and enjoyed her company, one should not delay regarding purification; the meaning is that one should perform purification immediately. Because of the prefix *vi-*, however, one may delay for as long as the pleasure does not cease. This delay regarding purification does not apply only to the matter of sexual intercourse; rather, the inclusion of the word "again" (*prati*) is for the purpose of indicating that one must not delay even regarding the discharge of urine, feces, and so forth. But is this not already established by the rule, "He is always pure" (GDh 9.2)?

To this it is replied: here, by the word *śauca* (purity), the mere removal of impurities is meant; the purpose of the commencement of this Sūtra is that when water fit for ritual rinsing (*ācamana*) is unavailable, the removal of its stains must be performed by whatever means possible. And thus, regarding the rule "always pure" (GDh 9.2), the meaning obtained is: "one should be always pure whenever possible. Consequently, there is no fault in being impure when such possibility does not exist. || 9.20 ||

Having united with his wife, he should not delay regarding purification; he should perform it at that very moment. Regarding purification, Āpastamba has stated: "Either by touching water, or by washing off the stains and sipping water, there is the sprinkling of the limbs" (ĀpDh 2.12.3; 2.2.1). || 9.26 ||
And one should not recite the Veda while lying on that bed. 9.27.

One should not study the Veda from the acquisition of its recitation on that bed where sexual intercourse was practiced; and because of the word "ca" (and), one should not seat those worthy of honor there either. 9.27.
In which sexual intercourse was practiced. || 9.27 ||
And having studied during the latter part of the night, he should not go back to sleep again. || 9.28 ||

Having studied during the latter part of the night, one should not sleep again. By the inclusion of the word "again," there is no prohibition against sleeping before that time. By the mention of the "latter part of the night," there is no fault in sleeping during the first part of the night. And just as one has previously lain down, so one should not lie down again—not even for the sake of rest; such is the meaning of the repetition. (9.28)

He who, having slept during the first watch of the night, rises during the last watch and studies, should not sleep again. Since there is a long duration of time remaining, he should not sleep again but should remain awake for the rest of the night. Because of the use of the word "again," there is no fault in sleeping if one was not already asleep during the first watch of the night. (9.28)
One should not take pleasure in an unvirtuous woman. 9.29.
