One should not take pleasure with a woman who is unwell, whose body is unadorned, or who is indisposed; for the word *abhī* signifies approaching [for sexual union]. Consequently, there is no prohibition against play intended for diversion. 9.29.
One should not take pleasure in a woman who is unwell due to illness or other causes; one should not engage in sexual union with her. 9.29
Nor one who is menstruating. || 9.30 ||
And one should not approach a woman in her courses (*udakyā*).
Now, it might be argued that the prohibition is already established by the rule for penance, namely: "In approaching a woman in her courses, there is a three-night [penance]" (GDh 23.35).

It is replied: because another Smṛti states, "A woman in her courses remains impure for three nights," the penance mentioned applies to intercourse occurring within those three nights. Here, however, the prohibition refers to cases where the menstrual flow has not yet ceased.

Others, however, say that a woman is *rajasvalā* (one who has menses) whenever blood appears at an improper time; but that is incorrect, because the term *rajas* applies only to blood appearing at the proper time, and because only that [blood] causes impurity. Thus, another Smṛti states: "The wise say that when blood occurs for women at an improper time..."
"But that [discharge] occurring at the proper time is declared to be *rajas*; therefore, she remains impure only during that period. Likewise, there is also a verse from the Bhārgava:
"One should declare that which occurs for women outside the proper time to be pure;
however, one should know that which occurs month after month to be impure."

Thus it is said. And likewise Vasiṣṭha states: "Women are an incomparable means of purification; they are never defiled. For month after month, their menstrual flow carries away their sins" (VaDh 28.4). And so says the Śruti: "This very sin of killing an embryo manifests itself month after month. Therefore, the prohibition applies from after the third night onwards. In this way, even after three nights, as long as the menstrual flow has not ceased, she remains indeed impure. And thus says Manu:

"When her menstrual flow has ceased, a virtuous woman who was menstruating becomes pure by means of a bath" (MDh 5.65). In this regard, after three nights have passed, she is indeed fit for touch even if the flow has not yet completely ceased; for the injunction regarding bathing—"on the fourth day, the menstruating woman shall bathe"—is intended for the purpose of touching. Although the status of the menstruating woman is already established by the preceding rule, this separate commencement is for the sake of what follows. (9.30)

One should not take pleasure even with a woman who is menstruating. Since the author will prescribe the penance for approaching a *udakyā* as "three nights" (GDh 23.33), this specific statement is made so that, although the matter is already established by that rule, intercourse is prohibited even after three nights have passed, provided the menstrual flow has not yet ceased. (9.30)
And he should not embrace her. 9.31.
Nor should he embrace her, nor a maiden. 9.31.

The phrase "her" (*enām*) is intended to include a woman who has become menstruating within the three-night period. This same purpose also applies to the separate injunction, "not a menstruating woman" (GDh 9.30). Thus, after the three nights have passed, there is no fault even if the embracing continues.

Now, one might object: since touching is prohibited by the rule beginning with "an outcaste, a Caṇḍāla, a woman who has recently given birth, a menstruating woman, or a corpse" (GDh 14.29), the prohibition of embracing is established by implication as well.

To this it is replied: the undertaking [of the ritual] is for the purpose of entering into the penance for the violation of the *snātaka* vows once the embrace has been performed. The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of conjunction, meaning "her and that which is unchaste. (9.31)
He should not embrace nor should he hug this girl while she is in her menses, even if she is unmarried. (9.31)
Nor a maiden. || 9.32 ||

This is for the purpose of making it known that there is no fault in embracing [a maiden] with a pure intention (*aduṣṭabhāva*). And thus, by the mere act of embracing with a corrupt intention (*duṣṭabhāva*), the defilement of the maiden occurs. Furthermore, it is logical that in the *paiśāca* form of marriage, "embracing" (*saṃgamana*) is indeed what is expressed by the word "union.
In this regard, is this person eligible for the penance for defiling a maiden, or rather for the penance for violating the vows of a *snātaka*?

To this it is replied: the qualification for the rite arises solely through the expiation for the breach of a *snātaka* vow, not through the expiation for sexual intercourse with a maiden, because another *smṛti* begins with the words "the emission of semen. As Manu says:
"The emission of semen in women of one's own kin, in virgins, and in women of the lowest castes...

One should avoid blowing on fire with the mouth, engaging in contentious speech, wearing perfumes and garlands, scratching oneself with the fingernails, eating together with one's wife, looking at anointing [the eyes], entering by a side door, washing the feet with the feet, eating while seated on a wooden bench, crossing a river by swimming with the arms, and climbing up or down trees or uneven places that require physical exertion of the vital breath. (9.33) — (9.32)
H reads: "together with his wife" and "entry."

Blowing upon fire with the mouth means blowing on the fire using one's mouth. Quarreling means a worldly verbal dispute, since the nature of idle chatter has already been established in the section concerning the religious student (*brahmacārin*). Wearing external perfumes and garlands means wearing fragrant flowers; thus another *smṛti* states: "One should not wear a garland that lacks fragrance, except for a golden garland. Scratching with something inferior means scratching the head or other parts of the body with an impure substance or object such as a piece of wood. Eating together with one's wife means consuming food from the same vessel as her. Since the scriptural statement, "The wife is indeed half of one's own self," establishes this practice, the present prohibition is intended to forbid it, rather than to grant permission for eating with someone other than one's wife, because another *smṛti* prohibits the general act of eating the remnants of women or *śūdras*. Looking at the application of unguents means looking at one's wife while she is using substances such as oil for anointing the body. Entering through a side door means entering a house or similar structure through an unauthorized entrance. Washing one foot with the other means washing one foot by means of the other. Eating while seated on a chair means consuming food placed on a support such as a stool or bench. Crossing a river by swimming means reaching the opposite bank using only one's arms. The mention of a "river" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) that includes ponds and other bodies of water. Climbing a tree and descending into a pit or other uneven place means going down into them. Exertion involving vital breath means obstructing the breath through activities such as jumping. One should avoid these [acts]. 9.33.

One should not blow upon fire with the mouth, nor cause it to blaze up. *Vigṛhyavādaḥ* is verbal quarreling. *Gandhamālyayor bahirdhāraṇam* means wearing perfumes and garlands openly. Āpastamba says: "One should be without visible garlands and ointments" (ĀpDh 1.32.5). *Avalekhanam pāpīyasā* is scratching the head and other parts of the body with an impure object such as a piece of wood; the absence of the *luk*-elision in the third case (*pāpīyasā*) is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). Eating together with one's wife means eating from the same vessel as one's wife. This prohibition applies even though the practice may be established by custom in certain regions. Others, however, maintain that *sahabhojanam* refers to eating at the same time. *Añjantyavekṣaṇam* is looking at a woman while she is being anointed—that is, while she is applying oil or being adorned with collyrium and the like. Some say this refers specifically to one's own wife; others say it refers to women in general. *Kudvārapraveśanam* is entering temples, houses, and so forth through a place other than the door, or entering cities, villages, and so forth by an unestablished path. As Āpastamba says: "One should not enter a village by a shortcut; if one should enter, one should mutter this verse, 'Homage to Rudra, the Lord of the Dwelling,' or another verse addressed to Rudra" (ĀpDh 1.31.21). *Pādapādadhāvanam* is washing one foot with the other. *Āsandīsthabhojanam*: an *āsandī* is a small stool; eating food while seated on it is *āsandīsthabhojanam*. Alternatively, it refers to placing the food vessel on whatever seat one is sitting on while eating. *Nadībāhutaraṇam* is crossing a river by swimming with the arms to reach the opposite bank. There is no fault in using a boat or similar means instead of swimming. The mention of a "river" is illustrative of ponds and other bodies of water as well. *Vṛkṣaviṣamārohaṇāvarohaṇe* means climbing a tree and descending into a pit or similar uneven place. By the mention of "trees and uneven places," very high elevations and deep depressions are indicated. *Prāṇavyāyacchanam* is exerting oneself to the point of obstructing the breath, such as jumping or climbing mechanical devices. One should avoid these acts, beginning with blowing on fire with the mouth. (9.32)
One should not board a boat that is doubtful [of its safety]. 9.34 — 9.33.

One should not board a boat that is doubtful [of its safety] because it is ruined by the defect of excessive loading for crossing to the other side; due to the use of the prefix *adhi*, one should not even step upon it, as there is no purpose in doing so. 9.34.
One should not board a boat that is doubtful of its ability to reach the other shore or is incapable of doing so. 9.33.

Having stated several duties that serve as means for protecting the body, he now speaks in brief, because it is impossible to recite every single rule: "One should protect oneself from all [harm]. (9.35) — [End of] 9.34.

One should protect the body from all calamities—for instance, as stated: “One should not set out on a journey alone,” “not accompanied by a woman,” and so forth. By the use of the word “all,” this includes even [the danger] arising from the practice of prohibited acts. By the word “even,” it is implied that one must also protect it through rites such as those for pacifying planetary influences. By the word “self” (*ātman*), the body is meant; the meaning is that its protection must be performed in such a way that it does not perish. Although time alone is the destroyer, the intention is that since the duration of life is difficult to discern, one should not be devoid of human effort. Likewise, there is the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*).
"Even the sages are bewildered regarding the knowledge of lifespan, the knowledge of age, and the characteristics of pregnant women; how much more so those who possess only the eye of flesh?

Some explain it otherwise: "By all means one should protect the Supreme Self; one should strive for victory," because verbal roots have multiple meanings. And thus says the Śruti: "The Self is to be reflected upon, it is to be meditated upon" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5).

Others, however, say that by the word "self" (ātman), four types are expressed: the Supreme Self (paramātman), the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), the individual self (jīvātman), and the elemental self (bhūtātman). As Manu says:
"That which causes this self to act is called the Knower of the Field;
but that which performs the actions is called the elemental self by the wise."
That which is known as the *jīva*, the inner self that is innate to all embodied beings,
by which one experiences all pleasure and pain throughout births;
[and] the ruler of all, subtler even than the subtlest—
"One should know that supreme Person, who has the luster of gold and is accessible through the intellect in a state of dream" (MDh 12.122). Thus ends section 9.35.
One should protect oneself from all means [of harm], based on such injunctions as: "One should not travel alone on a road" (MDh 4.60), and so forth. 9.34.
One should not wander about during the day with one's head covered. (9.36) — (9.35)

Having covered his head with a cloth or similar garment, he should not walk about on all sides during the day. Even if he must go through a narrow space, this is permitted because of the use of the word "pari" (all around). In that case, there is no fault if it is for the purpose of avoiding a headache, since it has been stated: "One should protect oneself from everything" (GDh 9.35). || 9.36 ||

It is forbidden to walk about during the day with one's head uncovered. One may sit as one pleases. However, if there is distress from rain, heat, or other such factors on the path, there is no fault in walking while covered, because it has been stated: "One should protect oneself in every way" (GDh 9.34). 9.35.
But having covered [it] at night. || 9.37 || — || 9.36 ||
H omits "tu.
This undertaking is for the purpose of restriction, even though [the meaning] is already implied: one should go only after having covered oneself, even if it is with a small amount of cloth. (9.37)
But at night, one should wander about only with the head covered.
And [he should not study] while voiding urine or excrement. 9.38–9.37.
The word "should do" is to be supplied as the ellipsis; by virtue of the word "and," it means specifically "having covered [the head]. 9.38.

*Mūtraṇam* means urinating; *uccāraḥ* refers to the act of voiding feces. This is a collective dvandva compound of these two. In that regard, the ellipsis is that one should perform the act with the head covered—that is, "with the head covered. (9.37)
From this point until 9.50, the order of the sūtras differs in M and H: "Furthermore,
during the day, one should perform [the rite] facing north" (9.39).
But during the day, one should void both urine and feces while facing the north.

If he performs it during the day, he should face north. This indicates that the facing [of the sun] is not mandatory in certain cases, because of the prohibition against facing toward the wind, fire, Brahmins, the sun, water, deities, or cows (GDh 9.13). For if this were a fixed rule, then facing the sun would never be possible. Thus, another Smṛti states:
"In shade, in darkness, and when there is danger to life."

"One should act facing whichever direction is comfortable"—thus the law is established. [Cf. MDh 4.5; VaDh 6.13] It should be understood that the sūtra beginning with "not toward wind or fire" (GDh 9.13) was composed with the intention that even when facing shadows and the like, one must avoid facing the sun and so forth. || 9.39 ||
If he voids urine or excrement during the day, he should do so facing north.
And during the two twilights. 9.40.
And during the two twilights. 9.42.
The word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of drawing in [the requirement of] facing north. || 9.40 ||
"One should perform [the rite] facing north. (9.42)
But at night, however, he should face the south. || 9.41 ||
At night, facing south. || 9.43 ||
The word *tu* has the sense of the word *ca*; it also serves to draw back the verb "he should perform" (*kuryāt*). (9.41)
This is clear. 9.43
Not without having vanished from the ground. || 9.42 ||
Not without having vanished from the ground. 9.38.

[He should void] with grass unfit for sacrifice. And thus another Smṛti states: "Having covered the ground with grass that is not a constituent of sacrifice, he may void urine or feces. Because of the mention of "ground," there is no fault in doing so on bricks and the like. (9.42)
One should perform the acts of voiding urine and excrement on the ground only after covering it with grass and the like; for another Smṛti states: "with sacrificially unfit grass" (VaDh 12.13). 9.38.
Nor while standing. || 9.43 ||
And while standing, one should not discharge urine or feces. 9.43.
And from a human habitation. 9.44.
And from a house belonging to a Nara. 9.39.
One should not do it near a house; because of the word "and," [it also means] not near a temple, an assembly hall, or the like. 9.44.
A dwelling is a house; one should not do [the aforementioned acts] near it. 9.39.
Nor [should one study] in places filled with ashes or cow-dung, in ploughed fields, or on paths frequented by travelers.
Nor [should one study] in places filled with ashes or cow-dung, on ploughed land, or in the shade desired by travelers.

One should not do so even on ashes and the like that are far removed from one's home. "Shade" refers to the shade of a tree providing livelihood. "Karīṣa" means dried cow dung. "Kāmya" refers to a desirable place, such as a marketplace and the like. The use of the plural in the word "kāmyeṣu" is for the purpose of including other locations taught in other Smṛtis. As Vasiṣṭha says: "One should not urinate in a river, nor on a path, nor on ashes; nor on cow dung, nor in a ploughed field, nor in a sown field, nor in the shade of grassy ground or of trees providing livelihood. (VaDh 6.12) || 9.45 ||

*Karīṣa* is dried cow dung. A *chāyopajīvya* is a place where travelers and others seeking shade take refuge. A *kāmya* is a desirable or beautiful spot. One should not perform the acts of voiding urine or excrement in these places, such as those containing ashes and the like. (9.40)
One should avoid using a seat made of palāśa wood, sandals, and a tooth-stick [made of palāśa]. 9.46 — 9.44.

One should not make a seat or other such items from *pālāśa* wood. By the use of the particle "iti," other similar objects such as a chariot are also included; by the use of the compound, a bed is included; and by the word "ca" (and), household utensils such as a ladle are included. Thus, another *smṛti* states: "One should avoid a seat, a bed, a vehicle, household utensils, sandals, and even a tooth-stick made of *pālāśa* wood."
Thus [ends the verse]. 9.46.
Based on the sense of "and so forth" (*itikārāt*) and other similar items, one should also avoid chariots and the like made of *pālāśa* wood. Regarding this, they recite:
"One should avoid a seat, a bed, a vehicle, as well as household utensils; likewise, one should avoid sandals and a tooth-stick made of *pālāśa* wood. (9.44)
And wearing shoes, one should avoid eating, sitting, saluting, and paying homage. (9.47) — (9.45)

One should avoid eating, sitting, saluting, or bowing to deities while wearing shoes; by the use of the word "and" (ca), it is also implied that one should not do so while standing on footstools. 9.47.

"Greeting" (abhivādana) has been explained previously; "salutation" (namaskāra) is prostration before a deity. One should not perform greetings and the like while wearing shoes. The mention of "shoes" (upānah) is also an elliptical expression for sandals and similar footwear. (9.45)
He should not let the forenoon, midday, or afternoon pass fruitlessly; he should devote them to dharma, artha, and kāma according to his ability. (9.48) — (9.46)

One should not fail to occupy oneself with dharma and the other [ends] during the divisions of the day, such as the forenoon, according to one’s capacity and in their respective order. Although it would have been sufficient to say "one should act according to one's power" (*śaktyā*), the inclusion of the word "yathā" (as) is intended to indicate that these should be practiced even in combination. Furthermore, because of the use of the dative case in "dharmādibhiḥ," it should be understood that one should apply oneself to dharma and the rest. In this regard, one should perform japa and similar practices in the forenoon as far as possible; at midday, the means for acquiring wealth; and in the afternoon, the enjoyment of perfumes, garlands, and so forth. (9.48)

The fourth or fifth case endings are used in the sense of the third. One should not, according to one's ability, make the three parts of the day—beginning with the forenoon—fruitless by means of the three [activities] beginning with dharma. Rather, one should make them fruitful, respectively. 9.46.
But among them, Dharma would be the superior one. 9.49 — 9.47.

Among those three—dharma, artha, and kāma—one should make dharma the primary concern. The intention is that even when the pursuit of the other two is impossible, dharma must necessarily be practiced. The word "tu" (but/however) implies that one should perform all three duties while remaining bound to dharma. 9.49.

The word *tu* (but) removes the charge of infinite regress. Among those three—dharma, artha, and kāma—one should have dharma as the highest; one should make dharma the primary concern. One should pursue artha and kāma only in a manner that does not conflict with dharma. And so Manu says: "One should abandon artha and kāma if they are devoid of dharma" (MDh 4.176). 9.47.
One should not look at another man's wife when she is naked. 9.48.

She is both "another" (parā) and a "woman" (yoṣit), hence "another's wife" (parayoṣit). Otherwise, widows, unmarried women, prostitutes, and so forth would not be [included]. He should not look at her while she is naked. (9.48)
One should not drag a footstool along. 9.49.
One should not bring a seat near oneself with one's foot. 9.49
One should not engage in the restlessness of the genitals, the stomach, the hands, the feet, speech, or the eyes. || 9.50 ||

The term *cāpala* (restlessness) is connected with each [of the following]. Restlessness of the genitals is the desire for sexual intercourse at an improper time. Restlessness of the stomach is the longing for various flavors. Restlessness of the hands is the longing to learn artistic crafts. Restlessness of the feet is wandering about aimlessly. Restlessness of speech is the speaking of dharma and so forth when unasked, or by one who asks in an improper manner. Thus says Manu: "One should not speak to anyone unless asked, nor to one who asks in an improper manner" (*MDh* 2.110). Restlessness of the eyes is an insatiable desire for seeing.
But is this not a partial redundancy with the rule, “restrained in speech, arms, and belly” (GDh 2.28)?

This is not so; for in that context, restraint of speech refers to the absence of idle chatter, restraint of the arms refers to the avoidance of crushing clods of earth and the like, and restraint of the belly refers to the avoidance of eating in excess or unwholesome food. || 9.50 ||

The term *cāpala* (restlessness) is connected with each [item]. Restlessness of the genitals is the desire for sexual intercourse at improper times. Restlessness of the belly is the constant craving to eat. Restlessness of the hands is the longing to practice crafts. Restlessness of the feet is wandering about. Restlessness of speech is engaging in discourse by transgressing the rule: "One should not speak to anyone unless asked, nor to one who asks improperly" (MDh 2.110). Restlessness of the eyes is the desire to see dancing and the like. One should not perform these. (9.50)
One should not, without cause, perform cutting, splitting, scratching, rubbing, or lashing. 9.51.

Cutting grass and the like; breaking [clay] pots and the like; scratching walls, the ground, and so forth with the fingernails and the like; crushing clods of earth and the like by rubbing them together; and cracking the joints of the fingers and the like—these one should not perform except for a specific purpose. Since it is already established in the section on the student (*brahmacārin*) that his arms must be restrained, this [verse] is intended as a permission for cutting and the other acts when there is a valid cause. 9.51.

Cutting refers to grass and the like; breaking refers to jars and the like; scratching refers to scraping with fingernails or similar objects on walls, the ground, and so forth; trampling refers to reducing clods of earth and the like to powder; snapping refers to stretching out the fingers with a sound. One should not perform these acts abruptly. However, there is no fault in snapping and the like when there is a specific reason; as for cutting and the other acts, they should be understood according to their respective possibilities. 9.51.
One should not walk over a rope made of calf-hair. 9.52.
The rope by which a calf is tied is called the *vatsatantrī*. One should not pass over it from above. The word "calf" (*vatsa*) is an indicative term for the bovine species.
The "calf-tether" is the rope for tying a calf; one should not walk over it. The word "calf" is an indicative term for the bovine species. 9.52.
He would not be one who goes from family to family. || 9.53 ||

The meaning is that he should not go from house to house. Alternatively, he should not go from house to house without a specific reason. Or, he is "one who goes from family to family" (*kulamkula*) because his [residence] is from family to family; the meaning is that even though he has the authority to practice the Dharma, he should not remain only within his father’s family. (9.53)

One who goes from family to family (*kulam-kula*) is called *kulamkula*. The suffix *mum* is added according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). Such a person [of this specific type] should not exist. This means that even when there is the opportunity for study and so forth elsewhere, he should not go to another place, but should remain within his own family. Another [teacher] says: a *kulamkula* is one who goes from one family to another—such as in the form of being given away in marriage—and such a person should not exist. He should not abandon his own *sūtra* (scriptural tradition) to resort to the *sūtra* of another. Regarding this, there is another *Smṛti*:
"He who abandons his own *sūtra* and practices the *sūtra* of another should be known as a *śākhā-araṇḍa* (one who has strayed from the branch), excluded from all ritual acts. (9.53)
One who has not been invited should not go to a sacrifice. || 9.54 ||
One should not go to a sacrifice unless invited. 9.54.
One who is not invited or formally requested should not go to a sacrifice. || 9.54 ||
But for the sake of seeing him, however, [I shall go]. 9.55.

"Kāmam" means "not necessarily"; even so, for one who goes [to the householder], lightness of digestion is inevitable. The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of restriction, indicating that it is only for the sake of seeing and not for the sake of eating as well. 9.55.
Even if uninvited, he may go to see a sacrifice at his pleasure; however, not out of a desire for the office of officiating priest or similar roles. 9.55.
One should not eat food from one's lap. 9.56.
Edibles such as *pṛthuka* (puffed rice) and the like—those which one is habituated to eating while holding them in one's lap—one should not eat after placing them upon the lap. 9.56.
One should not eat snacks such as *pṛthuka* and the like while holding them in one's lap.
Nor [should one eat] what has been brought by a servant at night. 9.57.

One should not eat anything brought at night by a servant, such as a Śūdra or others. Why is this so? Because, while the subject under discussion is "foods" (bhakṣān), there is a singular designation [of the act]. There is no prohibition, however, regarding what is brought during the day. 9.57.
Whatever has been brought at night by a servant or an attendant, he should not eat even a little of it; it is not only food that is prohibited, as indicated by the use of the singular number.
One should not eat oil-cakes from which the oil has been extracted, molasses, oil-cakes, buttermilk, and the like, when their potency has been removed. 9.58.
H reads: "vilapana" (lamentation).

Curd and the like from which the cream has been removed and the surface-scum (maṇḍa) taken off; "vilayana" refers to that produced from clarified butter (ghṛta) and so forth; "piṇyāka" refers to that from which the essence has been extracted, because there is no fault in the other kind. Thus says the explanatory Vedic passage (*arthavāda*): "On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, they should give piṇyāka from which the essence has not been extracted. "Mathita" refers to buttermilk, and that too must have its butterfat removed, because there is no fault in the other kind. Thus says the *Gṛhya-smṛti*: "Having churned curd, one should eat it without having extracted the butterfat. By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*prabhṛti*), items such as *kīlāṭa* and *kucaka* are included. The particle "ca" (and) is for the purpose of drawing in the prohibition regarding the night. The meaning is: one should not eat these at night.

Alternatively—the term "from which the oil has been extracted" (*uddhṛtasneha*) is connected with each [item]: the clarified butter from which the oil has been extracted, the oil-cake (*piṇyāka*), and those things beginning with churned curds (*mathita*). By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*prabhṛti*), curd and milk are meant. Their state of having the oil extracted consists in having the surface-scum (*maṇḍa*) removed. Although it would have been established by the rule "one should not eat things from which the oil has been extracted," the specific mention of clarified butter and so forth is for the purpose of permitting other items from which the oil has been extracted, such as mango fruits, molasses, and the like. One should not eat these at night; there is no fault in doing so during the day.

"Containing essence" (*āttavīryāṇi*): by the word "essence" (*vīrya*), the substantial core is meant. That in which this is contained is called "containing essence," such as the skin of the plantain fruit and so forth. It is mentioned separately because it is commenced even during the day. Now, one might object: "Should this not have been stated in the very section concerning the eating of forbidden food? To this it is replied: in the event of such a transgression, there would be the expiation for violating the *snātaka* vows, and not the expiation for eating forbidden food; therefore, it is included here. Furthermore, the separate commencement [of the rule] regarding "even those brought by one who is not sent, nor at night" applies to substances such as alkaline salts (*vilayana*) and the like. (9.58)

One should not eat foods that have lost their vigor (*āttavīrya*) or whose essential nutritive essence (*sāra-aṃśa*) has been extracted. What, then, are these? Here is an elaboration with examples: curd and milk from which the oil has been removed and the cream has been taken out; butter that is merely the residue of churning; the paste of sesame seeds pressed in a mill, which is oil-cake (*piṇyāka*); and also that which is churned but has had no contact with water—regarding which the lexicographers say: [the term *mathita* applies to both].

"For buttermilk (*takra*) is churned curd with one part water, half-part water, or without water at all. This [buttermilk] is of two kinds: that from which the butter has been extracted (*āttanavanīta*) and the other. Of these, the former is what is intended here, for it serves as an example of that which has had its potency removed (*āttavīrya*). By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*prabhṛti*), other similar substances in the form of a paste (*kalka*) are also included. One must consider whether buttermilk from which the butter has been extracted is edible or inedible; however, according to established custom (*ācāra*), it is indeed edible. Because it is mentioned here rather than in the section on forbidden foods (*abhakṣya-prakaraṇa*), the penance required for the breach of a *snātaka* vow applies to eating these, but not the penance occasioned by consuming forbidden food. (9.58)
In the evening and in the morning, however, he should eat food that has been honored, without finding fault with it. 9.59.
This undertaking is for the purpose of prohibiting eating in between [the two prescribed meals], because it is already implied by the sense [of the rules]. And so Manu says:
"For the twice-born, eating in the evening and in the morning is enjoined by the Veda;
one should not eat in between. This rule is equal to the Agnihotra sacrifice."

Thus [it is said]. The word *tu* (but) expresses a distinction: there is a prohibition regarding specific types of food, not regarding sweetmeats (*modaka*) and the like. "Abhipūjita" means with reverence; by the use of the prefix *abhi*, he indicates that it should be accompanied by a mantra. Thus Vasiṣṭha says: "One should honor the meals in the evening and morning with the words 'It is pleasing' (*rocate*)" [VaDh 3.69]. One should eat without censuring—that is, without disparaging it on account of defects such as being poor quality food. 9.59.

The word "tu" (but) is used for emphasis. One should eat at two specific times: evening, which is night, and morning, which is day. The phrase "not in between" serves as a restrictive rule (*parisaṃkhyā*) regarding the meal that would otherwise be understood as permitted. In this context, there is an injunction of a secondary quality (*guṇavidhi*): "honoring [the food] and not disparaging it. "Honoring" means finding it agreeable. "Not disparaging" means not reviling it on account of defects such as its being poor-quality food. Vasiṣṭha states: "One should honor the meals of morning and evening" (VaDh 3.69). 9.59.
One should never sleep naked at night. || 9.60 ||

Sometimes even when there is a specific cause [for sleeping naked]. The mention of "night" is for the purpose of restriction, meaning "only at night. If daytime were also intended, then by saying "one should never sleep naked," everything would be established; consequently, there would be no fault during the day. Furthermore, by this [mention of "night"], he also indicates that there is no prohibition against him sleeping during the day. Otherwise, if it were not so, then by saying "one should never sleep naked," since sleeping during the day would already be excluded by implication (arthatas), the remaining possibility (pāriśeṣyāt) would be only at night; thus, the mention of "night" would be redundant. (9.60)

One may sleep at night, but one should not sleep naked. Thus, this is a prohibition against sleeping naked specifically at night, whereas during the day it is prohibited altogether. This is understood because of the occasional mention [of the rule]; otherwise, it would have simply been stated: "One should not sleep naked at night. (9.60)
Or he may bathe. 9.61.
Because it is begun separately, this applies even during the day; by the word "or," descending into water is also included. And so says another Smṛti: "One should not descend into water naked.
It is not simply by being naked that one is so; for another Smṛti states: "A naked person should not enter the water. (9.61)
Now, because conduct is infinite and it is impossible to state it in its entirety, he speaks in brief:
"Since it is not possible to recite every single instance of conduct due to its infinity, he says in summary:
'Whatever those who are self-possessed, aged, well-disciplined, free from hypocrisy, greed, and delusion, and learned in the Vedas, declare—that one should practice. (9.62)

The word *ca* (and) has the sense of the word *tu* (but/also); that too expresses a distinction, namely: "with reference to what is unseen (*adṛṣṭa*). "Possessed of self" (*ātmavantaḥ*) means those who are devoted to the conjunction of knowledge and action. "Elders" (*vṛddhāḥ*) are those who possess the knowledge of reality established in the Vedas. "Properly disciplined" (*samyagvinītāḥ*) are those whose conduct has been well-trained by their teachers. "Deceit" (*dambhaḥ*) is the practice of dharma for the sake of pleasing the world. "Greed" (*lobhaḥ*) is the desire to obtain another's property through unjust means. "Delusion" (*mohaḥ*) is knowledge contrary to worldly consensus; they are "free from" these, meaning not pervaded by them. "Knowers of the Veda" (*vedavidaḥ*) are those who have studied the entirety of the Vedas. That which they declare with reference to an unseen purpose is: "Give grass to my cows," and so forth. An example of a visible purpose is: "Having given grass to my cows, take an *āḍhaka* [of grain]," and so forth. All of that, he should perform "without guile" (*amāyayā*). Since there is a constant syntactical connection between the relative and demonstrative pronouns (*yad-tad*), the meaning is already established by the employment of the word *yat*; nevertheless, because of the subsequent reference by the word *tat*, it is clarified. He should "practice" (*ācaret*) or perform that, having become well-disposed; this is due to the use of the prefix *sam-*. The irregular compound is intended to show that even in the absence of the possession of all qualities, it must be done when one possesses two or three qualities. One should not consider his purpose fulfilled merely by enjoining one person, but rather only by enjoining many; hence the use of the plural number. If such a person enjoins it himself, then that alone should be done, not the enjoining of another person. While one might have said "they say" (*vadanti*), the use of the term "they declare" (*ācakṣate*)—employing a heavy grammatical suffix (*sūtra*)—indicates that it must be performed repeatedly until death. While one might have said "it must be done" (*kartavyam*), the use of the verb "he should practice" (*ācaret*) indicates the commencement. Whether combined or separately, whether concerning a single object or various objects, whatever injunction is to be performed, that entire thing must indeed be performed. This is because, instead of saying "the word of those who are self-possessed, elders, properly disciplined, free from deceit, greed, and delusion, and knowers of the Veda must be followed," the author has expressed it in this specific manner. 9.62.

Those who possess self-control have conquered their senses; they are "elders" (*vṛddha*), meaning those whose age is mature, because in youth it is possible to be subject to the objects of the senses. They are "well-disciplined," having been instructed by their gurus. "Deceit" (*dambha*) is the cheating of the world under the pretext of righteousness; "greed" (*lobha*) is the desire for another's property through unjust means; "delusion" (*moha*) is ignorance or knowledge contrary to worldly consensus—they have abandoned these. They are "knowers of the Vedas" (*vedavid*), being those who have mastered the Vedas both in recitation and in meaning. Here, "elders" is the substantive. What such elders as these declare must be done. Because of the use of the plural number, this applies when there is a consensus among many. (9.62)
One should approach the Lord for the sake of security and well-being. 9.63.

Yoga is the acquisition of what has not been obtained; kṣema is the preservation of what has been obtained. The word *artha* signifies purpose; thus, it means "the purpose of yoga and kṣema. By the word *īśvara*, the king is meant. One should go to him, but not out of wretchedness (*kārpaṇya*), because of the use of the prefix *adhi*. (9.63)

The acquisition of what has not been obtained is *yoga*; the preservation of what has been obtained is *kṣema*. For that purpose, one should approach a lordly king. Because of the use of the prefix *adhi*—from the root *adhi* meaning "sovereignty"—one should go with independence, free from wretchedness. (9.63)
Except for [the sake of] gods, teachers, and those who follow the Dharma. || 9.64 ||

The other [type of person] is incapable of performing both [tasks]. By beginning with the negation of those who have not previously approached [the king], he indicates that one should seek out someone other than the king who is capable of performing both. "Excepting others" means excluding the deity, an image, a teacher, parents and the like, and a righteous person—one whose nature is the practice of the combination of knowledge and action—because approaching them serves a transcendental (adṛṣṭa) purpose. (9.64)

The phrase "he shall not find anyone else" is a restatement meaning that he should not seek out anyone other than [these], even if they are capable of providing security and prosperity (*yogakṣema*). "Gods" refers to Indra and others; "gurus" refers to fathers and others; "the righteous" refers to those whose nature is to practice dharma. "Other than these" means that he must indeed seek refuge in these alone. (9.64)

One should strive to dwell in a residence that has an abundant supply of fuel, water, fodder, kusha grass, and garlands; where people of noble character abound; which is free from laziness and well-provided for; and which is presided over by righteous persons. 9.65.

One should make a supreme effort to take refuge in a place that has abundant wood, water, grass, *darbha* grass, and flowers, which is pleasant for going out and about, where the three castes beginning with the Brahmins are numerous, which is crowded with people whose nature is devoted to religious observance, and which is protected by a king who acts according to justice. The lack of a compound [in the original] implies that one may dwell even in a place possessing only some of these qualities if they are available; for such a place alone will be sufficient for both dharma and pleasure. (9.65)

Fuel is wood; water is that suitable for bathing and drinking; grass is fodder for cattle; *kuśa* grass is well known; garlands are flowers for the worship of the gods and others; a place from which one goes out is an "exit" (*upaniṣkramaṇa*), meaning an open space outside for the purpose of walking and so forth. Where there are many such things as these, where noble people—meaning those of the three higher castes—are the very people who most abundantly fill it; where it is enriched by those who are not indolent, being the opposite of those who are lazy and lacking effort in their duties; where it is presided over by righteous ones whose nature is dharma; one should strive to dwell in a dwelling of such a kind. One should live with effort in a place of this description. (9.65)
One should circumambulate from left to right such things as places of praise, auspicious objects, temples, and crossroads. 9.66.

H reads: "Four-footed" refers to auspicious things such as cows, Brahmins, wise men, and trees. "Auspicious objects" refers to items such as curd, clarified butter, and full jars. A "temple" is a place for deities. A "crossroads" is well known. One should pass by these keeping them to one's right (pradakṣiṇa), not to the left (apasavya), so that as one goes, they are passed on the right; it does not mean that one should perform a circumambulation of each individual object, because the text begins with the word "āvarteta" (one should turn around). 9.66.
In going out, entering, and so forth, one should act in such a way that they remain on one's right side. || 9.66 ||
Or, as a rule for times of distress, he may observe that entire conduct mentally. 9.67.
If, however, due to haste one does not perform the circumambulation, then some explain that one should accomplish it by means of mental meditation alone.

That is incorrect, because the intended meaning is already obtained by the phrase alone: "or he should maintain [it] with the mind. Therefore, [the word] "or" (*vā*) implies that the word "which" (*yat*) must be supplied after the word "that" (*tat*): "whatever collection of practices has been stated as 'always pure' and so forth, all of that"—where the inclusion of the word "all" (*samagra*) is intended to prevent the rule from applying only to what immediately precedes it—and "the mention of 'practices' (*ācāra*) is intended to prevent the inclusion of the duties of a householder (*gṛhasthadharma*)"—[the phrase] "he should maintain" means "he should contemplate. An "alternative for times of distress" (*āpatkalpa*) is a rule for times of distress. Distress (*āpad*), due to its urgency, makes the performance of the regular rite impossible.

If it is argued that this meaning is already obtained by the word *vā* itself in the sense of an alternative (*vaikalpika*) regarding non-existence, and thus the mention of "alternative for times of distress" (*āpatkalpa*) is redundant, we say no. The mention of "alternative for times of distress" is for the purpose of showing that from the performance of rites prescribed for times of distress, there arises merely the absence of the fault of non-performance, and not spiritual merit (*abhyudaya*) as well. Its inclusion here, rather than at the end of the chapter, is for the purpose of excluding what will be stated later in the verse beginning with "one whose dharma is truth and whose conduct is noble" (GDh 9.68). 9.67.
But when it is possible, there should be direct performance alone. || 9.67 ||
One whose conduct is characterized by truth, righteousness, and nobility. || 9.68 ||
One whose nature is truth.

He is both one whose nature is truth (*satyadharman*) and one who possesses noble conduct (*āryavṛtta*), thus he is "one of truthful nature and noble conduct" (*satyadharmāryavṛttaḥ*). He is "of truthful nature" (*satyadharman*) because he is true to his word; the meaning is that he does exactly what he says or intends. He is "of noble conduct" (*āryavṛttaḥ*) because his conduct—consisting of pleasant speech and so forth—is such that he becomes dear to the noble ones (*ārya*) and the virtuous (*sādhu*). (9.68)
Its intrinsic nature is truthful speech; it depends on the word "it may be" which is to be mentioned later. || 9.68 ||
One who follows the noble conduct. || 9.69 ||

One whose conduct is like that of the noble ones—such as being the first to speak and speaking kindly—and so forth; [the compound] is formed by the elision of the middle term, as in the word *uṣṭramukha* ("camel-faced"). 9.69.
He should be a teacher of the cultured, purified by cleanliness, and devoted to the sacred revelation.
A teacher of the refined (śiṣṭa). || 9.70 ||

A teacher of the learned is one who instructs the virtuous, but not the unworthy; he is purified by water and other means and is devoted to that [purification]. Although it is established by the rule, “He is always pure,” and “Having engaged in sexual intercourse, he should not delay regarding purification” (GDh 9.2, 26), the rule “or mentally” (GDh 9.67) is taught again as an instruction on purification so that there may be no entry into a secondary alternative (āpatkalpa). He is devoted to the Vedas, meaning intent upon the study of the Veda. The mention of *śruti* is for the purpose of excluding Manu and others. (9.69)
He is a teacher for the virtuous, but not for those who are unworthy. 9.70.
One who is disciplined in purity. || 9.71 ||

One who possesses the purity prescribed by the scriptures is "śiṣṭa-śauca-vān. The reversal of the word order [in the compound] places *niṣṭhā* at the end. He is one endowed with that purity which is ordained by the scriptures. The repeated mention of "purity" (*śauca*) is for the sake of emphasizing the essential meaning. 9.71.
One should be devoted to sacred learning. 9.72.
Devoted to the study of the Vedas. || 9.72 ||
Always non-violent, gentle, firm in action, and characterized by self-restraint and generosity. (9.70–9.73)

Because of the inclusion of the word "constant" (*nitya*), he is non-violent (*ahiṃsra*)—that is, one whose character is to avoid harming living beings—even when there is a cause [for it]. He is gentle (*mṛdu*), meaning one whose character is to seek reconciliation even in the face of offenses. He is firm in action (*dṛḍhakārī*), meaning one who completes what has been begun, or one who undertakes tasks only after due reflection. He is self-controlled (*damaśīla*), meaning one who restrains the senses from excessive attachment to their respective objects. He is generous (*dānaśīla*), meaning one who delights in sharing even when his wealth is meager. The use of the irregular compound (*visamāsa*) is intended to indicate that one achieves the goal even by performing these practices according to one's capacity, should they all not be possible. (9.70)

"Always" means that even when there is a cause [for violence], he is non-violent, having non-violence as his habit. "Gentle" means patient even when an offense has been committed against him. "Firm in action" means one who completes what has been begun and is not merely impulsive. "Self-control" is the restraint of the senses. "Generosity" is sharing; the phrase "he should have such a character" is to be understood in connection with every [quality]. (9.73)
A Snātaka who conducts himself in this manner, seeking to liberate his parents and his ancestors and descendants from misfortunes, never falls from the worlds of Brahman; he never falls. 9.71–9.74.
H reads: "and the preceding and following parts."

"One who has such conduct and such actions is a *snātaka*": this is the connection with the word [placed] further on. The repetition of the subject already under discussion is for the purpose of making known that this is the fruit of the *snātaka* vows. If it is argued that the term "mother and father" (*mātāpitarau*) should result in a *ekaśeṣa* compound (meaning "parents"), we say no; for two fathers are intended here—namely, the progenitor and the teacher (*ācārya*). The "former relations" are the paternal grandfather and so forth; the "latter relations" are the maternal grandfather and so forth. Desiring to liberate these from sins, he indeed liberates them, and he himself does not depart from the worlds of Brahman. The mention of "conduct" (*ācāra*) is for the sake of including the fruits of all the duties of a *snātaka*, lest it be thought that [the fruit applies] only to the rule "he is always pure" and the like. The inclusion of the word "constantly" (*śaśvat*) is for the purpose of excluding a merely relative permanence. The double statement is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the chapter. (9.71)

One whose conduct is of the kind thus described is "one of such conduct" (*evamācāraḥ*). Being such, the *snātaka*—desiring to liberate his mother and father, his paternal ancestors (*pitāmahādayaḥ*) who are prior relations, and his sons and others who are subsequent relations, from misfortunes (*durita*) and sins (*pāpa*)—liberates those who have already existed from hell and other such states, and he becomes one who will liberate those sons and others who are yet to be born. The meaning of the future tense (*sapratyaya*) should be investigated; he is "one who will liberate. Such a *snātaka* does not fall from the worlds of Brahman for all time—that is, for a long duration. The repetition [of the word] is for the purpose of concluding the chapter. The mention of the *snātaka* again is for this purpose: that this is the fruit of the duties of the *snātaka* alone, and not of those combined with the duties of a householder. (9.74)
Now begins the tenth chapter.
The duties pertaining to the stages of life (āśrama-dharma) have for the most part been stated. Now he declares the duties pertaining to the social classes (varṇa-dharma):
for the twice-born, [the duties are] study, sacrifice, and giving. 10.1.

*Adhyayana* (study) consists of the acquisition, retention, practice, recitation (*japa*), and so forth of the Veda. *Ijyā* (sacrifice) is the performance of a sacrifice, namely the worship of the gods and ancestors. *Dāna* (charity) is the distribution of wealth to those who ask according to one’s capacity. The lack of a compound is intended to convey the sense of conjunction; it is not meant to imply a one-to-one correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhya*) with the twice-born classes. If it is argued that this [correspondence] is already understood from the inclusion of the word "moreover" (*adhika*), there is no fault, as it is for the purpose of making known the predominance of each specific duty for each individual class. For example—study is the primary duty of the Brāhmaṇa, as Manu has said: [Manu 1.88: "The study of the Veda is prescribed for the Brāhmaṇa, as well as the teaching of the Veda, the performing of sacrifices, and officiating at the sacrifices of others, and the giving and receiving of gifts. ...and so on. Thus, the duties of the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya are also established by implication. However, the specific duties of the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya are explicitly stated because they are not common to all twice-born classes. Sacrifice (*ijyā*) is common to all three, yet it is mentioned again here to indicate its particular importance for the Kṣatriya. Giving (*dāna*) is common to all three, yet it is mentioned again here to indicate its particular importance for the Vaiśya. Protection (*rakṣā*) is the specific duty of the Kṣatriya, while trade, cattle-rearing, and agriculture are the specific duties of the Vaiśya. The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the protection of the people, the administration of justice, and the like for the Kṣatriya; and for the Vaiśya, it includes serving the twice-born, money-lending, and the like. The term "and so forth" also serves to include other duties such as the service of the twice-born, the protection of the people, and the administration of justice, which are not explicitly mentioned. Furthermore, the mention of the word "and so forth" is for the purpose of including the specific duties of the Śūdra, such as service to the twice-born, which are not included among the aforementioned duties. The word "always" (*nityam*) indicates that these duties must be performed throughout one's life. The word "respectively" (*yathāvat*) means "according to their respective capacities. "A Brāhmaṇa shall attain perfection through recitation alone; there is no doubt in this matter" (MDh 2.87), and so forth. For the Kṣatriya, sacrifice is prescribed; thus it is said: "The king should sacrifice with rituals" (MDh 7.79). For the Vaiśya, giving is prescribed; and thus it is said:

"And he should diligently give food even to all living beings" (MDh 9.333). Furthermore, the use of the non-compound form (*visamāsa*) is intended to indicate that each preceding one is more powerful than the following; as Uśanas says: "Sacrifice is a hundred times more effective than giving, and recitation is a hundred times more effective than sacrifice."
Likewise, Manu also demonstrates the superiority of the sacrifice of recitation (*japa-yajña*) over other sacrifices:

"The four *pākayajñas*, together with the *vidhiyajñas*—all these are not worth even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of recitation" (MDh 2.86). Here, since for the twice-born, study, sacrifice, and giving are prescribed only after the initiation (*upanayana*), it should be understood that any gift given by one who is uninitiated is ineffective. 10.1.

The rule of correspondence by number does not apply here. Because of the inclusion of "more" (adhika) later on, it will be stated in that very place. Study (*adhyayana*) consists of the acquisition and practice of the Vedas. Sacrifice (*ijyā*) is the ritual offering and worship of the gods and ancestors. Giving (*dāna*) is the relinquishing of wealth to a worthy recipient (*pātra*). From the expression "of the twice-born" (*dvijātīnām*), it follows that these duties begin once they have become twice-born, that is, after the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) has been performed. Therefore, some maintain that those who have not been initiated have no entitlement even to giving; however, we say this is not so. The term "twice-born" is an illustration for those whose birth is from a twice-born parent. Consequently, even for one who has not been initiated, there certainly exists the duty of giving when he is capable and is prompted by those seeking his welfare. (10.1)
For a Brāhmaṇa, teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts are additional [duties]. 10.2.

The mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is intended to indicate that, because the right to perform these rites belongs to the twice-born (dvija), superiority accrues to him over the others who have already been mentioned.

But one might object: since the author will later state, "more for the Vaiśya" (GDh 10.48) and "more for the King" (GDh 10.7), this rite would thus belong to the Brāhmaṇa alone; therefore, the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" should not have been made.

It is said: as before, this is not for the purpose of indicating that these are duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-dharma*), but rather that they are duties of the social classes (*varṇa-dharma*). Consequently, even one who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*) has the entitlement to receive gifts; however, officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*) and teaching (*adhyāpana*) do not apply because they are impossible [for such a person]. Although it could have been stated simply as "for a Brāhmaṇa, teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts," the use of the term "additional" (*adhika*) is for the purpose of indicating that these also serve as means of livelihood (*vṛtti*). The compound was not formed—as in the previous sūtra—for the sake of performing them in combination, so that there might not be an option (*vikalpa*) based on their having a single purpose. "Teaching" (*pravacana*) means reciting after [the teacher] (*anuvacana*). The rest is explained by its own wording (*nigada-vyākhyāna*). 10.2.

"Teaching" (*pravacana*) means instructing; "officiating at sacrifices" (*yājana*) means performing priestly duties; "receiving gifts" (*pratigraha*) is well known. These are the additional [duties] of a Brāhmaṇa over and above the previous ones, such as study and so forth. What is meant is that these [additional duties] and those [previous ones] are to be combined. Even here, although one who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*) may receive gifts, officiating at sacrifices and teaching do not apply to him because they are impossible for him. Since the duties of a Brāhmaṇa—teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts—are already established [by general rule], the inclusion of the word "additional" (*adhika*) is intended to prevent them from being applied in their respective order [to the other castes]; thus, the former [duties] remain fixed first. (10.2)
But there is a restriction regarding the former [two]. || 10.3 ||

Regarding the first [duties], such as study and the like, there is a necessity to perform them; consequently, there is fault in their non-performance and spiritual merit (*abhyudaya*) in their performance. Regarding the [subsequent duties] such as teaching and the like, there is no such necessity; therefore, while there is spiritual merit in their performance, there is an absence of transgression (*pratyavāya*) in their non-performance. The word "but" (*tu*) expresses a distinction: that for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya there is a rule regarding these [latter duties] as well, whereas for the Brāhmaṇa it is especially so. For this very reason, the Sūtra was not formulated as: "For the twice-born, study, sacrifice, and giving are mandatory," lest the requirement of a rule (*niyamādhikāra*) would also follow for the subsequent [duties]. (10.3)

*Niyama* means that which must necessarily be performed. Previous duties, such as study and the like, are mandatory; by not performing them one incurs sin, and by performing them one prospers. However, activities such as teaching are for the sake of livelihood; therefore, there is no sin in their non-performance, nor is there spiritual prosperity in their performance. (10.3)

The giving away of a Brāhmaṇa girl in marriage may take place at the pleasure of the teacher, kinsmen, or elders, or for the sake of wealth or learning, or according to the prescribed rules; except in the case already mentioned. 10.4.

The *ācārya* is defined by the previously stated characteristics. A *jñāti* is one related through the mother or father. A *priya* is a dear friend. A *guru* includes the father, an elder brother, an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), and so forth. A "rule regarding wealth" (*dhananiyama*) refers to the exchange of wealth. A "rule regarding knowledge" (*vidyāniyama*) refers to the exchange of one branch of learning for another. The term "Veda" (*brahma*) refers to the meaning of the Vedas; consequently, there is no such rule regarding the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) and the like. "Bestowing" (*saṃpradāna*) means teaching; the word "must be performed" is to be understood as the remainder of the sentence. This applies "except as previously stated," namely, except for the service beginning with "having been permitted, he should sit down" [GDh 2.5]. Although it would have been sufficient to say "except as stated," the use of the word "yathā" (as) indicates that this exception applies only to that specific procedure by which the method of study was previously described, and not to the injunction "he should be a teacher of the disciplined" [GDh 6.69]. Consequently, even by the rules of wealth and knowledge, one must not give [instruction] to an unworthy person. 10.4.

*Brahma* is the Veda. *Saṃpradāna* is the correct giving of it. Beginning with the rule, "Having been permitted, he should sit down" (GDh 1.55), it has been stated that those who are desirous of learning are the ones to be taught; such is the aforementioned regulation. Therefore, the phrase "even otherwise than that" means that the *brahma* may be given by him to the teacher and others. The teacher has already been defined. *Jñātis* are brothers, paternal uncles, and so forth. A *priya* is a dear friend. *Gurus* are maternal uncles and others. To these, the *brahma* should be correctly given. Likewise, in the case of transactions involving wealth or knowledge: the exchange of knowledge for wealth is a transaction of wealth (*dhananiyama*); the exchange for another form of knowledge is a transaction of knowledge (*vidyāniyama*). To these as well, the *brahma* may be correctly given. Furthermore, even the transactions of wealth and knowledge apply only to qualified subjects, because it has been stated that "one who teaches refined persons" (GDh 9.70). Nor is this an exception to that rule; rather, since study was prescribed according to the rules of proper reception, this is an exception specifically to that. 10.4.
And agriculture and trade, provided they are not performed by oneself. || 10.5 ||
H reads: "Or [work] not done by oneself.

Agriculture and trade are well known; these, when caused to be performed by another, are permissible as additional occupations for a Brāhmaṇa. From the word "and" (ca), it follows that cattle-herding also must likewise not be done by oneself. (10.5)

Agriculture is the production of crops by plowing; trade is the business of buying and selling. These two are permissible for a Brāhmaṇa provided they are not performed by himself, as they can be carried out through another person. (10.5)
And laziness. 10.6.

Lending money for the purpose of accumulation is *kusīda*; this is indeed not performed by oneself, because of the use of the word "and" (*ca*) [in the verse]. Its separate mention is for the purpose of permitting even that which is done by oneself. And thus he will state later: "Interest on loans is lawful" (GDh 12.26). 10.6.
Lending money for the purpose of accumulation is a form of indolence; yet that too is superior for a Brahmin, provided it is not done by his own hand. 10.6.
The king’s duty is the superior protection of all living beings. 10.7

The protection and preservation of all beings—that is, all living creatures—is the duty of an anointed Kṣatriya king. Because of the use of the word "all," this includes even stationary things (plants and minerals) by extension; thus, the term "additional" (*adhika*) is employed [to indicate this]. 10.7.

For an anointed king, the protection of all beings is paramount; this includes, by the term "all," even stationary things such as the *aśvattha* tree and others, through the prohibition of cutting them down. (10.7)
Furthermore, as to how that should be carried out, he says:
"The state of administering just punishment. (10.8)

The wielding of punishment must not contradict worldly norms; it should not, however, be the infliction of punishment according to one's own will out of pride in sovereign power. And the author will state: "They say that 'punishment' is so called because of its capacity to subdue; therefore, one should subdue those who are unsubdued" (GDh 11.30). By the restraint of the unsubdued, the protection of others is accomplished. 10.8.

That which does not deviate from justice is "just" (*nyāyya*); the state of having a punishment that is not contrary to the scriptures is "the quality of having a just punishment" (*nyāyyadaṇḍatva*). The reading *nyāyadaṇḍatva* has the same meaning. And this is the duty (*dharma*) of a king: that there should be no punishment that is either too light or too heavy due to passion, hatred, and so forth. (10.8)
Furthermore:
He should support Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas. 10.9.

"Brahmins" refers to those endowed with the qualities of Brahman, who are learned in the Vedas and possess scriptural knowledge; by implication, they are residents of one's own territory. "Supporting them" means providing food and other necessities. (10.9)
He should support those Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the Vedas and have studied them by providing food and other necessities. 10.9.
And he should [deal with] non-Brahmins who lack enthusiasm. 10.10.
And [he should punish] Brahmins who lack energy. 10.10.

Lack of energy (*nirutsāhatva*) means the incapacity to perform actions for the sake of one's livelihood. "Non-Brāhmaṇas" refers to Kṣatriyas and others. Here, because of the mention of "non-Brāhmaṇas," the mention of "Brāhmaṇas"—though already obtained from the preceding sūtra—is repeated so that even those Brāhmaṇas who are not learned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*) may be supported when they are unable to earn a living. By the word "and" (*ca*), the poor and the helpless are also included. (10.10)

One should support even those who are not Brahmins if they are devoid of energy and unable to exert effort for the sake of their livelihood; how much more so, then, Brahmins? According to the previous sūtra, one should support learned Śrotriyas by summoning them equally, even if they are capable of working for themselves. 10.10.
And those who do not perform services, and those who do provide assistance. || 10.11 ||
And the causes. || 10.11 ||

Those who have gone forth [into the religious life] without [proper] characteristics are indeed not Brahmins, because the entitlement belongs only to them [who possess the characteristics]. However, it is not mentioned [here] for those who have gone forth as Brahmins precisely because they lack the entitlement to accept gifts. And one should support them with the giving of means of subsistence and so forth; by the word "and" (ca), those afflicted by disease, fear, and so on are also included. Those who are "beneficial" (*upakurvāṇāḥ*) are physicians and others who are helpful to the world; some say they are one's own attendants, but that is incorrect, because their status is already established by the context. By the word "and" (ca), those who know the [proper] time are also included. (10.11)

He should maintain as before those tax-exemptions granted by his predecessors to Brahmins and others, by removing any obstacles or impediments; furthermore, he himself shall not impose any new tax. (10.11)
And those who are students (*upakurvāṇa*). 10.12.

He should support with gifts of food and other necessities those students who are engaged in Vedic study (*brahmacārin*), specifically those who are "dependent" (*upakurvāṇa*)—provided they are seekers and capable of supporting themselves by avoiding such things as wild boars in the forest. Another teacher says: "The 'dependent' are those who benefit the world, such as physicians and the like. (10.12)
And there is yoga in victory. 10.12–10.13.

When victory is to be achieved, *yoga* must be practiced. *Yoga* is the acquisition of what has not yet been obtained. The meaning is that one should diligently collect taxes from forest-dwellers (*āṭavika*) and others who, due to favoritism or other reasons, have not paid them. By the word "and" (*ca*), the protection of what has already been obtained is also included; the meaning is that one must act so that thieves and others do not seize it. Thus, it should be understood that after first establishing both *yoga* and *kṣema*, effort should subsequently be directed toward the conquest of the enemy. (10.12)
Yoga is the means and yoga is the field of victory; this too is the preeminent duty of a king. || 10.13 ||
Especially in times of fear. || 10.13 || — || 10.14 ||
In that particular case, there is fear of being overcome by others; therefore, one must especially and with extreme effort attend to security and well-being.
One should practice yoga with particular intensity when there are specific causes for being overcome by others and so forth. 10.14.
And the movement is by means of the chariot and the bow. || 10.14 || — || 10.15 ||

*Car* means wandering everywhere throughout the kingdom. The mention of the chariot is an illustration for vehicles such as elephants and horses; the mention of the bow is an illustration for swords and other weapons. By the word "and" (*ca*), staying in one place is also included. The distinction between wandering and staying should be understood according to the requirements of the task at hand. (10.14)

*Carana* means movement. Moving in the outer area, he should move mounted on a chariot with a bow in his hand. The mention of a "chariot" is an illustration for elephants, horses, and so forth; the mention of a "bow" is an illustration for swords and other weapons. (10.15)
In battle, there is steadfastness and no retreating. || 10.15 || — || 10.16 ||

In battle—that is, in war—*saṃsthāna* means the fearless standing one's ground, and *anivṛtti* means the relinquishing of life right there; by the word "and" (*ca*), fighting itself is also included. Due to the lack of a compound, it also implies having a secure place of refuge. (10.15)
Battle is combat; therein, standing one's ground means risking one's life. Retreat is flight; its absence is "non-retreat. These two are the preeminent duties of a king. 10.16.
Now he states an exception to the rule that one must always be non-violent:
"There is no fault in killing in battle" (10.16–10.17).

*Āhava* means battle. The repetition of what has already been mentioned is for the sake of specification: there is no fault only in that situation where men proceed by challenging one another, and not in any other state. (10.16)

Where they call out to one another, that is a formal challenge (*āhava*). In such a battle, there is no fault even in the harming of enemies; this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule that he is always non-violent (*ahiṃsra*). (10.17)

Except for those who are without horses, charioteers, or weapons; those with joined palms; those with disheveled hair; those with their backs turned; those who are seated; those on dry ground; those who have climbed a tree; and messengers, cows, Brahmins, and those who are speaking. 10.17–10.18.

H reads: "The fault lies in one who strikes such [persons] as those 'mounted on a tree' (vṛkṣādhirūḍha). The word *vi-* is connected with three [terms]: *vyaśva* (without a horse), *visārathi* (without a charioteer), and *vyāyudha* (without weapons). With palms joined (*kṛtāñjali*) means with hands folded in reverence. With disheveled hair (*prakīrṇakeśa*) means with hair loosened. With face turned away (*parāṅmukha*) means facing another direction. Seated (*upaviṣṭa*) means sitting down. Mounted on dry land (*sthalārūḍha*) means mounted on a mountain. Mounted on a tree (*vṛkṣārūḍha*) is well known. And for him who says, 'I am a messenger,' or 'I am a Brāhmaṇa,' and he who makes the sound of a cow—apart from these, there is no fault. (10.17)

The word *vi-* is connected with three [terms]: *vyaśvaḥ*, *visārathiḥ*, and *vyāyudhaḥ*. He whose horse is killed is *vyaśvaḥ*; he whose charioteer is killed is *visārathiḥ*; he whose weapon is shattered or fallen is *vyāyudhaḥ*. With palms joined in fear; with disheveled hair, being unable even to restrain his locks; turned away (*parāṅmukhaḥ*), having turned his back and fleeing out of fear; seated (*upaviṣṭaḥ*), sitting down because he is unable even to flee; mounted upon a tree on high ground (*sthalavṛkṣādhirūḍhaḥ*)—high ground being an elevated place—and having climbed that tree; or a messenger (*dūtaḥ*), one who carries news; and those who say "I am a cow" or "I am a Brahmin" are the "proclaimers of cows and Brahmins" (*gobrāhmaṇavādinaḥ*). Indeed, there is no fault in causing injury in battle against anyone other than these; it is only toward these that there is fault. (10.18)

The duty of a Kṣatriya endowed with the qualities of consecration has been stated. Now he speaks of the other [type]: "If another Kṣatriya should subsist by that [other] means of livelihood... (10.18) — ... (10.19).

There is another connection based solely on birth; one may subsist upon that king by means of his service, according to the rule beginning with, "And [his] conduct [is defined] by the chariot and the bow" (GDh 10.14). || 10.18 ||

If another Kṣatriya were to subsist upon that king during a calamity of the country, then he should live endowed with the same mode of livelihood and conduct as that king’s—such as [wielding] chariots and bows—and so forth; for by that very king, he is thus approved. || 10.19 ||
The victor shall obtain the wealth of the battlefield. || 10.19 || — || 10.20 ||
If one, commissioned by the king, conquers an enemy and acquires wealth, he shall receive that war-booty. 10.19.
Whatever wealth a king’s servant or official appointed by the king acquires after defeating enemies in battle, that conqueror alone shall receive it, not the king. (10.20)
He states an exception to this:
"But [the theft of] a king's vehicle [is not an offense]. 10.20–21.

"Vāhana" refers to elephants and so forth. The word "tu" (but) expresses a distinction. Even highly valuable items such as jewels belong to the king alone, let alone vehicles; therefore, regarding vehicles, even the slightest [item] should be understood as belonging to him.
Having conquered vehicles such as elephants and horses, they belong to the king, not to the conqueror. || 10.21 ||
And there is extraction when there is no separate victory. 10.21–10.22.

Victory is not distinct from the king; victory belongs to the king. In this context, "extraction" refers to the king's essential wealth. The word "ca" (and) is used for the purpose of including the collection of vehicles. 10.21.

If all the soldiers, having joined together, should conquer and obtain something after the victory, then in that case where the victory is not shared individually, a special portion for the king must be given, chosen by himself. || 10.22 ||
But the king shall distribute the remainder as is appropriate. || 10.22 || — || 10.23 ||

He should give to the warriors in consideration of their valor and other qualities. The mention of the "king" is intended to show that by acting in this way, he becomes a king through the affection [of his subjects]. Or, it means that he should distribute [the wealth] himself for the sake of distribution, and not through others. (10.22)

Whatever gems such as rubies and so forth were chosen by himself, he should distribute the rest among them as is appropriate—according to each person's specific function or their degree of valor—so that they may share in a manner corresponding to those qualities. (10.23)
Now he describes his livelihood for the purpose of protection:
"The farmers shall give to the king a tenth, an eighth, or a sixth part [of their produce] as a tribute. (10.23–24)

The mention of the "king" implies that [the tax] is to be given to one who is appointed [to the office]. The mention of "tribute" (*bali*) implies that it is to be given every year. The remainder [of the sense] is that "giving" is to be performed. By "farmers" (*karṣakaiḥ*) are meant all those who live by agriculture, and not the Vaiśya alone. Whether it be a tenth, an eighth, or a sixth part, this alternative should be understood as being established according to the sequence of inferior, middling, and superior portions of land. (10.23)

The tenth, eighth, or sixth part of what is obtained by farmers in the field must be given to the king as a tax in the form of a tribute (*bali*). This is the livelihood of this king, based on the protection [afforded] by the farmers for what they have obtained in the field. This alternative arrangement is established according to the scope of excessive enjoyment, moderate enjoyment, or meager enjoyment of the cultivated land: in the case of excessive enjoyment, a tenth part; in moderate enjoyment, an eighth part; and in meager enjoyment, a sixth part. (10.24)
Some [teachers] maintain that for cattle and gold as well, the share is one-fiftieth. 10.24–25.

He should take a fiftieth part of the animals from those who subsist by cattle-rearing; or [he should take] gold from a moneylender. He who, having extracted goods at a fair price, sells them at a high price—[such a person is subject to punishment].

If it is argued that because of the prohibition of usury—namely, "He is indeed called a usurer, censured among those who discourse on the Veda" (VaDh 2.41)—it follows that such a person cannot exist at all, this is not a fault. For Vasiṣṭha has permitted it by another means, stating: "One may give [food] at will to one whose duties have been neglected and who is more sinful" (VaDh 2.43). Regarding the mention of "some" (eke), Gautama does not hold this view; thus, one should not accept food from those for whom there is no counter-exception. However, it should be understood that one may accept food from those for whom there is no prohibition, even if they might otherwise be considered usurers. 10.24.

Some maintain that those who live by means of livestock, or those who employ gold as usury, must give a fiftieth part to the king. For example: one who possesses fifty head of livestock should give one animal to the king every year; or one who employs fifty *niṣkas* at interest should give one *niṣka* each year to the king as a tribute. (10.25)
A twentieth part of merchandise shall be the toll. 10.25–26.

"Merchandise" (*paṇya*) refers to that which is to be sold, such as asafoetida and other goods sold by merchants; from these, he should take a twentieth part. The mention of "toll" (*śulka*) is for the sake of technical designation, and consequently, it ensures the validity of legal usage in such passages as "surety, merchant-toll, and so forth" (GDh 12.38). 10.25.

That which is sold by merchants is called *paṇya* (merchandise). A twentieth part of that must be given to the king; this [portion] being given is designated as *śulka* (toll/tax). Examples of places where tolls are levied include *pratibhāvya*, *vaṇikśulka*, and so forth. (10.26)
There are six [types of] theft regarding roots, fruits, flowers, medicinal herbs, honey, meat, grass, and fuel. 10.26–27.

The roots are turmeric and so forth; the fruits are black pepper and so forth; the flowers are safflower and so forth; the medicinal herbs are chebulic myrobalan and so forth; the grasses are whatever [plants] such as *kaṭa* and the like. The remaining items are well known. 10.26
