Roots include turmeric and the like; fruits include mangoes and the like; flowers include blue lotuses and the like; medicinal herbs include *bilva* and the like; the remaining items are well known. From these commodities, the seller must give a sixtieth part to the king. 10.27.
But why, then, should this be given to the king? To this he says:
"Why, moreover, should it be given to the king in this way? To this he replies: "Because it is his duty to protect it. (10.27–10.28)

The protection of those who pay taxes is "tadrakṣaṇa" (their protection); that itself is his duty, hence he is "tadrakṣaṇadharmī" (one whose duty is their protection). The state of being such is "tadrakṣaṇadharmitva" (the quality of having that as one's duty); therefore, "from tadrakṣaṇadharmitva" means because of having that as his character. The statement of a reason regarding a matter understood from the words is for the purpose of taking a smaller portion even than the previously mentioned measure, depending on the place and time; otherwise, the reason would be a general one, implying that the king protects everything. Thus Uśanas said: "He should determine taxes in accordance with the place, time, and profit. (10.27)
Because he possesses the dharma consisting of the protection of those who pay tribute, it is with the thought that "he is their protector" [that this is said]. || 10.28 ||
But one should be constantly devoted to them. || 10.28 || — || 10.29 ||

Regarding these offerings of oblations and the like, even when one is always preoccupied with other duties, one should remain intent upon them; the word "tu" (but/however) expresses a distinction, implying that one should likewise remain intent upon other means of acquiring wealth that are not inconsistent with dharma, though here it refers specifically to these [offerings]. 10.28.

Regarding those [subjects], such as farmers and others, he should be constantly diligent; he should always be attentive toward their protection. Another [commentator] says: "He should be constantly diligent regarding those [revenues], such as taxes and so forth; he should collect the toll with focused intent, thinking, 'For this is his wealth. (10.29)
There is no application [of the rule] when there is an excess. 10.29.
Livelihood by means of what is superior. 10.30.

The word "syāt" (should be) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. The meaning is that he should not take for the purpose of maintaining his family—except in times of distress—that which exceeds the requirements for family maintenance and has entered into the form of the treasury; he should not seize from that treasury [anything beyond what is needed]. And thus Vyāghra says: "He should constantly maintain his family and increase the treasury;
except in times of calamity, he should never seize the treasury."

Some explain that there might be a livelihood derived from the gate of protection provided by a superior; in that regard, it must be examined whether or not there is the consequence of redundancy by the phrase "the king’s superior [protection]. 10.29

Regarding what was stated—that the king’s protection is paramount—any wealth that comes in through that means shall be used primarily for his own maintenance, as well as for his dependents and for the upkeep of elephants, horses, and so forth; however, he should not live off the treasury accumulated and stored by his predecessors. Yet, in times of distress, he may indeed subsist upon it. Thus says Vyāghra: "He should constantly provide for the maintenance of his family and maintain the treasury;
except in times of distress, he should never draw from the treasury."
Thus [ends the verse]. 10.30.
Artisans shall perform one day's work each month. 10.30–10.31.
Artisans, such as blacksmiths and others, shall perform one day’s work for the king each month according to their own capacity; that alone shall be their tax, and nothing else whatsoever. (10.30)
One task is to be accomplished in one day. Artisans, such as smiths and others, must also perform one day’s work for the king every month; this constitutes their tax. (10.31)
By this, those who live off of others are explained. 10.31–32.

Those who subsist by their own labor include actors, dancers, and the like; they too should perform work for the king for one day. Although it would have been sufficient to say "those who subsist by their craft" (*śilpy-ātmopajīvinaḥ*), they are mentioned separately because those who subsist by their own labor provide only minor assistance and are not permanent members of the household. Nor was it formulated as simply "and those who subsist by their own labor," so that those craftsmen mentioned in other legal codes (*smṛti*) might also be included therein. As Uśanas says: "It is ordained that craftsmen perform one day's work every month; in their absence, they shall pay a *kārṣāpaṇa*. (10.31)

Those who live off themselves, such as wood-carriers and others who subsist through physical labor—they too, along with these artisans, are explained by the method already stated: they shall perform one day’s work every month. This same principle applies to dancers and the like as well. (10.32)
And those who possess the wheel of the boat. || 10.32 || — || 10.33 ||

A *cakra* is a cart; those who subsist by means of boats and carts [are included]. Because of the plural number, carpenters, barbers, and others are meant. By the word "and" (*ca*), hunters of wild animals and the like are included. They are mentioned separately so that, as in the previous case, they may not be considered merely temporary [outcastes]. (10.32)

A boat (*nau*) and a wheel (*cakra*) constitute *naucakra*; by the word *cakra*, a cart is likewise indicated. Those who possess these are *naucakrīvantaḥ*. The formation of the word is established in some way through the rule beginning with *āsandīvad-aṣṭhīvad-*. Those possessing boats are those who live by boats; those possessing wheels are those who live by carts. They too shall perform that work for the king for one day. (10.33)
One should give food to them. 10.33–10.34.
One should give food and wages as a fee to those artisans and others; this mention is made so that it may not apply only to those immediately following.
The king should provide food—namely, meals during the day—to those artisans who have been enumerated starting from the phrase "month by month," provided they perform their work. 10.34.
Merchandise shall be delivered by merchants at a reduced price. 10.34–35.

The phrase "one each month" is understood to carry over. This is in addition to the toll (*śulka*). "Depreciation of value" (*arghāpacaya*) means a price lower than the current market rate. And so says Bṛhaspati:
"They shall pay the toll, and then one [coin] each month for the merchandise itself;
those merchants shall pay separately according to a price that is half the market rate. (10.34)

The phrase "one each month" is understood to carry over. It has been stated that the toll (*śulka*) on merchandise is one-twentieth part; beyond that toll, merchants shall pay to the king one [part] every month, having calculated a slight reduction in the price obtained through a decrease in value. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
"Then they shall pay the toll, and every month the merchandise itself;
those merchants shall pay separately, with the price reduced by half."
Thus [ends the verse]. 10.35.
Having found a lost object that has no owner, they shall announce it to the king. (10.35–10.36)

"Lost" means gone away from the presence of its owner, being without an owner—that is, its owner being unknown; however, if the owner is known, one should inform the owner himself. Having found or recovered it, they should report it to the king through the ministers and others; by the use of the prefix *pra-*, they should report it without guile, saying: "This was obtained in such a manner in this place; let it be investigated as to whose it is. Because of the use of the plural number, it follows that the neighbors and others must also certainly speak [of it]. (10.35)

"Lost" means fallen away from the presence of its owner; "ownerless" means one whose owner is unknown. Having found it—that is, having discovered it fallen upon the ground—those appointed to the protection of the countryside should report it to the king; or whoever else has seen it, they too should speak of it. (10.36)
Thus it was said.
Then what should be done by the king?
Having made it known for one year, it must be protected by the king. (10.36–10.37)

Having made it known by means of a drum and having proclaimed: "An object of such-and-such a kind has been found; let him to whom it belongs come forward himself," it shall be guarded and protected for one year without disturbance. If the owner arrives before the end of the year, it must be returned to him, because the protection depends upon him and he possesses the right [to it]. Even though the king's name is used [in the proclamation], this is mentioned because trustworthy persons must be appointed to guard it. Thus Uśanas says: "One should appoint elders, endowed with learning and noble birth, whose integrity has been observed previously, to the guarding of treasure. (10.36)

Having made a proclamation by beat of drum throughout the city—“This object of such a kind has been found and is being guarded; let him to whom it belongs come forward”—it shall be kept for one year. If the owner arrives before the end of the year, then, having questioned him regarding its characteristics, if they match, it must be returned to him. In case of a discrepancy, he is to be punished. And so says Yājñavalkya:
“Property lost and found must be restored by the king to the owner.”

"If one does not disclose [the truth] after being interrogated by means of signs, one deserves a punishment equal to that [of the offense]. Thus, those who, having understood [the facts], do not declare them, are liable to punishment. 10.37.
Now, he states what is to be done after one year has passed:
"After [the year], the remainder belongs to the king for the fourth [time] of the seeker. (10.37–10.38)

After one year, the fourth part goes to him by whom [the thief] was identified; the remainder belongs to the king. Having given the fourth part to the informant, he should take the remainder himself. [The phrase] "the remainder belongs to the king" is stated to remove the doubt that might arise as to whether it should instead be given to an appointed official. 10.37.
To him by whom [the truth] has been realized and proclaimed, the king shall give the fourth part and take the remainder. || 10.38 ||
Now, as to how it is understood that he who says "this is mine" before the lapse of a year is the owner—[the author] states this:
"The owner [is established] by inheritance, purchase, partition, seizure, and finding. (10.38–39)

When these grounds have been established and recognized, he shall be the owner. "Inheritance" (riktha) is what has been obtained from the father. "Purchase" (kraya) is what has been bought for a price. "Partition" (saṃvibhāga) is what was lost and subsequently recovered as one's own ancestral property. "Appropriation" (parigraha) is the wealth of a woman. Regarding the appropriation of that which belongs to no other—such as trees and so forth in rivers and the like, according to some—it must be considered whether this is redundant because it is already included under "finding" (adhigama), or whether it is not. "Finding" (adhigama) is what is acquired from mines and the like, such as jewels and the like. (10.38)

Inheritance is the acquisition [of property] upon the absence of the father and others. Purchase is the acceptance [of an object] for a price. Partition is the mutual division of common property among brothers and others. Appropriation is the initial acceptance of wild things, such as trees, that have no owner. Discovery is the acceptance of lost items, such as treasure-troves, whose owners are unknown. Through these causes, the person who takes possession of the object becomes its owner. Consequently, it follows that in the case of a lost item found, ownership belongs both to the king and to the finder; this is the connection with the context. Crops and other produce grown in fields belong to the owner of the field, just like the field itself. By this, the case of salt and other products grown in mines is explained. These are the causes of ownership common to all social classes (*varṇa*).
These, first of all, are common to all castes; for a Brāhmaṇa, however, there is an additional [means of livelihood] consisting of what is obtained [as alms]. 10.39–10.40.

That which is acquired through receiving gifts [is impure], because that is its nature. What is meant is this: it should be understood that even what is acquired through officiating at sacrifices or teaching must be regarded in the same way. 10.39
Whatever is obtained in the form of a gift, that constitutes the Brāhmaṇa’s superior basis for ownership.
The conquest belongs to the Kṣatriya. 10.40–10.41.
That which is conquered by subduing with a weapon is the specific prerogative of a Kṣatriya.
That which is obtained by victory belongs more especially to the Kṣatriya. || 10.41 ||
It has indeed been explained for the Vaiśya and the Śūdra. || 10.41–10.42 ||

"Consumed" means acquired through one's own labor; for a Vaiśya, this is by means of agriculture and so forth, while for a Śūdra, it is by means of service and so forth. The term "excessive" (adhika) carries over [from the previous verse]. 10.41.
"Consumed" means acquired through labor—through agriculture and so forth for the Vaiśya, and through service and so forth for the Śūdra. That [wealth] is superior for these two. 10.42.
It has been stated that the fourth [portion] belongs to the finder of what was lost and found. He specifies that:
"Now, regarding 'the fourth [portion] belongs to the finder of what was lost and found,' he states the exception:
'[In the case of] finding a hidden treasure, it is the king's wealth. (10.42–10.43)

The discovery of a previously buried treasure is the "gain," and that belongs to the king alone; it does not belong to the fourth part for the finder. And thus, it should be understood that any other property besides the treasure also [belongs to the king], from which a fourth part is taken.
But one might object: how can the king obtain property other than the treasure, given that the discovery was declared to be common [to all], since it is taken by whoever first discovers it?

To this it is replied: one should report to the king that object in which signs of prior experience are seen, while one may take the other oneself; thus, there is a fault for one who takes [the object] after having stolen away the signs of experience. As Lokākṣi says: "For one who takes [an object] after stealing away the signs of experience, the punishment is the first *sāhasa* fine, and the king shall take double the value of that property. If the taking of wealth were not mentioned, then even though it was stated that the discovery of a treasure belongs to the king, a prohibition regarding one who is not a king might also be suspected. (10.42)
If a treasure-trove has been discovered, it belongs solely to the king; however, something should be given to the finder as a reward appropriate to his service. 10.43.
Not [the property] of a handsome Brahmin. 10.43–10.44.
H omits "na," likely a typographical error in the edition.

He is handsome and devoted to the six duties. And so Vasiṣṭha says: "If a Brāhmaṇa should acquire property while engaged in the six duties, the king shall not take it" (VaDh 3.14), because he is the means for performing those duties. 10.43.

He was handsome and devoted to the six duties. If that brahmin were to discover a hidden treasure, it would not be the property of the king; rather, it would belong to the brahmin who discovered it alone. (10.44)
Some say that even one who is not a Brahmin may receive the sixth share as a reciter. 10.44–10.45.

A non-Brāhmaṇa refers to a Kṣatriya or others. An "announcer" is one who previously informed [of the treasure]. Some maintain that he should receive a sixth part, for that is the fruit of his labor and hardship; however, because of the word "some," this is not Gautama’s view, since treasures have an immeasurable value. Therefore, whatever may be given to him is appropriate, but it is not necessarily a sixth part alone. By the use of the word "also" (api), it is implied that even a Brāhmaṇa who is unattractive [or lacks proper qualities] is included. 10.44.

Some traditionalists maintain that even a non-Brāhmaṇa, having discovered a treasure-trove, if he reports it, saying "this has been found in such a manner," shall receive a sixth part of that treasure; this rule is to be applied when the Brāhmaṇa is not worthy [to receive it]. (10.45)
The sequence of sūtras in M and H differs from this point until 10.51: *rakṣyaṃ bāladhanam ā vyavahāraprāpaṇāt samāvṛtter vā* || 10.45 ||.
The property of a minor must be protected until he reaches legal capacity.

A "child" (*bāla*) is one who has not reached the age of sixteen. The mention of him is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indication) for others as well who are incapable of protecting their own property. One should protect that wealth from kinsmen; as for protection from others, however, that is already established by the rule: "The protection of all beings" (GDh 10.7). This applies until he reaches legal capacity—that is, until the capacity for protection arises—or until his initiation (*samāvartana*), even though the characteristic of capacity may exist [after initiation]. The alternative options (*vikalpa*) should be explained with reference to his application to Vedic study and other such duties. (10.45)

A "child" is one who has not yet reached sixteen years of age. If he has no well-wishers or guardians such as his father and so forth, or if those who exist are foolish and unrighteous, then his wealth must be protected by the king. Until when? Until he reaches the legal age, that is, until he becomes sixteen years old. (10.48)
Or [the rule applies] until the completion of his studies. 10.49.

The particle *āṅ* is understood [from the previous rule]. *Samāvṛtti* is the return from the teacher’s house by one who has studied the Vedas; or rather, it is the period leading up to that [return]. 10.49.
Having recovered what was stolen by thieves, he shall restore it to its proper place. 10.46.
H reads: "caura-"

Having recovered from thieves and others what has been stolen, he shall restore it to the owner alone. He must not, however, live off even a small portion under the pretext of suppressing criminals (kaṇṭakamardana), on the basis of the rule: "The victor shall receive the prize of war" (GDh 10.19). Although one could simply say "having recovered" (ācchidya), the use of the term "having won back" (apajitya) implies that even one who recovers it by other means must cause it to be given to the owner. Although one could simply say "he shall give it to the owner," the introduction of the phrase "he shall restore it to its proper place" indicates that even in the absence of the owner, he should restore it to the owner's servants as is appropriate. The mention of "thieves" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for forceful seizure and other such acts. (10.46)

Property stolen by thieves, having recovered it from them, he should restore it to its proper place; he should give it back to the owner alone, while the victor receives some small portion as the fruit of his victory. (10.46)
Or he may give from the treasury. 10.47—10.47.

In cases where there is no possibility of recovery, because the property has been taken to difficult regions and the like, one should give back from his own wealth exactly as much as was stolen; it is not said "or from the treasury," so that the doubt might not arise: "Should he cause it to be paid from its proper place, or should he cause it to be paid from the treasury? (10.47)

If, even after searching, the thieves are not found, or if they have departed after defeating [the guards], then the king shall take from his own treasury and give that amount of wealth to the owner which was stolen by the thieves. || 10.47 ||

Thus, the king’s primary basis for ownership has been explained. Now he speaks of that of the Vaiśya: "For the Vaiśya, agriculture, trade, cattle-rearing, and money-lending are the primary [bases of ownership]. (10.48–10.50)
Agriculture and so forth are well known. "Agriculture and trade" (*kṛṣiś ca vaṇik ca*) is a dual compound treated as a singular. By the term "trade" (*vaṇij*), the activity of commerce is meant.

Agriculture is well known. "Vaṇij" refers to trade (*vāṇijya*). The work of a cattle-herder is *pāśupālya*. Lending money for the sake of interest is *kusīda*. Whatever is acquired through agriculture and the other [occupations] is the additional property of the Vaiśya. (10.50)
The Śūdra is the fourth caste. || 10.49 ||
The Śūdra is the fourth caste; he has a single birth. || 10.51 ||

The term *śūdra* is derived from the Veda (*śruti*) because he flows away (*dravati*). The term *varṇa* is intended to establish the designation of "caste" for the three beginning with the Brāhmaṇa. Therefore, the designation of *varṇa* applies only to these four, not to those born of intermediate unions (*antaraja*). Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "There are four castes: Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra. (VaDh 2.1) || 10.49 ||

Regarding the phrase "the fourth caste": although it shares the commonality of being a *varṇa*, the specific mention of the "fourth" is intended to establish that the three preceding castes—the Brāhmaṇa and the others—are distinct *varṇas*. Since the members of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) are already established [as having the status of twice-born], they possess a single birth; for them, initiation (*upanayana*) constitutes the second birth, which this [Śūdra] lacks. Because initiation is prohibited for him, the study of the Vedas, which precedes it, is likewise not permitted. Regarding this matter, the author of the *Gṛhya-sūtras* says: "For the Śūdra as well, the rites of conception (*niṣeka*), the rite for the male child (*puṃsavana*), the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), the naming (*nāmakaraṇa*), the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), and the tonsure (*caula*) are prescribed to be performed at their proper times, though without mantras. His marriage also takes place without mantras, according to custom. (10.51)
Of a single birth. || 10.50 ||

"A second birth does not exist for him," because even "initiation (*upanayana*)" is designated as a "second birth. Thus, there is a prohibition of initiation for him. And since it is that [initiation] alone which is prohibited, one should understand that the performance of the rites preceding it—which are performed without mantras—must take place at their proper times. Accordingly, the author of the *Gṛhyasūtra* states: "For the Śūdra as well, the rites of conception (*niṣeka*), the rite for a male child (*puṃsavana*), the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), the naming (*nāmakaraṇa*), the first outing (*upaniṣkramaṇa*), the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), and the tonsure (*caula*) are prescribed to be performed at their proper times without mantras. As for the subsequent rites, however, the prohibition is established precisely because they have initiation as their foundation. (10.50)
For him as well, truthfulness, freedom from anger, and purity [are required]. 10.51–52.

"Of that Śūdra"—by the word "also" (*api*), those of higher castes and intermediate mixed castes (*avāntarajā*) are included. This restatement here is for the purpose of establishing these as duties of caste (*varṇadharma*), even though they have already been mentioned in the section on students (*brahmacārin*) and among the duties of the *snātaka* for the twice-born; it is intended so that even those who are uninitiated (*anupanīta*) may be included. Truthfulness is speaking things as they actually are. Absence of anger is the disposition not to harbor malice toward others. Purity is by means of clay and other such substances. The use of the non-compound form (*visamāsa*) is for the purpose of including non-stealing, restraint of the senses, and so forth. And thus says Manu: "Non-violence, truthfulness, absence of anger, purity, and restraint of the senses."
"These are the duties in brief.
Thus [it is said]. And likewise Vasiṣṭha also states: "For all [castes], truthfulness, freedom from anger, charity, non-violence, and procreation. (VaDh 4.4) 10.51.

Lest there be a lack of conformity to the rules of conduct even in the absence of initiation (*upanayana*) and formal study, the duties of truthfulness and so forth belong to that Śūdra as well. Truthfulness is speaking of things exactly as they have been perceived. Freedom from anger is the disposition of not seeking to harm others. Purity consists of the previously mentioned purity of external objects, purity of mind, and so on. Vasiṣṭha, however, states: "For all [castes], truthfulness, freedom from anger, charity, non-violence, and procreation" (VaDh 4.4). 10.52.
Some say that for the purpose of sipping water (ācamana), one should simply wash the hands and feet. 10.52–53.

Some maintain that for the purpose of sipping water (*ācamana*) or bathing, one should perform only the washing of hands and feet; however, Gautama holds that a bath must indeed be performed without the recitation of mantras. This alternative should be understood as referring specifically to *sacchūdras* (virtuous Śūdras). Thus Uśanas says: "A *sacchūdra* should bathe; an *asacchūdra* should wash his hands and feet. This rule applies to the daily obligatory bath (*nityasnāna*). As for the occasional bath (*naimittika*), since there is no other option, the full bath itself must be performed.

Alternatively, it is simply the *ācamana* (sipping water) that is being discussed. Regarding this, some authorities maintain that washing the hands and feet alone suffices for its purpose, but Gautama does not hold this view. His intention is that after washing the hands and feet, one must also drink once. And so says Manu: "But a woman and a Śūdra [should sip] once each" (MDh 5.137). As for the alternative option, it should be explained as before. 10.52.

Some maintain that in the case where sipping water (ācamana) is prescribed for the preceding castes, for a Śūdra there is only the washing of hands and feet, and no other procedure for sipping water. Manu, however, prescribes drinking water once: "But a woman and a Śūdra, once each" (MDh 5.139). Regarding the matter of daily bathing, Uśanas states: "A virtuous Śūdra should bathe; an unvirtuous Śūdra should wash his hands and feet. (10.53)
The Śrāddha rite. 10.53–10.54.

"He will state [later], 'Now, the śrāddha' (GDh 15.1). The mention of *karman* (rite) is for the purpose of including all types of śrāddhas. As Kaṇva says: 'The obligatory, the occasional, the optional, the prosperity-śrāddha, and furthermore the pārvaṇa—thus the śrāddha is known to be remembered as fivefold. Since [the śrāddha] would already be understood by the mention of *śrāddha* alone, some say that the mention of *karman* is for the purpose of including the entire set of injunctions. Others hold that, lest there be a prohibition of the injunctions accomplished by those [rites] due to the prohibition of the mantras, [the word *karman* is used]. 10.53.
“Beginning with the words ‘on the new moon day’ (GDh 16.35), whatever Śrāddha rite is about to be described, that too must be performed by a Śūdra, excluding the sacred formulas. 10.54.
The maintenance of dependents. 10.54–55.

The maintenance of servants, wife, and so forth—this is stated even though it follows from the acquisition of wealth, lest one should become non-maintaining due to the rule regarding the consumption of leavings. 10.54.

A servant is one who must be supported, belonging to the class of those to be nourished; and his support must be provided. Therefore, he too must acquire wealth in a manner corresponding to that requirement. || 10.55 ||
One’s conduct should be restricted to one’s own wife. 10.55–10.56.

Since all subsequent [acts] are rooted in the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), a prohibition would otherwise apply to them all; therefore, a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) is made regarding the mere taking of a wife. By the use of the word "own" (*svā*), it is indicated that his wife must be of the same caste and not of a lower caste (*pratilomā*). Consequently, the taking of wives from different castes for Brāhmaṇas and others is established. Thus Manu says: "A Śūdra woman alone is the wife of a Śūdra; she and her own [woman] are prescribed for a Vaiśya."

"And those [wives] shall be his own, as well as the king's; and those [wives] shall be his own, as well as the Brahmin's. (MDh 3.13) Since the term *svadāra* ("one's own wife") was already established, the inclusion of the word *vṛtti* ("subsistence" or "conduct") is for the purpose of prohibiting appointment (*niyoga*) by a brother-in-law (*devara*) and others; that is, one's subsistence is with one's own wife alone, not with another's wife. The absence of a compound is for the purpose of including the giving of wealth for the sake of elders and so forth. The separate formulation of the rule indicates that the householder stage (*gārhasthya*) alone is his [the Brahmin's] life-stage, and not the others. (10.55)

His conduct is restricted solely to his own wife; he is subject to punishment if he indulges even with the wives of others who are of the same caste, or with prostitutes. Another teacher says: his conduct is indeed restricted to his own wife, and there is no attainment of another stage of life (āśrama) for him. 10.56.
And service toward those who are superior. 10.56–10.57.

Service, attendance, and obedience are the duties for the three higher castes; by the word "and" (*ca*), agriculture and so forth are also included. Some hold that service is for the virtuous Śūdra (*sacchūdra*), while agriculture and so forth are for the other [Śūdra]. Gautama’s intention, however, is this: he who is a virtuous Śūdra should perform both [service and agriculture] without conflict, whereas the other should perform only agriculture and so forth. Although the term "others" (*itareṣām*) would have sufficed, the inclusion of the word "higher" (*uttara*) is for the purpose of making known that the fruit is greater in each successive stage. Thus says Āpastamba: "In each preceding caste, the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*) is greater" (ĀpDh 1.1.8). || 10.56 ||
Service and attendance upon the three higher castes.
Now, as to how he who is to be served should conduct himself, [the author] says: "This very [service] is for the sake of livelihood;
one should seek a livelihood from them" (10.57–58).

One should desire to obtain one's livelihood from those very persons whom one serves; thus it is established that service is for one who seeks a means of subsistence, and not necessarily for everyone. 10.57.
From those who have been served, one should seek a livelihood. || 10.58 ||
In that regard, one should attend to each preceding one first.

And so says Āpastamba: "In each preceding caste, the highest good is greater" (ĀpDh 1.1.8). Thus, just as among the acts of officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and receiving gifts, receiving gifts is the primary means of livelihood for a Brāhmaṇa, so too is service the primary means for a Śūdra; and in that regard also, it is said: "in each preceding caste. (10.59)
What, then, should one request from these [ascetics], and what should they give to him? To this he says:
"Worn-out sandals, umbrellas, garments, brooms, and so forth. (10.58–10.60)

"Jīrṇāni" means worn out or used up. By the word "etc. (ādi), other items of little value are also included, as Manu says: "Leftover food should be given, as well as worn-out garments, the dregs of grain, and worn-out household utensils" (MDh 10.125). The mention of "umbrellas" (chatra) is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) that includes those made of peacock feathers. The rest is well known. 10.58.

A *kūrca* is a bundle of grass and the like; the rest is well known. Worn-out items, such as sandals and so forth, that have been used [by the master] should be given to the Śūdra who attends upon him. However, this rule applies to a Śūdra whose mode of life is service (*śuśrūṣā-vṛtti*), not to one whose mode of life is that of a householder (*gṛhastha-vṛtti*). For the latter, however, there is a distinction in terms of general form, provided it does not conflict with his means of livelihood. (10.60)
He returns once more to the subject at hand:
"Eating the remnants of others' meals and subsisting by a craft. (10.59)
Eating the remnants of another's meal. 10.61.

There is no restriction regarding water, because the word "food" (*aśana*) is specifically mentioned. "Leftover" (*ucchiṣṭa*) means what remains after eating; that too applies only to one who has not yet married, for others do not engage in this [practice] because they have the entitlement to perform *pākayajña* sacrifices. Why is this so? Because of the non-compounded designation [of the terms] and because of another *smṛti* text. As Vyāghra says: "Food that is leftover should be given to a Śūdra who is not a householder;
however, food that is not leftover should be given day by day to a householder."

The "occupation of crafts" (*śilpavṛtti*) refers to subsisting through the work of carpenters, blacksmiths, and the like; by the word "and" (*ca*), the work of artisans is also included. The lack of compound formation (*avisamāsa*) is intended to indicate that this is a provision for times of distress (*āpadkalpa*). And so Manu says: "But a Śūdra who is unable to perform service for the twice-born..."

"Having fallen into distress regarding his wife and children, he may live by the work of artisans. (MDh 8.250) If he is unable to perform service, he should subsist by the profession of a craftsman (*śilpa*). It should be understood that if livelihood cannot be secured even by that, he may resort to the profession of an artisan (*kāru*). The distinction between *śilpa* and *kārukarma* is to be understood from common usage: the works of artisans include those of barbers, dyers, painters, and so forth; because they are the occupations of those born of inverse unions (*pratiloma*), they are censured compared to the occupations of those born of direct unions (*anuloma*). The crafts (*śilpa*), however, such as those of carpenters and blacksmiths, are superior to the works of artisans because they are the occupations of those born of direct unions. (10.59)

That which remains after he has eaten in his food-vessel is his meal. As for the rule, "One should not give leavings to one who is not a Brāhmaṇa" (ĀpDh 1.31.22), that refers to a slave; others hold it refers to a Śūdra householder. And so Vyāghra says:
"Leavings of food should be given to a Śūdra who is not a householder;
but to a householder, non-leavings should be given day by day. (10.61)
And the livelihood of an artisan. || 10.62 ||
The crafts are painting and so forth; he may also subsist by means of these. In this regard, there is a specific rule from the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra]:
"But a Śūdra who is unable to perform service for the twice-born, having reached a state where his wife and children are in distress, may live by the work of artisans" (MDh 10.99). || 10.62 ||
And whoever one relies upon as a noble protector should be supported by him, even if he himself is impoverished. (10.60–10.63)

H reads: "One should resort to" means that one should resort to or serve a Brāhmaṇa or others; by him [the king] he is to be nourished. Because of the word "and" (ca), even a non-Aryan of one's own caste is included, since the instruction is for the service of Āryans alone through other activities. Although it would have been sufficient to say "whomever one should resort to," the inclusion of the term "Ārya" is for the purpose of indicating the distinction of the virtuous even among those of the same caste. "By him" is intended to indicate that this is an obligatory duty. "Even when exhausted" means even when afflicted by disease, old age, and so forth. (10.60)

If a Śūdra who lives by service becomes exhausted and is unable to perform his work, he must nevertheless be supported by the one whom he previously served and for whom he performed tasks, out of consideration for what was done in the past. (10.63)
And by him, Uttara [was saved]. 10.61–10.64.

And that Śūdra upon whom the Ārya might depend; this indicates that even for one whose means of subsistence are exhausted, there is recourse to a Śūdra. This dependence consists merely in showing oneself. As Jātūkarṇi says: "If a noble man should take refuge with a low-born person, he should always show himself [as an equal];
even the low-born person should behave toward him as if considering himself a servant."

Because of the word "ca" (and), one who is destitute (*anāśrita*) is also included as being in a state of distress (*avasanna*). Thus says Jātūkarṇi: "A poor Brāhmaṇa who is self-controlled and has mastered the Vedas must always be supported even by a Śūdra, even though he is not dependent [on him]. Therefore, although it would have been sufficient to say "the other," the inclusion of the word "uttara" (subsequent) is for the purpose of indicating that a Brāhmaṇa alone is to be supported as a rule, whereas the other is not so ruled. And thus says Jātūkarṇi:
"A wise man should always support a Brāhmaṇa with every effort;
even a Śūdra who possesses wealth should always do so for the sake of compassion toward others. (10.61)

And that Śūdra must support Uttara when his means of livelihood are exhausted by means of crafts and the like, taking into account what was previously done [for him]. On this point, Jātūkarṇya says: "If a noble man should take refuge with a low-born person, he should always show himself as such;
even the low-born person should behave toward him having made himself like a slave."
A poor Brāhmaṇa who is self-controlled and has mastered the Vedas must always be supported even by a Śūdra, even if he does not seek support.
"A wise man should always support a Brāhmaṇa with every effort;
even a Śūdra, if he possesses wealth, should do so out of compassion for others. (10.64)
His accumulation [of wealth] would be for that purpose. || 10.62 || — || 10.65 ||

"For his sake"—meaning for the sake of supporting him—there should be a "nicaya," that is, an accumulation, belonging to this Śūdra; this is what occurs. The word "because" (yasmāt) is to be supplied here. In this way, his acquisition of property for any other purpose is prohibited. Furthermore, the statement of the reason—as before—is that his maintenance is not to be carried out with worthless goods, but rather by the giving away of all his possessions without detriment to his own family. (10.62)
The accumulation of this Śūdra—the collection of wealth—would be for that purpose; it would be for the sake of supporting that subsequent [family]. This is the reason for the preceding sūtra. 10.65.
The mantra for his salutation is authorized. || 10.63 || — || 16.66 ||

The learned authorize this mantra for a virtuous Śūdra who has been initiated into the Veda, but not for one who is unworthy. The mantra called *namaskāra* is as follows: “Salutation to the deities, to the ancestors, and to the great yogis;

likewise, let there always be salutation to *svadhā* and *svāhā*. Its application is in rites for the ancestors (*pitṛkārya*). As the author of the *Gṛhyasūtra* says: “Having seated the Brāhmaṇas, he should mutter the mantra beginning with the deities. The mention of the word “mantra” is intended to prevent the doubt that the *namaskāra* alone might be authorized for him. (10.63)

For this Śūdra, in the Vaiśvadeva and other rites, the wise who know the Dharma have authorized a mantra consisting of the form "namo namaḥ," while mentally meditating upon the specific deity's name in the dative case. Another says: "To the deities, to the ancestors, and to the great yogis;

salutation to Svadhā, to Svāhā—always, salutation, salutation. This mantra is intended by the word "namaskāra" (salutation). It occurs in ancestral rites (*pitrya-karman*). And the author of the Gṛhyasūtra says: "Having seated the Brāhmaṇas, one should mutter the mantra beginning with the deities."
"According to some, he should himself perform the *pākayajña* sacrifices. (10.64–10.67)

The *pākayajñas* are sacrifices accomplished by means of cooked food, such as the *aṣṭakā* and others; with these, one should sacrifice oneself and not appoint another. In this way, the appointment of another is precluded. Because of the inclusion of the word "some" (*eke*), however, this does not apply according to Gautama. This option is to be explained as referring to the case of a virtuous Śūdra and an unvirtuous Śūdra respectively. (10.64)
The term *pākayajña* is well-established for domestic rites involving both cooked and uncooked substances; as Āpastamba says: "The term *pākayajña* applies to worldly [rites]. (10.67)
Not only the Śūdra alone should act in this manner; rather, all [the higher castes] should serve each other in the order of their succession. 10.65–10.68.

All those who are inferior should serve those of a higher caste. Now, one might object: since the Śūdra has already been mentioned and there is no subsequent [mention] for the Brāhmaṇa, this commencement must refer to the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya; therefore, the use of the plural number in the phrase "all should attend upon" is inappropriate. It is replied: the plural is used because even one of a lower caste should serve someone of the same caste who possesses superior qualities. Furthermore, by the word "all," those born in the direct order (anuloma) are also included; otherwise, since the context concerns the castes (varṇas), they would not be included. The particle "ca" (and) serves to include the Śūdra as well, for the purpose of his serving those of his own caste who possess superior qualities. (10.65)

Indeed, all those beginning with the Vaiśya—even not only the Śūdra—should serve each successive higher caste; however, for the Brāhmaṇa there is no one higher. Between them are the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya. Nevertheless, the plural number in the word "all" (sarve) is intended to include those of intermediate origin. Another says: even within the same caste, whoever is superior by virtue of his qualities, him each inferior person should serve; this is the meaning. 10.68.
In the case of the interchange between the noble and the ignoble, there is equality of action. 10.66–10.69.

In the case of the mixing, the intermingling, or the mutual exchange between a noble person of superior birth and a non-noble person of inferior birth, the equality or parity of their respective actions and conduct must be understood. Even a noble person, such as a Brāhmaṇa or others, if he performs the deeds of a non-noble person, should not be served by a Śūdra; likewise, even a non-noble Śūdra who acts according to what has been prescribed is to be relied upon. And so Manu, referring to Śūdras, says:
"But those who desire dharma, who know dharma, and who follow the conduct of the virtuous..."

"Except for the recitation of mantras, they do not incur sin and even receive praise. [MDh 12.127] Thus, by this, equality of caste is not asserted; rather, one should not perform what is contemptible by relying on the strength of one's caste. Nor should the other person, thinking "I am inferior," show disrespect. If there is a transgression—either the non-performance of what is enjoined or the practice of what is forbidden—the expiation that will be stated later should be understood to apply. 10.66.

The noble one is one of the three [upper] castes; the non-noble one is a Śūdra. When there is an interchange or reversal of their respective actions and conduct, equality alone results between them, and not the relationship of master and servant. Even a Brāhmaṇa or another [of the upper castes], if he performs the actions of a non-noble, should not be served by a Śūdra. Likewise, even a Śūdra, if he performs the actions of a noble, should not be despised by others of non-noble conduct on account of the inferiority of his birth. By this, the cases of the Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya, as well as the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya, are explained. [The repetition marks the end of the chapter. 10.69.
Now begins the eleventh chapter.

It was stated that the king is to be the one who prevents the transgression between the noble and the ignoble; now he describes the duties thereof. The king is the preventer of transgression between the noble and the ignoble; therefore, he describes those duties.
The king has authority over all, with the exception of the Brāhmaṇas. 11.1.

The King has been declared previously to be the master (*prabhu*) over all the people residing in his realm in matters of restraint and favor, conduct and the administration of taxes: in restraining offenders, in favoring those worthy of favor, in conduct (meaning the maintenance of social boundaries), in the collection of taxes, and in the appointment of men for service. The exception to this is "with the exception of Brāhmaṇas," meaning excluding Brāhmaṇas. Even when they have committed an offense, it should be understood that he should establish them in their own duty through conciliation first, and not by means of restraint as in the case of other castes. The purpose of this opening statement is to declare his independence in all administrative acts. And so says Nārada:
"All subjects are dependent; the lord of the earth is independent. (NSm 1.29) || 11.1 ||

An anointed king has authority over all the people residing in his own realm regarding matters such as punishment and favor. Is this without exception? No, he says: "excepting the Brāhmaṇas," meaning excluding the Brāhmaṇas. Therefore, even when they fall away from their own duty, they should be established [in it] through conciliation. This statement is for the purpose of declaring his independence in his own functions, as Nārada said: "All subjects are not independent; the lord of the earth is independent. (NSm 1.29) || 11.1 ||
Even though he possesses lordship, his autonomy exists only in matters not contrary to the scriptures; thus he says: "He shall be a doer of good and a speaker of good. (11.2)
One who performs good deeds and speaks words of praise. || 11.2 ||

A "doer of good" (*sādhukārī*) is one whose character is to act in accordance with what is prescribed in the scriptures. A "speaker of good" (*sādhuvādī*) is one who, at the time of presiding over legal proceedings, speaks without partiality. Although his sovereignty over all has been declared, nevertheless he must not transgress the boundaries prescribed by the scriptures; the meaning is that he should not engage in seizing the property of others, gambling with others, and so forth. Therefore, his independence pertains only to matters consistent with the scriptures, and not without qualification. (11.2)

One who acts rightly is one whose character is to conduct himself in accordance with the scriptures. One who speaks rightly is one who, at the time of legal proceedings, speaks impartially regarding both his own side and the opposing side. 11.2
Furthermore, he was thoroughly trained in the three Vedas and in the science of inquiry (ānvīkṣikī). || 11.3 ||

H reads: "abhivinītaḥ. The *trayī* consists of the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāman* [Vedas]. *Ānvīkṣikī* is the science of logic (*nyāyavidyā*) and the science of the self (*ātmavidyā*). One who is *abhivinītaḥ* in these two is one who is skilled (*kuśala*). Because of the lack of a compound, [it is understood] "and in the science of government" (*daṇḍanītyām*). From the word "and" (*ca*), it is also [implied] "and in the science of economics" (*vārtāyām*). And so Manu says: "From those learned in the three Vedas, he should learn the triple knowledge (*trayī vidyā*) and the science of government from those who know it."
"And he should learn from the world the science of inquiry (ānvīkṣikī), the knowledge of the self (ātmavidyā), and the undertaking of economic pursuits (vārtā). [MDh 7.43] Thus ends section 11.3.
Pure, with senses conquered, and endowed with virtuous companions and skillful means. || 11.4 ||

Pure and free from greed; having conquered his senses, he is devoid of vices such as hunting; possessing virtuous assistants, meaning he is endowed with ministers, vassals, envoys, and others who are possessed of virtues such as learning and good conduct; and skilled in means, meaning he is equipped with the expedients beginning with conciliation (sāma), applied according to the requirements of place, time, and circumstances. Although it would have been sufficient to say "possessing virtuous assistants and means," the inclusion of the term *saṃpanna* ("endowed with") is for the purpose of implying that his counsel is not leaked. 11.4.

Pure within, meaning free from longing for the property of others and so forth; pure without, meaning devoted to bathing and other such external rites; with senses conquered, meaning devoid of vices such as women, dice, hunting, and drinking; endowed with virtues such as tranquility and the like; accompanied by companions possessed of those same qualities, such as the three types of conciliation (sāma) and so forth; and endowed with the means (upāya) of conciliation and the rest, being one who employs them according to the requirements of place, time, and circumstance—this applies everywhere, as will be seen from what follows. (11.4)
He should be impartial toward all subjects. || 11.5 ||
In worldly affairs, one should maintain an equal disposition toward both the disliked and the beloved. || 11.5 ||
At the time of worldly dealings, one should be impartial toward both the disliked and the beloved. || 11.5 ||
And he should do what is beneficial for them. 11.6.

The meaning is that he should cause beneficial works—such as the digging of tanks, the building of embankments, and the planting of groves—to be carried out in every village. By the use of the word "ca" (and), it is implied that he should prohibit harmful activities such as gambling and the consumption of intoxicants. 11.6.
He should be intent upon the welfare and security of these subjects. || 11.6 ||
Others, besides the Brahmins, should sit below him as he sits above. 11.7.

The Kṣatriyas and others, remaining below and nearby, should serve that king who is endowed with such qualities and standing above them. Although it would have been sufficient to say "those other than Brāhmaṇas," the phrase "others than Brāhmaṇas" is used for the purpose of including those Brāhmaṇas who possess [such] qualities, and not merely those of the [Brāhmaṇa] caste. Since it was already established that they should sit below him, the inclusion of the word "above" (upari) is intended to indicate that they should remain in a superior position even during festivals and similar occasions. (11.7)

They should sit on the ground below that king—who possesses such qualities—while he is seated high upon a throne or similar seat. Is this without distinction? No; "others" refers to those other than Brāhmaṇas. Since it is already established that they should sit below, the phrase "seated above" is a restatement of the natural state [of the king], indicating that he is always seated above and not even on the ground when in private. || 11.7 ||
They too would think thus of him. || 11.8 ||
Even those virtuous Brahmins, considering him to be a portion of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), would regard him as standing above them and honor him with blessings and the like. As Manu says:

"Since this king was fashioned from portions of the lords of the gods" (MDh 7.5), and so forth. By the use of the word "even" (*api*), it is implied that even Brahmins who are devoid of virtue and stand below him [would do so]. 11.8.
Those brahmins too would consider him a king and honor him with blessings and the like. || 11.8 ||
He shall protect the social classes and the stages of life according to the law. || 11.9 ||

The *varṇas* are the Brāhmaṇas and others who have not yet undergone initiation (*upaneyas*). The *āśramas* pertain to the subsequent period of life. "In accordance with justice" means by a path that is not contrary to worldly custom or the scriptures; the meaning is that he should protect them in such a way that there is no interference with the performance of their duties as ordained by the scriptures, nor any disruption of the social order. The inclusion of the prefix *abhi-* (in *abhigrahaṇam*) is for the sake of emphasis, implying that he should protect them after having investigated the matter himself. The compound is analyzed as a non-coordinative (*visamāsa*) so as to include even those who possess neither the status of a *varṇa* nor an *āśrama*, namely the *pratilomas* (those born from inverse unions). Furthermore, the mention of *āśrama* is intended to include those *anulomas* (those born from natural unions) who do not possess the status of a *varṇa* but do belong to an *āśrama*. For regarding them, the status of a *varṇa* is excluded in the passage: "The Śūdra is the fourth *varṇa*" (GDh 10.49), while the status of an *āśrama* remains because the rite of initiation is prescribed for them in the passage: "But one born in the reverse order is devoid of *dharma*" (GDh 4.25); thus, since they are already included by the term *varṇa* alone, the separate mention of *āśrama* serves to include them. By the word "and" (*ca*), images of deities are also included. Thus says Vyāghra:

"A king should protect with diligence Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, as well as those born of intermediate castes, and even the images of deities. Since it has already been stated that "the protection of all beings" (GDh 10.7) entails protection from thieves and other dangers, the instruction given here is for the purpose of preventing mutual intermixture. 11.9.

The *varṇas* are the Brāhmaṇas and the others; the *āśramas* are the student (*brahmacarya*) and the others. He should protect them according to justice—that is, in accordance with the scriptures—by accepting for himself a sixth part of their produce and so forth, protecting them on all sides. This means he should ensure that they remain free from harm through the performance of the duties of their respective *varṇas* and *āśramas*. Alternatively, "according to justice" means he should protect them in such a way that the specific laws of the country and other regions are not violated. The intermediate castes, such as the *anulomas*, are included within these very categories. While the protection of all beings from thieves and the like has been mentioned previously, this present statement is intended to ensure that there be no confusion regarding the duties of the *varṇas* and *āśramas*. (11.9)
And he should establish those who have strayed in their own duty. || 11.10 ||

The meaning is that if those previously mentioned [duties] are not performed due to laziness or other such reasons, one should restrain them and compel them to perform their own specific duty; the word "and" (ca) implies this also applies when they engage in what is prohibited. 11.10.
If they should deviate from their own duty due to laziness or other such causes, then, as they deviate, he should restrain them by means of that very same duty and establish them in it. || 11.10 ||
Why does he act in this way? He says:
"Furthermore, why does he act thus? [The answer is:
"For it is understood that he becomes a sharer in a portion of the Dharma. (11.11)
H omits the word *vijñāyate*, but the commentary appears to presuppose it:

"The word *hi* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*). Since a sixth part of *dharma* accrues to the king from protection, it follows by implication that [a sixth part] of *adharma* accrues from non-protection. A 'part' (*aṃśa*) means a sixth portion. And so says Manu:
'A sixth part of *dharma* from all sources accrues to the king through his protection.'"

"Even from unrighteousness, a sixth part accrues to him who does not protect. (MDh 8.304) Since it is impossible for the formless *dharma* to be divided, one should understand that whatever *dharma* arises for the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*), a portion measuring one-sixth of that also accrues to the king from his performance of prescribed duties. The particle "iti" is intended to indicate a conclusion: "Since this is so, therefore he should protect and establish [the law]. The phrase "it is known" (*vijñāyate*) is for the purpose of indicating a scriptural source (*śruti*). That too is for the purpose of generating a sense of gravity regarding protection, because all *dharmas* have the Veda as their root. (11.11)

For it is known that a portion of *dharma* accrues to one who protects; this is an elliptical expression, and it should be understood that a portion of *adharma* also accrues to one who does not protect. On this point, Manu says:
"A sixth part of the *dharma* of all [subjects] accrues to the king from protecting them; likewise, a sixth part of their *adharma* accrues to him when he fails to protect. (MDh 8.304) || 11.11 ||
And he should appoint a Brāhmaṇa as his domestic priest. || 11.12 ||
And he should appoint as his domestic priest a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with learning, noble lineage, eloquence, beauty, youth, and good character, who is of righteous conduct and an ascetic. 11.12.
One should place a Brāhmaṇa at the forefront in all undertakings; by the word "and" (ca), one should also appoint a commander of the army. 11.12.

“‘He is one who is learned’ (GDh 8.4) — beginning with this, learning (*vidyā*) has been described. Noble birth (*abhijana*) is birth in a distinguished family. Speech (*vāk*) is refined *bhāratī*. Form (*rūpa*) is charming. Age (*vayas*) is middle-aged, neither too young nor too old. Character (*śīla*) is purity of the internal organ or external conduct. Endowed with these qualities—learning and the rest—he is accomplished (*samṛddha*). One whose conduct is righteous (*nyāyavṛtta*) follows behavior not opposed to the world. An ascetic (*tapasvin*) is one devoted to austerity rather than worldly enjoyment. Such a Brāhmaṇa one should place in front; that is, one should appoint as a domestic priest (*purohita*). (11.12)
Endowed with learning, noble lineage, eloquence, beauty, youth, and virtuous conduct.

By the word "learning" (vidyā), the Atharvaveda is meant; it alone is capable of rites for pacification and so forth. "Noble birth" (abhijana) refers to good character; one endowed with that engages in the task. "Endowed with speech" (vāk-saṃpanna) means he delights everyone by virtue of being a speaker of refined Sanskrit. "Endowed with beauty" (rūpa-saṃpanna) means that because he is pleasant to behold, his words become trustworthy. "Endowed with age" (vayas-saṃpanna) means neither too young nor too old; only such a person is fit for great tasks. "Endowed with conduct" (śīla-saṃpanna) means he is possessed of forbearance; for him, there is nothing unachievable. (11.13)
And what more?
[He was] an ascetic who lived according to the right way. || 11.14 ||

One who acts according to justice (*nyāyavṛtta*) is one endowed with conduct that does not contradict worldly custom; such a person does not abandon the king even in times of hardship. A "practitioner of austerity" (*tapasvin*) means one who approaches [his wife] only during her season (*ṛtu*); he is fit for entry into the inner apartments and other such duties. The grammatical analysis (*yogavibhāga*) indicates that other assistants as well should be of this same character. The compound is formed for the purpose of including those who are skilled in the treatises on Dharma (*dharmaśāstra*). (11.14)
He is called the *purohita* because he is placed in front (*puras*) for all ritual acts; this is what [the text] shows.
One should perform the rituals impelled by him. 11.15 — 11.13.

The word "tat" (that) is for the purpose of including all assistants. "Prasūtaḥ" means permitted; the meaning is that he should perform his duties—those with visible and invisible purposes—after they have deliberated upon them. || 11.15 ||

Impelled by that domestic priest—having been authorized and instructed as to how this or that must be performed—he should perform the rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, those belonging to the Purāṇas, the obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika), the propitiatory (śāntika), the nourishing (pauṣṭika), and the malevolent (ābhicārika). By the phrase "impelled by him," the author cites the Brāhmaṇa as the source for this statement. || 11.13 ||
Moreover, it is known from scripture: "The Kṣatriya power, born of Brahman, prospers and does not falter. 11.16 — 11.14.

The word *hi* has the sense of "because. Because [an action] undertaken as a kṣatriya’s duty with the permission of Brāhmaṇas succeeds—that is to say, it is necessarily joined with its fruit—[it] does not suffer, because it is performed according to rule and thus lacks defects such as those pertaining to the recipient (*pātra*). The meaning is that it does not turn out otherwise. The two particles *iti* and *ca* are for the purpose of indicating two scriptural citations (*śruti*). The word *vijñāyata* is for the purpose of indicating a scriptural citation. The presentation of the scripture is for the purpose of showing that these [duties] must indeed be performed after due deliberation. || 11.16 ||

The *brāhmaṇa* was produced from *brahman*; indeed, the *kṣatra*, being authorized by him, prospers—the *kṣatriya* caste prospers—and becomes fully successful; thus it does not falter, nor does it fear anything from any quarter. The meaning is that it shall be free from harm. It is understood in this manner, seen through traditional succession. 11.14.
Furthermore, he should pay heed to whatever those who contemplate divine portents might declare. || 11.17 || — || 11.15 ||

Those who contemplate fate are experts in the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*). Those who contemplate portents are those who know the omens and signs. "They should declare" means they should state with certainty; by the word "and" (*ca*), teachers are also included. "One should respect them" means one should have faith in them and act in accordance with their advice. (11.17)

Astrologers are those who contemplate fate; augurs are those who know omens. They understand beforehand the results of portents. Whatever they might declare—such as "this is a disturbance caused by other planets," "this today is an ill omen," "this today is a portent," and "this is the remedy for them"—he should respect all of that and not neglect it. || 11.15 ||
Why? Because:
"For some even maintain that security and prosperity depend upon that [the king]. (11.18) — [End of] 11.16.

The attainment of the fruits of action depends either on destiny (*daiva*) or on human effort (*puruṣakāra*). By the word "destiny," the karma acquired in previous births is meant; by the word "human effort," the karma performed in this life is meant. Thus says Kaṇva: "Karma performed in previous births is designated as 'destiny,' while that which is performed in this life is called 'human effort' here."

In this regard, because even those devoid of human effort (*puruṣakāra*), such as the lame and others, are seen to obtain treasures and the like, while even those who perform excellent deeds do not see the fruit [of their actions], they believe that the fruit depends solely on destiny (*daiva*) and not on human effort; thus, they maintain that it is dependent on that [destiny]. By the word "that" (*tat*), the speech of those who contemplate destiny and portents is meant, for by that alone the knowledge of results arising from the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) is obtained. Security and well-being (*yogakṣema*) are dependent on that. Acquisition of what has not been obtained is *yoga*; the preservation of what has been obtained is *kṣema*. First, *yoga* is dependent on that: when there is knowledge of the gain or non-gain of something through a sign (*nimitta*), one either exerts effort or fails to exert it accordingly. *Kṣema* also depends on that: when there is knowledge of an affliction through a sign, it can be removed by means of pacification and so forth. They "maintain" means they make a formal proposition. The word "also" (*api*) is used to indicate another underlying intention.

Others also speak thus: since the connection with food and other necessities is untenable without human effort (*puruṣakāra*), and because it is observed that even for those who have exerted themselves, results are sometimes fruitless, yet there is never a total absence of success, they consider [success] to be dependent solely on human effort. Conversely, because it is observed that the declarations regarding the portents of fate (*daiva*) are sometimes infallible, they hold that [success] is not dependent on that [fate].

Gautama maintains that [the result arises] from both, because of the mention of "either one. Neither destiny (*daiva*) nor human effort (*puruṣakāra*) is absolute in its predominance. What then? Sometimes destiny depends upon human effort, and likewise human effort depends upon destiny. Just as in agriculture and the like, human effort depends on destiny—for the accomplishment of the fruit through human effort alone in agriculture does not occur without rain and other such factors—so too, in the acquisition of food and the like, destiny depends upon human effort, since it is impossible for that [acquisition] to occur without it. This is Gautama’s intention: regarding destiny, one should heed the words of those who contemplate portents; regarding human effort, however, one should heed the words of the authoritative (*āpta*). (11.18)

It is not only the performance of prescribed duties such as protection that depends on this; rather, even the acquisition and preservation (*yoga-kṣema*) that is declared by those who contemplate divine portents and the like to be necessary when there is an anomaly of the planets and so forth, also depends upon it. *Yoga* is the gaining of what has not been gained; *kṣema* is the preservation of what has been gained. This is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*). In expressions such as “may she obtain *āyoga-prajā*” and “may *yoga-kṣema* be ordained for us” (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 7.5.18.1), the gender follows the final member of the compound, just as in the case of *ekaviṃśati* and other such numbers. For example: one and twenty is *ekaviṃśati*. Thus say some teachers regarding that *yoga-kṣema*. (11.16)

One should perform in the domestic fire (śālāgni) rites associated with prosperity—such as those for peace, a holy day, well-being, long life, and auspiciousness—as well as those associated with causing enmity, subjugation, malevolent magic, and the ruin of enemies. (11.19) — (11.17)

The word "connected" (*saṃyukta*) is to be construed with each [term]. That which is performed for the sake of averting misfortune indicated by divine portents, such as rites for the pacification of the planets (*grahaśānti*) and so forth, is "connected with peace" (*śāntisaṃyukta*). That which is performed at weddings and other occasions for the purpose of destroying defects of the day, such that through the destruction of those defects the rite becomes auspicious itself, is "connected with merit" (*puṇyāhasaṃyukta*). That which is performed during journeys and similar circumstances is "connected with well-being" (*svastyayanasaṃyukta*). Thus Vyāsa has said: "In a journey, the *Vāsava* [mantra]; likewise, the *Nārasiṃha* in battle."

"In times of fear, one should meditate upon Vāsudeva; this triad is remembered as a means of securing well-being (*svastyayana*). That which is performed on one's birth-star (*janmanakṣatra*) in conjunction with rites for longevity (*āyuṣya*) is for the purpose of increasing longevity. That which is performed in conjunction with auspicious rites (*maṅgala*) for the sake of wealth and so forth—such as the *Śrī-homa* and others—is precisely what constitutes "prosperous" (*abhyudayika*) acts, because they are the causes of prosperity. If it is argued that this should not be stated because [the performer] is himself the cause of prosperity, there is no fault, as it serves to indicate the absence of defect in the performer. Furthermore, this indicates that for subsequent [acts], there is some expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the performer. Thus says Paiṭhīnasi:
If the best of the twice-born performs a rite for the prosperity of a king,
even if it is said to cause suffering to others, he is not tainted by sin.

"Having committed an act that causes suffering to others, purification is declared by the wise to come either from the expiation prescribed by the Brahmins or from the king's permission. Thus [it is said].

The subsequent rites are mentioned separately because they cause harm to others. That which is joined with *vidveṣaṇa* (sowing dissension) is that by which another person becomes hostile toward his own subjects. That which is joined with *saṃvanana* (conciliation/enchantment) is that by which an enemy submits. That which is joined with *ābhicāra* (malevolent magic) is that by which an enemy dies. *Vyṛddhi* is the loss of prosperity; *dviṣad-vyṛddhi* is the hostility and misfortune of an enemy. That which is joined with this—such as *uccāṭana* (expulsion) and so forth—is that by which another person loses his power. Because of the mention of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) above, these [rites] should be performed by the domestic priest (*purohita*) in the *śālāgni* (the hall-fire). Due to the word "and" (*ca*), they may also be performed in the common fire (*laukika*). In this regard, it should be understood that the previously mentioned rites are performed in the common fire, while the others are performed in the *śālāgni*. (11.19)

Regarding this, Āpastamba, having introduced the topic with the words, “But we shall state the specific rules for the king” (ĀpDh 2.25.1), and referring to the three locations—the palace, the residence, and the assembly hall—states: “In all of these, the sacred fires should be perpetual, and the worship of the fire should be constant, just as in the domestic sacrifice” (ĀpDh 2.25.6–7). Among these, the fire used here is the *śālāgni* (the hall-fire), neither the *aupāsana* nor the *tretāgni*, because those two are restricted to domestic and *śrauta* rites respectively. [The following rites are performed in the *śālāgni*: 1. Those connected with *śānti* (propitiation), such as the *grahaśānti* and *mahāśānti*, which are performed to avert misfortune indicated by divine portents. 2. Those connected with *puṇyāha* (auspicious day), performed at weddings and other occasions to destroy defects of the day. 3. Those connected with *svastyayana* (well-being), performed during journeys and similar events. 4. Those connected with *āyuṣmat* (longevity), performed on birth-stars and so forth for the increase of life. 5. Those connected with *maṅgala* (auspiciousness), such as the *dūrvā-homa* and *vāstu-homa*, performed at house-entries and similar occasions. These are *ābhyudayika* (prosperous) rites, performed on account of prosperity. 6. Those connected with *vidveṣaṇa* (enmity), by which one’s enemy becomes hated by his own subjects. 7. Those connected with *saṃvanana* (conciliation), by which one’s enemies become submissive and prostrate. 8. Those connected with *abhicāra* (sorcery), by which one’s enemies perish. 9. *Vyṛddhi* is the absence of prosperity (*ṛddhi*). *Dviṣad-vyṛddhi* is the ruin of enemies; those rites by which one’s enemies lose their power. 10. *Uccāṭana* (eradication) and other such rites. These should be performed in the *śālāgni*. Who performs them? The king. And his status as the performer consists precisely in this: his role as the organizer through the provision of funds and other means. Just as even one who sits silently in a secluded place supervising the work of food, seed, and oxen is said to be “plowing with five plows. Another says: the domestic priest (*purohita*) should perform the *ābhyudayika* rites himself, while he should have the others performed. Furthermore, one does not perform the non-prosperous rites in the same fire where the prosperous ones are performed; rather, they are performed in another fire, distinct from those previously mentioned. (11.17)
As it has been said: "The officiating priests [perform] the others. (11.20) — (11.18)
The priests shall perform other rites, such as the Putrakāmeṣṭi, as prescribed; the phrase "as prescribed" is used so that the king may not be greedy for the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). 11.20.

As for other domestic (*gārhya*) and Vedic (*śrauta*) rites, as it has been stated, in whichever rite so many officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are prescribed, that many should perform it. For example: in the *aupāsana* and *agnihotra*, there is one *adhvaryu*; in the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, four; in the *cāturmāsya*, five; in the *paśubandha*, six; and in the *jyotiṣṭoma* and others, sixteen. Regarding this, Manu says:

"He should appoint a domestic priest (*purohita*) and he should indeed appoint officiating priests" (MDh 7.78). In those cases where there is an officiating priest, some say the *purohita* is the *adhvaryu* and the *brahman*. 11.18.
And its conventional practice consists of the Veda, the Dharmaśāstras, the auxiliary sciences (aṅgas), the Upavedas, and the Purāṇa. 11.21. — 11.19.

"Vyavahāra" (legal procedure) is that by which one transacts; these are the means for establishing the legal system of that king who is authorized to protect his subjects. The Vedas and the rest are well known: because in the Veda we see legal procedures such as "Like a pitfall for the winning of riches" (RV 1.124.7); because in the Dharmaśāstra there is the exposition of the castes, stages of life, and so forth; because in the Aṅgas there is the exposition of the rules governing words and other elements; because in the Upavedas there is the exposition of legal procedures regarding weaponry and the like; and because in the Purāṇas there is knowledge of the maintenance of the world. The non-compound form (visamāsa) is intended to indicate that each preceding item is more authoritative than the following. Consequently, in the event of a conflict between what is stated earlier and later, one should practice exactly what was stated first. In the observation of the true nature of legal procedure, the Vedas and the rest are called "vyavahāra" in the sense that they serve as its constituent limbs (aṅga). The meaning is that, having considered these, he should establish the legal procedures. (11.21)

That by which they conduct themselves is "vyavahāra" (legal procedure). For that king who is authorized to protect his subjects, the Vedas and other such sources are the means for conducting legal procedures. He should conduct himself according to what is declared in the Vedas and other authorities. Legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) is the establishment of the boundaries of worldly conduct. 11.19.
The laws of regions, castes, and families, when not in conflict with traditional scriptures, are authoritative. 11.22. — || 11.20 ||

The *deśadharma* (local custom) consists of festive rites, auspicious ceremonies, and the like. The *jātidharma* (caste duty) includes such things as the absence of red dye on the teeth among the Ābhīras and others. The *kuladharma* (family duty) is exemplified by such rules as "the topknot of the Vasiṣṭhas is on the right side," and so forth. By virtue of the use of the plural number in the word *āmnāyaiḥ*, these refer to the aforementioned Vedas, Dharmaśāstras, and other traditions; when they are not contradictory—that is, when they are not sublated—they are authoritative. The particle *ca* (and) is intended to indicate that even the duties of those to be mentioned later, such as farmers and others, are authoritative provided they do not contradict the *āmnāyas*. One should properly understand the local customs and the rest, and adopt them in accordance with the *āmnāyas*. The instruction is given for the purpose of setting aside those practices that are in conflict with the sacred tradition.

When local customs (*deśadharma*) and caste customs (*jātidharma*) are being observed as specifically prescribed for them, even if their foundational source such as the Vedas is not found, they must nevertheless be maintained provided they do not conflict with the Vedas; they are not to be rejected simply because their source is not explicitly enjoined. In this regard, *deśadharma*s are as follows: When the sun is situated in Aries (*meṣa*), girls in the land of the Caulas paint the sun together with his retinue on the ground using powders of various colors and worship him morning and evening. On the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa, adorned women wander through the village and offer whatever they have obtained to the deity. When the sun is in Cancer (*karkaṭa*), having worshipped the goddess Umā under the two Pūrvaphalgunī stars, they give sprouted grain and salt to beggars according to their means. When the sun is in Pisces (*mīna*), householders worship the goddess Śrī under the two Uttaraphalgunī stars. *Jātidharma*s are as follows: At a wedding, Śūdras drive a pillar into the ground in the middle [of the courtyard], place a thousand wicks in a single vessel, light lamps from each wick, take the bride by the hand, and circumambulate [the pillar]. Other practices of this kind are to be understood in the same way. *Kuladharma*s (family customs) include: some [members of a family] wear the topknot in the middle, others at the back; those who study the sacred texts (*pravacana*) and so forth wear the topknot on both sides depending on the occasion. And there is a connection between these individuals and their respective groups. However, those local customs which contradict the Vedic tradition (*āmnāya*), such as marrying the daughter of a maternal uncle or exerting effort in other pursuits without having studied the Vedas, are not authoritative here. (11.20)
Farmers, merchants, cattle-herders, usurers, and artisans [should be grouped] each in their own respective class. 11.23. — 11.21.

The term *pramāṇam* (authority) carries over from the previous context. This instruction is intended to show that when it is impossible to question the king, one should instead question those within one's own class (*svavarga*). *Karṣakāḥ* are those who live by agriculture; *vaṇijaḥ* are the well-known merchants; *paśupālāḥ* are cattle-herders; *kusīdinaḥ* are usurers; and *kāravaḥ* are artisans such as blacksmiths and the like. Although it would have been sufficient to say simply "one's own class" (*svavarga*), the use of the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) indicates that not only farmers and the others are authorities within their own class, but Brahmins and others as well. Even among them, however, only three or more must be questioned, based on the force of another Smṛti text and Prajāpati’s statement: "In their own class, three or more shall declare the laws.
