Since it has been stated that "what is not contradicted by the sacred traditions (*āmnāya*) is authoritative" (GDh 11.22), if they should speak in contradiction to that, then everyone must go before the Brahmins, for they alone have the capacity to speak in accordance with non-contradiction. This follows from the statement: "That is his legal proceeding" (GDh 11.21). If there is still dissatisfaction even with that, it should be understood that one must go before the king. In that case, since he too must speak in accordance with the sacred traditions, and because a single individual lacks the capacity to demonstrate such non-contradiction, it is established by implication that one should speak together with Brahmins who are experts in those traditions. And so says Manu: [Manu 8.39] "If the members of the court, being corrupted by wealth or passion, do not decide according to the law, the king himself shall take their property and give it to those who know the law. [Manu 8.40] "But if they decide according to the law, one should know that the merit of the deed belongs to them, while half of that merit goes to the king who acts according to justice. [Manu 8.41] "For a king who, through ignorance, does not inflict punishment upon those deserving of punishment, evil quickly seizes both his kingdom and himself. [Manu 8.42] "But a king who inflicts punishment according to the law upon those deserving of punishment gains merit in this world and in the next, provided he is guided by the sacred traditions. [Manu 8.43] "One should not, out of compassion, release a thief; for by releasing a thief, the king becomes associated with the thief's sin. [Manu 8.44] "By punishing the wicked and favoring the virtuous, the king obtains in this world fame and, after death, the world of Indra. [Manu 8.45] "The king must always exert effort to restrain the wicked, for by restraining the wicked, he attains the highest state. [Manu 8.46] "He should appoint as judges men who are pure, wise, self-controlled, well-versed in the sacred traditions, and impartial toward friend and foe alike. [Manu 8.47] "Those same persons, along with Brahmins learned in the Vedas, should investigate the legal proceedings of litigants, both in public and in private. [Manu 8.48] "When a judge, having entered the court, sits down upon his seat, he purifies the entire assembly, just as fire purifies metal. [Manu 8.49] "A man who knows the law should enter the court with composure, wearing his sacred thread, clean-shaven, and dressed in white garments. [Manu 8.50] "There, seated upon his seat, he should look upon the litigants with an equal eye, and examine the truth by means of witnesses and the like, in accordance with the sacred traditions. [Manu 8.51] "When the judge, having entered the court, sits down upon his seat, he purifies the entire assembly, just as fire purifies metal. [Manu 8.52] "A man who knows the law should enter the court with composure, wearing his sacred thread, clean-shaven, and dressed in white garments. [Manu 8.53] "There, seated upon his seat, he should look upon the litigants with an equal eye, and examine the truth by means of witnesses and the like, in accordance with the sacred traditions. [Manu 8.54] "If the judge, out of passion, greed, or delusion, or through negligence, decides a case unjustly, he falls headlong into hell. [Manu 8.55] "But if he decides according to the law, he attains the highest state; therefore, one should never decide a case unjustly, desiring to remain in the world of the righteous. [Manu 8.56] "The king should appoint as judges men who are pure, wise, self-controlled, well-versed in the sacred traditions, and impartial toward friend and foe alike. [Manu 8.57] "Those same persons, along with Brahmins learned in the Vedas, should investigate the legal proceedings of litigants, both in public and in private. [Manu 8.61] "If the judge, out of passion, greed, or delusion, or through negligence, decides a case unjustly, he falls headlong into hell. [Manu 8.62] "But if he decides according to the law, he attains the highest state; therefore, one should never decide a case unjustly, desiring to remain in the world of the righteous. [Manu 8.64] "Those same persons, along with Brahmins learned in the Vedas, should investigate the legal proceedings of litigants, both in public and in private. [Manu 8.65] "When a judge, having entered the court, sits down upon his seat, he purifies the entire assembly, just as fire purifies metal. [Manu 8.66] "A man who knows the law should enter the court with composure, wearing his sacred thread, clean-shaven, and dressed in white garments. [Manu 8.67] "There, seated upon his seat, he should look upon the litigants with an equal eye, and examine the truth by means of witnesses and the like, in accordance with the sacred traditions. [Manu 8.68] "If the judge, out of passion, greed, or delusion, or through negligence, decides a case unjustly, he falls headlong into hell. [Manu 8.69] "But if he decides according to the law, he attains the highest state; therefore, one should never decide a case unjustly, desiring to remain in the world of the righteous. [Manu 8.71] "Those same persons, along with Brahmins learned in the Vedas, should investigate the legal proceedings of litigants, both in public and in private. [Manu 8.72] "When a judge, having entered the court, sits down upon his seat, he purifies the entire assembly, just as fire purifies metal. [Manu 8.73] "A man who knows the law should enter the court with composure, wearing his sacred thread, clean-shaven, and dressed in white garments. [Manu 8.74] "There, seated upon his seat, he should look upon the litigants with an equal eye, and examine the truth by means of witnesses and the like, in accordance with the sacred traditions. [Manu 8.75] "If the judge, out of passion, greed, or delusion, or through negligence, decides a case unjustly, he falls headlong into hell. [Manu 8.76] "But if he decides according to the law, he attains the highest state; therefore, one should never decide a case
"But when the king desires to inspect legal proceedings, he should do so together with Brahmins," and so forth. (MDh 8.1) etc. 11.23.

Farmers are those who live by agriculture; merchants are those devoted to the business of buying and selling; cattle-herders are cowherds; usurers are moneylenders; and artisans are carpenters, washermen, and so forth. These are authoritative within their own respective classes regarding matters known to their own class. (11.21)

Now, if farmers and others were to approach the king directly, how would the king then decide? To this he says: "And thus, when there is a transgression of dharma among farmers and others, having brought their matters before him according to their respective jurisdictions, he establishes the law. (11.24) — [End of] 11.22.

From those [groups], such as the farmers and others; "according to their respective jurisdictions" means that whoever is authorized in a particular matter should be stationed for each category—this is the meaning. "Having brought forward the matters," that is, the customary practices (*ācāra*), having personally and correctly deliberated upon them individually—this is the meaning. Why is this so? Because instead of saying simply "having brought forward" (*avahṛtya*), the author uses the expression "having brought forward again" (*pratyavahṛtya*). From that, it follows that the settlement of the law (*dharma-vyavasthā*) must be made; this is the ellipsis. The intention is that the determination of the truth (*tattva-pariccheda*) must be performed. Although one could have said simply "he shall speak" (*brūyāt*), the inclusion of the term "settlement" (*vyavasthā*) is intended to prevent the reversal of what has already been decided by the king. Furthermore, this indicates that if there is dissatisfaction, there may be repeated proceedings even regarding a matter already settled elsewhere. The inclusion of the word "law" (*dharma*) signifies that he should settle the case solely with the intent of justice (*dharma-buddhi*), and not out of a desire for material gain (*artha-āśaya*). (11.24)

From among those respective groups, having brought back and ascertained the matters—the various modes of conduct—from those who are authorized as the established authorities within each group according to their jurisdiction, the settlement of the law (dharma-vyavasthā) must be carried out. When they have declared, "In this manner our own traditional practice (ācāra) is sufficient," the settlement should be established exactly in that way. || 11.22 ||
Now, if they should speak falsely out of partiality, how then is the truth to be known?
Reasoning (*tarka*) is the means for attaining right understanding. (11.25) — [End of] 11.23.
In the comprehension and ascertainment of that which is consistent with logic (*nyāya*), *tarka*—inference—is the means; that is to say, it is the primary means. Thus said Nārada:
"Just as a hunter tracks the path of a deer by drops of blood, so should a king track the path of *dharma* through inference" (MDh 8.44). 11.25.

In the comprehension and ascertainment of a matter established by logic (*nyāya*), reasoning (*tarka*) is the means of inference (*anumāna*). The prefix *abhi-* merely restates the meaning of the verbal root. Regarding this, Manu says:
"By outward forms, by gestures, by gait, by physical activity, by joy, and by changes in the eyes and face, the mind within is perceived. (MDh 8.26) // 11.23 //
And therefore:
"Having inferred that, he should cause it to go to its proper place. (11.26) — [End of] 11.24.
Having inferred by means of that inference, as Manu said:

"By outward forms, by gestures, by gait, by movement, and by speech, as well as by changes in the eyes and face, the internal mind is grasped" (MDh 8.26). He should cause it to reach its proper place and its true nature. 11.26.
Having reasoned by means of that logic and having determined that "this matter must be so," one should lead it to its proper place—that is, to whichever side the matter belongs. || 11.24 ||

Now, since the Self is difficult to comprehend even through reasoning when one is alone, one should resolve any conflicting views by consulting those who are elders among the knowers of the three Vedas, and thereby attain final certainty. (11.27) — (11.25)

"Contradiction" (*vipratipatti*) refers to the inability of a single person to determine [the truth] through reasoning alone, due to the extreme subtlety of the matter and because signs (*liṅga*) are observed in both ways. Regarding that [contradiction], "those who are elders among the knowers of the three Vedas" (*traividyavṛddhāḥ*) are those who have reached the further shore of all three Vedas; from them one should "withdraw"—that is, learn—having reflected: "This is the sign for this [matter]; this is the determiner of this; previously this was the sign for it, but now there is another sign; what does this determine? and so forth—the meaning is that one should know the reality after such deliberation. Those who were mentioned as assistants for the purpose of ensuring no contradiction with the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) and other authorities are here restated for the purpose of specifying the characteristics of the "knowers of the three Vedas. As Manu says: [text follows].

"Disciplined by ministers who are knowers of the mantras, he should enter the assembly. (MDh 8.1). If it is argued that this must be stated in that very place [in Chapter 8], there is no such fault; for the purpose of this instruction here is to show that they do not merely conduct deliberations on matters not contrary to the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*), but also on matters where there is doubt regarding the *liṅga* (indicative mark). When there is no doubt concerning the *liṅga* and no contradiction, the king’s own power of discernment should be understood as operative, because the assembly serves both purposes. However, when there is doubt regarding the *liṅga*, he should have the matter brought forward by those aged in the three Vedas (*traividya*) and not decide it himself; for although this was already established by the rule "he should cause [the litigant] to go to his proper place," the phrase "he should cause him to reach a final conclusion" is restated here [to emphasize this point]. (11.27)

When there is disagreement and the matter is difficult to ascertain, he should assemble those who are elders among the knowers of the three Vedas; having deliberated with them on the true nature of the matter and having received their consensus, he should bring it to a final conclusion. He should lead [the king] to whichever position the matter has been definitively settled upon. (11.25)
What happens for one who acts in this way? To this he says: "What happens for one who acts in this way?
Thus, his supreme good (niḥśreyasa) comes to be. (11.28)
For in this way, his supreme good comes to pass. || 11.26 ||

For one who makes this determination, there is the attainment of the supreme good and victory in both worlds: through the acquisition of merit in the hereafter, and through the affection of the people in this world. The word "iti" has the sense of a reason, meaning "because it is thus. (11.28)

For one who makes such a determination, there arises the highest good in both worlds: here, through the affection of the people, and in the hereafter, through the attainment of dharma; for this reason. (11.26)

Thus it occurs to the king: "What happens to those who are elders learned in the three Vedas, standing in the capacity of his assistants? To this, the Śruti provides an illustration corresponding to that. It is not only the success of the king; rather, what then? It cites the Śruti to show that it belongs to the Brahmins as judges as well:
"It is known that *brahman* joined with *kṣatra* sustains the gods, the ancestors, and human beings. (11.29) — [End of] 11.27.

H reads "saṃpṛktam" (joined). The Brahman characterized by the three Vedas is joined with, or associated with, the Kṣatriya king; the meaning is that it performs the discernment of dharma together with the king. By means of the performance of unimpeded rites, it sustains the gods and ancestors through oblations and the like, according to the principle: "The gods subsist on what is offered from here"; and it sustains human beings through the production of food. Therefore, it must be said that the discernment of questions regarding dharma belongs to kings. 11.29.

It is established by the Śruti that Brahman, characterized by the three Vedas, when joined with Kṣatra—that is, together with the king—discriminates the Dharma and sustains the gods, the ancestors, and human beings. When this determination has been made, men perform the actions as prescribed. And because of the principle that "the gods subsist upon that righteous action, and the ancestors do not perish," there comes to be the sustenance of all. || 11.27 ||

But if, even while such a rule is being established, they do not desist from immorality, then—since he does not approve of the rule on account of their immorality—it is said that "punishment is for the sake of subduing"; therefore, one should subdue those who are unsubdued. (11.30) — || 11.28 ||

*Daṇḍa* is that which subdues the unsubdued, or that wherein they are subdued; for Manu and others have stated that it is called *daṇḍa* because of its application as a means of subduing. As Manu says:

"Even gods, dānavas, gandharvas, rākṣasas, birds, and serpents are made fit for their respective enjoyments only when restrained by *daṇḍa* alone" (MDh 7.23). Therefore, in whatever manner one is subdued—whether by speech or by wealth and other means—as Manu has said: [MDh 7.15]... [text continues].

"First one should apply the punishment of reproach, then the punishment of verbal censure; third is the punishment of fines, and after that, the punishment of corporal chastisement. (MDh 8.129). In this manner, one should deal with those who persist in improper acts due to bad character and the like. 11.30.

Those who know the Dharma say that the term *daṇḍa* possesses the nature of *daṇḍa* (punishment) because of its connection with the act of subduing (*damanayoga*). Therefore, one should subdue those who are unsubdued and bring them under control. Although the meaning "one should subdue the unsubdued by means of punishment" is already established, [the text specifies]:

"One should first employ the punishment of censure (*dhig-daṇḍa*), then the punishment of verbal reprimand (*vāk-daṇḍa*), thirdly the punishment of fines (*dhana-daṇḍa*), and after that, the punishment of corporal death (*vadha-daṇḍa*). (MDh 8.129)
"Even the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, rākṣasas, birds, and serpents are made to serve for the enjoyment [of others] when oppressed by the rod alone. [MDh 7.23] Thus [ends verse 11.28].
Having established the subjects in this manner, [the author] asks: how do they proceed?

Furthermore, since the castes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*) are being established by the king in their own respective duties through the authority of the scriptures, he asks: how is their perfection achieved? To this, he says:

"The castes and stages of life, being devoted to their own duties, after death experience the fruit of their actions; then, by the remainder [of that karma], they obtain a birth distinguished by place, caste, family, form, lifespan, sacred learning, conduct, wealth, happiness, and intelligence."
H reads "varṇāśramāḥ sva-".

The *varṇas* are the Brāhmaṇas and so forth; the *āśramas* are the students (*brahmacārin*) and so forth. Those who are devoted to their own duties—that is, intent on the performance of their respective duties—after departing this life and experiencing the fruits of their actions in the other world, attain birth here in connection with distinguished places and so forth, by means of the remainder of that enjoyment of the fruits. The word "distinguished" (*viśiṣṭa*) is connected with each term: a distinguished place such as Āryāvarta; a distinguished caste such as Brāhmaṇa; a distinguished family endowed with Vedic study and the like; a distinguished form, meaning a pleasing appearance; a distinguished lifespan, such as a full hundred years; distinguished learning, accompanied by the understanding of the meaning of the Vedas; distinguished conduct, meaning excellent character; distinguished wealth, characterized by cattle, horses, and so forth; distinguished happiness, which is the successful attainment of desired objects without obstacle; and by the word "intellect" (*medhas*), health is meant—specifically, a distinguished health such that no disease arises even when eating desired foods. By speaking thus, it is established that there is a Self (*ātman*) distinct from the body, which is the agent of obligatory rites and the enjoyer of their fruits. Thus says the Śruti: "This great unborn Self, who consists of consciousness, is the agent and the enjoyer; he is indeed the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), composed of immortality, and established in the vital breath" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22). And likewise Manu.
For that which causes the self to act is designated as the *kṣetrajña*.

"He who performs actions is called the *bhūtātman* by the wise" (MDh 12.12), and so forth. When that eternal being's body—initiated by his past actions—falls due to the exhaustion of karma, he experiences the fruit of those actions, such as heaven and the like, through a body initiated by that very karma which is capable of experiencing its results, and which is accompanied by the powers of ego, the senses, mind, and vital breath (*prāṇa*). Having become composed of food (*annamaya*) by means of medicinal herbs and other substances, and having been transformed into the form of semen, he is drawn in by the wind residing therein—which had previously entered the mother’s womb—and, joined with the mother’s blood, this constitutes what is called "birth," the material cause of a body sustained by the remnants of previously experienced karma.

The meaning of the Sūtra being thus established, an objection is raised: the mention of "stages of life" (*āśrama*) is redundant, because the stages of life are prescribed only for those belonging to the social classes (*varṇa*), and even when one is in a stage of life, one does not lose the status of belonging to a class. Furthermore, the mention of "one's own" (*sva*) is redundant, since ownership is already established by the very fact of performance. The mention of "action" (*karman*) is also redundant, because its meaning is already established by the phrase "having experienced the fruit of action. The mention of "completion" (*niṣṭhā*) is likewise redundant, since it is impossible to perform an act without prior intention. The word "after death" (*pretya*) need not be used either, as its meaning is already established by the phrase "they obtain another birth. When it should have been said "having experienced the fruit," the inclusion of "action" is superfluous, because the fruit is produced by action. The word "therefrom" (*tataḥ*) is also redundant, as the reference to action is already established by the context. Moreover, a "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is logically impossible, because the entirety of the action is exhausted through the enjoyment of its fruit. Indeed, it is not possible for a portion of an action that has become ready to yield its fruit to remain over; for milk and the like do not begin to produce curds and other effects in only a single part. Nor can a "remainder" designated by the word *śeṣa* refer to a residue of impressions (*vāsanā*), because action is formless and thus a residue of impressions is impossible. Nor does the word "remainder" denote an action performed in a previous life, because there is no further eligibility (*adhikāra*) for such an action, and because it is impossible for something already used to have anything else remaining. It is not reasonable to determine that the mere interruption of the experience of the fruit constitutes a "remainder," for that would entail abandoning what is explicitly stated in the scripture and imagining what is not stated; for the scripture speaks of the fruit of the action, not of the interruption of the fruit. Furthermore, an interruption of experience cannot occur while the action remains unexhausted, since that [interruption] depends upon the action—just as a lamp, which depends on oil, is extinguished only by the exhaustion of the oil. Moreover, while there are "remains" in the form of moths and the like that might be gathered up, there is no such thing for the fruit of an action. Therefore, the interruption of the fruit cannot be denoted by the word "remainder. Nor can one divide the fruit of an action itself, thinking, "By this portion I shall experience happiness in the next world, and by this I shall obtain a connection with a specific place," etc., because the fruit is already accomplished. For a division is heard of regarding things that are not yet accomplished—such as, "This field is for rice, this is for barley"—but one does not say, "These rice-grains are being made into barley. If those who have completed their actions obtain another birth in this world due to a remainder of the experience of the fruit in the next, then, in the event of the consequence of the non-existence of liberation, there would be a contradiction with scriptures such as, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1) and "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8). If birth characterized by the attainment of specific places and so forth occurs due to a remainder of action, then the impossibility of the diversity of the world would follow, yet that diversity is clearly observed. And if it is admitted that the fruit belongs to an action already obtained, then human effort (*puruṣakāra*) would be entirely useless. Therefore, since there is no object to be denoted by the word "remainder," and since the intended meaning of the entire Sūtra is untenable, this Sūtra is inconsistent.

In this regard, the term *samādhi* (resolution) is as follows: first, the inclusion of both [categories] must be made, because there is a distinction between the duties (*dharma*) of the social classes (*varṇas*) and those of the stages of life (*āśramas*). Before initiation (*upanayana*), they are called classes; after it, they are called stages. Furthermore, even for those who have not been initiated, there is eligibility for certain duties of the classes. The lack of a compound (*asamāsa*) is for the purpose of including a copulative compound (*dvandva*), so that there may be no suspicion of a coordinate apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); for in the case of a *dvandva*, since both members are primary, the inclusion of both is established. And the word "and" (*ca*) is for the purpose of including the *sṛṣṭis* and *yantras*, since they too obtain excellence through the performance of their own specific duties. Thus says Manu:

"Renouncing the body for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa or for the sake of a cow, or in the rescue of women and children—even if unadorned—is the cause of success for those of the outer castes. (MDh 10.62) The inclusion of the word "own" (*sva*) is intended to include the primary alternative course of action. If it is argued that this is already established because penances are prescribed specifically for what is ordained in times of distress (*āpad*), we say no; for the prescription of penance applies only to the performance of the duties of another caste, not to one's own duty when performed defectively. Thus, the statement of Nārada says:
"When people have perished, a Brāhmaṇa may cross over his distress by the occupation of a Kṣatriya..."

“He should abandon that kṣatriya occupation, having performed purification for himself,” and so forth. Therefore, the mention of "one's own" (*sva*) is intended to exclude the fruit of a defective action. Thus, it should be understood that an action which is defective is neither a means to achieve its [intended] fruit—because there is no prescription of penance for it—nor is it a cause of sin. The inclusion of the word *niṣṭhā* (completion) is for the sake of continuity; for only he who performs the action until the fall of the body is connected with this fruit. The inclusion of the word *pretya* (after death) is to indicate that the fruit is inevitable; just as success is achieved here through visible fruits, so too there must be [success] there through invisible fruits. It does not mean, however, that an action once performed becomes fruitless. The mention of "action" (*karman*) is to show that the connection with this fruit belongs only to the action performed, and not to one who practices the combination of knowledge and action (*jñānakarmasamuccaya*). By this, it should also be seen that the objection regarding the impossibility of liberation is refuted, since such a person becomes truly liberated. The phrase "from that" (*tataḥ*) is also for the purpose of demonstrating the diversity of actions: by the remainder or surplus of each respective action. And thus, because of the gradation of actions, when there is a variety of fruits, the diversity of the world is logically established. The gradation of actions arises from differences in place, time, purity, substance, faith, recipient, and practice; and the word "remainder" (*śeṣa*) should be understood with reference to the aggregate of actions. How so? An action whose fruit is heaven yields its fruit right there; but an action whose fruit is worldly yields a birth connected with a specific place and so forth, and that is the "remainder" of that aggregate. Alternatively, the word "remainder" refers to the action that serves as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the primary action (*pradhānakarman*), such as the Agnihotra, etc., as in: "One desiring cattle should fetch water in a milking vessel" (*ĀpŚr* 1.16.2), or "One desiring vigor should make a sacrificial post of khadira wood" (*ṢaḍviṃBr* 4.4). In that case, the fruit of the primary action is enjoyed in the next world, while the fruit of the subsidiary is experienced here. This should be viewed like a tree: a tree is produced with many roots. When its principal roots are mostly severed, it falls because it cannot support the weight due to having only small, sapless roots. Similarly, when the primary form of an action is exhausted through experience, the residual form—which is unable to establish the agent in that state—yields a fruit connected with a specific place and so forth. Or it should be viewed like a jar of ghee: even when the jar of ghee has been used up, it continues to burn when touched by fire due to the residue of the oily scent; likewise, the performer of the action will experience a specific place and so forth solely due to the residue of the latent impression (*vāsanā*). Since action possesses parts, the existence of such a latent impression is logical, and its having parts follows from the fact that it is an effect.

As for what was said—that human effort (puruṣakāra) is purposeless—it is replied: only that which is endowed with human effort has a connection with the fruit; for one devoid of it, there is not even a connection with food and such. Therefore, since the previously mentioned cause for the bestowal of the fruit is [karma], while human effort is the cause of the connection, human effort is not purposeless; thus, this entire sūtra is indeed logically consistent. 11.31

The *varṇas* are the Brāhmaṇas and so forth; the *āśramas* are the stages of studenthood (*brahmacarya*) and so forth. Those who were devoted to their own duties—having performed the duties pertaining to their caste, those pertaining to their stage of life, and those pertaining to both—and having passed away, gone to another world after death, and experienced the fruit of each respective action such as heaven and so forth, thereafter, by means of the remainder (*śeṣa*)—the karma remaining after what has been enjoyed—they obtain a birth characterized by specific places and other factors. In this context, the word "specific" (*viśiṣṭa*) is connected with all the following: place, caste, family, form, lifespan, learning, conduct, wealth, happiness, and intelligence. A "specific place" is the Land of the Āryas (*Āryāvarta*) and so forth. A "specific caste" is the Brāhmaṇa caste. A "specific family" is one endowed with Vedic study and other virtues. "Specific form" means possessing beauty. "Specific lifespan" is one hundred and sixteen years, based on the observation that "he lived for one hundred and sixteen years. Being free from disease is also a quality of lifespan. "Specific learning" has been explained in the passage: "And the Brāhmaṇa who is very learned" (GDh 8.1). "Specific conduct" is a character free from ulterior motives. "Specific wealth" is that acquired through righteous means and employed for righteous purposes. "Happiness" is the enjoyment of permitted pleasures by abiding in a state free from misfortune. "Specific intelligence" is the capacity to grasp the meaning of texts; the form *medhā* ending in *s* is archaic (*ārṣa*), as seen in words like *sumedhas* and *durmedhas*. Actions being experienced—whether meritorious or non-meritorious—are experienced in this way along with their remnants, because even the taking of a body in this life is caused by merit and demerit. (11.29)
Moving in all directions, they perish, turned upside down. || 11.32 || — || 11.30 ||

Furthermore, those who do not perform their own duties themselves and are not established in them by the king are "all-pervasive" (viśvañcaḥ) animals that perish, due to the absence of connection with distinguished places and other such factors. Those who are the opposite are those who are either devoted to their own duties or otherwise. By speaking thus, it is shown that for those who are devoted to their own duties, there is the highest state; for those who are established in their own dharma by the king, there is the middling state; and for those who are neither devoted to their own duties nor established in them by the king, there is the lowest state. Thus it has been said in the Purāṇa:
Through auspicious deeds one attains the state of a deity; through mixed deeds, human birth;
and through inauspicious deeds, a person obtains a lower birth. (11.32)

Those belonging to the various castes and stages of life who do not perform their own duties properly become perverted and distracted; wandering into diverse wombs, they perish, experiencing a succession of misfortunes. || 11.30 ||
The teacher’s instruction and punishment protect them. || 11.33 || — || 11.31 ||

The instruction of the teacher protects those members of the castes and stages of life who are perishing through the non-performance of prescribed duties and the practice of forbidden ones; for others, however, there is punishment. (11.33)

The instruction of the teacher protects those castes and stages of life as long as they do not act contrary to what has been prescribed; even there, for one who does not abide [in that teaching], there is the punishment of the king.
Since this is so, therefore the king and the teacher are blameless; they are not to be censured. (11.34) — (11.32)

And because they serve as the cause of protection, even when the cause exists, harshness and the like may also be spoken; therefore, both the teacher who instructs even what is harsh and the king who maintains even what is fierce are not to be censured, owing to their being extremely beneficial. 11.34.

For this reason, the king and the teacher are to be honored and beyond reproach. Even though they may act as leaders at the time of restraint out of a desire for one's welfare, nevertheless, no criticism of them should be made. [The repetition marks the end of the chapter. 11.32
Now begins the twelfth chapter. It was stated in general terms:

"They say that punishment (*daṇḍa*) is so called because it subdues (*damana*); therefore, one should subdue those who are unsubdued" (GDh 11.30). In that regard, it must be explained what the punishment shall be for which offense; thus he says: "One should subdue those who are unsubdued by means of punishment. Since it has been stated there, for how much offense shall there be how much punishment? To this he says: [the following].
A Śūdra who, having deceived or struck twice-born men with verbal or physical violence, shall have that very limb by which he committed the offense cut off. 12.1.
H reads: “abhisaṃdhāyā-”

The Śūdra is mentioned. He, having deceived (*atisaṃdhāya*)—that is, having intentionally transgressed against—the twice-born (*dvijāti*), such as Brāhmaṇas and others, and not merely by way of jest or the like; and having "assaulted" (*abhihatya*)—the prefix *abhi-* being for the purpose of indicating intentional awareness; having assaulted, that is, having struck them, sequentially with verbal and physical violence. In this regard, the sequence should be understood as: having deceived through verbal violence and having assaulted through physical violence. Transgression through verbal violence means the uttering of harsh words and the like after having transgressed. The word *paruṣa* is a synonym for *ugra* (fierce). The meaning is: having transgressed with fierce speech and having assaulted with a fierce blow. Consequently, there is no fault [if the assault is] with a clod of earth or similar objects. A "limb" (*aṅga*) is a part of the body; it is "to be severed" (*mocya*)—meaning it is to be cut off—that hand or other member with which he might strike or cause pain. And thus, he makes known that physical violence (*daṇḍapāruṣya*) occurs even without an actual weapon or staff. In the case of verbal violence, the tongue is to be cut; in the case of physical violence with the hand or other members, that specific limb is to be severed—so it should be understood. From the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it follows that when both offenses are committed, both punishments are to be inflicted. (12.1)

The Śūdra is the fourth caste. If he, having intended to and having overcome the three twice-born castes—the Brāhmaṇas and the others—by verbal abuse, and having struck them with physical violence (daṇḍapāruṣya), that is, having intentionally and premeditatively beaten them; here the mention of "staff" (daṇḍa) is illustrative of the hand and other such instruments as well. Acting in this manner, he is to have a limb severed—that very limb by which he might strike or commit the offense must be cut off. If he strikes with the hand, his hand is to be amputated; if he strikes with the foot, his foot is to be amputated; if [he strikes] with speech, his tongue is to be cut off. On this point, Manu says:

"Whatever limb of a Brāhmaṇa with which a person of lower caste might offend, that very limb of his shall be cut off; such is the ordinance of Manu. (MDh 8.279). Because of the inclusion of the term "harshness," this does not apply in the case of speaking unpleasant words in jest, nor in striking [another] in jest or similar circumstances. 12.1.
For violating an Arya woman, the penis shall be excised and his property confiscated. 12.2.

If a woman of noble conduct (*āryavṛttā*) belongs to Āryas such as Brāhmaṇas and others, [the following applies]. Why is this so? Because, although one should have said "sexual intercourse with a woman" (*stry-abhigamana*), the text begins by saying "sexual intercourse with an Ārya woman" (*ārya-strī-abhigamana*). Consequently, if she is present in the form of a prostitute, there is no punishment. Since the term "intercourse" (*abhigamana*) is well-established as referring specifically to a woman, the inclusion of the word "woman" (*strī*) is for the purpose of indicating that this applies even to a Śūdra woman who has been taken into the household of an Ārya. The prefix *abhi-* in "intercourse" (*abhigamane*) signifies that the act was intentional. Therefore, in cases where it is done unintentionally, such as during sleep, a lighter punishment should be understood to apply. The "extraction of the organ" (*liṅgasyoddhāraḥ*) means its amputation, and "confiscation of all property" (*sarvasvaharaṇam*) must be carried out. Although it would have been sufficient to say "the extraction of that organ and [the confiscation] of wealth" (*talliṅgoddhāro dhanasya ca*), the expression used is "and the confiscation of his own property" (*svaharaṇaṃ ca*). The particle *ca* (and) serves to indicate conjunction; the lack of a compound is intended to prevent the implication of an option (*vikalpa*). Thus, in the case of approaching a Kṣatriya or Vaiśya woman, each respective penalty applies according to the order, whereas for a Brāhmaṇa, both penalties apply. (12.2)

The word "śūdra" refers back to the subject under discussion in the genitive case. "Āryas" refers to those of the three higher castes. If a Śūdra should have sexual intercourse with the wife of any of them, his punishment shall be the excision of his organ—the removal of the penis—and the confiscation of whatever property he possesses. Although the phrase "intercourse with an Ārya woman" would have sufficed, the inclusion of the word "strī" (woman) is intended to indicate that this applies even when the Śūdra approaches a woman who has been taken [as a wife] by an Ārya. In that regard, if she is a Vaiśya woman, there is confiscation of his property; if she is a Kṣatriya woman, there is excision of the organ; and if she is a Brāhmaṇa woman, both punishments apply. (12.2)
If he is a protector, the punishment is death. 12.3.
If he is their protector, then upon having sexual intercourse with them, he must carry out both the previously mentioned acts and, because of his superior status, the act of killing. 12.3.
If he is a Śūdra who acts as their protector, then he must be executed; because of the mention of "excessive," both of the previously mentioned punishments also apply. || 12.3 ||

Now, for one who eavesdrops upon his Veda, there shall be the filling of the ears with molten tin and lac; for reciting it, the cutting off of the tongue; and for retaining it, the destruction of the body. 12.4.
This [rule] applies after five years, because of the inclusion of the word "atha" (then). And so it is stated in another Smṛti:
"But if a Śūdra, having heard the Veda, should be five years old, he becomes liable to punishment;
one who has not reached five years of age does not deserve punishment anywhere."

The word *ha* is for the purpose of indicating that [the act] was intentional. This word is employed to show that [the penalty applies] not only to the protector. "Veda" means the Veda together with its auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga*). Why? Because of the observation in the Gṛhya-smṛti: "The Veda with its limbs should not be studied in the presence of women or Śūdras. By the prefix *upa*, which denotes proximity, he shows that the fault lies only in the hearing of the syllables. Consequently, there is no fault in merely hearing the sound. Since the infliction of punishment is prescribed only for intentional acts by the word *ha*, it should be understood that there is no fault even if syllables are heard occasionally through negligence. It should be understood as "with tin and lac," meaning with tin and with lac; and it should be understood as "with them heated," because of the force of the instruction regarding their filling [the ears]. The prefix *prati* is for the purpose of including both ears. In the case of reciting [the Veda], the cutting of the tongue must be performed along with the twice-born [who overhears]; in the case of memorizing it, the meaning is that the cutting must be performed by oneself alone. With an axe, the splitting of the body must be performed. 12.4.

Now, the word *atha* is used as a particle of emphasis (*vākyālaṃkāre*). "Upaśrutya" means the intentional grasping of syllables through listening. For this Śūdra who listens to the Veda, his two ears are to be filled with molten tin and lac (*trapu-jatubhyām*). By the term "upaśravaṇa," there is no fault in merely hearing the sound by chance. If he should utter or pronounce the syllables of the Veda together with the twice-born, his tongue is to be cut off. Once he has mastered them such that he is able to recite them even when gone elsewhere, then his body is to be split with an axe or similar weapon. (12.4)
One who seeks to obtain [another's] seat, bed, or path should be fined. 12.5.

Desiring equality with the noble ones at will regarding seats and other matters: "equality regarding seats and so forth" refers to equality in qualities such as height, which means equality of speech and simultaneous pronunciation; "equality on the road" means traveling together side-by-side, leaving them not behind; the "fine" should be understood as being less than one hundred [paṇas], depending on the circumstances of the place and so forth. (12.5)

If a Śūdra seeks equality with the twice-born in matters such as sitting and so forth—that is, if he desires a status equal to theirs—he should be punished for that. And the punishment has been shown by Āpastamba: “In speech, on the path, on the bed, and on the seat—if these are shared, there shall be a flogging with a rod” (ĀpDh 2.27.15). This means he is to be struck with a rod. Here, there is a specific rule from Manu: “An inferior who seeks to sit together with a superior, having been branded on the hip, should be banished; or else, one should cause his buttocks to be cut off” (MDh 8.281). 12.5.
A Kṣatriya [should pay] one hundred for insulting a Brāhmaṇa. || 12.6 ||

The word "committed" (*kṛta*) is to be supplied [to the verse]. Regarding verbal abuse (*ākrośa*), that is, harshness of speech; however, in the case of physical assault (*daṇḍapāruṣya*), double the fine should be prescribed, according to the force of other *smṛti* texts. And so says Bṛhaspati:

"When verbal abuse has been committed against someone, whatever punishment is ordained for that [abuse], one should cause double that punishment to be inflicted, except in the case of death. Likewise, Uśanas says: "In the case of threatening with a blow, the penalty is equal to that for verbal abuse; in the case of actually striking, it is double; in the case of drawing blood, it is triple," and so forth. A Kṣatriya should be fined one hundred *kārṣāpaṇas* for abusing a Brāhmaṇa. (12.6)

If a Kṣatriya should revile a Brāhmaṇa with harsh speech or insult him, he shall be fined one hundred [paṇas]. In all matters concerning fines, the traditional legal practice of the Smṛtis is that the copper *kārṣāpaṇa* is understood; thus, he is to be fined one hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*. In cases of physical assault, the fine is doubled. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
"When verbal abuse has been committed, whatever fine is prescribed for the offender, one should cause that very same fine to be doubled, except in the case of death. (12.6)
A Vaiśya [should give] one and a half [times]. || 12.7 ||
The phrase "insulting a Brāhmaṇa" continues [from the previous rule]. One hundred and fifty—that is, one hundred increased by half—is the fine for which a Vaiśya is to be punished. 12.7.
But a Vaiśya, for insulting a Brāhmaṇa, shall be fined one hundred and fifty; that is, he shall be fined one hundred and fifty, which is fifty more than one hundred. || 12.7 ||
But for a Kṣatriya, a Brāhmaṇa shall pay fifty.

The term "when reviled" (*ākruṣṭe*) carries over from the previous rule. When a Kṣatriya reviles a Brāhmaṇa who is not learned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*), [the Brāhmaṇa] shall be fined fifty [paṇas]. Why? Because of the inclusion of the word "but" (*tu*). Among those of equal caste, a fine of twelve [paṇas] should be prescribed; for those who are not to be reviled, double that amount should be prescribed. And so says Manu:

"In the case of an offense among the twice-born of equal caste, the fine is exactly twelve. In disputes regarding those who are not to be reviled, that same fine shall be doubled. (MDh 8.269) || 12.8 ||
But a Brāhmaṇa, when reviling a Kṣatriya, shall be fined fifty paṇas. || 12.8 ||
Half of that [period] for a Vaiśya. || 12.9 ||
If a Vaiśya is abused, a Brāhmaṇa shall be fined twenty-five [paṇas]. || 12.9 ||
For abusing a Vaiśya, he shall be fined half of that, namely twenty-five paṇas. || 12.9 ||
For a Śūdra, there is nothing [to be done]. || 12.10 ||

When reviled, a Brāhmaṇa is not to be fined at all. If it is argued that this is already established by the fact that he is not even to be addressed [with a fine], we say no; for this is intended to prescribe a punishment for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya. Thus, a punishment must be determined in their case: twenty-four paṇas for the Kṣatriya and thirty-six for the Vaiśya. Accordingly, Uśanas says: "Having reviled a Śūdra, a Kṣatriya shall be subject to a fine of twenty-four [paṇas], and a Vaiśya thirty-six," and so forth. (12.10)

When a Brāhmaṇa is reviled, he is not to be fined for anything whatsoever. This [rule] should not be stated [as a general principle], because the absence of punishment would be established simply by the fact that no penalty is prescribed; rather, it was stated for the purpose of prescribing a punishment for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who reviles a Śūdra. Thus it has been said by Uśanas: "Having reviled a Śūdra, a Kṣatriya shall incur a fine of twenty-four paṇas, and a Vaiśya thirty-six. (12.10)
The Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya are like the Brāhmaṇa and the Rājanya. || 12.11 ||

What has been stated regarding mutual abuse between a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya should also be understood to apply to a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya—namely, one hundred for the Kṣatriya and fifty for the Vaiśya. The same should be understood to apply to those born of intermediate castes as well. Thus says Jamadagni: "For those born in the natural order (anuloma), the [penalty] is equal to that of the mother; for those born in the inverse order (pratiloma), it is equal to that of the father. (12.11)

Whatever punishment is prescribed for mutual verbal abuse between a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya, the same applies to mutual verbal abuse between a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya. Accordingly, the rule should be adapted as follows: "A Vaiśya shall pay a hundred [paṇas] for abusing a Kṣatriya; but a Kṣatriya shall pay fifty for abusing a Vaiśya. This should be understood to apply likewise among those born of intermediate castes. On this point, Jamadagni says: "For those born in the direct order (anuloma), the status is equal to that of the mother; for those born in the inverse order (pratiloma), it is equal to that of the father. (12.11)
Having stated the punishment for violence, he now speaks regarding theft.
The punishment for violence has been declared; he now states the punishment for theft:
"The guilt of theft for a Śūdra is eightfold. (12.12)

That property which has been acquired through theft for the sake of unrighteousness is designated by the word *kilbiṣa*; "theft-taint" (*steyakilbiṣa*) means stolen wealth. An eightfold fine is the punishment for that. Regarding the rule "one who seeks to recover [what was taken] shall be fined" (GDh 12.5), the word "fined" (*daṇḍya*)—which is the subject here according to the analogy of a river's current—is understood here as "fine" (*daṇḍa*) to conform to the genitive case. Alternatively, the word *kilbiṣa* denotes the fine itself; thus "theft-taint" means the theft-fine. That [fine] should be taken as eightfold. In this context, however, one should exclude the gold of a Brāhmaṇa, because since its theft is taught among the mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*), the severity of the punishment for it is greater. (12.12)

*Steya* means theft. Property acquired through theft is called *kilbiṣa* (sin/impurity) because it is the cause of sin. A Śūdra must restore eightfold the property acquired by theft. This genitive case (*steyakilbiṣasya*) refers to the agent; the meaning is that the Śūdra shall pay eightfold for the sin of theft to the king as a form of punishment. Of that, one part is to be given to the owner, and the remainder to the king. And it has been stated: "Having recovered what was stolen by a thief," and so forth. (MDh 12.12)
For the other castes, the [distances] increase twofold for each successive class.

For the others—the Vaiśya, the Kṣatriya, and the Brāhmaṇa—the fine is doubled for each successive higher caste, as indicated by the beginning of the rule stating "for each caste in reverse order. Thus, the fine for a Vaiśya is sixteenfold, for a Kṣatriya it is thirty-twofold, and for a Brāhmaṇa it is sixty-fourfold. In all cases, the restoration of the wealth to the owner must be understood, because it has been stated: "Having recovered what was stolen by thieves, he shall restore it to its proper place" (GDh 10.46). 12.13.

For the others—the Vaiśyas and so forth—the sins of theft must be made to increase twofold for each successive caste: sixteenfold for a Vaiśya, thirty-twofold for a Kṣatriya, and sixty-fourfold for a Brāhmaṇa. (12.13)
Why is this so? He says: "In the case of a transgression by one who knows, the punishment is greater. (12.14)

Just as there is an increase in punishment based on the superiority of caste, so too it should be understood that there is an increase in punishment due to the superiority of knowledge, because another Smṛti text states: "That [punishment] for a learned man should be known to be one and a half times that prescribed for his own caste. And this is logical, since it says, "Having known [the value], he transgresses. Once it is established that there is a greater punishment for the learned, the inclusion of the term "transgression" (atikrama) is for the sake of restriction; this applies only to the subject of theft, not to the subject of violence (sāhasa), nor even to the subject of penance (prāyaścitta). By stating this, it is demonstrated that following the prescription of punishment, there is also a determination of the gravity or lightness of the penance. Furthermore, what was stated in the section on violence—"half the punishment for a Śrotriya"—is thus also justified. 12.14.

Just as there is a greater excellence of knowledge according to the excellence of one’s caste, so too does the severity of the punishment increase for the transgression of what is prescribed. For one who acts even after knowing the fault inherent in the prohibition, the fault is aggravated. However, for one who acts without knowing, there is leniency, like that afforded to one falling into a blind well; this is an exception to the rule regarding the "eightfold fine" (*aṣṭāpādya*) and so forth. (12.14)
He states the exception for this:
"In the case of taking fruits, green vegetables, grain, or potherbs, [the fine is] five *kṛṣṇalas* when the amount is small. (12.15)

H reads "alpam" (small amount) of fruits such as mangoes and the like, meaning unripe green grain such as rice and so forth; and for the theft of vegetables such as radishes and the like, the fine is one *māṣa*. Why? Because another Smṛti text states, "A *māṣa* consists of five *kṛṣṇalas*" [MDh 8.134]. In the case of a small amount—meaning merely enough to fill the stomach—or in the case of other substances, this very rule of "eightfold" [GDh 12.12] is to be understood to apply. || 12.15 ||

Fruit refers to mangoes and the like; green grain refers to rice and other crops while still standing on the stalk; vegetables refer to vāstūka and similar greens. For the theft or taking of these, the fine is five *kṛṣṇalas*. A *kṛṣṇala* is the size of a *guñjā* seed. Regarding the *māṣa*: "A *māṣa* should be known as one-twentieth of a *kārṣāpaṇa*; a *kṛṣṇala* is declared to be one-fourth of a *māṣa*. Thus it is said.

A collection of five *kṛṣṇalas* is called a *pañcakṛṣṇala*. If that is small—meaning it is merely enough fruit and so forth to fill the stomach—then [the fine is] as stated; but if it is more, then there is indeed the eightfold fine (*aṣṭāpādya*). || 12.15 ||
If cattle are harmed, the fault lies with the owner. 12.16.
When crops and other produce are damaged by cattle, the punishment for the owner of those cattle will be stated hereafter. (12.16)
When crops and other produce are damaged by cattle, the fault lies with the owner of the cattle; the measure of the fine will be stated [later]. (12.16)
But when that [body] is joined with a protector, || 12.17 ||

The meaning is that when the act is accompanied by a keeper, the keeper alone bears the penalty. The word "but" (tu) is intended to indicate that the penalty is greater when the act was caused to be committed by the keeper. This greater degree is indeed twofold, as seen in another Smṛti text stating: "When caused by a keeper, the penalty is double. (12.17)

If the animal has been entrusted to the herdsman by its owner, then the fault lies with that herdsman. A "pāla" is one who protects; here it refers to the cowherd. This applies when the act is committed through negligence; however, if it is done intentionally, the fine is double, as is seen in another Smṛti text. (12.17)
On a path or in an uncultivated field, the responsibility for damage rests with both the herdsman and the owner of the field.
The meaning is that because the protector acts without effort and the other likewise fails to act as a protector, they both shall pay half and half. 12.18.

The field-owner’s fields are his property, and the path shall be unenclosed; when cattle cause damage there, the punishment for both the keeper and the field-owner shall be equal—half and half—because of the keeper’s negligence and the field-owner’s failure to provide an enclosure.
For it is seen in the *Mānava* (Manu Smṛti): "And one should construct an enclosure there such that even a camel cannot look over it" (MDh 8.239). || 12.18 ||
Now he states the specific fines according to the particular animal;
he states the measure of the fine:
"Five māṣas for a cow. (12.19)
A *māṣa* is one-twentieth part of a *kārṣāpaṇa*. Thus says Uśanas:
"A *māṣa* should be known as one-twentieth part of a *kārṣāpaṇa*;
a *kākaṇī*, however, is proclaimed to be one-fourth part of a *māṣa*."
For these five offenses, he shall be punished with the five products of the cow. || 12.19 ||
Uśanas has set forth the *māṣa*:
"A *māṣa* should be known as the twentieth part of a *kārṣāpaṇa*;
a *kākiṇī*, however, is proclaimed to be a fourth part of a *māṣa*. Thus [it is said].
The fine for destroying crops and the like when they have been damaged by cows is five māṣas. || 12.19 ||
Six [mātrās] for a camel and a donkey. 12.20.
For an offense against a camel and for an offense against a donkey, the fine shall be six māṣas in each case. || 12.20 ||
The compound is treated as a singular collective (dvandvaikavadbhāva). However, if a camel or a donkey causes injury, the fine shall be six māṣas for each animal. || 12.20 ||
Ten [times] that of a horse or a buffalo. 12.21.
In this case as well, the fine for each individual is ten māṣas. || 12.21 ||
The gender is not intended to be significant. For a horse and for a buffalo, the fine is ten māṣas each. || 12.21 ||
In goats and sheep, there are two each.

The plural number is used for the purpose of excluding the calf; this should be understood to apply to the preceding cases as well. The fine is two māṣas each. The repetition at the end is intended to include the preceding items by extension; otherwise, there would be uncertainty. (12.22)

For two goats and two sheep that are kept together, the fine is two māṣas each; the plural number is used because they move about in a group. For each goat and each sheep, the punishment is two [māṣas] each. (12.22)
There is a fine for total destruction. || 12.23 ||

If there is the capacity for regrowth despite total destruction, the owner of the field shall be given a share of the produce proportionate to the extent that has been destroyed; and the king shall impose a corresponding fine. 12.23.

Furthermore, so that there may be no further growth [of the crop], the penalty for total destruction is *śada*. *Śada* is a term denoting a portion. Whatever portion would have arisen there, that much must be paid to the owner, and a corresponding fine must be paid to the king. (12.23)
If he fails to perform what is prescribed and engages in what is forbidden, his own property shall be confiscated after the [period of] alms-food and clothing has expired. 12.24.
H reads "cailapiṇḍād".

In the case of constantly failing to perform what is prescribed for the learned, or constantly failing to carry out what is enjoined—not merely once—and in the case of repeatedly indulging in prohibited acts such as eating forbidden food—not through negligence—the king shall confiscate whatever exceeds the mere necessities of food and clothing, such as a cloth or a lump of alms. However, his food and clothing must be released until the time when other property arrives for him; even after that, if he continues [the offense], his own property must again be confiscated. When this is done, out of fear of punishment, he will engage only in his own proper work. By the use of the word "and" (ca), it is implied that he must also be made to perform penance. (12.24)

The prescribed [duty] has been stated. Regarding the constant non-performance of what is prescribed and the constant practice of what is forbidden, one must effect the seizure of whatever property he possesses beyond the clothing and the food—where "clothing" means a garment and "food" means a morsel—and that which exceeds the amount necessary for their cessation. Whatever remains after setting aside what is required for clothing and seating must be taken from him; thus [the rule applies] until he desists. 12.24.

Now he states an exception to the prohibition against taking what is not given, which was mentioned in the section on the student (*brahmacārin*): "For the sake of cows or fire, one may take grass, fuel, and the flowers of shrubs and trees as if they were one's own; and likewise fruits from those that are not enclosed. (12.25)

Grass for the sake of cows; by the mention of "fire," both Vedic (*śrauta*) and traditional (*smārta*) fires are included, but not the worldly fire—for that purpose, fuel-wood; and the flowers of shrubs such as the *karavīra* and others—the word "vanaspati" here is a synonym for "tree," because flowers do not directly grow on [the category of] *vanaspati*s themselves, as Manu has stated.

"Those which bear fruit without flowers are known as *vanaspati*s. (MDh 1.47) Flowers are for the purpose of worshipping the gods, not for one's own enjoyment, because of their association with cows and fire. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), leaves are intended for the feeding of Brahmins. Although one could have said "the flowers of creepers and *vanaspati*s," the lack of a compound (in *oṣadhīnām*) indicates that even roots and other parts of herbs are for the sake of Brahmins. "As one owns" (*svavat*) means they should be taken in such a way that no injury occurs to them. As Vyāsa has said: "One should gather what is ripe again and again, but one should avoid cutting the root."

"Like a gardener in a grove, not like a charcoal-maker. Here, "fruits" refers to mangoes and the like; they are mentioned separately for the purpose of indicating times of distress. By the word "and" (ca), vegetables are also included. "Of those not enclosed" means those that have not been made into a formal garden (*ārāma*). This qualifies both [fruits and vegetables]. Thus, it is established that even grass and such are prohibited within a garden. (12.25)

The fire referred to here is that for Śrauta and Smārta rites, not the common (laukika) fire. Grasses are for the sake of the cows; fuel—consisting of shrubs and trees—is for the sake of the fire; and the flowers of creepers and trees are for the purpose of worshipping the deities, not for personal enjoyment. Because they are mentioned in conjunction with the cows and the fire, it is understood that they are for the sake of the deities. One may take these grasses and other items even if they have not been given by the owners; one should take them just as the owner takes them without hesitation. If those shrubs and trees are unenclosed, one may take their fruits as well as one pleases, without regard for the owner. This condition of being "unenclosed" applies specifically to the fruits and not to the grasses and so forth, because they are treated in separate sentences. (12.25)
Now, since taking the property of another is indeed theft even according to reason, this [rule] is commenced for the purpose of avoiding it:
Interest on a loan is lawful at the rate of five *māṣas* per month for every twenty [units]. (12.26)

Lending money at interest is *kusīda*. In this context, "interest" (*vṛddhi*) means accumulation; "lawful" (*dharmyā*) means not departing from dharma. When twenty *kārṣāpaṇas* are lent for one month, its interest per month amounts to five *māṣas*; that is to say, the interest per month is the measure of half a *guñjā* of a *niṣka*. By the word *māṣa*, an object measured by a grain of rice is denoted. And thus, the taking of exactly the eightieth part as stated by Manu is established. "One should grant the interest prescribed by Vasiṣṭha for the increase of wealth: a moneylender may take an eightieth part of a hundred per month" (MDh 8.140). Regarding that which was prescribed by Vasiṣṭha: "Or one may give at will to a most wicked person who has failed in his duties" (VaDh 2.43). In the case of gold and kārṣāpaṇas, it becomes a sixty-fourth part, according to the rule: "Sixteen of those [kārṣāpaṇas] make one suvarṇa" (YDh 1.358). || 12.26 ||

The term *kusīda* refers to capital lent for the purpose of interest. Uśanas stated: "A *māṣa* is the twentieth part of a *kārṣāpaṇa*. Where five *māṣas* are given as interest on twenty [coins], that is called *pañcamāṣikī*. In this sense—that "in this [amount], interest, profit, toll, or tax is given"—the suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.1.47 (*prāgvahateṣṭhak*). Although the elision (*luk*) would have occurred by Pāṇini 5.1.28 (*adhyardhapūrvadvigor lug asaṃjñāyām*), the seer did not apply it out of his own discretion. Thus, when twenty *kārṣāpaṇas* bear an interest of five *māṣas* per month, such being the case, it does not deviate from the legal rule regarding interest on loans. On this point, Manu says: [Manu 8.140] "One may take two in the hundred from the Vaiśya and three in the hundred from the Śūdra; but from a Brāhmaṇa, one must never take even one in the hundred. [Manu 8.151] "But he who, out of greed, takes more interest than the stipulated amount from debtors, becomes a *vṛddhi-jīvin* (one who lives by usury) and, after death, is born as a beast of burden for the duration of a hundred years. [Manu 8.152] "He who, having received the principal back, continues to take interest from the debtor, shall be made to pay a fine equal to that interest by the king. [Manu 8.153] "The king shall cause the creditor to forfeit the debt and impose a fine of sixty *paṇas* upon him who, through negligence, fails to recover his money within three years. [Manu 8.154] "Interest on a loan shall cease to accrue in the following cases: when there is a national calamity, when the debtor is imprisoned, when he has fled the country, or when the loan was secured by a pledge. [Manu 8.155] "If the debtor is unable to repay the entire debt at once, the creditor may, with the debtor's consent, cause the document to be altered so that the remaining balance bears interest. "One should grant interest prescribed by Vasiṣṭha for the increase of wealth; a moneylender (vārdhuṣika) may take one-eightieth part from a hundred per month. [MDh 8.140] Here too, this very same rate of interest is stated. How so? A *māṣa* is the twentieth part of a *paṇa*. Twenty *paṇas* amount to four hundred *māṣas*. Of those four hundred, five *māṣas* constitute the interest, which is one-eighthieth of the hundred. Thus it amounts to five percent. Yājñavalkya, however, states: "The interest shall be one-eightieth part every month when there is a pledge."

"One hundred [percent interest] according to the order of the castes, otherwise two, three, four, or five percent. (YDh 2.37) That gold and other goods which are deposited for the sake of gaining trust is called *bandhaka* (a pledge). When such a loan of wealth is mentioned, the principal becomes augmented by two, three, and so forth, respectively, according to the sequence of the castes among the debtors, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas. 12.26.
Some say that [the period of impurity] does not extend beyond one year. 12.27.

Some maintain that interest for a year should not be collected once a month has elapsed. This is what is meant: thinking, "Whatever is to be collected month by month, I shall collect all of that together only when the year is complete," one should not collect it every year. Because of this prohibition against annual collection, monthly and six-monthly collection is permitted. Therefore, the opinion of some is that interest should be collected month by month or every six months, but not every year. And this should be understood to apply specifically to the taking of monthly interest. Gautama, however, holds that as long as there is financial transaction with the debtor, interest must indeed be collected; but upon the cessation of that relationship, the established rule "not exceeding a year" (nātisāṃvatsarīm) is to be observed. (MDh 12.27)

Regarding this lawful interest characterized by the eightieth part [of the principal], you should not take it if it exceeds one year—that is, once a year has passed. Some hold the view that only the eightieth part may be taken every month within a single year, and nothing at all beyond that; such is the lawful practice. The grammatical derivation of the term *atisāṃvatsarīm* is to be considered. (12.27)
He states his own view:
"In the case of long-term storage, there is a doubling of the principal. (12.28)

If interest has not been collected for a long period, it shall cease to increase beyond the time at which the principal becomes double through that interest; it does not grow further than that. The mention of "lending" (prayoga) is for the purpose of allowing the doubling of the principal even when there is a change of the loan transaction, as Manu has said:

“Interest on a loan shall not exceed double [the principal], once it has been stipulated. (MDh 8.151) The mention of the term *sthāna* (place/position) is intended to indicate that the doubling limit applies specifically to gold (*hiraṇya*). Grains (*dhānya*) and other items continue to increase even beyond double their value. Thus Vasiṣṭha states: “Gold [may be increased] twofold; grain threefold; liquids are explained by [the rule for] grain; flowers, roots, and fruits likewise; and what is weighed on a scale [is increased] eightfold” (VaDh 2.44–47). By speaking in this manner, he demonstrates that the interest which is declared to be lawful (*dharmyā*) is universally applicable; otherwise, since the case of gold would already be established by the context, the mention of *sthāna* for its sake would be redundant. Consequently, one should understand that the one-eighth share (*aśītibhāga*) applies everywhere. The inclusion of the word *cira* (long time) indicates that it does not increase even after thousands of years. (12.28)

For as long a time as it takes for the lent capital to become double, for that same duration it increases by lawful interest; beyond this, it does not increase further. This refers specifically to items such as gold. On this point, Vasiṣṭha states: “Gold becomes double, grain becomes triple. By grain, liquids are explained. Roots of trees, fruits, and goods weighed on a scale become eightfold. Because of the mention of "long" [time], even after a thousand years, it does not increase beyond doubling. (12.28)
A pledge that has been used does not increase in value. || 12.29 ||
In that case, enjoyment itself constitutes the increase. || 12.29 ||

That which is deposited for the sake of trust, such as a brass ornament and so forth, is a pledge (ādhi). If it is used [by the creditor], the principal amount lent does not increase; in that case, the very use constitutes the interest. || 12.29 ||
Moreover: "And [the merit] of one who desires to give and of one who is obstructed. (12.30)

When a creditor who wishes to give [the loan] does not accept it due to greed for interest under some pretext, then [the debt] does not increase from that point either. He who wishes to give must establish a formal agreement (*saṃsthā*) with witnesses and a mark of identification, because of the potential failure of mental acuity through lack of awareness. And "of one thus obstructed" means of one who has become destitute and gone to another country; the word "and" (*ca*) is used so that there may be no suspicion regarding the preceding qualification. It should be understood as starting from that very day. Some say it refers to imprisonment by the king or others with fetters; in this matter, the Brahmins (*bhūmideva*) are the authority. (12.30)

The wealth of a debtor who wishes to pay a creditor does not increase. If the creditor, out of greed for interest, does not accept it under some pretext, then on that very day the debt must be placed in the hands of a third party; from that point on, the interest ceases to grow. Likewise, the property of a debtor who intends to give but is obstructed by the king or others, and is thus unable to pay, does not increase from that time forward. (12.30)
Now, in times of distress, the various forms of interest established by oneself are permitted. Next, he states other types of interest for times of distress:
"Interest on a revolving loan" (cakravṛddhi). 12.31.

The word "interest" (*vṛddhi*) is connected with each [term]. Compound interest (*cakravṛddhi*)—that application of capital in which the interest itself increases further is *cakravṛddhi*. As Nārada says:

"Furthermore, interest upon interest is declared to be *cakravṛddhi*. [NSm 1.89] *Kālavṛddhi* (time-based interest): Having made an agreement such as, "This must be paid to me either before this time by simple interest alone, or by the stipulated interest; if you do not pay it, then after that time, threefold or fourfold must be given," that in which a large amount of interest is taken is *kālavṛddhi*. The mention of "interest" (*vṛddhi*) even though the principal has already been specified is intended to show that this arrangement applies only to what was agreed upon by oneself, and not to that which is limited to five *māṣas*. The mention together with the principal indicates that if one means of livelihood is impossible, there is no fault in living by both.

But surely, this should have been stated right there [in GDh 12.26]: "The lawful interest on a loan is twenty [paṇas] for every five māṣas per month. Since it is taught separately here, it is understood that this refers to times of distress (*āpad*). Furthermore, by the maxim that "the understanding of a specific meaning arises from the commentary," it can be known through the commentary alone that the rule "not exceeding one year" (GDh 12.27) pertains specifically to interest measured in five *māṣas*.

To this it is replied: In the case of a lazy person, whether in times of distress or non-distress, and in the case of one who does not perform the work himself during non-distress, he should take only five māṣas; even in times of distress, he should not take interest such as that from a water-wheel (*cakravṛddhi*) when the work is not performed by himself—it is with this intention that the instruction is given. Furthermore, the instruction following the rule "not for more than a year" (GDh 12.27) is also for the purpose of clarifying that very point. 12.31.

The word "interest" (*vṛddhi*) is connected with each term. *Cakravṛddhi* (compound interest) is the interest on the principal itself, calculated upon whatever amount of interest has accrued over whatever period of time. As Nārada says: "Interest upon interest is declared to be *cakravṛddhi*" [NSm 1.89]. *Kālavṛddhi* (periodical interest) is that which is agreed upon by contract as being this much interest for this much time. 12.31.
And [the fruits] consisting of what has been done, bodily [action], the topknot, and the enjoyment of acquisitions. || 12.32 ||

*Kāritā* interest is that which is made by the debtor himself, independent of the creditor’s instruction, such as "one-quarter, one-half, or [another portion] of a *niṣka* shall be paid every year," and so forth. *Kāyikā* interest is that which, in addition to the agreed-upon interest, is taken day by day, month by month, or year by year; that is *kāyikā*. And thus says Nārada:

"Always not inconsistent with the physical object, beginning with a *paṇa* and a *pāda*," and so forth. [NSm 1.88] *Śikhā* (the crest) refers to a portion of grain, such as "the fifth of four *prasthas*" and so on. *Adhibhoga* (interest consisting of use) is that interest for which clarified butter or other items are taken daily; this is *adhibhogavṛddhi*. The particle *ca* (and) is intended to draw in the word *vṛddhi* (interest). The separate mention is for the purpose of showing its importance. || 12.32 ||

The word "for increase" (*vṛddhaye*) is the remainder [of the phrase]. Interest that has been agreed upon (*kāritā*) by the lender or the borrower themselves, taking into account the place, time, purpose, and circumstances, may be either large or small. Interest paid through bodily labor (*kāyikā*) is to be cleared through physical work. Thus Bṛhaspati says: "Interest paid through bodily labor is connected with work. Vyāsa, however, states:
"Interest paid through bodily labor is declared to be connected with the work of milking or carrying.
Kātyāyana speaks of interest on capital (*śikhāvṛddhi*).
That which is taken daily is known as *śikhāvṛddhi* (topknot-interest);
it increases perpetually like a topknot, but ceases upon the cutting off of the head.
"When the root [debt] has been paid, this interest on the principal is likewise remembered as 'śikhāvṛddhi' (interest like the growth of a crest). Thus it is said.

An example: "A handful of rice is taken daily from a *prastha* measure of rice. *Ādhibhoga* is the enjoyment or experience of the pledged field; in that case, the very experience constitutes the interest (*vṛddhi*). And that [interest] does not cease even after a hundred years. Furthermore, the field does not belong to the creditor (*uttamarṇa*); rather, whenever the principal is repaid, it belongs to the debtor (*adhamarṇa*). Others say it is *ādhibhoga*. It is called *ādhibhogavṛddhi* because it exists with reference to enjoyment (*bhoga*). In that case as well, the meaning is exactly this. Among these types of interest, such as *cakravṛddhi* and so forth, the interest may indeed continue even beyond the doubling of the principal due to the doubling of the interest itself. (12.32)
One should not lend [money] on interest exceeding five percent on cattle, wool, fields, and debtors who are not outsiders. || 12.33 ||

Although the term *kusīda* (loan) has already been introduced, it is mentioned again here to indicate that this particular application is of a different nature. The intention is as follows: when one buys livestock products such as ghee and so forth, and it is stipulated that "the price must be paid at such-and-such a time, and if it is not paid then, it shall increase," that is what is meant. The prefix *upa-* is used in the word *upajā* (livestock product) to prevent the inclusion of the calf itself. *Loman* refers to wool and the like; by the mention of the raw material (*prakṛti*), the inclusion of its derivatives (*vikāra*) should also be understood. This applies specifically to the purchase price of those items when it remains unpaid. Regarding *kṣetraśada*: when a field is leased for a fixed amount of grain, if the fee for it is not paid at the appointed time, it increases. *Vāhya* refers to that which serves as the means of transport, such as when someone causes grain to be conveyed by oxen and the like, and it is stipulated that "if the fee for this is not paid at such-and-such a time, it shall increase. The meaning is that among these, whatever loan (*kusīda*) was advanced is to be repaid later with interest; that [interest] does not exceed fivefold. Although the inclusion of wool is already established by the mention of "livestock products" (*paśūpaja*), its separate mention is for the sake of including items made from peacock feathers, as seen in the Vedic text: "O Agni, speak for me regarding the wings and the feathers of birds, as I have heard them. If it is argued that this should have been stated in the very rule, "In the case of long-term storage, the loan becomes double" (GDh 12.28), there is no fault in this; the instruction here is intended to indicate that for these items, there is neither compound interest (*cakravṛddhi*) nor a specific formal contract (*prayoga*). Since the fivefold limit is already established by the phrase "fivefold," the addition of the word *ati-* (exceeding) is to indicate that this limit may be exceeded in other types of transactions. (12.33)

*Paśūpaja* refers to products derived from livestock, such as ghee and milk. *Lomakṣetraśadaḥ* (the term for the field of wool) refers to the enjoyment of the field [of hair], such as woolen blankets, *kambala* cloths, chowries (*cāmara*), and fly-whisks (*bāla-vyajana*). *Vāhya* refers to draft animals such as oxen; although most read it as *bāhya*, the meaning remains the same.
