When these items, beginning with those derived from livestock, are lent out, that loan increases until it becomes fivefold, but it does not exceed the state of being fivefold. Another teacher says: regarding the goods designated as principal when lent as products of livestock, they increase until they become fivefold provided they are not returned at that time, and through lawful interest, they do not exceed the state of being fivefold. (12.33)

Now another legal proceeding is stated: Property belonging to one who is neither an idiot nor a minor, if it has been enjoyed by others for ten years in the presence of the owner, belongs to the enjoyer. (12.34)

The *jaḍa* is one whose mind is deluded and unfit for worldly transactions; the *pogaṇḍa* is one who has not attained legal capacity. Excluding these two, if the property of another is enjoyed by others who are unrelated to him—in the presence of the owner (meaning while the owner is residing in the same village)—that property belongs to the enjoyer alone after ten years. The intention is that such neglect for so long a time would not be possible if the ownership were still intact. However, the property of the idiot and the minor is not forfeited. The mention of these two is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the *ādhi* (mortgage) and other such properties. As Nārada says:

"A pledge, a boundary, the property of a minor, a deposit, an open deposit, women, royal property, and the property of a Vedic scholar do not become lost through enjoyment. [NSm 1.73] If it is argued that the property of one who is not mentally incapacitated (*ajaḍa*) was not included here, it is so that even after twenty years, its loss through prescription (*jīrṇatva*) shall not occur. As Nārada has said:

"And through actual enjoyment by the owner, twenty years pass; even mortgages and the like may be lost, except in the case of the property of a woman or a king. [NSm 1.74] Thus, after twenty years, the property of a minor is indeed lost. By the word "in the presence" (*saṃnidhau*) alone, the point for others is already established; however, the inclusion of the word "other" (*para*) is for the purpose of making known that there is no transgression when the relative himself enjoys the property. Because of the mention of "presence," there is no fault if the person is located in another village. (12.34)

One who is an idiot, one who is insane, or a minor whose legal capacity has not yet manifested—if the property of one who is neither an idiot nor a minor is enjoyed by others in his very presence for ten years, then it is determined that the property belongs to the enjoyer alone. That very enjoyment indicates that the property has departed from the owner’s possession in the form of a gift or some other transfer. Otherwise, how could he remain silent regarding such a matter in the world of the living for so long? Regarding this matter of land, Yājñavalkya says:
"For one who sees but does not speak, there is loss of land after twenty years;
for wealth being enjoyed by another, the loss occurs after ten years" (YDh 2.24).
Thus, he who, seeing another giving away land, does not prevent it—
Even though he is the master, he does not deserve to obtain that by means of a letter.
Thus says Bṛhaspati. On this point, Manu states:

"Whatever property a wealth-owner observes being enjoyed by others for ten years in his presence while remaining silent, he does not deserve to recover it" (MDh 8.147). However, such passages as "he who enjoys [property] without title," and so forth, refer to cases where the owner is absent or to those involving the mentally incapacitated and similar persons. (12.34)
He states an exception to this by way of a specific type of enjoyer:
The exception to this is:
"Not [with] men who are Vedic scholars, renunciants, or kṣatriyas. (12.35)

Even when being used by a *śrotriya* (one learned in the Vedas) and others, [the property] is not seized, because there exists a valid reason for indifference: the *śrotriya* and the renunciant (*pravrajita*) are overlooked due to their thirst for dharma, while the king’s officer is overlooked out of fear. If it is asked how this applies to the renunciant, it is said in response: it is indeed possible, because of the instruction regarding the impression (*vāsanā*) of an empty house for a renunciant who remains in the state of an empty house. 12.35.

When something is being enjoyed by a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) or others, it does not become theirs merely through that enjoyment, because it is possible for them to have indifference (*upekṣā*) as the underlying motive. Indifference on the part of the Vedic scholar and the renunciant arises from a thirst for dharma; on the part of the king’s official, however, it arises from fear. The mention of the king’s official is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all those who possess power. By this, violent offenders (*sāhasika*) are also explained. Furthermore, even for a renunciant who possesses no property, enjoyment of an ownerless object—such as an empty house—is possible. (12.35)
Now he states an exception based on the specific nature of the object being used: "In the case of cattle, land, and women, there is no offense for moderate use. (12.36)

By the word *paśu* (livestock), all four-footed animals fit for sacrifice are understood, based on the Vedic revelation: "Four-footed animals are indeed those fit for sacrifice. *Bhūmi* (land) refers to fields, gardens, and the like, but not the house, according to the statement of Auśanas: "Land does not belong to the occupant after ten years [of possession] regarding a dwelling. *Striyaḥ* (women) refers to female attendants. The meaning of "non-excessive enjoyment" (*anatibhoga*) of these is that ownership does not arise through ten years of enjoyment; thus says Nārada.
"But that which has been enjoyed without title, even for hundreds of years," [NSm 1.75]. This statement as well has been explained as referring specifically to cattle, land, and women. || 12.36 ||

Livestock consists of four-footed animals; land refers to fields, groves, and the like; women are female attendants or slave-girls. Regarding livestock and the other items, it is not required that one enjoy them excessively; even with a small amount of enjoyment, they become the property of the enjoyer. How could one neglect a cow seen in the house next door while personally purchasing and consuming buttermilk and such for it? Or how could one neglect a grove yielding abundant fruit? Or how could one neglect a young female servant who daily attends to one’s needs? (12.36)
The heirs of the inheritance shall discharge the debt.

The meaning is that those who enjoy or take possession of his wealth shall pay that debt, and not merely by virtue of being an heir. The plural number is used to include the son and the one who takes the wife as well. Thus says Nārada:
"Among the taker of wealth, the taker of the wife, and the son, he who takes the wealth shall bear the burden of the debt."

"The son inherits from those who have no [other] heirs; the woman inherits from those who have no wealth; the taker of the woman inherits from both the wealth and the son. [NSm 1.20] Thus, whether or not there is a son, the debt must necessarily be paid by the one who takes the woman and by the others who are heirs to the estate. Among sons, it should be understood that only those who possess the status of being heirs to the estate must pay the debt, and not merely by the son alone. 12.37.
Those who are the heirs of one's property must repay that debt; however, even in the absence of heirs, it must be paid by sons and grandsons. Thus says Bṛhaspati:
"A son must pay his father’s proven debt as if it were his own;
a grandfather’s debt is to be paid equally [by the grandson], but that debt is not to be paid by the latter’s son."
Nārada: Grandsons shall pay that debt of a grandfather which was contracted and incurred by his sons in due order; it ceases with the fourth generation. Yājñavalkya: [same].

"Even when the father is away, deceased, or overwhelmed by calamity, the debt must be paid by the sons and grandsons; if it is denied, it is established by witnesses. [Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.50] || 12.37 ||
Now he states an exception regarding the son:
"Surety-money, trade-duties, fines for liquor, gambling, and judicial penalties shall not devolve upon sons. (MDh 6.38)
Sureties for a guarantee, merchants, those who pay customs duties, those involved in liquor, gambling, or fines, shall not be liable for their sons' debts. || 12.38 ||
There are three types of sureties. As Vyāghra has said:
"The one who has seen the footprints, the one who is trustworthy, and the one who provides the funds—these are proclaimed [as the three].
Here, with the exception of the surety for payment (*dāna-pratibhū*), the other two are intended. Why?
When the master of the gift has died, one should cause even the heirs to give it away.

This is because of the statement of Manu: "That debt which is caused by a surety is *prātibhāvya*; likewise that caused by trade is for a merchant"—this is the meaning. For example, if a person, having agreed that he will pay the price, takes goods from someone and goes to another country to engage in trade, and then dies, and the son has not received those goods, then the intention is that this debt does not fall upon the son. Regarding the *śulka* (bride-price): if, after promising the *śulka* in an *āsura* or other form of marriage, one performs the marriage and then dies, that *śulka* does not fall upon the son. Regarding *madya* (liquor): since liquor is forbidden for a Brāhmaṇa, this should be understood as referring to Kṣatriyas and others. If, having said "I will give the money," one drinks liquor and then dies without giving the money, that debt also does not belong to the son. Likewise, there is the debt caused by gambling; likewise, the debt caused by a fine, which arises from losing a legal suit. "These shall not devolve upon the sons" means they do not fall upon the sons—provided, however, that the son is an inheritor of the estate (*rikthabhāk*). (MDh 8.161) 12.38.
Regarding this, Nārada says: "For attendance, for payment, and likewise for assurance—thus has the wise declared that a surety is of three kinds, pertaining to these three matters alone. (NSm 1.104)
"When his surety has died, one should cause even his heirs to pay," so says Manu (MDh 8.160). Viṣṇu and Yājñavalkya state:
"Suretyship is ordained for appearance, for confidence, and for payment.

In the case of the first being rendered void, the two [sureties] must be made to pay; in the case of the other, even the sons must pay" (YDh 2.53; ViDh 6.41). Therefore, this [rule] also should be understood as referring to cases other than those involving a surety for payment.

"I will show him this person"—having given such a guarantee (*prātibhāvya*) and having shown him, when the father has died, it is not for his son to show him. Or, as for wealth acquired by a merchant for the sake of trade, that too does not devolve upon his sons. When someone, having agreed "I will give back the principal with profit," takes wealth from another's hand and goes to another country for trade, and then dies, his son is not required to repay it. Likewise, having promised a bride-price (*śulka*) and having performed the marriage, if he dies, that bride-price does not devolve upon his son. Similarly, if one drinks much liquor and dies after promising "I will give the principal," it need not be paid by his son. Likewise, if one loses at gambling and dies without paying the stakes (*paṇa*), his son is not obliged to pay it. Just as one defeated in a legal dispute who dies without paying the fine to the king—that fine also does not devolve upon his sons. (12.38)
Deposits, pledges, borrowed items, purchases, and loans that have been lost—all these are not to be blamed [on the owner] provided no fault was committed by the person in charge. || 12.39 ||

A *nidhi* is a treasure-trove; a *nikṣepa* is a deposit; an *anvādhi* is a pledge; an *upanidhi* is a sealed deposit; a *yācita* is an ornament or similar item brought by request for festivals and other occasions; an *avakrīta* is something obtained without payment or with only half the price paid; and an *ādhi* refers to a pledge such as a bronze vessel or the like. If these are lost through theft, fire, or other such causes, they do not fall upon the sons alone. Rather, they must also be made good to those from whose presence the deposits and other items were taken—this is understood from the use of the term "all" (*sarva*). This applies provided they are "blameless," meaning they have been free from negligence. This is the case if the loss occurs without fault on the part of the person (the owner). "Fault on the part of the person" (*puruṣāparādha*) means the person's negligence, such as laziness and so forth. Thus, if the loss is due to those who are blameworthy and negligent, the heirs must indeed pay them back. (12.39)

A *nidhi* is a deposit (*nikṣepa*). It is that wherein one’s own property is deposited out of trust, without hesitation; that is a *nikṣepa*. An *anvādhi* is an *upanidhi*; it is well known as *aupanidhika* in another *smṛti*. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
"That which one should hand over by placing it in the hand without having described its contents while it remains in a container..."

"That deposited property must be returned exactly as it was" (YDh 2.65). A *yācita* is an ornament or similar item borrowed for festivals and other occasions. An *avakrīta* is that which has not been paid for in full, or for which only half the price has been paid. A *ādhi* is a pledge (*gopyādhi*). If these items—beginning with the deposit (*nidhi*)—are lost without any fault on the part of the person, such as being stolen by thieves and the like, they declare all of them to be "blameless," meaning free from fault. Not only should the sons not be held liable, but those to whom the deposits and so forth were entrusted shall likewise not be held liable. Regarding the term "blameless": if they have previously been observed to be guilty of faults, then this applies only to prior instances. However, as for "fault on the part of the person": if the holders do not protect the items as they would their own property; or if, in the event of danger from fire or the like, they take their own goods and neglect the deposit; or if they place their own goods in a secure spot and leave the deposit outside—in such cases of human negligence, they must indeed pay restitution. (12.39)

If no one were to discharge this paternal debt for these sons and others, he would become a thief; since a punishment has been prescribed for him in the rule, "The guilt of theft is eightfold" (GDh 12.12), it is in this very context that the punishment for a stealer of gold is also stated:
"A thief, with disheveled hair and carrying a club, shall go to the king confessing his deed. (12.40)

H reads "iyāt" [meaning] "the thief," specifically a thief of gold; for it has been stated that for those who steal other substances, there is "an eightfold loss," and because of the observation of another Smṛti text:
"A Brāhmaṇa who has committed the theft of gold, having approached the king..."
Proclaiming his own deed, he should say: "May your lordship instruct me.
In this section on punishment, the instruction regarding going [to the king] is for the purpose of penance. And so Manu says:
"But men who have committed sins, having been punished by kings..."

"Those who are stainless go to heaven, just as the virtuous do. [MDh 8.318] When theft has been committed, one becomes a thief. Theft is the taking away of another's property. This rule applies only to cases where there is intentional agency; unintentional theft is not possible here. However, this should be understood to apply when a great amount has been stolen, since no specific qualification is introduced. With disheveled hair—that is, with hair loose—and considering himself as good as dead, he should approach the king carrying a club in his hand as the means for his own execution, declaring his deed: "I am a thief. (12.40)

A thief is one who commits the theft of gold. Regarding this, the Code of Manu states: "But a Brahmin who has committed the theft of gold, having approached the king while proclaiming his own deed, should say: 'May Your Majesty punish me. (MDh 11.99). "With disheveled hair" means with loose, untied hair. According to another Smṛti, the club (*musala*) may be made of iron or of *khadira* wood; he is one who possesses such a club. Āpastamba says: "Having placed the club upon his shoulder" (ĀpDh 1.25.4). He should go to the king proclaiming his deed, saying: "I am a man of such deeds; please punish me. (12.40)
Then, having been thus approached, he was purified by both execution and release. 12.41.

"He becomes purified and cleansed. This refers to either being struck or killed, or alternatively, being released. "Striking" (*vadha*) means beating; and that too should be done only once, as seen in another Smṛti text: "Having seized a club, the king himself shall strike him only once" (MDh 11.100). In this regard, it should be understood that if he is struck by the king without hesitation and yet does not die, he nevertheless becomes pure. Furthermore, this striking applies to those who are not Brāhmaṇas, because it will be stated later: "There is no corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa" (GDh 12.43). And so says Manu:

"A thief is purified by execution, or a Brāhmaṇa by austerity alone" (MDh 11.100). Here, the Commentator has explained that because of the particle *eva* ("alone"), it means "a Brāhmaṇa by austerity alone. Consequently, it should be understood that for one who is not a Brāhmaṇa there is flogging, whereas for a Brāhmaṇa there is release. Nevertheless, in the case of a Brāhmaṇa who goes [to steal] of his own accord, there is release; but for one who is brought [there] by force, both release and austerity should be understood [to apply]. Thus, in all cases, when one goes of one's own accord, both punishment and penance (*prāyaścitta*) should be understood [to apply]. However, as for austerity, for a Brāhmaṇa who is not a learned scholar (*aśrotriya*), the *Sāntapana* penance should be understood if he steals gold. So says Manu: [Manu 11.100] "A thief is purified by execution, or a Brāhmaṇa by austerity alone. In this context, the Commentator has explained that due to the restrictive particle *eva*, the meaning is "a Brāhmaṇa by austerity alone. Therefore, it should be observed that for one who is not a Brāhmaṇa there is flogging, while for a Brāhmaṇa there is release. Nevertheless, in the case of a Brāhmaṇa who goes [to steal] voluntarily, there is release; however, for one who is brought [there] by force, both release and austerity should be observed. Likewise, in every instance, when one goes of one's own accord, both punishment and penance should be observed. As for austerity, if a Brāhmaṇa who is not a learned scholar steals gold, the *Sāntapana* penance should be observed. Thus spoke Manu.

"He shall perform the *sāntapana* penance after making restitution for the sake of self-purification" (MDh 11.124). It should be understood that the word "after making restitution" (*niryātya*) applies as a general rule to all forms of theft. Regarding the case of a learned *śrotriya*, one should refer to what is stated by Āpastamba: "Having committed theft, drunk liquor, or violated the teacher's bed—provided it is not the killing of a Brahmin—they should eat only at the fourth meal-time and so forth" (ĀpDh 1.25.9–10). If it is asked how there can be such weightiness regarding a *śrotriya*, it is because it has been stated: "In the case of an offense against a learned man, the punishment is more severe" (GDh 12.14). However, in the case of stealing gold from a *śrotriya* Brāhmaṇa, this same penance prescribed for a non-learned person (*aśrotriya*) should be observed for six years for a *śrotriya*. As Uśanas says: "One who commits the theft of gold, being a Brāhmaṇa, shall perform the vow for six years. Furthermore, when a penance is combined even for a Kṣatriya, then in the case of stealing gold from a non-learned person, the penance prescribed by Bhṛgu for a *śrotriya* should be observed.

"He who would take the property of a Brāhmaṇa should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa and other penances. Regarding the taking of the property of one who is not learned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*), the rule previously cited from Auśanasa is to be observed. However, for the theft of the property of one learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), this very same penance is doubled, according to the statement of Kaṇva: "In the case of stealing the property of a *śrotriya*, the penance is double. The case of a Vaiśya should also be understood as being like that of a Kṣatriya, based on the statement of Auśanasa: "The punishment for a thief who steals from a Vaiśya is the same as for a Kṣatriya. Regarding the theft of the property of a *śrotriya*: "But he who desires to remove the impurity born of stealing gold by means of austerity..."

Or it should be understood as stated by Manu: "A twice-born man, clothed in bark, shall perform the vow of a slayer of a Brahmin in the forest" (MDh 11.101). Regarding the expiation for a Śūdra, in all cases, that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha should be observed: "Alternatively, having smeared himself with clarified butter, he should burn himself from the feet upward using a fire of cow-dung, remaining naked" (VaDh 20.42). Furthermore, the gravity or lightness of the expiation must be determined according to the value of the stolen property. Why? Because, in the case of measurable things, there is death [as punishment] for stealing more than one hundred.

This is because of the indicative mark [in the text]. Punishment by the king applies only when the value exceeds one *kārṣāpaṇa*; in all other cases, however, only release (*mok�ṣa*) is to be understood. Entry into the entire expiation (*prāyaścitta*) occurs only when the value exceeds one *kārṣāpaṇa*. And it should be understood that "half [the penance] for half [the value], and a quarter for a quarter. For a *śūdra*, the rule should be fashioned like that for a *vaiśya*, according to the statement of Śaṅkha: "In the absence of a reduction, the rule for a *śūdra* should be fashioned like that for a *vaiśya*. (12.41)

*Vadha* is a beating that ends in death. Āpastamba states: "He should strike him with that very [weapon]" (ĀpDh 1.25.4). It is a single blow only, according to the traditional law (*smṛti*): "Having seized the club, the king himself should strike him once" (MDh 11.100). *Mokṣa* is release; namely, saying, "Do not do such a thing again; go. Through both these—beating and release—the thief becomes purified. For it is said: "Even when struck, he is purified; even when released, he is purified. (12.41)
A king who does not strike is a sinner. 12.42.

By failing to execute [the offender] out of compassion and the like, the king becomes a sinner; the meaning is that he incurs as much sin as the thief possesses. And so says another Smṛti: “He incurs the guilt of the thief” (NSm 19.56). Just as there is a fault in not killing one who deserves death, so too should a fault be understood in not releasing one who deserves release. And thus Vasiṣṭha says: “The guilt reaches the king who releases the offender” (VaDh 19.46). || 12.42 ||
If the king does not slay him out of compassion or similar motives, he himself becomes guilty; whatever guilt belongs to the thief, that becomes his. (12.42)
But this [rule] regarding punishment shows that it excludes the Brāhmaṇa;
corporal punishment is not the punishment for a Brāhmaṇa. (12.43)

Even for one who has appeared before him personally, that corporal punishment which is execution does not exist for a Brāhmaṇa; therefore, it must not be carried out. Now, an objection may be raised: "But surely, by the very prescription of other punishments such as the deprivation of rights and so forth, the cessation of the body's [function] occurs.
It is replied: True. However, this introductory statement is intended to prohibit corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa in cases of offenses other than those [specifically mentioned]. (12.43)
Even for a Brāhmaṇa who has presented himself voluntarily, corporal punishment must not be inflicted; rather, there must be release alone. And so says Manu:
"A thief is purified by execution, and a Brāhmaṇa by austerity alone" (MDh 11.100).

Here, by the force of the word "alone" (*eva*), the meaning is that even at such a time, for that Brāhmaṇa there is release through austerity; under no circumstance whatsoever, even when a specific cause arises, should [punishment] such as the cutting off of the hand be carried out. And so says Manu:

"These [penances] shall apply to the three [lower] castes; an unscarred Brāhmaṇa may depart [without punishment]. [MDh 8.124] This refers to the case of a Brāhmaṇa who is an ascetic (tapasvin). 12.43.
If that is so, how then is he to be disciplined? To this he says: "But for another, he prescribes punishment according to the offense:
disqualification from office, public proclamation of the crime, banishment, and branding. (12.44)

The meaning is that one must act in such a way that the person does not commit that deed again. "Proclamation" means causing him to wander everywhere with the mark of his theft. "Exile" means banishing him from the territory. "Branding" means making a physical mark upon him. As Manu says: "For violating the Guru’s bed, the mark of a female organ should be made; for drinking liquor, the sign of a tavern flag; for theft, the foot of a dog should be made; but for a slayer of a Brahmin, a headless male figure. [MDh 9.237] The appropriate punishment for these offenses should be determined in consideration of their repetition. 12.44.

Furthermore, "separation from the act" refers to acting in such a way that one no longer commits that act; this includes the confiscation of all property, taking a surety, and so forth. "Proclamation" is the public announcement in villages, cities, and other places by means of a mark of theft. "Banishment" is expulsion from a village, city, or kingdom according to the nature of the offense. "Branding" is the marking with a sign; regarding this, Manu says:
"In the case of violating the Guru's bed, the mark of a female organ should be made; in the case of drinking liquor, the sign of a tavern flag."

"But for theft, the mark of a dog's foot shall be made; for killing a Brahmin, the mark of a headless man" (MDh 9.237). Regarding these punishments—such as the removal of specific functions—the rule is that they are heavy for grave sins and light for minor ones, according to the principle of proportionality to the offense. This refers specifically to the category of mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*). However, the branding of the mark applies even to a Brahmin who performs penance. (12.44)
If he does not return, he must perform penance. || 12.45 ||

H reads "apravṛttau" (in the case of non-occurrence). When this has been done, that king becomes liable for penance (*prāyaścittī*). However, the specific penance is to be understood from another *Smṛti* text. As Vasiṣṭha says: "Upon the release of one who deserves punishment, the king shall fast for one night, the domestic priest for three nights; in the case of punishing one who does not deserve punishment, the domestic priest shall perform the *kṛcchra* penance and the king for three nights" [VaDh 19.40–43]. || 12.45 ||

However, that king who does not exercise such punishment within his territories becomes personally liable for penance (*prāyaścitta*) due to that failure to act. Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha states: "Upon the release of one deserving of punishment, the king shall fast for one night and the domestic priest (*purohita*) for three nights; upon the punishing of one undeserving of punishment, the domestic priest shall perform the *kṛcchra* penance and the king shall fast for one night and three nights" (VaDh 40–43). 12.45.
A minister who acts with deliberate intent is equal to a thief.
A minister or companion of a thief who intentionally provides food and other necessities should be punished like a thief; however, there is no fault if this is done unintentionally. (12.46)

"Assistance" refers to providing help such as shelter, food, and so forth. If that assistance is intentional—that is, if one provides aid even after knowing, "This person is a thief"—then he is equal to a thief and should be punished like a thief. However, in the case of ignorance, ignorance itself is the defense. (12.46)
The recipient as well [is at fault] when it is joined with unrighteousness. || 12.47 ||

The phrase "intentionally" (*matipūrva*) carries over from the previous context. Although the recipient is also included because the thief is the subject under discussion, the specific mention of "one associated with unrighteousness" (*adharmasaṃyukta*) is intended to show that for whatever sin a person commits, the recipient who accepts [the gift] intentionally from him must also perform the penance prescribed for one who has broken his vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*), and so forth. However, if the act was unintentional (*abuddhipūrva*), a lighter penance should be prescribed. (12.47)

By virtue of the word "api" (also), the phrase "intentionally" (*matipūrva*) is understood to carry over. He who, knowing full well that another's property has been stolen by this person, nevertheless accepts it from him, is equal to a thief in that unrighteous acceptance (*adharmasaṃyukta-pratigraha*). Although this is established by the context itself, the explicit mention of "unrighteous" is for the purpose of making it known that even in other sinful matters, the specific sin accrues to the recipient. (12.47)
The application of punishment follows from the knowledge of the persistence of human power, negligence, and transgression. 12.48.

The meaning is: having ascertained birth and so forth from the testimony of the person. "Capacity" refers to weakness and the like; "offense" refers to rash speech and the like. As Vasiṣṭha says: "A thief is not guilty if he entered by stealth; one who carries a weapon, one who was born together with the child, and one who has a wound—these are exceptions according to some. "Consequence" refers to the intent or resolve. Having taken these factors into account, the infliction of punishment must be carried out. (12.48)

"Person" refers to the caste of the individual, such as a Brahmin and so forth. "Power" concerns whether the punishment for wealth consists of much or little, and regarding the punishment for the body, whether one is weak or strong. "Offense" refers to whether there is direct agency or agency through complicity. "Consequence" refers to repetition. Having ascertained these factors—person and the rest—a punishment corresponding to them must be applied. (12.48)
Or rather, there is permission [to eat], because of the statement of an assembly of those who know the Vedas; because of the statement of an assembly of those who know the Vedas. || 12.49 ||
Alternatively, liberation may be achieved through the words of the assembly of those who know the Vedas. An "assembly" (*saṅgha*) is a gathering of four or three. As Manu has said:
"Whether they be four or even three, those who have mastered the Vedas—if they declare something, that should be known as Dharma, and not the words of thousands of others."
Or [it may be done] with the permission of the assembly of at least ten members to be mentioned later; and in this way, the fault in performing it oneself should be observed. 12.49.
A *saṃgha* is an assembly of three or four who are knowers of the Vedas. Regarding this, Manu says:
"Whether they be four or even three, whatever those who have mastered the Vedas declare, that should be known as *dharma*, and not the word of thousands of others."

One must either grant permission at the request of that Saṃgha, or state the rule regarding non-obstruction. If they should say this, then one should say: "I give you permission; go as you wish. [The repetition is for the purpose of concluding the chapter. 12.49

Now begins the thirteenth chapter. Punishment has been declared for verbal abuse when there is agreement; but when they disagree, how is it to be? To this he says: "In case of disagreement, the determination of the truth depends upon witnesses. (13.1)

"Vipratipatti" refers to various types of conflicting claims made by the plaintiff and the defendant. When such a conflict exists, a determination of truth must be established—that is, the truth must be settled—by means of witnesses. There are five kinds of witnesses, as Nārada has stated:
"The written witness, the reminded witness, the incidental witness, and the cognizant witness..."

"The secret witness, the public witness, and so forth—the witness is declared to be of five kinds" (NSm 1.130). The meaning is that one must examine them in order to ascertain the truth. Although it would have been sufficient to say "truth is based on witnesses," the inclusion of the term *vyavasthā* (settlement/decision) is for the purpose of indicating that when witnesses disagree, the testimony of the majority is authoritative; and even in the event of doubt regarding that, it is for the purpose of establishing that the matter must be resolved by those very witnesses through an oath. 13.1.
In the event of a dispute, witnesses are to be questioned; the truth is to be established exactly as stated by them. On this point, Nārada says:
"Eleven kinds of witnesses are seen in the treatises by the wise;
among them, five are said to be appointed (appointed witnesses), and six are said to be unappointed (unappointed witnesses)."
The written witness, the reminded witness, the incidental witness,
the secret witness, and the corroborative witness— thus the witness is declared to be of five kinds.
Furthermore, other witnesses have been declared who are not specifically designated:
the village headman, the presiding judge, and the king for those engaged in legal proceedings.
"One who is an insider in the affairs, one who has been sent by the plaintiff, and those involved in disputes between kinsmen and non-kinsmen—these too may be witnesses. (NSm 1.129–132) [13.1]
Furthermore, as to how many they are and what their characteristics are, he says:
"How are they and how many are they? He says:
They should be many, blameless in their own duties, and trustworthy to kings. (13.2)
There should be many blameless men, trustworthy in their own duties toward the kings, who feel neither affection nor resentment toward either side.
The meaning is that there should be many, at least three; as Manu has said: "There should be at least three witnesses in the presence of the king and the Brāhmaṇas. [MDh 8.61]

The inclusion of the word *syuḥ* (should be) is for the purpose of dispelling doubt. "Blameless" (*aninditāḥ*) means those who perform their own duties according to the prescribed injunctions. The inclusion of the word *sva-* (own) implies even wealth, sons, and so forth; as Manu says: "Householders, having sons, and being blameless... [MDh 8.62], and so on. The plural number in *karmasu* (in duties) is for the purpose of including even those duties prescribed for times of distress (*āpad*). "Trustworthy" (*prātyayikāḥ*) refers to those who act with confidence (*pratyayena*); the meaning is that they have been tested by kings in many tasks and are determined to be entirely vigilant in all matters. Because of the plural number, this also includes members of the court and others appointed by the king. (13.2)

One's own duties—those pertaining to caste (*varṇa*), those pertaining to the stages of life (*āśrama*), and those pertaining to both, whether based on the *Śruti* or the *Smṛti*—are blameless when performed correctly, provided they are not omitted or performed otherwise. Now, Yājñavalkya says:
"Witnesses should be known as at least three in number, devoted to the performance of rites prescribed by the *Śruti* and the *Smṛti*. (YDh 2.69)

*Pratyaya* means trust; those who act with that are *prātyayika*s. Such persons are trustworthy to kings because they are free from the fault of partiality. They should have no affection for, nor any attachment to, nor any resentment toward either the plaintiff or the defendant—being without hatred. Many such persons may serve as witnesses. On this point, Yājñavalkya says:
"Even a single person who knows the law may be a witness if he is agreed upon by both parties" (YDh 2.72).
However, in the case of a deposit, even a single person who is an insider is declared to be a witness.
A witness sent by a litigant becomes valid even if he is alone, provided he has been formally requested.
Thus says Kātyāyana:
"Even a single person may be authoritative, especially in cases of violence.
Thus says Vyāsa. (13.2)
And in either case, there is freedom from both delight and distress. (13.3)

"Free from affection and free from aversion" means they have neither formed attachments nor enmities; by the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that they are also not related by wealth. Thus Manu says: "Neither those related by wealth, nor friends, nor allies, nor enemies... [MDh 8.64], and so forth. "In one of the two" means whether the plaintiff or the defendant. 13.3.
Even Śūdras [may do so]. 13.4 — 13.3.

Such are even the Śūdras; how much more so the twice-born (dvijātayaḥ)! Thus, it should be understood that when twice-born men and others endowed with good qualities are unavailable, even such Śūdras may serve as officiants. || 13.4 ||

"If even Śūdras who possess such qualities may be witnesses, how much more so the twice-born? Thus it should be understood that in the absence of virtuous twice-born men, even Śūdras who possess such qualities are eligible. 13.3.
But a Brahmin, if he is unattached and not bound [by ties], cannot be restrained on account of the words of a non-Brahmin. 13.5 — || 13.4 ||

A non-Brāhmaṇa is one such as a Kṣatriya and so forth. Although the term "non-Brāhmaṇa" alone would have sufficed, the inclusion of the word "Brāhmaṇa" is for the purpose of including those who are learned in the Vedas (śrotriya). The meaning is that others are indeed acceptable [as witnesses], but specifically Brāhmaṇas are not. Because of the mention of the "non-Brāhmaṇa," one who is not to be excluded is not to be accepted; the sense is that if a non-Brāhmaṇa says, "This Brāhmaṇa is a witness to this matter," he must not be accepted by the king as a witness. Furthermore, if the Brāhmaṇa is "unregistered," meaning he has not been entered upon the official document (patraka), then he is certainly to be included—this is the intended meaning. || 13.5 ||

"A Brāhmaṇa here is not one learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*). When an un-Brāhmaṇa says, "That Brāhmaṇa is the witness to this matter," he should not be constrained by the king to serve as a witness, nor should he be accepted through persistence, provided he is not recorded in writing. If he is not entered in the document, he is not a witness; however, if he is indeed set down in the writing, he is certainly a witness. There is no reason for this other than the statement itself being the authority. On this point, Nārada says:
"Even those who are non-witnesses are seen in the legal treatises (*śāstra*) to be of five kinds by the wise:
[one excluded] by word, by defect, by division, by self-statement, and by a different opinion."

Where there is a conflict among witnesses in a legal dispute, it may arise from a learned priest’s testimony being based on hearsay, or from a thief’s testimony being tainted by the perception of guilt, or from their internal divisions leading to contradictory statements.

"One who speaks of his own accord, unappointed, having come of his own volition, is one whose testimony is suspect; he is like one who has died while the claimant is still alive, or one who is about to die, unless he was previously made aware of the case. [NSm 1.137–139] Regarding this, Nārada’s position is that a *śrotriya* can never be a witness here. However, since it has been stated here that "on account of the exclusion of non-Brāhmaṇas," even a *śrotriya* who is a Brāhmaṇa may indeed serve as a witness. (13.4)
Those who are not members of the assembly shall not speak unless they have been questioned. 13.6 — 13.5.

However many witnesses may have assembled together, even if they are gathered in one place, they shall not speak unless questioned by the king or the presiding judge (*prāḍvivāka*). The inclusion of the prefix *pra-* in the word *prabrūyuḥ* indicates that they must remain silent regarding their involvement in the matter until the questioning is concluded. (13.6)

Those who are not assembled together, not gathered, and have not been questioned by the king or the judge shall not speak; however, those who are assembled and questioned shall declare [the truth]. 13.5.
Moreover: "And they would be at fault for not speaking. (13.7)—(13.6)
Even at the time of questioning, by the force of the word "and" (*ca*), those who remain silent or speak otherwise shall be guilty and subject to punishment. Thus says Manu:

"One should either not enter the court, or one should speak what is just; for a man who remains silent or speaks falsely becomes a sinner. (MDh 8.13). Therefore, the intention is that one must speak only the truth. 13.7.

If such persons, knowing the truth, were not to speak it, or were to speak otherwise, they would be guilty and wicked; they would be punished by the king in this world and become denizens of hell in the next. (13.6)
It is not merely that there is an absence of punishment for truthful speech; rather, in the opposite case, one is subject to punishment. What then?
Heaven results from truthful speech, and hell from its opposite. (13.8) — (13.7)

From the dharma caused by truthful speech, heaven is attained; in the opposite case, from the adharma caused by false speech, hell is attained. This result belongs to the witnesses because of their speaking, and not to the king as the cause of the legal decision. (13.8)
If those who speak indeed speak the truth, then heaven comes to be; in the opposite case, by speaking untruth, hell comes to be. || 13.7 ||
Now, as to how it should be in a case where even the five kinds of witnesses are not available, he says: "It should also be stated by those who are unattached. (13.9) — [End of] 13.8.

"Nibaddhāḥ" means firmly bound; the meaning is that they are recorded as being of five kinds. Those who are not recorded as being of five kinds are "anibaddhāḥ," meaning those who know of their activities in some way or another and reside in their village. They too must speak. The word "api" (also/even) is intended to indicate the absence of being formally recorded. Although it was said "even the unrecorded," since this occurs in the context of witnesses, it follows by implication that they would be witnesses; yet, even though the full sense is thus obtained, the explicit mention of "must speak" (vaktavyam) is used because—within that category as well—it is only the speech of those whose testimony is designated as authoritative that is to be accepted, not the speech of mere interested parties. Consequently, they must speak only while free from defects such as having a personal interest in the matter. (13.9)

Those designated as "appointed" (*nibaddha*) are those specified [by the litigants] as witnesses here. Those who are the opposite, the "unappointed" (*anibaddha*), must also give testimony; they are to be understood as described by Nārada, beginning with the words, "Others, moreover, are the unappointed. (13.8)
There is no binding [of the mind] for the sake of causing pain. 13.10 — || 13.9 ||

In this context, by the word *bandha* (bond/obstruction), a formal restriction is meant. *Nibandha* refers to a fixed rule regarding acts such as violence that cause suffering. The meaning is that there is no *nibandha*, that is, no prohibition [against speaking]. The intention is that one must certainly speak even when faced with other fivefold types of objections, such as those involving contradictions with the facts or the purpose. And so says Uśanas: "In matters of violence, all [rules] cease to apply. (13.10)

"Causing pain" means inflicting injury. "Connection" (*nibandha*) refers to a relationship with the subject matter and so forth. In cases of causing pain—that is, regarding acts of violence—the connection of witnesses need not be scrutinized; no defect whatsoever arises from their relationship to the matter and so on. Vyāghra says:

"In cases of theft, violence, association [with outcasts], and likewise in matters concerning women, as well as in the administration of poisons and the like, no fault is recorded regarding the witnesses. (13.9)
Likewise: "And [the word] spoken by one who is intoxicated" (13.11). — [End of] 13.10.

"Negligent" means ignorant or acting through deception, because of the inclusion of the word *pra-*. When witnesses are kept secret and, by various means, cause a person to fall into a private situation, then even those standing by who are connected to the matter through wealth and so forth become witnesses. "Spoken by one who is negligent" means that he has been overpowered; the word *ca* (and) implies this also applies to the act of sexual intercourse with a woman. Thus Vyāghra says: "In cases of theft, violence, association [with outcasts], and likewise with women, and in the administration of poisons and the like, no fault is recorded regarding the witnesses."
In the opposite case, hell is said [to be the result]; that [result] is not for them alone. 13.11.

Negligence is a lack of careful attention. Even regarding that which was spoken by a witness incidentally in a subsequent sentence, there is no formal binding; thus, there is no defect such as a lack of connection to the subject matter. || 13.10 ||
What then?
It is stated that hell [awaits] in the case of the opposite. That [sin] does not belong to the witness alone; what then?
"In the oppression of the system of dharma, the fault lies with the witnesses, the members of the court, the king, and the judge" (13.12). — [End of verse 13.11]

Wherever an injury to the administration of justice (*dharmatantra*) is committed through the failure to examine legal proceedings properly, there the perpetrator is tainted by the fault in exactly the same way as the witnesses and others.
Now, it may be asked: "Has the fault of the witnesses not already been stated? For what purpose is it mentioned again here?"

It is said: if the mention of "witnesses" were not made here, then it would follow that the fault stated applies only to judicial proceedings lacking witnesses, and not to those with witnesses; therefore, [the term is used] for the purpose of extending the fault to cases with witnesses as well. It should be understood that to whatever extent the fault attaches to the perpetrator, that same degree of fault accrues to the members of the court (*sabhyas*) and others individually due to their own negligence, and not merely in part. By the word *tatra*, worldly legal procedure (*lokavyavahāra*) is meant; and thus, the inclusion of that term is for the purpose of stating that such harassment must not be inflicted. (13.12)

*Tantra* refers to worldly legal procedure (*lokavyavahāra*). When there is an injury to both the Dharma and the *tantra*, guilt falls upon all—the witnesses, the members of the court (*sabhyas*), the king, and the perpetrator. The mention of the "perpetrator" is for the sake of illustration; just as great is the guilt of the perpetrator, so too is it for the witnesses and the others. Although the guilt of the witnesses was stated previously, their inclusion here is for the purpose of including the members of the court and others even in cases involving witnesses. Otherwise, it would have been said that in a lawsuit without witnesses the guilt lies with the members of the court and others, whereas in a lawsuit with witnesses it lies with the witnesses alone. (13.11)
Some perform truthful deeds by means of an oath. 13.13. — 13.12.

But when there is a total disappearance of other means of proof such as witnesses and the like, then some authorities maintain that one should establish the truth of the matter through an oath, a *kośa* ordeal, or similar means. An oath is employed because the other party has made a determination [to the contrary]. Although one should simply say "truth" (*satyam*), the inclusion of the word "action" (*karman*) is intended to allow for the application of the oath even outside of formal legal proceedings, in cases of doubt regarding ordinary worldly transactions. Thus says the Śruti: "If I am a sorcerer, may another woman... and so forth. Gautama, however, maintains that it is by logic alone. In this regard, it should be understood that an oath is used when there is a slight trace of evidence, whereas in its absence, logic alone prevails. (13.13)

Where there is no such confidence in the witnesses, some hold the view that the matter of truth should be settled by means of an oath; having caused an oath to be taken, the truth must be declared. 13.12.
That [offering] should take place in the assembly of Brahmins and the king of the gods, not among those who are non-Brahmins. 13.14 — 13.13.

And that oath [should be taken] in an assembly of gods, in the presence of the gods. By the term "gods" (deva), either images of deities or the Ādityas and other celestial beings are meant. The "king" is the one who presides over the legal proceeding. The "Brāhmaṇas" are the members of the court and others. The mention of these is for the purpose of excluding ordinary worldly transactions. Thus, it should be understood that this applies when a legal proceeding takes place in the presence of deities and so forth, whereas in worldly matters, it may be anywhere. A legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*) is caused by a dispute over property, while a worldly matter is caused by an offense. "Non-Brāhmaṇas" refers to Kṣatriyas and others. The use of the particle *syāt* ("may be") is for the purpose of removing the fixed order. In that regard, if a deity is available, [the oath is taken] in an assembly of Brāhmaṇas; if not, it should be understood as being in an assembly of kings. And so it is stated in another Smṛti:
The king should cause non-Brahmins to undergo the ordeal properly in the presence of the deity;
and in the absence of that, he should have them take the oath in the presence of a Brahmin.

"In the absence of those, the Blessed Kāśyapa then said regarding the king. This "absence" should be understood as referring to cases where [the king] is occupied with other duties. Although one should have said "of non-Brahmins," the use of the word *guru* (teacher) in the sūtra is intended to include even a Brāhmaṇa who is not a *śrotriya*, so that he may enter into the presence of the deity. And thus, it should be understood that for a *śrotriya* Brāhmaṇa, an oath occurs merely by the utterance of the word "truth.
Some say the inclusion of the word "syāt" (should be) is for the purpose of incorporating other Smṛtis, just as Manu says:
"One should cause a Brāhmaṇa to swear by truth, a Kṣatriya by his vehicle and weapons..."
"A Vaiśya by means of cows, seeds, and gold; a Śūdra by all sins.

[MDh 8.113] Although it could have been stated "in the presence of the king, the deity, and the Brāhmaṇas," the inclusion of the term *saṃsad* (assembly) is for the purpose of including a place where a deity is present, as well as an assembly free from defects such as deception. As Nārada says:
"That is no assembly where there are no elders..."
"Those who do not speak the Dharma are not elders; that is not the Dharma wherein truth is absent; and that is not truth which is pierced by deceit. [NSm Mātṛkā 3.17] Thus ends [verse] 13.14.

That act of swearing occurs in an assembly of gods, in the presence of formidable deities, or in an assembly or council of Brahmins. For Kṣatriyas and others, there is an option depending on the gravity or lightness of the matter at hand: in a major matter, it takes place in the presence of deities; in a minor one, elsewhere. Because of the expression "of non-Brahmins," the act of swearing does not apply to Brahmins. Regarding this, Viṣṇu states: "The king should question the Brāhmaṇa, saying 'Speak'; the Kṣatriya, saying 'Speak the truth'; the Vaiśya, with [threats regarding] cattle, seed-corn, and gold; and the Śūdra, with all sins. Thus, O King, he should question witnesses according to the order of their castes" [ViDh 8.20–23, 38]. Manu, however, says:
"One should cause a Brahmin to swear by truth; a Kṣatriya, by his vehicle and weapons; a Vaiśya, by cattle, seed, and gold; and a Śūdra, by all the mortal sins" (MDh 8.113). Thus [ends verse 13.13].
The defect of witnesses has been stated in general terms. Now he speaks for the sake of specific cases:
"In the opposite case, there is hell"—thus the defect of witnesses was stated generally. Now he states the specific defect in a specific legal proceeding:
"In the case of a lie regarding small cattle, the witness kills ten. (13.15) — [End of] 13.14.

Small animals are goats, sheep, and the like. Regarding false testimony concerning them, one "slays ten men. Because no distinction is made, it is understood that he slays his own kinsmen. The meaning is that he incurs as much sin as would result from the slaughter of ten of his own kinsmen; this applies everywhere in similar cases. Consequently, the determination of punishment and penance should be made in accordance with that. The mention of "witnesses" is intended to include members of the court and others as well. (13.15)

Small livestock refers to goats, sheep, and the like. Regarding false testimony concerning them, the witness kills ten; that is, he incurs as much guilt as would result from the slaughter of those ten. Both the punishment and the penance should be understood to correspond accordingly. (13.14)
In the case of cows, horses, humans, and land, [the fines] increase tenfold for each subsequent one. || 13.16 || — || 13.15 ||

Each subsequent [falsehood] becomes ten times [more serious] than the preceding one; in the case of cattle, it is a hundredfold; in the case of horses, a thousandfold, and so forth. As for what has been stated in another Smṛti—“In the case of falsehood regarding five animals, he destroys [the merit of] five; in the case of falsehood regarding cattle, he destroys ten; in the case of falsehood regarding horses, he destroys a hundred; in the case of falsehood regarding men, he destroys a thousand” (MDh 8.98)—that should be understood as being with respect to the specific nature of the possession or with respect to the purpose [for which the animal was used]. 13.16.

Regarding the witnesses who have been mentioned, [the sin] increases tenfold for each successive category of objects. In the case of lying regarding cattle and other such things, the witness incurs a fault equal to the sin of killing those respective animals, increasing tenfold over what was previously stated. This is what is meant: by lying regarding a cow, the witness incurs the sin of killing a hundred cows; by lying regarding a horse, the sin of killing a thousand horses; by lying regarding a human being, the sin of killing ten thousand men; and by lying regarding land, the sin of killing a hundred thousand of the inhabitants of that land. "By lying regarding small livestock one kills five; by lying regarding a cow one kills ten."

"He kills a hundred horses by a lie regarding [the theft of] a horse, and a thousand men by a lie regarding [the theft of] men"—this [rule], however, refers to the case of extremely small animals and the like. 13.15.
Or everything on the ground. 13.17 — 13.16.

Regarding the subject of the earth, one hundred thousand [units] or the entire human race should be understood as a conceptual distinction based on the division of cultivated and uncultivated fields. || 13.17 ||

Or, if one lies regarding land, it destroys the entire human race; there is an option [regarding the gravity of the offense] depending on whether the land is a village, a district, or a large territory. (13.16)
In taking [it] away, there is hell. || 13.18 || — || 13.17 ||

"Of the earth" refers to its transformation. Because there is no distinction [in the rule], this occurs until the end of the kalpa. This was stated in connection with the discussion of the mention of defects. 13.18.

This is incidental. The word "of the land" (bhūmeḥ) is connected [to the verb] by transposition. By the theft of land, one goes to hell; the limit of the duration of time is to be understood from other scriptures. 13.17.
Now he states the subject at hand: "And in water, in sexual union. (13.19)
As with the earth, so with water. || 13.18 ||

"In waters" means in reservoirs such as wells and the like; "in sexual union" means in approaching the wives of others and so forth. By the inclusion of the term "union," it also includes [acts] such as violating a virgin. The word "and" (*ca*) is for the purpose of ensuring that the mention of "waters" does not become a qualification of "sexual union" alone. And thus, hell should be understood to result even from the act of abduction. (13.19)

In the case of falsehood regarding water, the fault is equal to that of killing a hundred men for land; likewise, for its theft, it is equal to [the sin of] hell. By the word "water" (ap), bodies of water such as wells and ponds are indicated. (13.18)
And in connection with sexual intercourse. 13.19.
In such cases as "he goes to another's wife" when there is a falsehood connected with sexual intercourse, it is understood from the word "and" (*ca*) that [the sin] is like that of the soil. (13.19)
As with animals, so it is with honey and clarified butter. || 13.20 ||
Regarding honey and ghee, the fault is equal to that of lying about small livestock.
In the case of honey and ghee, there is a fault equal to that of lying for the sake of a small animal. (13.20)
As in the case of a cow, so it is with clothing, gold, grain, and the property of a Brahmin. || 13.21 ||

In the case of a falsehood regarding clothing and such items, the fault is equal to that of a falsehood regarding cattle; this is stated in reference to a falsehood regarding Brahmanas, whether they have studied the Veda or not. (13.21)

"Brahman" means the Veda. Regarding matters such as clothing and the like, falsehood entails a fault equal to that of killing a cow. To say "I have not studied this" after having indeed studied it, and so forth, constitutes falsehood regarding the Veda (brahmānṛta). (13.21)
Like horses in vehicles. 13.22.

In the case of a falsehood regarding vehicles such as elephants, the fault is equal to that of a falsehood regarding horses. The use of the plural "vehicles" (*yāneṣu*) is intended to include even insentient objects such as palanquins. Some explain it otherwise: beginning with the rule "as in the case of animals, so for honey and clarified butter," they hold that the fault in seizing honey and clarified butter is like that of seizing an animal; likewise, the fault in seizing clothing and other goods is like that of seizing a cow. In this context, by the word "brahman," they mean the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅga*), as well as written books. And in the case of seizing vehicles, the fault is equal to a falsehood regarding horses. (13.22)

Vehicles such as elephants, carts, and palanquins: regarding falsehood concerning these, the fault is like that [of lying] about horses. Others, however, begin with "falsehood concerning small cattle" and apply this to the exhortation of witnesses: "In the case of falsehood concerning small cattle, there is the fault of killing ten cattle; therefore, you must speak only the truth"—thus the witness is to be exhorted. This applies everywhere, even in subsequent cases. (13.22)

If, even after this fault has been stated, the witness nevertheless speaks a falsehood, then—having thus declared the fault regarding the unseen realm—he states the punishment for the witness regarding the visible realm:
"A witness who speaks falsely is to be censured and punished. (13.23)

When a false statement has been made, the witness is to be censured and reproached in the presence of all people for the purpose of terminating legal transactions. Furthermore, he is to be fined according to the value of the object, based on an assessment of the man’s capacity and other factors. The word "and" (ca) is used to indicate that the penalty may be calculated either collectively or individually, depending on the purpose of the transaction and the specific nature of the property involved. Since this is already established by the general context, the explicit mention of the "witness" (sākṣin) serves to show that it is he alone who is both to be censured and fined; whereas the members of the court and others are subject to punishment alone. (13.23)

When a witness is seen speaking falsely, he is to be censured and reproached by all as one with whom no legal transaction may be conducted, and he is to be punished by the king. On this point, Manu says: "For lying through greed, he should be fined one thousand; for lying through delusion, the first amercement;
for fear, two middle amercements; and for friendship, four times the first."
Ten times the former [fine] for desire, twice that for anger;
two full hundreds for ignorance, but only one hundred for childishness. Furthermore, a righteous king should punish the three social classes who give false testimony as follows: [MDh 8.120–121].

"Having punished him, he should banish [the offender]; however, a Brāhmaṇa he should exile. [MDh 8.123]. Viṣṇu states: "For false witnesses and for those who live by bribery, there shall be confiscation of all property. [ViDh 5.180–181]. 13.23.
He states an exception to this: "There is no fault in speaking untruth if life itself depends upon it. (13.24)

When the life of another would necessarily be cut short by speaking the truth, then even a falsehood must be spoken by the witness; when that is said, the previously mentioned fault does not apply. (13.24)

When, by speaking the truth, there would be mutual slaughter, whereas by speaking a falsehood the life of another—dependent on that lie—is preserved rather than his death, then in that instance of lying there is no fault as previously described. On this point, Yājñavalkya says: "In a case where the execution of those belonging to the [four] castes would otherwise occur, there a witness may speak falsely. To purify himself from that sin, the twice-born should offer a *caru* oblation to Sarasvatī" (YDh 2.83). 13.24.
But not the life of an evil person. 13.25

The word "tu" (but) has the sense of specification; it makes known this: although there is certainly a fault in speaking untruth, nevertheless, even so, untruth is indeed superior to truth that would cause death, because its fault is much smaller. And thus Manu says:
"In cases where the execution of a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, a Kṣatriya, or a Brāhmaṇa would result from speaking the stated truth..."

"In that case, one must say what is untrue, for that is distinguished as superior in such a situation" (MDh 8.104). The intention is this: one should think thus—"Even while living, this person is devoted solely to evil deeds and performs only theft and the like"—and in that event, one must speak the truth. The use of the superlative suffix in the word *pāpīyasaḥ* ("more wicked") indicates this. Truth must be spoken even when it causes pain to another; it does not refer merely to the non-performance of what is enjoined, nor merely to the performance of what is prohibited. 13.25.

But if by speaking an untruth the life of one who is more wicked, more sinful, and intent on harming others is preserved, then it is not the case that there is no fault; rather, there is indeed a fault. || 13.25 ||
The witnesses have been described; now, as to by whom they are to be questioned, he says: "The king, the judge, or a Brahmin learned in the scriptures. (13.26)

One who asks (*pṛcchati*) is a *prāṭ*. One who discerns (*vivekti*) what has been asked is a *vivāka*. Or, he is a *prāḍvivāka* because he examines (*vicārayati*) that which has been stated by the litigants or the witnesses; he should be the king himself. When the king is exhausted or engaged in other duties, it may be a Brāhmaṇa learned in the scriptures—that is, one of great erudition. And so says Manu: "When the king does not personally conduct the investigation of legal cases, then he should appoint a learned Brāhmaṇa to investigate the cases" (MDh 8.9). 13.26.

He asks, thus he is a *prāṭ* (questioner). He speaks after having deliberated, thus he is a *vivākaḥ* (judge). Because [the word] is seen among the *nyaṅku*-class, there is the substitution of *vṛddhi* and the change to *k*. A king shall be the *prāḍvivākaḥ*. However, when he is occupied with other matters, a Brāhmaṇa learned in the scriptures who has been appointed by him [shall act]. On this point, Manu says: "Or, if the king himself does not perform the decision of legal cases, then he should appoint a learned Brāhmaṇa for the decision of legal cases" (MDh 8.9). 13.26.
One should approach the judge who possesses the characteristics thus described. 13.27.

*Adhyābhavet* means he should go above him; that is the sense. This also applies to the case of a Brahmin; however, in the case of a king, it has been stated: "They should wait upon him while he is seated above" (GDh 11.7). Since the meaning "he should go above him" was already established, the specific mention of the *prāḍvivāka* (judge) is for the sake of a restrictive rule (*niyamārtham*): he should go only above him, and not even above his assistant. The inclusion of the prefix *āṅ* indicates that he should merely decide the case for the plaintiff and should not reopen it. And so Manu says: "He should not himself initiate a legal proceeding," and so forth (MDh 8.43). || 13.27 ||

*Upari* means in a superior position or in authority; *āṅ* has the sense of "coming toward. A person seeking justice, being subordinate for a long time, should approach this aforementioned judge (*prāḍvivāka*) who is seated above while standing below; however, the judge himself must not initiate a case nor summon anyone. Thus says Manu: "Neither the king nor his official shall himself initiate a legal case" (MDh 8.43). 13.27.
If there is no immediate realization [of the truth], one should wait for a year.

When the defendant, the plaintiff, or the witnesses lack presence of mind—that is, when there is a failure to respond—then one should wait for them for one year. After a year has passed, one should decide the case according to their subsequent mental state; this is the meaning. || 13.28 ||

When a defendant, a plaintiff, or a witness lacks presence of mind (*apratibhā*), such that they say, "It does not occur to me," either because they are personally afflicted by dullness and so forth, or because the matter is difficult to determine due to having occurred long ago, then one should wait for a year. After this much time has passed, one should grant them time, saying, "Deliberate and then speak. Regarding this, Kātyāyana states:
"For those who are dependent, the dull-witted, the insane, children, those initiated for sacrifice, and the sick, the time limit may be less than a year, according to their own desire."

Nārada says: "Because of the profundity of legal disputes and because even the memory [of the facts] may fail, one may take as much time as desired in matters such as debts, out of a desire to ascertain the truth. Thus [says Nārada, Mārgaṇā 1.38]. Prajāpati says:
One day, or two, or three, or five, or seven;
however, in cases such as debts and the like, when the matter is complex, the time limit is traditionally held to extend even up to three fortnights.
The exception to this is: "And [there is no fault] when it concerns a cow, a bull, or a woman's generative organ, provided it is done quickly. (13.29)

In legal transactions involving a milch cow (*dhenu*) and the like, one should not wait for a full year; for if time is delayed, the period for the enjoyment of the milch cow and other items passes away. A *dhenu* is a cow that yields milk. An *anaḍvān* is a draft ox; this too becomes worn out through a year’s use. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "connected with the procreation of women" (*strī-prajanana-saṃyukte*), the term "connected" (*saṃyukta*) is to be construed with each [of the preceding terms]. "The procreation of women" refers to the marriage of a maiden; if one waits for a year, there would likewise be a lapse of the proper time for that as well. If it is argued that one should have simply said "marriage" (*vivāha*), we say no; for the purpose here is to include those who are capable of procreation. Thus, there is no fault in waiting for a year even in the case of an incapable girl. The mention of "women" (*strī*) is intended to include those born of the same caste (*savarṇa*). Consequently, this indicates that in the case of a woman of a different caste (*asavarṇā*), one must wait. The particle *ca* (and) serves to indicate that [the terms] apply individually. [This is shown by the examples: "connected with a milch cow," "connected with a draft ox," and so on, so that the rule does not apply only to the collection of all items together. The inclusion of "quickly" (*śīghra*) is for the purpose of including those born of the same caste. (13.29)

The word "connected" (*saṃyukta*) is to be construed with each [term]. In a dispute concerning property connected to a cow and so forth, one should settle the dispute quickly. "Procreation" refers to marriage, because it is the cause of it; "woman" refers to a female slave and the like. Thus says Kātyāyana:
"In the case of a cow, a bull, a field, women, and procreation, as well as in the case of a deposit, a loan for use, a gift, and likewise in sale and purchase."
In cases of violating a maiden, theft, quarrel, acts of violence, embezzlement of a deposit, fraud, and perjury, one should bring a lawsuit immediately.
Thus [ends the verse]. 13.29.
And in cases of urgency. 13.30.

The meaning is that one should reach a decision quickly. "Urgent business" (*atyayakarma*) refers to cases such as when someone who was traveling with another departs for half the journey, or when one of the parties is in a state of death, or when a village is under siege, and so forth. It is treated separately because, due to the urgency, it must be investigated even before a case involving cows and the like. The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to include theft, violence, assault, and other such matters. Accordingly, another legal text (*smṛti*) states:
"In cases of violence, theft, assault, false accusations regarding cattle, urgent matters, and women..."
"One should institute a lawsuit immediately; in other cases, the time is said to depend on one's own will. [YDh 2.12] Thus ends verse 13.30.
Where dignity departs, as does destruction and even abandonment,
one should not waste time there, for that matter is urgent.
Thus says Kātyāyana: "In such urgent matters as these, one should litigate immediately and should not grant time. Yājñavalkya says:

"In cases of violence, theft, verbal or physical assault, a false accusation involving a cow, an emergency, or matters concerning women, one should litigate at once; in other matters, time is prescribed according to one's wish. (YDh 2.12) || 13.30 ||
Truthfulness in speech before the judge is weightier than all other dharmas; truthfulness in speech, truthfulness in speech! 13.31.

The meaning is that, among all duties taught in the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* which serve as the means for accomplishing dharma, the most important is the judge’s—i.e., the observer of legal proceedings—vision of things as they truly are; or rather, it is the speaking of truth by witnesses and others when the judge is present. (13.31)

This is more important than all the duties enjoined by the Śruti and Smṛti: that one should speak the truth when questioned by the presiding judge. The repetition [of the word "truth"] is for the purpose of indicating the conclusion of the chapter. 13.31.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.

Punishments and expiatory rites for the non-performance of prescribed duties have been stated. To address the question of at what time these two are not desired for one who fails to perform what is prescribed, he says: "Now follows the determination of impurity (āśauca)."
The impurity due to death lasts for ten nights for the sapinda relatives, except for those who are officiating priests, consecrated for a sacrifice, or lifelong students.

The state of impurity caused by a corpse lasts for ten days and nights. For whom? For those who are *sapiṇḍas*. Its specific nature will be explained later. [This applies] to those excluding the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) and others. Here, the "officiating priest" is understood as one who has already engaged in the ritual action (*pravṛttakarman*), because of his association with the "initiated" (*dīkṣita*). If the status of having previously been such were accepted here—as in the case of "the officiating priest and the father-in-law"—then the same would apply to the initiated and the student (*brahmacārin*). Consequently, since everyone has at some point been a student, the separate mention of the officiating priest and the initiated would be redundant. Therefore, all those who have actually engaged in the ritual action are included. The "initiated" is the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). The "student" is so until the completion of his studentship. Since Kṣatriyas and others are mentioned later on, this refers specifically to Brāhmaṇas. Since the impurity of birth (*sūtaka*) will be discussed later, the phrase "impurity lasts ten nights" already establishes the period of impurity caused by a corpse; however, the explicit mention of "corpse" (*śāva*) is for the purpose of indicating that the counting of days should begin from the moment the corpse is encountered.
But surely, in another Smṛti, it is heard regarding the rites performed prior [to cremation], beginning with the consecration (*saṃskāra*):

"Having abandoned him in the forest like a log, one should let him remain for three days" (MDh 5.69). Likewise: "If one who has maintained the sacred fires should die while away from home, having performed the rite of re-consecration (*punaḥ-saṃskāra*), purification is to be carried out as in the case of a corpse" (VaDh 4.37). Therefore, this [latter rule] appears contradictory. To this it is replied: there is no contradiction because of the distinction of subject matter (*viṣaya-vibhāga*). Thus, in the *Vyāghra-dharma*, a statement is heard that is intent upon establishing such a distinction of subject matter.
"Only death should be performed for one whose union with the sacred fires has not occurred;
only cremation should be performed for one for whom the Vaitānika rite was prescribed.

Since impurity is already established by the rule "one who has touched an outcaste, a Caṇḍāla, a woman who has recently given birth, a menstruating woman, or a corpse" (GDh 14.29), which prescribes bathing upon touching a corpse, the specific mention of "impurity" (*āśauca*) is intended to establish that one is also disqualified from study and other such activities during that state of impurity. And so says Manu:
"In both cases, for ten days the food of the family is not eaten;

giving, receiving, sacrifice, and Vedic study are suspended. Although it should have been stated as *śāvāśauca* (impurity caused by a corpse), the use of the non-compound form *śāvam āśaucam* is intended to indicate that the state of impurity regarding mutual touch lasts only until the collection (*saṃcayana*) of the bones which constitute parts of the corpse. And so says Saṃvarta:
"Touching of the limbs is prescribed after the collection of the bones. The nature of the collection of the bones is to be understood from another *smṛti* text. And so Vyāghra says:
"On the first, second, third, and fourth [days]..."

"One should perform the collection of the bones by relatives desiring their welfare. In this regard, it should be understood that for those entitled to immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*), it occurs on the first day; for those related by a one-day period, on the second day; for those related by a three-day period, on the third day; and for those related by a four-day period as well as those related by a ten-day period, on the fourth day. Likewise, another statement is heard in that very same source: "On the fourth, the fifth, the seventh, and likewise the tenth."

"One should perform the collection of bones according to the sequence of the social classes (*varṇa*). In this regard, it should be understood that for a Brāhmaṇa it is on the fourth day, for a Kṣatriya on the fifth, for a Vaiśya on the seventh, and for a Śūdra on the tenth. What has been stated for the Brāhmaṇa applies likewise to the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya; based on their conduct and Vedic study, the principle "for those with shorter periods of impurity, [the rite] is shorter" should be applied. The mention of the *brahmacārin* (celibate student) is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*) and others. Thus says Bṛhaspati: "For lifelong students (*naiṣṭhika*), forest-dwellers (*vanastha*), ascetics (*yati*), and celibate students..."

"No impurity is declared for one in *sūtaka* (birth), nor likewise for one in *śāva* (death). The mention of "initiated" (*dīkṣita*) is intended to include those who have already begun the *Cāndrāyaṇa* and other such observances. Thus Vasiṣṭha says:
"There is no fault of sin for kings, nor for those observing vows, nor likewise for those engaged in sacrificial sessions (*satrin*)."

“Those who occupy the station of Indra are indeed always purified by Brahman. [VaDh 19.48]; and from the indicative marks of the texts, “after the tenth day” [GDh 14.24] and “for a Kṣatriya, eleven nights” [GDh 14.2], it is possible to understand that the period is ten nights. The mention of ten nights serves as a restrictive rule (niyama) to ensure that even for a Kṣatriya or others, the period of impurity for a Brāhmaṇa is exactly ten nights. Thus, another Smṛti states:
“Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who are heirs or kinsmen of a Brāhmaṇa...”

"In their case of impurity, the *sūtaka* for a Brāhmaṇa shall last ten days. The meaning here is that when impurity has befallen a Brāhmaṇa, the period for those [others] is exactly ten days. Manu also says: "All [those of lower castes] should respectfully observe the impurity of the highest caste (the Brāhmaṇa), but they themselves should observe their own purification according to the rules prescribed for their own caste among their own kin. Since it is taught that their [the Śūdras'] impurity lasts ten days during the impurity of a Brāhmaṇa, one must look to what is stated in other Smṛtis regarding the Brāhmaṇa's impurity during the impurity of those others. As Lokākṣi says:
Impurity due to death lasts ten days among those of one's own caste;
for the castes of Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra, it is declared to be six, three, and one day respectively at birth or death.
Thus [ends the section]. 14.1.

*Śāva* refers to that which pertains to a corpse (*śava*). *Āśauca* is the state of impurity.
