It lasts for ten nights—that is, ten days and nights—for those who are *sapiṇḍas*, excluding the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) and others. An *ṛtvij* is a sacrificer engaged in a ritual act. A *dīkṣita* is one who has undergone the initiatory rite (*dīkṣaṇīya*) and is engaged in the ritual act. A *brahmacārī* is well known [as a student]. For the first two cases, it lasts until the final purificatory bath (*āvabhṛtha*); for the other, it lasts until the completion of the period of studentship (*brahmacarya*). What, then, is the definition of this *āśauca*? It is the lack of eligibility for ritual acts, the state of having food unfit for consumption, untouchability, and the lack of eligibility for giving gifts and so forth. On this point, Manu says:
In both cases, for ten days the food of the family is not eaten;
giving, receiving, sacrifice, and Vedic study are suspended.
"And those who are not near should not touch the relatives near the deceased. Thus [says the law]. And Aṅgiras says:
"But when a Brahmin, especially a student (brahmacārī), unknowingly drinks water, eats food, or touches [an impure person] during a period of birth-impurity (sūtaka)..."

"One should consume the *pañcagavya* while drinking water; for eating [food from such persons], it is prescribed for three nights; having touched them, bathing is ordained. Thus says Yājñavalkya: "One should bathe if touched by those who are menstruating (*udakyā*) or impure due to death or birth (*āśaucin*); if touched by them, one should sip water (*upaspṛśet*). [YDh 3.30] Saṃvarta says:
"After the collection of the bones, the touching of the limbs is prescribed"—thus says Vyāghra.
"For one whose connection with the sacred fires does not exist, [the rite] must be performed immediately after death;
for one whose Vaitānika ritual exists, it must be performed immediately after cremation."
Śaṅkha says: "In the fourth [generation], there should be ten nights; in the fifth [generation] for a male, six nights;

in the sixth, purification occurs after four days; but in the seventh, after three days. All of this refers to those who lack specific qualities (*nirguṇa*). Regarding those who possess qualities (*guṇavat*), Parāśara states:
A Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires and possesses the Vedas is purified in one day;
one who possesses only the Vedas is purified in three days, but one devoid of qualities is purified in ten days.
Thus says Bṛhaspati:

"A Brahmin who maintains the Veda and the sacred fires is purified in three nights; one who lacks the sacred fires is purified in five days; and one who merely claims to be a Brahmin is purified in ten days. In this context, the mention of the *brahmacārin* (celibate student) is intended as an illustration for the other stages of life (*āśrama*) besides that of the householder. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati states:

"For lifelong celibates (*naiṣṭhika*), those established in vows (*vratastha*), ascetics (*yati*), and students (*brahmacārin*), no impurity is declared in the case of a birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), nor likewise in the case of a death-impurity (*śāva*). The mention of "initiated persons" (*dīkṣita*) is intended as an illustration for those engaged in vows such as the *cāndrāyaṇa*. On this point, Vasiṣṭha says:
"There is no fault for kings, nor for those observing vows, nor likewise for those engaged in sacrificial sessions (*satrin*)."
"Those who occupy the station of Indra are never indeed impure. [VaDh 19.48] Thus ends section 14.1.
For a Kṣatriya, it is eleven nights. || 14.2 ||
The impurity on account of a birth or death (śāva-āśauca) applies to all sapindas, with the exception of the officiating priest, the initiated sacrificer, and the student. 14.2.

For a Kṣatriya other than one who has been initiated (*dīkṣita*) or is a student (*brahmacārin*), the period of impurity upon the death of a relative lasts eleven nights. Yājñavalkya says, "By twelve nights" (YDh 3.22); Vasiṣṭha says, "By fifteen nights" (VaDh 4.28); Parāśara says, "By ten nights"; and Paiṭhīnasi says, "Sixteen days. Among these, there is an option depending on whether the fire-sacrifices and Vedic study have been maintained collectively or separately.
For a Vaiśya, it is twelve nights. || 14.3 ||
For a Vaiśya, it is twelve nights; some say it is half a month.
It continues as before. 14.3.
“Eleven nights,” says Parāśara; “twenty nights,” say Vasiṣṭha and Paiṭhīnasi. As before, there is an option between these. 14.3.
Some [say] for half a month. 14.4.

"Others say fifteen days. This alternative should be understood as depending upon one's conduct (*vṛtta*) and Vedic study (*svādhyāya*). And thus it is understood that even for Brāhmaṇas and others, there is a dependence on conduct and Vedic study. Accordingly, Parāśara says: "A Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with the sacred fires and the Vedas is purified in one day; one who possesses only the Vedas in three days; but one devoid of virtues is purified in ten days. (PārSm 3.5). Likewise, Manu also says:
Impurity on account of a death is ordained for ten days among the sapinda relatives.

“Before the collection of the bones, [the impurity lasts] for three days or even one day” (MDh 5.59). Here, the phrase “before the collection of the bones” is an elliptical expression for four days. When there is the presence of one quality [of the deceased], purification occurs after four days; when two qualities are present, after three days; but when all qualities are present, after one day. The Commentator has explained that when all qualities are present, there may even be a restriction of livelihood (*vṛttisaṃkoca*), in which case there is immediate purity (*sadyaḥśauca*). Similarly, a set of four statements is also commenced for a Kṣatriya: Gautama says, “After eleven nights” (GDh 14.2); Vasiṣṭha says, “After fifteen nights” (VaDh 4.28); Yājñavalkya says, “After twelve nights” (YDh 3.22); and Parāśara says, “After ten nights. Just as ten nights apply to a Brāhmaṇa, for a Kṣatriya fifteen days is the constant rule. In that regard, when there is the presence of one quality, it is twelve nights; when two qualities are present, eleven nights; when all qualities are present, ten days; and for one devoid of qualities, fifteen days. Likewise for a Vaiśya: when there is the presence of one quality, “some say half a month,” thus half a month; when two qualities are present, “twelve nights for a Vaiśya,” thus twelve days; when all qualities are present, the eleven nights mentioned by Parāśara; and for one devoid of qualities, twenty nights as stated by Vasiṣṭha. This should be understood as the conceptual framework for what is the constant rule. 14.4.
For a Śūdra, [the penance lasts] one month. 14.5 — 14.4.

Because this [individual] lacks initiation (*dīkṣā*) and other such rites, the rule applies to the *sapiṇḍas* alone. And because he lacks proper conduct (*vṛtta*) and so forth, this very same rule applies. This refers to the case of an unworthy Śūdra, based on the statement of Auśanas: "For worthy Śūdras, [the impurity lasts for] half a month. (14.5)

“[For] *sacchūdras*, [the impurity lasts] for half a month,” says Uśanas. Those who serve members of the three higher castes and seek their livelihood from them are *sacchūdras*; for we have stated that this is their highest mode of livelihood. Regarding the subject of slaves, Bṛhaspati says: “Slaves, apprentices, laborers, and students living together are purified by the same degree of purity as their master in cases of death or birth-impurity.”
Regarding marriage in this sequence, Baudhāyana states:
"If those belonging to the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes are the relatives of a Brāhmaṇa,
it is prescribed that the Brāhmaṇa's purification from their impurity occurs after ten days."
"Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas likewise, when [dealing with] kinsmen of lower castes, should observe their own period of impurity for the sake of purification; of this there is no doubt. As for Bṛhaspati:
"A Brāhmaṇa becomes pure in ten days upon the birth or death of those born of his own caste."

"But for those born of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes, it is by seven, five, and three nights respectively. Regarding this, Viṣṇu states a specific rule: "For a Brāhmaṇa, purification occurs after six nights, three nights, and one night among Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras; for a Kṣatriya, it is by six nights and three nights among Vaiśyas and Śūdras; and for a Vaiśya, purification from a Śūdra is after six nights"—this is the subject at hand. The application of these rules is determined by considerations such as conduct (*vṛtta*) and so forth. Regarding the case of a higher caste, Manu says: "But all should respectfully observe the period of impurity for those of the highest caste."

"Regarding their own impurity among those of their own birth, they shall act according to the manner prescribed by the rules for that caste. This means that those of higher castes shall observe the impurity occasioned by a death according to the method prescribed by the rules for that specific caste; however, regarding those of their own birth (svayoni), they shall observe their own impurity—that which is caused by their own jāti. From this very point, it is understood that the duties of those born in the direct order (anuloma) are conjoined with the caste of the mother. 14.4.
If that [period] should recur within it, they shall be purified by the remainder. 14.6 — 14.5.

That very same [period] should be understood as death in the case of a death of the same kind, and birth in the case of a birth, because of the inclusion of the word "that" (tad). Furthermore, the meaning of "again" (punar) is "once more" or even "repeatedly. It would "fall upon" (āpated), i.e., it would arrive. Consequently, purification would occur by the very time remaining from the previous period of impurity; the meaning is that one need not wait for the arrival of the new period. The inclusion of the word "within" (antar) is for the sake of clarity, since the intermediate case could have been known from these very rules: "They are purified by the remainder" (GDh 6.7), and "If a night remains, by two days; at dawn, by three" (GDh 18.8).

Others, however, maintain that since this is already established by the extension (*atideśa*) in the rule, "The same applies to birth" (GDh 14.14), the explicit mention of that [birth] refers to cases where the two [impurities] coincide in time. For example, when there is an impurity lasting ten nights, it is said, "an impurity lasting ten nights. This means that if a longer period of impurity occurs during a shorter one, the former shall not be superseded by the latter. Accordingly, the *Paiṅgi-gṛhya-smṛti* states: "In the case of an increase in impurity, one should complete [the rite] according to the latter. By the expression "in the case of an increase in impurity," it should be understood that even when there is a small amount of impurity, one must indeed observe the full duration. (14.6)

When there is a requirement for a correlate regarding an interrupted period, the phrase "impurity due to death (*śāva*) lasts ten nights" is connected to the context of the ten-night period and so forth that has been introduced. If, while one such impurity of ten nights or the like due to death is still ongoing, another impurity due to death—either of equal or shorter duration—should again occur or arrive, then they shall be purified by the remainder; that is, by those very days that remain of the previously ongoing ten-night period or the like. It does not mean, however, that one must wait for the completion of the time of the newly arrived impurity. Here, because of the extension (*atideśa*) that "the same applies to birth," if during the midst of a full period of impurity due to birth, another period of impurity due to birth of equal or shorter duration should arrive, they shall be purified by the remainder. In a case where a full period of impurity should fall during the midst of a shorter period of impurity, one proceeds by means of the latter itself. On this point, Manu says:
"If death and birth should both occur within ten days, the Brahmin shall remain impure until that period of ten days has passed. [MDh 5.79] Devala says:
"But when the initial [impurities] coincide, the purification should be understood as being according to the more serious [cause]."

Thus says Aṅgiras: "If the mother dies first and the father subsequently dies while still impure, his purification shall be by the remainder of the father's period; however, he should observe a *pakṣiṇī* (two days with the intervening night) for the mother."

"Impurity due to death (śāva) is twice that of birth (sūtaka); impurity due to menstruation (ārtava) is twice that of death; impurity due to childbirth (sūti) is twice that of menstruation; and for one who burns a corpse, it is even greater than that. Thus says Vṛddhātri: "By this, the purification of the cremator and the woman in childbirth occurs through the specific prior period of impurity [of the deceased or the fetus]. In this regard, there is the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
When impurity due to birth occurs while impurity due to death has already arisen, the birth-impurity is purified by the death-impurity;
the birth-impurity does not purify the death-impurity.
Thus [ends the section]. 14.5.
At the end of the night, [he should recite] two [verses]. 14.7 — 14.6.

If another impurity should occur when only one night remains of a previous period of impurity, then purification does not take place by the first alone; rather, it occurs after two nights. In this way, the three-night period is fully completed. (14.7)
If another impurity should occur while the preceding period of impurity still has one night remaining, then they shall be purified after two days. || 14.6 ||
At dawn, with three [verses]. 14.8 — 14.7.

"Before dawn" means before the *saṅgava* period, as seen in the explanatory passage (arthavāda): "Having bathed at the *saṅgava* time, those who have committed a sin should enter the village. If [the death] should occur then, purification is not achieved by the remainder of that night; rather, it is by three nights. 14.8.

Now, if ten days or more have elapsed, and on the following morning at the time of *saṃgava* (the third muhūrta after sunrise) another death occurs, they shall be purified in three nights. Regarding this, Manu says:
"But he who hears that one who was abroad has died before the ten days have passed shall remain impure only for as long as remains of those ten days. (MDh 5.75). Thus ends verse 14.7.
For those killed by cows or Brahmins, [the purification is] immediate. 14.9 — || 14.8 ||

For those killed for the sake of cows or for the sake of Brahmins, the period of impurity lasts only until they are seen; that is to say, there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*). And so says Manu: "In the case of [death] for the sake of cows or Brahmins, or for whomsoever the king desires. [MDh 5.95] This was stated under the heading of immediate purification: "for those killed by cows or Brahmins, or caused to be killed by either of these. And thus Uśanas: "There is immediate purification for those killed by cows and for those killed by a Brahmin. (14.9)

For those who are *sapiṇḍas* of persons killed for the sake of cows or for the sake of Brahmins, the period of impurity (*āśauca*) lasts as long as the corpse is visible. "As long as it is visible" (*anvakṣa*) means as long as the corpse is perceived; at the conclusion of the funeral rites, they become pure after bathing. Regarding this matter of immediate purity (*sadyaḥśauca*), Manu says: "In the case of one killed for the sake of cows or Brahmins, or for whom the king desires it... (MDh 5.95). The meaning is that for the kinsmen of those killed by a cow or by a Brahmin, the impurity lasts as long as the corpse is visible. Likewise, Uśanas states: "There is immediate purity for those killed by cows or killed by Brahmins. (14.8)
And [there is no offense] due to the king’s anger when there is no combat. 14.10.
And because of the king’s wrath. 14.9.

The term *anvakṣam* (immediately) is understood to carry over. The word *ca* has the sense of *api* (also), and its position is displaced. This means "even in the absence of battle due to the king’s wrath"; by the force of the word *api*, it also includes "even in battle. Thus says Manu:

"But for one slain in accordance with the duty of a Kṣatriya while weapons are raised in combat, the sacrifice is immediately completed; such is the rule regarding that impurity" (MDh 5.98). Alternatively, the word *ca* may have the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). Consequently, there is immediate purification for a king who causes someone to be killed out of wrath even when not in battle, and also for one who is killed in battle even without wrath.

Some explain it thus: "killed by royal wrath" refers even to those killed in battle, while "killed by disturbances of the populace and so forth" refers to others. And so says Manu: "And for those killed in a riot or battle, by lightning, or by the king... (MDh 5.95). Others, however, say it refers to the time of marriage: there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) for those killed by royal wrath outside of battle, and immediate purification at the time of marriage. And so says Bṛhaspati:
In times of distress, at a marriage, during a sacrifice, in battle, during a national calamity,
and even in the face of dire adversity, immediate purification is ordained.
Thus [ends the section]. 14.10.

The word "hatānām" (of those killed) is to be understood as connected [to the preceding]. For the kinsmen of those who have been killed due to the king's wrath, there is also immediate impurity. (14.9)
In battle. || 14.10 ||

The word *ca* (and) is carried over [from the previous rule]. Furthermore, for those killed in battle, impurity lasts for the duration of immediate perception (*anvakṣam*). On this point, Manu says: "And for those killed in a riot, in battle, by lightning, or by the king" [MDh 5.95]. *Ḍimba* means a crowd or a tumultuous gathering. Immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) is the subject under discussion. However, an alternative reading does not appeal to us; or rather, if that indeed is the reading, the division of the compound would be *ā-yuddha*. *Āyuddham* means a place of combat (*āyodhana*), that is to say, a battle. In any case, a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*) is not appealing. 14.10.
For those who desire [liberation] through fasting, weapons, fire, poison, water, hanging, or falling [from a precipice]. || 14.11 ||

The term *anvakṣam* (immediately) carries over from the previous context. For those who intentionally bring about their own death by means of fasting and the like, there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*). "Fasting" (*prāya*) refers to the Great Departure (*mahāprasthāna*); this may occur even against one's will due to fear of the king or other causes, which is why the phrase "of those who desire it" is used. "Fasting unto death" (*anāśaka*) is the refusal of food; this too may occur even against one's will during a famine or similar circumstances. "Weapon" (*śastra*) refers to a sword and so forth; even in that case, death may occur through negligence. "Hanging" (*udbandhana*) is by means of a rope and the like; here too, it may occur even against one's will through jesting or other such causes. "Falling" (*prapatana*) is from a mountain or a tree; even in that case, it may occur even unintentionally due to fate. Thus, it should be understood that for those who die by these means unintentionally, the rules are exactly as they apply in each case. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it should be understood that [the same applies] to other such causes of self-destruction. (14.11)

"Prāya" refers to the Great Departure (*mahāprasthāna*). Since this may occur even against one's will due to fear of the king or other causes, the phrase "of those who desire it" is stated [to exclude such cases]. In the same way, for the subsequent items as well, desire and lack of desire should be understood according to the circumstances. *Āśa* means eating; thus *āśana* is "eating," and *āśaka* is that very state. Its opposite is *anāśaka*. This refers to the cessation of eating out of anger or similar motives while edible food is actually present. Weapons, fire, poison, water, and hanging are well known. *Prapatana* is falling from a tree or a mountain. Through these—starting with fasting (*prāya*) and so forth—in the case of self-destruction, as well as by other similar means indicated by the word "and" (*ca*), there is immediate impurity (*anvakṣam āśauca*). Regarding this, in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
Out of anger, those lowest of men who resort to fasting, poison, fire, weapons, hanging, water, or falling from mountains and trees [are reborn as such].
Those who have been struck down by the rod of Brahmā, those who have been slain by Brāhmaṇas,
and those who are great sinners— they are proclaimed to be the fallen (patita).
"For those who have fallen [from their caste], there shall be no cremation, nor shall there be a collection of bones;
there shall be no shedding of tears, no offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), and no performance of śrāddha rites. On this point, Aṅgiras says:
"If someone should die through negligence by fire, water, or other such means..."
"Her impurity must be observed, and the water-libation rite must be performed. (14.11)
Now he states the nature of the *sapiṇḍa* relationship.
It was stated, "of the *sapiṇḍas*"; who are those *sapiṇḍas*, and he says:
"The cessation of the *piṇḍa* occurs at the seventh or the fifth [generation]. (14.12)

When one has passed beyond six persons and reaches the seventh, the offering of the *piṇḍas* is made to three ancestors beginning with the father. Others hold that while those [ancestors] are living, the son offers to the same ones as his father does; thus, there are six persons connected by the *piṇḍa*. When, for one whose father is living, the rule "one does not offer beyond a living person" is applied such that the father who is living offers to the grandfather and the great-grandfather, then the cessation occurs at the fifth. This is the same for women; or rather, on the paternal side, the cessation is at the seventh, and on the maternal side, it is at the fifth. (14.12)

Sapiṇḍya extends from the *kūṭastha* (the common ancestor) down to the sixth degree; at the seventh, it ceases. At the seventh degree alone, there remains the status of being a *sodaka* (a water-relation), because it is stated: “But it ceases at the seventh” (*MDh* 5.60). Beyond that, there is only the status of being a *sagotra* (a lineage-relation). As for what was said regarding the fifth degree, that refers to cases other than those involving an *aurasa* (legitimate son); even there, it should be understood according to the specific circumstances. And thus is the meaning: one should offer the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) to the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, and beyond them to two more—thus, including oneself, up to the sixth degree. But at the seventh, there is cessation. The rule “or at the fifth” refers specifically to the case of the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā-putra*). On this point, Baudhāyana says: “How, then, is the offering of the cake performed by the son of an appointed daughter? ‘This, O Father of such-and-such, is for you; and for my grandfather, and for those who follow you. This, O Grandfather of such-and-such, is for you; and for my great-grandfather, and for those who follow you. This, O Great-grandfather of such-and-such, is for you; and for my great-grandfather, and for those who follow you. For him who offers the cake in this manner, the cessation of the cake-offering occurs when the fifth degree is reached. In the *Mātsyapurāṇa*:

"Those beginning with the fourth [descendant] are partakers of the unguent; those beginning with the father are partakers of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa); the seventh among them is the giver of the cakes. Thus, the sapinda-relationship extends for seven generations. (14.12)
The same applies even to birth. 14.13.

The period of ten days alone is extended [to the mother]. Otherwise, immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) would apply to the mother as well, which contradicts established practice and the *Gṛhya-smṛti*, which states: "For ten nights, both husband and wife remain in a state of birth-impurity (*sūtakin*). Therefore, it should be understood that whatever ten-day period is prescribed for impurity due to death (*śāva*) applies to all *sapiṇḍas*. Likewise, Manu says: "When a child dies after teeth have emerged, or after they have been born [but before teeth], or after the tonsure ceremony (*caula*) has been performed, all relatives are impure; and the same is declared regarding birth-impurity (*sūtaka*). [MDh 5.58] Vyāghra also says the same.

"In the case of birth-impurity (sūtaka), however, for the sapindas, or for the parents, or for the mother alone, the impurity shall last ten nights; for those who offer water, it shall last three days. In this context as well, the exclusion of those initiated (dīkṣita) and others should be understood from the word "api" (also/even), as in the rule: "If that [impurity] should occur again within [the first period]," etc. (GDh 14.6). 14.13.

This is an extended application (*atideśa*) of the rules beginning with "impurity due to death lasts ten nights" and ending with "in the morning, with three [verses]"; it should be understood that just as it is with impurity due to death, so it is also with birth. || 14.13 ||
That [belongs] to the mother and father. || 14.14 ||
[The inheritance] belongs to the mother and father, or [in their absence] to the mother alone. || 14.14 ||

"Or the birth-impurity (sūtaka) of the mother and father. The word "or" (*vā*) from above should be supplied here as well. Accordingly, Vasiṣṭha also used the word "or" in this very context: "Or that of the mother and father, because it is caused by them" [VaDh 4.21–22]. 14.14.

"The impurity resulting from that birth belongs to both parents, or to the mother alone; because of the mother's preeminence, it pertains to the father even more so. Regarding kinsmen in that case, Vyāghra says:
'But the *sūtaka* (birth-impurity) belongs to the *sapiṇḍas*, or to the parents, or to the mother alone.
[The phrase] 'or to the parents' is because they are the cause of that [birth]. But Manu says:"

"Even in the case of birth, for those who desire precise purity, the impurity due to death (*śāva-āśauca*) applies to all, while the impurity due to birth (*sūtaka*) applies only to the mother and father. [MDh 5.61–62] Yājñavalkya says:
"The impurity due to death is prescribed as lasting either three nights or ten nights."

“For a child less than two years old, the impurity (*sūtaka*) belongs to both; however, for the mother alone. [Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.18] Baudhāyana says: “Regarding birth, there is a ten-day period of impurity for both the mother and the father. Some say it belongs to the mother alone, because she carries the child. Others say it belongs to the father, because of the predominance of the seed (*śukra*). For it is heard in scripture that there are even sons not born from a womb. But [the view] that it belongs to both the mother and the father is correct, due to their common connection through contact. [Baudhāyana Dharma Sūtra 1.11.19–23] Aṅgiras says: “Impurity is not declared for *sapiṇḍas* in the case of birth in any way.
There shall be impurity for the mother and father, and the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) belongs to the mother alone.”

"The impurity due to death applies to all, but the *sūtaka* (impurity due to birth) applies to the mother and father; or rather, the *sūtaka* belongs to the mother alone, for after touching her, the father becomes pure. Thus [says the text]. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "The same applies to birth. In that case, both the mother and father are impure; some say it is the mother alone. Paiṭhīnasi states:
"At birth, the *sapiṇḍas* are pure, but the mother and father are subject to *sūtaka*."

"The impurity (sūtaka) belongs to the mother alone; having performed the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśya), the father becomes pure. In this regard, the ten-day period is dependent on one's conduct and other factors; it is not an option for these [others]. Others say that the impurity characterized by loss of eligibility (anadhikāra-lakṣaṇa) applies to everyone, because of the observation in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra]: "In both cases, the food of the family is not to be eaten for ten days. However, the impurity characterized by untouchability (asparśitā-lakṣaṇa) applies only to the mother and father. And it is said that for the father who lives in another house and does not come into contact with them, there is no [impurity]: "During a birth-impurity (sūtaka), contact is not forbidden, provided one avoids the person who is actually in the state of birth-impurity. Thus they recite. (14.14)
Or from his mother. 14.15

The meaning is that the impurity belongs to the mother of that very child born, and not to the stepmother. A fixed alternative (*vyavasthitavikalpa*) is to be understood here: if all [the relatives] are devoid of good conduct (*vṛtta*), then there shall be birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) for all; if all possess good conduct but the father is devoid of good conduct, then [it applies] to both parents; when the father possesses good conduct but follows a restricted livelihood (*saṅkocavṛtti*), then it applies to the mother alone. However, if the father is a maintainer of the sacred fires (*agnihotrī*) and does not follow a restricted livelihood, then, having touched [the child] and offered the fire-oblation, he should again observe the period of impurity. (14.15)
The nights equal in number to the months of gestation [are required] for the falling away of the embryo. 14.16 — 14.15.

In the case of a miscarriage, however, there are as many days and nights as the number of months the fetus has been in the womb. One should understand that miscarriage occurs up to the fifth month, whereas after that it is a fall of the fetus (*garbhapātana*). Why? Because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the Brāhmaṇa: "Therefore, in the fifth month, fetuses undergo transformation. Consequently, the meaning is that for as many months as the fetus has miscarried, there are an equal number of days and nights [of impurity]. (14.16)

"Up to the fourth month there may be a *srāva* (a miscarriage); in the fifth and sixth months it is a *pāta* (a fall/miscarriage). Beyond that, for women, it is called *prasava* (birth). Thus, there are three types of fetal misfortunes (*garbhavipad*), all of which are designated by the term *sraṃsana* (miscarriage). For whichever month the miscarriage occurs, the period of impurity (*āśauca*) lasts for as many nights as the number of those months. The accusative case is used here to denote duration (*atyantasaṃyoga*). From the second month onwards, the days correspond to the number of the respective months. (MDh 5.67)
Or for three days. 14.17 — 14.16.

In the case of a miscarriage occurring at two or three months of pregnancy, the impurity lasts for three days; beyond that, the rule should be understood to be equal to the number of months elapsed. Even in the case of a full-term birth (patana), the impurity should be understood to last for a period equal to the months [of gestation], based on the statement in the *Paiṅgi-gṛhya-sūtra*: "When the fetus is dead, the day of impurity is equal to the number of its months. This impurity belongs to the mother alone, because she is the one authorized [in the rite]. Thus says the *Devagṛhya-sūtra*: "When the fetus is dead, the impurity shall belong to the mother alone. By the same logic applied to the period equal to the months, the ten-day period is established even for one who dies after the time of birth. From the use of the restrictive particle (*eva*) in the phrase "when the fetus is dead, [impurity] belongs to the mother alone," it is understood that after the time of birth, it pertains to both parents. And so says Vyāghra:
"When an infant dies, immediate purification (sadyaḥśauca) is prescribed for the sapindas;
however, for a husband and wife, as well as for uterine brothers, it lasts for ten days."

The mention of the ten-day period for uterine siblings (sodarāḥ) should be understood as applying only after the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*). Thus says the *Paiṅgi-gṛhya-smṛti*: "If the fetus dies while still in the womb, the impurity belongs to the mother alone; if born, to both; and when the name has been given, also to the uterine siblings. Some say this applies even before the name is given. When teeth have appeared and the tonsure (*cūḍā*) has been performed, it applies to all. This and other such rules should be understood to mean that when teeth have appeared and the tonsure has been performed, the ten-day period applies to all twelve types of sons. Since the rule "the nights [of impurity] are equal to the months [of pregnancy] in the case of a miscarriage" (GDh 14.16) already establishes this, the specific mention of "fetus" (*garbha*) here is for the purpose of restriction, indicating that this impurity applies only to the mother who is closely connected to the fetus. (14.17)
In the second month as well, it lasts for three days; however, in the fourth month, there is an increase.
And having heard [the news], for ten days and the subsequent two days (the "winged" period), one should remain [in restraint]. || 14.18 || — || 14.17 ||

The mention of the tenth day is for the purpose of indicating all periods of impurity (*āśauca*). A *pakṣiṇī* is a night situated between two days, or a day situated between two nights. Upon hearing of the birth or death of a *sapiṇḍa*, there is a *pakṣiṇī* period of impurity. Because of the word "and" (*ca*), and because it has been stated that "for those who have not undergone the tonsure ceremony (*caula*), [impurity lasts] three nights," this [rule of *pakṣiṇī*] should be understood to apply to those who have undergone the *caula*. Even among them, this should be understood to apply to those related by a four-day period of impurity. However, for those related by a three-day period, one should follow what was stated by Vasiṣṭha: "If one hears of a deceased person residing in another country after ten days have passed, the impurity lasts for one night. For those related by a one-day period, there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) according to the rule: "In the case of a child residing in another country... For those related by a ten-day period, however, [the following applies]:

Regarding the statement by Manu, "But when ten days have passed, one shall remain impure for three nights" (MDh 5.76), it should be understood as referring to a period of three days. For after a year has elapsed, there is only bathing;
according to the words of Manu: "But when a year has passed, one becomes pure simply by touching water" (MDh 5.76). 14.18.

The mention of the "tenth day" (*daśamī*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the full period of impurity (*āśauca*) beginning from ten days. A "pakṣiṇī" is either a night situated between two days, or a day situated between two nights. As before, the application of the second [period] follows from the context of calamities. If, after the ten-day period of impurity caused by a death has passed, one hears of the death of a relative, then there is impurity for a *pakṣiṇī*. If the news is heard by day, it consists of that intervening day, the following nights, and the day on the next morning; if heard by night, it consists of that night and the full day-and-night (*ahorātra*) of the next day. On this point, Manu says:
"But when ten days have passed, one shall be impure for three nights" (MDh 5.76).
Likewise, Jābāli says:
"When the period of birth-impurity has elapsed, one shall be impure for three nights according to each respective [period]."

In this context, the word *sūtaka* is a synonym for *āśauca* (impurity). Viṣṇu, however, states: "But when more than one year has passed, it is removed by a single night" [ViDh 22.40]. This regulation is determined in view of the specific place, time, and local custom. Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha says: "In the case of three months, there is impurity for three nights; in six months, it shall be for a *pakṣiṇī* (two days with the intervening night).
And all of this applies prior to one year. On this point, Manu says:
"But when a year has passed, one becomes pure simply by touching water. [MDh 5.76] Regarding this, Paiṭhīnasi states:
"If both parents should die, even a son who is far away, upon hearing of it, shall remain in a state of impurity for ten days starting from that day. In another Smṛti:
O best of the twice-born, when the wife of one's father has passed away, excluding one's own mother,
one shall remain impure for three nights once a year has elapsed.
Having heard that his kinsmen had died ten days ago and that a son had been born.
But this refers to the case of those who are *samānodaka* (sapindas beyond the seventh degree).
[One should offer water] to a kinsman not related by the *sapinda* bond, to one related by birth, and to a fellow student. (14.19) — [End of 14.18]

One who is not a *sapiṇḍa* but a *samānodaka* (a kinsman by water) is meant here. When such a person dies, the impurity for the *samānodakas* lasts for a "bird-night" (*pakṣiṇī*). This also applies to those related by a four-day period; however, for those related by a one-day period, the impurity lasts until the same time the next day. By the rule, "In the case of a child or one residing in another country," a three-day period is prescribed for non-relatives, while for those related by a ten-day period, it should be understood that the impurity lasts for three days according to the rule, "But for those who offer water, it is after three days" (MDh 5.64). Regarding blood relations: maternal uncles, maternal aunts, their daughters' sons, and paternal aunts' sons—when these die, the impurity lasts for a *pakṣiṇī*. The same applies to a fellow student (*sahādhyāyin*), who is one who has studied under the same teacher. From the word "and" (*ca*) in the verse, it is also implied to include a friend. (14.19)

One whose sapinda relationship has ceased is an asapinda, who is a samānodaka (a distant relative). Kinship by birth includes the maternal grandfather, the mother’s sister, her sons, and so forth; for married women, it includes their father and siblings, etc. A fellow student is one who has studied the entire Veda under the same preceptor. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), others mentioned in other Smṛtis—such as the father’s sister, her offspring, and so on—are also included. When these persons die, there is a period of impurity lasting for a "winged day" (*pakṣiṇī*) among themselves. However, once that period of the *pakṣiṇī* has passed, there is only bathing required. Manu, however, prescribes three nights of impurity for a *samānodaka*.

"Those who touch a corpse are purified by one night and day, or indeed by three triple-nights; but those who offer water [for the deceased] are purified after three days. (MDh 5.64). The application of these two rules is to be determined as before. Both of these refer to the death of one who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*). Prior to that, there is merely bathing. Regarding birth as well, a period of three days for *samānodaka* relations is shown by Manu:
"In the case of a birth, however, purification for those related by water is held here to occur after three days. (MDh 5.71). || 14.18 ||
For a fellow celibate practitioner, one day. 14.20 — 14.19.

A fellow religious student (*sabrahmacārī*) is one who practices the same observances; the meaning is that upon his death, one should observe impurity for one day and night, because the word "should observe" (*gṛhṇīyāt*) is supplied everywhere [in the context]. (14.20)
A fellow student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) who is a companion in the Veda and a friend—when he has died, there is impurity for one day and night. || 14.19 ||
And [the same applies] when a learned Śrotriya has arrived. || 14.21 || — || 14.20 ||

"One should stay for one night" is understood [from the previous rule]. In the case of a *śrotriya*—one who has studied the Veda with its six auxiliary limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), who is accomplished in knowledge and practice, and who is not a fellow student (*asabrahmacārī*)—[one may stay]. Or, "accomplished" (*upasaṃpanna*) means one who has taken refuge for some reason or is a neighbor-student. By the word "and" (*ca*), it is also [permitted] in the case of a king. (14.21)

A *śrotriya* is one who has studied the Veda. "Dependent" (*upasaṃpanna*) means one who relies [on him] through living in his house and so forth. Upon his death, there is impurity for one day. By the word "and" (*ca*), the phrase "for one day" is carried over [from the previous rule]. Regarding this, Aṅgiras says:
"If anyone dies in someone's house, that person's *sapiṇḍas* should likewise be known to be impure for three nights; there is no doubt in this matter."

Manu says: "But upon the death of a learned Śrotriya who has arrived, one shall remain impure for three nights" (MDh 5.81). The statement of Aṅgiras as well refers to the subject of a Śrotriya. On this point, Viṣṇu also states: "Marriage is the purificatory rite for women; among women who have undergone that rite, there is no impurity on the paternal side. However, if their birth or death occurs in the father's house, then there shall be one night and three nights respectively" (ViDh 22.32–34). This is a settled option: one night for a birth and three nights for a death. 14.20.
Upon touching a deceased person, there is impurity for ten nights, provided that one did so intentionally. (14.22) — (14.21)

"Upon touching a *preta* (a deceased person)" means upon carrying out the corpse; this is because of the use of the prefix *upa*, which indicates that it does not refer to mere touching. "Impurity (*āśauca*) lasts for ten nights," provided that he touches the body intentionally—that is, having seen it and accepted it—whether out of duty, for wealth, or out of affection. Here, the impurity refers only to contact, and not to the rules to be stated later, such as "they shall sleep and sit on the ground" (GDh 2.27), because the term "impurity" is used again within this section on impurity. In this very context, the distinction of cases should be understood: among the *sapiṇḍas*, there is no special rule for one who carries the corpse or performs the funeral rites, as there is no statement to that effect. However, for those who are *samānodakas* (distant kinsmen), the impurity lasts for ten nights.

"By one day and night, and by three periods of three nights, those who touch a corpse are purified; but those who offer water are purified after three days" (Manu Smṛti 5.64). According to this statement of Manu, and because the Commentator has explained that for those *samānodaka* (sapinda) relatives who carry out the removal of a deceased person or perform the funeral rites (*saṃskāra*), the period of impurity (*āśauca*) is ten nights, whereas for others it is three nights, it should also be understood that for those other than the *samānodaka*, the rule stated by Manu applies: "A Brahmin, having carried out a deceased twice-born person who is not a *sapiṇḍa* like a kinsman..."
One becomes pure after three nights, as do the maternal relatives who are closely related to the mother.
He who eats their food becomes pure after ten days.

"He shall not eat food [from that person], nor shall he dwell in that house for even a single day" (MDh 5.101–102). In this context, if one performs the removal of the corpse or the funeral rites (*saṃskāra*), and furthermore prepares the funeral mat (*kaṭa*) or eats that person's food, the period of impurity is ten days. If one performs only the preparation of the funeral mat but does not eat that person's food, it is three days. If one neither prepares the funeral mat nor dwells in that house, but merely enters the village, it is one day and night; the use of the particle "even" (*eva*) in the phrase "for even a single day" indicates that the impurity lasts as long as the light of day (*sajyotis*). This rule is to be understood as applying to one who, for the sake of a visible purpose, carries a corpse—whether it be a *sapiṇḍa* or a non-*sapiṇḍa*. This applies specifically to a Brāhmaṇa touching another Brāhmaṇa, because separate rules are prescribed for Vaiśyas and Śūdras. As for a Kṣatriya, when touching another Kṣatriya, his own specific rule applies; for when the beginning and end are explicitly stated, the middle case is understood by implication. (14.22)

In this context, by the word *upasparśa*, mere touching is not intended; for regarding that [touching], bathing with one's clothes on will be prescribed later in the passage beginning with "one who has touched an outcaste (*patita*) or a *caṇḍāla*. What then? *Upasparśana* here means the carrying away of a corpse. In that case, there is impurity (*āśauca*) for ten nights. If that carrying away is done with a worldly motive, such as the expectation of wages and the like, and not for the sake of dharma—then, although the subject of impurity is already established, the repetition of the term "impurity" is for the purpose of making known its distinction from the previous [types of] impurity. Consequently, the rules to be mentioned later, such as sleeping and sitting on the ground, do not apply in this instance; it is characterized solely by the subject of untouchability (*aspṛśyatā*). (14.21)
The [rules] for the Vaiśya and the Śūdra have been stated. 14.23 — 14.22.
The meaning is that upon touching a deceased person of the same caste, the impurity belonging to oneself alone—which has been taken up as a constant rule—occurs. (14.23)

With reference to this matter of touching a *preta* and so forth, the previously mentioned period of impurity for Vaiśyas and Śūdras—twelve nights or half a month—is not explicitly stated here. (14.22)
Or [the verses] beginning with "ārtavīḥ. 14.24 — || 14.23 ||

Or else, for the Vaiśya and the Śūdra, the period of impurity lasts for as many nights as there are seasons; that is, six. Although it could have been stated simply as "six," the inclusion of the term *ārtava* (seasons) is for the purpose of making known that there are five seasons. In this regard, it should be understood that for the Śūdra it is six [nights], and for the Vaiśya it is five. Among these, for a Vaiśya who possesses the proper conduct (*vṛtta*), it is five; for one who lacks such conduct, it is his own [standard] period. Regarding the Śūdra as well, for a virtuous Śūdra who possesses proper conduct it is six; for another, it is half a month; and for a base Śūdra who lacks proper conduct, it should be understood that it is indeed a full month. (14.24)
Or the period of impurity lasts for as many nights as there are seasons; there are six seasons, or five by combining the cold and dewy seasons into one. (14.23)
And [the same applies] to the two preceding [cases]. 14.25 — 14.24.

For the two previously mentioned [castes], the Brāhmaṇa and the Kṣatriya, the officiating priest (ārtvij) or that which was stated before [is prescribed]. The word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of drawing in the alternative options. 14.25.

The period of impurity (*āśauca*) has been stated for the two preceding castes, the Brāhmaṇa and the Kṣatriya, whether it be the [standard] impurity or the impurity lasting for the nights of menstruation (*ārtavī rātrīḥ*). Although the Brāhmaṇa was already mentioned, the phrase "of the two preceding [castes]" is repeated again for the purpose of establishing the option (*vikalpa*) regarding the nights of menstruation. As before, this option depends on factors such as place, time, and circumstances. Regarding the carrying out of a corpse when there is no payment for the service, Manu says: "A Brāhmaṇa, having carried out the corpse of a deceased person who is not a *sapiṇḍa* relative, as if he were a kinsman, becomes pure after three nights; likewise for the maternal relatives of his mother."

"He who eats their food becomes pure after ten days; but if he does not eat their food and does not dwell in that house, he becomes pure in a single day" (MDh 5.101–102). "Like a kinsman" means out of affection and so forth. Regarding those carrying the corpse while dwelling outside the village, purification occurs as long as the light lasts (*sajyotiḥ*). As Hārīta says: "Those who have touched a corpse shall not enter the village until the appearance of the stars at night, or until the appearance of the sun by day; thereafter there is purification. But regarding entry into the village, the one-day period according to Manu applies: "if he does not eat their food, he becomes pure in a single day. Regarding the case of one who is destitute (*anātha*), Parāśara states:
Those twice-born who carry a deceased brahmin who is without a protector obtain,
step by step in succession, the fruit of a sacrifice.
"A Brāhmaṇa is not defiled by touching a corpse or performing the funeral rites;
both the carrier of the body and the giver of the fire become pure immediately after bathing. (14.24)
Or for three days. 14.26 — || 14.25 ||

The phrase "of the two former" carries over [from the previous rule]. In that regard, for a Brāhmaṇa who has not completed his studies, the period is ten nights; for one who has completed them, five; and for one who has established the sacred fires, three days. The same should be understood to apply to a Kṣatriya as well. || 14.26 ||
Starting from the rule "upon touching a corpse" (GDh 14.21), for all castes there is a period of three days; this refers to the case of an extremely eminent person.
The same applies toward the teacher, his son, his wife, one for whom he performs sacrifices, and his pupil. (14.27) — (14.26)

When the teacher, his son, or his wife has died; when the person for whom one performs sacrifices (the *yājya*) or a pupil has died; and by the word "and" (*ca*), when the teacher’s teacher has died—as well as by the word "thus" (*evam*), which extends the period of three days alone, based on the observation of the Vasiṣṭha Smṛti stating, "And when the teacher has died, there is a three-night [period]" (VaDh 13.39). || 14.27 ||

The *ācārya* is one who possesses the characteristics described in the verse: “But he who, having initiated a pupil... (MDh 2.140). The son of such a teacher is the *ācāryaputra*. The wife of the teacher is the *ācāryastrī*. The *yājya* is one worthy of being sacrificed for; in relation to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), this refers to the patron of the sacrifice (*yajamāna*). The *śiṣya* is well known. When these have died, the period of impurity is likewise three days. || 14.26 ||
This was previously stated regarding those of the same class;
however, regarding those of different classes, he speaks of the domain of the removal of dissimilar [elements]:
"If a lower caste should touch a higher caste, or a higher caste a lower one, in that case..."
The impurity resulting from a corpse has been declared [in the preceding rule]. (14.28) — (14.27)
H reads "pūrvavarṇam".

The *avara* (lower) is the inferior one, such as a Kṣatriya and so forth. By the mention of "caste" (*varṇa*), it is not intended merely that there is impurity (*āśauca*) in the case of a *pratiloma* union; rather, there is also the necessity of penance (*prāyaścitta*). Although those born in the *anuloma* order are also not denoted by the word "caste," nevertheless, because of the rule "But those born in the *pratiloma* order are devoid of religious duties" (GDh 4.25), which establishes that only *pratiloma* offspring lack religious status, it is inferred that for *anuloma* offspring, the mother’s status prevails. One should touch or carry the "prior" caste—the Brāhmaṇa and so forth—or the "prior" person carries the "inferior" one, such as a Kṣatriya and so forth. This is due to the use of the prefix *upa*. In that case, regarding their mutual carrying, whatever impurity has been stated for a corpse (*śāva*) applies here as well. Thus, when a Kṣatriya touches a Brāhmaṇa, the impurity lasts ten nights; likewise, when a Brāhmaṇa touches a Kṣatriya, it lasts fifteen days. This applies everywhere. Since this occurs within the section on impurity, the repetition of the term "impurity" is for the purpose of indicating that it is an impurity of that specific kind, and not merely the suspension of Vedic study and other activities. While it would have sufficed to say "impurity from a corpse" (*śāvāśauca*), the inclusion of the word "stated" (*ukta*) is to include such impurity even in the context of ordinary activities like eating. Furthermore, when penances are heard in other Smṛtis—such as "for a *pāraśava* within ten days" (VaDh 4.32)—they should be understood as applying after the period of impurity has passed. Here, while it would have been sufficient to say "the stated impurity," the inclusion of the word "corpse" (*śava*) is to ensure that everything caused by a corpse is included. Therefore, having accepted the visible purpose of mutual carrying, the rules stated in other Smṛtis should be observed. Thus says Vyāghra: [He who carries a corpse] becomes pure after ten days, provided he does not eat the food of the family, does not sleep in the same bed, and does not perform the funeral rites.]

"If one of lower caste carries a person of higher caste, or if one who is superior carries one who is inferior, he shall observe impurity for a period equal to that of a corpse; if it is for a visible purpose, it shall be double.
Thus it is also in the case of an invisible purpose.
Those twice-born who carry a deceased brahmin who is without a protector obtain,
step by step, the fruit of a sacrifice in due order.

And so forth. Although it should have been stated simply that "the impurity is as declared for the corpse," the inclusion of the word *tatra* (in that case) is intended to prevent the application of the impurity that pertains specifically to conduct and Vedic study. And thus, just as the ten-day period is mandatory for a Brāhmaṇa, so too should the fifteen-day period and others be understood to apply to Kṣatriyas and the rest. Whatever impurity has been stated regarding the carrier of the corpse, that same impurity should be understood to apply to the one who performs the funeral rites (*saṃskartṛ*). Why? Because of the identical instruction in the *Auśanasa*: "Both the performer of the rite and the husband [of the deceased] become pure after three nights. (14.28)

The "lower" (avara) is one of inferior status, such as a Kṣatriya or others, in comparison to a Brāhmaṇa; the "higher" (pūrva) is one of superior status, such as a Brāhmaṇa or others, in comparison to a Kṣatriya or others. When these two carry out each other's corpses, the impurity (āśauca) prescribed for the specific caste of the corpse applies. For instance, when a Kṣatriya carries out the corpse of a Brāhmaṇa, his impurity lasts ten nights; when a Brāhmaṇa carries out the corpse of a Kṣatriya, his impurity lasts eleven nights, and so forth. Regarding this very matter, Vyāghra states concerning service: "If a lower person carries out the corpse of a higher caste, or if a higher person carries out the corpse of a lower caste, he must observe the impurity pertaining to that corpse; however, if it was done for a visible purpose (dṛṣṭārtha), the impurity shall be double. (14.27)
The impurity caused by carrying a corpse has been declared for those of the same caste as well as for those of a different caste. Now he states [the rule] regarding touching it intentionally.
He declares the purification for the mere intentional touch of a corpse, along with incidental cases:

upon touching an outcaste (*patita*), a *caṇḍāla*, a woman who has recently given birth (*sūtikā*), a menstruating woman (*udakyā*), a corpse, or one who has touched them, or one who has touched the person who touched them.
One is purified by touching water while wearing one's clothes. || 14.29 || — || 14.28 ||
H reads: "by touching water with one's clothes on."

An outcast (*patita*) is one who has killed a Brahmin and so forth. A *caṇḍāla* is as previously defined. A woman who has recently given birth (*sūtikā*) is one whose period of ritual impurity (*āśauca*) has not yet expired. A menstruating woman (*udakyā*) is one who has her menses. By the mention of "the corpse" (*śava*), everything caused by it is intended: namely, the corpse itself, those who are subject to its impurity, those who prepare the funeral pyre, those who carry it, and those who perform the cremation, and so on. The term "touching" (*upasparśana*) is connected with each of these individually. Thus, "touching an outcast, a *caṇḍāla*, a woman who has recently given birth, a menstruating woman, or a corpse" refers to touching them directly, touching one who has touched them, or touching one who has touched the one who touched them. The prefix *upa-* implies intentional action; the intentional touching of a corpse occurs for the purpose of decoration or out of mere whim. Whether the corpse belongs to one's own caste or a different caste makes no difference, as there is no distinction made. However, in the case of unintentional contact, the rule stated by Manu should be observed. As he says:
Having touched one whose praises are sung at dawn (a *divākīrtya*), a woman in her courses, an outcaste, a woman who has recently given birth,
a corpse, or one who has touched a corpse, one becomes pure by bathing.

Thus, impurity (*āśauca*) is prescribed for two [classes], whereas Gautama prescribes it for all three. "With his clothes on" means with his garment; if it is argued that one should rather say "by bathing" (*snānāt*), this is not a fault. The phrase "by touching water" (*udakopasparśanāt*) is stated so that, having first immersed himself like a staff, he should bathe again properly. While it could have been said simply "he should touch water with his clothes on," the use of the term "touching water" is intended to include libations (*tarpaṇa*) even within the occasional bath (*naimittika-snāna*). And thus says the *Bhārgavīya*:
Bathing is said to be of three kinds: daily, occasional, and optional;
Prajāpati declared that libation (tarpaṇa) belongs to all three as well.
Thus [ends the verse]. 14.29.

An outcast (*patita*) is one who has killed a Brahmin and so forth. A *caṇḍāla*, a woman recently delivered (*sūtikā*), a menstruating woman (*udakyā*), and a corpse (*śava*) are well known. Upon touching these, upon touching those who have touched them, and upon touching those who have touched the latter, one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on (*sa-caila*) after performing the ritual sipping of water (*upasparśana*). Purity through bathing while wearing one's clothes is intended here; therefore, reading this as an adverbial modifier (*kriyā-viśeṣaṇa*) is incorrect. For unintentional contact, the rule of Manu applies: "A person who is impure due to childbirth, a *divākīrti* (outcast), a menstruating woman, an outcast, and likewise a woman recently delivered..."
"Having touched a corpse or one who has touched it, one becomes pure by bathing. [MDh 5.85] Thus [ends the verse]. 14.28.
And also when following a corpse. 14.29.
"Even if one follows this relative or even a non-relative out of one's own desire, one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter. (MDh 5.103)

Some authorities maintain that bathing should take place even after consuming the clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśana*); however, the source for this must be sought. Yājñavalkya also states only this much: "Having touched fire and consumed clarified butter, one becomes pure" (YDh 3.26). This refers to cases involving those of the same caste (*sajātīya*). Regarding a Brāhmaṇa following a Kṣatriya, Vasiṣṭha says: "Upon touching a human bone, there is impurity for three nights; but if the bone belongs to a killer, it is for a day and night, and the same applies to following a corpse" (VaDh 23.24–26). The phrase "the same applies" extends the rules of three nights and one day-and-night to this case. Here, the settled rule is that following a Kṣatriya requires one night, while following a Vaiśya requires three nights. Regarding following a Śūdra, however, Aṅgiras says:
But a Brāhmaṇa who, weak in knowledge, follows a Śūdra who has become a corpse while being carried away,
shall remain impure for three nights.

"But when three nights have passed, having gone to a river that flows into the ocean and performed a hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), one becomes pure by consuming clarified butter. Thus it is said. For a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya following a Vaiśya or a Śūdra woman, the penance should be determined as being like that for a Brāhmaṇa. For a Kṣatriya following a Śūdra woman, the penance is one night and a hundred breath-restraints. Manu says:
"Having touched a human bone that still has marrow upon it, one should enter the water with one's clothes on."
"Having sipped water, one who is free from oiliness should touch a cow or look at the sun. (MDh 5.87). This refers to cases where the act was unintentional. Vṛddha-Manu states:
"Furthermore, one who has borne a child in his wife becomes pure by performing the cremation or the carrying away of another's corpse."
One should not perform both [rites] there; one should always perform only that which pertains to the father.
"Or [the impurity lasts for one day] for an elder brother who is childless, or for the son of a maternal uncle.
The term "father" is indicative of the mother as well. Regarding weeping for the deceased, Pāraskara states:
"If one weeps before the collection of the bones, one should perform a ritual bath."

"Within ten days for a Brāhmaṇa, sipping water (ācamana) is prescribed after [the period of impurity]. This rule applies equally to all castes who weep for a deceased Brāhmaṇa within ten days. Regarding this, Viṣṇu states: "For every deceased person, having shed tears along with the relatives, purification is attained by bathing; if the collection of bones has not yet been performed, by bathing with one's clothes on" [ViDh 22.61–62]. From the context, it is understood that this refers to "purification. This applies to those of equal or lower status weeping at the death of a Kṣatriya or others, with the exception of Śūdras. They cite the *Brahmapurāṇa* regarding weeping for a sick person belonging to the three higher castes.
If a Brahmin cries over a heap of bones belonging to a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya,
he becomes pure after bathing with his clothes on on the second day.

"But when the collection [of bones] has been performed, the Brahmin becomes pure by bathing alone. This same principle should be inferred for a Kṣatriya even when there is the manifestation of illness in a Vaiśya. Regarding the manifestation of illness in a Śūdra, Pāraskara says:
"If a Brahmin should shed tears before the collection of the bones..."
If a Śūdra has died, having gone to his house, one becomes pure after three nights.
After the collection of the bones, for up to one month,
the twice-born become pure by means of a single day and night, as well as by the washing of their clothes.
Thus, enough of this digression following upon a digression. || 14.29 ||
And [the same applies] to dogs. 14.30.

Regarding "purification through touching water with one's clothes on" (*upasparśane sacela udakopasparśanāt*): the word "he shall be purified" (*śudhyet*) carries over from the previous context. The separate mention [of the dog] is for the purpose of excluding those who have touched the one who touched it. The mention of the "dog" (*śva*) is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for jackals and the like as well. By the word "and" (*ca*), "bone" (*asthi*) is also included, provided it is moist (*sasneha*). As Manu has said: "Having touched a human bone that is moist, a Brahmin is purified by bathing; but having touched one that is dry, he is purified simply by sipping water (*ācamya*), or by touching a cow, or by looking at the sun. (MDh 5.87)

This, however, applies to touching [human bone] unintentionally. But regarding intentional contact, Vasiṣṭha says: "Having touched moist human bone, there is impurity for three nights; but if it is dry, for a day and a night" (VaDh 23.24). By the use of the word "and," blood and so forth are also included. Some say this refers to following a corpse; in that case, bathing with one's clothes on and consuming clarified butter should also be understood as required. Thus Manu says: "If one intentionally follows a deceased person, whether they be a relative or not..."
"Having bathed with his clothes on, touched fire, and consumed clarified butter, he becomes purified. (MDh 5.103)

This rule applies to all [castes] only in the case of following a corpse of their own caste. However, in the case of following a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha should be observed. Thus he says: "But in the case of following one who is not a relative, or in the case of following a corpse, it is likewise for a day and a night" (VaDh 23.25). In that context, the extension of the rules for three nights and one night applies to following a corpse. Consequently, one should observe one night as the penance for following a Kṣatriya, a *pakṣiṇī* (two days with the intervening night) for following a Vaiśya, and three nights for following a Śūdra. Thus Aṅgiras says: "A Brāhmaṇa weak in knowledge who follows a Śūdra who has become a corpse..."
One who follows a corpse being carried away shall remain impure for three nights.

"But when three nights have passed, having gone to a river that flows into the ocean and performed a hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), he becomes pure after consuming clarified butter. Thus it is said. For a Kṣatriya following a Vaiśya, and for a Vaiśya following a Śūdra, the penance should be determined as being like that of a Brāhmaṇa. For a Kṣatriya approaching a Śūdra woman, one should observe a hundred breath-restraints accompanied by one night. (14.30)

Even when combined, it requires [purification]. Upon touching a dog, one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on; the separate mention is for the purpose of precluding the rule regarding those who have touched such a person. (14.30)
Some say that one should strike [the ground] with it. 14.31.

Some, however, maintain that whatever limb a dog touches must be washed; this is an alternative view (vikalpa) to be understood as follows: bathing is required if the upper body is touched, whereas washing is sufficient if the lower body is touched. The same applies to contact with birds. Likewise, Jātūkarṇi states:

"If a bird touches any part of the body above the navel, excluding the hands, bathing must be performed there; for the remainder, one becomes pure by washing. This principle regarding dogs should likewise be understood to apply to all parts except the hands. (14.31)

Some, however, maintain that if a dog should defile a limb, one should wash only that specific part. Regarding this, there is a specific rule from Āpastamba: “One defiled by a dog should immerse himself with his clothes on; or, having washed that spot and touched it with fire, and having washed his feet again and sipped water, he becomes pure” (ĀpDh 1.15.16–17). Jātūkarṇya states the following distinction: “If a donkey touches a limb above the navel—excluding the hands—one must bathe; if below, one should merely wash [the affected part].”
"In that case, a bath must be performed; otherwise, one becomes pure by washing [the hands]. (14.31)
The offering of water for one who has grown matted hair is performed by his sapinda relatives.
The offering of water for one who has undergone the tonsure ceremony is performed by the sapinda relatives.

On account of the context, water must be offered by the *sapiṇḍas* for the deceased who has had his hair matted (*jaṭila*) or whose tonsure (*caula*) has been performed; it is not to be done by all those who are impure (*aśuci*). Impurity (*āśauca*) is also to be understood from the injunction regarding the water-rite (*udakakriyā*), because Vasiṣṭha mentions them together in the statement: “The water-rite and impurity” (VaDh 4.9). The purpose of that joint mention is that whoever performs the water-rite also undergoes impurity. Similarly, based on another *smṛti*, it should be understood as lasting three nights. Thus Manu says:

"But for those who have ceased wearing the [student's] cloth, purification is held to occur after three nights" (MDh 5.66). This same rule applies equally to Kṣatriyas and others as well, because there is no distinction. And thus, all the alternative periods of impurity heard of in scripture—such as three days and so forth—which depend on the stage of life, should be understood as applying equally to everyone, precisely because there is no distinction. Likewise, those periods such as fifteen days which are prescribed depending on one's conduct (*vṛtta*) and other factors, are to be understood as referring to one who has died after having received the initiation (*upanayana*). The same applies to impurity due to being in another country (*deśāntara*). And so Vyāghra says:

"For all [the deceased], it is equal when their age has passed; likewise, it is equal when they have been initiated (*upanīta*); but in that very case, if the time has elapsed, there is inequality. Regarding what was stated, prior to the completion of the period of impurity (*āśauca*), that which is heard such as "whatever remains of the ten nights" (MDh 5.75) and so forth, should be understood to apply even before initiation. Furthermore, the cremation (*saṃskāra*) of one who has grown matted hair (*jaṭā*) should also be observed based on another Smṛti. Thus says Lokākṣi:
"One should offer water silently and likewise [dispose of] the fire silently;

for all those who have undergone the *cūḍā* ceremony, both [rites] may also be performed according to one's wish in other cases. Thus, it should be understood that for one whose hair has been matted (*jaṭā*), the cremation with fire and the offering of water are mandatory, whereas for one whose tonsure (*caula*) has not been performed, they are not mandatory. And so says Manu:
"The water-rite (udakakriyā) should not be performed by relatives for one who has not reached three years of age;
however, they may perform it for one whose teeth have emerged, or even when the naming ceremony (nāman) has been completed. [MDh 5.70] || 14.32 ||

For that deceased person whose tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*) has been performed, the offering of water (*udakadāna*) must be carried out by his *sapiṇḍas* for as long as the period of impurity (*āśauca*) lasts; not before then. His cremation (*agnisaṃskāra*) is likewise to be performed for him. As Laugākṣi says:
"One should offer water silently, and likewise the fire silently."

"For all those whose tonsure (*cūḍā*) has been performed, [the rites] are mandatory; otherwise, however, both are optional according to one's wish. Thus, for one whose tonsure has been performed, the consecration by fire (*agnisaṃskāra*) and the offering of water (*udakadāna*) are obligatory; for one whose tonsure has not been performed, they are not obligatory, and there is no transgression (*pratyavāya*) in their omission. By the mention of the "tonsure," the third year is indicated, as that is seen in many *smṛtis*. Manu also says:
"The water-rite (*udakakriyā*) should not be performed by Brahmins for one who is less than three years old."

"Or one may perform it for one who has teethed, or even when the naming ceremony has been performed" (MDh 5.70). The mention of fire and water is an elliptical expression for the funeral rites (*aurdhvadehika*). Regarding this, Devala states a specific rule:

"If death occurs while the child is still in the *paugaṇḍa* stage (before the age of sixteen) prior to the twelfth year, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite shall not take place; one should instead perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rites."
Thus [ends the verse]. 14.32.
And that [is the rule] for women as well. 14.33.

That offering of water is accompanied by the cremation rites, because it is included therein. And this must be performed for women as well; the word "and" (*ca*) is used for the purpose of including the pulling out of matted hair (*jaṭā*). It is mentioned separately for the purpose of lightening the period of impurity (*āśauca*), which is to be understood from other *smṛti* texts. In that regard: "In the case of an immature girl, immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) is ordained.
Thus, before the performance of the tonsure (*caula*), there is immediate purification. By the word "immature" (*prauḍhā*), the performance of the tonsure ceremony is meant.

Regarding the verse, "But for unmarried girls and children, purification is one day" (YDh 3.24), this means that for those who have undergone the *cūḍākaraṇa* ceremony but have not yet reached the time of being given in marriage, purification is one day. However, by the rule, "For female relatives who are uninitiated, the kinsmen are purified after three days" (MDh 5.72ab), it is established that for an unmarried girl after the time of marriage, purification takes three nights.

"In the very manner already stated, those of the same *nābhi* (uterine kin) are purified" (MDh 5.72cd). In this context, by the logic of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpika*), it should be understood that regarding women, the period of impurity for both parents is ten days. Regarding *sapiṇḍas* as well, the limit should be seen as three generations (*tripūruṣa*), based on the statement of Vasiṣṭha: "But for unmarried women, it extends to three generations" (VaDh 4.18). 14.33.
That offering of water should also be performed for women whose tonsure ceremony has been completed.
Some [say it belongs] to those who have been given away. 14.34.

Some authorities maintain that even for those girls who have been given away with water and speech, the rites must be performed by the bridegroom's family alone. Gautama, however, states: "If the groom should die first after she has been given away by water and word, she should be given to another according to the prescribed rule; such is the case with a maiden."

Thus, because of the extension [of rules] from the case of a maiden (*kanyāvat*), it follows that the gift should be given by the father and others themselves; in that regard, it should be understood that in the absence of the paternal side, it must be performed by the groom’s side. (14.34)
Some maintain that the offering of water is for married women alone, and not at all for unmarried ones; and for those who are married, it should be given by the families of their husbands.

Now, as to how they should conduct themselves during a period of impurity, he says: "Furthermore, during the time of impurity, all kinsmen should sleep and sit on the ground and remain celibate. (14.35)

They should sleep and sit only on the ground and avoid sexual intercourse for as long as the period of impurity lasts. The inclusion of the word "all" is intended to indicate that this applies even to those who are *samānodaka* (sapindas beyond the seventh degree). 14.35.

They should sit on the ground itself, not on mats, seats, or similar objects; they should also avoid sexual intercourse. The inclusion of the term "all" is for the sake of including those who are *samānodaka* (sapindas up to the seventh degree). 14.35.
They should not wipe [it]. 14.36.
The meaning is that they should not wear bright or gaudy clothing; or rather, they should avoid the removal of bodily impurities. 14.36.
Washing is the removal of bodily impurities; and they should not perform that. 14.36.
They shall not eat meat until the [final] offering has been made. 14.37.
Until the performance of the *śrāddha* rite, they should not consume meat, even in cases such as when life is at stake. || 14.37 ||
The offering is the *śrāddha* ceremony. They should not eat meat until that [ceremony] is completed. (14.37)
The water-rites are performed on the first, third, fifth, seventh, and ninth days.
The water-libation rite is performed on the first, third, seventh, and ninth days.

It should be understood that on the first and subsequent days, the rite is to be performed by the sapinda relatives, whereas on each day it is to be performed by the sons. The inclusion of the term "rite" (kriyā) is for the purpose of including the procedure for the offering of water as prescribed in the Gṛhyasūtras, such as: "The sons offer water once for the deceased," and so forth. (14.38)

On the first and subsequent days, water mixed with sesame seeds must be offered by the sapindas for the deceased, saying: "To the deceased of such-and-such gotra and such-and-such name, I give this sesame-water. On the first day, three [handfuls] are given; on the third, nine; on the seventh, thirty; and on the ninth, thirty-three. Thus, seventy-five handfuls of water are to be offered. However, according to custom, three are given on the first day, and from the second day onwards, one more is added each time.
And there is the relinquishing of garments. 14.39.

There is the discarding of garments worn at the time of the water-offering; the meaning is that other [garments] are to be worn. By the word "and" (*ca*), hair and so forth are also included. And thus it is stated in another *Smṛti*:
"On the second day, the shaving of the head should be performed with diligence;
on the third, the fifth, or even the seventh, until the offering [of the *pinda*]. (14.39)
The garments worn at the time of the water offering should be discarded on the first, third, fifth, and ninth days; other garments should be put on in their proper sequence. 14.39.
But for the last [of the vowels], it is before the final [consonants]. || 14.40 ||

"Before the ninth [day], for the lowest castes, the Śūdras, there is the discarding of the garments"—this phrase continues [from the previous rule]. The word "but" (tu) is for the purpose of specification. The offering of water is to be performed on the first day and so forth; however, the discarding of the garments occurs only at the end. The use of the plural "of the lowest" (antyānām) indicates that this same rule applies even to those born in the direct order (anuloma) who are entitled to wear the sacred thread (savyavahārya). 14.40.
Among the castes, for the lowest, the Śūdras, the discarding of clothes occurs on the ninth day after their final impurity.
The appearance of teeth and so forth [are determined] by the mother and father. || 14.41 ||

From the time of the eruption of the teeth onwards, the parents must invariably perform the offering of water; it should be understood that prior to this, there was no such obligation for them either. 14.41.
From the time of the eruption of the teeth, the mother and father should offer water for their son; the mother [offers] silently. 14.41.
There is immediate purification for children, those living in a foreign land, renunciants, and those who are not sapinda relations. (14.42)

A "child" (*bāla*) is one prior to the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*). And from that point, after the naming ceremony but before the eruption of teeth, the period of impurity mentioned in another *Smṛti*—namely, "one day"—should be understood: "For men who have not yet had the tonsure performed, impurity is declared to last for one night" (MDh 5.67).
