After the eruption of teeth but before the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*), the period lasts for three days.

"Having abandoned him like a log in the forest, they should pass three days [in impurity]. [MDh 5.69] One who has died in another country and is not heard of at that very time is "one gone to a foreign land. An ascetic, a perpetual student, a forest-dweller, and a wandering mendicant—when such a person has died, there is immediate purification for those who are not *sapiṇḍas*. A non-*sapiṇḍa* is one who shares the same water-libations (*samānodaka*); the scope regarding him has already been stated. 14.42.

An "infant" (*bāla*) is one whose tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*) has not been performed. One who is "separated by region" (*deśāntarita*) is one who is obstructed by distance, residing in another country. "Renunciants" (*pravrajitāḥ*) are those who have taken lifelong vows (*naiṣṭhika*), forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*), and wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*). Those who are "not *sapiṇḍas*" are those who are "common-water relations" (*samānodaka*). Upon their death, there is immediate purification for the kinsmen; purity is attained through bathing. Regarding infants, Yājñavalkya states: "One should bury a deceased child less than two years old, but no water libation should be offered thereafter. Until the eruption of teeth, purification is immediate; until the tonsure ceremony, it is declared to last one night. [YDh 3.1–2]
"Three nights until the instruction in the vows, and ten nights beyond that. [Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.23]. Āṅgiras says:
"Even if he has not had his tonsure ceremony performed, if he has died after teeth have appeared, one should cremate him and observe impurity for three days. But Manu says:
Relatives should place a deceased child who has not yet reached two years of age outside the village,
having adorned it, upon pure ground, except for the collection of bones.
For him, no cremation with fire is to be performed, nor is the water-rite to be performed.

“Having abandoned them like a piece of wood in the forest, one should pass three days [in impurity]. [MDh 5.68–69] Āśvalāyana says: “In the case of one who has died before the eruption of teeth, or after it has erupted, [the impurity lasts for] one day. Āpastamba, however, states: “For those related to the mother through the womb and to the father up to the seventh person, or as far as the relationship is known—if they have died, there is the touching of water; this excludes fetuses less than a year old. Among these, the parents alone and the heirs [are affected]. [ĀpDh 2.15.2–4] The application of these rules depends on the customs of the region and the family. Regarding the case of a maiden, Āpastamba says:

"But in the case of an immature girl, immediate purification is ordained. Here, "immature" means one whose *cūḍā* (tonsure) ceremony has not been performed. [Yājñavalkya]: "In the case of unmarried girls and young children, purification occurs after one day. [YDh 3.24]. This refers to the period after the *caula* ceremony. Vyāghra says:
"When a child dies, immediate purification is ordained for the *sapiṇḍas*."
"By ten days alone [the impurity ends] for a husband and wife, and likewise for uterine brothers.
This, however, refers to the case of death occurring within the ten-day period of *sūtaka*. And so it is said:
"If the *niṣkramaṇa* (first outing) of a newborn infant takes place within the ten-day period..."
"Śātātapa declared that for the parents, purification occurs through the very same period of birth-impurity. || 14.42 ||
And because of the conflict with the duties of kings. || 14.43 ||

The term "immediate purification" (sadyaḥśauca) continues to apply here. The plural form "of kings" (rājñām) is intended to include ministers who resemble kings; this is also indicated by the word "and" (ca), which implies "and of whomever [the king] desires. Thus Manu says: "And of whomever the king desires" (MDh 5.95). For one, there is no obstruction or impossibility regarding duties such as protection and so forth. (14.43)

And for a king, there is immediate purification because of the conflict with his duties; "duty" refers to the protection of the subjects and so forth. Because of the use of the plural number, this applies also to others such as ministers who have similar duties. As Manu says: "Whomever the king desires [to be pure]" (MDh 5.95). 14.43.
And for the sake of the Brahmin’s non-cessation of Vedic study, for the sake of the non-cessation of Vedic study. || 14.44 ||

The statement of the reason is for the purpose of making it known that impurity occurs with respect to the study of the Veda as it has been performed. By the word "and" (ca), the aforementioned subjects are established for the purpose of allowing even Kṣatriyas and others to enter [the rite] on account of their own Vedic study. The repetition [of the concluding verse] is for the purpose of marking the completion of the chapter. 14.44.

And for a Brāhmaṇa, there is immediate purification so that his study of the Veda may not be interrupted; this was stated with reference to one who has many pupils and is teaching. [The repetition marks the end of the chapter. Thus ends the section on impurity. 14.44.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter.
Now, one should offer the Śrāddha to the ancestors on the new moon day. 15.1.
Now, the Śrāddha ceremony. 15.1.

The *śrāddha* is of five kinds, as Vyāghra has stated: "The daily (*nitya*), the occasional (*naimittika*), the optional (*kāmya*), the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, and likewise another, the *pārvaṇa*; thus the *śrāddha* is known to be remembered as being of five kinds. Among these, that which is performed day after day is the *nitya*, as Manu has said:
"One should offer the *śrāddha* day after day with food and drink, or even with milk, roots, and fruits, bringing satisfaction to the ancestors" (MDh 3.82). Likewise, it is stated in that same work:
"In the context of the five great sacrifices (*pāñcayajñika*), one should feed even a single Brahmin for the sake of the ancestors."
"And one should not feed anyone here on account of the Vaiśvadeva offering to the gods. Thus [it is stated in] MDh 3.83. And likewise, another Smṛti also says:

"Except for celibacy and the suspension of Vedic study, [one should perform] the daily *śrāddha*. Regarding that which is called the occasional (*naimittika*) *ekoddiṣṭa*—so named because it is performed with reference to a single person—as Kātyāyana says: "Now, the *ekoddiṣṭa*: there is one twice-born man, one vessel, one purifier, even one *arghya* offering, one *piṇḍa*; there is no invocation (*āvāhana*), nor the offering into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*). This should be performed starting immediately after the period of impurity (*āśauca*) and prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite; as Lāṭyāyana says: "The *ekoddiṣṭa*, however, should be performed every month for a year."
"And likewise every year, on the eleventh day from the first. Similarly, Vyāghra also says:
"It should be performed on the eleventh day, and likewise after three fortnights."

"And likewise, for six months, one should diligently perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* [rite]. Thereafter, when the year is complete, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* must be performed. And so says Jātūkarṇi: "Then, when the year is full, or after three fortnights, or even earlier, one should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*; if it occurs before [the year], it would be a cause for prosperity (*vṛddhi*). The phrase "three fortnights" refers to the case of one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*). Why? Because of the statement of Bṛhaspati. He says thus:
If the new moon should occur during the tenth night,
the son who maintains the sacred fires must perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* on that very day.
"In the absence of that [the first anniversary], the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is prescribed after three fortnights.

Thus it is heard in the *Jābāla* tradition: "The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* occurs after three fortnights"—this is the revealed scripture (*śruti*). After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, on occasions such as the *saṃkrānti*, one should perform the *śrāddha* by offering three rice-balls (*piṇḍa*). On the anniversary of the death each year, the *ekoddiṣṭa* should be performed. As Uśanas has said:
"At the *saṃkrānti*, during an eclipse, at the *parvan*, at the solstice (*ayana*), and during the *mahālaya*..."

"One should offer three rice-balls there; however, if [the day] has been missed, only one. Thus, the Aṣṭakā rites must be performed every year after the Āgrahāyaṇī full moon. To this effect says the author of the Gṛhyasūtra: "There are three dark fortnights following the Āgrahāyaṇī; in each of these, there is one Aṣṭakā: the Śākāṣṭakā, the Māṃsāṣṭakā, and the Apūpāṣṭakā," and so forth. Among these, *kāmya* is that which is performed out of desire, such as "one desiring a son on the eleventh day," and so on. *Vṛddhiśrāddha* is the *Nāndīmukha*. *Pārvaṇa* is the monthly *śrāddha*. Alternatively, whatever is performed by means of the offering of three rice-balls—such as the Aṣṭakā and others—all the remainder is *naimittika* (occasional).

While this fivefold [classification] stands—“Now, on the new moon day, one should offer the *śrāddha* to the ancestors”—the word “now” (*atha*) means immediately after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Why? Because of the opening statement, “On the new moon day, one should offer the *śrāddha* to the ancestors,” it can be understood that this refers to the monthly *śrāddha* (*māsi-śrāddha`); furthermore, because other *smṛtis* prohibit the monthly *śrāddha* prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. As Bṛhaspati says: “But he who performs the *pārvaṇa* [śrāddha] prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*...”

"Having become a worm in a dog's excrement, one sinks down together with the ancestors. If it is argued that, in that case, only those *śrāddha* rites which take place prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* should be mentioned, [the answer is] no; for the purpose of indicating the absence of such rites for some, it is stated immediately thereafter that the *pārvaṇa* alone should be performed. And so says Bṛhaspati:
"For ascetics who have died, no funeral rite whatsoever is seen;
when the eleventh day arrives, the *pārvaṇa* is prescribed."
"For those who have taken lifelong vows (naiṣṭhika), forest-dwellers, and likewise for those who are liberated,
the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite is not prescribed, nor is the ekoddiṣṭa rite."

*Śrāddha* is the name of a ritual act, so called because it is accomplished through extraordinary faith (*śraddhā*). For it is only one who possesses faith who undertakes it, as seen in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*): "By means of food given by their sons, the ancestors, wherever they may be, dwell in happiness through its enjoyment. On the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), when the sun and moon are at their closest approach, [one should offer] to the *pitṛs*; that is, for the sake of the ancestors. Because of the plural number, the offering should also be made for the grandfather and great-grandfather. (15.1)

The word *atha* (now/then) signifies the commencement of a topic (*adhikāra*). The rite named *śrāddha* is now introduced. That in which faith (*śraddhā*) is present is called *śrāddha*. It is of five kinds:
the obligatory (*nitya*), the occasional (*naimittika*), the optional (*kāmya*), the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, and furthermore, the *pārvaṇa*; thus the *śrāddha* is known by the wise to be of five types.
Regarding this, Manu has declared: "One should offer the śrāddha daily with food and drink,
or even with milk, roots, and fruits, thereby bringing satisfaction to the ancestors."

"One should feed even a single Brāhmaṇa for the sake of the ancestors during the *pāñcayājñika* rite; however, one should not feed anyone there for the sake of the *vaiśvadeva*. [MDh 3.82–83] That which is performed on occasions such as eclipses is *naimittika* (occasional). Its performance is like that of the *pārvaṇa* rite. The *ekoddiṣṭa*, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, and the *aṣṭakā*—these too are indeed occasional rites. Among them, the *ekoddiṣṭa* is of sixteen kinds. It should be performed on the anniversary of death every month for a year.

"And thus, every year, on the eleventh day, the first [rite] is performed," says Yājñavalkya. "But the *ekoddiṣṭa* must be performed," says Laugākṣi in the first quarter [of his verse]. Vyāghra states:
"It should be performed on the eleventh day, and likewise in the third fortnight;
thereafter, one should diligently perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* at the sixth month."

"Then, when a year has passed, or after three fortnights, or likewise even before that, one should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, or earlier if a festive occasion (*vṛddhi*) arises. Thus says Jātūkarṇya:
"In the fourth, the fifth, the ninth, and likewise the eleventh [month]."
Whatever food is given to a living being is called a *navaśrāddha*.

And so they recite: these four [rites] are established according to the sequence of the [lunar] days. That very *śrāddha* performed on the eleventh day is the primary one. The mention of the "eleventh day" is an indicator for the end of the period of impurity (*āśauca*). And in that [period], at the same time [within] the month, is the monthly rite (*māsika*). At the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, there is a single-offering (*ekoddiṣṭa*) for the deceased and a *pārvaṇa* for the ancestors and others. There too, at the same time within the month, is that very monthly rite. In between, there are ten monthly rites—at the third fortnight, at the sixth month, and each year; and another, the annual rite (*sāṃvatsarika*), on the anniversary of death—thus there are sixteen *ekoddiṣṭas*. And they recite:
Through sixteen śrāddha rites— performed at nine fortnights, three fortnights, six months, one year, and monthly intervals— the deceased is released from the state of being a piśāca.
For him for whom these sixteen *ekoddiṣṭa* rites are not performed, [the ancestors do not accept his offerings].

"His state as a *piśāca* remains firm even by performing hundreds of *śrāddhas*. The *Aṣṭakā* rites are performed on the eighth days of the four dark fortnights (*aparapakṣa*) of the Hemanta and Śiśira seasons, or on a single one. When performed on the first day [of the dark fortnight], it results in the birth of female offspring; such performances, when undertaken for the sake of specific desires, are called *kāmya*. These too are exactly like the *pārvaṇa* rite. On the day before marriages and other rites of prosperity (*vṛddhikarma*), the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* should be performed. The Brāhmaṇa source states: "Therefore, it is performed for the ancestors on the previous day. In that case, an even number of Brāhmaṇas are invited, barley is used instead of sesame seeds, and the rest is like the *pārvaṇa*. The *pārvaṇa*, however, will be described later.
On the new moon day, one should make offerings to the ancestors.

The *Amāvāsyā* is that [lunar day] on which the sun and the moon dwell together. Because of the plural form "to the ancestors" (*pitṛbhyaḥ*), one should offer [the oblation] to the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather. The procedure for the offering is stated in the *Gṛhyasūtras*: "The fire-oblation, the feeding of Brahmins, and the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*). However, in this context, there is a specific rule regarding the feeding of Brahmins. (15.2)
Or from the fifth day onwards of the dark fortnight, according to the śrāddha rites.
Or [the rites may be performed] during the latter fortnight, beginning from the fifth day. 15.3.

Or one should offer [the śrāddha] beginning from the fifth day of the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa). The meaning is that it should be performed according to the śrāddha and according as faith exists. The intention is that the Aṣṭakā-śrāddha should be offered starting from the fifth day. The mention of the "latter fortnight" (aparapakṣa) is so that [the rule] does not apply to the former fortnight (pūrvapakṣa), because of the context of the new moon (amāvāsyā). 15.2.
The latter fortnight is the dark fortnight; one should give [the food] starting from its fifth day. 15.3.
Or [it may be] in all [of them]. 15.3.
According to one's faith, or in its entirety. || 15.4 ||

The meaning is that one should perform [the rite] either during the entire second fortnight or beginning from the first day (pratipad). This is to be understood as applying to one who possesses abundant wealth. 15.3.
Or one may give on every day of the dark fortnight, according to one's faith, as faith arises. || 15.4 ||
Or [it may be performed] when there is the presence of the substance, the place, and a Brāhmaṇa. || 15.4 ||
Or, when there is an abundance of wealth, a suitable location, and the presence of Brahmins, there is no restriction regarding the time. 15.5.
Of the substance, such as silver and the like; and likewise Vyāghra says:

"Silver, black śāka-vegetables, rhinoceros meat, fish, honey, and all kinds of hermit-food (muni-anna) are prescribed for the sake of infinite [merit]. Of the place, such as Puṣkara and the like; as Vyāghra has said:
"A śrāddha performed at Puṣkara is inexhaustible, as is one performed at Kurukṣetra;
likewise at a river, in the ocean, in a lake, in a cow-pen, or on a mountain. Thus [it is said]. Regarding Brāhmaṇas and ascetics who purify the company (paṅktipāvana), as Vyāsa has stated:
"The *svadhā* call, a silver vessel, a daughter's son, a *kutapa* blanket, and sesame seeds..."

"And [he should provide] clothing and purifying materials, as well as a triple staff and a mendicant. This means that he should do so when [the recipient] is present, when there is an opportunity, or even during the first fortnight (pūrvapakṣa). || 15.4 ||
"Starting from the phrase *tilamāṣa* [GDh 15.15], each specific substance that is about to be mentioned is praised. A sacred place (*deśa*) is Gayā, Puṣkara, and so forth. It is said:
'A Śrāddha performed at Puṣkara is inexhaustible, and likewise at Kurukṣetra;
one should also offer it at the great ocean, in a lake, in a cow-pen, or on a mountain.'"
Thus says Vyāsa.

"Whatever one who is staying at Gayā gives, he enjoys all that as infinite," so says Yājñavalkya (YDh 1.261). The Brāhmaṇas who purify the company (paṅktipāvanas) are those to be mentioned later, such as those learned in the six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍaṅgavid) and so forth. In the proximity or assembly of these—referring to the substances and other factors—the rule regarding time is that proximity itself constitutes the time. The word "vā" (or) is used in the sense of an alternative. || 15.5 ||
The restriction of time is according to one's capacity. || 15.5 ||
One should increase the excellence of the food through the application of qualities and refinements according to one's ability. 15.6.

When there is an absolute impossibility of the requisite materials and so forth for him, then the previously stated restriction of time—namely, "after the full moon of Āgrahāyaṇī"—does not apply. The intention is that the rite should be performed in whichever month those materials are absolutely available. Just as there is no specific restriction regarding the fortnight when materials are unavailable, the intention is that there is likewise no specific restriction regarding the month. By this same principle, the absence of any restriction regarding the lunar day (*tithi*) is also established. (15.5)

Regarding food, there are rules for its qualities, such as being milk-rice (*pāyasa*), pure, or well-prepared; and rules for its preparation, such as roasting it or making it fragrant with black pepper, cumin, salt, and so forth. One should bring these to excellence—that is, one should make them superior—according to one's ability. (15.6)
And at all times during a funeral rite,
he should enhance the qualities, preparations, and methods of the food.

One should "exalt" (prakarṣet), that is, perform with excellence: the qualities of the food, such as its specific types like vegetables or cakes; its preparations, such as being well-cooked or fragrant; and the ritual rules, such as the use of *darbha* grass, sesame seeds, water, and the leftward circumambulation (*savyatva*). || 15.6 ||
One should feed at least nine persons. || 15.7 ||
He should feed an odd number of guests, at least nine.
This is so when there is capability. 15.7.

Those for whom nine is the maximum number are "nine-at-most" (navāvara); he should feed that many Brahmins. "Odd" means an odd number. In the case of nine, there are three for the father, three for the grandfather, and three for the great-grandfather. Because of the inclusion of the term "at most," there may be more as well, such as fifteen, twenty-one, and so forth. By the statement "odd," the exclusion of twelve and other even numbers is intended. (15.7)
Or [they may be] uneven, or according to one's energy. || 15.8 ||
Or according to one's enthusiasm. || 15.8 ||

"Odd-numbered [guests] according to one's enthusiasm and according to one's capacity," meaning fewer than nine, because the term "fewer" (*avara*) is used in the preceding [rule], and because there is no possibility of [obtaining more] beyond nine.

Now, one might object: should it not simply say "or odd-numbered"? For since [the rule] does not apply beyond nine, the very purpose of this commencement would be to prescribe a smaller number; thus, the option would be necessitated by incapacity alone, making the phrase "according to one's enthusiasm" redundant. It is replied: even when one has the enthusiasm, one should feed [the guests] without contradicting the requirements of hospitality and so forth. As Vasiṣṭha says: [he cites the verse].
One should feed two at a rite for the gods and three at a rite for the ancestors, or one at each; even if very wealthy, one should not be overly attached to a large company.

"Hospitality, the proper time and place, purity, and the excellence of the Brahmins—these five are destroyed by prolixity; therefore, one should avoid it. [VaDh 11.27–28] The "gods" are the Viśvedevas, who constitute a part of that rite. As Vyāsa says:
"The virtuous daughter of Dakṣa is celebrated by the name Viśvā."
Her sons were the high-souled Viśvedevas, possessed of great strength.
Kratu, Dakṣa, Vasu, Satya, Kāla, Kāmya, Śuci, Ruci,
Purūravas, and Ādruvas— these should be known as the ten immortals.
In the *iṣṭi-śrāddha*, Kratu and Dakṣa; in the *aṣṭakā*, Kāla and Kāmyaka;
in the *nāndīmukha*, Vasu and Satya; and in the optional (*kāmya*) rite, Śuci and Ruci.
Purūravas and Āyus are indeed proclaimed [as the presiding deities] during the Pārvaṇa [Śrāddha].
"One should call them by name according to their respective assignments in each instance.
And likewise, another Smṛti states:
"The Śrāddha should begin and end with the gods; it should not begin and end with the ancestors."
"If it should end with the ancestors (pitr-anta), then indeed the Rākṣasas consume it. Likewise, there is also a verse by Bhārgava:

"When there is only one Brāhmaṇa and a second is not available, one should assign the portion for the ancestors to that Brāhmaṇa and assign the portion for the gods to his hand. And likewise, Bṛhaspati says:

"One should seat two Atharvan Brahmins facing east for the rite to the gods (daiva), and three twice-born men who chant the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman Vedas facing north for the rite to the ancestors (pitrya). (15.8)

According to one's capacity, one may feed even fewer than nine; because of the continued application of the rule "an odd number," one may feed exactly three. Thus says Āpastamba: "An odd number, at least three. In other scriptures, the feeding of Brahmins for the Viśvedevas and for the maternal grandfathers is prescribed. As Yājñavalkya says: "Two for the gods facing east, three for the ancestors facing north, or even one for each."

"The same applies to the maternal grandfathers; or else, the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the *vaiśvadeva* [deities] may be performed. (YDh 1.228) Two Brahmins should be seated facing east for the rite to the gods (*daiva*). For the sake of the ancestors (*pitṛ*), those [seated] there should face north. "One for each," or "only one"—meaning one for the gods and one for the three beginning with the father. The same applies to the maternal grandfathers as in the *śrāddha* for the paternal ancestors. There are two for the gods and three for the sake of the maternal grandfather and others. Or, the ritual procedure (*tantra*) of the *vaiśvadeva* may apply to both the *śrāddha* for the father and the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfather. 15.8.
He states what kind of brahmins one should feed.
What kind should he feed? Regarding this, he says:
those who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and endowed with eloquence, physical form, age, and virtuous conduct. 15.9.

One should feed Brahmins who possess these qualities: those learned in the Vedas, who have studied the meters; those endowed with speech, who speak refined Sanskrit; those endowed with beauty, whose forms are pleasing; those endowed with age, who are advanced in years; and those endowed with character, whose minds are tranquil. (15.9)

"Learned in the Vedas" means those who have studied the Vedas. "Perfection of speech" refers to well-trained expression, such as speaking in Sanskrit and so forth. "Endowed with beauty" means having a pleasing appearance, being neither deficient nor excessive in limbs, and not marred by skin diseases such as vitiligo; they should be endowed with youth, meaning not too young. "Character" (śīla) refers to purity of the internal organ; one should feed those endowed with such qualities. || 15.9 ||
He states an exception to the rule regarding being endowed with youth:
"The gift [of food] is for the young first. (15.10)
That which is the first *ekoddiṣṭa* should be given to those who are young.
The primary rule for the offering of a *śrāddha* is that it should be given to young men endowed with such qualities as these.
Some [behave] like fathers. 15.11.

Some maintain that one should offer [the oblation] at the same ages at which the father and others passed away. This rule should be understood as referring specifically to the *ekoddiṣṭa* performed during the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Indeed, the *ekoddiṣṭa* within the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has already been stated in another Smṛti. As Yama says:
"When the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is reached, one should likewise perform two *śrāddhas*;
at the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, one should feed the Brahmins just as in a *pārvaṇa*."

"And one should prepare separate food according to the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite. Alternatively, "like [the rite for] the father" means that one should feed the young [ancestor] with the father in mind, the elder with the grandfather in mind, and the eldest with the great-grandfather in mind. (15.11)

Some believe that the gift should be according to the ancestors, corresponding to the father and so forth; for example—youths [should give] to the father, the elderly to the grandfather, and those even more aged to the great-grandfather. (15.11)
And he should not perform the work of a friend with that [wealth]. || 15.12 ||
That faithful person should not engage in mutual activities with friends; by the use of the word "and," [it is implied that] one should also avoid forming alliances with enemies. 15.12.

And one should not perform a friendly service for that faithful person; one should not feed someone with whom friendship is to be cultivated while having regard for material gain. The meaning is that one should not feed them for the sake of creating a bond of friendship through greed. Āpastamba, however, states specifically: "One should feed them without regard for material gain. (15.12)
In the absence of a son, the *sapiṇḍas*, the mother’s *sapiṇḍas*, and the disciples shall offer [the funeral oblation]. || 15.13 ||

This is first of all the primary rule: that sons perform the *śrāddha*. In their absence, however, the *sapiṇḍas* are mentioned. In their absence, the mother’s *sapiṇḍas*, such as maternal uncles and others. In their absence, the disciples; because of the use of the word "relation" (*saṃbandhi*), [the teacher is included], and because of the word "and" (*ca*), the sacrificer (*yājya*) and the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) are also included. This refers specifically to the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, because the mother’s *sapiṇḍas*, the disciple, and the sacrificer are taught as the givers [of the offering]. For the mother’s *sapiṇḍa* of one person is not necessarily the mother’s *sapiṇḍa* of his father. The same applies to the disciple and the sacrificer. Thus, in the case of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* and other rites, a different order should be observed. As Uśanas says: "In the absence of sons, the *sapiṇḍas*, the *samānodakas*, those of the same *gotra*, and those of the same *ṛṣi* lineage," and so forth. The *ekoddiṣṭa* should be performed by a single individual alone, and not by all of them together as in the case of impurity (*āśauca*); this is the meaning of the compound. (15.13)

"Sons shall offer [the funeral cakes]—this is the primary rule (prathamaḥ kalpaḥ). In their absence, the sapinda relatives, such as brothers and their sons; in their absence, the mother’s sapinda relatives, such as the mother’s brothers and their sons; in their absence, the disciple. 15.13.
In their absence, the officiating priest (ṛtvij) and the teacher (ācārya).

The officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) for one who is to be sacrificed for, and the teacher (*ācārya*) for his pupil; in their absence—that is, in the absence of the preceding relative—the mention of "separate performance" is intended to indicate that there is no need for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) in the case of the officiating priest and the teacher when one performs a *śrāddha*. Thus, it should be understood that expiation must necessarily be performed for the preceding relatives. Furthermore, for those performing a *śrāddha* for an officiating priest or a teacher, prosperity (*abhyudaya*) ensues by virtue of the force of the injunction. The inclusion of the phrase "in their absence" in the preceding rule—"maternal sapindas and pupils" (GDh 15.13)—is also intended to indicate their eligibility (*adhikāra*). It should be understood that the *śrāddha* is for those who are indeed eligible. Why? Because of the force of another Smṛti text. As Prajāpati has said:
And for those killed by cows, Brahmins, lightning, or a sovereign,
as well as for those who have committed suicide and likewise for the fallen (patitas).
For Brahmins killed by serpents, for those who wander according to their own lusts,
and for those who have resorted to heretical sects, no funeral rites are prescribed.
If that lowest of men should perform [the rite] out of affection, fear of consequences, or other such motives,
I shall declare the expiation even for one who has been killed by a Caṇḍāla.
Whoever should carry or cremate any one of these deceased persons shall perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance; if it was done intentionally, he must perform the Taptakṛcchra.
Having merely touched such a corpse, or likewise caused it to fall, one should not eat for one night;
however, if it was done intentionally, one should fast for three nights.
"Having performed a *śrāddha*, one should perform a *kṛcchra* penance; if done intentionally, one should perform a *sāntapana*.
Likewise, for those who eat at a *śrāddha*, and for students (*brahmacārin*s), the penance is double. (15.14)
In the absence of a disciple, the officiating priest; and in his absence, the teacher shall give [the gift].

One should not feed a thief, a eunuch, one who has fallen from his caste, an atheist, or one who lives by such [heretical] means; nor one who has killed a hero, one whose younger brother is married before him, one whose elder brother's wife is married before him, one who has sexual intercourse with women, a priest for a multitude, one who neglects the *japa* and the sacred fires, a drunkard, a rogue, a false witness, or a professional messenger. (15.15)

One should not feed a thief, a eunuch, one who has fallen from his caste, an atheist, one who lives as such, one who has killed a hero, one who marries before his elder brother, one who officiates for women or for a multitude, a goat-herd, one who has abandoned the sacred fires, a drinker of liquor, a rogue, a false witness, or a juggler. (15.15)

Since these individuals might otherwise be eligible for initiation through their possession of qualities such as Vedic learning (*śrotriya*), they are here prohibited. A *stena* is one who steals gold and the like; he is excluded because he is already considered fallen (*patita*). A *klība* is one whose vigor is broken; thus the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva said, "Do not yield to weakness, O son of Kuntī" (BhG 2.3), and so forth. This does not refer to a person of the third gender (*tṛtīyaprakṛti*), because such a person lacks Vedic learning and thus would not have been eligible in the first place. A *patita* is a killer of a Brahmin and the like. An *nāstika* is one whose intellect is fixed on the non-existence of the next world and so forth; he too has a corrupted mind, whereas one whose actions are corrupted is taught to be fallen due to the habitual performance of censurable acts. One who lives by that very profession—that is, by means of the Lokāyata philosophy out of that same atheism—is also included. A *vīrahā* is a slayer of any human being, since the word "hero" (*vīra*) is applied to a man in such passages as "and of a woman who has no hero" (MDh 4.213). Alternatively, it refers to one who performs the Soma-pressing in vain, based on the Vedic text: "He who presses the Soma is indeed a slayer of the heroes of the gods. An *agredidhiṣū* is the husband of a younger sister whose elder sister is still unmarried; the word "husband" (*pati*) applies to each term. Thus, the elder sister who was previously given in marriage is the *agredidhiṣū*, and she, the elder sister, is the *didhiṣū*. So says Manu.
"If a younger sister is married while the elder remains unmarried, she is to be known as *agredidhiṣū*, whereas the elder is remembered as *didhiṣū*.
[The term refers to] the husband of those two; or rather, he alone is designated by the word "husband" (*pati*), as Prajāpati has said:
He who, out of lust, becomes attached to the wife of his deceased brother—
even if she has been appointed to him according to dharma— is to be known as a *didhiṣūpati*.
"He is known as a *jīvat-pati* (one whose husband is living), and he is also remembered as an *agredidhiṣū*. Or, as stated by Vyāghra:
"The wise call the husband of a woman who previously had another husband a *didhiṣūpati*."
A Brahmin whose wife is the younger sister married before her elder sister is called an *agredidhiṣū*.

A "sacrificer for women" (*strī-yājaka*); the word "sacrificer" (*yājaka*) is to be connected with each [term]. One who performs sacrifices for women, such as for Kāmadeva and others, is a sacrificer for women. A "village-priest" (*grāma-yājaka*) is one who performs sacrifices for many people. An "ajapāla" is one who subsists by guarding goats. An "one who has abandoned the sacred fires" (*utsṛṣṭāgni*) is one who, contrary to the scriptures, abandons either the *śrauta* or *smārta* fire. A "liquor-drinker" (*madyapa*) is one who subsists by means of selling liquor made from coconuts and so forth, or one who consumes intoxicants other than *surā*. A "wicked person" (*kucara*) is one of reprehensible conduct; reprehensible conduct includes being habitually devoted to serving as a son, a teacher, or a deity, or to begging, and so on. A "false witness" (*kūṭasākṣin*) is well known. A "magician" (*prātihārika*) is one who subsists by means of sorcery. One should not feed these. Since the prohibition of feeding them is already established by the prohibition of touching those who have fallen (*patita*), this [new] undertaking is for the purpose of prohibiting the feeding of those who have performed penance (*prāyaścitta*). (15.15)

A thief is one who steals gold. A *klība* is one whose virility is futile; he is not a third gender (*tṛtīyā-prakṛti*). One who has fallen [from his caste] due to the lack of Vedic learning is a slayer of a Brahmin and so forth. An atheist (*nāstika*) is one who denies the existence of life after death. One who follows that way is an atheist by conduct. Even though one accepts the existence of life after death, he is one who does not act in accordance with it due to the influence of association. A destroyer of heroes (*vīra-hā*) is one who intentionally extinguishes the sacred fires even when there is a possibility for them to continue; for it is heard in scripture: "He who extinguishes the fire is a destroyer of the heroes of the gods. Some read the word *agredidhiṣū* ending in a long vowel; the word *pati* (husband) is connected to each [term]: *agredidhiṣū-pati* and *didhiṣū-pati*.

"If a younger sister is married while the elder sister remains unmarried, she is to be known as an *agredidhiṣū*, whereas the elder is recorded as a *didhiṣū*. The two [terms] refer to the husbands of these two. However, the etymologists (*naighaṇṭukas*) say:
"A *punarbhū* is a woman remarried; her husband, having married her twice, is called a *didhiṣū*.
A twice-born man whose wife is such a woman is an *agredidhiṣū*. Thus it is said.

One who officiates for women; one who instructs women in religious observances (*vrata*) and causes them to perform them is a "woman-officiant" (*strīyājaka*). A village-priest (*grāmayājaka*) is one who performs sacrifices for many people. A goat-herder (*ajāpāla*) is one who makes his living by guarding goats. One who has abandoned the sacred fires (*utsṛṣṭāgni*) is one whose fires have been extinguished due to impurity or through negligence. A drinker of intoxicants (*madyapa*) is one who drinks substances other than *surā* that cause intoxication; however, a drinker of *surā* (*surāpa*) is said to be an outcaste (*patita*). One of evil conduct (*kucara*) is one whose behavior is contemptible. A false witness (*kūṭasākṣin*) is one who speaks untruthfully when giving testimony. A doorkeeper (*pratihārika*) is one whose livelihood is guarding the gate. One should not feed these. This prohibition regarding those such as the outcastes—whose sight, touch, and so forth are forbidden—is intended to exclude them even if they have performed penance (*prāyaścitta*). (15.15)
And he whose [birth] is that of an intermediate state being (upapatti). || 15.16 ||
The paramour. || 15.16 ||
A paramour is a lover; and "he to whom she belongs" refers to one whose wife is unchaste. One should not feed these two. 15.16.
An *upapati* is a lover (*jāra*). || 15.16 ||
And he belongs to whomsoever it may be. || 15.17 ||
He is the paramour in whose domain she lives, and he is her actual husband; both of them must not be fed. || 15.17 ||

Those who subsist on the remnants of sacrificial offerings, those who sell Soma, arsonists, poisoners, those who have broken their vows of chastity, servants of a multitude, those who approach women who should not be approached, those who are violent, an elder brother whose younger brother marries before him, a younger brother who marries before his elder, one who causes his wife to be superseded by another, one who supersedes his wife, one who abandons himself, one with deformed hair, one with a deformed nail, one with black teeth, one with a missing limb, one with three folds [on the belly], one born of a remarried woman, a liar, one defeated in a wager, a servant, a counterfeit maker, the husband of a Śūdra woman, one who has renounced the Vedas, one afflicted with leprosy, a usurer, a merchant, one who lives by manual crafts, and those whose habits consist of lute-playing, instrumental music, clapping, dancing, and singing. || 15.17–15.18 ||

H reads: “*śyāvadantaśvitri*”; the mention of the *kuṇḍa* is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the *golaka*. He who eats the food of such a person is a *kuṇḍāśin*. By the prohibition against the *kuṇḍāśin*, the prohibition of both the *kuṇḍa* and the *golaka* is established by implication. Their specific nature is to be understood from another *smṛti* text, as Manu says:
“Two types of sons, the *kuṇḍa* and the *golaka*, are born from the wives of others.”

"A *kuṇḍa* is one born while the husband is alive; a *golaka* is one born after the husband has died" (MDh 3.174). A *somavirakī* is a seller of the *soma* plant, or a seller of the rituals performed with it. An *agāradāhī* is one who sets fire to a house. A *garada* is a giver of poison. An *avakīrṇī* is a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) who intentionally violates his vow of chastity. As Manu says: "The intentional emission of semen by a twice-born man established in his vows..."

Those who know the Dharma and expound the Veda declare these to be transgressions of the vow: [MDh 11.120] A *gaṇapreṣya* is one who performs service for groups. An *agamyāgāmī* is one who has sexual intercourse with a woman who should not be approached, such as a girl who has been defiled. Some say it refers to one who approaches a woman of the same *pravara*. This is because of the instruction regarding equality in the rule: "With respect to the wife of a friend, a uterine sister, a woman of the same *gotra*, a pupil’s wife, a daughter-in-law, and a cow, it is equal to violating one's own bed" (GDh 23.12); since this teaches equality, such a person is included under the category of "outcastes" (*patita*). A *hiṃsra* is one who delights in the slaughter of living beings. A *parivitti* is an elder brother whose marriage remains unperformed when a younger brother marries; that younger brother is the *parivettṛ*, and consequently, the elder brother is the *parivitti*. A *paryāhita* is an elder brother whose *agnyādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires) remains unperformed when a younger brother performs the *ādhāna*; that younger brother is the *paryādhātṛ*.
But surely the terms *parivitti* and *parivettṛ* also apply respectively to the *paryāhita* and the *paryādhātṛ*, since this is observed in another Smṛti; as Manu says:

"He who enters into the union of wife and *agnihotra* while his elder brother remains [unmarried] is to be known as the *parivettṛ*, and the elder brother is the *parivitti*. [MDh 3.171] Consequently, a separate treatment of the *paryāhita* and the *paryādhātṛ* would be purposeless.

To this it is replied: both are mentioned for the purpose of including both him who performs the sacrifice and him who gives the girl in marriage. As Manu says: "The elder brother who marries before his younger brother, the younger brother who so marries, she by whom he is superseded, and the giver and the officiating priest as the fifth—all these go to hell. [MDh 3.172] An exception to this rule should be observed, as Uśanas says:
"Regarding the sons of a paternal uncle, the sons of a co-wife, and likewise the sons of another's wife,
there is no fault in superseding them for the purpose of marriage and the maintenance of the *agnihotra*.
Thus also says Vasiṣṭha:

"One who is insane, one who is sinful, one afflicted with leprosy, one who has fallen from his caste, and likewise one who is impotent, as well as one suffering from consumption—these are not fit to be waited upon. Thus [says the law]. Śātātapa also says:
"In the case of one who is impotent, one ruined by his country, one who has fallen from his caste, and likewise one who has renounced the world..."
"And there is no fault in marrying [a younger sister] when one is enjoined by the Yogaśāstra.
Likewise, Kaṇva says:
"If one whose mind is addicted to vices, or who might be an atheist..."
There is no fault in superseding a younger brother who has failed in his duties.

And so forth. One who has abandoned his own self is a reckless person. According to some, this refers to one who carries a weapon in his hand. *Durvāla* is *śipiviṣṭa*; according to some, it means one whose generative organ is deficient. A *kunakhī* is one whose nails have become deformed for no apparent reason. *Śyāvadan* is one with black teeth, even in the absence of disease. A *paunarbhava* is the son of an unchaste woman. A *kitava* is a gambler. This term is also indicative of those who trade in clay elephants, horses, and similar items. An *ajapa* is one who, having merely been initiated (*upanīta*), lacks Vedic learning (*aśrotriya*). A *rājapreṣya* is one who performs the king’s errands, such as a messenger and the like. A *prātirūpika* is one who deals in false weights and measures, or one who is a cheat by any means whatsoever. A *śūdrāpati* is one for whom a Śūdra woman is his wife. A *nirākṛti* is one who does not abide in any stage of life (*āśrama*). A *kilāsin* is a leper or a usurper of land. A *kusīdin* is a usurer who operates by forbidden means. A *vaṇij* is one who lives by the occupation of a Vaiśya, provided that such an occupation is possible. A *śilpopajīvī* is one who lives by crafts such as carpentry or painting, as well as one who learns those arts from them; this is indicated by the use of the prefix *upa*. A *jyāśīla* is one who lives by the science of archery. A *vāditraśīla* is one who lives by instruments such as the flute or the lute. A *tālaśīla* is one who lives by beating drums and the like. A *nṛttaśīla* is one who lives by dancing. A *gītaśīla* is one who lives by singing. One should not feed these. From this very prohibition, it is established that they perform improper acts. Therefore, theft and other such deeds must not be committed. (15.17)
Two types of sons, the Kuṇḍa and the Golaka, are born from the wives of others.

"While the husband lives he is a *kuṇḍa*; when the husband is dead, he is a *golaka*"—thus says Manu (MDh 3.174). One who eats the food of such a *kuṇḍa* is a *kuṇḍāśin*. The mention of the *kuṇḍa* is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the *golaka*. The prohibition against those such as the *kuṇḍa* is established by the maxim of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpikayā*). Another says: A *kuṇḍa* is a cooking vessel; in a certain region, those who eat from it and do not leave it behind are *kuṇḍāśins*. A *somavikrayin* is one who sells *soma* at a sacrifice. An *agāradāhin* is a burner of houses. A *garada* is a giver of poison. An *avakīrṇin* is one who has fallen from his vow; or alternatively, one who, being a religious student (*brahmacārī*), approaches a woman. A *gaṇapreṣya* is one who performs errands for groups. An *agamyāgāmī* is one who approaches a woman with whom he should not have intercourse, specifically one who shares the same *pravara* lineage. A *hiṃsra* is one who delights in the killing of living beings.
A younger brother who takes a wife while his elder brother remains unmarried is called a *parivettṛ*; the elder brother, however, is a *parivitti*.

Thus says the *Nighaṇṭu*: "If the elder has not performed the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) while the younger has performed it, the younger is the *paryādhātṛ* (the one who causes the consecration) and the elder is the *paryāhita* (the one for whom the consecration was caused). [In such a case], the elder remains the *vasiṣṭha* (the most excellent). Śātātapa states: "One who is insane, a sinner, a leper, an outcast, a eunuch, or likewise afflicted with consumption—such a person should not be abandoned even after examination."

And also: "There is no fault in superseding [an elder brother] in the case of one who is impotent, one who has perished in a foreign land, one who is outcasted, one who has entered the life of a wandering mendicant, or one who is devoted to the study of Yoga scriptures. Thus it is said.

One who has abandoned his life is a reckless person who engages in such acts as hanging himself. A *durvāla* is one who is bald; others say it refers to one whose penis is covered [by skin]. A *kunakhī* is one whose nails are discolored without cause; others say it means one with deformed nails. A *śyāvadant* is one whose teeth are naturally black. A *śvitrī* is one afflicted with white leprosy (*śvitra*). A *paunarbhava* is the son of a *punarbhū*, that is, a woman who has married a second time. A *kitava* is a gambler—one who deals in *kita* (stakes)—or one who lives by means of gambling. An *ajapa* is one who does not perform the prescribed recitation (*japa*) of the *Sāvitrī* and other mantras. A *rājapreṣya* is a messenger or the like employed by the king. A *prātirūpika* is one who deceives by using false weights, measures, and so forth. A *śūdrāpati* is one for whom a Śūdra woman alone is his wife. A *nirākṛti* is one who neglects Vedic study. Although the term "learned in the Vedas" (*śrotriya*) was already mentioned, because of this further prohibition, even if one possesses speech, appearance, age, and character, he is excluded from being invited if he lacks [the required qualities]. *Kilāsa* is a skin disease known among the Dravidians as *balalī*. The suffix here denotes abundance. A *kusīdī* is a usurer, one who lives by interest. A *vaṇik* is a merchant who lives by the occupation of a Vaiśya, namely trade; [the text refers to] one who lives off such merchants. A *śilpopajīvī* is one who lives by crafts such as painting. The word *śīla* (habit/occupation) is connected individually with each of the following: *jyā*, *vāditra*, *tāla*, *nṛtya*, and *gīta*. One whose habit is the bow is one who lives by the science of archery. One whose habit is musical instruments is one whose livelihood is beating drums and the like. One whose habit is rhythm is one whose livelihood is keeping time. Those whose habits are dancing and singing—these one should not feed. 15.18.
Those who have been divided against their father's will. || 15.18–19 ||

H reads "pitrā vākāmena," meaning those who have been separated from their father against his will; by the word "ca" (and), it is implied they were also separated from their mother. One should not feed them [at a śrāddha]. 15.18.
And those who have been separated from their father against his will, one should not feed them. || 15.19 ||
And some [teach] their disciples and those of the same lineage. 15.19–20.

By the word *ca* (and), the *yājyās* are included; by the second *ca*, those of the same *ṛṣi*-lineage (*samānārṣeya*) are included. Gautama holds that by the use of the term "some" (*eke*), only those worthy of being fed (*bhojanīya*) are meant. In this regard, it should be understood that if they possess good qualities, one should feed them; if they are devoid of good qualities, they are not to be fed. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "One should also feed disciples who possess good qualities" (VaDh 11.33). Here, too, because of the word *api* (also), those of the same *gotra* are included as well. 15.19.

Some teachers say that disciples and those of the same *gotra* are persons with whom one should not eat; however, our own view is that they may be eaten with because they belong to the same *grāmaṇī*. In this regard, it means "provided they possess good qualities" when such qualified persons are unavailable. Thus says Āpastamba: "Even a uterine brother who has been duly initiated should be fed" (ĀpDh 2.17.5). 15.20.
He should feed more than three [guests]. 15.20–15.21.

Since the rule "or an odd number according to one's enthusiasm" (GDh 15.8) applies without distinction, this [present rule] is stated for the sake of specification: even in the absence of enthusiasm, one should feed an odd number of guests beyond three. 15.20.

By the phrase "according to one's enthusiasm," there arises the possibility that even a single person might suffice for all purposes; to preclude this, [the text] says, "one should feed at least three," following the observation in the *Āpastamba* [Dharmasūtra] that "at least three" must be fed. 15.21.
One who possesses virtuous qualities. || 15.21 || — || 15.22 ||

"One should feed even one," because of the use of the singular number. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "Or else, one should feed a single Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas, who is endowed with learning, conduct, and character, and who is free from inauspicious marks" (VaDh 11.29).
The non-inclusion of the word "or" (*vā*) is for the purpose of permitting both [options]. Thus Manu says:
"One should feed even a single learned man at a rite for the gods or for the ancestors; one obtains abundant fruit, but not from many who are ignorant of the mantras. (MDh 3.129) || 15.21 ||
By the use of the singular number, if there is one who possesses the required qualities, he may feed even a single person. Vasiṣṭha also says:
"Or else, he may feed a single Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas, who is endowed with good character, conduct, and virtues, and who is free from inauspicious marks. [VaDh 11.29] Manu also says:
"One should feed even a single learned man at a rite for the gods or the ancestors; one obtains abundant fruit, but not by feeding many who are ignorant of the mantras. [MDh 3.129] || 15.22 ||
One who performs a Śrāddha immediately after [the period of impurity] and has sexual intercourse with a Śūdra woman causes his ancestors to dwell in her excrement for a month. || 15.22–15.23 ||
By this, celibacy is prescribed for both the eater and the giver; and so Manu says:
"A twice-born man invited to a rite for the ancestors should always remain self-restrained."

"And one should not study the Vedic hymns (*chandas*) at whose *śrāddha* ceremony he may be present" (MDh 3.188). The word "immediately" (*sadyas*) is an adverbial modifier meaning that he leads [the ancestors] away immediately. The mention of the *śūdra* is for the purpose of defining the duration of time; in the case of other women, the period is somewhat shorter. The mention of the "bed" (*talpa*) refers to a wife. Consequently, the fault is more severe in the case of another woman. The meaning is that by dwelling near her for a month, he becomes connected with as much sin as the ancestors themselves possess. || 15.22 ||

He by whom a *śrāddha* has been eaten is called a *śrāddhin* for that day and night; [the suffix] *ini* or *ṭhan* is applied because of the sense "one by whom a *śrāddha* was eaten. If he should approach the bed of a *śūdra* woman on that same day—where the mention of "bed" (*talpa*) signifies a wife—if he should approach even a married *śūdra* woman, he leads his ancestors into her excrement for a month immediately.
This [rule] is to be applied to the other wives. Therefore he says: "On that day, he should remain celibate. 15.23–15.24.
Since this fault exists, one should avoid sexual intercourse on that day even during the fertile period, because of the statement of the underlying reason. 15.23.
A rule has also been stated for the giver among men:
"The twice-born man invited to a rite for the ancestors (pitrya) should always remain self-restrained; he should not recite the Vedic hymns, and that [rite] shall be his śrāddha" (MDh 3.188). 15.14.
It is defiled by looking at a dog, a caṇḍāla, or one who has fallen [from his caste]. 15.24–25.

H reads: "If food or a *śrāddha* offering is looked upon by a *caṇḍāla*, a dog, or similar creatures, it becomes defective. In the case of ordinary food, it is unfit to be eaten; in the case of a *śrāddha*, however, the meaning is that it becomes as if it were never performed. (15.24)

Food looked upon by dogs and other such creatures becomes defiled and unfit for consumption; likewise, a Śrāddha ceremony looked upon in this manner becomes defiled and as if it were never performed. || 15.25 ||
Since this is so, therefore one should give [the gift] in an enclosed space. 15.25–26.
Since this is so, one should give [the food] in a concealed place. The statement of the reason is that, even other than at a *śrāddha*, one must eat only in an enclosed space. 15.25.
*Pariśrayaṇam* means the screening or concealment by means of a curtain (*tiraskariṇī*) or similar object. || 15.26 ||
If that is impossible, one should scatter sesame seeds instead. 15.26–15.27.
It serves to pacify faults that have not been expiated. Furthermore, by the power of other Smṛti texts, the ancestors attain satisfaction. As Bhṛgu has said:
"Even water, when offered to a twice-born man mixed with sesame seeds, becomes a cow of plenty for the ancestors;
therefore, this is what the ancestors accept. (15.26)
On this point, Bhṛgu says:
"Even water, when given to a twice-born man mixed with sesame seeds, becomes a cow of plenty for the ancestors; therefore, this is a secret of the ancestors. (15.27)
Or one who purifies the assembly (paṅktipāvana) may pacify it. 15.27–15.28.
The one who purifies the assembly, who will be described below, shall pacify the fault of being unenclosed.
He by whom a row [of diners] is purified is a "purifier of the row"; he shall neutralize that defect which arises from the sight of a dog or similar creature. (15.28)
Who, then, is that person? He says:

"Those who purify the assembly (paṅktipāvana) are: one who knows the six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍaṅgavid), a singer of the Jyeṣṭhasāman, one who has thrice performed the Nāciketa fire-sacrifice, one who knows the three Madhu verses, one who knows the Trisuparṇa hymn, one who maintains the five sacred fires (pañcāgni), a graduate (snātaka), one who knows the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas, one who knows the Dharma, and one who is the offspring of a woman married according to the Brahma rite. 15.28–29.

H reads "jyeṣṭhasāmikas. And these, while being learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), are called *paṅktipāvanas* because they purify—that is, make faultless—the company (*paṅkti*) by virtue of possessing superior qualities. One who knows the six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*) is one who understands the meaning of at least one of the six auxiliary sciences. Likewise, it is said in the Purāṇa: "Even he who has mastered one of the fourteen branches of knowledge..."
And those who know the absolute liberation of the Self—all these are purifiers of the company. Thus it is said.

A *jyeṣṭhasāmaga* is one who studies the *jyeṣṭhasāman*, which is a specific *sāman* chant of the *chandoga* (Sāmavedins). A *triṇāciketa* is a specific *ṛk* (verse) of the *adhvaryu* priests. A *trimadhu* is a specific *sūkta* of the *bahvṛcas* (Ṛgvedins). A *trisuparṇa* belongs to both the *bahvṛcas* and the *taittirīyas*. A *pañcāgni* is one who maintains five fires, including the *sabhyāvasathyas*. A *snātaka* is one who has completed his studies and vows. One who knows the *mantras* and *brāhmaṇas* is so even without knowledge of the auxiliary sciences (*aṅgas*). One who knows the *dharma* is one who knows the meaning of the *dharmaśāstras*. One whose lineage is descended from a *brahmadeyā* is the progeny of a woman married according to the *brāhma* rite. The particle *iti* indicates manner; as Vasiṣṭha says: "One who knows the *triṇāciketa*, the *pañcāgni*, the *trisuparṇa*, the *caturmedha*, the *vājasaneyin*, one who knows the six auxiliary sciences, a *chandoga*, a *jyeṣṭhasāmika*, one who knows the *mantras* and *brāhmaṇas*, one who studies his own duties, and he whose maternal and paternal lineages for ten generations are known to be learned *śrotriyas* and *snātakas*—these are the purifiers of the assembly (*paṅktipāvanas*). This is intended to include other such persons mentioned in other *smṛtis*. (15.28)

The six ancillary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*) are: phonetics (*śikṣā*), ritual science (*kalpa*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), astronomy (*jyotiṣa*), etymology (*nirukta*), and metrics (*chandovicitir*). One who knows these both by their recitation and by their meaning is a "knower of the six ancillaries" (*ṣaḍaṅgavid*). A "knower of the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*" (*jyeṣṭhasāmika*): among the Talavakāras, one who sings the two [hymns] beginning with "ud u tyam" and "citram" is a singer of the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*; among the Chandogas, however, the *Jyeṣṭhasāman* consists of the [hymns] beginning with "tad id āsa" and "tad yogayā," and one who knows that is a knower of the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*. One who has performed the *Nāciketa* fire-sacrifice three times (*triṇāciketa*): the *Nāciketa* is prescribed in many recensions, such as in the Taittirīya, the Kaṭhavallī, and the Śatapatha. He who knows this together with a Brāhmaṇa is a *triṇāciketa*. The verse beginning with "madhu vātā ṛtāyate" is the "Threefold Honey" (*trimadhu*), for there are three instances of the word "madhu" in each verse. Āśvalāyana also says: "Having known them to be satisfied, he should cause the 'Honeyed' verses to be heard. Here, however, a person who studies that is a "Threefold Honey" (*trimadhu*). The "Three Suparṇas" (*trisuparṇa*): in the Ṛgveda, it is the triplet beginning with "ekaḥ suparṇaḥ sa samudram āviveśa"; in the Taittirīyaka, it refers to the three sections (*anuvākas*) beginning with "brahmam etu mām. For it is heard there: "He who should give this *Trisuparṇa* unasked to a Brāhmaṇa... As before, the application is to the person. "One who maintains the five fires" (*pañcāgni*): one who studies five sections including the *Sabhya* and *Āvasathya* fires. An "initiated student" (*snātaka*) is one who has completed both his studies and his vows. "One who knows the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas" is one who knows the meaning of the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas. "One who knows the Dharma" is one who knows the meaning of the Dharma-śāstras. "Of a lineage descended from a Brahmā-gifted wife" means one whose lineage descends from a woman wedded in the Brāhma form of marriage. By the use of the word "etc. (*iti*), anyone else who is similarly endowed is included. Those who have practiced for ten years on both sides—maternal and paternal—in learning, austerity, and meritorious deeds, such that they would not allow anyone who is not a Brāhmaṇa to sit in their row; those characterized by such qualities as "on the father's side" and so forth—all these are "purifiers of the assembly" (*paṅktipāvana*). || 15.29 ||
And likewise with the oblations. 15.29–15.30.

Regarding the oblations in rites for prosperity (*abhyudaya-karman*): the plural number indicates that this applies not only to the *daiva* rite which is an ancillary part of the ancestral rites (*pitrya*), but rather to all rites for prosperity whatsoever. Although the meaning is already established by the word "and" (*ca*), the word "only" (*eva*) is used for the purpose of excluding those who are merely seated in the enclosure (*pariśrita*) or are mere purifiers of the row (*paṅktipāvana*). (15.29)

By the word "oblation" (havis), both divine and human rites are meant. Thus, even those who are senior [in age] should be fed only if they are Brahmins possessing the aforementioned characteristics; however, those who are prohibited—such as thieves and the like—are not to be fed. (15.30)
Some say that one should offer *durvālā* and other such items specifically at the *śrāddha* ceremony; some say specifically at the *śrāddha* ceremony. || 15.30 ||

"Only at the *śrāddha* [rite], according to some, those beginning with Durvāla. (15.31) Those who have been enumerated starting from Durvāla should be fed only at the *śrāddha*, and not at the *daiva* rite. Because of the inclusion of the term "some," this is not the view of Gautama; rather, it is an option based on the possibility or impossibility [of obtaining other guests]. (15.30)

Some, however, hold that those who have been enumerated beginning with the Durvālas should be fed only at a *śrāddha* rite, but not at rites for the gods or humans; in our own view, though, they are not to be fed even in those cases. (15.31)
And likewise in the case of a śrāddha where cooked food has not been prepared, it is thus and thus. || 15.32 ||
The repetition is as before. || 15.32 ||
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.
Since this dharma is common to the twice-born, he says:
"Having performed the upākaraṇa ceremony on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa or Proṣṭhapada, one should study the Vedas for the duration of the rainy season. (16.1)
H reads "śrāvaṇādi."

The full moon day conjoined with the asterism Śravaṇā is called *Śravaṇā*. One should understand this as a derivative formation (*taddhita*) used in a specific sense. Starting from that day, what occurs during the rainy season is "rainy-seasonal" (*vārṣika*); this too is for the sake of technical designation, and thus the conventional usage in the rule "on both sides of the *vārṣika*" (GDh 16.40) is established. Alternatively, having begun from the full moon day of Proṣṭhapadī, one should perform the *upākaraṇa*—that is, the opening rite—and then study. Study consists of both the acquisition of what was not previously learned and the rehearsal of what has already been mastered. The "Vedas" refer to the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas. This is what is meant: having performed the *upākaraṇa* on either the full moon of Śrāvaṇa or Proṣṭhapadī, one should carry out the study of the Vedas beginning from that point throughout the period of the rainy season. (16.1)

The full moon day conjoined with the asterism Śravaṇa is called *śravaṇā*. Regarding the rule "the suffix *aṇ* [is applied] when time is conjoined with an asterism," the elision (*lup*) occurs according to the rule "there is elision of *aṇ* when no specific distinction is intended. However, the designation of the word as being like that which it denotes (*yuktavat*) does not apply here, because of the specific grammatical instruction: "optionally so for *phālgunī* and *śravaṇā*. Thus, the form *śrāvaṇī* also occurs. For in the case of *paurṇamāsī*, the elision does not apply, as indicated by the examples *phālgunī*, *kārtikī*, and *caitrī*. But in the word *śravaṇa*, both possibilities occur.

"Whichever new moon (*darśa*) occurs while the sun is situated in Aries and the following signs, those twelve lunar months ending with that respective [new moon] are traditionally known as Caitra and the others."
Among those, whichever day is the full moon is traditionally designated as Caitrī and so forth;
this is the established conclusion regarding the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) based on its occasional conjunction.

Thus, when the sun is situated in Leo (Siṃha), the new moon occurs; at the end of that lunar month, the full moon is called *Śrāvaṇī*, because it is associated with the asterism Śravaṇā. Whether there is actually a conjunction with Śravaṇā or not is irrelevant. By this, the *Proṣṭhapadī* is also explained. In the term *proṣṭhapadīm*, the accusative case is used in the sense of location (*adhikaraṇe*), or perhaps to express continuous connection (*atyantasaṃyoge*). Having performed the rite known as *upākarma*—the commencement of study—on either the full moon of Śravaṇā or Proṣṭhapadī, according to the rules of the Gṛhyasūtras, one should then study the Vedas characterized by the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas. The teacher should teach them, and the students should study. This study is called "the annual" (*vārṣika*), meaning it takes place during the rainy season (*varṣartu*) or every year. Teaching, too, is "study" from the teacher's own perspective, like the recitation of a complete text (*pārāyaṇa*), whereas from the perspective of the student, it is "teaching. 16.1
He states for how long a time one should study: "For how long a time should one study?
For four and a half months, or for five months during the southern course of the sun. (16.2)
The option [regarding the disposal of the skin] after the *upākaraṇa* ceremony is to be understood as depending on whether the purpose has been fulfilled or not. || 16.2 ||
"Those for whom the fifth is half" means four months plus a half, or full five months, or as long as the sun's southern course; studying in this manner. 16.2.
While studying, the student, having shaved his body hair, shall not eat meat. 16.3.

A *brahmacārī* is one who avoids sexual intercourse; he has not had his body hair removed and has not grown a beard. By the mention of "hair," nails and so forth are also included. He shall not eat meat, even that which remains after the worship of the gods. This is a rule for the householder, as there is no possibility of its application to the *brahmacārī*. Regarding the preservation of celibacy, there is the practice of approaching one's wife only during her fertile period (*ṛtu*). Why? Because of the traditional law (*smṛti*) which states: "They teach that for the householder, approaching [one's wife] only during the fertile period constitutes celibacy. If, by the term "having removed body hair" (*utsṛṣṭaloman*), the state of having trimmed the hair were intended, then since this would already be established by the rule "he should not suddenly have a grown beard" (GDh 9.7), the present rule would be redundant. Therefore, by the force of its inclusion here, it is understood specifically as "not having the hair trimmed. (16.3)

He should be a *brahmacārī* (celibate student); he should avoid sexual union with women. He should have his hair removed and not let it grow long. Regarding the phrase "unexpectedly" (*akasmāt*), the practice of grooming the hair mentioned here is what is meant by "removed"; one who has performed this is called *utsṛṣṭalomā*. Being such, he should not eat meat. This is an instruction for the teacher, since there is no possibility of a [student] *brahmacārī* being present [at that time]. Āpastamba also says: "One engaged in teaching should avoid sexual intercourse during the rainy season and autumn" [ĀpDh 1.32.1]. Furthermore, for the purpose of including even one who, having completed the mere vows, marries and subsequently studies, it is said "also" (*api*). Āśvalāyana also says: "Having returned home, [he should live] according to the rule of the *brahmacārī*. In that case, however, approaching [one's wife] during her fertile period (*ṛtu*) is accepted as optional. Thus it is said: "Some say one may approach one's wife; that is the *prājāpatya* [form of marriage]. (16.3)
Or the observance may last for two months. 16.4.

This observance of celibacy lasts for two months; there is an option depending on one's capacity. The inclusion of the term "observance" (niyama) is intended to signify that it must necessarily be performed. And thus, in the absence of this observance, the cessation of the inclination toward study is to be understood. 16.4.

The word *dvimāsyaḥ* means "lasting for two months," referring to either what has occurred (*bhūta*) or what will occur (*bhāvin*). According to the rule *māsād vayasi yat-khañau*, the suffixes *yat* and *khañ* are applied after the word *māsa* when denoting age. Furthermore, they also employ the suffix *ya* after a *dvigu* compound when denoting age; thus, it is also *dvaimāsyaḥ*. This observance of celibacy and so forth may last for two months; this option depends upon one's capacity. (16.4)
Thus he should study.
Now, the occasions when study is forbidden are stated:
one should not study during the day when the wind carries dust.

As long as a wind that carries dust blows during the day, one should not study. Although the phrase "one that carries dust" (*pāṃsuhara*) would have sufficed for the daytime, the inclusion of the word "wind" (*vāyu*) is for the purpose of indicating that one should not study even when there is a whirlwind (*vātyā*). Thus Uśanas says: "A whirlwind is a *piśācī*; therefore, one should not study during it. Because of the mention of "day," there is no fault at night; if [study] were intended for the night as well, it would have been established simply by not mentioning "day" at all. (16.5)

"Carrying away dust" means *pāṃsuhara*. When the wind blows carrying away dust during the day, one should not study; when it does not carry away dust, there is no fault. Even when it carries away dust at night, there is no fault. || 16.5 ||
At night, [one should speak] so that it is heard by the ear. || 16.6 ||

Regarding "karṇaśrāviṇi": when the wind is audible at night—that is, when it fills the ear with sound—one should not study. Because of the mention of "night," there is no fault during the day. || 16.6 ||

This is an instance of a verbal suffix used in the sense of the agent despite the rule governing the object; thus, "karṇaśrāvī" means that which is heard by the ears. When such a great noise is blowing in the wind, one should not study at night. || 16.6 ||
In the sounds of arrows, kettledrums, clay drums, and the cries of the distressed; || 16.7 ||

The *vāṇa* is a lute (*vīṇā*), as seen in the *Mahāvrata* ritual where it is stated, "the *vāṇa* consists of a hundred strings. The *bherī* and *mṛdaṅga* are well known [types of drums]. The word *garta* refers to the sound of a chariot, or an indistinct noise. The word *ārta* refers to the sound of wailing, or such things as shouting. The word "sound" (*śabda*) is connected to each of these; as long as their noise persists, there is no study [of the Veda] (16.7).

The *vāṇa* is a particular kind of lute, as seen in the *Mahāvrata* [section] where it is stated that "the *vāṇa* has a hundred strings. The *bherī* and *mṛdaṅga* drums are well known. The *garta* is a chariot, as seen in such passages as "O Varuṇa and Mitra, ascend the chariot (*garta*)" and "Praise the famous one who sits upon the chariot (*gartasat*). An *ārta* is one distressed by the death of a kinsman or similar causes. When the sound of these is heard, one should not study for that duration of time. (16.7)
In the clamor of dogs, jackals, and donkeys. || 16.8 ||

The word *hrāda* is to be connected with each [term] individually: in the case of the sound of dogs and so forth when they are gathered together—that is, in a *śvasaṃhrāda*, a *sṛgālasaṃhrāda*, and a *gardabhasaṃhrāda*. This is because the prefix *sam-* implies a beginning (*ārambha*), as the author of the Bhāṣya has stated that "*sam* denotes oneness" (*ekībhāva*). By the logic of the "stick and cake" (*daṇḍāpūpikā*), this should be understood to apply to all three when combined. And thus, there is no fault in taking them one by one. || 16.8 ||

"Saṃhrāda" means making a noise together. One should not study during the simultaneous barking of dogs, jackals, and donkeys; however, the prohibition regarding these three together is established by the maxim of the "stick and the cake" (the inclusion of the third implies the others). 16.8.
In the red rainbows and mists. || 16.9 ||
H reads "rohit-":

one should not study when there is a red [phenomenon], such as a rainbow (*indradhanus*) or mist (*nīhāra*). Regarding the redness of the sky (*lauhityam ākāśasya*), that is its state of being red in color; when that is seen, one should not study. Likewise with the moonbow (*indudhanus*); that is well known. Mist (*nīhāra*) is snow. As long as these are visible, one should not study. (16.9)
When the sky is red, when Indra’s bow (the rainbow) is visible, and during mist or heavy snowfall—one should not study for as long as those conditions persist. 16.9.
And when clouds appear outside the rainy season. || 16.10 ||

When there is an unseasonal appearance of clouds accompanied by water—this applies to anyone—and because of the word "and," also upon seeing lightning, there is no study for as long as that appearance lasts. Thus Kaṇva says: "One should not study when lightning is seen. (16.10)
The period from the end of the hot season until the rainy season is *apartu*. During that time, one should not study upon seeing a cloud accompanied by water. 16.10.
He has urinated and defecated. || 16.11 ||

As long as urine or feces have arisen, there is a suspension of study even if they have not been voided; however, once they have been voided, it is because it will be stated later that "one is impure even mentally" (GDh 16.47). || 16.11 ||

If one urinates when there is only a small amount of urine remaining, or likewise if one voids excrement, even Śreyas should not study there. For it will be stated later that after voiding, one is impure even in mind. (16.11)
In the night, at the twilight, and in water. || 16.12 ||
At night, in the twilight waters. || 16.12 ||

By the word "niśā" (night), midnight is meant, not the night in general, because there is no commencement of specific exceptions such as "during lightning and at night" [GDh 16.25]. Therefore, one should not study while standing in water at midnight or during the twilight. 16.13.
The middle portion of the night is *niśā*; during that time, at twilight, and while standing in water, one should not study. || 16.12 ||
And it rains. || 16.13 ||
One should not study as long as the rain-rite (varṣakarma) lasts; and because of the word "ca" (and), [one should also refrain] during the non-seasonal rains for a day and a night. 16.13.
Furthermore, one should not study while it is raining; only the general meaning of the root [√vṛṣ, "to rain"] is intended here, not a specific measure [of rainfall]. (16.13)
Some [say] it is the continuity of the straw mat. || 16.14 ||

Some maintain that one should not study when it rains in an unbroken stream; Gautama, however, maintains that one may study. This option depends on whether one’s purpose has been fulfilled or not. (16.14)
Some think that "valīka-saṃtāna" refers to the *valīka*—the edge of the roof-covering, the eaves—at which the stream of rain extends; when it rains in such a manner, one should not study. 16.14.
When serving food to the teacher. || 16.15 ||

The two teachers of the gods and the asuras are Śukra and Bṛhaspati; one should not study while they are serving food. Some say that "serving food for a teacher" refers to the taking away of food from a sub-teacher (upādhyāya). 16.15.

Some think that *valīka-saṃtāna* means the *valīka*, which is the roof-ridge at the edge of the house-covering; when rain falls in such a way that the stream of raindrops extends along it, one should not study while it rains. 16.14.
And [the same applies] to the two luminaries. 16.16.

He is equal to the sun and the moon because they are mentioned in the dual number; one should not study during an eclipse, and according to the word "and" (ca), also when the teacher has met with misfortune. 16.16.

The sun and the moon are the well-known luminaries. One should not study while they are eclipsed. In the second alternative of the preceding sūtra, one must accept a difference in the meaning of the word *pariveṣaṇa*, which was previously understood as "serving food. [16.16]
One who is afraid, one standing in a vehicle, one lying down, or one with feet raised [should not recite]. || 16.17 ||

"Frightened" means one who is currently in fear; "mounted on a vehicle" means one who has ascended a horse or the like; "lying down" means one who is occupying a bed; "with feet upraised" means one who has placed one foot upon another, or whose feet are resting upon a stool or similar object. The compound is analyzed as a non-regular (visama) compound in order to include one who has climbed a tree as well. (16.17)

One who is afraid is one experiencing present fear. One standing in a vehicle is one mounted on a horse or similar conveyance. One lying down is one occupying a bed. One with legs crossed is one who places one foot upon the other, or one whose feet are placed upon a stool, seat, or similar object. One in such a state should not study. (16.17)
In cremation grounds, at the outskirts of villages, on great highways, and in places of impurity. || 16.18 ||

A *śmaśāna* is a place where corpses are burned; near that. A village boundary (*grāmānta*) is the limit of a village; near that. A *mahāpatha* is a royal road; an *āśauca* is a place of impurity. One situated in these places should not study. Some say that *āśauca* is caused by birth or death; that is incorrect, because it has already been mentioned previously. Others say it is for the purpose of indicating the absence of study even in the case of immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*), since even when there is immediate purification, only giving, receiving, and eating are to be performed, but not study.
