Others say it refers to the period before ten nights have passed. Regarding the view that it applies to the mother and father, or specifically the mother, some maintain that this is intended to indicate the absence of study for *sapiṇḍas*. This instruction is for the purpose of stating that one should not study in the vicinity of someone who is under *āśauca*, similar to the expression "a hamlet on the Ganges. Furthermore, the mention of the *śmaśāna* is for the sake of a prohibition based on past status, since the prohibition for a current location is already stated by the rule: "And also while studying in a cremation ground" (GDh 1.66). Therefore, one should not study in a place that is traditionally known through oral tradition to have been a cremation ground. 16.18.

A cremation ground is a place where corpses are burned. The edge of a village is its boundary. A great road is well known. Impurity is the absence of purification; one should not study in these places. Alternatively, impurity refers to that caused by birth or death, characterized by untouchability; one should not study even when that exists. (16.18)
In the presence of a Śūdra, one should avoid foul odors, internal corpses, and those of ill repute.

"Fetid odor" means a foul smell. "In a village containing a corpse" refers to one where a dead person has not yet been removed. "Divākīrtya" refers to a barber, even if he is a Śūdra, but not a Caṇḍāla; for since the prohibition of the Caṇḍāla is already established by implication through the prohibition of the Śūdra, his inclusion here would be redundant. One should not study in his vicinity. Alternatively, by the mention of *divākīrtya*, his occupation is intended; thus, the meaning is that one should not study after shaving but before performing purification rites. Some, however, explain the word *divākīrtya* as referring specifically to a Caṇḍāla, interpreting the prefix *anta-* to mean "in a village containing a Caṇḍāla. Āpastamba says: "There is no study in a village containing a corpse or a Caṇḍāla, but there is no study within the boundary of those who have not yet removed [the corpse]. Why is there a prohibition against a deaf person being nearby, when this is already established by the rule: "Now, [there is no study] while he listens to the Veda"? Because this rule is commenced again here [despite the previous one]. (16.19)

“Foul-smelling” refers to a stench that offends the sense of smell. “Divākīrtya” means a Caṇḍāla. The word “inside” (*antaḥ*) is connected with both: “in a village where there is a corpse inside, or where there is a Caṇḍāla inside. Furthermore, one should not study in the presence of a Śūdra. This is a dvandva compound treated as a singular. Āpastamba also says: “In a village where there is a corpse inside, or where there is a Caṇḍāla inside” (ĀpDh 1.16.20). || 16.19 ||
And [the same applies] when there is spitting or belching. 16.20.
And when there is belching after one has eaten. || 16.20 ||
One should not study when there is an acid eructation; by the use of the word "and," it is implied that one should also not study during other conditions such as fever. 16.20.
One should not study when food has been eaten that is sour, nor when a sour eructation occurs. 16.20.
And for the Ṛgveda and Yajurveda, the term "Sāman" applies as far as [the end of the section]. 16.21.

There is also a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) for the *Ṛg* and *Yajus* as long as the sound of the *Sāman* is heard. The particle *ca* (and) serves to indicate that there is likewise a suspension of study for the *Sāman* itself according to other recensional branches (*śākhā*). Thus, another *Smṛti* states: "And there is a suspension of study for the *Sāmans* in other branches. Although the dual number should have been used, the plural form "*ṛgyajuṣām*" is employed to include their ancillary texts such as the *Sūtras* and so forth. The inclusion of the word "as long as" (*yāvat*) implies that one must not study even upon hearing the mere sound; otherwise, he would have said "*ṛgyajuṣāṃ ca sāmaśabdaḥ*" ("and the word *sāman* [is heard] for the *Ṛg* and *Yajus*"). 16.21.

*Ṛk* and *yajus* together constitute *ṛgyajuṣam*; this is a *nipāta* (irregular formation) according to the rule beginning with *acatura*. As long as the word *sāman* is heard, one should not study the *Ṛgveda* and the *Yajurveda*. However, the reading with the genitive case-ending does not appeal to us.
Thunderbolts, earthquakes, the appearance of Rāhu, and meteors are not immediate [in their results]. || 16.22 ||

From the time these occur until the second [recurrence], they cause a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*); thus they are "time-bound" (*ākālika*). A thunderclap is the falling of lightning; an earthquake is the shaking of the earth; the appearance of Rāhu is an eclipse; a meteor is the falling of a meteorite.

"One should not recite the Veda for three days during the impurity (*sūtaka*) of a king or of Rāhu. (MDh 4.110) In light of such other Smṛti texts which prescribe longer periods, an option (*vikalpa*) should be understood depending on whether the purpose has been fulfilled or not. (16.22)

A thunderclap is the falling of lightning; an earthquake is the shaking of the earth; the appearance of Rāhu is an eclipse; a meteor is the falling of a firebrand. From the context, it is understood that these are causes for the suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) that last until the same time the following day. That period during which these occur is called *ākāla* (the improper time); that which is connected to it is *ākālika* (lasting until that time). 16.22.
And when thunder, rain, and lightning appear while fires have been kindled. || 16.23 ||

"When the fires have been kindled" means at the time of the Agnihotra oblation, that is, during the twilight (saṃdhyā). These [inauspicious events], beginning with thunder, being present, cause the rite to be repeated until the same time the next day. The word "and" (ca) is for the purpose of including all of them together, so that the rule does not apply if only one or two occur. (16.23)

*Stanayitnu* is the sound of thunder; the rest is well known. When the fires have been kindled at the time for the *agnihotra* oblation, the occurrence of thunder and so forth during the twilight constitutes a cause for the suspension of study (*adhyāya*) for each case until the same time the following day. This applies when it is not the rainy season. 16.23.
He says "ṛtau" at the beginning of the day; "ahar ṛtau" [is said] at the end of the day. 16.24.

During the rainy season, at the time of twilight (*saṃdhyā*), these [phenomena] do not constitute an interruption of study (*anadhyāya*) for the rest of the day. They cause a suspension of study for the duration of the day alone. By the word "day" (*ahaḥ*), the night is also implied, as seen in Vedic texts such as, "The day is black, and the day is white. Therefore, it should be understood that when these phenomena are observed at the morning twilight, there is no study during the day; when they are observed at the evening twilight, there is no study during the night. (16.24)

If these [clouds] should appear during the twilight of the rainy season, then there is a suspension of study for the duration of the day if they appear in the morning; however, if they appear in the evening, the suspension lasts for the night—this being established by the sense of the matter, it was not explicitly stated.
And during lightning at night, from the latter part of the night [until sunrise]. || 16.25 ||

When lightning is seen during twilight or during the rainy season, the night is unfit for study for three parts [of its duration]. Because of the word "and" (ca), when it is perceived in the morning, the entire day is unfit for study—not just for three parts as in the case of the night—since the *Jābāli-gṛhya* states: "In the morning, when there is lightning, the day is unfit for study. (16.25)

If lightning is seen at night but not during twilight, then from the latter part of the night—the third division of the night—there is no study until that [end of the third part]; after that, one may study. Regarding lightning at dawn, however, Jābāla says: "When there is lightning at dawn, the day is unfit for study. (16.25)
In the case of the commencement [of the vow] at one-third [of the night] and so forth, all [the rules apply]. 16.26.
If that [thunder] which is perceived at twilight has its onset after the first part of the day has passed, then the entire night is a time unfit for study. 16.26.
If lightning begins to flash starting from the third part of the day—neither during the twilight alone nor at night—then there is a suspension of study for the entire night. || 16.26 ||
According to some, a meteor and lightning occur together. 16.27.

A meteor is equal to lightning. According to the opinion of some, just as there is a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) during lightning, so it should be understood to apply to the fall of a meteor as well; however, this is not the view of Gautama. The option (*vikalpa*) depends on whether the purpose has been fulfilled or not. (16.27)

A meteor is equal to lightning. Just as there is a suspension of study during lightning and at night from the latter part of the night onwards, so too is it during the fall of a meteor; such is the opinion of some. 16.27.
The thundering occurs in the afternoon. || 16.28 ||
When thunder occurs in the afternoon, it becomes equal to lightning; the meaning is that it causes a suspension of study until the end of the night.
If thunder occurs in the afternoon, but not at twilight, then it is equal to lightning; it causes a suspension of study until the latter part of the night.
Even at nightfall. || 16.29 ||
The meaning is that even during the first part of the night, one should observe a suspension of study as before, until the latter part of the night. || 16.29 ||
Even at dusk, thunder and lightning are equal; until the end of the night, they constitute a cause for the suspension of study. 16.29.
Everything [is considered night] until midnight. 16.30.
Starting from the first part of the night until midnight, he makes the entire night a time for non-study. || 16.30 ||
Thunder that begins from the first part of the night until midnight is a cause for the suspension of study throughout the entire night.
If it is by day, he should do so while there is still light. || 16.31 ||
If thunder occurs during the day before the afternoon, then there is a suspension of study as long as the light lasts; that is to say, for the entire day. || 16.31 ||
If there is thunder during the day before the afternoon, then there is a suspension of study for as long as the light lasts; that is to say, for the entire day. (16.31)
And when the king residing in his domain has died. || 16.32 ||

"Residing in the realm" means residing in one's own kingdom; [this refers to the period] when the king has died. The word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of drawing in the rule regarding the suspension of study until the same time [the next day]. Consequently, there is a suspension of study lasting until that same time. 16.32.

When the king who is the sovereign of the region where one resides himself dies, there is a suspension of Vedic study for as long as the light lasts; others say it is until the same time the next day.
And having been away from home, they shall reunite with one another. || 16.33 ||

When a teacher and pupil, or fellow students, travel together without being separated from one another, then there is a suspension of study for the duration of that time; by the use of the word "and" (ca), it is also [a suspension] when they have come together [after being apart]. 16.33.

When fellow students dwell apart from one another, yet some remain together with their teacher, then there is a suspension of study for as long as the light lasts. According to some, this continues until they have reunited; according to others, it lasts for the duration of that day and night. 16.33.
In the case of eating at a *śrāddha* where the Veda has been recited by a crowd, or at a human sacrifice (*manuṣya-yajña*), the penance lasts for one day and night.

A "disturbance" (*saṃkula*) is a calamity affecting a village or similar place caused by some reason. A "fire-panic" (*agnisaṃbhrama*) is a conflagration; it refers to the completion of the Veda, meaning the conclusion of a section within the Veda, as in the expression "the village has been burnt," or the completion of a recensional branch (*śākhā*). Vomiting (*chardiḥ*) is well known. A *śrāddha* is a rite such as the *ekoddiṣṭa*; [the prohibition applies] there for the one who eats. At a "sacrifice to men" (*manuṣyayajña*), that is, at a gathering of friends, and at a "meal" (*bhojana*), meaning a meal where many Brahmins are fed—in these cases, there is no study for a day and a night. || 16.34 ||

A "disturbance" (*saṃkula*) refers to an affliction such as a village being harassed by thieves and the like. "Imposed" (*upāhita*) refers to a fire set by arson. "Completion of the Veda" (*vedasamāpti*) means the completion of a recensional branch (*śākhā*). "Vomiting" (*chardana*) is the regurgitation of what has been eaten. "Śrāddha" refers to the *ekoddiṣṭa* and other funeral rites. "Human sacrifice" (*manuṣyayajña*) refers to spring festivals and the like. The word "eating" (*bhojana*) is connected with both; thus, there is "eating at a śrāddha" and "eating at a human sacrifice. On account of these causes, there is no study for a day and a night. Others hold that a "human sacrifice" is a sacrifice to deities who have humans as their nature. As Āpastamba says: "Some say that one should not eat after a sacrifice to deities who have humans as their nature" (ĀpDh 1.11.3). This refers to those who, having been humans, became gods through eminent asceticism; a "sacrifice to them" is the feeding of Brahmins for the sake of pleasing them. (16.34)
And on the new moon day. 16.35.
There is no study for a day and a night; and because of the word "ca" (and), also on the full moon day.
On the new moon day, there is a suspension of study for a full day and night.
Or for two days. 16.36.

On the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) and the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), there is a suspension of study for two days, or for the aforementioned single day and night; it should be understood that this applies to the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*) in both cases. In this regard, a fixed option (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*) should be observed: for the Veda, the suspension lasts for two days, while for the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) and so forth, it lasts for only one day and night. Thus Uśanas says: "There is a suspension of study for all branches of knowledge (*vidyā*) except for the *itihāsas* on the days of the lunar changes (*parvan*). (16.36)

On that day and on the preceding day, there is a two-day suspension of study. Regarding the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, however, another basis for the suspension of study must be sought; the same applies to the first days of the lunar fortnights. 16.36.
The full moon days of Kārttika, Phālguna, and Āṣāḍha. || 16.37 ||

Because of the word "ca" (and), since the previous [rule] had established the prohibition of study on the new-moon days, the term "full-moon day" here includes the first lunar day (*pratipad*). On these [days], there is no study. Thus, there is no fault on other *pratipads*. In this regard, the option [between studying or not] should be understood as depending on whether the purpose has been achieved or not, according to the statement of Auśanasa: "On the *pratipads*, one should not reflect [on sacred matters]. (16.37)

The three full-moon days beginning with Kārttikī are causes for the suspension of study (anadhyāya) for a day and a night; regarding the suspension of study on other full-moon days, the source must be sought.
The three Aṣṭakās last for three nights each. || 16.38 ||

The three Aṣṭakās during the dark fortnights following the Āgrahāyaṇī full moon cause a suspension of study for three nights; therefore, there is a suspension of study for three nights on those [days], namely on the seventh, the eighth, and the ninth. 16.38.

After the full moon of Āgrahāyaṇī, during the three dark fortnights, there are three Aṣṭakās; these are causes for a three-night suspension of study, as well as on the day [of the Aṣṭakā] itself, on the preceding day, and on the following day. (16.38)
Some say it is the last [syllable]. 16.39.
They maintain that only the final *aṣṭakā* causes a suspension of study; as before, there is an option. 16.39.
Some consider the final Ekāṣṭakā to be a cause for the suspension of Vedic study.
On both sides of the rainy season. || 16.40 ||

"At the beginning and at the end" is the meaning. "Vārṣika" means that which occurs during the rainy season; thus, the study connected with that time is referred to. By the word "abhitaḥ" (on both sides), both that which is performed before and that which is commenced at the beginning and end are included. The phrase "a three-night suspension of study" (*trirātram anadhyāyaḥ*) is understood to follow. Thus, the meaning is that there is a three-night suspension of study both at the *upākarma* and the *utsarga*. Accordingly, Uśanas says: "At the *upākarma* and the *utsarga*, there is a three-day suspension of study. (16.40)

Regarding what was stated as "the period of the rains begins with the Śravaṇa [full moon]," that refers to the cessation of study during the rainy season. Some maintain that for three days there should be no study even before and after the two rites performed on either side of it—namely, the *upākaraṇa* (commencement) and the *utsarjana* (conclusion). Thus says Manu:

"At the commencement and at the conclusion, a three-night suspension of study is prescribed" (MDh 4.119). Uśanas states: "At the commencement and at the conclusion, there is a three-day suspension of study. (16.40)
All [these] occur when there is a conjunction of rain, lightning, and thunder. || 16.41 ||

H reads "varṣā. All teachers maintain that when rain and the other phenomena occur together, there shall be a three-night suspension of study. Gautama, however, states: "When thunder, rain, and lightning appear while the sacred fires have been kindled, the suspension lasts as long as those conditions persist" (GDh 16.23). In this case, there is an option as before. 16.41.
All teachers agree that when the three [seasons] beginning with the rainy season coincide simultaneously, there shall be a suspension of study for three nights. 16.41.
In that which is flowing. 16.42.

The phrase "for three nights" continues [from the previous rule]. On whichever day the god rains only sparsely, yet on that very same day there is a conjunction of lightning and fire, they likewise desire [the observance] for three nights in that case as well.
*Prasyanda* refers to heavy rain and the time during which it occurs; as long as that flow continues, there is no study for two days, three days, or four days. (16.42)
After a meal, during a festival. || 16.43 ||

On a festival or on every occasion of prosperity, there is a suspension of study for that day and night after eating; the meaning is that on a festival such as the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) and the like, there is a suspension of study for the period following the meal. (16.43)
On festive occasions such as the initiation ceremony (upanayana) and others, there is a suspension of study for that day after the meal. || 16.43 ||
And [the same applies] to that which has been studied. || 16.44 ||
And for one who has studied [the Veda], [the time for study] during the night is four muhūrtas.

Furthermore, for one who has already begun his studies—that is, one who has commenced learning—the suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) occurs after a meal even when it is not a festival; the word "and" (*ca*) implies that for one studying the Vedānta as well, there is a suspension of study after a meal.

Having performed the *upākaraṇa* (the rite of commencing study), one who has begun to study is called *prādhīta*. The suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the beginning of an action and refers to the agent. For him, during the night, for four *muhūrtas*—that is, four *muhūrtas*, which are eight *nāḍikās*—there is a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*). This is identical in meaning to the rule of Āpastamba: “Having performed the *upākaraṇa* on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, one should not study during the first month at nightfall” (*ĀpDh* 1.9.1). By the use of the word “and” (*ca*), the prohibition for four *muhūrtas* during the night is also shown to apply to the nightfall of the thirteenth lunar day. (16.44)
At night, for four muhūrtas. || 16.45 ||

One should not study during the first four *muhūrta*s of the night, because of the force of another *smṛti* text regarding the thirteenth lunar day. As Uśanas says: "On the thirteenth [lunar day], one should not study during the first four *muhūrta*s. (16.45)
Some [say it is] always in the city. || 16.46 || — || 16.45 ||

Some maintain that there is always a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) in a city or a village; but Gautama does not hold this view, because it would result in a perpetual suspension of study for those living in villages. In this regard, it should be understood that where Śūdras and others predominate, there is a suspension of study, whereas where the twice-born (*dvijāti*) are numerous, one should study. (16.46)
Some teachers maintain that one should never study in a town; the inclusion of the word "always" (nityam) is for the purpose of excluding the period of night. 16.45.
Even the mental [act] is impure. || 16.47 || — || 16.46 ||

One should not perform recitation even mentally when one is unpurified. Thus, mental recitation is not prohibited during other occasions of non-study (*anadhyāya*). Alternatively, the mention of "mental" is for the sake of the obligatory (*nitya*) recitation; that is, being impure, one should not recite even the obligatory prayers. And so it should be understood that there are no other prohibitions regarding non-study in the case of the obligatory recitation. Thus Manu says: "There is no prohibition of study in the case of the obligatory [recitation], nor indeed in the case of the *mantras* for the fire-oblation.
There is no prohibition of study in the obligatory [recitation], for that is remembered as the 'Brahma-sacrifice' (*brahmasatra*). (MDh 2.105–06) || 16.47 ||
Being unpurified, one should not perform even mental study; likewise, among other causes for the suspension of study, mental recitation is not prohibited.
For those who perform the ancestral rites (śrāddha), [the impurity lasts] until the same time the next day. 16.48 — 16.47.

Regarding the givers and the eaters, however, because it has been stated that they are "crowded together" (GDh 16.34), the plural number is used for the purpose of indicating all types of *śrāddha* rites, so that it may not apply to the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite where there are only givers. 16.48.

One who possesses *śrāddha* is called *śrāddhī*, meaning the performer of a *śrāddha*; this is according to the rule "the suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan* are added after a word ending in *a*. It does not mean "one by whom *śrāddha* has been eaten," because eating [at a *śrāddha*] has already been prohibited for such a person previously. For those givers of *śrāddha*, there is a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) lasting until the same time the next day. Another [teacher] says: the previous prohibition of one day and night applies to those who have merely eaten at a *śrāddha* and were not invited as vessels for the sake of the ancestors; however, this present prohibition until the same time applies to those who have eaten as vessels for the sake of the ancestors. (16.47)
And [the same applies] when there is contact with one who has performed a śrāddha for which no food was prepared. 16.49–48.
H reads "even in the case of a connection" (*-saṃyoge ’pi*).

When food that has not been prepared is given with reference to the ancestors in the absence of a formal meal, that is a *śrāddha* consisting of unprepared food (*akṛtānnaśrāddhika*). Because of the mention of the "connection" (*saṃyoga*) of both the giver and the recipient, there is a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) for as long as they remain together. By the word "and" (*ca*), it is also [prohibited] in other cases for the sake of the ancestors. As Manu says:
"Whether it be animate or inanimate, whatever constitutes a *śrāddha* offering..."

"Even after accepting [the gift], there is no suspension of study; for Brāhmaṇas are traditionally said to have their hands as their mouths. (MDh 4.117). This very [rule] is the indicative mark of the *āmaśrāddha* (funeral rite with raw food). 16.49.

When food is unavailable, if uncooked food is given to the ancestors, that is an *akṛtānna-śrāddha*. Even when such a rite is performed, there is a suspension of Vedic study for the duration of the day; it is not only when one has eaten. Regarding this, Manu says:

"Whether it be animate or inanimate, whatever constitutes a *śrāddha* offering—having touched even that, there is a suspension of study; the Brāhmaṇas who have partaken are said to be impure for a day. (MDh 4.117). This very same [rule] is the indicative mark for an *āma-śrāddha* (a śrāddha consisting of raw food). 16.48.
And whatever vehicles they remember, those very ones they remember. 16.50 — 16.49.

One should not study those days of suspension from study (*anadhyāya*) which the authors of the Gṛhyasūtras prescribe for each Veda and each branch (*śākhā*), and—by virtue of the word "and" (*ca*)—those prescribed in other legal codes (*dharma*); such is the connection [of the verse]. 16.50.

Regarding each specific science and each treatise on dharma, one should not study during those periods of non-study (*anadhyāya*) that the authorities (*smartāraḥ*) prescribe; one should also refrain from studying for those reasons mentioned therein. On this point, Vasiṣṭha says: "In the case of a conflagration, a mountain collapse, or falls of stones, blood, and dust, the interruption lasts until the same time the next day" (VaDh 13.35). Furthermore: "One should never study under a *śleṣmātaka*, a *śālmali*, or a *madhūka* tree, nor ever under a *kovidāra* or a *kapittha* tree."
In this same way, it should be understood in other cases as well. || 16.49 ||
Now begins the seventeenth chapter.

It has been stated that even the mind is impure; since that impurity can also be produced by food, the author speaks with the intention of distinguishing between what is fit to be eaten and what is not.
Having declared that even the mind is impure, and noting that such impurity may also arise from food, the section concerning what is edible and what is inedible is commenced.
A Brāhmaṇa may eat at the houses of twice-born men who are praiseworthy in their own duties. 17.1.

The meaning is: those who are highly praised for their own duties—not for the duties of Kṣatriyas and others—and who, having renounced wealth and pleasure, are devoted to the performance of their primary duties; [this refers to] those twice-born ones (*dvijāti*) who have been initiated (*upanīta*). Since eating is already implied by the context, this statement is for the purpose of an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*). The mention of "Brāhmaṇas" is for the purpose of indicating the twice-born in general. Some say it is for the purpose of permitting Kṣatriyas and others when they are not otherwise praised. "He should eat" means he should perform the act of eating. When it is said "of the praised," since people might become "praised" merely through self-aggrandizement (*āhopuruṣikā*), the phrase "their own duties" is used. Although "their own" would suffice for "the praised," the inclusion of the word "duties" (*karman*) is for the purpose of excluding optional rites (*kāmya*). The plural in "in their own duties" (*svakarmasu*) is for the purpose of proclaiming the preeminence of those who practice the combination of knowledge and action (*jñāna-karma-samuccaya*). (17.1)

A Brāhmaṇa should eat in the house of those twice-born men who are praised for their own duties—whether those duties pertain to their caste (*varṇa*), their stage of life (*āśrama*), or both—with the thought, "Ah, this man performs his own duty! The purpose of engaging in eating is merely to ward off hunger; and it is possible for anyone to ward off hunger by eating in the house of just anyone. In this regard, he specifies: "A Brāhmaṇa should eat only in the houses of these [praised ones], and not in the houses of others. (17.1)
And he should accept it. 17.2.
The particle "ca" (and) has this meaning: "their wealth [belongs to them]," and "one should teach these [Vedas] and cause them to perform sacrifices. || 17.2 ||
Acceptance [of gifts] is also from these alone, and not from others. || 17.2 ||

Even so, there is this exception: fuel, water, fodder, roots, fruits, honey, things offered out of fear, bedding, seats, dwellings, vehicles, milk, curd, parched grain, fish, *priyaṅgu* seeds, garlands, paths, and vegetables are not to be refused by anyone. (17.3)
H reads "śaparī."

Fuel is wood; water is that contained in jars and the like; fodder is grass; roots and fruits are well known; honey is that produced by bees; "abhaya" means protection; beds and seats offered for use are well known; a dwelling is a shelter and so forth; vehicles and the like are well known; the *śapharī* is a particular kind of fish; *priyaṅgu* is a particular kind of grain; a garland consists of strung flowers; "mārga" is venison; vegetables are well known. These are "not to be refused"—that is, they are not to be rejected—because of the inclusion of the term "not to be refused" (*apraṇodya*). In this Sūtra, by the word "offered" (*abhyudyata*), that which is brought into the presence of the recipient is meant. In that regard, there is no distinction of species. Thus says Manu:

"Prājāpati has declared that alms which are offered spontaneously, brought forward, and not previously announced, may be eaten even from one who has performed evil deeds. (MDh 4.248) An exception to this rule is:
"One should eat the food of a person who is full of faith, especially even if he is a thief."
"But certainly not from one who performs many sacrifices, nor from one who initiates many. [VaDh 14.17] Likewise, another [verse]:

"The food of a physician, a hunter, a surgeon, a snarer, a eunuch, and an unchaste woman is not accepted even when offered. [VaDh 14.19] In this context as well, it should be understood that the referent is specifically the *bhojya* (food fit for consumption), based on the indicative mark [of the text]: "Prajāpati considered [these] to be edible" [MDh 4.248]. Thus, even when offered, such food is not to be accepted. Since the rule concerns what is not to be rejected (*apraṇodya*), there is a fault in rejecting it. And so says Vasiṣṭha:

"The ancestors do not eat for fifteen years, nor does the fire carry his oblations, for him who treats her with contempt. [VaDh 14.18] In that case as well, one should accept only foodstuffs, because of the separate mention of "unpraiseworthy twice-born men" (*dvijāti*). Because of the use of the word "all," this includes even from a Śūdra. Although it would have been sufficient to say "from all" (*sarvebhyaḥ*), the use of the form "of all" (*sarveṣām*) is intended to indicate a connection to oneself. Thus, there is no fault in not accepting a gift from one who, having stolen another's property, gives it away. 17.3.

*Edhas* means firewood. *Udaka* (water) includes that contained in jars and other vessels. *Yavasa* refers to grass and the like. *Mūla* refers to fresh ginger and the like. *Phala* refers to mangoes and the like. *Madhu* is honey. *Abhaya* is protection. *Abhyudyata* is that which has been brought by the giver himself, even without being asked, with the words, "Take this. *Śayyā* is a mat and the like. *Āsana* is a stool and the like. *Āvasatha* is a shelter or dwelling. *Yāna* is a cart and the like. *Dadhi* and *payasī* are well known. *Dhānā* are parched barley grains. *Śapharī* is a species of fish. [The word *priyaṅgu* refers to black mustard. *Sraṅ* is a garland. *Mārga* is venison, or alternatively, the word *mārga* means a path. *Śāka* refers to *vāstūka* and other leafy vegetables. These items, beginning with firewood, are not to be rejected; they are to be accepted from everyone, even if one must ask for them. Regarding food that is already prepared (*abhyudyata*), it is not to be rejected and must not be refused; there is a fault in refusing it. And so says Āpastamba:
Prajāpati considered alms that are being offered, brought forward, and not previously announced as fit to be eaten even from one who has committed evil deeds.
"The ancestors do not eat for fifteen years, nor does the fire carry his oblations, for him who treats such a person with contempt. [ĀpDh 1.19.13] An exception to this rule is stated:
"[One may eat the food] of a physician, a hunter, a surgeon, and a snarer..."
"And the food of an unchaste woman and of a eunuch is not to be eaten. [ĀpDh 1.19.14] Thus [ends the section]. 17.3.
And another [use] is for the maintenance of one's parents, gods, teachers, and dependents. 17.4.
H reads: “-bharaṇe ’py anyat”

The mention of "support" (bharaṇa) refers to necessary duties: the support of ancestors consists of the *ekoddiṣṭa* and other rites, as well as the uninterrupted performance of *śrāddha*; the support of the gods consists of the morning and evening *agnihotra* oblations and so forth; "elders" (*guru*) refers to fathers and others; "dependents" (*bhṛtya*) refers to sons, slaves, and so forth; the support of these consists of giving them food, clothing, and the like. On account of these causes, even other things [such as fuel] are not to be refused; this is understood from the word "and" (*ca*). Because "support" has been mentioned, one should not become nourished by taking [fuel] for oneself from those sources. Some say that the word "and" (*ca*) is for the purpose of including hospitality (*ātithya*). Thus says Vasiṣṭha:

“Desiring to abandon his wife for the sake of his guru, or wishing to honor the deities and guests, he may accept gifts from anyone; yet he should not satisfy himself with that. [VaDh 14.13] In times of distress, however, acceptance by means of begging is prescribed by the rule: “For all [castes], officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and accepting gifts [are permissible]. [GDh 7.4] Here, however, the point is the non-rejection of what is being offered. Thus, it is demonstrated that even in times of distress, acceptance after having begged applies only when there is no acquisition without begging. Since this refers specifically to times of distress, it should be understood that one must not accept [gifts] when not in distress. 17.4.

The support of one’s ancestors consists in performing the *śrāddha* rites without interruption; the support of the gods consists in the *agnihotra* and other such sacrifices. The "teachers" (*guru*) are the father and others; the "dependents" (*bhṛtya*) are the sons, slaves, and so forth. Their support is the giving of food and other necessities. On these occasions, even things other than those already mentioned must not be refused. As Manu says: "One who intends to support teachers and dependents, or to honor the deities and guests, may accept gifts from anyone; yet he himself should not find satisfaction therein. (MDh 4.251) || 17.4 ||
If there is no other means of livelihood, [he may accept it] from a Śūdra. || 17.5 ||

The phrase "not to be rejected" (*apraṇodyam*) continues [from the previous rule], but not the phrase "if there is no means of livelihood" (*vṛttiś cet*) from the preceding one. If one's livelihood cannot be maintained without accepting gifts from a Śūdra, then in that case one may accept from a Śūdra; however, one must not perform sacrifices for him, eat his food, or teach him. Thus says Manu: "A wise man should not eat cooked food from a Śūdra, even if he is impure; he may take only raw food from him when there is no other means of subsistence, sufficient for one night. (MDh 4.223) And likewise Vasiṣṭha:

“He who engages in sexual intercourse while the food of a Śūdra remains in his stomach—his sons belong to the one whose food it was; for from food, semen is produced. [VaDh 6.27] Regarding officiating at sacrifices for them, he will state: “One who performs sacrifices for a Śūdra, one who performs sacrifices for the sake of a Śūdra,” and so forth [GDh 20.1]. Likewise, regarding teaching them, he will state: “A Śūdra student, and likewise a teacher [of a Śūdra],” and so forth [MDh 3.156]. || 17.5 ||
If one's livelihood—that is, one's means of subsistence—cannot be maintained without accepting gifts from a Śūdra, then one may accept them even from a Śūdra. (17.5)
The exception to this is as follows: cattle-herders, field-plowmen, family associates, those who cause work to be done, and personal attendants are those whose food may be eaten. 17.6.

A cattle-herder is one who protects livestock; he is entitled to eat the food of the owner of the animals. Likewise is the field-plougher. Thus said Uśanas: "One's own cowherd and the plougher of one's own field are [those whose] food may be eaten," and so forth. One who has come through family connection is one who has arrived in the form of a friend by way of tradition. A barber is a "causer to act" (kārayitā). An attendant is a slave. From these indicators, the Śūdra status of the barber is determined. And so Manu says: "The field-plougher, the family friend, the cowherd, the slave, and the barber..."

"These are those among Śūdras whose food may be eaten, as well as he who offers himself," and so forth. From the context, if the maintenance of life were not possible without eating the food of a Śūdra, then the food of these [categories] may be consumed. Why? Because, although it would have been sufficient to say "the food of those who cause one to associate with their family and of female servants is to be eaten," the use of the term *bhojyānnāḥ* (those whose food is fit to be eaten) indicates that it should be understood as "that which is to be eaten" (*bhoktavyam*). 17.6.

He who tends another's cattle and cultivates his field; he who has been associated with one's family through tradition, having come as a friend; and he who is one's attendant or slave—these are those whose food may be eaten. They may eat even cooked food from them. The artisan (*kāru*) is the one who causes work to be done. For it is observed that "the barber (*nāpita*) shaves the beard upwards. He who is born to a Brāhmaṇa from an unmarried Vaiśya woman is also one whose food may be eaten. Regarding this, Manu says: "The owner of the field, the family friend, the cowherd, the slave, and the barber..."
"These are those among Śūdras whose food may be eaten, as well as one who offers himself [to the Brāhmaṇa]. (MDh 4.253). And this refers to a situation of extreme distress. 17.6.
And a merchant who is not an artisan. 17.7.

The phrase "whose food may be eaten" (bhojyānna) is to be supplied [to each clause]. A Śūdra who lives by trade is one whose food may be eaten, provided he is not a craftsman such as a potter and so forth. By the word "and" (ca), it is implied that even a non-Śūdra who is a craftsman is one whose food may not be eaten. 17.7.
And a merchant whose food may be eaten, provided he is not a craftsman such as a potter and so forth. 17.7.
In this very context, he mentions another thing that is unfit to be eaten.
Now he states what is unfit to be eaten: "It is always unfit to be eaten. (17.8)

That which is given day after day to one who is without a protector must not be eaten as a regular habit. Or rather, one should never eat in another’s house at all times except in times of distress. As Manu says:
"Those foolish householders who subsist on the cooked food of others... and so forth. (MDh 3.104) || 17.8 ||

One should never eat in another's house. This prohibition applies specifically to the householder, as seen in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra]: "Those foolish householders who subsist on the cooked food of others... (MDh 3.104). Whatever is given daily to others is always unfit to be eaten. 17.8.
[Food] into which hair or insects have fallen. 17.9.

The mention of "hair" (*keśa*) is intended to include the hair on all parts of the body. The mention of "insects" (*kīṭa*) is also for the purpose of indicating impure living beings. "Spoiled" (*avapanna*) means that it has already become fit for consumption at the very time of cooking; this is the intended meaning. And it is "unfit for eating. By stating this, it is made known that after the time of cooking, food prepared with such things may be eaten provided an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) has been performed. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "But one may, at will, remove hair and insects, wash them with water, scatter ashes over them, and then consume that which has been commended by word as fit for eating" (VaDh 14.23). In the case of a large quantity of food, an expiation should also be observed even if the contamination occurred at the time of cooking itself. As Manu says:

"Food that has been burnt by birds, smelled by a cow, blown upon, sneezed at, or defiled by hair or insects, becomes pure by the scattering of earth. [MDh 5.125] In this context, the mention of "birds" should be understood as referring to [birds] other than crows, since a different penance is seen prescribed for the latter. As Parāśara says:
If food exceeding one *droṇa* has been prepared by dogs and crows, it must not be discarded; for the sake of its purification, one should offer it to Brahmins.

"Food that has been sprinkled with water purified by the *gāyatrī* mantra recited eight thousand times, and over which fire has been carried by Brahmins, [is fit for consumption]. The plural number [of Brahmins] should also be understood as depending on the circumstances of place, time, and so forth. As Vyāghra said:
"Place, time, as well as the measure, the substance, and the purpose of the substance..."
Having understood the origin and the state [of the recipient], one should determine the appropriate purification.
Thus [ends the section]. 17.9.

Furthermore, food that is covered with hair or insects is also unfit for consumption. Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha states: "One may, at will, remove the hair and insects, sprinkle it with water, scatter ashes over it, and then consume it after it has been verbally commended" (VaDh 14.23). Manu, however, says:
"That which has been pecked by birds, smelled by a cow, blown upon, or sneezed at..."

"And that which is contaminated by hair or insects is purified by the addition of earth. (MDh 5.125). Thus, there is an arrangement according to preference among these. Another says: regarding that which is contaminated by hair or insects starting from the point of cooking, the rule of Gautama applies; but for what follows, the rules of Vasiṣṭha and Manu apply. 17.9.
[The ground] was defiled by the footprints of a menstruating woman and a black bird.

The term "unfit for consumption" applies throughout. The mention of a menstruating woman is intended to illustrate all types of impurity; the mention of a "part" (pada) is likewise intended to illustrate any part of the body that is impure. "Defiled by these" means touched by them. (17.10)

A *kṛṣṇaśakuni* is a crow. The mention of "feet" (*pada*) is an elliptical expression intended to include other parts such as the beak and so forth. Food that has been defiled—that is, touched—by a menstruating woman or by the word "black bird" (*kṛṣṇaśakuni*) itself is unfit for consumption. However, regarding an abundance of food, Parāśara states: "Food exceeding one *droṇa* in measure, even if defiled by dogs or crows, need not be discarded; for the sake of its purification, one should present it to Brāhmaṇas."

"Having sprinkled that food with water purified by the Gāyatrī mantra recited eight thousand times, and having performed the circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa), it should be offered by the Brahmins. This [act] should be performed after removing the defiled portion. (17.10)
That which has been looked upon by a killer of a fetus, smelled by a cow, or is corrupted in its essence. || 17.11 ||
[Food] looked upon by a killer of an embryo. 17.11.

A *bhrūṇahan* is one who kills a Brahmin. And so Vasiṣṭha says: "By killing a Brahmin, one becomes a *bhrūṇahan*" (VaDh 20.23). That specific mention is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for dogs, Caṇḍālas, and outcasts, because they are taught together in the rule: "Looking at a dog, a Caṇḍāla, or an outcast is defiling" (VaDh 23.33).

But surely, if this were the case, then even those mentioned together would be subject to such inclusion; for instance, in the sūtra "Caṇḍālas and the fallen" (VaDh 23.33), because of their being mentioned together, and in the sūtra "Dogs and Caṇḍālas" (VaDh 23.33), since the mention of either one—Caṇḍāla or the fallen—would suffice by implication (lakṣaṇā) to include the other, the inclusion of both would be redundant.

To this it is replied: the present undertaking is for the purpose of restriction; the prohibition applies only to the three [categories] mentioned in the act of looking, and not to those such as women who have recently given birth included in the sūtra on outcasts (*patita*). Therefore, it is entirely logical that by the mention of the "destroyer of an embryo" (*bhrūṇahan*) here, dogs and the like are also included. This being so, since there is no contradiction, in the sūtra "a menstruating woman, a black bird... (GDh 17.10), by the mention of the "menstruating woman," those included in the same sūtra such as outcasts and the like are also included. Consequently, it should be understood that what is merely touched by a menstruating woman and the like is not [necessarily] looked at, whereas what is looked at and touched by a destroyer of an embryo and the like is indeed [defiled]. And [food] smelled by a cow because of its proximity, food defiled in its nature (*bhāvaduṣṭa*), food given with ill-will by the one who feeds, or food that causes dissatisfaction to the eater's mind. || 17.11 ||

A *bhrūṇahan* is a slayer of a Brahmin. And so Vasiṣṭha says: "By killing a Brahmin, one becomes a *bhrūṇahan*" (VaDh 20.23). Therefore, even food looked upon by such a person is unfit to be eaten. 17.11.
Defiled by intention. || 17.12 ||
That which is given with contempt by the giver, or which causes impurity of mind to the eater, is "defiled in its nature" (bhāvaduṣṭa); that too is unfit to be eaten. || 17.12 ||
Smelled by a cow. || 17.13 ||
And food smelled by a cow in her proximity is unfit for consumption. 17.13.
Sour gruel alone, without curd. 17.12–17.14.

That which becomes sour is *śukta* (fermented gruel), but it is not inherently sour [by its own nature], because there is an exception seen in the rule "not [if it is] curd" (*adadhi*). That which is merely untouched by other substances, like *kāñjika* and the like, is unfit for consumption. Curd that is not curd—that is, even pure curd when touched by another substance such as buttermilk—is fit for consumption. || 17.12 ||

That which has become sour by the power of time is merely *śukta*; that is unfit for consumption. Because of the use of the word "merely," even a sour substance mixed with milk, water, and so forth, is fit for consumption. Curd (*dadhi*), however, is fit for consumption even when it is not sour. Since buttermilk (*takra*) and sour gruel (*kāñjika*) are not [sour] through the process of cooking, this prohibition does not apply to them. Furthermore, the practice regarding buttermilk is undisputed; regarding sour gruel, however, there is dispute. (17.14)
Again, it is established. 17.13 — 17.15.
That which attains a state equal to its previous cooking, and not due to coolness or lack of cooking, because of being taken up again. || 17.13 ||

If the same kind of cooking is performed again for that which was already once cooked—namely, that which was previously cooked with sour gruel—that is "re-cooked" (*punaḥsiddha*). That is unfit to be eaten. However, there is no fault in performing another cooking, such as roasting, for something that was cooked in a different manner.
Stale food, vegetables, cooked grains, oils, meat, and honey [are not to be consumed]. (17.14–17.16)

"Stale" means that which has been kept overnight, with the exception of vegetables and the like. Vegetables and the like may be eaten even if stale. "Vegetables" refers to those not mixed with oil; "eatables" refers to flour-based foods and the like; and "oil" refers to ghee and so forth—it should be understood that these may also be consumed when mixed [with such oils], as seen in other Smṛtis. As Manu says: "Whatever food or eatable is mixed with oil and is not otherwise censured..."

"That which has become stale is also fit to be eaten, as is what remains from an oblation" (MDh 5.24). This includes meat even when it is not mixed with fat. Although honey is already included by the mention of "fat," its separate mention is for the purpose of prohibiting the consumption of stale honey by women. Thus, there is also an Upaniṣadic passage of the Kalpakāras: "Therefore, women do not eat honey. 17.14.

That which has remained overnight (*paryuṣita*) is that which has passed between sunrise and sunset. What is cooked by day is "cooked by day," and what is cooked at night is "cooked at night"; such food is unfit for consumption even if it is not sour. However, vegetables and the like, though they have remained overnight, are fit for consumption. "Vegetables" have been mentioned [above]. "Edibles" (*bhakṣa*) refers to flattened rice, cakes, and so forth. "Fat" (*sneha*) refers to ghee, oil, and the like. "Meat" is well known. And "honey. These, when they have remained overnight, are unfit for consumption. Since fats, honey, and the like do not become "overnight-remained" simply because they are uncooked, the mention of fat and honey here is intended to exclude those items when they are mixed with other things that have remained overnight. Therefore, that which is mixed with them remains fit for consumption even if it has remained overnight and is not censured.
"That which has stood overnight may be eaten, as may whatever remains of an oblation.
Having spoken of that which is defiled by association and that which is defiled by time, he now speaks of that which is defiled by its source:

"Of those who have abandoned [their vows], of prostitutes, of those accused of crimes, of those whose occupation is unmentionable, of executioners, of carpenters, of misers, of jailers, of physicians, of hunters, of those who live by arrows, of those who eat the leavings of others, and of those who hate their own group. (17.15–17)

"Abandoned" means ownerless. A "prostitute" (*puṃścalī*) is an unchaste woman; by this very term, a courtesan is also included as a matter of course. And so says Vasiṣṭha: "The food of a *gaṇa* (a group) and the food of a prostitute... [VaDh 14.10]. "Accused" (*abhiśasta*) means one who is notorious for a fault. "Indescribable" (*anapadeśya*) means one who cannot be designated as either female or male; the meaning is a person of the third gender (*tṛtīyā prakṛtiḥ*). A "constable" (*dāṇḍika*) is one appointed by the king to inflict punishment. A "carpenter" (*takṣan*) is a chariot-maker. A "miser" (*kadarya*) is one addicted to vulgar speech, according to the observation in the Brāhmaṇa: "One should not utter what is indecent; if one utters what is indecent, they call him a miser. A "jailer" (*bandhanika*) is a guard of the prison. A "physician" (*cikitsaka*) is a Brāhmaṇa doctor, according to the observation in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa: "Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should not practice medicine. And likewise says Vasiṣṭha:
"A Brahmin does not become crooked by being a merchant, nor by being an actor;
nor by serving a Śūdra, nor by being a thief, nor by being a physician" (VaDh 3.3). Some say [he becomes so] by living as a thief; others say by being a surgeon.

[This is known] from the observation of the rule: "The physician, the hunter, the surgeon, and the snarer" (VaDh 14.19). Here, a *mṛgayu* is a hunter; if he is one who does not shoot with arrows, he is a trapper. An *ucchiṣṭabhojī* is one who eats the remnants of food. A *gaṇa* is a multitude of people. A *vidviṣāṇa* is an enemy. The food of these persons is unfit to be eaten. Since there is an instruction regarding the non-eating of both those who are praised and those who are not praised, their food must not be eaten even in times of distress. 17.15.
"Utsṛṣṭaḥ" means abandoned by his parents;
the abandonment of those born upon a goitre is prescribed.

For these reasons—such as being unable to provide protection during a famine, or due to hostility—a *puṃścalī* is a woman who is unfaithful to men, a wanton woman, or a courtesan. An *abhiśasta* is one who is notorious for a fault, whether real or imagined. One who is *anapadeśya* is unfit for designation, such that one cannot say, "This person is of such-and-such a kind. Others hold that a *tṛtīyā prakṛti* (third gender) is an indeterminate nature that cannot be designated as either female or male. A *daṇḍika* is one appointed by the king to the office of punishment. A *takṣā* is born from a *śūdra* father and a *vaiśyā* mother through inverse (*prātilomya*) order. A *māhiṣya* is born from a *vaiśya* father and a *kṣatriyā* mother. A *karaṇī* is born from a *vaiśya* father and a married *śūdrā* mother; a *rathakāra* is born from a *māhiṣya* father and a *karaṇī* mother. Others maintain that he is a *takṣā*. A *kadarya* is a miser, concerning whom Manu has spoken.

[The text says: "Of a Śrotriya who is miserly, and of a usurer who is generous... [MDh 4.224]. A *bandhanika* is a guard of a prison. A *cikitsika* is a physician or a surgeon. One who is a hunter (*mṛgayu*) but does not move with arrows, but rather moves with snares, is a fowler (*vāgurika*). An eater of leavings (*ucchiṣṭabhojī*) is self-evident. A *gaṇa* is a multitude of people. A *vidviṣāṇa* is an enemy. The food of these—beginning with those already mentioned—is unfit to be eaten. The mention of those here who are not among the praiseworthy twice-born is for the purpose of prohibiting what has been previously stated. Thus says Āpastamba: "Of a physician and of a hunter," [ĀpDh 1.19.14], and so forth. Others hold that this is for the purpose of prohibition even in times of distress (*āpad*). 17.17.
Those unworthy of the company [are to be excluded] prior to Durvāla. (17.16–17.18)

The food of those previously designated as unfit for the company (*apāṅktya*), beginning with thieves and ending with those who have abandoned their own selves, is not to be eaten as long as they have not performed penance; however, this applies even to those such as the slayers of Brahmins once they have performed penance, according to the statement of Āpastamba: "For him, there is no restoration in this world, but his taint is removed" (ĀpDh 1.24.25). || 17.16 ||
Furthermore, the food of those previously designated as unfit for the company (apaṅktya), beginning with the thief and ending with the one who has abandoned his own self, is also not to be eaten [cf.
[These acts] are rendered in vain by [the omission of] rinsing the mouth with water and rising [from one's seat]. || 17.17–19 ||

"Vain food" is that which is cooked for one's own sake without intending it for guests and the like. Thus, there is a Rigvedic verse for those who know many hymns: "The thoughtless man gains food in vain;
I speak the truth: that is his destruction."
He nourishes neither Aryaman nor his friend.

"He becomes one who eats only sin, eating alone" (RV 10.170.6). That which is interrupted by sipping water (*ācamana*)—when, having eaten half, one sips water and then eats that same food again; that which is interrupted by rising (*utthāna*)—when, having already eaten half, one rises and then eats again—all three of these types are unfit to be eaten. Although it should have been stated as "interrupted by sipping and rising," the plural form indicates that if either sipping or rising is performed by one person at a single row (*ekapaṅkti*), the food of the other person becomes unfit to be eaten. Thus says Uśanas: "And that which is performed with those who are not elders, regarding sipping and rising. In this way, there is no fault when these acts are performed by elders. 17.17.

That which is cooked for one's own sake and not for the sake of guests and others is "vain food" (*vṛthānna*). For it is heard in scripture: "The witless man obtains food in vain," and so forth. When, during the course of a meal, one sips water again due to anger or the like, or stands up, that is called *vyapeta*—meaning "departed" from what was joined [with the company]. These two cases involve food from which one has departed by sipping water or standing up; such foods as these, beginning with "vain food," are unfit to be eaten. Regarding this, Uśanas says: "By those who are not elders, there is [the fault of] sipping water or standing up. When many are eating in a single row, if even one person other than an elder performs sipping or standing up, the food of the others also becomes unfit to be eaten; however, if it is done by elders, there is no fault.
Through equal and unequal [offerings], there arise the unequal and the equal, resulting from worship. || 17.18–20 ||

Having performed unequal honor—such as providing seats and attendance—toward those who are equal in terms of learning, family lineage, and so forth, and having performed equal honor toward those who are unequal, one must not eat at a place where food is served if that honor is either unequal or equal [to what it should be]. || 17.18 ||

One who is equal in terms of family, conduct, and so forth, is *sama*; one who is the opposite is *asama*. The words *viṣama* and *sama* refer to the states [of inequality and equality]. *Viṣamasama* is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*). Regarding honor—consisting of such things as providing a seat and attending upon—one for whom equality is practiced with respect to both the equal (*sama*) and the unequal (*asama*) in that honor, his food is not to be eaten. (17.20)
And [the same applies to] that which is not honored. 17.19–17.21.

It is not honored with the food-mantra (*annamantra*) nor with a salutation. As Vasiṣṭha says: “One should honor the meals with the words ‘it is pleasing’ in the evening and in the morning” (VaDh 3.69). By the use of the word “and,” it is also proclaimed: “Who will eat? And so Vasiṣṭha says: “And it is proclaimed: ‘Who will eat? (VaDh 14.9). 17.19.
That which is given without honor, such as saying, "O son of a widow, eat this," is also unfit to be eaten. This applies equally to receiving gifts as well. As Manu said:

"He who accepts a gift with honor and he who gives with honor—both of them go to heaven; but in the opposite case, they go to hell" (MDh 4.235). Vasiṣṭha says: "One should honor food in the evening and in the morning" (VaDh 3.69). Others maintain that failing to do so constitutes giving without honor. 17.21.
And the milk of a cow during the ten-day period of impurity following birth [is forbidden]. 17.20–17.22.
The milk of a cow that has recently calved and whose ten-day period has not yet elapsed is unfit for consumption; by the use of the word "and," curds and other such products are also included. 17.20.
*Sūtaka* means birth. The milk of a cow that has recently calved and whose ten-day period has not yet elapsed is unfit for consumption. (17.22)
And [the same applies] to goats and buffaloes. 17.21–22.

The milk of goats and buffaloes that have not passed ten days since calving is unfit for drinking, as is their curd and other products. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to include goats within the scope of the rule. Their separate mention is intended to indicate that cow's milk may sometimes be consumed after seven nights have elapsed without fault.
The milk of goats and buffaloes must not be drunk during their period of birth-impurity, nor until ten days have passed.
The milk of sheep, of camels, and of one-hoofed animals is always unfit for drinking. 17.22–17.23.

The inclusion of the word "always" (*nitya*) indicates that this prohibition applies not only for ten days; because of the use of the suffix denoting a modification (*vikāra-pratyaya*), even urine and the like are not to be drunk by these women. In this way, it is understood that for the aforementioned [period], urine and such may be drunk. "Single-hoofed" (*ekaśapha*) refers to those with one hoof, such as mares and the like. The others are well known. The compound *viṣama* is intended to include all wild animals, such as deer and so forth. And thus says Manu:

"And among all wild animals, except for the buffalo. [MDh 5.9] By the use of the word "and" (ca), the milk of a human woman is also included. Although the term "unfit to be drunk" (apēya) was already under discussion, it is repeated here for the sake of establishing a permanent rule. Consequently, this establishes that even in cases of extreme distress, the milk of goats and buffaloes is permitted, even if they have not passed their ten-day period of impurity after calving. 17.22.

Because of the inclusion of the word "always" (*nitya*), it is not only the milk of those who have not yet passed ten days that is forbidden. A ewe is a female sheep; a camel is well known; "single-hoofed" (*ekaśapha*) refers to those with one hoof, such as horses and the like. The milk belonging to ewes and the others is always unfit to be drunk. However, Manu says:
"But among all wild animals, except for the buffalo, the milk of females must be avoided, as must all sour substances. (MDh 5.9) 17.24.
And [the same applies] to the words *syandinī*, *yamasū*, and *saṃdhinī*. 17.23–25.

"Always" means [the milk] of cows and so forth that are constantly pregnant; "milk" is to be understood as something not to be drunk. *Syandinī* is a cow whose udders are excessively swollen with knots. *Yamasūḥ* is one that gives birth to twins. *Sandhinī* is one that is milked after an interval of one period, or by means of another calf; according to some, a *sandhinī* is one that is milked while she is pregnant. By the word "and" (*ca*), those that are diseased are also included. (17.23)

That cow from whose udders milk flows spontaneously is called *syandinī*. A woman who gives birth to twins is called *yamasū*. A pregnant cow that is milked is called *saṃdhinī*; others say it is one that is milked at the same time [as her calf]. The milk of such cows and other animals is unfit for drinking. (17.25)
And [the same applies] to one who has no offspring. 17.24–17.26.

That which has lost its calf, and that which has been separated from its calf by loss or death—of these, [the milk] is not to be drunk. The separate mention is for the purpose of avoiding a prohibition against curds and so forth; otherwise, there would be a prohibition only of milk itself. The word "and" (ca) is for the purpose of including the milk of goats and buffaloes as well. 17.24.

One whose calf has been separated from her is "without a calf" (*vivatsā*); the milk of such a cow or similar animal is unfit for drinking. In this context, some authorities maintain that even curd and other products derived from prohibited milk are likewise forbidden. However, the customary practice regarding a cow within the ten-day period of impurity is as described, while elsewhere it is unrestricted. (17.26)
Now those things which are inedible by their very nature are being stated. He now declares those things that are inedible by their very nature:
"And five-clawed animals, except for the śalyaka, the hare, the porcupine, the iguana, the rhinoceros, and the tortoise. (17.25–17.27)

He will state later on that these are "not to be eaten" (*abhakṣya*); this [term] is drawn forward here [to the present context]. Those who have five nails on their hands and feet—namely, the five five-toed animals such as the jackal, the monkey, and so forth—are not to be eaten, with the exception of the porcupine and others. The word "and" (*ca*) is for the purpose of including milk, urine, and leavings. The *śalyaka* is the thorny boar; the hare (*śaśa*) is well known; the *śvāvit* is the bat; the *godhā* is well known; the *khaḍga* is the horned deer; the tortoise (*kacchapa*) is well known. Of those which are not to be eaten, their urine and other [secretions] should be understood as unfit for drinking.
The urine of animals whose meat is unfit for consumption, as well as their vomit, is declared to be inedible;
and likewise, their excrement is also inedible.

This is because of the words of Vatsa. The use of the nominative case in the phrase "and those with five claws" (*pañcanakhāś ca*) is intended so that all the limbs of the body may be included. If only the flesh were intended, then the use of the genitive case would have been appropriate. In this way, blood and other such substances are also indeed unfit for consumption; thus it should be understood in all cases. (17.25)

He will state later that these are not to be eaten. Those five-nailed animals whose nails on their hands and feet are five are "five-nailed," such as monkeys and the like; these are not to be eaten, with the exception of the *śalyaka* and others. The *śalyaka* is a particular kind of boar whose hair is shaped like iron arrows (*nārāca*). The hare (*śaśa*) is well known. The *śvāvit* is a porcupine, whose skin is used to make armor. The *godhā* is large-bodied and resembles a lizard. The *khaḍga* is a specific type of wild animal (a rhinoceros). The tortoise (*kacchapa*) is well known. Regarding this, they recite:
"The urine of those whose flesh is forbidden to be eaten, as well as their leavings, are likewise declared to be unfit for consumption; and their excrement is especially so. (17.27)
Animals with teeth in both jaws, those with hair on their bodies, those without hair, and those with solid hooves; as well as the kalaviṅka, the plava, the cakravāka, and the haṃsa. || 17.26–17.28 ||

"Those with two rows of teeth" refers to humans and the like. Since their prohibition is already established by the fact that they have five claws (*pañcanakha*), they are mentioned again for the sake of emphasizing the gravity of the expiation (*prāyaścitta*). This should be understood similarly in other cases where specific distinctions are made. "Hairy ones" (*keśin*) refers to those possessing an excess of hair, such as the *camari* (yak) and others. "Hairless ones" (*aloman*) refers to snakes and the like. "Single-hoofed ones" (*ekaśapha*) refers to horses and the like. The *kalaviṅka* is the village sparrow. The *plava* is the *śakaṭabila*. The *cakravāka* and the *haṃsa* are well known. (17.26)

Horses and the like have teeth in both jaws; the change to *dadbhāva* (the form *dadbhiḥ*) is an archaic Vedic usage (*ārṣa*). Keśins are animals such as the *camarī* deer that possess an abundance of hair. Those without hair include snakes and the like. One-hoofed animals are those with a single hoof. This [list] is intended to exclude those that do not have teeth in both jaws. The *kalaviṅka* is the village sparrow. The *plava* is the bird known as the *śakaṭabila*. The *haṃsa* and *cakravāka* are well known. These are also not to be eaten. (17.28)
Crows, herons, vultures, hawks, water-birds with red feet and beaks, domestic cocks, and pigs. || 17.27–29 ||

Crows and other such birds are well known. "Aquatic" refers to all [birds] without distinction. "Red-footed" refers to pigeons and the like; "red-beaked" refers to chakoras and the like. The word "domestic" (grāmya) is connected with both the cock and the pig. Thus, there is no prohibition against wild [cocks and pigs]. The lack of compound [in the term for domestic animals] is for the purpose of prohibiting others as well, such as carnivorous beasts and the like. (17.27)

Crows and the like are well known. Water-birds are also indeed birds because of their proximity to crows and the rest; they are qualified as "red-footed and red-beaked. That which occurs in a village is "village-born" (*grāmya*). This is a qualification for the two following [terms]: the village cock and the village pig. There is no prohibition regarding those that are wild (*āraṇya*). (17.29)
And [the forms] *dhenu* and *anaḍuh* [are used in the dual]. 17.28–30.

A *dhenu* is a milch cow; an *anaḍvān* is a bull. The mention of these two is also indicative of calves and other such animals. If it is asked, "In that case, should one simply say 'and a cow'?", it is replied here: the word "and" (*ca*) is for the purpose of including them as edible. This instruction is intended so that, in the context of being edible, only those two are included and not the calves and others. And thus says Vasiṣṭha: "But the cow and the bull are to be eaten, for they are known to be pure in the Vājasaneyaka" (VaDh 14.46). In this regard, it should be understood that when they have arrived in the form of guests, the cow and the bull are edible, whereas for others they are inedible, based on the indicative mark of Vasiṣṭha: "One may likewise kill animals even for the worship of ancestors, gods, and guests—this is the teaching of Manu" (VaDh 4.5); and "Furthermore, for a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya who has arrived as a guest, one should cook a large bull or a large goat; in this very way they provide hospitality to him" (VaDh 4.8). || 17.28 ||

A *dhenu* is a milch cow; an *anaḍvān* is a bull fit for drawing a cart. Regarding the form *dhenvanaḍvāhau*, one might object that it is not obtained because of the rule prescribing the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) *ac* in the *dvandva* compounds beginning with *acatura-*; however, that objection is disregarded, or else it is a corrupt reading. Furthermore, both the cow and the bull are inedible. In the *Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra*, however, having stated that meat from cows and buffaloes is edible, it says: "But according to the Vājasaneyakas, the meat of a *dhenu* and an *anaḍvān* is edible, and the meat of an *anaḍvān* is pure" (ĀpDh 1.17.30–31). The meaning is that the meat of an *anaḍvān* is not only edible but also pure. It is heard in the *Bahvṛca Brāhmaṇas*: "Just as when a king of men or another worthy guest has arrived, they slaughter a bull or a barren cow. In that context, it is the guest who may eat it, while for others it is inedible. Indeed, even killing was permitted there: "The *dāśa* and the *goghn* are included in the category of recipients," where the *goghn* is the guest for whom the cow is killed. Such, indeed, was the former practice; nowadays, even the smell [of such meat is forbidden]. (17.30)
Meat from animals that have not been slaughtered for sacrifice, meat from those that have died of exhaustion, and meat obtained in vain. || 17.29 ||
Meat from animals that have not been slaughtered for sacrifice, meat from animals that have died naturally, and meat obtained for no purpose [are forbidden]. || 17.31 ||

"Whose teeth have fallen out" means one whose teeth have dropped out. "One who has succumbed" means one who is diseased; others say it refers to one who has died naturally. "Meat prepared in vain" (vṛthāmāṃsa) means meat cooked solely for one's own sake. Although this is already established by the inclusion of the word "vain," the instruction is repeated again for the purpose of emphasizing the severity of the penance. And this should be understood as referring to edible meat, since there is no possibility of consuming what is inedible. (17.29)

The *apannadan* is one whose teeth have not fallen out; even though it is not explicitly forbidden, it is not to be eaten. For the *Bahvṛca-Brāhmaṇa* states: "When the teeth of an animal fall out, then it becomes fit for sacrifice. And Āpastamba says: "It is known that what has its teeth fallen out is the 'impurity' of animals. *Avasanna* means diseased. "Meat not [offered] in sacrifice" (*vṛthāmāṃsa*) is explained by reference to "food not [prepared] in sacrifice" (*vṛthānna*). The repeated prohibition of meat, however, is intended to ensure the severity of the penance. (17.31)
The red exudations from the shoots of the *kiśalaya* and *khyākula* trees were flowing forth. || 17.30 ||
The exudations from the shoots of the śuna trees were mixed with young sprouts.

*Kisalaya* refers to the first sprout of all plants. *Kyāku* is the *ahicchatra*, that is, the *chatrāka* mushroom. *Laśuna* is well known. If they are red exudations from trees, then likewise Manu says: "Red exudations from trees" (MDh 5.6), and so forth. Thus, there is no prohibition regarding asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) and similar substances. || 17.30 ||

*Kisalaya* is a sprout, a new shoot at the tip. *Kyāku* is a mushroom. *Laśuna* is well known (garlic). *Niryāsa* is the sap of a tree that has become solidified, such as asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) and the like. Sprouts and the others mentioned are also unfit for consumption. (17.32)
And [the word] *vraścana* [is used]. 17.31.
The red ones are the felling tools. 17.33.

"Produced from felling" means those trees which grow from [the site of] a cut; these, whether red or not red, are unfit for consumption. Thus, because camphor and similar substances are neither produced from felling nor are they red, they are not prohibited. Some make a division of the sūtra as "red and produced from felling"; even in their view, there is no prohibition of camphor and the like. Others explain that "resins are [those derived from] trees. According to them, there is a prohibition of asafoetida and so forth. By the word "and" (ca), onions, *gṛñjana*, and other items taught in other Smṛtis are included. (17.31)

Resins (*niryāsa*) produced in the incised parts of trees and the like are called *vraścana*; if they are red, they are not to be eaten. Resins that exude spontaneously (*svayaṃsūna*), whether red or non-red, are not to be eaten; however, those originating from incisions (*vraścanaprabhava*) are [forbidden] only if they are red. Manu, moreover, says:

"Red tree-exudations as well as those produced from incisions. [MDh 5.6] Some, however, include the word "red" (lohita) even for sprouts and the like. It should be considered whether asafoetida (hiṅgu) is an exudation or not one produced from an incision; in any case, even the learned eat it. Camphor, however, is neither an exudation, nor is it produced from an incision, nor is it red; therefore, it is certainly edible. 17.33.
The *nicu*, woodpecker, crane, *balākā* heron, *śuka* parrot, water-hen, *tiṭṭibha* sandpiper, *māndhāla*, and nocturnal prowlers are not to be eaten.

H reads "māsthāla" for "māndhāla. The *nicudāru* is the woodpecker; the *madgu* is one whose nature is to dive into water; the *ṭiṭṭibha* is one who habitually imitates the sound "ṭiṭṭibha"; the *mandhāla* is the *vāgguda* (the cackling goose); *naktaṃcarāḥ* refers to owls and the like; others are well known. It has been stated that the verb "are not to be eaten" (*abhakṣyāḥ*) is connected with the phrase beginning from "five-toed animals" (*pañcanakhāḥ*). 17.32.

The *nicudāru* is a woodpecker; the *madgura* is a water-crow; the *māsthāla* is a "talkative" [bird]; the *naktaṃcaras* are owls and the like; others are well known. The phrase "not to be eaten" (*abhakṣyāḥ*) connects back from the passage beginning with "those with five claws" (*pañcanakhāḥ*).
Those that peck with their beaks, those that scratch with their claws, and those that walk on webs of toes are edible. (17.33–17.35)

Since one [category] is established by the teaching of the other, the teaching of both categories is for the purpose of favoring those for whom there is neither a specific injunction nor a prohibition. "Piercers" (*pratudāḥ*) are those such as peacocks that eat by pecking repeatedly with their beaks. "Scatterers" (*viṣkirāḥ*) are those such as quails that eat by scattering [the food] repeatedly. "Non-web-footed" (*ajālapādāḥ*) are those that do not have webbed feet, such as gourds (*tumbaka*). || 17.33 ||

Those that eat by pecking repeatedly with their beaks are *pratuda*s. Those such as peacocks that eat by scattering [food] with their feet are *viṣkira*s. Those whose feet are webbed are *jālapāda*s. These are edible. Although it is understood from the mention of non-edible animals that others are edible, the explicit inclusion of the term "edible" is so that eating may occur only in times of distress (*āpad*), and not when there is no distress. (17.35)
And fish that are not altered [by cooking]. 17.34–17.36.

"Deformed" refers to those whose form is different from that of the hand. The word "ca" (and) has the purpose of including those with scales. The meaning is that only those possessing both qualifiers—being scaled *and* undeformed—are edible; those possessing only one qualifier are not. Since "those without webbed feet" was stated previously, here one should understand that there is a prohibition of webbed-footed animals and of those possessing only one of the two qualifiers. This should be understood in the same way for what follows as well. (17.34)
Those with deformed human heads and so forth are "altered" (vikṛta), while those opposite to them are "unaltered" (avikṛta) and thus fit for consumption. || 17.36 ||
And those who deserve execution may be slain for the sake of dharma. 17.35–17.37.

Those animals previously killed on account of dharma, such as at the beginning of a sacrifice, though otherwise unfit to be eaten, are permissible to eat; the word "and" (ca) implies also in cases of danger to life. Thus Manu says: "One may eat consecrated meat, or at the desire of Brāhmaṇas, or when one is engaged according to rule [in a rite], or indeed when there is danger to one's life" (MDh 5.27).
But is it not the case that since [the merit] for those killed in sacrifices and the like is already established by the injunctions of the Śruti itself, this instruction here is purposeless?

To this it is replied: those [acts] which are performed specifically for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) entail no penance (*prāyaścitta*) when eating the remnants of such [acts], but not when eating the remnants of acts intended for a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭaprayojana*). For this very reason, instead of saying "for the sake of sacrifice" (*yajñārtha*), it is said "for the sake of dharma" (*dharmārtha*). By this alone, the eating of the flesh of the animal sacrificed by one who has broken his vow of celibacy (*avakīrṇin*) is also excluded, because that [act] is for the purpose of penance and does not have an unseen purpose. And thus, just as there is an application of the Smṛti-prescribed penance in the case of eating meat for a visible purpose, it is understood that the same applies to the violence (*hiṃsā*) committed in that context as well. With this very intention, it was also stated by Manu:
"One should offer a ghee-animal in times of distress; likewise, one may offer an animal made of flour," and so forth. [MDh 5.37] 17.35.

Those animals which are declared as edible are not only to be eaten when they have died naturally or been killed by others, but may also be slain for the sake of dharma, such as in the honoring of guests and similar rites. Another [author] says: "Those which are to be slain for the sake of dharma, such as in sacrifices and the like, are edible even for those who are not officiating priests.
