Because of the expression "for the sake of dharma," the meat of the *avakīrṇin*-animal (sacrificed by one who has broken his vow of celibacy) is inedible, since its purpose is for the performance of an expiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*). (17.37)
One should consume food that has been killed by a predator, or that whose defects are unseen, after sprinkling it with water and pronouncing words of praise; one should consume it. 17.36–17.38.
H reads "praśastān".

One may eat the meat of an animal killed by predators—such as lions and the like—after merely sprinkling it with water. The qualification "killed by a predator" applies specifically to cases where no visible defect exists, as well as when it is commended by word. The meat of an animal killed by a predator is fit for consumption provided that it is free from visible defects and is commended by word. "Free from visible defects" means it has not been taught among the list of forbidden foods, since its fitness for consumption is established precisely by the present instruction. "Commended by word" means it is so declared by others. Thus, this is an authorization for that which is not mentioned in either the list of permitted or forbidden foods, but is prescribed for times of distress; it does not apply when one is not in distress. Furthermore, the plural number indicates that purity belongs only to meat possessing all three qualifications, and not to that possessing only one. Likewise, in the rule "one may even consume dog-meat" (GDh 3.31), the same criteria regarding the absence of visible defects and so forth should be understood. While one could have simply said "he should eat," the use of the term "upayuñjīta" (may consume/utilize) implies that abstaining from eating is better than eating. And so says Manu:
"There is no fault in eating meat, nor in liquor, nor in sexual intercourse; for this is the natural inclination of living beings, but abstention bears great fruit. [MDh 5.56] || 17.36 ||

One should feed and eat even with guests, but one must avoid the leftovers of dogs and other such animals. Manu also said: "A dog is pure when it catches game" (MDh 5.130). This has been stated twice. On this point, Manu says:
"The one who consents, the one who dismembers, the killer, the buyer and seller, the one who prepares, the one who serves, and the eater—all these are slayers" (MDh 5.51).

"There is no fault in eating meat, nor in liquor, nor in sexual intercourse; this is the natural inclination of living beings, but abstention bears great fruit" (MDh 5.56). The meaning is that even regarding those things not explicitly forbidden, abstaining from consumption is indeed superior. 17.38.
Now begins the eighteenth chapter.
The general and specific duties of the stages of life (*āśrama*) have been declared. Now, it is said that the duties of women must be stated;
thus, he declares the duties of women.

A woman is not independent in matters of dharma. (18.1) "Not independent" means she is dependent on another; regarding dharma pertaining to the next world, her entitlement to perform religious duties is in conjunction with her husband, and not through independence as a man is. Thus Manu says:
"For women there is no separate sacrifice, no vow, nor even a fast."

“By whatever means she serves her husband, by that she is glorified in heaven. [MDh 5.155] Śaṅkha also stated: “Neither vows, fasts, observances, sacrifices, nor the duty of giving bestows favor upon women except through service to the husband; however, with the husband’s permission, the practice of vows, fasts, observances, and so forth is indeed the duty of women.”

Now, an objection may be raised: since the Vedic and Smṛti injunctions are prescribed with reference to the male person, there is no independent entitlement for the woman; therefore, a prohibition [of her independence] would be inappropriate. If it is argued that the statement regarding her lack of independence is intended to mean that the woman also shares in the fruit of performing religious duties together with her husband, that is incorrect, because this very point is already established by her status as a "companion in dharma" (*sahadharmacāriṇī*). Furthermore, if she is not independent, it is not known to what she is dependent. If one says she is dependent on her husband, we say no, because her subordination to the husband will be stated later in the passage, "She must not transgress against her husband" (GDh 18.2). If it is argued that by this [present verse] non-transgression is being enjoined, we say no, because transgression concerning dharma, artha, and kāma has already been prohibited.

To this it is replied: This undertaking is intended for the sake of enabling a woman to perform religious means (*dharmasādhana*) such as fasting and giving, provided she has her husband’s permission; for the duties of the stages of life (*āśramadharma*) are attained by means of the husband. Thus, the statement of Śaṅkha which was cited, beginning with “But at will, with the husband’s permission,” and so forth, applies here. Likewise, regarding the matter of giving, Nārada says: “They declare that transactions performed by a woman are invalid in the absence of an emergency, especially the giving, mortgaging, or selling of a house or field,” and so forth. This refers to property belonging to the husband.

If it is argued that this is because of the statement of Kaṇva—"The woman shall be the mistress of her own property, and the husband is entitled to enjoy and protect it with her permission; he is not entitled to consume it, nor to destroy it"—we say no, for another Smṛti text is observed. Thus Vyāghra says:
"Woman's property must never be given away by anyone, nor should it ever be offered as a sacrificial gift."
"If it has previously been authorized by the husband, that [property] must indeed be given by the woman.
And likewise Lokākṣi says:
"A woman is declared to be the mistress of wealth, except in matters of mortgaging, giving, and buying."
"Therefore, ownership resulting from that [gift] and so forth is never established.

Thus, even according to the words of Kaṇva, ownership should be understood as existing only after excluding gift, mortgage, and sale. As for what was asked, "Under whose authority must she remain?", there too she is dependent upon her husband, son, and father at the appropriate times. Manu says accordingly:
"In childhood she shall remain under the control of her father; in youth, under her husband."
“When her son has reached old age, a woman does not deserve independence. [MDh 5.148] And likewise, there is another [verse] in that same place:
“Whether she be a child, a young woman, or even an elderly woman, no action whatsoever should be performed by a woman independently, even within the household. [MDh 5.147] || 18.1 ||

In both the Vedic (*śrauta*) and domestic (*gārhya*) duties, a woman enters into the performance of her husband alone. Even through Smṛti-based and Purāṇic duties such as vows (*vrata*) and fasts (*upavāsa*), she is not authorized to act independently without the permission of her husband. Śaṅkha says: "Neither through vows, fasts, observances, sacrifices, gifts, nor religious merit do women gain favor, except through service to their husbands. However, the practice of vows, fasts, observances, and so forth with the husband's permission is the duty of a woman. Nārada also says:
They say that transactions involving women are invalid when not in times of distress,
especially those concerning the giving, receiving, studying, or selling of houses and fields.
"These indeed are the authorities, provided the husband approves. Thus [it is stated in NSm 1.22–23]. Manu, however, says:
"In childhood she shall remain under the control of her father, and in youth under that of her husband."

"In the absence of a son, an elderly woman does not deserve independence. [MDh 5.148] "Whether she be a child, a young woman, or even an old woman, no action whatsoever should be performed by a woman independently, even within her own home. [MDh 5.147] Thus [ends the citation]. 18.1.
And since such unrestricted conduct would otherwise result in acting contrary to dharma, he says:
"She must not transgress against her husband. (18.2)

The meaning is that she should not engage in anything whatsoever without her husband’s permission, or even when it is forbidden by him. Although one could simply have said "the master" (*pati*), the term "husband" (*bhartṛ*) is used to indicate that this applies to whomever provides her maintenance. (18.2)
She should not transgress against her husband, nor should she think of anyone other than her husband even in her mind. || 18.2 ||
Moreover: "Restrained in speech, sight, and action. (18.3)

The word "syāt" (should be) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the verse]. One who speaks only as much as is necessary for the purpose is restrained in speech (*vāk-saṃyatā*). One who does not look at those who witness improper acts and so forth is restrained in sight (*cakṣuḥ-saṃyatā*). One who is engaged in household duties is restrained in action (*karma-saṃyatā*). || 18.3 ||

Speech that speaks only as much as is necessary is restrained in speech (*vāk-saṃyatā*). Not looking at spectators and the like is restrained in sight (*cakṣuḥ-saṃyatā*). Not performing actions other than those required for the sake of one's own family is restrained in action (*karma-saṃyatā*). She should be such as this. (18.3)
Now, this is an exception to the rule that "she must not transgress against her husband": "If she is without a husband and desires offspring, [she may obtain one] from her brother-in-law. (18.4)
"Without a husband" (*apatih*) means one whose husband is absent or one who has an unsuitable husband. And so says Bṛhaspati:
"When the husband is lost, dead, has renounced the world, is impotent, or has become an outcast—under these five calamities, another husband is ordained for women."

The meaning is that if a woman who is childless and desires offspring should wish for a child, she may procreate one through her brother-in-law (*devara*). The brother-in-law is either the elder or the younger brother of her husband. (18.4)

If a woman who is childless and whose husband has died should desire offspring, she may seek to obtain them through her husband’s brother; the instruction is that the husband’s younger brother is the *devara*. (18.4)
He states by what procedure one should produce [the seed]: "In that regard, the method is: she who has been authorized by the guru should not let her fertile season pass. (18.5)

"Permitted by her elders" means she has been authorized by both her husband's kin and her father's kin. "She should not let the fertile season pass" means she should not fail to engage [with her husband] except during the period of her menses. Even there, if conception occurs on a single day, it happens precisely then; if not, it does not happen during that entire season. Thus says the *Talavakāra-Brāhmaṇa*: "If semen is emitted on the first day, it results in conception; therefore, what is emitted thereafter is in vain and is cast away. In this case as well, it should be understood that she is anointed with clarified butter (*ghṛta*). As Uśanas says: "Having anointed himself with clarified butter on all his limbs, he should approach her who has been authorized and anointed with clarified butter on all her limbs. (18.5)

Being appointed by her husband’s kinsmen or her father’s kinsmen, she should unite with him; even then, she should not let the season pass, nor should she exceed the fertile period. Furthermore, conception occurs upon the first union. For it is heard in the *Tālavr̥kārāṇām Brāhmaṇa*: "If semen is emitted on the first day, that results in a conception; but where it is emitted thereafter, it is emitted in vain. Therefore, even during the fertile season, there should be union only once. Regarding this, there is a specific rule from *Uśanas*: "She who is appointed [to procreate] should have all her limbs anointed with clarified butter; having thus anointed her entire body, she should approach him. (18.5)
He states those who should be approached in succession in the absence of a husband's brother:
"From among those related by funeral offerings, lineage, or sages. (18.6)
From those related by funeral offerings, lineage, or seers, or from the mere fact of being born of the same womb. || 18.6 ||

In the subsequent sūtra, the particle *vā* (or) carries forward the sense of optionality (*vaikalpika*) as well as non-existence (*abhāva*). Consequently, by virtue of this governing context (*adhikāra*), in the absence of a brother-in-law (*devarā*), one who desires offspring may take [the seed] even from a mere *sapiṇḍa*; in his absence, from a mere *sagotra*. Here, by the word *sagotra*, one should understand a *samānodaka* (distant relative), because another Smṛti text is seen stating, "One should take [the seed] from the nearest [relative]. Those related to a seer (*ṛṣi*) are those connected through a seer; they are one's own kinsmen (*svakulyāḥ*). (18.6)

One who shares the *piṇḍa* (ancestral offering) is a *sapiṇḍa*; one who shares the *gotra* (lineage) is a *sagotra*; one who shares the connection to a *ṛṣi* (ancestral seer) is one of the same *pravara*, such as Harita, Kutsa, and others. From these, in due order, he should seek offspring; or else, from one who possesses only the [maternal] womb. Regarding this, another *smṛti* states: "In the absence of all [these], from one who possesses only the womb—that is, from one belonging merely to the Brāhmaṇa caste. (18.6)
Or [the rule applies] from the mere womb. || 18.7 ||

In the absence of all [suitable candidates], she may go even to one who belongs merely to the Brāhmaṇa caste. The word *mātra* (merely) expresses the sense of "only" with respect to dharma; therefore, it should be understood that in the absence of one possessing qualities (*guṇavat*), she may go to one devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*). The separate mention [of the Brāhmaṇa caste] is for the purpose of prohibiting her from going to another [caste] when a man of noble birth (*kulīna*) is available. And so Vasiṣṭha says: "Indeed, while a man of that same lineage exists, she must not go to another. (VaDh 17.80) [18.7]
Some say [the prohibition applies] to one who has not been consecrated by his elder brother. 18.8 — 18.7.

Some maintain that one should not procreate offspring from a non-kinsman such as a brother-in-law; however, the Teacher [Vasiṣṭha] holds that in the absence of a brother-in-law, one may do so even from another.
Some think that one should seek [wealth] only from a non-king, not from a king. 18.7.
The offspring does not belong to the progenitor beyond the second [generation]. || 18.9 ||
Not more than twice. 18.8.

Having passed over the second, one should not produce a third; in this way, the second is permitted. If one produces a third, it belongs to the progenitor, such as the husband's brother, and not to the owner of the field (*kṣetrin*). Therefore, that [third] becomes unfit; this much is intended here. 18.9
"One should not produce a second offspring after having passed over the first.
The offspring belongs to the progenitor. || 18.9 ||
That offspring belongs to the progenitor, not to the owner of the soil. Āpastamba also states: “For the Vedic text says, ‘The son belongs to the progenitor’” (ĀpDh 2.13.5), and so forth. 18.9.
[The fruit belongs] to another because of the agreement. || 18.10 ||

If an agreement has been made in the form, "Your pleasure [is mine], my offspring [is yours]," then even a third [son] belongs to the other, the owner of the field (*kṣetrin*). Therefore, the intention is that this is not faulty. || 18.10 ||

If kinsmen, having made an agreement, commission [a man], thinking "let there be offspring for the owner of the field," as in the case of Vicitravīrya’s field, Satyavatī, and the offspring produced in her by Vyāsa—[that is the case]. 18.10.
And [the property] of one who is alive in his own field. || 18.11 ||

The word "ca" (and) serves to draw in the phrase "of another. The intention is that the offspring produced in the field—that is, in the wife—of a living husband who is incapable of procreation belongs to the owner of the field alone, even without a formal agreement, and this applies even if there is more than one [offspring] from a second [man]. (18.11)

And when the owner of the field, while still living, being either barren or diseased, requests, "Produce a son in my field," then the offspring belongs to the owner of the field alone, not to the owner of the seed. 18.11.
Of that [self], from another. || 18.12 ||

If offspring is produced even while the husband is alive, either from another man—distinct from the husband such as a brother-in-law—or through transgression, that child belongs exclusively to the biological father alone, even if he is the second, and not to the owner of the field (the husband). 18.12.

From another man—that is, one distinct from the husband or the king—even if she has not been authorized by him, the son born to her, whether she has offspring already or is childless, belongs again to that very progenitor (bījin) and not to the owner of the field (kṣetrin). || 18.12 ||
Or [it may be] for two. 18.13.
Thus, the offspring so produced belongs either to the progenitor or to the owner of the field; the meaning is that it becomes a *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa* (belonging to two lineages). || 18.13 ||

Thus, offspring so produced belongs to both the seed-giver and the owner of the field; this refers to the case of a woman appointed for the purpose. And so says Yājñavalkya: "A son begotten by appointment upon the wife of another by one who is childless is, according to dharma, the heir to the property and the giver of the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to both. (YDh 2.127) || 18.13 ||
But because of the protection of the husband alone. || 18.14 ||

When protection, maintenance, nourishment, and sacramental rites are performed by the husband, any offspring born from another through a lapse belongs to that husband alone; the word "tu" (but) is for the sake of specification. Even if he is unprotected—such as in the case of one who has gone forth [into homelessness], is lost, or has fallen—[the child] belongs specifically to him who is capable of protecting it. || 18.14 ||

If the husband alone performs the protection, maintenance, nourishment, sacraments, and so forth for the field, and not the progenitor, then that offspring belongs to the husband alone; the same applies when he has died. (18.14)
If her husband has disappeared, the penance lasts for six years.

When the husband has departed for another land, offspring should not be produced for six years. After that period, if she so desires, she may produce offspring after obtaining the authorization of her elders; this is the intended meaning. Why? Because of the observation of the Vasiṣṭha-smṛti: "They say that a son born of a woman who has not been authorized belongs to the progenitor" (VaDh 17.63). || 18.15 ||
When it is being heard, there is the approach. 18.16 — || 18.15 ||
If, after six years, the husband is heard from, she should go directly to him while he is still being heard from; the intention is that she should not procreate offspring with anyone else. 18.16.
But when it is heard that her husband is staying in that country, then she should go to him. || 18.15 ||
But upon his renunciation, there is cessation [of the debt], because it would otherwise follow as an undesirable consequence. 18.17–18.16.

If the husband has renounced the world (*pravrajita*), there is a cessation of approaching him due to that specific circumstance; the meaning is that she should not go to him. Alternatively, there is a cessation of procreating offspring due to that circumstance; she should not produce offspring. The word "but" (*tu*) is for the sake of specification. Some explain that she should not procreate in the absence of desire, and that she must remain self-restrained (*saṃyatā*). [The rule] "she should not procreate offspring when he has renounced the world" implies, by virtue of the word "but," that she herself may also renounce the world, since it would be impossible to know the intention of one residing in another country.

But if the husband has gone forth, having entered the stage of liberation (mokṣāśrama), then there must be a cessation from all worldly attachment; she herself also, being oriented toward renunciation, should remain truly self-restrained. || 18.16 ||
Twelve years for a Brāhmaṇa in connection with the acquisition of knowledge. 18.18. — 18.17.

It should be understood that for the wife of a Brāhmaṇa who has gone abroad for the purpose of acquiring knowledge (*vidyā*), she may wait for twelve years; however, she should bring about the cessation of waiting upon the birth of a child or his return. But in the case of one who has renounced the world (*pravrajita*), she should bring it about immediately. Here, because of the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa," it is understood that previously this applied to Kṣatriyas and others. Alternatively, because of the mention of "knowledge" here, it applies specifically to a Brāhmaṇa who has gone for the sake of learning. By the force of other *Smṛtis*, there is no such waiting period in the case of one who has gone for the sake of pleasure (*kāma*). As Vasiṣṭha says: "The wife of one who has gone abroad shall wait for five years; after five years, she may go to her husband's presence. If he went away for the sake of dharma or wealth, then she may go; but if he went for the sake of pleasure, she should behave as if he were dead" (VaDh 17.75–77). And thus, even for a Kṣatriya or others who have gone for the sake of knowledge, half and half [of the period] should be assigned compared to the Brāhmaṇa and others. For one who has gone for the sake of wealth, the rule stated by Vasiṣṭha should be observed. As Vasiṣṭha says: "In this way, a Brāhmaṇa woman who has not borne children waits five years, and six if she has borne children; a princess who has not borne children waits four, and five if she has borne children; a Vaiśya woman who has not borne children waits three, and four if she has borne children; a Śūdra woman who has not borne children waits two, and three if she has borne children" (VaDh 17.78). By this same logic, even in connection with the pursuit of knowledge, a reduction of one year should be observed for those who have not borne children. (18.18)
The wife of a Brāhmaṇa who has gone abroad for the purpose of acquiring knowledge shall wait for twelve years; there shall be neither procreation of offspring nor sexual intercourse. 18.17.
And likewise, when the elder brother is present, the younger brother may perform the rites of marriage, the establishment of the sacred fire, and the taking of a wife. (18.19) — (18.18)

If the eldest brother has not married, has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), or is away on a journey, the younger brother may do exactly the same. By the use of the word "exactly" (*evam*), there is a complete extension (*atideśa*) of the rules; however, from that [extension], it should be understood that if [the elder] is present, he must be approached, whereas if he has renounced the world (*pravrajita*), the requirement to approach him ceases. If it is argued that, in the case of one who has renounced the world, the obligation of self-restraint (*saṃyatatva*) would also apply [to the younger brother], we say no, because of the observation of other *smṛtis*. As Uśanas says: "When the eldest brother has renounced the world, there is no waiting period (*kṣapaṇa*); he should marry immediately," and so forth. Even so, if it is argued that for one who has gone abroad for the sake of wealth, a six-year period would apply, we say no, because of the force of yet another *smṛti*. As Vasiṣṭha says: [He should wait] for twelve years... [and so forth].
"Indeed, for twelve years he has been devoted to dharma and artha;
it is right that he be awaited by his brother, even though he hears [of him] again and again. Thus [it is said].

By the use of the word "and" (ca), there is an inclusion of those [periods] mentioned in other Smṛtis. As Vasiṣṭha says: "If one does not wait for his eldest brother who has not yet married for eight, ten, or twelve years, he becomes liable to penance. In that context, twelve years should be understood when [the elder brother's marriage] is frequently heard of, because of the repeated mention; ten years when it is heard of only slightly; and eight years when it is not heard of at all. For Kṣatriyas and others, half and half [of these periods] should be calculated as before. This is the exception [to the rule].
One who is insane, a sinner, a leper, an outcast, a eunuch,
or afflicted with consumption should not be waited upon.

This should be understood as stated in other Smṛtis beginning with these words. Since the status of the younger brother is established by implication through the mention of the "eldest" alone—because the term is a relative one—it is for the purpose of making known that the fault applies only to one who shares the same mother. The plural number is used to include even the fire-altar (agni) prescribed in the Smṛtis. (18.19)

If an elder brother has not taken a wife, has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), and is away on a journey, the younger brother shall wait for him for twelve years. After that, he may marry a maiden and establish the sacred fires. Regarding this, there is a specific rule from Vasiṣṭha: "One who does not wait for an elder brother who has not married for eight, ten, or twelve years becomes liable to penance.
And also: "An elder brother who is capable of fulfilling religious and worldly duties is properly to be waited for for twelve years, provided he is heard from again and again. (18.18)
"Some say there are six. 18.20 — || 18.19 ||

Some maintain that one should wait for exactly six years; in that case, it should be understood that if the one who has gone abroad is extremely old, he should wait for six years, but if not, for twelve years. (18.20)
Some think that one should wait for only six years; this [rule] applies when the husband has gone abroad, is extremely aged, or remains excessively devoted to dharma. (18.19)
Having spoken incidentally, he now states the duties of women. The incidental discussion is concluded; he speaks again of the duties of women:
"A maiden, having passed three menstrual periods, may unite herself with one who is blameless, after renouncing her paternal ornaments."

The meaning is that if, after three seasons have passed, the father or others do not give her away, the maiden—remaining blameless and endowed with noble lineage and other qualities—should herself choose a husband. She should do so having relinquished the ornaments given by the father and others. The mention of the "father" is for the sake of illustration; thus Manu says: "A maiden choosing her own husband (svayaṃvarā) must not take ornaments belonging to her father, nor those of her mother, nor those given by her brothers; if she should take them, it would constitute theft" (MDh 9.92). 18.21.

If her father or others do not give her away, then after three menstrual periods have passed, she may herself unite with a blameless husband endowed with noble lineage, learning, and virtuous conduct, having cast aside the ornaments received from her paternal kin. Regarding this, Manu says:
"A maiden choosing her own husband must not take the ornaments belonging to her father;
those given by her mother or her brother—if she takes anything at all, it shall be theft" (MDh 9.92). 18.20.
At what time should she be given away by her father and others? To this he says:
"For this very reason, the giving [of the girl] should take place before puberty. (18.22) — [following] (18.21).
One should give her away before the appearance of her menses. 18.22.
A maiden should be given away in marriage even before the appearance of her menses. 18.21.
For:
"One who does not give is at fault. (18.23) — (18.22)

Not only is there an absence of merit for one who does not give [a daughter in marriage], but rather, for the couple, there arises a sin equal to the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*). As Vasiṣṭha has said:
"As many seasons as touch a maiden who is of equal status and solicited by one who desires her..."
"As many embryos as have been killed by those two, the mother and father," such is the declaration of the Dharma. [VaDh 17.71] Thus ends [the section]. 18.23.
At that time, one who does not give her—such as the father and so forth—becomes guilty of a fault. On this point, Yājñavalkya says:
"The father, the grandfather, the brother, a *sakulya* (distant relative), and likewise the mother;
in the absence of each preceding one, each subsequent person is the giver of the maiden, provided they are of sound mind."
"By not bestowing her, he incurs the guilt of killing an embryo at every menstrual period. [Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.63–64] || 18.22 ||
Some say [it should be done] before the acquisition of the garment. 18.24 — 18.23.

Because the proper time is difficult to discern, she should give [the garment] before putting on her clothes; the meaning is that she should give it at the very moment she feels bashful. Thus some maintain. This is an option depending on the presence of a suitor. 18.24.
Some think that she should be given away at the very moment when the girl puts on the garment or feels bashful. || 18.23 ||
It has been stated that when the father or others give her away, they should do so after she has been clothed and adorned. To the question of what should be done in the absence of wealth, he says:
"The acceptance of wealth is for the purpose of accomplishing the marriage. (18.25)
The acceptance of wealth from a Śūdra is permitted for the purpose of accomplishing a marriage or when engaged in matters concerning religious duties.

The taking of another's property means the appropriation of what has not been given; the meaning is that for the sake of accomplishing a marriage, one may take as much as is required to complete the marriage and give it away, provided one lacks one's own property. (18.25)

Even without permission, goods such as clothing may be taken from a Śūdra for the purpose of accomplishing a marriage; one may take as much as is necessary for the marriage to be completed. To take more than that constitutes a fault. Likewise, when a ritual such as an animal sacrifice has begun, whatever equipment or subsidiary part—such as a horse—is required, one may take even without permission from a Śūdra as much as is needed to complete it so that the rite is not interrupted. To take more than that constitutes a fault. (18.24)
Moreover: "And in attachment to the system of Dharma. (18.26)

The interruption of an established ritual tradition (*tantra*), such as the *agnihotra* and others, constitutes "attachment" (*saṅga*). When that occurs, one may take the property of another. The inclusion of the term *tantra* indicates that this applies only to attachment to what has already begun and is obligatory to perform, and not for the purpose of initiating what has not yet begun. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to draw forward the phrase "for the sake of success" (*siddhyartham*). One should take only as much as is required to complete it, and nothing more; for if one takes more than that, it is indeed theft. (18.26)
From where is that to be taken? To this he says: "from a Śūdra" (18.27).
For wealth is for the sake of sacrifice, and a Śūdra has no entitlement to Vedic rites; therefore, one should first take it from a Śūdra. (18.27)
In the absence of such a person, [one may accept it] even from another, provided he is not a Śūdra. 18.28.
Even in other cases, [this applies] to a Śūdra who possesses many cattle but performs inferior work.

Although it could have been stated simply as "in other cases as well," the specific mention of the *śūdra* is for the purpose of including the *vaiśya* and the *kṣatriya*. In the absence of that [the *brāhmaṇa*], [one may take from] a *vaiśya*; in the absence of that, from a *kṣatriya*. (18.28)

The suffix *tral* is used here for the ablative case (*pañcamī*) according to the rule: "It is also seen after other [stems] as well. Wealth may be taken from someone other than a Śūdra, provided that he possesses many cattle and is thus of low character—meaning he does not perform his appropriate duties or engages in forbidden actions. The mention of the Śūdra is so that this specific rule may apply; therefore, in the absence of a Śūdra, one may take it from a Vaiśya, and in the absence of that, from a Kṣatriya. (18.25)
In that case as well: "Of one who has many cattle but whose ritual action is deficient. (18.29)
One of inferior action is he who performs unsuitable work, or he who does not do anything at all; from such a person one should receive [alms]. (18.29)
He demonstrates the very meaning already stated by means of an illustration: "Of one who owns a hundred cows but has not maintained the sacred fires" (18.30)—[end of section] 18.26.

Even for one who has performed other rites but has not established the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*), [the fine is] "one hundred cows. The mention of "hundred" is intended as an illustration of the quantity of the substance; the meaning is "one hundred *niṣkas*. This applies everywhere in this manner. (18.30)

The mention of "cows" is illustrative. This applies first to one who possesses wealth but does not establish the sacred fires; as for one who indulges in forbidden acts, he is explained by the maxim of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpika*). || 18.26 ||
And for one who does not drink soma, [the penance is] a thousand cows. 18.31–18.27.

One may also take from one who, though he maintains the sacred fires and possesses a thousand [cows], does not drink the Soma; the word "also" (ca) implies that it may be taken from others as well. One may likewise take from one who, despite possessing abundant wealth, does not perform the corresponding religious duties.
The preceding has been explained. It is because he possesses a thousandfold [merit] yet does not drink the Soma that this is so. || 18.27 ||
Not only are there these two causes for taking another's property, but furthermore: "And without having enjoyed the seventh [requisite], one does not store it up. (18.32) — (18.28)

On the seventh occasion, having not eaten due to the depletion of his own wealth, he may take the property of another. Thus says Manu: "Likewise, when he has reached the seventh meal-time without having eaten the previous six, he may take from one of low conduct according to the rule of 'no provision for tomorrow' (an-aśvastana). [MDh 11.16] The word "and" (ca) is intended to include those who are otherwise ineligible for such acts. Furthermore, the verse of Manu cited there states: "It is for the sake of non-accumulation, merely to fill the belly. (18.32)

The accusative case is used here in the sense of the locative. Having failed to obtain food during six meal-times, one may take as much as is necessary for sustenance during the seventh meal-time, even if it has not been permitted. Furthermore, one must not accumulate; no store should be made by him. Even food for the following day must not be taken. On this point, Manu says: "Likewise, when he has reached the seventh meal-time without having eaten the previous six, he may take what is needed by one who follows the rule of not providing for tomorrow, from a person of low conduct" (MDh 11.16). 18.28.
Even from those whose actions have not been deficient. 18.33 — 18.29.
In this state, even for those who perform their prescribed duties—as indicated by the word "even" (api)—as well as for those who maintain the sacred fires and those who drink the Soma juice. 18.33.

In this state, one may accept [gifts] even from those whose actions are deficient; the word "even" (api) indicates that this is permitted only under certain circumstances. Therefore, this applies only when there is a danger to life. 18.29.

If, while taking [the goods], he is led before the king by a royal officer and questioned on account of the theft, then, being questioned by the king, he should speak [the truth]. 18.34. — || 18.30 ||
Being questioned, he should declare and speak [the truth], but he must not deny it out of fear; nor, however, should he go of his own accord to report it. 18.34.

If, while acting in this way, he is seized by his masters and brought before the king, and is asked by him, "Why have you done this?", then he should describe his own situation; he must not speak falsely. (18.30)
For this reason:
"Therefore, he should indeed be supported, provided he is endowed with learning and virtuous conduct. (18.35) — [End of] 18.31.

The word *hi* has the sense of "because. Because of that, he must be supported, according to the statement: "One should support Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas" (GDh 10.9). This applies if he is endowed with learning and good conduct—that is, if he is fully possessed of learning, which is the understanding of the meaning of the Veda, and of good conduct, which is the performance of the actions enjoined therein. If it is argued that the quality of being endowed with learning and good conduct is already established by the very mention of him as one to be supported—since the instruction to support those learned in the Vedas is given in the passage, "One should support Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas" (GDh 10.9)—we reply: No, because there is also an instruction to support even those not learned in the Vedas, as in: "Brahmins who lack energy [and non-Brahmins]" (GDh 10.10). Thus, it is demonstrated that in the case of stealing another's property, a non-Brahmin need not be supported. By the use of the word "by him," it is shown that his support is for the sake of dharma alone, and not for the sake of his livelihood.

The word *hi* is used in the sense of "and. Therefore, that man was not only unpunishable by the king, but rather, from that time forward, he was to be supported [with the words]: "This condition of yours was not known to me," thus consoling him. And this applies if he is endowed with learning (*śruta*), conduct (*vṛtta*), and character (*śīla*). *Śruta* is the thorough knowledge of the scriptures; *śīla* is conduct consistent with that. Even another [type of offender] is not to be punished, but his maintenance should not be of such a kind [as the former]. The absence of punishment is common to both of the two preceding grounds as well. (18.31)
In the case of an affliction of the Dharma-tantra, there is no fault in performing it; there is no fault. || 18.36 ||
In the case of an affliction of the Dharma-tantra, there is a fault in not performing [the remedy]; there is a fault in not performing it. || 18.32 ||

Because he is to be maintained, therefore, in the case of an injury to his *dharma* or *tantra*—whereby the word *dharma* refers to the *agnihotra* and other rites, the word *tantra* refers to marriage, and the word *pīḍā* (injury) refers to injury to oneself, as expressed by the phrase "without having enjoyed the seventh [year]"; the meaning is: in the event of the interruption of religious duties (*dharma*) for the sake of accomplishing marriage, or in the event of injury to oneself—the act of theft toward him is without fault. The meaning is that there is no punishment. The intention is that when an injury to *dharma* or *tantra* occurs through the negligence of the king, and the theft has been committed such that the thief's own fault has resulted, it is not proper to inflict punishment upon the Brāhmaṇa.

Some explain it thus: if one is endowed with learning and virtuous conduct, he may speak because he is to be supported; even one who is not learned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*) may speak. Therefore, even for one who is not learned in the Vedas, there is no punishment when there is an obstruction to the performance of his religious duties (*dharmatantra*).

Others explain it thus: "He should support those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*). This means that whoever is one who ought to be supported must indeed be supported even for such an offense. The word *hi* has the sense of *eva* (indeed). The meaning corresponding to that is: "An appropriate reward must also be given to him. One should not punish even a non-learned person (*aśrotriya*), because for him too there is no punishment for that offense. Why? Because the commencement of this rule, "when there is injury to the system of Dharma," is intended for the sake of the non-learned person. || 18.36 ||

If, while one is engaged in a duty such as the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*), an animal part—such as a side of meat—is harmed, killed, or stolen by someone, and this is reported, the king must immediately provide a remedy for that. If he fails to do so, a fault arises. The repetition [of the word] is for the purpose of concluding the chapter. (18.32)
Now begins the nineteenth chapter.

The fivefold Dharma was introduced as the subject to be explained; therein, four types have been described. Now, the fifth type of Dharma, the *naimittika* (contingent), must be stated. To introduce that, he provides a summary of what has already been said.

Dharma is fivefold: the dharma of caste (*varṇadharma*), the dharma of life-stage (*āśramadharma*), the dharma pertaining to both (*ubhayadharma*), the dharma pertaining to specific qualities (*guṇadharma*), and the occasional dharma (*naimittikadharma*). Among these, the dharma prescribed for a particular caste is the *varṇadharma*, as in: "The initiation (*upanayana*) of a Brāhmaṇa is in the eighth year" (GDh 1.6). The dharma prescribed for a particular life-stage is the *āśramadharma*, such as the kindling of the sacred fire (*samidādhāna*) and so forth for the religious student (*brahmacārin*) and others. The dharma prescribed for both is the *ubhayadharma*, such as the staff made of *pālāśa* wood for a Brāhmaṇa who is a religious student, and so forth. The dharma pertaining to specific qualities is the *guṇadharma*, such as the protection of subjects and so forth, which is connected with the quality of royal consecration (*abhiṣeka*). The occasional dharma is the *naimittikadharma*, such as expiation (*prāyaścitta*), which is to be performed when a specific occasion arises, such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa. Now, intending to explain the occasional dharma, he restates what has already been mentioned.
The duty of the social classes and the duty of the stages of life have been explained. 19.1.

Furthermore, what is accomplished by this sūtra? If it is argued that this is a restatement of what has already been said for the purpose of introducing a topic not previously mentioned, that is incorrect, because the subsequent portion could have been stated even without such a summary. If it is argued that it serves to remove the listeners' desire for further information, that too is incorrect, since that is already achieved simply by the commencement of the specific treatment (naimittika). Moreover, the mention of "caste and stage of life" (varṇāśrama) need not be made, because dharma is being expounded in connection with them; the summary would be complete by merely saying "dharma has been explained. For, if there were a summary of the whole, the exposition of both the general duties of caste and stage of life and the specific qualities of dharma would also have to be performed.
"Because they serve no purpose, the two *ca*s are also meaningless; therefore, this sūtra is inconsistent. To this we reply:

some first explain that [the *ca*s are for] the sake of establishing the substratum (*ādhāra*). This is incorrect, because it is already known from the very commencement of the sūtra: "The castes (*varṇas*) and the stages of life (*āśramas*)," [GDh 11.31].

Others, however, explain that this is for the purpose of establishing the absence of penance for a Śūdra who consumes forbidden food. That too is incorrect; for in the passage, "Of the twice-born who are praised in their own duties" (GDh 17.1), the mention of the Brāhmaṇa is stated for the purpose of illustrating the twice-born in general, not for the purpose of illustrating the Śūdra. Why? Because of the observation of other Smṛtis. As Manu says:

"Thus has been stated in its entirety what is edible and inedible for the twice-born" (MDh 5.26). Since a Śūdra lacks the qualification regarding what is edible and inedible, his lack of liability for penance follows as a matter of course. Others explain that this [text] is intended to establish the qualification for certain duties of caste even prior to initiation; however, that too is incorrect, because it has already been stated in the very passage, "The castes and the stages of life... (GDh 11.31).

Others explain that this is for the purpose of ensuring that women also obtain the duties (*dharma*) of the castes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*). That too is incorrect; for since she remains uninitiated prior to marriage, her status as a member of a caste is already established by the inclusion of the word "castes" (*varṇa*) in the rule, *varṇā āśramāś ca* (GDh 11.31). Furthermore, because the word "stages of life" (*āśrama*) is used, it follows that after [marriage], having been initiated, she is entitled to the duties of the stages of life. Regarding this, Manu says: "The rite of marriage is declared to be the initiation (*upanayana*) for women," and so forth. Since this is already established from that very source, what is the purpose of this present sūtra?

Others say: "This restatement is for the sake of what follows; that which is to be stated hereafter applies only to those for whom duties have been declared according to the division of social classes (*varṇa*). And from this, they conclude that the accomplishment of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is possible even for a *śūdra*. That too is incorrect, because there are only two causes for expiations: the non-performance of what is enjoined and the practice of what is prohibited. Regarding the non-performance of what is enjoined, Manu says:
"In the case of neglecting the obligatory rites prescribed by the Veda, and in the case of violating the vows of a *snātaka*, fasting is the expiation. (MDh 11.203)
Regarding the practice of what is forbidden, Bṛhaspati says:

"But he who performs what is forbidden, especially a Brāhmaṇa, shall undergo fasting for one night if no specific penance has been prescribed; however, if a specific penance has been prescribed, it shall be applied separately for each offense."
And therefore, since [the application of penance] is already established for a Śūdra as well, this [text] was not commenced for the purpose of prescribing it for him.

To this it is replied: This is for the purpose of removing a doubt. Later on, Vedic rites such as the *punaḥstoma* and others will be cited; those do not apply to a Śūdra. Therefore, lest the same exclusion apply to others as well, this doubt is removed. Alternatively, the mention of caste (*varṇa*) is for the sake of favoring the penance with regard to specific stages of life (*vayaḥ-avasthā*). As Bhṛgu says: "He who is eighty years old, or a child less than sixteen..."
"Women and the sick deserve only half of the expiation.
Or [this applies] with regard to a specific degree of strength, as Bhṛgu said:
"That which has been prescribed even for the weak is stated to apply to children and the elderly."
"Or even by one whose conduct is contracted, likewise during a reversal of time. Vyāsa also says:
"Place, time, age, power, as well as knowledge and that which is produced by the intellect..."
"Having recognized that practice is performed without intelligence, one should speak of renunciation. Thus it is said.

The word *ca* (and) is intended to include intermediate [classes of] people (*avāntaraja*). Their inclusion is for the purpose of ensuring that they also receive half of the prescribed penance (*prāyaścitta*). Consequently, they should be considered as belonging to the caste of their mother. The mention of the stages of life (*āśrama*) is for the purpose of establishing the possibility of penances; just as penances are ordained for the destruction of sin, so too are they ordained with respect to the stages of life. Thus, there is a distinction based on what is possible for those engaged in recitation (*japa*) and other such acts. Indeed, fire-offerings (*homa*) and giving (*dāna*) are not possible for one who subsists on alms (*bhikṣuka*), because he possesses no sacred fires and owns no property. Likewise, giving is not possible for students (*brahmacārin*). The second *ca* is intended to draw in the duties of women. Since these are already established by the very mention of caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*), this further restatement is for the purpose of ordaining specific penances. In this regard, the statement of Bhṛgu has been cited: "He whose years are eighty," and so forth. And likewise Aṅgiras.
"Even a woman who has approached [a man] unintentionally shall incur half the sin; but before twelve years have passed, even a man shall become a sharer in half [the sin]. (19.1)

This is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for both the *dharma* of the two [castes] and the *dharma* of the qualities. Although it is stated elsewhere that what will be said later need not be repeated because it can be spoken even without being restated, nevertheless, it is restated here to remove any doubt. Otherwise, since the divine penances such as the *punastoma* and others will be cited later on, someone might suspect that—just as those do not apply to a Śūdra—other penances like the *punastoma* would likewise not apply to him. Another says: That which has been declared is the *dharma* of the castes and the stages of life (*āśrama*), whereas what is about to be declared is the *dharma* common to all human beings. As he says: "Now, indeed, this person... (GDh 19.2). What is established by this? It is established that even those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*) have the right to perform penances. Even though they lack the discrimination between what is fit and unfit to eat, they certainly must undergo penance for killing cows or Brāhmaṇas, or for stealing gold and other such things from a Brāhmaṇa. However, if they fail to perform the penance, they are to be executed by the king. Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, non-possessiveness, and so forth, which are the *dharma* common to all humans, are not restricted to specific castes or stages of life. Therefore, it is entirely appropriate that there be penance for their transgression. As for what was previously stated, "But those born in the inverse order are devoid of *dharma*" (GDh 4.20), that is intended to mean the cessation of their entitlement to those actions that accomplish worldly and otherworldly excellence. 19.1.
Now he states the cause for expiation; he states the occasions for expiation: "Furthermore, this person is defiled by a blameworthy action. (19.2)

Now, indeed, this person is tainted by a blameworthy action, such as: officiating at sacrifices for those for whom one should not officiate, eating what is unfit to be eaten, speaking what is censurable, failing to perform the duties of the instructed, and practicing what is forbidden. (19.2)

But is it not the case that the non-performance of what is prescribed and the practice of what is forbidden are the causes for expiation (*prāyaścitta*), and since this will be established in the subsequent aphorism, this present aphorism is indeed redundant? To this it is replied: The connection with action belongs only to one who performs action without knowing the Self, but not to the knower of the Self; for there is no connection with defilement (*lepa*) in the case of either the non-performance of what is enjoined or the practice of what is forbidden. Therefore, this [aphorism] is intended to establish that only the non-knower of the Self has the qualification for expiation. And so says the *Atharva-upaniṣad*:
"The knot of the heart is broken, all doubts are cut asunder,
and his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen.
Therefore, this [teaching] is for the ignorant.

Now, following the performance of ritual action—*khalu* being used here for emphasis—it is this very person. By the word "this," he points to the embodied knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) through direct perception; by the emphatic particle, he excludes the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Thus says the Upaniṣad:
"Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree."

"Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit of the *pippala* tree, while the other looks on without eating" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1). He is called *puruṣa* because he dwells within the city (*puri*). Thus says the Upaniṣad: "He who knows Him hidden in the cave, in the highest heaven" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4.1). [The objection: Although he is tainted—that is, connected—by blameworthy action (*yāpa*), even though he is also tainted by righteous action (*dharma*), nevertheless, since there is no expiation (*prāyaścitta*) regarding the connection with *dharma*, only *adharma* is mentioned. If it is argued that the word *atha* is redundant because, once it has been stated that "this person is indeed tainted by blameworthy action," there is an inevitable connection with whatever action has been performed, we say: No. It is for the purpose of enjoining the performance of recitation (*japa*) and so forth, even when the occasion for expiation has not been specifically observed. And so Manu says:

"A twice-born man should perform even a single *kṛcchra* penance during the course of a year for the sake of purifying food eaten unknowingly; but for that which is known, it is especially so. (Manu Dharma Śāstra 5.21).
Thus, it is made known that there is indeed an expiation even for what is done unintentionally. And so says Manu:
"The wise know that expiation is prescribed for a sin committed unintentionally;

some say it is also required for one committed intentionally, based on the evidence of the Śruti. (MDh 11.46). Therefore, it should be understood that the penance is more severe for an intentional act and lighter for an unintentional one. And so he will state: "For approaching a woman of the lowest caste (antāvasāyinī), there is a year-long Kṛcchra penance if done unintentionally, but twelve nights if [intentional]," and so forth. The inclusion of the word *karman* (action) is for the purpose of making known the connection even with actions performed in a previous birth. And thus Manu says: "Some [suffer] here due to misdeeds in this life, and others likewise due to those committed in the past."

“Evil-souled men undergo a transformation of their physical form. Thus [it is said in Mānava Dharma Śāstra 11.48]. In that same context, he says: “The killer of a Brahmin suffers from consumption,” and so forth [Mānava Dharma Śāstra 11.49]. And thus, when signs such as consumption are observed, the instruction must be given for the purpose of prescribing penance even for deeds committed in a previous birth; this is the meaning. While it could have been stated simply that one is “stained by sinful action,” the inclusion of the term *yāpya* (curable/contemptible) is for the sake of making known that even a righteous act becomes unrighteous if it is censured by the world. And so Manu says:
One should renounce wealth and pleasure if they should be devoid of righteousness.

"And also a dharma that results in unhappiness and is censured by the world. [MDh 4.176] The term *yāpyena* is a compound with an irregular (visama) formation. This is intended to make it known that even if one has not committed the act oneself, one becomes liable for penance (*prāyaścitti*) merely through being accused, because the act is condemned by others. And so Vasiṣṭha says: "Having falsely accused a Brāhmaṇa of a sin causing loss of caste (*patanīya*) or a secondary sin (*upapātaka*), one should subsist on water for a month and repeat the *Śuddhavatī* verses; thus he is purified—so it is known. By this, the case of one who is falsely accused is explained. [VaDh 23.37–39] || 19.2 ||

Now, the word *atha* (then) is used as a phrase-filler (*vākyālaṃkāre*). The phrase "this person" (*ayaṃ puruṣaḥ*) points to the inner self (*pratyagātmānaṃ*) residing within the aggregate of the body. "Blameworthy" (*yāpyaṃ*) means contemptible. One is "stained by blameworthy sinful action"; when one is stained by the unrighteousness (*adharma*) produced by that, the expression "stained by action" is a figurative statement (*bhākto vādaḥ*). The detailed expansion of examples for such blameworthy action begins with "such as this" (*yathaitat*) and so forth. *Yathā* is used in the sense of an example. "Sacrificing for those unfit to sacrifice" (*ayājyānāṃ yājanaṃ*) refers to officiating at sacrifices for outcasts (*patita*) and the like. "Eating what is not to be eaten" (*abhakṣyāṇāṃ bhakṣaṇaṃ*) refers to eating garlic and the like. "Speaking what is censurable" (*avadyasya vadanaṃ*) refers to speaking falsehoods, vulgarities, and so on. "Omission of what is prescribed" (*śiṣṭasyākriyā*) refers to the failure to perform prescribed duties such as the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsanā*). "Practicing what is forbidden" (*pratiṣiddhasya sevanaṃ*) refers to the performance of violence and other prohibited acts. The word *iti* marks the conclusion, signifying: "blameworthy action consists of just these. Since the phrase "practicing what is forbidden" alone would suffice, the specific mention of "sacrificing for those unfit to sacrifice" and so on is intended to indicate that officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and receiving gifts are permitted for all in times of distress (*āpadi*), even though they require expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Regarding this, Uśanas says: "Having crossed over the distress by performing actions prescribed for times of distress, one should subsequently perform a fourth part of the expiation for those [acts]. The inclusion of "eating what is not to be eaten" also refers to the consumption of garlic and the like during distress or illness. As for the inclusion of "speaking what is censurable," [it refers to...]

This also applies to cases such as when one must give false testimony where the killing of living beings would otherwise occur. Likewise, where people, thinking someone is a Brāhmaṇa, might beat him or seize his property, one may speak an unseemly falsehood for the sake of protecting him; having thus averted that calamity by speaking such a lie, he should later perform a penance consisting of a fourth part [of the prescribed expiation].
If it is asked, "How is one tainted by a blameworthy action? [the answer is: "By resorting to its means. If it is asked, "What is that means? he says:

"For example, officiating at sacrifices for those unfit to sacrifice, eating what should not be eaten, speaking what should not be spoken, failing to perform what is prescribed for the learned, and practicing what is forbidden. (19.3)

The phrase "such as these" (*yathaitat*) is for the purpose of providing examples. Sacrificing for those unfit to sacrifice (*ayājyayājana*) means officiating at sacrifices for outcasts (*patita*). Consuming what should not be eaten (*abhakṣyabhakṣaṇa*) means eating garlic and the like. Speaking what should not be spoken (*avadyavadana*) means speaking falsehoods and so forth. Non-performance of what is prescribed (*śiṣṭasyākriyā*) refers to the failure to perform enjoined duties such as the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*). Performance of what is prohibited (*pratiṣiddhasya sevana*) refers to the practice of violence and the like. The particle *iti* serves to indicate completion, signifying that "this much constitutes the means to unrighteousness (*adharma*). Now, one might object: since the mention of "what is prohibited" (*pratiṣiddha*) already includes sacrificing for those unfit to sacrifice and the rest, their separate enumeration is redundant.

It is said: these are mentioned by their own names in order to make it known that they are not to be performed even though they have been permitted. Consequently, it is established that even for one who lacks knowledge (*avidyā*), there is an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) when these are practiced in times of distress (*āpad*); for in that regard, it has been permitted that "sacrificing for others, teaching, and receiving gifts are for all" (GDh 7.4). Likewise, the eating of forbidden foods (*abhakṣya*)—even those not included in the category of permitted foods—is permitted in times of distress. Similarly, even speaking untruth (*anṛta*) is permitted in times of distress according to another Smṛti; as Vyāghra says:

"If speaking to someone always causes pain to their speech and mind, then one may speak untruth there, as was the word of the tiger. By the force of this permission, there is a lighter penance; that too consists of a fourth part of what was previously prescribed. As Uśanas said: "Having crossed over the calamity by means of actions permitted in times of distress, one should perform a fourth part of the penance for those [actions]. (19.3)
In this regard, they deliberate whether one should perform an expiation or not. 19.4 — 19.3.
Regarding that connection with a curable act, the exponents of the Veda deliberate and investigate whether an expiation must be performed for its removal, or whether it need not be performed. 19.4.

In that regard, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for that defilement resulting from a palliative act (*yāpyakarman*) is as follows: "Penance" (*prāya*) is said to be austerity (*tapas*), and "mind" (*citta*) is called determination (*niścaya*).
Through the conjunction of austerity and determination, it is traditionally known as *prāyaścitta*.
Thus do the exponents of Brahman deliberate upon that which is characterized in this way: "It should be done" and "It should not be done. || 19.3 ||
Regarding this, some say: "One should not do it. (19.5) — (19.4)
First, some say that one should not perform [the rite] by the power of rebirth alone. || 19.5 ||

In the case of a time of distress (*āpatkalpa*), there is no fault, because [the practice] is prescribed as a rule for such circumstances. But even in the absence of distress, if one fails to perform what is enjoined or engages in what is prohibited, the penance (*prāyaścitta*) would be rendered useless. Why?
The reason for this is:
"For action is not exhausted" (19.6). — [End of 19.5]

The word *hi* signifies "because. Because an action performed does not perish without yielding its fruit—nor is it destroyed by expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*)—therefore, an action residing within the self yields its fruit until its destruction. Thus says Śaṅkha:
"Just as seeds remain in the earth and jewels in the ocean, so do actions reside in the self and from there they manifest."

It perishes of its own accord immediately after yielding its fruit, just as the potency of a seed vanishes upon the emergence of the sprout. Thus says the Śruti: “One becomes virtuous by virtuous action and sinful by sinful action. Furthermore, no one is observed here to experience mere pleasure alone, such that one could infer from this that his inauspiciousness is diminished by expiation (prāyaścitta). As for those scriptural expiations, such as “he offers an oblation when [the vessel] is broken” or “he offers an oblation when [the rice] is spilled,” these are subsidiary parts of the ritual (*karmāṅga*) contingent upon specific occasions, not intended for the removal of defects. Even in the world, when a hole in a jar is plugged with lac or similar substances, only the capacity for functional efficiency is restored; there is no return to the original state. Moreover, it is impossible to remove the inauspiciousness that resides pervading the self, just as it is impossible to remove salt that has permeated water. By means of merit produced through expiation, demerit is merely suppressed, not destroyed, just as the coldness of water is suppressed by heat, since coldness is seen to return once again. (19.6)
The word *hi* indicates the reason: because performed action—whether merit or sin—is not exhausted without being experienced. And so says Śaṅkha:
"Just as seeds, jewels, and treasures remain in the earth, even so do actions reside within the self and bring forth their results."

But once the fruit has arisen, it perishes just as a seed does in the sprout; whereas expiations (prāyaścitta) are distinct rites performed on account of a specific occasion, such as the Kṣāmavati offerings and others in the event of a house fire and similar incidents. (19.5)
"One should act"—this is another [reading]. 19.7 — 19.6.

"One should perform penance"—this is another view. "There is nothing higher than this"—this is another established conclusion (*siddhānta*); such is the meaning. First, regarding the performance of duties according to the rules for times of distress (*āpatkalpa*), penance is shown by one scriptural statement even while another statement prescribes those very duties. Even when not in a state of distress, penance is indeed purposeful. How so? It is exhausted precisely through the experience of suffering caused by recitation (*japa*) and other such acts, because the experience of suffering caused by *japa* and the like has that [expiation] as its instrument. Even a long-term [impurity] is exhausted by a short-term [remedy], just as in the world a long-term disease is cured by the drinking of medicine that causes only brief pain.

But how is it understood that unrighteousness (*adharma*), which yields abundant results of suffering, is exhausted through the experience of even a small amount of suffering? It is understood from scripture (*āgama*). And he demonstrates this: "It is known that 'having sacrificed with the *Punarstoma*, they return to the *Savana*'; 'having sacrificed with the *Vrātyastoma*; he who sacrifices with the *Aśvamedha* crosses over all evil, he crosses over even the murder of a Brahmin'; and 'one should cause one who is being falsely accused to sacrifice with the *Agniṣṭut*'. [GDh 19.8–11]

This is his intention: that this matter—namely, "this is a means for accomplishing dharma" and "this is a means for accomplishing adharma," or "when this is done, adharma is destroyed"—is accessible only through scripture (*āgama*), and not accessible through reasoning (*upapatti*), because it is not an object of other means of valid cognition such as perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, all the arguments stated regarding the non-performance of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) are refuted precisely on account of their contradiction with scripture.
As for what was said—that there is no restoration of a jar that has been pierced merely by filling it with lacquer and the like—[that too is refuted].

To this it is replied: In that context, what is intended is precisely the production of fitness (*yogyatā*), and not the actual production of a jar; thus there is no contradiction. Furthermore, even through expiation (*prāyaścitta*), it is simply the fitness of the person that is produced by way of the destruction of demerit (*adharma*). As for the objection that the removal of qualities pervading the self is impossible—like salt pervading water—that is not contradictory, for it is like the removal of dye from cloth by means of alkaline substances and the like. As for the "overpowering" (*abhibhava*) mentioned, that too is refuted by the very scriptural statement: "He overcomes all evil" (*sarvaṃ pāpmānaṃ tarati*). If only overpowering were effected, then the verbal expression "he overcomes" (*tarati*) would be untenable. As for the claim that expiations are auxiliary parts of ritual acts (*karmāṅga*), that is not universal; for where the occasion (*nimitta*) is either the non-performance of a prescribed act or the performance of a prohibited one, there the expiation serves to destroy that specific fault, as in: "He who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice overcomes the murder of a Brahmin" (*tarati brahmahatyāṃ yo ’śvamedhena yajate*). Where neither of those two conditions exists, it should be understood that the expiation is an auxiliary part of the ritual with respect to that occasion.
Now, if this point is established by scripture, then a single example alone would be appropriate; one must state the purpose for providing a multiplicity of examples.

It is said that the presentation of multiple examples is for the purpose of demonstrating the variety of objects [of transgression]. Furthermore, by means of the example of the *punaḥstoma*, he demonstrates first that the fault incurred from accepting what should not be accepted is destroyed, based on the Vedic revelation: “Having accepted much from one from whom one should not accept, one should sacrifice with the *punaḥstoma*. The mention of accepting what should not be accepted is also intended to illustrate eating what should not be eaten and speaking what is blameworthy, because another Vedic text is seen which states: “One crosses over the eating of forbidden food and the speaking of what is blameworthy by means of the *punaḥstoma*. (19.7)
"One should perform penance"—this is another view; "there is nothing beyond this"—this is another established conclusion. 19.6.
And when, consequently, they become disqualified for all ritual acts, then he cites Vedic passages as authoritative evidence on that point:
"It is known from scripture: 'Having sacrificed with the *punar-stoma*, they return to the *savana* [sacrificial session]'. (19.8) — (19.7)

By the word *savana*, ritual action (*karman*) is meant. "Re-attaining that" means that one once again becomes fit for the performance of rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti. The plural form "they come" (*āyanti*) is intended to indicate [other transgressions such as] eating what is forbidden and speaking what is blameworthy. The phrase "it is known" (*vijñāyate*) is intended to point to the Vedic revelation (*śruti*). (19.8)

It is heard in scripture: “Having accepted a gift from one who should not be accepted, one should sacrifice again with the *punarstoma*. And: “One crosses over the eating of what is unfit to be eaten and the speaking of what is blameworthy by means of the *punarstoma*. Those defiled by the fault of accepting improper gifts and the like, having performed the one-day sacrifice named *punarstoma*, return to the *savana*. By the word *savana*, ritual action (*karman*) is meant. They return to—that is, they attain—the Śrauta and Smārta rites; they become fit for them once more. (19.7)
And having performed the Vrātyastoma sacrifices. 19.9 — 19.8.

The particle *ca* (and) serves to draw back the phrase "coming for the sake of purification" (*savanam āyanti*). The plural number in "by the Vrātyastomas" (*vrātyastomaiḥ*) indicates that there are four Vrātyastomas well-known from the Śruti. Those who have passed the time for initiation are called *vrātyas*; because they are to perform sacrifices [with these rites], they are called *vrātyastomas*. And so Vasiṣṭha says:

"One whose *sāvitrī* has fallen should perform the *uddālakavrata*: he should subsist for two months on *yāvaka*, for one month on milk, for half a month on *āmikṣā*, for eight nights on clarified butter, for six nights on unpolished grain fit for sacrifice, for three nights on water, and fast for one day and night. Or he may go to the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of an *aśvamedha* sacrifice; or he may perform the *vrātyastoma* sacrifice. [VaDh 11.76–79]. The mention of the *vrātya* here is also an illustration for those who have committed minor offenses (*upapātaka*). This is because the *vrātya* is listed among the minor offenders in the *Gautama Dharma Sūtra*: "Minor offenses consist of being unworthy of sitting in the same row as the twice-born (*apāṅktya*), with the exception of those before Durvāsas, namely: the killer of a cow, the abandoner of a Brahmin, the composer of spells, the student who breaks his vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*), and one whose *sāvitrī* has fallen" (GDh 21.11); and because another *Smṛti* states: "By the *vrātyastoma*, the minor offense is destroyed. Thus, it is demonstrated that by this [penance], the faults arising from minor offenses are destroyed. (19.9)

The phrase "returning again to the Soma-pressing" is to be supplied as a connective. The *vrātyas* are those who have not been initiated at the proper time. For them, there are expiatory sacrifices to be performed called the *vrātyastomas*. Because of the use of the plural number, it should be understood that there are many such [sacrifices]. 19.8.
"He who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice overcomes all evil and overcomes even the murder of a Brahmin. (19.10) — (19.9)

By the phrase "all evil," he shows the destruction of that sin which arises from the non-performance of what is enjoined and the practice of what is forbidden. The separate mention of "even the killing of a Brahmin" (brahmahatyā) is for the purpose of making known that among all unrighteous acts, the killing of a Brahmin is the most grievous; otherwise, since it would already be included under the category of practicing what is forbidden, it need not have been stated. Thus says Vyāsa:
"There is nothing greater than the killing of a Brahmin among sins, nor than the horse-sacrifice among merits. (19.10)
The words "iti ca" (and thus) require what is about to be stated; "is understood" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
And one should cause him who is being falsely accused to sacrifice with the Agniṣṭut [offering]. 19.11 — 19.10.

By citing the Agniṣṭut sacrifice, [the author] demonstrates the destruction of defects caused by the demerits of other bodies; for false accusation does not occur without some transgression on the part of the person. The word "ca" (and) serves to draw forward the phrase "is known. The particle "iti" is intended to indicate that each [instance] points to a different scriptural source. For thus, since such scriptural evidence is seen in every case, an expiation must certainly be performed.

But surely, regarding a matter that is to be understood through scriptural injunction, what is this deliberation concerning the performance or non-performance of the penance? That [deliberation] is not tenable. If it were performed, then—starting from the rule "The initiation of a Brāhmaṇa"—it would have to be performed from that point onward.

It is said: this discussion is intended to make known that there is no expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the repetition or the combination of mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*). Because of the scriptural observation that "indeed, action is not exhausted," one should not perform expiation when there is repetition or combination of mortal sins; rather, it should be performed separately for each. Thus, expiation does exist for the repetition or combination of other offenses, such as minor sins (*upapātaka*). Some say, however, that this discussion is for the purpose of praising expiation.
Others say: "Expiation applies only to what is done unintentionally, not to what is done intentionally.

This is incorrect, because it would result in contradiction with such passages as: "In the case of approaching an outcaste woman, a year-long *kṛcchra* penance for unintentional action, and twelve nights for intentional action" (GDh 23.33); "If it was preceded by knowledge, then three nights" (GDh 20.9); and "And in the case of a blameworthy act performed with prior intent" (GDh 25.10). Others say: "This discussion is intended to demonstrate the greater gravity of an intentional act."
That is incorrect, because it has already been made known in this very passage: "Now, moreover, this person... [GDh 19.2]. || 19.11 ||

The one-day sacrifice named Agniṣṭut—one should cause one who is being falsely accused to perform it. Since here the *punarstoma* and other elements are prescribed for the purpose of destroying defects, even through expiation (*prāyaścitta*), as through the consumption [of the sacrificial remains], a sinful act is destroyed. Furthermore, the statement of Śaṅkha refers to cases where no expiation has been performed and to matters concerning merit. Now, why is an inquiry made regarding a matter that is established by scriptural authority—namely, whether one "should" or "should not" perform it? It is said: this inquiry is for the purpose of praising expiation; for such an inquiry was not made regarding the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) and similar rites. (19.10)
Now he teaches the penances for those acts for which no specific penance has been prescribed:
"The means of expiation for that are recitation, austerity, burnt offerings, fasting, and giving gifts. (19.12) — [End of] 19.11.

The "expiations" (*niṣkrayaṇāni*) for that act which requires atonement are the means of purification; just as in the world there are purifiers such as ashes for bronze and other metals, so too are these [rites] for unrighteous acts (*adharmāṇām*). Regarding the word "for that" (*tasya*), if it were not used, there would be doubt as to whether the expiations consist of the *punar-stoma* and other sacrifices, or of silent recitations (*japa*) and the like. "Recitation" (*japa*) refers to the repeated practice of the Upanishads and other texts to be mentioned hereafter, characterized by being either loud, whispered, or mental. As Manu says: "The sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*) is superior to the ritual sacrifice (*vidhiyajña*) by tenfold."

"The whispered [recitation] is a hundredfold [more effective], and the mental is recorded as a thousandfold" (MDh 2.85). Austerity (*tapas*) refers to that which will be described, such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and so forth. An oblation (*homa*) is the casting of substances such as clarified butter (*ājya*) into the fire, preceded by mantras such as the *vyāhṛtis*. Fasting (*upavāsa*) is the restraint of all the sense organs. And thus say the authors of the Purāṇas:
"In this world, turning away from faults and dwelling together with virtues—that is to be known as fasting; it is not the mere emaciation of the body."

As for that which they recite among the forms of austerity (tapas) as "fasting" (anāśaka), it refers to the complete renunciation of food, because it is taught together with [other] difficult practices and is designated as "fasting. Giving (dāna) is the bestowing of substances such as gold and so forth upon a worthy recipient (pātra). The use of the distributive compound (visamāsa) is for the purpose of making known that each [of these] is a means of redemption. || 19.12 ||
For that curable offense, there are five means of expiation and purification, beginning with the recitation of mantras (japa). || 19.11 ||
In that regard, he first states the nature of recitation (*japa*).
Regarding what was called "recitation" there, he specifies the recitations:

the *Upaniṣads*, the Vedāntas, the *Saṃhitās* among all the meters, the *Madhu* hymns, the *Aghamarṣaṇa*, the *Atharvaśiras*, the *Rudras*, the *Puruṣasūkta*, the *Rājan* and *Rauhiṇa* *Sāmans*, the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara*, the *Puruṣagati*, the *Mahānāmnīs*, the *Mahāvairāja*, the *Mahādivākīrtya*, any one of the *Jyeṣṭhasāmans*, the *Bahiṣpavamāna*, the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* hymns, the *Pāvamānī* verses, and the *Sāvitrī*—these are the purifiers. (19.13) — (19.12)

The *Upaniṣads* are the secret *Brāhmaṇas*. The *Vedāntas* are the *Āraṇyakas*. Among all the meters (*chandas*), it is the *Saṃhitā*, not the *Pada-pāṭha* or the *Krama-pāṭha*.
