The qualification "among all the meters" is for the purpose of making it known that this applies not only to one's own branch (*śākhā*) of the Veda. The "Honey-hymns" (*madhūni*) are those joined with the word "honey," such as "The winds blow honey for the righteous one" (*madhu vātā ṛtāyate*, RV 1.90.6). The *Aghamarṣaṇa* begins with "Righteousness and Truth" (*ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ ca*). The *Atharvaśiras* is well-known in the *Atharvaveda*. The *Rudras* are those joined with the word "Rudra," beginning with "Obeisance to you, O Rudra, to your wrath" (*namas te rudra manyave*, VS 16.1). The *Puruṣasūkta* begins with "The Puruṣa has a thousand heads" (*sahasraśīrṣā puruṣaḥ*, RV 10.90). The *Rājarauhiṇe* are the two *Sāmans* sung upon this verse: "Men call upon Indra at the distribution of the spoils" (*indraṃ naro nemadhitā havante*, RV 7.27.1). Although these are *Yajus* verses, they are called by these names; therefore, the term "*Sāman*" is used here. The *Bṛhat* is sung upon the verse "Verily, we invoke thee" (*tvām iddhi havāmahe*, RV 6.46.1). The *Rathantara* is sung upon the verse "We praise thee, O Hero" (*abhi tvā śūra nonumaḥ*, RV 7.32.22). The *Puruṣagati* are sung upon the verse "I am the first-born of Righteousness" (*aham asmi prathamajā ṛtasya*, RV 7.27.1). The *Bṛhat* is formed from the two verses beginning with "Verily, we invoke thee" (RV 6.46.1), and the *Rathantara* is on "We praise thee, O Hero" (RV 7.32.22). That which is sung upon the verse "I am the first-born of Righteousness" (TaitBr 2.8.8.1) is also included. The *Mahānāmnyas* are the *Sāman* on the verse "Know, O Maghavan" (*vidā maghavan*, AitĀ 4.15). The *Mahāvairāja* is sung upon the verse "Drink the Soma" (*pibā somam*, RV 6.17.1). The *Mahādivākīrtya* is the *Sāman* on the verse "Shining forth, drink the great [Soma]" (*vibhrāḍ bṛhat pibat*, RV 10.170.1). Any one of the *Jyeṣṭhasāmans* is intended, being a single *Sāman* among the three-verse hymns (*ṛcaḥ*) beginning with "May the goddesses be auspicious to us" (*śaṃ no devīḥ*, RV 10.9.4) and "The bright [light] of the gods" (*citraṃ devānām*, RV 1.115.1). The *Bahiṣpavamāna* consists of the verses beginning with "Sing unto him, O men" (*upāsmai gāyatā naraḥ*, RV 9.11.1). The *Kūśmāṇḍas* are the *Yajus* formulas beginning with "Whatever offense against the gods, O gods" (*yad devā devahelanam*, VS 20.14). The *Pāvamānyas* are those characterized by the mark of "purifying" (*pavamāna*), beginning with "With the sweetest, most intoxicating [draught]" (*svādiṣṭhayā madiṣṭhayā*, RV 9.1.1). The *Sāvitrī* is well-known. The word "and" (*ca*) is for the purpose of including those not explicitly mentioned; consequently, the *Sāmans* and others mentioned in other *Smṛtis* should be understood. The word "iti" indicates a class; thus, only those of this kind are meant. Accordingly, it should be understood that only those recited in other *Smṛtis*, such as the *Śivasaṃkalpa*, are to be taken, and not those not so recited, such as the *Śrīsūkta*. The irregular compound (*visamāsa*) is for the purpose of indicating that each individual item is purificatory.

But is it not the case that since recitation has been stated to be their price, and since these [elements] are the means for that [recitation], their purifying nature is already established? Thus, the mention of "purifying" (pāvana) is redundant.
It is said in reply: the mention of "purifying" is intended to make known their status as purifiers even on occasions other than [the payment for] the cause [of recitation]. 19.13.

The *Upaniṣads* are the secret Brāhmaṇas concerning the supreme self (*ādhyātmika*). The portions of the *Āraṇyakas* distinct from those are the *Vedāntas*. Among all the *Chandas* (Vedic meters) and all the recensions (*pravacana*), the *Saṃhitā* refers to the *saṃhitā-pāṭha* (the continuous text), not the *pada*, *krama*, and other modes of recitation. The "Honey" (*madhu*) consists of the *yajus* mantras containing the word "honey," such as "May the Brahman protect me" (*brahma metu mām*). The *Aghamarṣaṇa* is the hymn of six verses beginning with "Righteousness and Truth" (*ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ ca*), seen by the seer Aghamarṣaṇa. The *Atharvaśiras* is well-known in the *Atharvaveda*, beginning with "The gods indeed went to the heavenly world. The *Rudras* consist of eleven sections (*anuvākas*) beginning with "Obeisance to you, O Rudra, to your wrath. These are recited in all one hundred and one branches of the *Yajurveda*. The *Puruṣasūkta* begins with "Thousand-headed" (*sahasraśīrṣā*). The *Rājatarauhiṇa* Sāmans are sung upon this verse: "Men call upon Indra at the sacrifice. The *Bṛhat* Sāman is sung upon these two verses beginning with "Verily we call upon you. The *Rathaṃtara* is sung here: "We praise you, O Hero. The *Puruṣagati* is on the verse: "I am the first-born of the Cosmic Order. The *Mahānāmnīs* are the verses beginning with "O Maghavan, know [us]. The *Mahāvairāja* is the Sāman sung upon the verse "Drink the Soma. The *Mahādivākīrtya* is on the verse "Shining forth, may the Great One drink. The *Jyeṣṭhasāmans* of the Talavakārin school are those sung upon the two verses "Upwards that [sun]" and "The Bright One. However, the *Chandogas* say: the three Sāmans beginning with *Ājyadoha* are sung upon the verse "The head of heaven," because it is so heard in the Brāhmaṇa. The *Bahiṣpavamāna* is sung upon the verses beginning with "Sing for him, O men. The *Kūṣmāṇḍas* are the three sections in the *Svādhyāyabrāhmaṇa* of the Taittirīyaka: "Whatever offense against the gods," "Whatever debt while not gambling," and "They have bestowed life upon you from every side. The neuter gender is used with the intention of referring to the *yajus* nature. Among them, in the section called *Acchidra*, the verses in the section beginning with "Whatever offense against the gods" are the *Kūṣmāṇḍyas*. Those whose deity is the purifying Soma (*pavamāna*) are the *Pāvamānyas*, beginning with "With the sweetest, most intoxicating [draught]," extending to the end of the *maṇḍala*. The verse "That excellent splendor of Savitṛ" is the well-known *Sāvitrī*; it does not refer to any verse whatsoever having Savitṛ as its deity. The word "iti" indicates a manner; thus, there are other *Pāvamānas* of this kind as well. Regarding this, Manu says:
By reciting the *Kautsa* hymn beginning with "āpaḥ," as well as the three-verse *Vāsiṣṭha* hymn,
the *Māhitra*, and the hymn containing pure [purificatory] signs, even a drinker of spirituous liquor is purified.
By reciting the Āsyavāmīya and the Śivasaṃkalpa even once,
one becomes stainless in an instant, even after having stolen gold.
By practicing the Haviṣyāntīya hymn and the verse beginning with "na tamaṃhaḥ," and by reciting the Puruṣasūkta, one who has violated the Guru's bed is liberated from sin.

"But by practicing the *soma-raudra* [mantras] for many months, one is purified" (MDh 11.249–250, 254), and so forth. Furthermore, because of the statement "the *pāvamānī* hymns" in the section on penances (*prāyaścitta*), these [mantras] are to be recited daily even apart from penance by one who desires prosperity. 19.12.
Now he states the rules for diet for one engaged in recitation (*japa*) and other practices;
he states the rules for diet for one engaged in recitation:
subsisting on milk, subsisting on vegetables, subsisting on fruits, eating a handful of barley-gruel, or consuming gold.
Consuming clarified butter and drinking Soma are purifying acts. 19.14 — 19.13.

*Payovrata* is the practice of subsisting on milk. Because of the mention of a *vrata* (vow), the procedure for fasting (*upavāsa*) should be understood to apply here as well. *Śāka* is well known [as vegetables]. *Phala* refers to mangoes and the like. Regarding *prasṛtayāvaka*: although one should have said "eating a handful of barley-gruel" (*prasṛtayāvakāśana*) based on the context, this specific expression is used in order to include the rules mentioned in other *smṛtis*. Thus Uśanas says: "Having bathed and become pure, when the stars have risen, one should cook a handful of barley-gruel in a copper vessel so that it becomes like thin gruel (*yavāgū*). At the time of cooking, one should perform a protection rite with this mantra: 'Salutation to Rudra, the lord of beings, the lord of mountains; may you protect this! Then, having poured it out with the syllable *praṇava*, having purified it with the mantra beginning 'Of the god Savitṛ,' and having sprinkled it with clarified butter while reciting the *Sāvitrī*, one should then consecrate it."
You are barley; you are the king of grains; you belong to Varuṇa and are joined with honey.
You are the cleanser of all evils, remembered by the seers as a purifier.
Whatever deed has been done by speech, whatever deed has been done by action, and whatever has been ill-conceived by the mind—
may the barley grains purify all that misfortune and the dark-throated goddess of ill-fortune.
O barley grains, purify for me everything— my terrible royal offense joined with great sins, as well as my conduct toward women and children and all my religious duties.
The theft of gold, the violation of vows, officiating at the sacrifice of one for whom it is forbidden,
and reviling Brāhmaṇas— may all these be purified for me by barley.
May the barley grains purify for me all [the sins] of having been cast away by a dog or a pig, as well as the leavings of crows and other such creatures, and my failure to serve my mother and father.

May the barley grains purify for me all this: food from a communal group, food from a courtesan, food from a Śūdra, food at a funeral or birth-impurity, and likewise the food of a thief, as well as everything that is unfit to be eaten.

With these six [verses], and then having sipped [water] with the verse, “Brahmā among the gods...,” and then with the verses beginning with “For breath thee...,” one may thereafter eat everything according to one’s desire. By doing so for six nights, one is liberated from all sin arising from the transgression of rules, from the practice of what is forbidden, from eating what should not be eaten, and from minor offenses (*upapātaka*). Having drunk it for seven nights, one purifies oneself of killing an embryo, violating the Guru’s bed, stealing gold, drinking liquor, and so forth. Having drunk it for eleven nights, one casts off sins committed in the past. Having drunk it for twenty-one nights, one beholds the *gaṇas*, one beholds the Lord of the *gaṇas*, one beholds the sciences (*vidyās*), and one beholds the Lord of the sciences. Thus, day after day, without overeating, one should consume barley-gruel.”

Gold and the other items are well known. By means of the particle *iti*, which denotes manner, the consumption of others such as the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth is also to be understood. The repetition of the verb is for the purpose of making known that each individual item possesses the quality of purity. (19.14)

*Payovratatā* means subsisting on milk as one's food; this follows the rule for fasting because of the mention of the term "vow" (*vrata*). *Śāka* refers to potherbs such as *vāstuka* and the like. *Phala* refers to the fruit of the plantain tree and others. *Prasṛtayāvaka* is boiled rice prepared with barley measured by a *prasṛta*. Regarding this, there is a specific rule from the *Auśanasa*: "Having bathed and become pure, when the stars have risen, one should cook *prasṛtayāvaka* in a copper vessel so that it becomes gruel (*yavāgū*). At the time of its cooking, one should perform a protection rite [with the mantra]: 'Salutation to Rudra, the lord of beings, the lord of mountains; may you protect this. Once it is cooked, having poured it out and purified it with the mantra beginning 'Devasya tvā Savituḥ,' one should then consecrate it with a mantra."
You are barley; you are the king of grains; you belong to Varuṇa and are joined with honey.
You are the cleanser of all evils, declared a purifier by the seers.
The action performed by speech, the deed committed by hand, and the evil thought conceived by the mind—
may the barley grains purify all of this for me, as well as misfortune and the black-throated goddess.
May the barley grains purify for me everything— whether it be joined with great sins, terrible royal offenses, the conduct of children, or unrighteousness.
Stealing gold, violating one's vows, officiating at the sacrifice of one for whom it is forbidden,
and reviling Brahmins— may barley grains purify all of these for me.
May the barley grains purify for me all [the sins] of having become a dog or a pig, of eating the leavings of crows and the like, and of failing to serve my mother and father.
The food of a group, the food of a courtesan, the food of a Śūdra, food from a funeral rite or one in impurity, and the food of a thief— all such forbidden food, may the barley grains purify for me.
Thus, by these six.

Then, having tasted [the water] with the mantra "Brahmā, the god of gods," he should consume everything as prescribed for six nights with the mantras beginning with "To Prāṇa, svāhā. Thereby he is liberated from all sin arising from the transgression of rules, from the consumption of forbidden things, and from the eating of impure food. Having drunk it for seven nights, he purifies the killing of an embryo, violating the Guru's bed, stealing gold, and drinking liquor. Having drunk it for eleven nights, he drives away all committed sins. Having drunk it for twenty-one nights, he beholds the Gaṇas, he beholds the Lord of the Gaṇas, he beholds Vidyā, and he beholds the Lord of Vidyā. Thus, day after day, subsisting on nothing else, he should consume the gruel.

Rubbing gold on clarified butter and then consuming it is "eating gold" (*hiraṇyaprāśana*). Consuming clarified butter is well known. Drinking Soma is prescribed in the context of a sacrifice. Others [say] even outside [of such rites]. Because of the use of the particle "iti," whatever else has been stated in this manner—such as the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) or *śaṅkhapuṣpī*—its consumption should be understood as purifying (*medhya*). (19.13)

Now he states the locations for recitation and other rites: "All mountain peaks, all rivers, sacred lakes, holy fords, dwellings of seers, cow-pens, and sacred enclosures—these are the [suitable] places. (19.15) — [End of 19.14]

H reads *ṛṣinivāsāḥ*. "All mountain peaks" refers to all mountains; the inclusion of the word "all" is for the purpose of including even those that are not meritorious, since the text specifies "meritorious above. Meritorious [mountains] are Kailāsa and others; non-meritorious ones are those not intended here. Meritorious rivers are the Gaṅgā and others; non-meritorious ones are small streams. Meritorious lakes are those that do not dry up, such as the illustrious Puṣkara and others. Holy fords (*tīrthas*) are those such as Kanyātīrtha and others. "Abodes of sages" are the hermitages of Vasiṣṭha and others. A "cow-pen" (*goṣṭha*) is well known. A "shrine" (*pariṣkanda*) is a temple, as in the passage: "The shrine of the gods and the Brāhmaṇa, the lord of the forest."

"One should always perform circumambulation of Vārāha as well as Vāmana," because of this traditional teaching of the learned (*śiṣṭasmaraṇāt*). The use of the particle *iti* is an elliptical indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for other sacred forests and the like; thus, Naimiṣāraṇya and others are to be understood [as included]. The irregular compound (*visamāsa*) serves the purpose already stated. (19.15)

"Masses of rock" refers to mountains; "streams" refers to rivers. Because of the inclusion of the word "all," no distinction between meritorious and non-meritorious [sites] is to be observed. "Meritorious lakes" refers to lotus ponds and the like. "Sacred fords" (tīrtha) refers to Prayāga and other such places. "Abodes of sages" refers to the hermitages of Vasiṣṭha and others. "Cow-pen" is a place for cattle. "Enclosure" is a temple. By the use of the particle "iti," Naimiṣa forest and other such sites are included. (19.14)
Now he states the nature of austerity (*tapas*).
Recitation (*japa*) has been explained along with its accessories. He states the nature of austerity:
celibacy (*brahmacarya*), truthful speech, and the ritual touching of water at the [three] libations (*savana*).
Wearing wet clothes, sleeping on the ground, and fasting—these are the ascetic practices. 19.16. — 19.15.

*Brahmacarya* and so forth are well known. By the word *savana*, the forenoon, midday, and afternoon are meant, because of the plural number. The particle *iti* is for the purpose of including breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and other such practices. Thus Kavaṣa says: "One should perform three breath controls (*prāṇāyāmas*) every day, morning and evening, for sins committed by the generative organ, the anus, the mind, speech, the ear, the skin, the nose, the eye, and the tongue. For eating the food of a Śūdra, having sexual intercourse with his women, or accepting gifts from him—if these are combined—one should perform seven breath controls for seven days; if they are separate, three days each. For consuming what should not be eaten, what should not be drunk, or what should not be licked, and for selling impure things—excluding honey, meat, clarified butter, oil, lac, salt, curd, alkaline substances, and milk—one should perform twelve breath controls for twelve days, twelve for each. For minor offenses (*upapātakas*), one should perform twelve breath controls for half a month, twelve for each. For those equal to mortal sins (*pātaka-samānas*), one should perform twelve breath controls for four months, twelve for each. Then, for acts causing loss of caste (*patanīyas*), one should perform twelve breath controls for six months, twelve for each. For acts equal to violating the Guru's bed (*gurutalpa*), one should perform twelve breath controls for one year, twelve for each. Furthermore, they cite this:"

"Sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), accompanied by the vyāhṛtis and the praṇava, performed day after day, purify even the slayer of a Brahmin within a month. Thus, the specific timing for other daily recitations and such acts is to be understood.
And so say the authors of the Purāṇas.
Breath control, celibacy, silence, and fasting;

"Such is the nature of austerity and meditation for the Supreme Lord. The *homās* (fire-oblations), such as the *kūṣmāṇḍa-gaṇa-homa* and others, are well known from other *smṛtis*. As Uśanas says: "In the case of approaching a woman who should not be approached, stealing gold, misappropriating a deposit, eating forbidden food or the like, consuming what should not be eaten, sexual intercourse on sacred festival days (*parvan*), approaching a woman during her menses, or officiating at a sacrifice for one for whom one should not officiate—one should, having had one's hair, nails, and beard shaved, bathe, and from that time forward offer clarified butter once with each of the four *kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras for seven days, twelve days, half a month, or a full month. As Vyāghra says: "For sins of mortal transgression (*pātaka*), minor transgression (*upapātaka*), great transgression (*mahāpātaka*), and all other sins—even those previously committed—one should perform the *gaṇahoma*. By performing it even once, one overcomes everything; how much more so by repeated practice! Furthermore, they cite this:
Performing the Vaiśvānarī, the Vrātapatī, and likewise the Pavitreṣṭi sacrifice at every season, one purifies ten generations of one's lineage.
Thus it is known, it is known. Because it is already well-established, it is not mentioned here; the same applies to the fast as well. 19.16.

Celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is the renunciation of sexual intercourse. Truthfulness (*satyavacana*) is speaking of things as they have been perceived. Bathing at the *savanas*—that is, at dawn, midday, and evening—is the touching of water. Wearing wet clothes (*ārdravastratā*) means wearing the garment put on at the time of bathing exactly as it is, without wringing it out. Sleeping on the ground (*adhaḥśāyitā*) means sleeping upon the bare earth. Eating (*aśanam*) is "food" (*āśa*). The absence of that food is "non-eating" (*anāśaka*), which is fasting. Here too, by the inclusion of the particle "iti," practices such as breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and others are understood. Regarding this, Manu says: "Sixteen breath controls (*prāṇāyāmas*), accompanied by the *vyāhṛtis* and the *praṇava* [should be performed]."

"Even for a killer of a learned Brahmin (bhrūṇahan), these performed day by day purify within a month. The *homa*s such as the *kūṣmāṇḍagaṇahoma* and others are not mentioned here because they are well known. Regarding this, the Śruti says: "One who considers himself impure should offer oblations with the *kūṣmāṇḍa* verses," and so forth. The *gaṇahoma*, however, is that which was taught by Baudhāyana:
"The *kṣāpavitra*, the *sahasrākṣa*, the *mṛgāra*, and the two *aṃhomuc* groups;
the *pāvamānī* verses, the *kūṣmāṇḍya* verses, and those verses addressed to Vaiśvānara."

"Offering oblations of rice cooked with ghee three times a day for seven days—observing a vow of silence, eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), and restraining the senses and their activities—one is released from all sins, even from the most grievous crimes. [BDh 4.7.5–7]. Yājñavalkya says:

"And wherever a person considers himself to be defiled, there one should perform an oblation of sesame seeds and the daily recitation of the Sāvitrī mantra. [Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.309] — thus says Manu.

"There is no recitation equal to the Sāvitrī, no oblation equal to the offering of clarified butter, no gift equal to food and water, and no austerity superior to non-violence. Here, fasting (*upavāsa*) means the renunciation of food. It is mentioned repeatedly among the various forms of austerity (*tapas*) for the sake of emphasizing its importance. Another [commentator] says: "Fasting," as recited among the means of atonement (*niṣkrayaṇa*), refers to the restraint of the senses;
it is that dwelling with virtuous qualities by one who has indeed turned away from faults.
They call that alone true fasting, not the mere emaciation of the body.
"Because it is seen thus in the Purāṇa. (19.15)
Now he shows the means for practicing generosity. Next, he states the things to be given:
gold, a cow, clothing, a horse, land, sesame seeds, clarified butter, and food—these are the things to be given. 19.17 — 19.16.
Gold and the other items are well known. The particle *iti* is used for the purpose of including gems and so forth. 19.17.
This has been explained by the [very] words [of the text]. 19.16.
Now he states the duration of time.
To the question, "How long is the time for the recitation (*japa*) and other rites? he says:
"A year, six months, four, three, two, or one; twenty-four days, twelve days, six days, three days, and a day and night—these are the durations. (19.18) — [End of] 19.17.
H reads: "Because of the particle 'iti' in the phrase 'two or one,' only the night and the day are understood. (19.18)
For as long as he considers himself pure in these matters, for that long [the period lasts]. || 19.17 ||

Now, since it is impossible to teach an expiation for every single sin because of their infinite number, he says: "In the absence of a specific instruction, these very [penances] shall be performed as alternatives; they are heavy for heavy sins and light for light sins. (19.19)
These very [rites] should be performed optionally when there is no specific instruction. || 19.18 ||

These very [acts], such as recitation (*japa*) and the rest. The word *eva* (only/very) serves for the purpose of restriction. For if it were merely stated, “these [apply] when there is no specific instruction,” then the application of recitation and the rest would occur only in those cases where penances have not been taught by their own specific names. By the use of the particle *eva*, the fulfillment [of the penance] through repetition is established even when [the penance] has been specifically taught. “When there is no specific instruction” (*anādeśe*) means where another penance has not been taught. This being the case, when there is no specific instruction, they [the penances] occur together with those [others]. “By way of option” (*vikalpena*) means by various combinations; in some cases only recitation, in others only austerity (*tapas*), and so forth, should be performed. In the absence of this [rule], there would be no possibility of combining two or three of the taught recitations and so forth. But when it exists, the establishment of combinations—such as in some cases recitation, in others austerity, and in others giving (*dāna*)—is achieved. Where, then, is the application of these? To this he says: “In sin” (*enasi*), that is, in evil; “heavy” (*gurūṇi*) means great penances, and “light” (*laghūni*) means small penances. If it is asked how the heaviness or lightness of an unrighteous act (*adharma*) is to be known, it is said: by intention (*abhisaṃdhi*), lack of intention, repetition (*abhyāsa*), and so forth. As Āpastamba says: “He who kills while negligent incurs the fruit of the fault; it is greater when done intentionally. The same applies to other blameworthy acts, as well as to those resulting in merit, according to the repetition of the act” [ĀpDh 1.29.2–5, 18]. However, where there is only a prohibition, the heaviness and so forth should be understood in relation to royal punishment, or through the description of censures, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and the ripening of results (*vipāka*) in other Smṛtis, or in view of the excessiveness of suffering and the like. (19.19)

These very acts, such as recitation (*japa*) and the rest, serve as ransoms (*niṣkrayaṇa*) in cases where no specific expiation has been prescribed; that is, in those instances where a particular penance has not been explicitly mentioned, they are to be performed as alternatives. The particle *eva* is used for emphasis. For example: "Let Devadatta go to the village; he himself [shall go] to the forest. What is established by this? It is established that even in those cases where a specific penance has been expressly stated for fixed causes (*nimitta*), when there is a requirement for a full restoration due to repetition, connection with consequences, and so forth, the inclusion of recitation and the other acts is established. (19.18)
Is the expiation the same for all? No; he says:
"In the case of heavy sins, the penances are heavy; in the case of light sins, they are light.

An offense committed intentionally is grave; its opposite is light. This should be understood to apply as well to cases involving habitual practice and so forth. As Āpastamba says: "He who kills unintentionally incurs the fruit of the fault together with his intention; likewise in other sinful acts, as well as in those resulting in merit, according to the repetition of the action" (ĀpDh 1.29.2–5). || 19.19 ||
The Kṛcchra, the Atikṛcchra, and the Cāndrāyaṇa constitute the universal penance; this is the universal penance. 19.20.

The author will describe the nature of the *kṛcchra* and other penances. The meaning is that the "universal expiation" (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) applies not only when no specific penance has been prescribed; rather, depending on the capacity [of the offender] and other factors, it may be either heavy or light, and whether public or secret. The separate mention of the *cāndrāyaṇa* is for the purpose of prescribing the *cāndrāyaṇa* alone in place of the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra*. And thus, its prescription in place of those two is also established. The particle *iti* is used for the purpose of allowing them to be prescribed individually as well. Consequently, the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* together constitute a universal expiation, and the *cāndrāyaṇa* alone is also a universal expiation. The singular number is used for the purpose of prescribing them collectively. Some explain that the particle *iti* is intended to include the manner [of performance] as well, as Manu says: [Manu 11.209].

"Abstaining from food for twelve days by one who is self-restrained and vigilant—this is the penance called *parāka*, which destroys all sins. (MDh 11.215) The *parāka* should be understood as a substitute for the *prājāpatya* and the *cāndrāyaṇa*. Why? Because of the observation of equal punishment. As Lokākṣi says:
"One should cause thirty-three *paṇas* to be paid for a *prājāpatya*."
Likewise, for the Sāntapana penance, one hundred and twenty-five [paṇas] shall be made to pay.
For the *atikṛcchra* penance, the fine is likewise four hundred and sixty-seven;
for both the *kṛcchra* and the *atikṛcchra*, it is five hundred *paṇas*.

"And one should cause [the offender] to pay five hundred *paṇas* as *parāka*, along with a fine of thirty-three more; so say those who expound the Veda. Here, *prāyaścitta* means "expiation" (*niṣkrayaṇa*). If it is argued that, this being the case, one ought to say "expiation for everything," it is replied: this is for the purpose of making known that whatever is performed for the sake of expiation receives the designation *prāyaścitta*. A technical term is established to convey its literal meaning. Thus Vyāghra says:
"Penance (*prāya*) is said to be austerity (*tapas*), and *citta* is said to be self-restraint (*saṃyama*)."
"The wise know that penance conjoined with self-restraint is expiation. (10.20)

The *kṛcchra*, *atikṛcchra*, and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances will be described below. Because of the use of the word "all," these apply not only when no specific penance has been prescribed. Furthermore, all these heavy sins taken together constitute a single penance; for lighter offenses, there is an *atikṛcchra*, and for the lightest, a *kṛcchra*. Manu also says:
"An excellent twice-born man shall perform even a single *kṛcchra* for the sake of purifying food eaten unknowingly, but especially so for that which was known. (MDh 5.21)
By the use of the word "iti," whatever else has been stated in this manner is included. Regarding that, Manu says:
"For one who is self-controlled and vigilant, fasting for twelve days is the penance called Parāka; it destroys all sins. [MDh 11.215]. [The repetition marks the end of the chapter.]
Now begins the twentieth chapter.

The rule for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) has been stated in connection with curable acts (*yāpyakarman*). In that regard, if the father is involved in a curable act, what should the son do? To this he says:
Now, if one who has committed a curable act does not undergo expiation, what should be done with him? He says: "He is to be abandoned."

One should abandon a father who is a regicide, a priest for a Śūdra, one who sacrifices for the sake of a Śūdra, a corrupter of the Vedas, a killer of an embryo, or one who lives with outcastes or with a woman of the lowest caste. (20.1)

H reads: "And [one should abandon] a woman of the lowest caste (antāvasāyinī)"—one should abandon her according to the rule to be stated hereafter. By the mention of the "father" (*pitaram*), the abandonment of the son and others is established by implication (*daṇḍāpūpikayā*). A "king-killer" (*rājaghātaka*) is one who harms a king who conducts himself according to justice through malevolent magic (*abhicāra*); he is to be abandoned. Thus, there is no abandonment for one who causes death through malevolent magic against a king who conducts himself unjustly. Likewise, it is said in the *Purāṇa*: "He who harms a king because a member of the fourfold assembly (*cāturvidya*) has been killed by him..."
"That evildoer must be excluded by everyone; he is not [admitted] through the mantra. Thus it is said.

As for what he will say, “There is never a lack of subsistence for one’s mother and father” (GDh 21.15), that is to be understood as referring to other circumstances. Regarding the *śūdrayājaka*—one who causes a *śūdra* to perform the *Niṣādasthapati-iṣṭi*, because there is an injunction for that sacrifice. If this is so, then in the case of killing an embryo (*bhrūṇahatyā*), it should be understood as applying to everyone, just like the injunctions. A *śūdrārthayājaka* is one who performs a sacrifice after obtaining wealth from a *śūdra*. Thus says Manu: “Those who, having obtained wealth from a *śūdra*... (MDh 11.42). A *vedaviplāvaka* is a teacher who teaches those who should not be taught. A *bhrūṇahan* is a killer of a Brahmin; the mention of that term is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for those who have fallen from their caste (*patita*). As Manu has said:

"The sapinda relatives and kinsmen shall perform the water-libation for one who has fallen [from his caste] outside [the village], on an inauspicious day, in the evening, in the presence of agnates, officiating priests, and gurus. [Manu Dharma Śāstra 11.182] "And he who dwells with outcastes (antāvasāyin). Outcastes (antāvasāyinaḥ) are Cāṇḍālas and others; as Aṅgiras says:
"The Cāṇḍāla, the Śvapaca, the Kṣattṛ, the Sūta, and likewise the Vaidehaka..."
"The Māgadhas and Yogins—these seven are the Antāvasāyins.
He dwells together with them in one place; by the use of the word "and" (ca), this includes the Cakrikas and others. As Kaṇva says:
"The Cakrika, the Pulkasa, the Jambha, the Kharajīvī, and the Pradīpaka..."

"And these, born of Śūdras, are proclaimed to be untouchable. The connection is "he shall live with an Antāvasāyinī," which means he practices sexual intercourse with her. Now, there arises a doubt: when these causes such as killing a king and so forth exist, does the state of being fallen (patitatva) occur, or does it not?

What follows from this? If he does indeed become an outcast (*patita*), then having included them in the very passage beginning with "the slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of spirituous liquor" (GDh 21.1), one need only say, "one should abandon a father who has become an outcast"; in that case, the term "slayer of an embryo" (*bhrūṇahan*) would not need to be mentioned here. If, however, he does not become an outcast, then abandonment is not appropriate. In another Smṛti as well, the rule for abandonment is stated only in connection with being an outcast; and thus the verse of Manu is shown: "The water-libation (*udaka*) should be performed for the outcast" (MDh 11.182), and so forth.

To this it is replied: first of all, the status of being an outcast (*patitatva*) does indeed occur in these cases. Nevertheless, they are not listed among the "sinners" (*pātakins*) for the sake of lightening the penance. The mention of the "feticide" (*bhrūṇahan*) is for the purpose of making known that the penance is the same as that for him, by establishing equality with him. Where one is equated with another, there a degree of inferiority is also understood, as in the expression "the minister is equal to the king. Among these, the penance for some is heard in the texts, such as "for killing a Kṣatriya, a six-year penance" (GDh 22.13), and likewise "for sexual intercourse with a woman of the lowest caste (*antāvasāyinī*), a year-long *kṛcchra* penance" (GDh 23.33). For those for whom no penance is found, a universal penance (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) must be prescribed. Thus, in every case where an equation is made, the universal penance alone is to be understood. If it is argued that, in that case, because the penances are equal, the enumeration here of false witness (*kauṭasākṣya*) and so forth would follow as a consequence, it is replied: the distinction is made so that a father should be abandoned only when these specific individuals have become outcasts, and not otherwise. In this context, the status of being an outcast should be understood to apply even to the killing of a king and other such acts when committed unintentionally. Why? Because among those taught together, we see that the status of being an outcast applies to even one of them in the case of an unintentional act. As Manu says: [Manu 11.89–90] "By slaying a Brahmin, by drinking liquor, by stealing the gold of a Brahmin, and by having sex with the Guru’s wife—one becomes an outcast; the fifth [act] is association with these. "By approaching women of the Caṇḍāla or other lowest castes, by eating their food, and by accepting gifts from them, a Brahmin falls through ignorance; but through knowledge, he becomes equal to them. [MDh 11.175] Thus ends section 20.1.

A king is one who has been consecrated here; he is not merely one who lives by his birth. One who kills such a person is a "king-killer" (*rājaghātaka*). One who officiates at a sacrifice for a *śūdra*—as in the passage, "One who would officiate for a *śūdra*, let him officiate for a *niṣāda-sthapati*" and so forth—is a "sacrificer for a *śūdra*" (*śūdrayājaka*). One who, having obtained wealth from a *śūdra*, performs a sacrifice is a "sacrificer for the sake of a *śūdra*" (*śūdrārthayājaka*). One who causes the Veda to fall into ruin or confusion by studying during forbidden times (*anadhyāya*) or by teaching those unfit to study is a "corrupter of the Veda" (*vedaviplāvaka*). A "fœticide" (*bhrūṇahan*) is a killer of a Brahmin; this term is also indicative of other great sinners (*mahāpātakin*). Furthermore: the Caṇḍāla, the Śvapaca, the Kṣattṛ, the Sūta, and likewise the Vaidehika.
The Māgadha and the Yogava—these seven are the Antyāvasāyins.

Thus says Aṅgiras. One who dwells in the same place with them is so described. [The phrase] "of those who dwell at the end" (antyāvasāyinām) requires the sense of "one who dwells together. Co-dwelling with them means engaging in sexual intercourse. On account of these causes, one should abandon even one's father; by the mention of the "father," it is implied how much more so the son and others. 20.1.
Now, the procedure for his renunciation is stated.
This is the manner of renunciation:
having assembled his teachers of knowledge and those related to him by birth, [he should perform] all the rites beginning with the water libations.
They should perform the funeral rites. || 20.2 ||

Of that person who is to be abandoned—not his own self—the *vidyā-gurus* (teachers of sacred knowledge), namely the *ācārya*, *guru*, and *upādhyāya* (the plural being used to include all three); the *yonisambandhas* (blood relations), such as maternal uncles, maternal grandfathers, and so forth (here too the plural serves the same purpose as mentioned before); and by the word "and" (*ca*), the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and those for whom he performs sacrifices (*yājya*), and so on—having assembled them together and having made it public by saying, "This man has committed such an act; I shall abandon him"—his sons and other kinsmen shall perform all the funeral rites, such as the offering of water and the *śrāddha*, while he is still alive. 20.2.

Having assembled together all those who are his teachers of learning—namely the ācāryas, upādhyāyas—and those related by birth, such as maternal uncles and others, they shall perform all the funeral rites for the deceased, beginning with the offering of water and ending with the śrāddha. Who [are they]? His sons and other kinsmen; this is because the passage begins with "the father" and because of the use of the plural form. 20.2.
And they would overturn his bowl. || 20.3 ||

The very same relatives who are the recipients of what is to be abandoned would themselves undergo a reversal; "reversal" here means the failure to offer water. The particle *ca* (and) has the sense of conjunction with the offering of water. One should understand that it must not occur immediately after the *śrāddha* rite; therefore, having first performed the offering of water and the reversal of the vessels, one should then perform the *śrāddha*. 20.3.
Having devised some vessel for this thing to be discarded, they themselves would overturn it; "overturning" means turning it face down, so that it becomes devoid of water. 20.3.
To explain how they should be overturned, he says:

"In this regard, the method is as follows: A slave or a laborer, having brought a vessel of impurity from a refuse heap and filled it from a female slave’s water-jar, should, facing south, overturn it with his foot while pronouncing the name [of the deceased], saying: 'I render so-and-so devoid of water. (20.4)

A slave (dāsa) includes those such as the "flag-bearer" (dhvajābhṛta) and others. As Manu says: "The flag-bearer, the slave for food (bhaktadāsa), the one born in the house, the purchased, and the one given [as a gift]..."

"The paternal slave and the slave by punishment—these seven are the origins of slavery" (MDh 8.415). A *karmakara* is a hired laborer; there is an option between these two depending on the circumstances. From a refuse heap—that is, from a place for excrement—one should take some impure vessel, fill it from the jar of a female servant (*dāsī*) who is an attendant, and turn it upside down with one's foot while facing south, casting it away in the *apasavya* manner after reciting the mantra: "I deprive this Devadatta of water. Since the word "this" (*amum*) already establishes the taking of the name, the phrase "by name" (*nāmagrāham*) is for the sake of clarity; it does not mean that one should mutter it in a low voice (*upāṃśu*). 20.4.

A *dāsa* is well known [as a slave]. A *karmakara* is a hired laborer (*bhṛtaka*). From one of these two, from a refuse heap (*avaskara*)—for *avaskara* means a place for excrement (*varcaska*)—having taken some impure vessel from an unclean spot, and having filled it with water drawn from that jar by which the female servant brings water, he should turn facing south and overturn it with his left hand; that is, he should cast it down, turned face-downward. The mantra for this is: "I make so-and-so waterless. [This is done] by mentioning the name. In the word "so-and-so" (*amuka*), one should take the name of the person to be abandoned in the accusative case. [The suffix] *ṇamul* is applied according to the rule *nāmny ādiśigrahoḥ*. If the reading is *grāha*, the formation of the word must be considered. 20.4.
All of them, wearing their sacred threads over the right shoulder and with their topknots loosened, should touch it. || 20.5 ||

All the *sapiṇḍa* relatives—not only the son—should touch that slave or laborer; this is the meaning of "they should lay hold of" (*anvālabheran*). Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītinaḥ*), they should have their sacrificial threads placed on the left (*apasavya-yajñopavītinaḥ*). With their topknots loosened (*muktaśikhāḥ*), having let down their hair-tufts. By this very indicative mark, it should be understood that for other auspicious rites such as sipping water (*ācamana*) and so forth, one with a loosened topknot is unfit. (20.5)
As he was being carried out, all his kinsmen, wearing their sacred threads over the right shoulder and with their hair-locks loosened, should follow him, touching him. || 20.5 ||
The teachers of sacred knowledge and those related by birth should look on [her]. 20.6.
But the meaning is that they should not touch [it]; and by the word "and" (ca), the officiating priests and others are also included.
But they should not touch it. 20.6.
Having touched water, they enter the village. || 20.7 ||

Having performed this rite in this manner, they then bathe and go home. All the funeral offerings (*śrāddha*) and so forth are completed on that very same day. And because of the instruction regarding the entry into the village, it follows that this [rite] must be performed outside [the village]. (20.7)

Having thus performed this rite, having touched water and bathed, they enter the village; that is, they should go inside. From this very fact it is known that this rite is to be performed outside the village. 20.7.
After that, having conversed with him, he should remain for one night reciting the Sāvitrī mantra, provided it was done unintentionally.

After that renunciation, having conversed—that is, having engaged in speech—with him who has been renounced; this penance is to be understood as applying when done through ignorance. Because of the singular number in the word "he should stay" (*tiṣṭhet*), it refers to someone other than a kinsman or similar relative; yet, by virtue of the context, the kinsmen themselves are intended. "For one night" means for a full day and night (*ahorātra*); the meaning is that he should not eat. While muttering the *Sāvitrī*. 20.8.

Therefore, after that renunciation, having conversed with the one who has been renounced out of ignorance, he should remain for one day and night without eating, without sleeping, and without sitting. Because of the expression "out of ignorance" and because of the use of the singular number, this applies even to someone other than a relative. 20.8.
If it was done intentionally, [the penance lasts] for three nights. 20.9.
And if it was done intentionally, [the penance lasts] for three nights. || 20.9 ||

But he who intentionally converses with such a person shall observe the rule prescribed for this case for three nights. And this shall remain so until that person has performed the penance. This refers to conversation regarding other matters, not to inquiries on the road and the like; in those cases, that which was stated by Parāśara should be observed:
"Upon sneezing, upon spitting, upon touching the teeth, likewise upon speaking an untruth, and upon conversing with outcasts, one should touch the right ear" (PārSm 12.19). || 20.9 ||

But he who converses with such a person intentionally shall remain for three nights according to the procedure already stated. This applies to cases such as determining what ought or ought not to be done; however, regarding inquiries and similar matters, that which was spoken by Parāśara applies:
"Upon sneezing, upon spitting, upon touching the teeth, and likewise upon conversing with outcasts, one should touch the right ear. (20.9)

But he who is purified by means of an expiation—once he is purified—they should fill a vessel made of gold with water from a most sacred pool or from flowing rivers, and then cause him to touch that water. 20.10.

The word *tu* (but) is for the purpose of restriction. That is, one who is purified by penance (*prāyaścitta*) is not [purified] by royal punishment. By stating this, it is implied that in other cases, even royal punishment is a cause of purification. Consequently, it should be understood that in those other cases, purification applies even to one who has been punished by the king. When he is purified, the meaning is that he has performed the penance in the presence of the public. Having filled a vessel made of gold (*śātakumbha*)—that is, a golden vessel—from an exceptionally meritorious lake that is practically inexhaustible, or from flowing rivers with constant currents; because of the plural number, from many [streams]. There is an option according to what is possible. Then, they should bathe him—who has performed the penance—with the mantras to be mentioned hereafter, using that vessel. By implication, this refers to those who previously abandoned him. (20.10)

Because of the statement "by means of expiation," the procedure for acceptance to be described below does not apply to one who has been purified by royal punishment; for such a person, purification occurs only in the hereafter. As it is said: "But men who, having committed sins, have been punished by kings..."

"The pure ones go to heaven, just as the virtuous who have performed good deeds. [MDh 8.318] In that case, in the presence of the people, having filled a pure vessel made of *śātakaumbha*—that is, gold—with water brought from the most meritorious lakes or rivers, the kinsmen should then cause him, whose penance has been performed, to touch those waters drawn from it; they should bathe him with those waters. 20.10.

Then they should give him that vessel; having accepted it, he should recite these sacrificial formulas: "Peaceful is the sky, peaceful is the earth, peaceful and auspicious is the intermediate space; I take here that which is the radiant realm," as well as the *pāvamānī* verses and the *taratsamandī* verses.

Then they should give him that vessel; having accepted it, he should recite: "Peaceful is the sky, peaceful is the earth, peaceful and auspicious is the intermediate space; I accept this which is the radiant realm. || 20.11 ||

Then, immediately after, they should give that full vessel to him who has bathed. Having accepted it, he should mutter this mantra. With which mantras? He will say: "Peaceful. It is with these very *yajus* verses already mentioned, beginning with "Peaceful is the sky," with the eight *pavamānī* verses beginning with "Pavamāna, the winner of light," and with the four *taratsamandī* verses. || 20.11 ||

Then, immediately after the ritual bathing, his kinsmen should give that golden vessel to him who has been bathed. Having accepted that vessel, he should recite the mantra beginning with "The sky is peaceful" (śāntā dyauḥ) and ending with "I accept" (gṛhṇāmi). || 20.11 ||
With these Yajus verses—the Pāvamānīs, the Taratsamandīs, and the Kūṣmāṇḍas—one should offer clarified butter as an oblation and give gold to a Brāhmaṇa. || 20.12 ||
At the conclusion of the fire-oblation, there is a gift. || 20.12 ||
And one should offer clarified butter with the Kūśmāṇḍa verses.

Because of the singular number used in the instruction "one should offer," only one person should offer, not all the kinsmen and others. Among them, this should be understood as applying to the one who is qualified. With the *kūṣmāṇḍa* verses beginning with "Whatever offense against the gods, O gods... (*yad devā devaheḍanam*), one should offer clarified butter (*ājya*); and because of the word "and" (*ca*), also with the *mahāvyāhṛtis*. (20.12)
One should give gold to a Brāhmaṇa, and a cow to the teacher.

At the conclusion of the *homa*, one should give gold to a Brāhmaṇa endowed with exceptional qualities; for although the right to receive gifts belongs to the Brāhmaṇa alone, the specific mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" here [indicates this]. This applies to the one who has performed the penance (*prāyaścitta*), not to the performer of the *homa*. Or, one should give a cow to the teacher (*ācārya*). The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to include gold as well. One should give either a cow or gold to the teacher, that is, to the performer of the *homa*. Both of these are primary options; it should be understood that both the cow and the gold are alternatives, as they are presented as equal choices. (20.13)
Or a cow. 20.13.
Conceptual construction ends with desire. || 20.13 ||
And to the teacher. || 20.14 ||
One should also give gold or a cow to him who is one's own teacher.
But for one whose penance ends only with death, he becomes pure upon dying. 20.14–15.

H reads “sa mṛtaḥ. For one to whom a penance ending in life—that is, ending in death—is prescribed, if he should die while striving [to perform it], he is purified by that very death. This is stated even though it is already known: for the purpose of prohibiting *sapiṇḍa* relationship even when there is a recovery [from illness]. The word "tu" (but/however) is for the sake of specification. Even if one dies in the midst of performing a penance having resolved upon a penance ending in life, then too he is purified; specifically, because he died after having performed the penance. Thus says Vyāsa:
If one who is always striving in the Dharma should die in the interim, they will certainly attain all of that; of this I have no doubt.
Thus [ends the verse]. 20.14.
This is stated with the intention of providing a further explanation: since penance has purification as its purpose, purification is established by that very fact. (20.15)
They should perform all the funeral rites for him, beginning with the offering of water and so forth. || 20.15 || — || 20.16 ||

All the rites for the consecration of the deceased (*preta-saṃskāra-karma*), beginning with the water-libation (*udaka-śrāddha*) and so forth—whatever they may be—all these are to be performed for him who has been purified by the penance ending at death (*maraṇāntika-prāyaścitta*), as well as for one who has been rescued (*pratyuddhṛta*), and for one who dies in the interval (*antarā-mṛta*). By implication, these are not to be performed for anyone other than these. From the use of the word "all," the *sapiṇḍas* should also observe the period of impurity (*āśauca*). (20.15)

Even though there is no restoration for him in this world, he is nevertheless purified by death alone; therefore, all the funeral rites (*pretakarman*) must be performed. By the use of the word "all," the period of impurity (*āśauca*) is also included. Regarding one who has begun a penance (*prāyaścitta*) such as that lasting twelve years but dies in the interim, Vyāsa says concerning that case: "If the sacrificer dies in the midst of a righteous act, he attains the full merit of it; of this I have no doubt. (20.16)
This very same water for pacification [is prescribed] for all minor offenses (upapātaka). || 20.16–20.17 ||
H reads: "In all secondary sins (upapātaka), in all secondary sins.

This very thing which was mentioned in the interval as "the water for pacification" (*śāntyudaka*)—namely, that water prescribed for bathing which has been consecrated with the mantras beginning with "The sky is peaceful" (*śāntā dyauḥ*) and so forth—is [to be used] in all cases. By the word "all," this is to be performed even in the case of those secondary sins equal to great sins (*mahāpātaka*) which will be mentioned later, at the beginning of their respective penances (*prāyaścitta*). Thus ends verse 20.16.

This very rite just described, consecrated with the mantras beginning with "The sky is peaceful," is to be performed at the conclusion of the penance for all minor offenses (upapātaka). Others say it should be performed at the beginning. The repetition is as before. 20.17.
Now begins the twenty-first chapter.
The rule for the abandonment of those who have fallen [from their caste] has been stated. But who are they? To this he says:
"The rule for the abandonment of those who have fallen has been stated; but who are they? He states them.

The slayer of a Brahmin, a drinker of spirituous liquor, one who violates the bed of his guru, one who has sexual relations with the female relatives of his mother or father, a thief, an atheist, one who habitually performs censurable acts, one who abandons those who are not outcasts, and one who abandons an outcast—these are outcasts (patita). 21.1.

A "brahmahā" is one who has committed the murder of a Brahmin. A "surāpa" is one who has drunk *surā* of any of the three types; whichever kind of *surā* is forbidden for a particular person, if he drinks that, he is so designated. As Manu says: "The three kinds of *surā* should be known as those made from molasses (*gauḍī*), honey (*mādhvī*), and flour (*paiṣṭī*)."

"Just as one [portion] must not be drunk, so all [portions] must not be drunk by the best of the twice-born" (MDh 11.94). *Gurutalpagaḥ*: "One who approaches the teacher's bed"—the word *talpa* (bed) denotes the wife of the teacher (*guru*, i.e., the *ācārya*); he who approaches her for sexual intercourse. *Matṛsaṃbandhagaḥ*: One who marries a girl on the mother’s side within five degrees of descent. *Pitṛsaṃbandhagaḥ*: Likewise, one who marries a girl on the father’s side within seven degrees of descent. *Yonisaṃbandhagaḥ*: A sister’s husband. *Stenaḥ*: A thief of gold. *Nāstikaḥ*: An atheist, one who denies the existence of the next world and so forth. *Ninditakarmābhyāsī*: One who habitually and intentionally practices censurable acts—that is, prohibited acts—continuously. Because of the mention of "acts," this refers only to physical misconduct, not to transgressions of speech or mind. *Patitātyāgī*: One who does not perform the renunciation of those who have become outcasts (*patita*), such as the slayers of Brahmins and others. *Apatitatyāgī*: One who, out of hatred or other motives, performs the abandonment of those who are not outcasts. These individuals, beginning with the slayer of a Brahmin, are the outcasts (*patita*).
The killer of a Brāhmaṇa is a Brahmaghātaka.
Surā should be known as threefold: that made from molasses (gauḍī), that made from honey (mādhvī), and that distilled from flour (paiṣṭī).

"Just as one [type of liquor] must not be drunk, so all [types] must not be drunk by the best of the twice-born" (MDh 11.94)—so says Manu. In this context, he who drinks that specific *surā* which is prohibited for him is a *surāpa*. "Guru" refers to the father and the teacher. By the word *talpa*, the wife is indicated. "Going" means sexual intercourse. Those related through the mother are those born on the mother's side within five generations; those related through the father are those born on the father's side within seven generations. Those related by birth (*yonisaṃbandha*) are sisters and others. He who approaches these as wives is one who has committed an offense against those related through mother, father, or birth. A *stena* is one who steals the gold of a Brāhmaṇa. An *nāstika* is one who denies the existence of the afterlife. "Blameworthy" (*nindita*) means prohibited. One who intentionally and continuously performs such an act is a practitioner of blameworthy acts. One who does not abandon those who have fallen (*patita*), such as sons and others, out of affection and so forth, is a "non-abandoner of the fallen. But he who abandons those who have not fallen, out of hatred and the like, is an "abandoner of the non-fallen. These, beginning with the killer of a Brāhmaṇa, are the "fallen" (*patita*). 21.1.
And those who associate with such sinners. 21.2.
Those who employ others in sinful acts; and by the word "and," also the one who consents [to them].

Regarding those who, through sinful actions, involve others [in sin]: they incite them there by means of giving wealth and so forth, saying, "Kill my enemy in this manner; this is the means for killing your enemy. Likewise, he who stops someone fleeing while being pursued by a killer, and the one stopped is killed, is also an instigator (*prayojaka*). He whose consent is required for an act to be accomplished is the thinker (*mantṛ*). That person is not mentioned here separately, as he is included within the category of the instigator. Āpastamba, however, has stated that very person separately based on a certain internal distinction: "The instigator, the thinker, and the doer are sharers in the fruits of actions leading to heaven or hell; whichever of these initiates more [of the action], to him belongs the specific fruit" (ĀpDh 2.21.1–2).
And practicing with them for one year. || 21.3 ||
By associating with them for a year through the use of vehicles, seats, and beds, one likewise falls; as Kaṇva says: "One falls by associating with an outcaste for a year;
those who discourse on Brahman say this applies constantly through the use of vehicles, seats, and beds."

By virtue of the word "and" (*ca*), [the loss of caste occurs] even immediately through officiating at sacrifices and so forth. Thus says Vṛddha-Yājñavalkya: "By officiating for [an outcaste], forming a matrimonial alliance, studying the Veda together, or eating together with an outcaste—one falls immediately by associating with such a person."

Because there is no distinction between intentional and unintentional acts, the penance for an unintentional act should be regarded as lighter. As Vasiṣṭha says: "Regarding association with outcasts—whether through the Brāhma (Vedic) or Yauṇa (matrimonial) ties—whatever property was received from them must be abandoned; one should not dwell with them. Having gone toward the northern direction, fasting and reciting the *Saṃhitā*, he becomes purified; so it is known. [VaDh 20.45–46] In this context, the second word "or" (*vā*) in the phrase "through the Brāhma or the Yauṇa" is intended to include [association] by means of eating, sitting, or lying down together. Since the recitation of the *Saṃhitā* is possible only for one who has already studied the Veda, for one who has not yet studied the Veda, the repetition of the *Sāvitrī* should be observed for as long as it takes to complete the study of the *Saṃhitā* of his own *Śākhā*. This is because another Smṛti text states: "One should recite the *Saṃhitā*; for that same length of time, one should mutter the *Sāvitrī*. Furthermore, there is a characteristic mark (*liṅga*) in the *Svādhyāyabrāhmaṇa* of the Taittirīyas: "Fasting, one should study the Veda, the *Svādhyāya*, three times; or else, for three nights, the *Gāyatrī* [Sāvitrī]," and so forth. Thus, because of the observation of this characteristic mark of a Brāhmaṇa text, even though the Vasiṣṭha-smṛti does not specify it, the recitation of the *Saṃhitā* should be understood as being performed three times. One *Prājāpatya* penance should be understood for each single recitation. As Kaṇva says: [text follows].
"One should perform a single *adhyayana* of the Veda, or likewise a *prājāpatya* penance;
or else, a wise man should give ten thousand cows as a gift. However, in the case of intentional contact, that which was stated by Manu should be observed:
"Whatever man enters into association with any one of these outcasts..."

"He should perform that very same vow for the sake of purification from contact with him" (MDh 11.181). This should be understood as referring to what was stated by Vyāghra regarding cases occurring within one year.

However, if one enters into association with an outcaste without knowing it, he should abandon whatever he has received from him and perform the Sāntapana penance. But in the case of intentional association, that which was stated by Kaṇva should be observed.

"But if association with an outcast has been intentionally entered into, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow after having performed the rite for the renunciation of what was received. Regarding eating together, Lokākṣi says:
"Having eaten food together with outcasts, one is purified by the Parāka penance."
"Having understood that, one should perform the vow; thus the knowers of Dharma understand."
Thus [ends the section]. 21.3.
He who, for a year, associates with those fallen persons (patita) by sharing their vehicles, seats, beds, and so forth, is also fallen. Regarding this, Kaṇva says:
"By associating with a fallen person through constant use of vehicles, seats, and food, one falls within a year; so say the exponents of the Veda."
Regarding officiating at sacrifices and similar acts, Yājñavalkya says:

"By officiating for a fallen person, by forming a matrimonial alliance with one, by studying together with one, or by eating together with one—by engaging in these acts with a fallen person, one falls immediately. [MDh] Here, "eating together" means eating from a single vessel.
One becomes an outcast by associating with an outcast for a year through officiating at sacrifices, teaching, or marriage; but not by sharing a vehicle, a seat, or food.

Thus, even this verse from the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra] should be explained in this manner: one falls [from caste] in a year due to riding in vehicles and the like, but not due to officiating at sacrifices and the like; rather, by those [latter acts], one falls immediately. 21.3.
To the question, "What is their state of being fallen? he says: "Furthermore, what is their state of being fallen? Falling is the loss of the duties of the twice-born. (21.4)

"Loss from the duties of the twice-born" means loss of eligibility for those rites prescribed by the Vedas, such as the Agnihotra, and those prescribed by the Smṛtis, such as the Aṣṭakā. While it would have been sufficient to say "loss from duties," the inclusion of the term "twice-born" indicates that his status is like that of a Śūdra. For even a Śūdra is considered fallen and exists in the same condition as one of the inverse castes (pratiloma). 21.4.
The loss of the duties of the twice-born—namely, those rites such as Vedic study, whether they be Śrauta, Gārhya, or Smārta—consists in their lack of entitlement to perform them. 21.4.
And it is unestablished in the other case as well. || 21.5 ||

H reads: “Likewise in the next world”: there is non-attainment [of results] in the next world because there is no connection with the fruit of whatever merit was performed by him even prior to the service of a *patanīya* (one who causes loss of caste). From the word "and" (*ca*), it follows that there is infamy in this world as well. This determination of the essential nature of the category of sin is for the purpose of establishing the disqualification from the duties of the twice-born and for the purpose of encouraging the performance of penance. 21.5.
The loss of those duties—namely, the rites of the twice-born such as Vedic study, whether they be Śrauta, Gārhya, or Smārta—which constitutes their disqualification for them. 21.4.
Some [call] that hell. 21.6.

They consider hell to be that state where one lacks the capacity for action and does not experience the fruits of merit in the next life, because of the arising of extreme suffering for one abandoned by friends and kinsmen; for hell, too, is a cause of suffering. As the author of the *Niruktabhāṣya* said: "Hell is humiliation, it is going down low; no delight is found in it. Gautama, however, considers it to be a portion of hell (*narakabhāga*). 21.6.

Some consider that very thing to be hell: namely, the loss resulting from one's actions and the failure to achieve success in the next world. Because it shares the same grammatical referent as "hell," it is expressed in the masculine gender and the singular number. For one who has fallen away from his duties and been abandoned by his kinsmen, suffering arises; because he fails to achieve success in the next world, not even a trace of happiness remains, and thus this state is indeed hell. However, our own view is that hell is the dwelling of one who is single-mindedly devoted to suffering in a specific place. (21.6)
The first three [stages] are indefinable, according to Manu. (21.7)
The first three are not to be designated as such subsequently.

Among these heinous crimes (*pātaka*), the first three—killing a Brāhmaṇa, drinking liquor, and violating the teacher’s bed—are "indefinable" (*anirdeśya*) because no expiation can be prescribed for them. Manu says:
"For the intentional killing of a Brāhmaṇa, no atonement is ordained. (MDh 11.89) The same applies to the drinking of liquor.

"Intentional [killing], which cannot be specified [as a particular penance], is remembered as resulting in the end of life" (MDh 11.145). Passages such as this are to be understood. Alternatively, it is stated that they "cannot be specified" because there is no possibility of restoration (pratyāpatti). As Āpastamba says: "In this world, there is no restoration for him; however, his stain is destroyed" (ĀpDh 1.24.25). The mention of Manu is intended to show that Manu is the one who remembers (smarta) the entire meaning of the Smṛti. Regarding this, the authors of the Purāṇas say: "The Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, the Sāman-chants, and those mantras belonging to the Atharvans..."
"Whatever was proclaimed by the Seven Sages as Smṛti, that Manu declared. (21.7)

Among the heinous sins (*pātaka*) enumerated, the first three—killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, and violating the Guru’s bed—are *anirdeśya*, meaning their expiation is not to be prescribed. Regarding these, it is said that "their expiation is not to be prescribed. Concerning the killing of a Brahmin, Manu says:
"For the intentional killing of a Brahmin, no atonement is ordained" (MDh 11.89).
Regarding the drinking of liquor:

"Intentionally, it is indescribable, and ends with death; such is the settled rule. Thus [it is stated in MDh 11.146]. Regarding sexual intercourse with the Guru's wife, it is to be sought [in the same manner]. 21.7.
Some say that one who does not violate the bed of his guru does not fall [into hell] on account of women. 21.8.
The H edition reads *agurutalpam*, but the commentary presupposes *agurutalpaḥ*:

"Some hold that for one who engages with women other than his teacher’s wife—provided he avoids the teacher’s wife—he does not fall [from his caste]; but Gautama says that he falls in every case. This distinction is to be understood as being based on the difference between intentional and unintentional action. Since the term *agurutalpa* alone would have sufficed, the inclusion of the word *strī* (woman) is for the purpose of including women of all four castes, so that the status of having fallen may apply even in the case of women born of inverse unions (*pratiloma*). Thus Manu says:
Having approached women of the Caṇḍāla or lowest castes, having eaten [with them], and having accepted gifts from them;

"A Brahmin falls through ignorance; through knowledge, however, he attains equality. [MDh 11.175] If it is argued that one falls only after committing these three acts and not merely by going [to her], that is incorrect, because expiation is prescribed for the mere act of going itself. As Vasiṣṭha says: "Furthermore, in the case of killing an embryo, one should subsist on water for twelve nights, fast for twelve nights, or go to the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of an Aśvamedha sacrifice; by this same rule, sexual intercourse with a Caṇḍāla woman is explained. [VaDh 23.38, 40–41] This should be understood to apply to a single instance of unintentional intercourse. In the case of repetition of that very act, the expiation for violating the Guru's bed (*gurutalpa*) should be observed. As Manu says:

"One should perform the vow for violating the Guru’s bed after having emitted semen into one's own female relatives, into the wives of a friend or a son, into virgins, and into women of the lowest castes" (MDh 11.170). Therefore, because the penance for an outcast is extended to both repeated practice and a single act, one certainly becomes an outcast by the mere act of sexual intercourse. The plural number in the word "women" (*strīṣu*) is used for honorific purposes. One indeed becomes an outcast even with women who are not themselves outcasts. As Kavaṣa said:
"A twice-born man becomes an outcast through ignorance by approaching a woman who is an outcast."

"In the case of repeated practice, one should perform that vow for violating the Guru's bed with full knowledge. Here, since the extension of the vow for violating the Guru's bed applies to repeated practice when it is unintentional, in the case of a single act, that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha should be observed: "Having approached the wife of a Guru, the female friend of a Guru, an outcast woman, or an outcaste woman, one should perform a quarter of the Kṛcchra penance for one year" (VaDh 20.16). It should be understood that even in the case of a single act committed intentionally, one must perform that same vow. 21.8.

Some maintain that one who has sexual intercourse with women [belonging to his teacher's family] falls by violating the teacher’s bed (*gurutalpa*) alone and not otherwise; however, [the author] himself holds that one falls even in other cases. Manu also says:

"Having approached the women of *caṇḍālas* or other outcastes, having eaten [their food], and having accepted [gifts from them], a Brahmin falls through ignorance; through knowledge, he becomes their equal. (MDh 11.175) [21.8]
Now he states the cause for the downfall of a woman:
"By causing an abortion or by serving a man of a lower caste, a woman falls. (21.9)

Whatever has been taught regarding the killing of a Brahmin and so forth should be understood to apply equally to women as it does to men. However, that which is additional for her is now stated: "She falls [from her caste] by associating with a *bhrūṇahan*. The term *bhrūṇahan* (one who kills an embryo) is an elliptical designation for one who is fallen (*patita*). A person of inferior caste is a Śūdra. Some say, based on the use of the prefix *upa-*, it refers to a man of inverse caste (*pratiloma*). As Vasiṣṭha says: "But four [wives] must be abandoned: one who goes to a pupil, one who goes to a teacher..."

Because of the instruction on abandonment in the passage: "And especially she who strikes her husband, and she who has approached a degraded man" (VaDh 21.10), for if one does not abandon such a woman, the consequence would be that he himself becomes an outcast (*patita*). The word "and" (*ca*) serves to include [these acts] together with the killing of a Brahmin and other such crimes. Some say it refers to causing an abortion; as Vasiṣṭha says:
"Those who know the Dharma recognize three sins for a woman in this world:
the killing of her husband, the killing of an embryo (*bhrūṇahatyā*), and the causing of an abortion of her own fetus" (VaDh 28.7).

In that regard, regarding contact with those who have fallen from their caste (*patita*) or those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*), the penance should be understood to be the same as for men, because of the statement of Manu:

"One should know this very rule to apply even to women who have fallen. Although a woman who serves a Śūdra—that is, one who maintains contact with a Śūdra—falls [from her status], nevertheless, the penance should be observed until the birth of a child. As Vasiṣṭha has said:
"The wives of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas who have united with a Śūdra..."
"Those who have not given birth are purified by penance, but others are not. Thus it is said; likewise, the penance for that very case is also stated in that same work.

“They should perform, for each respective caste, the Kṛcchra penance followed by the Cāndrāyaṇa. (VaDh 21.13) The phrase *cāndrāyaṇottaram* means that the Cāndrāyaṇa is the subsequent [penance], or that there are successive Cāndrāyaṇas. This should be applied in order to a Brāhmaṇī, a Kṣatriyā, and a Vaiśyā. Since it has been stated, “Those who have associated with a Śūdra are purified if they have not conceived,” (VaDh 21.12), it should be understood that those who have associated with a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya are also purified even if they have conceived. In this regard, one should infer that for a woman who has associated with a Kṣatriya, the Cāndrāyaṇa is the subsequent [penance], and for one who has associated with a Vaiśya, there are two successive Cāndrāyaṇas. Likewise, in the case of a Kṣatriyā who has associated with a Vaiśya, one should infer that the Cāndrāyaṇa is the subsequent [penance]. As for men who engage in intercourse in the reverse order (*pratiloma*), the rule stated by Vasiṣṭha, beginning with “A Śūdra [who approaches] a Brāhmaṇī,” (VaDh 21.1) should be observed. Regarding intercourse in the natural order (*anuloma*), however, he will state later: “Two [years’ penance] for adultery with another’s wife,” (GDh 22.31) and so forth. In this context, even among those who have become outcasts (*patita*), only the four [wives] are to be abandoned. Why? Because by the word *tu* (“but”) in the restrictive phrase “But the four,” (VaDh 21.10), Vasiṣṭha establishes that only these four are to be abandoned. For the others, however, the rule stated by Manu should be observed.

"One should apply this very same rule even to women who have fallen [from their status]; food and clothing should be given to them, and they should dwell near the house. [MDh 11.188]. He will also state later: "And a woman who is unfaithful... [GDh 22.37], and so forth. 21.9.

The term *bhrūṇahā* refers to the state of being a killer of an embryo (*bhrūṇa*); here, "embryo" means a fetus. A woman falls [from her caste] by killing a fetus with regard to herself. She also falls by serving one of inferior caste—such as a Kṣatriya or the like—to a Brāhmaṇī, a Vaiśya or the like—to a Kṣatriyā, or a Śūdra—to a Vaiśyā. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that she also falls for killing a Brāhmaṇa and other such crimes. Another [commentator] says: she who serves a killer of an embryo or one of inferior caste ceases to be his wife; she falls. By the use of "and," it is meant that she falls for killing a Brāhmaṇa and so forth. The mention of the "killer of an embryo" is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for those who have fallen from their caste. (21.9)
Giving false testimony, malicious tale-bearing that reaches the king, and making a false accusation against one's teacher are equal to mortal sins (pātaka).
The H edition reads "mahāpātakasamāni," but the commentary omits "mahā."

Perjury is the speaking of falsehood when one is called upon to bear witness—this being so because of the exception stated in the rule, "There is no fault in speaking untruth in certain cases" (GDh 13.24). Slander reaching the king is the reporting of another's faults to the royal court; by using the term "reaching the king" (*rājagāmi*) instead of simply "to the king" (*rājani*), that which reaches the king indirectly through others is also included. Speaking directly to the teacher—that is, the preceptor—of some false accusation or fault is also included. These acts should be understood as equal to mortal sins (*pātaka*), that is, equal to the great mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*).

"And false accusations against a guru are equal to the killing of a Brahmin" (MDh 11.55); because of this observation from another Smṛti text, these acts are equal to a mortal sin only when committed intentionally, not through negligence, delusion, and so forth—this is the purpose of the compound formation. And thus, there is no fault when [the act] occurs through negligence and the like. (21.10)

Perjury (*kauṭasākṣya*) is the state of being a false witness, that is, a witness speaking untruthfully. Slander (*paiśuna*) is the disclosure of another's fault, whether real or unreal. The expression "one who goes to the king" (*rājagāmī*), which should have been "one who informs the king" (*rājanī*), is used so as to include even those cases where the report reaches the king through an indirect succession; such cases are also to be avoided for this reason. False accusation of a teacher—that is, of one’s father or preceptor—by means of an untruth, meaning the proclamation of their wickedness, is "false accusation of a teacher. These are equal to the great sins (*mahāpātaka*). According to the Smṛti tradition, when there is an extension of equality [with a great sin], the penance is half [of that prescribed for the great sin]. (21.10)

Among those unworthy of the company at a meal, up to the point of Durvāsas, the killing of a cow, the abandoning of a Brahmin, the composition of heterodox mantras, violating a vow of chastity, and the loss of the Sāvitrī—these constitute minor offenses (upapātaka). 21.11.

Among those unworthy of the company at a meal, from Durvāla onwards—namely, the killer of a cow, the slayer of a Brahmin, the composer of spells against him, the student who has broken his vow of chastity, and one whose Sāvitrī initiation has lapsed—their offense is a minor sin (upapātaka). 21.11.

Those previously mentioned as persons whose food should not be eaten—beginning with one who has a weak digestive power (*durvāla*)—are to be excluded from the list, except for the outcaste (*patita*) and the false witness (*kūṭasākṣin*). However, atheists (*nāstika*) are indeed listed among those whose food is not to be eaten separately from the category of "sinners" (*pātakin*). Why? Because there are three kinds of atheists. As the authors of the Purāṇas have said:
"Atheists are declared to be of three types by those who know the Dharma and perceive the truth:
