the one corrupted in action, the one corrupted in mind, and likewise the one corrupted in speech."
"But one who is corrupt in speech is a minor offender (upapātaka), while one who is corrupt in mind is an offender (pātaka).
Through repetition, however, one who is corrupt in action is called a great offender (mahāpātaka). Thus it is said.

In this context, one who is corrupt in speech is listed among the minor offenses (*upapātaka*), one who is corrupt in mind among the major offenses (*pātaka*), and one who is corrupt in action is described by the very rule: “one who habitually performs censurable acts” (GDh 21.1). Regarding him who is listed among the minor offenses, the penance prescribed by Vasiṣṭha should be observed: “An atheist, having performed the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights, shall desist from atheism” (VaDh 21.29). As for him who is listed among the major offenses, that which was stated by Āpastamba should be observed: “This same [penance applies] to others who have fallen [from their status] as well” (ĀpDh 1.28.14). However, regarding a person guilty of a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*), before its repetition, the general penance should be observed. But in the case of repetition, the penance for killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) as stated by Vasiṣṭha—beginning with “Now, furthermore, regarding the killing of an embryo” (VaDh 23.38)—should be observed. Enough of this digression; we shall now explain the subject at hand.

A *gohantā* is a cow-killer. A *brahmojjha* is one who, having studied the Veda, forgets it through negligence; he is thus categorized. However, one who intentionally abandons it is indeed an atheist (*nāstika*); his fault is more severe. Thus, regarding the one who forgets it through negligence, that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha should be observed: "A *brahmojjha*, having performed the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights, should receive the Veda again from a teacher" (VaDh 20.12). For the other, that which was stated by Manu should be observed.
Denying the Vedas, reviling the Vedas, giving false testimony, and the killing of a friend.

"Eating forbidden food and drink, and the six acts equal to drinking liquor" (MDh 11.56). Among these, "one who performs mantras" refers to one who officiates at sacrifices for a killer of a cow or for one who has killed a Brāhmaṇa. An "avakīrṇin" is a student (*brahmacārī*) who has violated his vow of celibacy. He is mentioned again here because he was previously included among those excluded from the company at a meal (*apaṅktya*); the purpose of this repetition is to indicate that even if such a student has performed the prescribed penance, he must still be avoided as one guilty of a minor offense (*upapātakin*) until he has performed the specific expiation for that particular minor offense. Some explain it thus: the repetition is intended to distinguish between heavy and light penances based on whether the student is a lifelong celibate (*naiṣṭhika*) or not; that is, the penance is light for a student who is still under formal training (*upakurvāṇa*) and heavy for a lifelong celibate. However, that view is incorrect, because the penalty for a lifelong celibate is double—as seen in the *Kavaṣadharma*: "The punishment for an avakīrṇin is double. A "Vrātya" is one whose *Sāvitrī* initiation has lapsed due to falling away. On these grounds, a minor offense occurs. The assignment of these specific names is for the purpose of prescribing the appropriate penances. (21.11)

In the section on *śrāddha* offerings, fifty-one individuals beginning with the thief (*stena*) and ending with those of bad character (*gītaśīla*) are stated to be unworthy of being fed at the row (*apaṅktya*). Among those unworthy of the row, from Durvāla back to the one who has abandoned himself—making thirty-one in total—the false witness (*kūṭasākṣin*) is included. In that regard, the state of being an outcast (*patitatva*) is declared for the outcast, and the same status applies to the false witness. For those other than these, the sin is a minor offense (*upapātaka*). An atheist (*nāstika*) is also listed among them; he is of three kinds, as the authors of the Purāṇas have said: [text follows].
"Those who know the Dharma and perceive the truth should recognize that there are three kinds of atheists (*nāstika*):

one corrupted in action, one corrupted in mind, and one corrupted in speech—these are the three. In this context, the one corrupted in speech is intended to mean a minor offender (*upapātaka*), while the other two are indeed major offenders (*pātaka*). "Killer of a cow" refers to striking [her] with a staff, a wooden stick, or the like. A "killer of the Veda" (*brahmaghna*) is one who, through negligence, has struck or forgotten the Veda (*brahman*) which he had studied. If [the act was] intentional, the rule of Manu applies.
"Being a slayer of a Brahmin, reviling the Vedas, giving false testimony, killing a friend, and eating forbidden food or drink—these six are equal to the drinking of liquor. Thus it is said.

One who performs sacrifices for those who have composed heretical mantras, for killers of cows, or for those who have stolen the Veda; one who is a religious student (*brahmacārī*) who approaches a woman is an *avakīrṇin*. The repetition of this person—who is already listed among those unworthy of sitting in a row—is for the purpose of indicating that even when the penance for an *avakīrṇin* has been performed, the penance for a minor offense (*upapātaka*) must also be performed separately. And this should be understood to apply to sexual intercourse resulting in the procreation of offspring. One whose *sāvitrī* has fallen away because he was not initiated at the proper time is a *vrātya*. Among these, there is the sin of a minor offense (*upapātaka*). (21.11)
The officiating priest and the teacher are to be abandoned for teaching what is unknown and for serving those who have fallen from their caste. || 21.12 ||
H reads: “due to ignorance and due to not teaching.”

On account of ignorance, one may abandon the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*); on account of failing to teach, one may abandon the teacher (*ācārya*). Even for these two causes, there is no fault in abandoning them. Since it is impossible for an ignorant person to perform the duties of an officiating priest, there is no sin for the sacrificer who abandons him. Likewise, if a teacher does not teach properly due to laziness or other such reasons, there is no fault for the student who abandons him. Regarding "service to those whose conduct leads to loss of caste" (*patanīyasevā*)—that is, the performance of acts leading to loss of caste, such as traveling or sitting together with an outcaste—why is this mentioned? For while one might simply say "the two outcastes are to be abandoned," the specific mention of "service to those whose conduct leads to loss of caste" indicates that this explanation is intended for abandonment even before the full year [of impurity] has passed, since the status of an outcaste and the abandonment of one who is not yet an outcaste would otherwise be established by the previous rule. If it is argued that in this case too the fault of abandoning one who is not an outcaste would follow, it is replied: No, what is intended here is not the abandonment of sitting together and so forth. What then? It is the taking of another officiating priest and going to another teacher. In that regard, the fault applies to one who abandons sitting together and so forth, but not to one who takes another officiating priest or goes to another teacher. By the word "and" (*ca*), those whose conduct leads to minor offenses (*upapātakin*) are also included. (21.12)

"Due to ignorance or due to not teaching": if the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) who has engaged in the ritual does not know the mantras or the manual of the rite (*karmapaddhati*), and if the teacher (*ācārya*) does not teach [the student] out of laziness or the like, both of these are to be avoided and abandoned. This is for the purpose of abandoning, even before a year has passed, those who engage in activities such as lying on the same bed or sitting together with an outcast (*patita*). If that were so, the statement "one becomes an outcast after a year" would be meaningless. It is not such an abandonment that is intended here; rather, another officiating priest and teacher are to be taken up. For there is a fault in not taking them up. (21.12)
Elsewhere, one falls away from what has been abandoned. || 21.13 ||

Except in the case of the previously mentioned ignorance or teaching [with wrong knowledge], and except for abandonment or renunciation, one falls; therefore, one must not abandon those two in any other circumstance. || 21.13 ||
Except in cases of ignorance or failure to teach, one must not abandon those two; by doing so, one falls. 21.13.
And some say that he is the recipient of that [gift]. 21.14.

And for one who abandons his officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) or teacher (*ācārya*), the meaning is that he who receives [the property] from him, or the priest or teacher who performs the officiating or teaching for him, falls. According to some, by the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it is understood that the fellow student (*sahādhyāyī*) also falls. Gautama maintains that one falls through intentional knowledge (*jñānāt*), but not through ignorance (*ajñānāt*).

Some maintain that for one who abandons such a sacrificial priest (*ṛtvij*) or teacher (*ācārya*), even the recipient—who accepts him as a patron (*yājya*), a pupil (*śiṣya*), or as a priest/teacher—also falls. Because of the inclusion of the word "some," it is understood that this loss of status (*pātitya*) occurs through acceptance [of the abandoned person] when one knows [his status], and not otherwise. (21.14)
There was never any lack of livelihood for his mother and father. || 21.15 ||

"In no state whatsoever" means even in a state of having fallen [from virtue]. "Non-service" means lack of obedience; that must not be practiced. The meaning is that they are to be served even in that state. Service consists of salutation and so forth. (21.15)

Under no circumstances whatsoever should one fail to serve or show obedience to one’s parents; rather, even if they have fallen from their status (*patita*), one must still perform services such as saluting them. Thus says Āpastamba: “A mother undertakes many tasks; service toward her is obligatory even when she has fallen. (ĀpDh 1.28.9) || 21.15 ||
But they shall not divide the inheritance.

The meaning is that they should not divide—that is, they should not take—that inheritance, which is her property. "Inheritance from the mother" refers to the woman's wealth (*strīdhana*). The inclusion of the word "but" (*tu*) implies that in the absence of such inheritance, food and clothing must be provided even from one's own property. Since there is an injunction for providing food and clothing even when both parents are destitute or in a state of being outcastes (*patita*), it follows by implication that this applies even when they are not outcastes. In this regard, it should be understood that there is no abandonment of the mother even if she has become an outcaste. Why? Because of the observation of another *smṛti* text. As Vasiṣṭha says: "But a mother does not become an outcaste with respect to her son" (VaDh 13.47), and so forth. That was stated with the intention that even in a state of being an outcaste, the mother must not be abandoned by the son. (21.16)
But in the absence of him, his sons and others shall not divide that wealth; it shall go to the king. || 21.16 ||
In the case of falsely accusing a Brahmin, the fault is as great as that [of killing a Brahmin]. 21.17.

If one accuses a Brāhmaṇa of a fault, saying, "This sin was committed by you," then whatever demerit (adharma) belongs to the accused, the accuser incurs exactly that much as well. For example, if one accuses another of being an outcast (patita), he himself becomes an outcast. Just as he is to be shunned by people, so too must the accuser be shunned; yet, even through his own penance, he may regain his status. || 21.17 ||

He who accuses a Brahmin first reveals an existing fault; his own fault becomes as great as that of the perpetrator. As Āpastamba has said: "Having seen a fault, one should not be the first to proclaim it to others regarding one who has fallen; rather, one should avoid him in religious duties" (ĀpDh 1.21.20). 21.17.
Twice [he is] sinless. || 21.18 ||

But for him who makes a false accusation, the guilt of the accuser becomes twofold, both because of speaking untruth and because of the accusation itself. Here, the mention of the *brāhmaṇa* is intended to indicate any member of the twice-born (*dvijāti*). Likewise, another *smṛti* text has been recited without distinction:
"Having called an outcast an 'outcast,' or a thief a 'thief' again..."

"By speaking thus, one incurs an equal fault; by lying, one incurs a double fault. (VaDh 20.30). Here too, the mention of a "fallen person" (*patita*) is an elliptical expression for one who has committed a minor offense (*upapātaka*). This is indicated by the passage in another *Smṛti*: "It is known that having falsely accused a Brāhmaṇa of a sin causing loss of caste (*patanīya*) or a minor sin (*upapatanīya*), one becomes pure by subsisting on water for a month while reciting the *Śuddhavatī* verses; by this, the case of one who is falsely accused is explained" (VaDh 23.39, 41). Thus, it should be understood here as well that the fault applies only to the false accusation of a mortal or minor sin, and not in all cases. Furthermore, this fault belongs only to the one who first reports it, not to everyone who subsequently deals with the matter. As Āpastamba says: "Having recognized the fault, the first person shall not report the fallen person to others" (ĀpDh 1.21.20). (21.18)

In this matter of falsely accusing one who is innocent, he incurs twice the offense; that is, double the penalty. Here, the offense is stated for the mere act of accusation. However, in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra], it is said:
"Having called an outcast an 'outcast,' or again, having called a thief a 'thief'..."

"By speaking falsely, one incurs the same fault as the scales; by lying twice, one becomes a partaker of the fault. Thus it is said. Accusation regarding the grounds of loss of caste (*pātitya*) or theft has been described. Vasiṣṭha, however, states: "Having falsely accused a Brāhmaṇa of an offense causing loss of caste or an offense not causing loss of caste, one shall subsist on water for a month and repeat the *Śuddhavatī* verses; thus he becomes purified. So it is known. (NSm 15–16.22) [VaDh 23.39] 21.18.
And if one is capable, there is a fault in failing to protect those who are being harmed by the weak. || 21.19 ||
The H edition reads: *ca vimocane*. However, the commentary (*com.*) requires the negative [particle]:

"For where there is injury or destruction of one who is weak, if one is capable of liberating them—that is, rescuing them—from that, yet does not liberate them, then whatever fault belongs to the killer, that much fault belongs to this person as well. Furthermore, because of the word *ca* ("and"), if one is capable of providing food, medicine, clothing, and so forth for one who is afflicted by hunger, disease, and the like, yet kills them instead, then whatever fault belongs in that killing, that very same fault belongs to this person as well.
[Objection: But surely, if one causes death for the sake of food, would a fault not also accrue even in the mere cutting off [of such sustenance]?

It is said: because of the inequality between the interruption of food and the interruption of life. When food is interrupted, the cessation of hunger can still be achieved even by means of roots and the like; however, when life is interrupted, there is no remedy whatsoever.
For when a weak person is being harmed by one who is powerful, he who is capable but does not liberate him incurs as much fault as the one who inflicts the harm. (21.19)
For threatening an angry Brāhmaṇa, there is a lack of heaven for a hundred years.

H reads "abhigoraṇaṃ" [as] "by one who is enraged," not by way of jest or the like; regarding the threatening of a blameless Brāhmaṇa, that is, the raising of a weapon—there is no fault in the case of one who is guilty, due to the contingency of being an assailant (*ātatāyin*). "A hundred years" refers to a fall into hell, which excludes heaven. This refers to the case of a person of the same caste. When committed by Kṣatriyas and others, it is double, triple, or even fourfold.
When the killing of a Brāhmaṇa has been committed by those of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes...

This is because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) found in the *Smṛti* of Prajāpati. One should likewise postulate that for years, there may be a doubling or tripling [of the period]. By this same principle, when a crime is committed by a Brāhmaṇa against those of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes, it should be understood as three-quarters, one-half, and one-quarter [respectively]. Just as it is between a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya, so it should be postulated for a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya; and likewise, as between a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya, so it should be postulated for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra. In this manner, it should be understood for every higher caste when a killing is committed by a lower caste. (21.20)

If one, being enraged, raises and brandishes his hand or a weapon to strike a Brāhmaṇa, that threatening gesture results in the loss of heaven for a hundred years; it obstructs the attainment of heaven. The meaning is that it destroys the merits (*sukṛta*) caused by that [act]. By the term "non-heavenly" (*asvargya*), a fall into hell is also indicated. This refers to the case of those belonging to the same caste (*sajātīya*). However, in the case of a different caste (*vijātīya*), [the duration is] double, triple, or even fourfold.

"Regarding the castes of Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, [the penalty] is prescribed for the killing of a Brāhmaṇa. By this same principle, when a Brāhmaṇa has committed an act of threatening (*avagoraṇa*), it should be understood that the penalties are three-quarters, two-quarters, one-quarter, and one-quarter [of the full penalty], respectively, for Kṣatriyas and the others. In the same way, in other cases as well, a proportional gradation should be determined according to the distinction between inverse (*pratiloma*) and direct (*anuloma*) order, based on the relative status of higher and lower. 21.20.
In the case of a blow, the fine is one thousand.
If one strikes with a weapon or with the hand, it results in the loss of heaven for a thousand years, because that [act] is what has been prescribed [as the offense]. 21.21.
For one who kills with gold, there is a lack of heaven for a thousand years; the word "year" (varṣa) is understood to apply to each preceding term [of the scale]. 21.21.
Upon seeing blood, he should plunge into it as far as he can and gather up the dust. || 21.22 ||

When blood is caused to flow from a Brāhmaṇa, that blood, having flowed out from him, shall gather as many particles of dust as it can form into clumps; for that many thousands of years there is a fall into hell—meaning for an immeasurable time. This statement regarding the specific gravity of the offense is for the purpose of making known the specific expiation. As Kaṇva says: "One should perform the Kṛcchra penance after threatening [to strike], and the Atikṛcchra upon striking;
one should perform the Kṛcchra and Atikṛcchra upon causing blood to flow from a Brāhmaṇa. From the specific expiation, a specific punishment should be understood [to follow]. 21.22.

If, by that blow, he should cause blood to flow, then for as many years as that blood, having spilled and flowed out, should take up particles of dust and form lumps, for so many years does that act become non-heavenly. Therefore, one should not threaten a Brāhmaṇa, nor strike him, nor cause him to bleed; this is understood from the context and thus is not explicitly stated. [The repetition marks the end of the chapter. 21.22.
Now begins the twenty-second chapter.
The causes for expiation have been stated; now, therefore, the expiations must be declared for each specific offense. Regarding that, he first speaks of the very first:
thus the causes for expiation have been stated; now the expiations themselves are being declared.
Expiation: For a slayer of a Brahmin who has been thrice shorn, there is attachment to the fire. 22.1.
Expiation. 22.1.

The term "expiation" (*prāyaścitta*) serves to define the scope of the subject; that is, this is indeed an expiation and not for some other unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). "Attachment to fire" means clinging or falling into it. The word "three times" is a qualification of the falling. Furthermore, in the act of falling, one should understand that the head is turned downwards. As Manu has said:

"Or he should throw himself three times headlong into a kindled fire," [MDh 11.73]. For whom is this expiation intended? For the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa, that is, for the killer of a Brāhmaṇa. "Emaciated" means one whose body has been weakened by the abandonment of food. And so says the Kāṭhaka Śruti: "One emaciated by fasting should ascend the fire. 22.1.
This is the heading: penance (*prāyaścitta*) is the performance of austerity (*tapas*) after having reached a firm resolution. And so says Aṅgiras:

"Austerity (*prāya*) is said to be *tapas*, and *citta* is called resolution (*niścaya*); because of the conjunction of austerity and resolution, it is traditionally remembered as *prāyaścitta*. (22.1)
The attachment of a slayer of a Brahmin to fire lasts for three lives after being cut away.

*Śaktiḥ* means attachment; *patanam* means falling. *Avacchātaḥ* means one who has become emaciated through the abandonment of food, being worn away. A killer of a Brahmin, having become emaciated by the abandonment of food, shall fall into the fire three times, rising again and again. This is his expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Regarding this, there is a specific rule from Manu: "Or he may throw himself headlong into a blazing fire three times" (MDh 11.73). The *Kāṭhaka-śruti* states: "Emaciated by fasting, he should ascend the fire. This does not imply death as the end, because of the restriction "three times"; for even while living, he becomes purified by falling three times. 22.2.
Or he might become a target for those who bear weapons when [the battle] arises. || 22.2–22.3 ||

The "target" (lakṣya) is that which is to be pierced by arrows; it may be situated either in a battle (*janya*) or in the midst of an army (*senāmadhya*). The phrase "of those bearing weapons" refers primarily to a combat involving bows, not one involving other types of weapons. (22.2)

*Janya* means battle. *Śastrabhṛtaḥ* refers to archers. From the word "target" (*lakṣyam*), it follows that in battle he should stand as a target for archers discharging arrows. Pierced by them, whether living or dead, he is purified. Yājñavalkya says:
"Or, slain in battle while serving as a target, he shall obtain purification;
even if living, one who is struck down and near death is purified" (YDh 3.248). 21.3.
Or, carrying a skull-topped staff and a skull-bowl in his hands, he shall enter a village for alms for twelve years as a celibate student, proclaiming his deed. 22.3–22.4.

The *khaṭvāṅga* is well known. The *kapāla* is a human skull; as Manu says: "Having made a human skull his banner" (MDh 11.72). Its wearing is for the sake of a mark. He should practice in this manner for twelve years. Remaining a celibate student (*brahmacārī*), he must avoid sexual intercourse. He should enter the village solely for the purpose of begging; that alone shall be his food. Even when wandering for alms, he should use an earthen vessel; as Śaṅkha says: "An earthen vessel. At other times, he should remain in the forest. Because of the instruction regarding celibacy and begging, it should also be understood as a religious vow (*vrata*). As Kaṇva says:

"One who holds a sacred grass-broom (pavitra) in hand, carries a staff, has clay-stained teeth, is covered in dust, dwells at a holy ford, wears a garment of *kuśa* grass, and has matted hair, shall become a killer of a Brahmin (*brahmahā*).
Thus it is said; "proclaiming his deed" means always saying, "I am a killer of a Brahmin."

The *khaṭvāṅga* (skull-topped staff) is well known among the Pāśupatas. The *kapāla* is the skull of a Brāhmaṇa whom he has himself slain. He who holds these in his hands is called *khaṭvāṅgakapālapāṇi*. The *khaṭvāṅga* is in the right hand and the *kapāla* in the left, for the purpose of begging, drinking water, and eating. Thus says Āpastamba: “Having taken a human head for the purpose of drinking and a *khaṭvāṅga* for the purpose of a staff” [ĀpDh 1.28.21–29.1]. Manu, however, says: “Having made a corpse’s head his banner” [MDh 11.72]. According to that view, the banner is at the top of the *khaṭvāṅga* and the corpse’s head is at its base. As for wandering for alms, it is done with a red broken bowl, according to the view of Āpastamba. Being thus equipped, he should enter a village for alms; such is his entry into a village, otherwise he remains in the forest. And he should wander for alms while proclaiming his deed.

“I stand at the door of the house seeking alms, a slayer of a Brahmin,” thus says Parāśara. Wandering in this manner for twelve years, he shall remain a celibate student (*brahmacārī*); he must not become attached to women. Regarding the practice of begging for alms, Āpastamba states: “Seven houses are to be visited without prior intention. Saṃvarta, however, says:
“He may enter the village for the sake of alms if he cannot subsist on forest-grown food. Vasiṣṭha states: “He should eat only one meal a day. (22.4)
He should step aside from the path so as not to be seen by the noble one. || 22.4 || — || 22.5 ||

One should avoid the path from which a noble twice-born man might fall by his gaze; by this same principle, it should be understood that one should avoid him from behind, from the side, and from afar. In that regard, when he is within the distance of a cow-tail whisk (*govālavyajana*), a bath with one's clothes on (*sacelasnāna*) should be observed. As Vyāghra has said:
"One should avoid a Caṇḍāla and an outcast (*patita*) from afar;
within the distance of a cow-tail whisk, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on."

It should be understood that one must avoid even a Śūdra by touch. As Lokākṣi says: "In the case of contact with those who have committed mortal sins (mahāpātakin), bathing is prescribed for all social classes; if one eats without having bathed after such contact, one should perform the Taptakṛcchra penance."
One should drink water mixed with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for three nights;
this same [penance] is prescribed even for contact with menstrual blood, a caṇḍāla, or a corpse.
Thus [ends the section]. 22.4.

Upon seeing that [outcaste], a noble person of the three higher castes should depart from the path and withdraw. On this point, Vyāghra says: "Having seen a Caṇḍāla or one who has fallen [from his caste], one should avoid him from afar;
within the distance of a cow-tail whisk, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on."

Even a Śūdra should avoid physical contact [with such persons]. As Laugākṣi has said: "In the case of contact with those who have committed a mortal sin (mahāpātakin), bathing is prescribed for all castes; if one eats without having bathed, one should undergo a penance for seven nights."
"If it is unintentional, there should be a three-night fast, and one should drink milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* [flowers].
One should declare this same rule to apply even in the case of menstrual blood, a *caṇḍāla*, or a corpse.
By subsisting on standing and sitting postures and bathing at the three daily libations, he shall become pure. 22.5–22.6.

Except during times of conflict or for occasions such as sipping water (ācamana), he should remain standing throughout the entire day; likewise, he should pass the night in a seated posture. By performing the ritual bath at the three periods of the day, he is released from the sin caused by the killing of a Brahmin. The phrase "he shall be purified" serves as a concluding summary. 22.5.

“He should stand during the day and sit during the night” (GDh 26.6). According to his ability, he should perform the three daily junctures (*trisandhya*)—in the morning, at midday, and in the evening—by touching water, that is, by bathing. By practicing this for twelve years, he becomes pure at the end. It is understood that by the very prescription of bathing, the acquisition of the mantras and other elements included therein is implied. Furthermore, the requirement that “it must be performed by one who is pure” is common to all ritual acts. Therefore, the worship of the *sandhyā* also pertains to him; for it is said: “One who neglects the *sandhyā* is perpetually impure and unfit for all ritual acts.”
Whatever action one performs, one shall not partake in its fruit.

Thus, according to the recollection of Dakṣa: "Falling away from the duties of the twice-born is degradation. By this statement, however, what is meant is the loss of those actions that are not auxiliary to the performance of penances and vows, and not the loss of all [actions]. And in this regard, he who has committed two killings of a Brāhmaṇa should perform the vow for twenty-four years; he who has committed three, for thirty-six years. But there is no extension of the single penance [tantratā] based on the identity of the body, time, and agent. He who has committed four [killings] finds no atonement in this world. He should perform this very vow until his last breath. And so says Manu:
"For the second [offense], one should perform double the penance prescribed for the first;
for the third, it is declared to be triple; for the fourth, there is no atonement. Thus says Yājñavalkya.
"But for a Brāhmaṇa who is present at a Soma-sacrifice, one should prescribe double the penance. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.252). Thus ends section 22.6.
Or when his life is at stake, or for the sake of obtaining it, [he may take] from a Brāhmaṇa. 22.6–22.7.

Or, he may be purified when there is the recovery of life for a Brāhmaṇa caused by that [act], meaning having rescued one who was being killed by thieves, tigers, or the like; that is, the life of one person, which had been severed, is restored to another. By this same principle, it should be understood that purification occurs through the liberation of all [beings] from death—that is, from the severance of their vital breaths—when they belong to the same species as the victim. 22.6.

If a Brāhmaṇa who is being killed by thieves, tigers, or the like should regain his life on account of that [act], then he would be purified. For what difference is there here between one whose life-breaths are severed and another to whom they are restored? By this same logic, it should be understood that purification occurs for all [offenders] when, upon the killing of someone, a member of that same class regains his life through that very cause.
Or, in the case of a deficiency of materials, he should perform at least three [additional] oblations. 22.7–8.
H [the commentator] omits "vā" (or).

By virtue of the context, whatever property of a Brāhmaṇa there may be—such as gold and so forth—if that too is sufficient for his livelihood—that wealth (*draviṇa*) is also of the nature of life, according to the scriptural insight: "For these external things are indeed the vital breaths. When such property is being carried off or has been carried off by robbers, one is purified by its recovery or by its restitution. If restitution is impossible, then "three times attempted" means that human effort has been exerted three times. As Manu says: "Or having attempted at least three times, or having conquered all their property..."

"Or, by saving the life of a Brahmin for that purpose, he is liberated. [MDh 11.80] From this very indicative mark, it should be understood that purification occurs even through the gift of wealth sufficient for the experience of a poor man without causing him distress. 22.7.

The term "of a Brāhmaṇa" carries over from the previous context. When the property of a Brāhmaṇa is being diminished or stolen by thieves and others, one who has gone to the presence of those thieves and others for the purpose of recovering it, having been wounded by them with weapons and the like, is exempted [from the rule] if he has been struck once; however, if he has been attacked three times—meaning fewer than three times—he is purified even if the property is not recovered. But if the property is recovered, he is purified even if the attempt was made only once. Or, if he has been attacked at least three times, or having conquered all their possessions... [MDh 11.80]
Thus says Manu. By this same principle, purification should be understood as occurring even through the gift of one's own property. And so Manu says:
"Or he should bestow his entire property upon a Veda-knowing Brāhmaṇa;
or wealth sufficient for a livelihood, or a house together with its furnishings" (MDh 11.76).
But Yājñavalkya says:
"Having given sufficient wealth or a vessel, one may obtain purification;
and for the sake of the purifier's own purification, the Vaiśvānara sacrifice is prescribed. (YDh 3.250) || 22.8 ||
Or at the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*). || 22.8 || — || 22.9 ||

The mention of the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) is for the purpose of excluding other ritual actions. By the force of the statement itself, they should cause him to touch water; the word "he shall be purified" (*śudhyet*) is understood to carry over. Because of the inclusion of the word "or" (*vā*) and because these are mentioned as complete [acts], these penances (*prāyaścitta*) are indeed independent. Some say this refers to one who has already commenced the twelve-year penance. And so Śaṅkha, having stated that "one attains purification at the end of twelve years," says: "Or, in the interim, by releasing a Brāhmaṇa from danger or by saving twelve cows. In that case, in the event of repetition, it should be understood as a specific qualification for the completion of the commenced twelve-year penance; however, in the absence of repetition, they are indeed independent. (22.8)

The word "having bathed" (*snātvā*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. One may become pure by bathing oneself at the *avabhṛtha* (concluding purificatory bath) of another's horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*). In the sūtras beginning with "the recovery of life," the word "or" (*vā*) signifies an option. Regarding this, there is a specific rule from the *Mānava-dharmaśāstra*: "Or, having confessed his own sin in the assembly of the gods of the earth and the god of men, he is released from it after bathing at the *avabhṛtha* of a horse sacrifice. (MDh 11.82) The "gods of the earth" (*bhūmideva*) are the Brahmins who serve as officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). The "god of men" (*naradeva*) is the king who is the patron of the sacrifice (*yajamāna*). In their assembly, one should "confess" (*śiṣṭvā*)—that is, make public—one's own sin. 22.9.
Even at another sacrifice, if it ends with the Agniṣṭut [stotra], [the same applies]. 22.9–10.

That which has another sacrifice as its [concluding] bath is called "another-sacrifice-bath" (*anyayajñāvabhṛtha*). And that sacrifice is one which ends with the *agniṣṭut*; the meaning is that the *agniṣṭut* is in the middle. And that is either a *sarvamedha* or a *sattra*; having bathed there as well, one would become pure. (22.9)

One may become pure by bathing at the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) even in a sacrifice other than the Aśvamedha. Is this so without distinction? No; provided that within the interval of that sacrifice there occurs a one-day rite (*ekāha*) named Agniṣṭut. This refers to the inclusion of the Pañcadaśarātra and others. Another says: "Ending with the Agniṣṭut" means having the Agniṣṭut as its conclusion. According to this view, the Sarvamedha and others are included. And here, because the phrase "one may become pure" is prescribed after concluding the twelve-year penance (*dvādaśavārṣika*), and because there is no mention of the word "or," all these [penances] should be understood as independent alternatives, applicable either as primary options or as pertaining to specific cases such as those who instigate the crime. Others, however, say they apply to one who has already commenced the twelve-year penance. Thus Śaṅkha, after stating, "He attains purity in the twelfth year," says: "Or in the interim, by releasing a Brāhmaṇa, or by rescuing twelve cows. The word "or" (*vā*) here serves to indicate an alternative in relation to the other options. (22.10)
A slayer of a Brahmin does not become so merely by the taking of life; what then?
If he has been incited to the killing of a Brahmin, he becomes a slayer even without having killed him. 22.10–22.11.

"Created" means determined or resolved; that is the sense. If one has formed the resolution, "A Brāhmaṇa must be killed," regarding the matter of killing a Brāhmaṇa, he becomes a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa even without having actually killed him. The intention is that this very same penance applies to him as well, because his intention (saṃkalpa) is what is observed [as the cause]. By this same principle, in the case of the killing of any living being whatsoever, that very same penance for that specific act should be understood, since the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" here is intended merely as an illustration. || 22.10 ||

*Sarga* means resolve and determination; one who possesses that is called *sṛṣṭa*. If, in the case of killing a Brāhmaṇa, he has resolved [to do it] and is prevented by someone through fate or other circumstances, he becomes a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa even without having killed him. Therefore, among the penances mentioned immediately above, the lightest one applies to him as well. (22.11)
And likewise in the case of an Ātreyī woman. 22.11–22.12.

The H edition reads *ātreyyāś*, but the commentator assumes the locative *ātreyī*—meaning a Brahmin woman who has reached her menses (*ṛtumatī*)—as Vasiṣṭha says: "They call a woman who has bathed after her menses an *ātreyī*, for it is in her that future offspring is to be found" [VaDh 20.35–36]. When she is killed, one becomes a slayer of a Brahmin (*brahmahā*). The particle *ca* (and) is intended to include Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas as well when they have arrived at a Soma sacrifice (*savanagata*), as Manu says: "Having killed an embryo whose sex is unknown, one should observe this very same vow."

"Also a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who has committed murder, and likewise a woman who is an Ātreyī. (MDh 11.87). The word "thus" (*evam*) is intended to indicate that this applies to the instruction for the complete penance. Others, however, say that an *ātreyī* is one belonging to the lineage of Atri. From the mention of the term *ātreyī*, it should be understood that if she is not an *ātreyī*, one does not become a slayer of a Brahmin (*brahmahā*). 22.11.

“[They] call her who has bathed after her menses an *ātreyī*; whatever offspring is born therein [is significant],” says Vasiṣ�ṭha (VaDh 20.35–36). When even such a Brāhmaṇa woman is killed, one becomes a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmahā*); therefore, the penance for that very act applies. For the killing of a Kṣatriya or others who are *ātreyīs*, the penance is that which is prescribed for the killing of those respective persons. Others, however, say that an *ātreyī* is one belonging to the Atri lineage. 22.12.
And [the same applies] when the pregnancy of a Brāhmaṇa woman is unknown. 22.12–13.
The *H* edition omits the word "brāhmaṇasya.

When a Brāhmaṇa’s fetus is killed by means of medicine or other methods before it can be identified as male, female, or neuter, one becomes a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmahā*), provided that [the fetus] was indeed conceived in a Brāhmaṇa woman. However, once [the sex] is known, it should be understood that the penance corresponds exactly to the gender. The particle *ca* (and) is for the purpose of extending the application of the penance. This penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa, which is of many kinds, is to be applied according to the circumstances, such as whether the killer or the victim acted with intention (*abhisaṃdhi*) or without intention.

On this point, some say: First, regarding the killer, it is appropriate to consider whether he should act or not, because the gravity or lightness of the offense has been stated in relation to acting out of desire or without desire. Furthermore, by the rule "one who habitually performs censurable acts" (GDh 21.1), it is heard that even in the case of repetition, the gravity of the fault increases. However, the calculation of gravity or lightness with respect to the victim being killed is improper, as there is no indicative authority for it. Moreover, in the injunction "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed," a prohibition against killing is prescribed with reference to the Brāhmaṇa. And an attribute of the subject being referred to is not intended to be significant—whether he be virtuous or devoid of qualities—just as in the case of "He cleanses the cup with the *daśāpavitra*," where singularity is not intended to be significant. Therefore, the prohibition is based solely on the caste of Brāhmaṇahood; the quality is not accepted as a factor.
This is incorrect, because there exists [a rule] that makes known the gravity of the offense with respect to the quality of the person being harmed. As Manu says:
"A teacher, or a child, or an elderly person, or a Brahmin of great learning..."

"One should indeed kill an approaching assassin without hesitation" (MDh 8.350). Here, although the killing of even those who are highly learned (*bahuśruta*) and so forth is established by the very permission to kill an assassin, their specific mention is for the purpose of making known that there is a particularly grave fault in killing those who are highly learned and so forth. Just as greater gravity is understood in relation to praiseworthy actions—by which the expiation for killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā-prāyaścitta*) is prescribed for the killing of even a *Rājanya* or a *Vaiśya* engaged in a *savana* sacrifice, according to the rule "if they are a *Rājanya* or a *Vaiśya* engaged in a sacrifice" (MDh 11.87)—so too is it here. As for example:

"A superior twice-born man shall perform this very same penance for one year after killing a Vaiśya established in his duty, and he shall give one hundred cows. Since this has been stated separately regarding the killing of a Vaiśya established in his duty, for the killing of any other [Vaiśya], however, the penance for a minor offense (*upapātaka*) applies by virtue of the rule: "The killing of a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya" (MDh 11.66).

As for the claim that an attribute of that which is being designated is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*), that too is incorrect. By the very injunction regarding penance (*prāyaścitta*), the prohibition of killing a Brāhmaṇa is inferred; for there is no explicit statement prohibiting the killing of a Brāhmaṇa in which one could say that the attribute is unintended to be significant. Even if such a statement did exist, the attribute could certainly be intended to be significant by the very force of the aforementioned indicator (*jñāpaka*). Furthermore, just as the attribute would be unintended to be significant, so too would the number be unintended to be significant; consequently, the same penance would apply equally whether one person is killed or two. And this is not desired. Therefore, even in the case of "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed," it is indeed possible to know that the fault is more severe when killing one who possesses [distinctionary] qualities; thus, everything stated is entirely logical. 22.12

If a Brāhmaṇa’s embryo—whether male, female, or neuter—is not yet known to be such, and it is destroyed by means of medicine or other methods while still within the Brāhmaṇa woman, the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmahatyā*) applies. However, if the sex is known, the penance is according to the specific gender. The same applies, with appropriate adjustments, to embryos of Kṣatriyas and others. Furthermore, the killing of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who has entered the *savana* (the stage of conception) entails this very same penance. As Manu says: "Having killed an embryo whose sex is unknown, one should perform this very vow;
likewise for those born from the seed of Kṣatriyas or Vaiśyas, and also for a woman of the Ātreyī lineage. [MDh 11.87]
On this point, Parāśara says:

"But for one who has committed the murder of a Brahmin and is endowed with knowledge of the four Vedas, one should prescribe the journey to the bridge over the ocean as the penance, performed according to the rules."
On the path to Setubandha, he should collect alms from the four castes,
avoiding those engaged in forbidden occupations, and remaining without an umbrella or sandals.
"I am indeed one of evil deeds, a perpetrator of great sins;
standing at the door of your house, I, a slayer of a Brahmin, seek alms."
In cow-pens and cattle-sheds, in villages and cities,
in penance groves and sacred fords, and by rivers and springs.
Having gone to the ocean, one should confess this sin among these [sacred sites];
by bathing in that great ocean, even a slayer of a Brahmin shall be liberated.
Then, purified, having returned home and performed a feeding of Brahmins,
he gave a hundred cows as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to one learned in the four Vedas.

"In this way, one who is approved by the four castes attains purification. [PārSm 12.65–69] Regarding this, Sumantu says: "A killer of a Brahmin shall perform the *kṛcchra* penance for one year, sleeping on the ground, bathing three times a day, proclaiming his deed, subsisting on alms, and dwelling among the sandy banks of celestial rivers, confluences, hermitages, cow-pens, mountains, springs, groves of asceticism, and forests; he shall not sit in the *vīrāsana* posture. When the year is complete, he should give gold, gems, cows, grain, sesame seeds, land, and clarified butter to Brahmins; thus he becomes purified. Regarding specific castes and specific stages of life (*āśrama*) in this context, Aṅgiras says:
The assembly for Brahmins is considered to be [one person]; for kings, it is held to be double that;
for Vaiśyas, it is declared to be triple. And the penance is remembered to be in accordance with the assembly.

"If those belonging to other stages of life commit the same sins as householders, they should perform purification twice as much as the householder, until the realization of Brahman. This is the purification for householders; it is double for students.
"It should be triple for those living in the forest and quadruple for ascetics. On this point, Bhārgava says:
"He who is eighty years of age, or a child under sixteen,"
"Women or those who are ill deserve [the rites] for the purpose of expiation. Thus says Hārīta:
"But if one who has set out for expiation should die in the midst of it,"
"On that very day he becomes pure in this world and in the next. Thus it is said. (22.13)
The penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa has been stated. Now, regarding the killing of a Rājanya:
for killing a Rājanya, the standard vow of celibacy (brahmacarya) is to be observed for six years. 22.13.
For killing a Kṣatriya, one shall observe the standard vow of celibacy for six years and give a thousand cows with a bull as the eleventh.

When the killing of a Kṣatriya has been committed, "six-yearly" (ṣaḍvārṣika) refers to the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) lasting for six years; furthermore, that is "ordinary" (*prākṛta*), meaning natural and devoid of the skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) and other such emblems. Thus, the meaning is that the very expiation for the murder of a Brāhmaṇa must be performed for six years. This applies to a case where the act was intentional and to the killing of one who possessed [Vedic] conduct (*vṛttavat*). Regarding the killing of one who lacks such conduct (*avṛttavat*):

“Killing a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya, as well as atheism, constitute minor offenses (upapātaka). Thus, the penance for minor offenses is to be understood. The same applies hereafter. In that regard, for a killing committed intentionally, one should look to what will be stated: “The same applies to those who extinguish the sacred fires, those who are excluded from society, and those who have committed minor offenses” (GDh 22.34). But for an unintentional act, that which was spoken by Manu is to be observed: “Twice-born men who have committed minor offenses shall perform this very vow.”

"Or else, for the sake of purification, the *avakīrṇin* shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance. (MDh 11.117) Because of the governing term "of a Brāhmaṇa," this refers specifically to the Brāhmaṇa caste. However, for one of the Kṣatriya caste, a twelve-year penance is to be understood; for a Vaiśya, eighteen years; and for a Śūdra, twenty-four years. This same principle is to be applied in subsequent cases as well. 22.13.

When the killing of a *rājanya* (kṣatriya) has been committed, that same vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) prescribed for the killing of a Brāhmaṇa must be performed for six years. That too means one should perform the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa for six years, which is the standard, natural [penance] devoid of the skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) and other such [emblems]. One should give a thousand cows with a bull as the eleventh (*ṛṣabha-ekasahasrāḥ*). On this point, Uśanas says: "For the killing of a *rājanya*, the Brāhmaṇical vow lasts for six years, and at its conclusion, the gift of a thousand cows with a bull. This applies to the intentional killing of a consecrated (*abhiṣikta*) Śrotriya who observes vows. For the killing of that same person if he is not a Śrotriya or is devoid of vows, there is only the gift of cows. For the killing of one who is devoid of both [Śrotriya-hood and vows] and is unconsecrated, there is only the six-year penance. However, for the killing of one who is unconsecrated but possesses both [qualities], the rule of Vasiṣṭha applies: "A Brāhmaṇa, having killed a *rājanya*, shall observe the vow for eight years. For these same cases, if the act is unintentional, half [the penance] should be assigned. In the case of killing someone by birth alone [without qualities], [the following applies]:
"Killing a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya, as well as atheism (nāstikya), are minor offenses (upapātaka).
Having stated this, [the text continues]:
"Twice-born men who have committed such minor offenses shall perform this very same vow."

One should observe what was stated by Manu: "For the sake of purification, one may perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, with the exception of the Avakīrṇin rite" (MDh 11.117). In the case of killing someone who possesses some minor merit, one should perform the standard one-year period of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) which will be mentioned later in the verse: "The same applies to those who extinguish the sacred fires, those who neglect their duties, and those guilty of secondary sins" (GDh 22.34). This should be understood to apply in subsequent cases as well. In all instances, if the act was unintentional, the penance is half; if intentional, it is full. (22.14)
And he should give cows numbering one thousand and one bulls.
Regarding those who possess virtuous conduct (*vṛttavantaḥ*): as before, this should be understood as referring to cases where the act was unintentional. As Manu has said:
"A fourth part of the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa is prescribed for the killing of a Kṣatriya;
an eighth part for a Vaiśya who maintains his conduct; but for a Śūdra, it should be known as a sixteenth part. (MDh 11.126)
Having said this, he spoke again:
"But if a preeminent twice-born man unintentionally causes the death of a Kṣatriya,
he should give one thousand cows with a bull as the eleventh for the sake of his own purification."
Or, with self-restraint, one may perform the vow for the slayer of a Brahmin for three years, wearing matted hair.

"One should live at a great distance from a village, making one's dwelling at the foot of a tree" (MDh 11.127–28)—thus it should be understood. In this manner, in all cases, the six-year period of ordinary *brahmacarya* accompanied by gifts should also be understood from the word "and" (*ca*). As Uśanas says: "For the killing of a Kṣatriya, one shall observe the vow of a Brahmin-killer for six years, and at its conclusion, give a gift of one thousand cows plus a bull. This applies to the intentional killing of one endowed with the quality of consecration (*abhiṣeka*). But for unintentional killing, he himself says: "Or one should perform it for eight years. (22.14)
In the case of a Vaiśya, [the fine] is for three years' worth [of grain]. || 22.15 ||
But for a Vaiśya, he should give three years' worth of provisions and one hundred cows with a bull as the hundred-and-first.
The ordinary form of celibacy is to be understood as applying to the Kṣatriya class. 22.15.
This [penance] applies to the intentional killing of one who possesses supreme virtues; by this, the case of others is explained. || 22.15 ||
And he should give one hundred and one cows, including a bull.

As before, this refers to the case of intentional killing. And so it has been stated and cited by Manu: “He shall perform this very [penance] for one year,” and so forth. By the use of the word *ca* (and), it is understood that this applies even to the preceding case. That too applies to the intentional killing of one who possesses extreme virtues. However, in the case of unintentional killing, this very rule—“They shall perform this very vow” (MDh 11.117)—is to be observed. For it would be improper to prescribe the same penance for a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya; thus, it might be argued that it would not apply to those who have not practiced [the Veda]. If it is asked: “In that case, does it follow from the rule ‘And likewise in the case of those who extinguish the sacred fires, the *nirākṛti*, and minor sins’ (GDh 22.34) that equality applies to the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya who have not practiced? To this it is replied: the deficiency must be filled by means of austerity (*tapas*). And so says Manu.
"In whatever action he has committed that causes unease in his mind, he should perform penance for it until it becomes a source of satisfaction. (Manu Dharmaśāstra 11.233)

In this manner, it should be inferred in all cases. This being established, regarding the unintentional killing of a virtuous Vaiśya, that which is stated in another Smṛti should be observed. As Uśanas says: "Having killed a Vaiśya, one should perform the vow for the killing of a Brāhmaṇa for seven months. In all cases, when there is an abundance of qualities or when an act is repeated, an increase in the recitation of prayers (*japa*) and so forth must also be prescribed. Although the obligation to give is already established by the general heading [of the rule], the explicit mention of "he shall give" is for the purpose of including other substances as well in the absence of cows. And thus Vyāghra says:
In the absence of cows, he should give a gold *niṣka*, or half a *niṣka*, or even a quarter;
or whatever else the recipient might accept, that he should give to a *śrotriya*.
In the case of a Śūdra, [the penance lasts] for one year. || 22.17 ||
For killing a Śūdra, one should give a cow for each year of age and eleven bulls as a fine.
This [penance] applies to the intentional killing of a servant of a twice-born man. 22.17.

This [penance] also pertains to the killing of one who possesses extreme virtues. Regarding the killing of a *śūdra* who is utterly devoid of qualities, the *Auśanasa* states: "Having killed a *śūdra*, one should perform the *taptakṛcchra*. Now, regarding the case of those born in the direct order (*anuloma*), Vyāghra says: "In the case of all those born in the direct order, for the killing of their respective mothers, the learned man should prescribe that very same penance; and for women, half of that."

"Regarding the killing of an Ātreyī woman, one should state that which is prescribed for the [killing of a] husband; and likewise when the fetus is known [to be alive], it is according to the word of Vyāghra. Thus [it is said]. Regarding the killing of those born in the inverse order (pratiloma), Laugākṣi says:
"In the case of killing those born in the inverse order, such as those born of Śūdras, how should it be?"
If it was done intentionally, the Parāka penance shall be performed; if done unintentionally, however, the Aindava is prescribed by tradition.
For the others, the wise have declared that a fourth part shall belong to the father.
Thus [ends the verse]. 22.16.
Regarding that very same [act] when done unintentionally, he says:
"He shall give cows with a bull as the eleventh. (22.18)
Since cows have already been the subject of discussion, the mention of "cows" again is for the purpose of specifying the gift of a cow of a particular color, namely white. And so Manu says:
"Having killed a Śūdra, one should perform this very same vow for six months."

“And one should also give white cows, with the bull as the eleventh, to a Brahmin. (MDh 11.130) By the word “also” (*ca*), it should be understood that what was previously mentioned applies to the intentional killing of that same person who lives according to the prescribed conduct. However, for unintentional killing, the rule beginning with “one who extinguishes the sacred fires” (GDh 22.34) applies. For the intentional killing of a woman without a husband, they should perform this very same vow; but for unintentional killing, a *taptakṛcchra* penance is to be observed. As Uśanas says: “Having killed a Śūdra, one should perform a *taptakṛcchra*. In this regard, the rules stated in other Smṛtis concerning the direct and inverse orders of castes (*anuloma-pratiloma*) should be consulted. As Vyāghra says:

But for all those [offenses] committed in the direct order, as well as for the killing of their mother, the learned one should prescribe that same penance; and for women, half of that very same [penance].
"Regarding the killing of an Ātreyī woman, one should declare that which is prescribed for [the killing of] a mother;

and likewise when the fetus is unknown, it is according to the statement of Vyāghra. This same principle is to be understood regarding women born of inverse (pratiloma) unions. Regarding men in that regard, Aṅgiras says:
"But upon approaching, eating with, or killing those of the lowest castes..."

"Purification shall be by means of the *parāka* penance; so said the Blessed Aṅgiras. This refers to cases where the offspring of Śūdras act intentionally (*buddhipūrva*). However, in cases of unintentional action (*abuddhipūrva*), a *cāndrāyaṇa* penance should be observed. As Lokākṣi has stated: "In the case of killing those born of Śūdras from inverse unions (*pratiloma*), what should be done? If intentional, there should be a *parāka*; if unintentional, likewise an *aindava* (cāndrāyaṇa). For the offspring of Śūdras, since their status is equal—according to the rule, "But from a Śūdra, one of fallen conduct is born of a non-equal woman" (GDh 4.27)—an equality of penance is indeed appropriate. Regarding others as well, he says in that very same place:

"For others, one-fourth [of the penance] is prescribed by the wise for the killing of those of their own caste; the rule for a Śūdra is stated to be the same as that for killing [members of] other castes. The meaning here is that whatever penance has been prescribed for a Śūdra in the case of killing those born in the natural (anuloma) or inverse (pratiloma) orders, that very same penance should be understood to apply even in the case of killing one's own kind. Regarding the Śūdra, it is stated in that very same context:
"The vow [of penance] shall be the whole, half, three-quarters, or indeed a quarter [of the full term]."
Abstention from injury, sexual intercourse, and eating, which are inherent within the [observances of] caste and the measures [of time].
Thus [ends the section]. 22.18.
And likewise in the case of an *anātreyyā*. 22.19–22.17.

Since the extension (*atideśa*) is already established by the word *eva*, the inclusion of the word *evam* is for the purpose of extending the penance for killing a Kṣatriya, so that what was mentioned immediately prior [the penance for killing a Śūdra] might not apply. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: “In the case of injuring a Kṣatriya who is not an Ātreyī, [one should perform the penance] for injuring a Kṣatriya; in the case of injuring a Vaiśya, [the penance for injuring] a Vaiśya,” and so forth. If it is asked, “In that case, this should have been stated in that very place,” we reply: It is stated at the end for the purpose of indicating that even after the penance has been performed, one should not live together [with such persons]. And thus says Manu: “Those who kill a Brāhmaṇa and those who are ungrateful, even if they are purified according to the Dharma...”
"And one should not dwell with those who kill those who have sought refuge, nor with those who kill women. [MDh 11.190] || 22.19 ||

And likewise for the killing of a woman other than an *ātreyī*, a Śūdra shall perform penance for one year and give ten cows with a bull as the eleventh. This applies to the intentional killing of a virtuous Brāhmaṇī who is a housewife. Yājñavalkya also says:
"Having killed a woman who is not corrupt, one should observe the vow prescribed for the killing of a Śūdra" (YDh 3.269).
And: "A killer of a Śūdra should also perform this for six months, or else give ten cows" (YDh 3.267).

"Having killed women of the Brāhmaṇa, Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, or Śūdra castes who have behaved wickedly, one should give, for the sake of purification, in order, a leather water-bag, a bow, a goat, or a sheep. (YDh 3.268) As for that which was stated by Hārīta: "For killing a Kṣatriya, the standard period of studenthood (*brahmacarya*) is six years; for a Vaiśya, three; for a Śūdra, one and a half years; for Brāhmaṇas, as for a Kṣatriya; for a Kṣatriya woman, as for a Vaiśya; for a Vaiśya woman, as for a Śūdra; and having killed a Śūdra woman, nine months"—that refers to the case of an extremely eminent teacher or similar person. (22.17)
And [the penance for killing] a cow is like that for a Vaiśya. || 22.20 || — || 22.18 ||

Having killed a cow, one should perform the penance as prescribed for a Vaiśya. In this context, the killing refers to one committed by a person of such conduct (*vṛttavān*). Furthermore, the element of intentional action (*buddhipūrvatva*) is established from the context. In that regard, for the intentional killing of a cow endowed with the quality of yielding much milk, the three-year period of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) mentioned for a Vaiśya should be understood to apply. And in that case, for one who possesses wealth, there is the gift of one thousand cows plus one bull. Why? Because, in the case of killing a Kṣatriya king, the observance of celibacy for three years is seen to serve as a substitute for the gift of a thousand cows. Likewise, the verse of Manu has been cited: “One thousand cows plus one bull,” and so forth. [MDh 11.127]
If it is asked how it is known that there is a heavier penalty for [killing] a cow yielding much milk, it is said:

"For the killing of small animals, however, the fine is two hundred [paṇas]. [MDh 8.297]. In this context, by the term "small animals" (kṣudrapaśu), cows of little utility are meant, not goats and sheep.

"However, for donkeys, goats, and sheep, the fine shall be five *māṣakas*" (MDh 8.298). Since a separate fine is seen for these animals, it is understood from the observation of a lighter penalty in their case that the fault is more serious when the animals serve many purposes. In the case of killing that very cow unintentionally, it should be understood that one must give "one hundred and one cows with a bull. In the absence of that, one may observe celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for a year. That which was prescribed for a Vaiśya regarding the combination of giving gifts and performing penance should also be understood to apply here. Its scope, however, is the intentional killing of this very cow when she has been taken under the protection of a Brāhmaṇa; for there is greater gravity in the case of a cow protected by a Brāhmaṇa.

This is indicated by the mark [in the text]: "In the case of cows belonging to Brāhmaṇas, and in the breaking of a *sthūrikā* [a small herd]. Here, regarding the inability to give a cow, it should be understood that one *niṣka*, half a *niṣka*, or even a quarter (*pāda*) [is the fine]. Likewise, the statement of Vyāghra has been cited: "In the absence of cows, a *niṣka*, or half a *niṣka*, or even a quarter," and so forth. In that regard, for a king, there is the gift of a thousand cows or a thousand gold pieces; for one of equal status, the position is that it is half a *niṣka*. But for an ordinary person, it is a quarter. Why? Because of the statement of Jātukarṇi concerning this subject matter.
"A thousand cows and a thousand gold pieces are declared for a king;
half of that is said for one of middle rank, while a quarter should be for an ordinary person.
And likewise, Manu also says in a certain context:
In a case where another ordinary person would be fined one kārṣāpaṇa, [he shall be fined ten].

"In that case, the king shall be punished with a fine of one thousand; this is the settled rule" (MDh 8.336). By this also, it is understood that the punishment for the king is greater than that for an ordinary person. When all other options are impossible, the observance of the standard *brahmacarya* for four years should be understood to apply to an ordinary person. This applies everywhere. Regarding the unintentional killing of that same [cow], the rule stated by Vasiṣṭha should be observed. As Vasiṣṭha says: "If a cow should be killed, he who was wrapped in its raw hide should perform the *kṛcchra* or *taptakṛcchra* penance for six months," and so forth (VaDh 21.18). The understanding that this refers to an unintentional case is due to the governing term "unintentionally" (*aprekṣāpūrvam*) in the passage: "If a Brāhmaṇa [is killed] unintentionally" (VaDh 21.16). In that context, because of the dual number in "the two should give a bull and a cow" (VaDh 21.22), two killers are understood. Therein, in the case of killing a bull, a bull should be given; in the case of killing a cow, a cow and so forth—this is how it should be understood. Or else, the rule stated by Vyāghra may be applied.

"If a man should kill a cow through ignorance, he should then give seven hundred *paṇas* to a poor *śrotriya* for the sake of his own purification. Regarding the word "cow" (*gām*), by the force of the particle "and" (*ca*), that which was stated concerning a *śūdra* should also be understood here. In that context, for the intentional killing of a cow of little utility, one should understand the gift of eleven cows with a bull as the eleventh, accompanied by a year-long penance. For the unintentional killing of that same [cow], that which was stated by Jātukarṇya should be understood, as he said: "If one should kill a cow unintentionally, then, with the permission of Brāhmaṇas..."

"Having performed three *prājāpatya* penances, he should present a cow to a Brāhmaṇa. This [penance] should be understood as prescribed by Manu for the intentional killing of that very same cow when she has been accepted by a Brāhmaṇa. As he says:
"A cow-killer who is afflicted by a minor offense (*upapātaka*) shall drink barley-gruel for a month;
having taken up his residence in a cow-pen, he shall be covered with a wet hide."
One should eat a measured amount of food, free from pungent seasonings and salt, at every fourth mealtime;
for two months, with senses restrained, one should perform one's ablutions using cow urine.
He should follow those cows during the day, and while standing, he should inhale the dust rising from them;
having performed service and paid homage, he should remain in the vīrāsana posture at night.
While they stand, he should stand; while they walk, he should walk;
likewise, while they sit, he should sit—self-restrained and free from longing.
Whether she is afflicted by illness or consecrated for sacrifice, or threatened by dangers such as thieves and tigers,
or fallen or mired in the mud— he should liberate her with all his vital strength.
Whether it be hot, raining, cold, or when a fierce wind blows,
one should not seek protection for oneself without first providing protection for the cow to the best of one's ability.
Whether it be one's own or another's, whether in a field, a house, or a threshing floor,
one should not speak of a cow that is eating, nor of a calf that is drinking.
But he who, following this rule, attends upon cows,
removes the sin committed by killing a cow within three months.
"One who has properly observed the vow should give eleven cows along with a bull;
if these are unavailable, he should offer his entire property to those learned in the Vedas. (MDh 11.108–109).

However, in the case of unintentional [killing], the standard period of *brahmacarya* for one year should be observed. If the death of the calf occurs unintentionally, then the gift of eleven cows and a bull should be observed. Furthermore, there is a mitigation regarding the calf.
For calves, the fine shall be half; for milch cows, the fine shall be equal.
For draft oxen and breeding bulls, the same has been declared by the wise.

Thus, from the observation of the *Prājāpatya-smṛti*: "But if a man intentionally kills a calf, he should then perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for his own purification, or he should give five hundred paṇas."

Thus, what is stated in the *Kavaṣasmṛti* should be observed. He must be made to pay its value to the owner, based on the indicative mark [of the text]: "And he shall be made to pay that wealth to him" (MDh 8.176). In this case of killing, the punishment for Śūdras is half; this is according to the statement of Lokākṣi:
"But for all the twice-born, the full punishment is ordained;
those who know the Dharma understand that for Śūdras, the punishment shall be half."
Thus [ends the section]. 22.20.

Having killed a cow, one should perform that penance prescribed for the killing of a Vaiśya: "For the killing of a Vaiśya, one should live for three years or give a hundred cows and a bull" (GDh 22.15). This applies to the intentional killing of a cow that gives much milk, is young, and belongs to a poor man with a large family who is devoted to his conduct and Vedic study. For the killing of such a cow that yields a single crop [of milk], is pregnant, or is used as an auxiliary to a ritual, the penance is that of Yama: "One who has well-performed his vow should give a thousand or even a hundred cows;
if these are not available, he should offer his entire property to those learned in the Vedas. (MDh 11.134)

A two-month vow is the subject here. In this very context, however, for an intentional act, there is the three-year penance prescribed by Kātyāyana, which excludes the gift of a cow. Furthermore, the killer of a cow shall dwell in a cow-pen, clothed in its hide, or he shall constantly follow the cows, wearing a girdle of muñja grass, rags, a deerskin, and so forth.

“Afflicted by the fear of rain, cold, heat, suffering, fire, mud, and [other dangers], one who rescues [a cow] with every effort is purified in three years. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: “If he should kill a cow, he shall remain for six months wrapped in her raw hide, performing either the *kṛcchra* or the *taptakṛcchra* penance; and in the case of a bull or a *vehat*, he shall give them away. A *vehat* is a cow that has been harmed by a bull. In the phrase “he shall give them away,” the agentive suffix (*kartṛ-pratyaya*) is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). Yājñavalkya says:
A cow-killer, drinking the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), shall remain self-controlled for one month;
sleeping in a cow-pen and following the cows, he is purified by the gift of a cow.
"Or, being composed, one should perform the Kṛcchra and Atikṛcchra penances;
or, having fasted for three nights, one should give eleven cows along with a bull. Thus [says Yājñavalkya, 3.263–264]. Jābāla says:
"If one has killed a cow unintentionally, he shall perform the Prājāpatya penance for a month;
he should follow the cows for their benefit and is purified by the gift of a cow," so says Viṣṇu.
"For one who has killed a cow, there shall be three palas of the five products of the cow for one month,
or else a Parāka penance, or even a Cāndrāyaṇa."

Kāśyapa says: “Having killed a cow, one should be clothed in its hide, sleep in a cow-pen for a month, bathe at the three periods of the day, and constantly subsist on the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). Śātātapa says: “One should subsist on the five products of the cow for a month. Śaṅkha and Pracetas say: “The killer of a cow should subsist on the five products of the cow; he should fast for twenty-five nights, have his hair shaved including the top-knot, be clothed in a cow-hide, follow after cows, sleep in a cow-pen, and give a cow as a gift. Paiṭhīnasi says: “A cow-killer becomes purified by eating for a month gruel made from a handful of rice, while doing what is pleasing to cows. Manu [says]:
One who has committed the minor offense of killing a cow shall subsist on barley-gruel;
having shaved his head, he shall dwell in a cow-pen, covered with a wet hide.
"Having restrained his senses, he should eat a measured amount of food, free from pungent salt, at the fourth mealtime,
and perform his bath with cow urine for two months.
Beginning thus, [the text continues].
He who, being a killer of a cow, follows cows according to this rule,
removes the sin committed by killing a cow within three months.

"One who has successfully observed the vow should give eleven cows along with a bull. [Manu Dharma Śāstra 11.115–116] Sumantu says: "For the killer of a cow, there is the gift of a cow, sleeping in a cow-pen for twelve nights, consuming the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and following after the cows. Saṃvarta says:
"Eating barley-meal, barley-gruel, alms-food, milk, curd, clarified butter, and cow-dung—one should consume these in sequence for half a month with a well-composed mind."

"Having fed the Brāhmaṇas, one should give a cow for the sake of one's own purification. Bṛhaspati says: "For twelve nights, one should subsist on the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). The appropriate distribution of these [penances] according to the subject matter should be inferred based on the distinction between intentional and unintentional acts, and according to whether a Brāhmaṇa or other [caste] was involved. There is a specific rule in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*: "If a miscarriage occurs immediately after conception, it is one quarter; if it becomes firm, it is two quarters; having killed an insentient fetus, a penance of three-quarters is prescribed."
When the fetus is complete with all its major and minor limbs and endowed with consciousness, one should perform a double cow-vow; this is the atonement for a killer of a cow.
Bṛhatpracetā says:
"When a calf one year old is killed, a quarter-penance (kṛcchrapāda) is prescribed;
for a man acting unintentionally, it shall be a half-penance when the calf is two years old."
"In the case of a three-year-old cow, it shall be three-quarters; beyond that, it shall be a *prājāpatya* penance. Thus says another *Smṛti*:
"An excessively old cow, one that is excessively emaciated, one that is excessively young, and one that is diseased..."
Having killed [it], the twice-born man shall perform the half-vow according to the previously prescribed rule.
"One should feed Brahmins according to one's ability and likewise give gold and sesame seeds.
Thus say Saṃvarta and Āpastamba.
"If a single woman is somehow killed by several people through fate," [and so forth].
But for each step of the killing, they shall perform penance separately.

"But if many [cows] have perished through confinement or even through being bound, and if a physician has administered a wrong treatment, one should perform the *govrata* twice over. By the force of this statement, even in the case of killing many [cows], it is precisely double; however, it is not a repetitive application (*nauprettikāvṛtti*) for each individual cause. Vyāsa says:
"Medicine, salt, and even food, even if intended for the sake of merit..."
One should not give more than required; rather, one should cause only a small amount to be given at the proper time.
"If there is injury when [the amount] exceeds [the limit], a *kṛcchra* penance for one quarter is prescribed.
Thus says Āpastamba.
"Whether by means of stones, clubs, weapons, or anything else, [if it is done] by force..."
Those who cause cattle to perish must indeed perform a vow in that regard.
"One quarter [of the penance] should be performed for obstructing, two quarters for binding,
one-quarter less for yoking, and one should perform the whole for causing a fall," so says Vasiṣṭha.

"Cows should not be tied with coconut fibers, nor with hempen cords, nor even with those made of muñja grass, nor with leather thongs or chains. Having tied them, one should stand guard over them, holding an axe. (22.18)
And [the same penance applies] for the killing of frogs, mongooses, crows, crabs, mongooses, mice, and dogs. || 22.21 || — || 22.19 ||

In this context, the mention of the "crow" (*kāka*) by Manu is an elliptical designation (*upalakṣaṇa*) for those animals mentioned in the verse concerning "flesh-eaters" (*kravyāda*), those mentioned in the verse concerning "domestic pigs" (*viḍvarāha*), and those mentioned in the verses concerning the "cat" (*biḍāla*) and the "wild cat" (*mārjāra*).
[Manu Smṛti 11.154: "Having consumed the urine or excrement of a domestic pig, a donkey, a camel, a jackal, a monkey, or a crow, a twice-born man shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance."
For eating the flesh of carnivorous animals, pigs, camels, and cocks,
as well as that of hell-beings, crows, and cranes, the *taptakṛcchra* penance is the means of purification.
Having consumed the leavings of a cat, a crow, a mouse, a dog, or a mongoose, one must likewise perform this penance.
"One should drink *brāhmī* and *suvarcalā* [if one has consumed food] contaminated by hair or insects.
Having killed a cat, a mongoose, a blue jay, a frog, a dog, an iguana, an owl, or a crow, one should perform the penance prescribed for killing a Śūdra. (MDh 11.159; 11.131) Thus it is said.

It should be understood that for the killing of these [animals] collectively, one should perform the penance prescribed for the killing of a Śūdra. The word "ca" (and) serves to extend the rules regarding the expiation for killing a Śūdra. This remains the same whether the act was intentional or unintentional. However, in the case of killing each individually, specific penances for certain animals such as the village-pig and others are prescribed in another Smṛti for unintentional killing:
