"Having killed a boar, one should give a jar of ghee; a tittiri bird, a droṇa of sesame; a parrot, a two-year-old calf; and having killed a krauñca crane, a three-year-old calf."

"Having killed a swan, a crane, a heron, and likewise a peacock, as well as a monkey, a hawk, and a vulture, one should offer a cow to a Brāhmaṇa. (MDh 11.134–35). This [penance] applies to the killing of many; however, for the killing of each individual, only a *kārṣāpaṇa* should be given. Thus says Vyāghra:
"In the case of swans, peacocks, and aquatic birds..."
For the killing of monkeys, hawks, or vultures, a twice-born man shall pay a fine of one paṇa.
Having killed a horse, one should give a garment; for killing an elephant, five dark-colored bulls; and for killing a goat, a sheep, an ox, or a donkey, a one-year-old calf.
Having killed carnivorous wild animals, one should give a milch cow;
for non-carnivorous animals, a heifer; but having killed a camel, one should give a *kṛṣṇala* of gold.
Thus it is said. In cases of intentional [harm], a punishment proportionate to the offense should be determined. As it is stated in the section on assault (*daṇḍapāruṣya*):
"In the case of killing a human being, the guilt shall immediately be equal to that of a thief;
for large living beings such as cows, jackals, camels, horses, and the like, it shall be half."
For the killing of small animals, the fine is two hundred;
for the slaughter of living beings [of larger size], the punishment has been determined accordingly.
For killing auspicious deer or birds, the fine shall be fifty [māṣakas];
for donkeys, goats, and sheep, the fine shall be five māṣakas.
"But the fine for killing a dog or a pig shall be one *māṣika*. (MDh 8.296–98).
For those who have committed these acts intentionally, it is said: "One should drink milk for three nights, or travel a distance of one *yojana* on the road."

"One should touch water in a flowing river, or mutter a hymn addressed to the waters" (MDh 11.132)—this is how it should be understood. In that regard, drinking milk or traveling on foot should be understood as applying when the act is intentional (*buddhipūrva*); however, when unintentional (*abuddhipūrva*), bathing and the muttering of a hymn apply. This is similar to the injunction regarding sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). Even in the case of killing calves, a gradation of severity should be observed. What has been stated for humans according to the distinctions of caste (*varṇa*) and so forth, will also be stated for boars: "In the case of a boar, a jar of ghee" (GDh 22.26). Here, this also should be observed: as for the statement that a *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance applies to the consumption of urine or feces, there too the inclusion of all these [animals] is intended, and the *Cāndrāyaṇa* should be understood as applying when the act is intentional. In that context, a *Taptakṛcchra* has been prescribed for eating [the meat]; and where the drinking of *Brahmasuvarcalā* is prescribed for eating leavings, here too the inclusion of all these is intended. Furthermore, since the *Cāndrāyaṇa* is mentioned separately for consuming the urine or feces of a human, it should be understood to apply to those other than humans. In that case as well, by the mention of "urine," semen is also included, because its instruction is identical to the instruction for the penance for consuming human urine or feces.

"Having eaten the food of any one of these [outcastes], if unintentionally, one should fast for three days; but having eaten it intentionally, or having consumed semen, feces, or urine, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance. [MDh 4.222] This author will also state later: "And in the case of consuming urine, feces, or semen" [MDh 11.154]. In the case of intentional consumption, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance is to be understood; however, in the case of unintentional consumption, the Sāntapana penance applies, as Lokākṣi has said: "In the case of pigs, donkeys, camels, and likewise monkeys..."
"Having consumed urine or feces, a twice-born man shall perform the Sāntapana penance. Thus [it is said].

In this case as well, all of these are to be included. The prescription for the *taptakṛcchra* penance also applies only when the act is intentional; furthermore, in that instance, a re-consecration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*) must also be observed. Thus, he will later state, with reference to the *taptakṛcchra* accompanied by re-consecration: "And [the penance for eating] the flesh of beasts of prey, camels, and donkeys" (GDh 23.5). However, in the case of unintentional consumption, that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha should be observed: "Upon eating the flesh of dogs, cocks, village pigs, herons, vultures, *bhāsa* birds, crows, pigeons, humans, or owls, there shall be fasting for seven nights, evacuation of the bowels, and re-consecration" (VaDh 23.30). In this way, the inclusion of those mentioned here within those [other rules] should be understood. But even where the drinking of *brahmasuvarcalā* is prescribed, that too excludes what has been left over by a human. As Uśanas says:

If one eats the remnants of a Brāhmaṇa’s meal, one should perform a hundred *prāṇāyāmas*; if the remnants of a Kṣatriya’s meal, a thousand *prāṇāyāmas*; and if the remnants of a Vaiśya’s meal, ten thousand *prāṇāyāmas*. If this was done intentionally, the penance is a *Prājāpatya*, an *Atikṛcchra*, or a *Kṛcchrātikṛcchra*. Upon eating the remnants of a Śūdra’s meal, one must drink barley-gruel (*yavāgū*) for seven nights; if intentional, the penance is a *Parāka*. Likewise, when a twice-born person eats the remnants of another twice-born person’s meal, or when Śūdras drink water that has been the remnants of a Brāhmaṇa’s meal, they should perform sixteen *prāṇāyāmas*. For Kṣatriyas, it is thirty; for Vaiśyas, forty; and for Śūdras, they should drink *kuśa* water for three days. If intentional, the sequence of penances is drinking the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) for three, four, five, and seven days respectively. Upon eating the remnants of those of the lowest castes (*antyaja*), if intentional, the penance is a *Mahāsāntapana*; if unintentional, a *Cāndrāyaṇa*. Thus it is said.
Manu has also stated something:

"Having drunk water that is the leavings of a Śūdra, one should drink water infused with Kuśa grass for three days. And having eaten the food of those whose food should not be eaten, as well as the leavings of a woman or a Śūdra... [MDh 11.148].

"Having eaten forbidden meat, one should drink barley-gruel for seven nights" (MDh 11.152). Thus, even the drinking of *suvarcalā* [leaves], if unintentional, lasts for only one night as there is no distinction; however, if intentional, it requires the *sāntapana* penance. As Jātūkarṇi says:
"A twice-born man who has intentionally consumed the leavings of a jackal, a crow, a cat, a dog, a monitor lizard, or even cows, shall perform the *sāntapana* *kṛcchra*."
In this regard, what was stated by Kavaṣa should also be observed:

"The penance for a Kṣatriya shall be half that of a Brāhmaṇa, and for Vaiśyas it is half of that; the wise know the penance for Śūdras to be exactly half of that. This is to be understood as applying everywhere. The mention of "violence" (hiṃsā), although its status as a qualifying condition is already established, is included here to show that [the rule applies] only in cases of violence and not even when one has merely touched [an animal]. 22.21.

The *bimba* is a lizard capable of changing its form at will; the *dahara* is a mouse of very small body—some say it is a muskrat (*chucchundarī*), while others are well-known by these names. For the killing of all these together, the penance is that of a Vaiśya. This refers to cases of intentional and repeated practice. In other instances, the rule of Āpastamba applies: "For the killing of a crow, a crane, a heron, a peacock, a ruddy goose, a swan, a vulture, a frog, a mongoose, a *sairika* bird, or a horse, the penance is that of a Śūdra" (ĀpDh 1.25.13). Manu also says: "Having killed a cat, a mongoose, a blue jay, or a frog..."

"And for killing a dog, a monitor lizard, an owl, or a crow, one should perform the vow prescribed for the killing of a Śūdra. (MDh 11.131) But in the case of each of these being killed intentionally, [the rule is]:
"Having killed a cat, a monitor lizard, a mongoose, a frog, a dog, or a bird, one should drink milk for three days or perform a quarter-Kṛcchra penance. (YDh 3.270)
Thus, the statement of Yājñavalkya is to be understood. Regarding intentional acts, the rule of Manu applies:
"Or he should drink milk for three nights, or he should travel a distance of one yojana on the road" (MDh 11.132). || 22.19 ||
Having killed a thousand vertebrate animals. || 22.22 || — || 22.20 ||
For the killing of a thousand other beings possessing bones, there is the penance prescribed for the murder of a Śūdra. || 22.22 ||
Having killed a thousand vertebrate creatures such as lizards and the like, one must perform the penance prescribed for a Vaiśya.
And [the same applies] to boneless animals and to the carrying of a load by oxen. 22.23. — 22.21.

If one kills boneless creatures such as worms and the like, equal in number to the load of an ox, this penance for killing a Śūdra applies. It should be understood that the penance for killing a Śūdra applies here [only] when done intentionally, and not otherwise; the same should be understood regarding all such extended applications (*atideśa*). || 22.23 ||

For those boneless creatures such as gadflies and mosquitoes, having killed as many as one is able to carry on a bullock, the penance is the same as for a Vaiśya. Both of these cases refer to instances of repeated practice. In other circumstances, that which was stated by Yājñavalkya applies: "A thousand [boneless creatures], or likewise a cartload of those with bones; or one should perform the six-month vow prescribed for killing a Śūdra, or give ten cows. (YDh 3.269). || 22.21 ||
Or rather, one may give something small to each of those who possess livestock. 22.24. — 22.22.

Now, it is not necessary to complete a thousand or to complete a load of oxen; rather, immediately thereafter, one should give something small—something like a single cowrie shell—to each individual. From the word "vā" (or), one may perform recitation (*japa*) and so forth. From the word "api" (also/even), this applies even to those creatures that have no bones. Thus Manu says:
"But for the killing of creatures with bones, one should give something small to a Brahmin."

"Indeed, for the killing of boneless creatures, one is purified by means of *prāṇāyāma*. (MDh 11.141). In this regard, for the intentional killing of creatures possessing bones, a *kākaṇikā* coin or more should be given; however, if it was unintentional, six *prāṇāyāmas* are required. For boneless creatures, three *prāṇāyāmas* should be observed for intentional killing, but only one *prāṇāyāma* for unintentional killing. Thus says Kaṇva: "Upon killing creatures with bones, a man should give a *kākaṇikā* intentionally; but if unintentionally, he should perform six *prāṇāyāmas* for them."
Those who know the Dharma understand that if one intends to kill boneless creatures, one should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas); if it was unintentional, one should then perform one.
Thus [ends the section]. 22.24.

The word *api vā* indicates an alternative. One should count however many of those possessing bones have been killed—whether a thousand or more or less—and give something small to each one. This expiation for those with bones may be performed either before or after [the previous rites]. A small amount (*kiṃcit*) is eight handfuls (*muṣṭi*); eight of those make a *puṣkala*;
four *puṣkalas* are proclaimed to be an *āḍhaka*.
Four āḍhakas constitute a droṇa; such is the definition of measurement.
Thus says the Smṛti. For boneless creatures, however, there are as many breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) as there were bones. And so Manu says:
"In the case of killing a creature with bones, one should give something small to a Brahmin;
for in the injury of boneless creatures, one is purified by a breath-restraint" (MDh 11.141). || 22.22 ||
In the case of a eunuch, there shall be a load of straw and a māṣa of lead. || 22.25 || — || 22.23 ||

The term *ṣaṇḍa* refers to one of the third gender (*tṛtīyā-prakṛti*), but not to a eunuch (*klība*); for the latter, since he might otherwise qualify as a *śrotriya*, he is specifically prohibited from the *śrāddha* rite, and because he is connected with the performance of sacraments (*saṃskāra*). When such a person is killed, there is no distinction of caste regarding the penance: "A load of straw, a cow, a *sīsa*-bean, [and] a *brāhmaṇa*. Because they are mentioned without being compounded, they are separate; and by the word "and" (*ca*), their equality is also indicated. In that regard, it is separate when done unintentionally, and combined when done intentionally. (22.25)
Regarding this, Devala said:

"One who is a *ṣaṇḍha* (impotent) and possesses deficient sexual organs is not at all fit for the sacraments (*saṃskāra*). Thus, when such a person is killed intentionally, both a load of straw and a *māṣa*-weight of lead—these two combined—must be given as a fine; otherwise, [if unintentionally], only one of the two. Lead is a specific type of metal resembling silver that melts instantly. The measure of a *māṣa* has already been explained previously. Furthermore, no distinction regarding the species is heard of anywhere in the *Smṛti*; only "a *ṣaṇḍha*" or "*ṣaṇḍhaka*" is mentioned. In that regard, just as a sacrament prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa or others does not apply even when there is a commonality of species, so too the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) occasioned by killing them does not apply; rather, only what has been specifically stated takes effect. Others consider this to concern wild animals and birds—that is, when those among wild animals and birds which are *ṣaṇḍhas* are killed. (22.23)
In the case of a boar, there is a jar of ghee. || 22.26 || — || 22.24 ||
When a pig has been killed, a jar filled with clarified butter should be given to a Brāhmaṇa; the specific scope for this [act] has already been stated. 22.26.
When a boar has been killed, a jar filled with clarified butter should be given.
An iron staff [is used] against a snake. || 22.27 || — || 22.25 ||
By the word *loha*, black iron (*kārṣṇāyasa*) is meant. As Manu says:

"Having killed a snake, the best of the twice-born should give a sickle made of black iron" (MDh 11.133). This applies when the act is intentional; however, if it was unintentional, only a *māṣa* weight [of iron] should be given, according to the statement of Auśanas: "Having killed a snake, one should give a *māṣa* weight. || 22.27 ||

When a snake has been killed, an iron rod (lohadaṇḍa) must be given. By the word "iron" (loha), black iron (kārṣṇāyasa) is meant, as seen in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra]: "Having killed a snake, the best of the twice-born should give a black-iron spade" (MDh 11.133). The statement from the *Auśanasa* [Dharmaśāstra], "Having killed a snake, one should give a māṣa," refers to a case where the act was intentional. 22.25.
The suffix *jīla* is applied after the word *brahmabandhū* when it denotes instability. 22.28.
In the case of a woman who is a nominal Brahmin (brahmabandhū) and is fickle, [the son born] is Nīla. || 22.26 ||

"Calanā" means unchaste behavior. Regarding Kṣatriyas and the other castes, that which was stated by Manu should be observed, as he said: "Having killed women of the four castes who are not under restraint, one should give for purification a leather water-skin, a bow, a goat, and a sheep, respectively. [MDh 11.138] "Jīla" means a leather bag. "Calanā" also refers to being served by many men due to her being hidden from view, as Prajāpati has said:
“That woman who approaches many men in secret should be known as an *vyabhicāriṇī* (adulteress) and, in effect, a courtesan.

Thus, for intercourse with fewer than three men, the previously mentioned penance involving death (*hanana-prāyaścitta*) alone should be understood to apply; beyond that, this [present] one applies. Even for intercourse with fewer than three men, half of the previously mentioned [penance] should be assigned for each [subsequent man]. As Kaṇva says:
"Every penance is prescribed for a woman who remains established in her conduct;

however, for one who has become active with multiple men, it shall be reduced by half. This refers to intentional action. But in the case of unintentional action, that which was stated by Vyāghra should be observed:
"For an unchaste woman, the sin is halved when she has intercourse with prostitutes."
Having killed an unfaithful woman of any of the four castes, one is purified.
And for the purification of these, one should respectively give a conch shell, mother-of-pearl, and a goat. Thus [ends verse 22.28].

A *brahmabandhū* is a woman who is a Brāhmaṇī by birth alone. A *calanā* is an unchaste woman. When she has been killed, a blue bull must be given; that is, a blue ox. Manu, however, states the sequence according to the castes:
"Having killed women of the four castes who are not steadfast, one should give separately for purification a blue bull, a bow, a goat, and a sheep" (MDh 11.138). 22.26.
In the case of the Vaiśika, there is nothing [to be done]. || 22.29 ||
Something according to the style of a courtesan. 22.27.

If a Vaiśya woman who lives by her own work is killed, nothing at all need be done [by way of penance]. This refers to an unintentional act. But in the case of an intentional act, half of what has been prescribed for an unchaste woman should be understood to apply;
"half the sin of an unchaste woman shall be incurred in approaching a prostitute.
This is the eternal law for all four castes.

This is because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) regarding the dharma of Prajāpati. Alternatively, "vaiśika" means that which is performed with courtesans; thus, when sexual intercourse is performed openly with a *brahmabandhū* (a woman of low caste), the meaning is that no penance whatsoever for approaching another's wife need be performed. And from this, it is understood that there is some penance for intercourse performed secretly with her. That too should be determined analogously to [the penance for] violence (*hiṃsā*). Here, since the penance for approaching another's wife is prohibited, it is understood that there is indeed something else [required]. Thus says Śaṅkha:
"A twice-born man shall perform a Prājāpatya penance for approaching a female animal or a prostitute.
This [rule] applies to a single instance of such an act; however, in the case of repeated practice, that which was stated by Saṃvarta should be observed. As he said:
"In approaching a female animal or a prostitute, one should perform a Prājāpatya penance."

"But for a human being who has committed [the act] with a *gogāmī* (a woman who has intercourse with cattle), one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance followed by the *cāndrāyaṇa*. Regarding the case of extreme habitual practice (*atyantābhyāsa*) with her, the penance for a minor offense (*upapātaka*) prescribed by Manu should be observed. As he says: "The theft of grain, base metals, or cattle, and consorting with women who drink liquor... [MDh 11.66]. For one who has fathered a child with her, that which was stated by Kaṇva should be observed. As he says: "But he who has fathered a son with a *veśyā* (courtesan) should subsist on alms, with his senses restrained..."

"By practicing the Sāvitrī mantra ten thousand times, one attains purity. Thus it is said. That which was stated regarding the practice of courtesanship with a *brahmabandhu* (one who is a Brahmin in name only) should be understood to apply equally to the practice of courtesanship with those who are *kṣatrabandhus* (Kṣatriyas in name only) and others as well. To this effect, Kavaṣa says: "When the practice of courtesanship has been performed by relatives of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras..."

“The learned man should perform the Prājāpatya penance, but in the case of repeated practice, he should indeed perform the Kṛcchra. For Kṣatriyas and others, half and half [of the penance] should be prescribed respectively. Regarding this, some explain as follows: “In the case of a Brāhmaṇī woman’s contact with a Śūdra, loss of caste (pātitya) is declared: ‘A woman falls [from her status] by killing an embryo or by serving one of a lower varṇa’ (GDh 21.9). Therefore, for those who enter into a relationship with others while she—a Brāhmaṇī—has become connected to the Śūdra varṇa, the penance for approaching a fallen woman must be performed.
That is incorrect.
Having approached women of the Caṇḍāla or lowest castes, having eaten [with them], and having accepted gifts from them;

"A Brahmin falls through ignorance, but through knowledge he attains equality"—from this indicative mark (liṅga) [it follows]. And thus, it is understood that even upon intentional contact with a Śūdra woman and the like, there is equality with the Śūdra and others for those of Brāhmaṇa status and so forth, whereas through unintentional contact, there is subordination to them. If it is argued that, even so, the same penance prescribed for having sexual intercourse with an unfaithful Śūdra woman would also apply to a Brāhmaṇa woman who has entered into a connection with a Śūdra—here it is said: it does not apply because of the statement regarding "equality. Therefore, the previously stated penance alone applies.

Others explain it thus: for one who has sexual intercourse with a Śūdra or similar person through unintentional contact with them, there is the penance for a mortal sin (pātaka); however, if it is done intentionally, there is the penance for approaching a Śūdra woman, based on the statement: "But through knowledge, she attains equality" (MDh 11.175).

That too is incorrect; for even here, if unintentional contact were held to be more serious than intentional contact, that would contradict such statements as, "more so by design" (ĀpDh 1.29.3). This being the case, the meaning of the verse, "Having approached a Caṇḍāla woman or a woman of the lowest castes... (MDh 11.175), must also be understood as follows: the meaning is that one becomes fallen (*patita*) through unintentional contact with Caṇḍālas and the like, and is thus no longer entitled to the rites of the twice-born (*dvijāti*), but it does not mean that the sin of killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) or similar crimes has occurred. As it has been said: "The falling away from the duties of a twice-born is 'falling' (*patana*)," (GDh 21.4); this refers to the loss of eligibility for caste-rites, not the loss of the caste itself; therefore, there is a penance (*prāyaścitta*). However, in the case of intentional contact, there is indeed a loss of the caste itself, and therefore there is no penance. By the phrase "one falls through ignorance" (MDh 11.175), it is stated that one is disqualified from the duties of the twice-born, not that the sin of killing a Brahmin has occurred. Furthermore, because of the statement regarding equality—namely, that by intentionally having contact with someone, one attains equality with them and is not made eligible again by penance—it follows that there is an absence of penance by way of this attainment of equality. In the case of women of the Brāhmaṇa and other castes having intentional contact with a Śūdra, this equality should be understood to apply only when she has given birth; for it is taught that purification occurs for her if she has not conceived.

"The women of the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya castes who have had sexual union with a Śūdra are purified by penance if they have not conceived; others are not. Since this establishes the purification for one who has had union with a Śūdra but has not conceived, it should be understood that one who has had union with a man of a lower caste remains impure. Because it specifies "of the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya," the purification applies even to a Śūdra woman who has conceived. Furthermore:
"In the case of a woman who has conceived, that [penance] shall be reduced by half for each successive person [with whom she has consorted]."

In this regard, regarding sexual contact with a Kṣatriya woman, one should calculate that half [of the penance applies]; half of that in relation to a Vaiśya woman; and half of that again in relation to a Śūdra woman. Regarding the rule, “associating with a woman who drinks liquor” (MDh 11.66), an objection is raised: when one approaches a Brāhmaṇa woman who drinks liquor, the penance for approaching an outcast (patita) ought to apply, rather than the penance for a minor offense (upapātaka), because she becomes an outcast through the act of drinking liquor.
To this it is replied: her outcasting consists in being equal to a Śūdra, not in being equal to a killer of a Brāhmaṇa, as Manu has stated.
He whose Brahma residing in the body is once drenched with liquor—

“His Brahminhood departs and he attains the state of a Śūdra” (MDh 11.97). Therefore, because of his equality with a Śūdra, the penance already mentioned applies, and not the penance for approaching a fallen woman (*patitāgamana*). Likewise, it is stated here as well: “In the case of an interchange between an Ārya and a non-Ārya, there is equality of action” (GDh 10.66). An interchange, however, occurs when drinking liquor—which is not prohibited for a Śūdra but is prohibited for Brāhmaṇas and others—is involved; in that situation, when the Śūdra has abstained from drinking while a Brāhmaṇa or other has indulged in it, there is equality on account of that cause. Thus, it should be understood that a Brāhmaṇa or other who drinks liquor is equal to a Śūdra who abstains from it. Even though he is equal to a Śūdra, he must nevertheless be understood to be untouchable (*aspṛśya*), because he is included under the term *patita* in the rule: “A fallen man (*patita*) and a Caṇḍāla... (GDh 14.29). If it is argued that this refers only to those other than the Śūdra, we say no, because of the force of other Smṛti texts. Thus Kaṇva says:

The killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of intoxicants, the thief, and likewise the violator of the Guru’s bed—these are indeed outcasts and untouchable; and one who associates with them is equal to them.
That woman who goes about in secret with many men should be known as an unchaste woman, and she is explicitly called a courtesan.

Thus says Prajāpati: When a nominal Brahmin woman who lives by the work of a courtesan—that is, by the profession of a prostitute—is killed, something must be given; this is what is meant by the statement, "Something shall consist of eight handfuls. (22.27)
For [the theft of] a bed, food, or wealth, the years [of penance] are distinct. || 22.30 || — || 22.28 ||

The term *lābhavadha* (obstruction of gain) is connected with each [of the preceding items]: obstruction of the bed, obstruction of the acquisition of wealth, and so forth. By the word *talpa*, which denotes a bed, the wife is meant; however, because she is the cause [of the husband’s pleasure], the maiden is included here by figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). *Anna* refers to food, whether prepared or unprepared. *Dhana* refers to gold, cattle, and the like. *Lābha* means acquisition. *Vadha* means creating an obstacle. This is what is intended: when a maiden, food, or wealth is being obtained, one must perform a year-long period of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) separately for each case after having created such an obstacle or prohibition. This applies when the act is intentional (*buddhipūrva*). But in the case of unintentional action, that which was stated by Uśanas should be observed: “In the case of obstructing the acquisition of a maiden, food, or wealth, a *Prājāpatya* penance is required. This refers to the obstruction of the acquisition of a Brahmin; for Kṣatriyas and others, the appropriate degree of sin should be determined according to their respective status. (22.30)

By the word *talpa*, which denotes a bed, the wife is indicated. *Anna* means prepared food; *dhana* refers to gold and the like. Regarding the "obstruction of their acquisition"—that is, one who prevents these from being obtained by raising objections on account of some fault—he shall perform the standard vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for one year, separately for each distinct cause. The rule of Auśanasa, "In the case of an obstacle to [obtaining] a maiden, food, or wealth, [one shall perform] a *Prājāpatya*," applies to cases where the act is intentional. This present rule, however, concerns the obstruction of obtaining a Brāhmaṇa. For Kṣatriyas and others, the penance is reduced by half for each respective case. (22.28)
For the loss of a bed, food, or wealth, the penances are distinct for each year. (22.30) — (22.28)

The word *lābhavadha* (obstruction of gain) is connected with each [term]; thus, there is the obstruction of the gain of a bed, the obstruction of the gain of wealth, and so forth. By the word *talpa*, which denotes a bed, the wife is meant. Because she is the cause of that [act], a maiden is included here by figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). "Food" means prepared or unprepared; "wealth" means gold, cattle, and the like; "gain" means acquisition; "obstruction" means creating an impediment. This is what is meant: when a maiden, food, or wealth is being obtained, one must perform a year-long period of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) separately for each, after having created an obstacle or prohibition. This applies to intentional acts. However, in the case of unintentional acts, that which was stated by Uśanas should be observed: "In the case of obstructing the acquisition of a maiden, food, or wealth, [one should perform] a Prājāpatya penance. This refers to the obstruction of the acquisition of a Brāhmaṇa; for Kṣatriyas and others, the rule should be determined according to whether the act is contrary to or in accordance with their specific duty (*dharma*). (22.30)

By the word *talpa*, which denotes a bed, the wife is indicated. *Anna* means prepared food; *dhana* refers to gold and the like. Regarding the "obstruction of their acquisition"—that is, one who thwarts these when they are being obtained by means of attributing faults and so forth—he shall perform the standard vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for one year, separately for each distinct occasion. The rule from the *Auśanasa* Smṛti, "In the case of an obstruction to a maiden, food, or wealth, [one should perform] a *Prājāpatya*," applies to cases where the act is intentional. This present rule, however, concerns the acquisition of a Brāhmaṇa. For Kṣatriyas and others, the penance is reduced by half for each respective category. (22.28)
Two [cases of] adultery with another's wife. || 22.31 || — || 22.29 ||

For approaching another's wife, the penance is ordinary celibacy (*prākṛtabrahmacarya*) for two years. This should be understood to apply when conception occurs from approaching a Brāhmaṇa woman; prior to conception, the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances are required. As Vyāghra has said:
"If a Brāhmaṇa should intentionally approach a Brāhmaṇa woman who is unwilling, he should perform the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances; if it was through negligence, he should perform only half."
If he approaches her once with mutual desire, he shall perform half of the *taptakṛcchra* penance;
for approaching the wives of kings and others, a Brahmin shall perform half of that [half] for each respective case.

“One should observe this vow together with the wife of a *śrotriya*; if she is not a *śrotriya*, it is double; and if she is protected [by another], it is exactly half. Regarding the birth of a child in the wife of a Kṣatriya, one should understand that half of the rule “two [years] for the wife of another” (GDh 22.31) applies, based on the indicative mark: “half, half for the King and the others. Regarding the wife of a Vaiśya, the penance for a minor offense (*upapātaka*) prescribed by Manu should be observed, starting with: “They should perform this very vow” (MDh 11.117). For the wife of a Śūdra, it is an *atikṛcchra* penance, according to the statement of Kaṇva.

"A Brahmin who has approached the wife of a Śūdra should perform the *atikṛcchra* penance; for a Vaiśya [approaching a Śūdra wife], the *cāndrāyaṇa*; and for a Kṣatriya, the vow is the same as that for a Brāhmaṇa. If the sons born of the four castes have been produced by a Brāhmaṇa in the proper order [of marriage], then regarding the Brāhmaṇa’s approach to a Brāhmaṇī wife, whatever has been prescribed [as a penance] should be understood to be reduced by one quarter when approaching a Kṣatriyā wife and so forth, according to the statement of Vyāghra: "Those born of the four castes who have been produced by a Brāhmaṇa alone..."
"One should observe the vow among them, decreasing it by one quarter in each successive case. Thus it is said.

This same principle should be understood to apply to Kṣatriyas and others as well. If a Brāhmaṇa approaches a Śūdra woman who is the wife of another Brāhmaṇa, he should perform a Prājāpatya penance, according to the statement of Vasiṣṭha: "If a Brāhmaṇa, unintentionally, approaches the wife of a Brāhmaṇa, he shall perform a Kṛcchra if his religious duties have been suspended, and an Atikṛcchra if they have not been suspended" (VaDh 21.16). This refers to a single act of approaching her unintentionally. However, if it is intentional, the penance is doubled, based on the indicative mark: "Half only in the case of negligence. In the case of repetition, the principle of reduction by one-quarter should be observed. Whatever has been stated regarding a Brāhmaṇa’s approach to the wives of Kṣatriyas and others should likewise be understood to apply to Kṣatriyas and others when they approach the wives of their own caste. Why is this so?
Whatever a Brahmin commits in sexual union with the wife of a king,
a Kṣatriya likewise commits when he has united with her in that very same manner.
Thus, because of the characteristic marks of Prajāpati’s dharma. 22.31.

For approaching another's wife, the penance is two years of ordinary celibacy (*prākṛta-brahmacarya*); this applies when the act is intentional and during her fertile period. However, for one who lacks desire, this same penance should be applied by reducing it by half. (22.29)
Three [are the duties] of one learned in the Vedas (śrotriya). 22.32 — || 22.30 ||
This applies specifically to the occasion of conception during sexual union. It has already been stated even prior to conception:
"One should observe this vow together with a wife who is well-versed in the Vedas" (Vyāghra under 22.31).

After conception, this very same rule is to be understood as applying until the birth of the child. If it is argued that it is improper for there to be an identical penance for repeated practice, it is said in response: even in the case of women, identity of penance is observed despite repeated practice prior to conception.

Regarding the statement, "The women of the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya castes who have had sexual union with a Śūdra... (VaDh 21.12), there is likewise no fault here in this case. Similarly, there is also the statement of Kavaṣa: "Whatever has been prescribed regarding the conception of a fetus, that very same penance one should perform until death."

"A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, and likewise a Śūdra. Thus it is said. Alternatively, fulfillment may be achieved through recitations (*japa*) and other such means. As it is stated in the *Mānava* (Manu-smṛti): "In whatever action has been performed, there should be no lightness of heart in his mind," and so forth. In that regard, if one who was previously guilty of a fault and has performed penance becomes guilty of that same fault again after a year has passed, then he must perform double the penance from the previous one. Why?

"Double the fine for a wicked man who has been accused for a year" (MDh 8.373). Because of this observation regarding punishment, it should be understood that starting from one year, the penalty remains exactly at that same level. Regarding the period prior to one year, the Commentator (Bhāruci) has explained that for the first month, the twelvefold fine itself is divided into monthly portions. Thus, a three-month fulfillment should be calculated for each month. This applies only to one who has performed penance (*prāyaścitta*), because of the use of the two terms "accused" and "wicked. For one who has not performed penance, however, the fulfillment occurs through recitations (*japa*) and other such means. In that regard, for a *śrotriya* Brāhmaṇa, falling from his status (*pātitya*) should be understood to occur before the fourth act of approaching the wife by force—provided she has children and is devoted to her husband—according to the statement of Āpastamba: "They teach that in the case of a single union with a woman of the same caste who has had another husband previously, one quarter falls away; likewise, for repetition, a quarter falls away for each instance; on the fourth, all [is lost]" (ĀpDh 2.27.11–13). || 22.32 ||

In the case already mentioned, for one who approaches the wife of a *brāhmaṇa* learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), there shall be a period of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for three years. In this case as well, if it was unintentional, the penance is half. Regarding this, Śaṅkha says: "One who has spilled his seed upon a Vaiśya woman shall observe celibacy for one year and perform the ritual bath at the three periods of the day (*triṣavaṇa*). For a Kṣatriya woman, two years; for a Brāhmaṇa woman, three years. And for a Śūdra woman married to a Brāhmaṇa, the penance is the same as for a Vaiśya. Saṃvarta states:
"A Brāhmaṇa having approached a Śūdra woman shall [observe celibacy] for a month or even for half a month."

"Subsisting on cow’s urine and barley-gruel, he shall remain [in this state] until released from that sin. Thus, there is a fixed alternative: one month for intentional [intercourse], and half a month for unintentional. However, in the case of twice-born women such as Brāhmaṇīs during a period other than their fertile season, the penances are those lasting three months, two months, or the Cāndrāyaṇa, according to the rules of Manu. For Kṣatriyas and others having intercourse with Kṣatriya women and so forth, the penance is the same as for Brāhmaṇas. Regarding this, Uśanas says:
"Whatever vow there may be for sexual intercourse, one should perform double that if it results in conception. (22.30)
And upon obtaining wealth, there shall be its relinquishment. 22.33. — 22.31.

And if property has been obtained from another's wife, its relinquishment must be made; and "relinquishment" (tyāga) means abandonment without the formal rite of acceptance (pratigraha). From the word "and" (ca), it follows that whatever food and other things have been consumed should also be restored. 22.33.
And if any property whatsoever has been obtained from another's wife, its relinquishment—that is, its renunciation—must be performed. || 22.31 ||
Or he should cause it to go to its proper place. 22.34 — || 22.32 ||
The meaning is that one should offer food and so forth to the master himself under some pretext. 22.34.
Or he may send whatever was obtained at that bathing place. || 22.32 ||
If one performs the recitation of the *sahasravāka* when the application of mantras has been prohibited. 22.35 — 22.33.

The "application of mantras" (*mantrayoga*) refers to the acts of officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*) or teaching (*adhyāpana*) for one of a prohibited and disreputable twice-born caste. If this is performed, one must observe the standard period of studentship (*brahmacarya*) for one year. This applies when the act is done unintentionally; otherwise, the status of an outcast (*patita*) would ensue. Furthermore, if this "application of mantras" consists of a "thousand recitations" (*sahasravāka*), the word *vāka* denotes a *pada* (verse/word), and the word *sahasra* signifies plurality. Therefore, the meaning is: if he studies a large volume of text. In this way, for a small amount, the study of the aforementioned *saṃhitā* should be understood as the penance. This rule concerns those who are outcasts (*patita*); however, regarding those who have committed minor offenses (*upapātakin*), the rule stated by Vasiṣṭha should be observed.

“It is known from scripture that upon hearing of a fallen person (*patita*), a *caṇḍāla*, or a corpse, they should remain silent and fasting for three nights; by practicing this [recitation] up to a maximum of one thousand times, they become purified. By this very rule, those who teach what is censurable or act as priests for such persons are explained; it is also known that they become purified by the renunciation of their fees (*dakṣiṇā*). In this case as well, if it was done through ignorance, they should remain silent and fasting for three nights, provided it is less than one thousand recitations. However, beyond that, for as much as has been taught, a recitation of up to one thousand times should be understood for those eating sacrificial food (*haviṣya*). But in the case of intentional knowledge, once it exceeds one thousand recitations, they should be regarded as having committed a secondary sin (*upapātaka*). This is stated in the verse: “He who composes mantras for him [is also tainted]. Therefore, for cases below that [limit], a recitation of three thousand times should be understood, according to the statement of Auśanasa: “One should practice three thousand repetitions of the *anuvāka* concerning what is forbidden.”

Others, however, explain "mantra-yoga" as studying together or performing sacrifices together; and thus, having studied together with or performed sacrifices together with one who is prohibited, it is called "ordinary brahmacarya.

In this case as well, that same penance previously mentioned should be understood to apply according to the distinction of the subject matter, because studying together and performing sacrifices together are equivalent. 22.35.

In the practice of mantra (*mantrayoga*), if one engages for a year in the study, teaching, officiating at sacrifices, or acting as a priest for those who are prohibited and fallen (*patita*)—characterized by such activities as studying or teaching together with them—and if that mantra-practice consists of a thousand utterances (*vāka*); here, *vāka* means a word or phrase (*pada*). If it consists of a thousand words (*sahasrapada*), then this refers to an act committed unintentionally. However, if it was done intentionally, the status of being "fallen" (*patitatva*) would apply. Regarding minor offenses (*upapātaka*), the *Vasiṣṭha-smṛti* states: "Upon hearing of a fallen person, a *caṇḍāla*, a corpse, or a birth-impurity, they should remain silent for three nights; it is known from tradition that by reciting [the Veda] at least a thousand times, they become purified. By this same rule, teachers of censurable subjects and officiating priests are explained. It is also known from tradition that they become purified by the renunciation of their sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). Others, however, explain *mantrayoga* as joint study and joint sacrifice. (22.33)
And the same applies to those who extinguish the sacred fires, those who have been expelled from their caste, and those who have committed minor offenses (upapātaka). || 22.36 ||—|| 22.34 ||

One who, due to the calamity of his country or similar causes, remains separated from his Vedic fires for a long period is an *agnyutsādī* (one whose fires have been extinguished). He has already been described as a *nirākṛti*. He is not classified here as a minor sinner (*upapātaka*), because he is mentioned after Durvāsas and others. On the other hand, the *utsṛṣṭāgni* (one who has abandoned the fires) is explained differently, as one who has renounced the Vedic fires out of atheism (*nāstikya*). In this regard, the distinction between the subjects must be understood as follows: for one who abandons the rites out of atheism, or for whom a long time passes due to the calamity of the country and such, there is ordinary *brahmacarya* for one year; however, if the period is short, the *prājāpatya* penance applies. As Vasiṣṭha says: "He who casts away the fires, having performed the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights, should have them re-consecrated" (VaDh 1.23). For one who abandons them out of laziness or similar motives—even in the absence of atheism or national calamity—the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance is to be observed, as Manu has stated.

"A Brāhmaṇa who, out of desire, neglects the sacred fires for a month should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, for that is equal to the killing of a hero. [MDh 11.41]. This refers to one who has neglected them for a month; therefore, it should be understood that after this, a more severe Kṛcchra penance follows.
If an Agnihotrin intentionally neglects the sacred fires for more than a month,
he must perform both the Kṛcchra and the Cāndrāyaṇa penances without hesitation.

Because of this statement, even before a month has passed, the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance alone is required; for the author of the *Bhāṣya* has stated, "Or rather, the mention of 'month' is for the sake of clarity. Furthermore, in all such cases, the re-establishment of the sacred fires (*punarādheya*) and the expiation for the lapse of the proper time (*atītakālahoma*) are to be understood. And so says Jātukarṇi: "One should offer the sacrifice into the fire, or provide wealth to a Brahmin, [for the lapse]."

"When the fire has been lost, the twice-born man, having performed the *ādhāna* again according to rule, should offer [the oblations]. This statement is to be understood as applying both to the *śrauta* and the *smārta* fires. Thus, when a long period of time has elapsed, the gravity of the penance (*prāyaścitta*) becomes significant; therefore, no supplementation by means of recitations (*japa*) and the like is required here. For the *smārta* fire, however, there is only the re-establishment (*punar-ādhāna*) and the expiation for the lapse of time; there is no other penance. But in the case of atheism (*nāstikya*), a *prājāpatya* penance is to be observed. Thus Vyāghra says:
"The twice-born man who abandons the fires out of atheism should perform a *prājāpatya*."
"Furthermore, for others, there is the re-establishment of the sacred fires, as well as giving and likewise [other penances].

For those who have been excluded from the *nirākṛti* category and those mentioned as being unfit for the company at meals (*apāṅktya*), provided they are not guilty of minor offenses (*upapātaka*), one should observe what was stated by Manu:
"Eating only at every sixth mealtime for a month, and the recitation of the *Saṃhitā*."
"And *śāla* oblations performed daily are the purification for those excluded from the company at meals" (MDh 11.200).
The plural number in the term "upapātakas" (minor sins) is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) of those mentioned in other Smṛtis. As Manu has said:
"Killing a cow, sacrificing for those unworthy to sacrifice, adultery, and selling oneself;..."
Abandoning one's guru, mother, father, one's own Vedic study, the sacred fires, and one's son.
Being superseded by a younger brother, as well as superseding him;
giving away one's daughter to either of them, and officiating at a sacrifice for either of them.
Violating a maiden, usury, the breaking of a vow,
and the sale of a tank, a garden, one’s wife, or a child.
The state of being a *vrātya*, abandoning a wife who bears children, teaching for a fee,
receiving instruction for a fee, and the sale of goods that should not be sold.
Authority over all forms [of crafts], the operation of great machines,
the sale of harmful medicinal herbs, livelihood through women, malevolent magic, and rites of eradication.
Felling trees that are not yet dry for the sake of fuel,
undertaking actions for one's own sake, and likewise eating censured food;
Not maintaining the sacred fires, theft, non-payment of debts,
studying improper scriptures, and engaging in the arts of the stage.
“Stealing grain, base metals, or cattle; associating with women who drink liquor;

killing a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya; and atheism—these are minor offenses (upapātaka). [MDh 11.59–65] Regarding these, for some specific cases, an expiation is heard directly in another Smṛti. As Vasiṣṭha says:

A younger brother who has married before his elder brother (parivitta) shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights, then marry that same woman and live with her. Now, an elder brother whose younger brother has married before him (parivividāna) shall perform the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra penances, give [the bride-price] to that [younger brother], and then marry again and live with that same woman. The husband of a younger sister whose elder sister remains unmarried (agredidhiṣūpati) shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights, then marry that same woman and live with her. The husband of an elder sister whose younger sister has already been married (didhiṣūpati) shall perform the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra penances and give [the bride-price] to that [younger brother], and then marry again. [VaDh 20.7–10]

And so forth. Regarding the killing of a cow, this has been stated here; likewise, it has been stated for officiating at sacrifices for those unfit to sacrifice (*ayājya*), for adultery, and for the abandonment of one's Vedic study and sacred fires. And regarding the defilement of a maiden, Vasiṣṭha says: "Having approached the wife of a teacher, the female friend of a teacher, a woman who is outcasted, or one who is fallen, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance for one-quarter of a year" (VaDh 20.16). This should be understood to apply when the act is committed unintentionally. But if done intentionally, [one should say]: "Having discharged semen in women of one's own [lineage], one should perform the vow prescribed for violating the Guru’s bed."

Regarding the verse by Manu: "In the case of the wives of a friend, a son, or among women of the lowest castes (*antyajā*) and maidens" (MDh 11.170), the penance for violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa-vrata*) is to be understood. Although this is stated in general terms, specific penances must nevertheless be observed according to the particular caste: "The full [penance] for a Brāhmaṇa girl, half for a Kṣatriya girl," and so forth. Furthermore, regarding the state of being a *vrātya*, that which was spoken by Vasiṣṭha has been cited: "One whose *Sāvitrī* initiation has lapsed shall perform the *Uddālaka-vrata*" (VaDh 11.76), etc. Manu also says:

“Those twice-born men for whom the Sāvitrī has not been recited according to the rule—having made them perform three *kṛcchra* penances, one should initiate them according to the rule. [MDh 11.191] In this regard, it should be understood that if a long period of time has elapsed, the Uddālaka-vrata is prescribed; for a middling period, the three *kṛcchras*; and for a very short period of delay, the Vrātyastoma sacrifice. Regarding teaching for wages, it is stated that such a person is a “corrupter of the Veda” [GDh 20.1]. If this is done repeatedly, he incurs loss of caste (*pātitya*), and his exclusion is declared by the injunctions beginning with, “one should abandon the father” [GDh 20.1]. On another point, Manu says:

"Having abandoned one who has come for refuge and having caused the Veda to be corrupted, a twice-born man removes that sin by subsisting on barley for one year. [MDh 11.198] Regarding malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) as well, Manu says: "Having performed the sacrifice for those who have lost their caste (*vrātya*), or having performed the funeral rites for others..."
“He removes both malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) and the *ahīna* sacrifice by means of three *kṛcchra* penances.

[MDh 11.197] This refers to the killing of a twice-born person. However, for the killing of a Śūdra and others, one should follow the statement of Paiṭhīnasi: “Having performed malevolent magic against a Śūdra, one should perform a *prājāpatya* penance. Regarding the eating of forbidden food, however, he will state later: “In the case of eating what should not be eaten, there is the state of being purged of all excrement,” [GDh 23.23] and so forth. In that regard, if this is done intentionally and repeatedly, it is equal to the drinking of liquor. As Manu says:
“Eating forbidden foods and things censured—these six acts are equal to the drinking of liquor. [MDh 11.58]

[MDh 11.56] Thus, this should be understood as applying to the repeated commission of a minor offense (*upapātaka*) unintentionally. For those minor offenses for which no specific penance has been prescribed, this standard period of celibacy (*prākṛta-brahmacarya*) lasting one year should be observed; and this refers specifically to cases of repetition. In other instances, that which was stated by Manu applies:
"Twice-born men who have committed minor offenses shall perform this very same vow."

"Or else, for the sake of purification, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, with the exception of the Avakīrṇin penance. (MDh 11.117). In that case as well, the Cāndrāyaṇa is to be understood for unintentional acts; otherwise, the penance for cow-slaughter is to be observed. Since the extension [of the rule] is already established by the word "and" (*ca*), the use of the word "thus" (*evaṃ*) is for the purpose of extending the entire [set of rules]. Consequently, the rule "Upon obtaining wealth, there is relinquishment" (GDh 22.33), and so forth, is to be observed. 22.36.

One whose nature it is to extinguish the sacred fires is called an *agnyutsādī* (one who extinguishes the fires) when done intentionally. A *nirākṛti* is one who, despite having the capacity, does not study the Vedas. Regarding the minor offenses (*upapātakas*), those such as the slayer of a cow or the committer of Brahman-murder, which precede Durvāla among those unworthy of sitting in the company of the virtuous (*apaṅktyas*), have been explained [GDh 21.11]. For these very cases, beginning with the extinguisher of the fires, the rule is that there shall be a year-long period of celibacy (*brahmacarya*). This refers to one who, out of atheism or due to a calamity in the country and so forth, abandons the fires and does not re-establish them for a long time even after they have been pacified. In that same context, regarding a shorter period, the Vasiṣṭha-smṛti states: "He who abandons the fires, having performed a *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights, should re-establish them again" [VaDh 21.27]. For one who abandons them out of laziness, the rule of Manu applies.

"A Brāhmaṇa who is an *agnihotrī*, having intentionally abandoned the sacred fires, shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance for one month; for that is equal to the killing of a hero (*vīrahatyā*). [MDh 11.41] The grammatical construction is "having abandoned [the fires] for a month.
However, if an *agnihotrī* intentionally abandons the fires after a month has passed...

"One should perform the Kṛcchra and the Cāndrāyaṇa penances here without hesitation. Thus it is said; they maintain that the Cāndrāyaṇa is required even for abandoning the fire within a month. Regarding the Smārta fire, however:
"A twice-born man who, out of atheism, abandons the fire shall perform the Prājāpatya penance;
otherwise, there is simply the re-establishment of the fire (punarādhāna) and likewise the giving of gifts."

But for a human being, the purification from those unworthy of the company at meals is as follows: "Eating only at every sixth mealtime for a month, the recitation of the *Saṃhitā*, and daily fire-offerings with *Śākala* wood—this is the constant means of purification. (MDh 11.200) || 22.34 ||
And a woman who is unfaithful, even if she is guarded, shall receive only a morsel of food. || 22.37 || — || 22.35 ||
H reads "yāticāriṇī".

A woman should perform this same penance. This applies to one who has transgressed—that is, one who has committed adultery. Since adultery with a Śūdra has already been mentioned, this refers to adultery with members of the twice-born castes. If the act was intentional and occurred only once, this applies to adultery with someone of the same caste, as the rule for adultery with another’s wife has already been stated elsewhere: "Whatever [penance] is prescribed for a man regarding another's wife... [MDh 11.176]. However, in the case of a Brāhmaṇa woman’s adultery with a Kṣatriya, that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha should be observed: "In the event of sexual intercourse, she should wear a garment smeared with ghee for one year; she should sleep on a bed of Kuśa grass in a pit filled with cow-dung. After a year, having submerged herself in water, she should offer oblations with her head [submerged] eight thousand times while reciting the Sāvitrī; she then becomes purified" [VaDh 21.8]. In the case of adultery with a Vaiśya, that which was stated by Auśanas should be observed: "An unchaste woman shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for one year. Furthermore, in the case of approaching a woman of lower status than oneself, half of the prescribed penance should be assigned. Likewise, it is heard in the scriptures regarding mere conversation: [the following rules apply].

"In the case of a transgression against her husband committed through the mind, she should eat barley-gruel or milk-rice for three nights and sleep on the ground; after the three nights, while submerged in water, she should offer oblations with one hundred and eight repetitions of the Sāvitrī verse for each head [of the mantra]; it is declared that she thus becomes purified. In the case of verbal connection [with another], having performed this same penance for a month, after the month, while submerged in water, she should offer oblations with four sets of one hundred and eight repetitions of the Sāvitrī verse for each head. [VaDh 21.6–7]. This also applies to a single instance of speaking; however, in the case of repetition, that which was stated by Manu applies, because of the hearing of the word "again" (punar). As he said:
"But if she should become thoroughly corrupted after being approached by a man of equal status, the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances are declared to be her means of purification" (MDh 11.177).

In the case of conversation with an inferior man, double that [penance] is to be observed; in the case of conversation with a superior man, half [of it] is to be understood. Thus, a woman who has committed adultery and is not purified shall, while being kept guarded, receive only enough food for the maintenance of life—merely a *piṇḍa*—and, because of the word "tu" (but), she shall also receive clothing for the purpose of covering her private parts. 22.37.

A woman who transgresses against her husband—that is, commits adultery by consorting with another man—must perform this same penance: celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for one year. And as long as that penance is being completed, she, remaining concealed, receives only a mere morsel of food. This applies to a single instance of intentional intercourse; otherwise, [the rule is different].

"That which applies to a man regarding the wives of others, that same vow he should cause her to perform" (MDh 11.176)—this refers to the case of a woman of the same caste. Regarding a Brāhmaṇī woman in the case of a Kṣatriya, Vasiṣṭha states: "In the event of sexual intercourse, she should wear a garment smeared with ghee for one year; she should eat while sitting on a bed of cow-dung mud or on a layer of *kuśa* grass, and sleep on the ground. After half a year, she should offer oblations with her head submerged in water, reciting the *Sāvitrī* eight thousand times" (VaDh 21.8). Regarding a Vaiśya, however, Auśanasa says: "An unchaste woman should perform the *Kṛcchra* penance for one year. On this point, Bṛhat-Pracetās says:
If Brahmins have sexual union with a Śūdra woman, she is not born from that [union as a true Brahmin];
for her, an atonement is prescribed: the Kṛcchra penance and three Cāndrāyaṇas.
For a Brahmin woman’s sexual union with a Vaiśya, two Cāndrāyaṇas and one Kṛcchra are prescribed;
for her union with a Kṣatriya, there should be one Kṛcchra and one Cāndrāyaṇa.
A Kṣatriya woman who has had sexual contact with a Śūdra shall perform the Kṛcchra penance and two Cāndrāyaṇas;
one who has united with a Vaiśya shall perform a Cāndrāyaṇa and a Kṛcchra.

"Having approached a Śūdra, a Vaiśya woman should perform the Kṛcchra penance followed by the Cāndrāyaṇa; she should perform the Kṛcchra reduced by one quarter for each successive degree of proximity (ānulomya). Regarding a Brāhmaṇa woman who has given birth [to such a child], there is a specific rule in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
In the case of killing a Brahmin embryo, the penance for a Kṣatriya shall be a Parāka;
likewise, for a Vaiśya, it shall be an Aindava and a Parāka, provided the act was unintentional.

"If there is an abortion from a Śūdra womb, one becomes a Caṇḍāla; therefore, in the case of an abortion due to defects of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), one should perform three *Cāndrāyaṇa* penances. However, in the case of intentional action (*kāmakāra*), one should perform double the Parāka and other penances. Vasiṣṭha, however, states:
"The wives of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas who have had sexual intercourse with a Śūdra..."

Those who have not yet given birth are purified by penance, but others are not. However, for a woman who has already conceived, if she subsequently engages in intercourse with a Śūdra or similar person,
or if a pregnant woman is approached by a lustful man,
she shall not perform penance until the fetus has been delivered.
Once the child is born, one should subsequently observe the vow of eating only barley-gruel for one month;
there is no defect in the fetus in that case, and the child should be consecrated according to the prescribed rite.
Thus, what is stated in another Smṛti should be understood. However, when one does not perform penance due to immorality, then the following applies:
"In the case of an inverse [mixture], there shall be death for men, and for women, the cutting off of the nose and so forth" (YDh 2.286).
"She who has been enjoyed by one of inferior caste shall be branded or even put to death"—thus says Parāśara. Branding consists of marking with the male organ. (22.35)

In the case of non-human females—with the exception of cows—for the sake of intercourse with them, there shall be an oblation of ghee with the *kūśmāṇḍa* mantras; [an oblation of ghee]. || 22.38 || — || 22.36 ||

If sexual intercourse is practiced for the sake of a woman with non-human females such as mares and the like—excluding cows—one must perform an oblation of ghee with the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras beginning with "yad devā devaheḍanam. It should be understood that due to repetition, the oblation must be repeated. || 22.38 ||

When sexual intercourse is practiced for the sake of a woman with non-human females—such as female buffaloes and others—with the exception of a cow, an oblation of clarified butter (*ghṛta-homa*) must be performed with *kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras. The statement "with the exception of a cow" is for the sake of clarity; he will state later: "And in the case of a cow, it is equal to violating the Guru’s bed" (GDh 23.12). Consequently, that same penance will apply to the act of approaching a cow. This [penance] applies to a single instance of intercourse; in the case of repetition, that which was stated by Śaṅkha applies: "In approaching a female animal or a prostitute, one should perform the *Prājāpatya*. On this point, Kaṇva says: "But he who has procreated in a prostitute, being self-controlled and subsisting on alms..."
"By practicing the Sāvitrī a hundred thousand times, one attains purity. Thus, the repetition has been stated. 22.36.
Now begins the twenty-third chapter.
He now states the expiation for drinking liquor, which follows in the proper sequence.
He states the expiation for drinking liquor, which follows in the proper sequence.
In the case of a Brāhmaṇa who has drunk spirituous liquor, they should pour hot liquor into his mouth; he becomes pure when he dies [from it]. 23.1.
By the word *surā* here, the three types of liquor are intended, because of the mention of the Brāhmaṇa and because all three types are prohibited for him. As Manu says:
"The liquor made from molasses (*gauḍī*), that from honey (*mādhvī*), and that from flour (*paiṣṭī*)—these are to be known as the three kinds of *surā*."

"Just as even a single drop must not be drunk, so all [liquors] must not be drunk by the best of the twice-born" (MDh 11.94). Since it will be stated later, "In the case of drinking unintentionally" (GDh 23.2), it is understood that this [penance] applies to intentional drinking. This same penance for drinking *paiṣṭī* liquor should be understood to apply to Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas as well, because that specific type of liquor is prohibited for them. As Manu says: "Liquor is indeed the filth of foods, and sin is called filth;
therefore, a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, and a Vaiśya should not drink liquor" (MDh 11.93). Likewise:
A twice-born man who has drunk liquor through delusion shall drink liquor that is the color of fire.

"When his body has been consumed by that [fire], he is then released from the sin. (MDh 11.90) Since the term "twice-born" (*dvija*) is used in the injunction for penance, it is understood that for whichever person a particular drink is forbidden, drinking that very same drink when it is fire-colored, provided it was done intentionally, constitutes the penance. This should be understood to apply here as well to a Brāhmaṇa’s intentional repeated consumption of *gauḍī* or *mādhvī*, and to the intentional single consumption of *paiṣṭī*. Why? Because other penances are seen for the intentional single consumption of *gauḍī* or *mādhvī*. As Vasiṣṭha says: "In the case of drinking liquor (*madya*), however, if it is *asurā* or *surā* and done unintentionally, there is the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* penances, the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and a re-initiation (*punaḥsaṃskāra*). (VaDh 20.19). Here, because it is stated "if it is *surā* and done unintentionally," it follows that the drinking of *madya* [in this context] was intentional. Furthermore, the *atikṛcchra* mentioned here is the *taptakṛcchra*, as seen in another Smṛti: "Having drunk *madya*, one should perform the *kṛcchra* or the *taptakṛcchra*," according to the statement of Paiṭhīnasi. It should be understood that "hot" means "fire-colored," because the passage begins with "he is purified when dead. "They should pour [it]" means they should pour it upon him face-to-face. This is a designation of the causal agent rather than the direct agent; the one who drinks does so by himself. As Āpastamba says: "The drinker of *surā* should drink *surā* that is fire-colored. (ĀpDh 1.25.3). The plural number in "they should pour" is intended to indicate the plurality of those who instruct [the penance]. Thus says Manu.

"That which those three who know the Vedas declare as the expiation for sins shall serve as their means of purification, for the speech of the learned is indeed purifying. [MDh 11.85] Śaṅkha also says:

"Having been approved by the assembly and having duly confessed his offense according to the facts, whatever those who know the rules prescribe shall be the supreme means of purification for him. [The word] *āsye* means "in the mouth"; one who has died shall be purified; he becomes pure through death alone. In the phrase "having drunk *surā* in the mouth," the word *surā* is intended to include cow urine and other such substances as well. As Manu says:
"Or he may drink cow urine the color of fire, or even water [the same color]."

“Milk, ghee, or even the juice of cow dung [should be drunk by her] until death. [MDh 11.91] Since the word *brāhmaṇa* denotes a caste (*jāti*), this same penance applies to a Brāhmaṇī woman as well for drinking *surā*. As Śaṅkha says, referring specifically to women: “She should avoid *surā*, garlic, onions, leeks, meat, and other forbidden foods; she should subsist on food [only], for the body consists of what it eats, or rather, it is said to be composed of that. Likewise, Vasiṣṭha also states: “Half the body of him whose wife drinks *surā* falls [with her].”

"No atonement is prescribed for one whose body has fallen [into such a state]. [VaDh 21.15]. Likewise, in that same work: "The gods do not lead a Brāhmaṇī woman who drinks liquor to the world of her husband; indeed, having exhausted her merit, she wanders here, becoming a leech in the waters or a pearl-oyster shell.
[VaDh 21.11]. Others, however, observing the customs of other regions, say:
"In former times, women were enjoyed by the gods—by Soma, Gandharva, and Agni."
Thereafter, they go to the world of men; therefore, women are free from blemish.

Furthermore, because of the observation in the *Vasiṣṭha-smṛti*: "Soma gave them purity, Gandharva taught them speech, and Agni [granted] the state of being food for all; therefore, women are free from blemish" (VaDh 28.5–6), they do not accept this expiation for a Brāhmaṇī woman. In that regard, an option based on regional distinctions (*deśavyavasthā*) should be understood. 23.1.
There are three kinds of *surā*. As Manu has said:
"The *gauḍī*, the *mādhvī*, and the *paiṣṭī*—these should be known as the three kinds of *surā*.

Just as one [type] is not to be drunk, so all are forbidden for the best of the twice-born" (MDh 11.94). The "best of the twice-born" are the Brāhmaṇas; however, for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, it is only the *paiṣṭī* that is forbidden. As he himself has stated:
Surā is indeed the impurity of foods, and evil is said to be impurity.

"Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, and a Vaiśya shall not drink *surā*. [MDh 11.93] *Surā* made from flour (*paiṣṭī*) is the dregs of grains. Here, the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all twice-born (*dvijāti*) castes. One who drinks that specific *surā* which has been forbidden for him is a *surāpa*. Into the mouth of such a twice-born person, they should pour that very same *surā* while hot. This act of pouring is prescribed for the instructors; for they indeed pour the *surā* into his mouth. They instruct: "This is the expiation for that *surāpa* by whom the *surā* must be drunk while very hot. However, he himself is the one who performs the pouring. And so says Āpastamba: "The *surāpa* shall drink *surā* that is touched by fire. [ĀpDh 1.25.3] The plural number in "they should pour" (*āsiñceyuḥ*) indicates the plurality of the instructors. Manu also says:
"Those three who are knowers of the Vedas shall declare the expiation for their sins;

for that is their means of purification, since the speech of the learned is indeed purifying. (MDh 11.85) Because of the statement "the dead man shall be purified," liquor must be heated until the drinker dies. Paiṭhīnasi says: "He should drink while wearing wet clothes. Prajāpati says: "With a vessel made of iron or copper. Then Yājñavalkya says:
"Of liquor, water, ghee, cow-urine, and milk, [he should drink that which is] like fire..."
Having drunk any one of these intoxicants, one attains purification through death.

"Clad in hair-cloth or with matted locks, he shall perform the vow for killing a Brāhmaṇa; or he shall eat oil-cake or grain-particles at night for a year. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 4.253–254). Among these, the penance ending in death applies to the case of intentional and repeated practice. In that same context, the twelve-year vow for killing a Brāhmaṇa applies to the case of drinking [liquor] once. Regarding women here, Śaṅkha says: "One should avoid non-edible things such as *surā* liquor, garlic, onion, leek, meat, and so forth; this body consists of food. Vasiṣṭha also says:

"Half of the body of that man whose wife drinks *surā* falls; for one whose half-body has fallen, no expiation (*nikṛti*) is prescribed. [VaDh 21.15] In this regard, *surā* is forbidden for women as well, and there is an expiation. It was stated previously that for women, the expiation is half. In that context, since it is impossible to calculate half of an expiation ending in death, for intentional drinking on a single occasion, the expiation is half of the twelve-year penance. For repetition, it is the repetition of that very same penance. 23.1.
If one drinks milk, ghee, water, or air for three days each, that is the *taptakṛcchra*. || 23.2 ||
If he drinks milk, ghee, water, or air for three days each while they are heated, that constitutes the Kṛcchra penance; thereafter, his consecration (saṃskāra) takes place. || 23.2 ||

The ministers [hold that this applies] through ignorance regarding the Gauḍī and Mādhvī liquors, because the word "drinking" is mentioned again in the context of the qualification for drinking. And so says Manu: "Having drunk Vāruṇī through ignorance, one becomes pure by means of the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) alone; but having done so intentionally, the penance is not to be prescribed otherwise—the rule is that it ends only with life. [MDh 11.146] Regarding this, the commentator Bhāruci has explained: "By means of the purificatory rite accompanied by the *Taptakṛcchra* penance. And thus, this should be understood to apply to a Brāhmaṇa who drinks the *paiṣṭī* liquor once unintentionally. As Manu says:

Or he may eat grain husks, or oil-cake once at night for a year, wearing hair-cloth, with matted hair, and carrying a skull-topped staff, in order to remove the sin of drinking liquor. However, regarding Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, the penance as stated by Vasiṣṭha—beginning with "In the case of unintentional [drinking] of *surā*" (VaDh 20.19)—should be observed. Even in the case of intentional and repeated practice of that [drinking], the penance ending in death must be understood to apply to all three [classes]. As Vasiṣṭha says:

"But in the case of repeated practice of liquor, the twice-born shall drink it when it has reached the color of fire" (VaDh 20.22). Here, the word *tu* (but) expresses a distinction. For the twice-born classes, in the case of unintentional repeated practice of *paiṣṭī* liquor, that liquor must be drunk when it has specifically reached the color of fire; however, for a Brāhmaṇa, in the case of unintentional repeated practice of *gauḍī* or *mādhvī* liquors, purification occurs only through death from drinking it when it has reached the color of fire. Thus Vyāghra says: "Having intentionally or unintentionally drunk liquor again, the best of the twice-born..."

"Then, having drunk that [liquor] which has the color of fire, he shall be purified from his sin when dead. Thus it is said. However, for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, there is no prohibition against *gauḍī* (molasses-based) and *mādhvī* (honey-based) liquors. To this effect Vyāsa says:
"Both Keśava and Arjuna were seen by me intoxicated with honey-liquor, both anointed with sandalwood paste, and both reclining upon the same couch."

Consequently, for a Brāhmaṇa who unintentionally drinks Gauḍī or Mādhvī liquor even once, he must perform the penance of subsisting on milk and the other items for three days each. The arrangement of the milk and other items in unequal durations is intended to preclude a sequential progression. Thus Vasiṣṭha says:
"For three days he should drink hot water; for three days he should drink hot milk;
having drunk hot ghee for three days, he should subsist on air for the final three days."

"Thus is the *taptakṛcchra*. [VaDh 21.21] Here, only water, ghee, and milk are to be heated, because that is possible; not air. "That is the *kṛcchra*" is intended to include the general injunction for the *kṛcchra* penance, such as "he should stand during the day and sit during the night," and so forth. 23.2.

But he who drinks *surā* unintentionally—that is, without prior conscious intent—mistaking it for *yavāgū* or the like, must drink four substances—milk and so forth—while they are heated and hot. Because of the use of the accusative case, it is understood that he "should drink" them. For three days each: on the first three days milk, on the second ghee, on the third water, and on the fourth air. The heat of the air is obtained by staying in a place exposed to the sun. This *kṛcchra*, being of such a nature, is the *taptakṛcchra* penance for him. After that *kṛcchra*, a re-consecration—that is, a second initiation (*punar-upanayana*)—must be performed for him. In this regard, there is a specific rule from the *Mānava*.

"Shaving, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging for alms, and the vows—these indeed are discontinued in the rite of re-consecration. (MDh 11.151). This refers to the case of slight repetition. As for the statement in the *Mānava* code: "Having drunk *vāruṇī* through ignorance, one is purified by the rite of re-consecration alone" (MDh 11.146), that refers to the case of drinking it once. As for that which...

"Or he should eat oil-cake or even grain-particles for an entire year at night," such is the statement of Yājñavalkya. And as for that of Āpastamba: "Having committed theft or having drunk liquor," etc., both of these refer only to repeated practice (*abhyāsa*). Rules such as those of Manu: "Or he should eat grain-particles for a year, or oil-cake once at night;

for the purpose of removing the sin of drinking liquor, wearing hair-cloth, with matted hair and carrying a banner," etc., are to be applied to cases of unintentional acts (*abuddhipūrva*) alone, according to the degree of repetition. (23.2)
Then, for him, there is volitional formation. || 23.3 ||

The word "tataḥ" (then) means immediately after the period of penance (*kṛcchra*). The mention of "his" (*asya*) is for the sake of clarity, meaning "of him whose [liquor] was drunk. Furthermore, even for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, this applies to the performance of the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) when drinking *paiṣṭī* liquor intentionally and only once; this is so that their exclusion—which might follow from the fact that the qualification [for the penance] is stated specifically for Brāhmaṇas—does not occur. Alternatively, it is for the sake of what follows: namely, that in the case of consuming urine and such, the purificatory rite (*punaḥsaṃskāra*) applies to the Brāhmaṇa alone. This purificatory rite consists merely of the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), and does not include the observance of Vedic vows (*vedavrata*) and so forth. The specific nature of the *punaḥsaṃskāra* is to be understood from other Smṛti texts. As Manu says:

"Shaving the head, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging for alms, and the vows—these are indeed discontinued upon the performance of the rite of re-initiation. [MDh 11.151] Thus ends section 23.3.
And [the same penance applies] for consuming urine, feces, or semen. || 23.4 || — || 23.3 ||

This same penance applies to the consumption of urine and other such substances. The word "ca" (and) is intended to include the rite of re-initiation (*punaḥsaṃskāra*). This refers to intentional acts. Why? Because of the statement of Manu: "But having unintentionally eaten the food of any one of these, one should fast for three days."

"Having consumed semen, feces, or urine intentionally, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance. [MDh 4.222].
