Since the Commentator (Bhāruci) has stated here that by the word *kṛcchra* the *taptakṛcchra* is intended, and because other penances for consuming forbidden foods are taught subsequently, it should be understood that this refers to the consumption of the urine and so forth of humans. And this applies when done unintentionally.

"Having eaten the food of any one of these, however unintentionally, he shall fast for three days" (MDh 4.222). By this very rule, a three-day penance is to be understood; for if the act were intentional, a different penance would be observed. As Kaṇva says: "In the case of unintentionally consuming semen, urine, or feces, a twice-born man shall not eat for three days, but if intentionally, he shall perform the *taptakṛcchra*. Furthermore, even in cases of unintentional consumption, a re-initiation (*punaḥsaṃskāra*) is to be seen as required. As Manu says:

"Having unintentionally swallowed feces, urine, or that which is mixed with *surā* liquor, the three twice-born castes deserve to undergo the purificatory rite (*punaḥsaṃskāra*) again. (MDh 11.150). Some maintain that this very penance applies here; however, that too should be understood as referring to a single instance of swallowing. And thus, where a penance for swallowing urine or feces is prescribed in such passages as "of crows, donkeys, and camels," etc., it should be understood to apply to everything except humans. 23.4.

And for consuming urine and the like, the penance is a rite of re-consecration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*) accompanied by the *taptakṛcchra* austerity. This refers to cases where the act is intentional. As it is said: "Having unintentionally eaten the food of any one of these, one should fast for three days;
having eaten it intentionally, or semen, feces, or urine, one should perform the *kṛcchra*. (MDh 4.222)
"Having unintentionally swallowed feces, urine, or that which is mixed with *surā* liquor, the three twice-born castes deserve to undergo the purificatory rite again. Thus it is said;
and Kaṇva has also stated this clearly:
"If one intentionally consumes semen, urine, or feces, a twice-born man shall not eat for three days; having done so intentionally, he must perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance. (23.3)
And [the same applies] to the limbs of beasts of prey, camels, and donkeys. 23.5 — 23.4.

The term *prāśane* (in the case of eating) is understood to carry over from the previous context. *Śvāpadāḥ* refers to those whose feet are like those of a dog (*śveva padāḥ*), namely jackals and other such animals with dog-like feet. *Uṣṭra* and *khara* (camel and donkey) are well known. For the consumption of their limbs—such as flesh, skin, and so forth—this very same penance applies. Since they are specified by the rule regarding those with dog-like feet, the case of the dog is established by implication; furthermore, by the use of the word "and" (*ca*), this also applies to humans. (23.5)

Tigers and the like are wild beasts that roam the forest; camels and donkeys are well known. Regarding their limbs—such as flesh, skin, and so forth—if one consumes them, there is the *taptakṛcchra* penance and a rite of re-consecration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*). If the act is repeated intentionally, both [penances] are combined. If it occurs once intentionally or if it is repeated unintentionally, there is the *taptakṛcchra*. If it occurs once intentionally, there is only the rite of re-consecration. (23.4)
And [the same applies] to the village cock and the pig. 23.6 — 23.5.

In the case of divination by means of the limbs of the body, this same expiation applies. The separate formulation [of this rule] is for the purpose of excluding these two cases from the previous rule, "and of one bitten by the aforementioned [animals]" (GDh 23.8). Regarding this [present case], [the expiation] beginning with intentional acts has already been stated previously. The word "ca" (and) serves to carry over the requirement of re-initiation. || 23.6 ||
And for consuming the flesh of a village cock or a pig, this same penance applies; and the determination of the specific case is as before. 23.5.
If one who has drunk liquor smells a fragrance [of it], he must perform breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and consume clarified butter (ghṛta). 23.7. — 23.6.

Because the term *surāpaḥ* (wine-drinker) is not further specified, it refers to every such person. Regarding "smelling the odor" (*gandhāghrāṇe*), it means smelling the odor of *surā*, but not the odor of the body. Even in that case, it does not refer to smelling the odor of *surā* situated elsewhere; for while one might have simply said "smelling the odor of *surā*," the specific designation *surāpasya* (of the wine-drinker) is used. Consequently, the loss of caste (*jātibhraṃśakara*) should be understood to apply to the smelling of the odor of *surā* situated elsewhere. As Manu says: "Having caused injury to a Brāhmaṇa, or having smelled what is unfit to be smelled, or [the odor of] intoxicants... (*MDh 11.56*).
"Deceit and sexual intercourse with men are recorded as acts that cause loss of caste. (MDh 11.67). Likewise, regarding the penance:
"Having intentionally committed any one of the acts that cause loss of caste..."

"One should perform the *sāntapana* or the *prājāpatya* penance if [the act was committed] unintentionally" (MDh 11.124). It should be understood that for whichever substance is forbidden for a particular person, smelling its odor constitutes the offense, since no specific distinction is made. For the twice-born (*dvijāti*), the same penance for acts causing loss of caste (*jātibhraṃśakara*) is to be observed. There is no application here of the rule "half for a Brāhmaṇa, a quarter for a Kṣatriya," because of the observation of other Smṛti texts. As Kaṇva says: "A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or likewise a Vaiśya..."

"Having smelled the odor of *surā*, one should perform the *sāntapana* vow. Here, three *prāṇāyāmas* are to be understood, since the plural number is satisfied by that alone. The consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśana*) is merely a ritual bathing of the body; having performed that, one may eat, as there is no rule prescribing a fast. The non-compound form of the particle *ca* is intended to allow for the interpretation of the items both individually and collectively. Therefore, for a Brāhmaṇa the whole [set] applies, for a Kṣatriya the *prāṇāyāmas*, and for a Vaiśya the consumption of clarified butter. Even in that regard, a distinction must be observed for a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*). As Manu says:

"But a Brāhmaṇa who has drunk Soma, having smelled the odor of one who has drunk liquor, becomes purified by suppressing his breath three times in water and consuming clarified butter" (MDh 11.149). There is no distinction for the Kṣatriya and others, because there is no such statement. 23.7.

But as for one who has drunk *surā*, he smells that odor of *surā* [from the sinner], yet not the odor of the sinner's body, nor the odor of the liquor remaining in the vessel; for him, the penance consists of three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) and the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśana*). This applies to a Brāhmaṇa when both [smelling the odor and consuming the butter] are combined; for a Kṣatriya, there are breath-restraints; for a Vaiśya, the consumption of clarified butter. A specific rule regarding the Soma-drinker is shown by Manu: "Having smelled the odor of a Brāhmaṇa who has drunk *surā*, the Soma-drinker becomes pure by sipping water three times, performing breath-restraints, and consuming clarified butter" (MDh 11.149).

"Causing pain to a Brāhmaṇa, smelling things that should not be smelled or drinking intoxicants, crookedness, and sexual intercourse with a male—these are recorded as acts causing the confusion of castes (jāti-saṃkara). Having intentionally committed any one of these acts that causes the loss of caste... [MDh 11.67]. Thus. Having performed any one of the acts that cause the degradation of caste, intentionally...

"One should perform the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra or the Prājāpatya penance if one unintentionally smells the scent of liquor contained in a vessel"—this is the rule from the Code of Manu regarding the smelling of the fragrance of liquor residing in a vessel. 23.6.
And for one bitten by [the aforementioned creatures] previously [listed]. 23.8 — 23.7.

This same penance applies to one bitten by wild beasts and the like, including humans. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it includes domestic carnivorous animals as well. Thus says Manu: "One bitten by a dog, a jackal, or a donkey, or by domestic carnivorous animals, or by a human, a horse, a camel, or a pig, is purified by breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*). [MDh 11.199]. In this case too, the scope should be understood in the same way. For a Brāhmaṇa bitten by these, that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha should be observed.

"But a Brāhmaṇa bitten by a dog becomes pure by going to a river that flows into the ocean, performing one hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), and consuming clarified butter" (VaDh 23.31). Since the mention of the "dog" is intended as an illustration for these [other animals] as well, this [prescribed] triad of breath-restraints should be understood to apply to a Kṣatriya. For a Vaiśya, one breath-restraint should be understood as prescribed by Manu, because of the use of the singular number in the word "by a breath-restraint" (*prāṇāyāmena*). However, there is no fault for a Śūdra. And for a woman, a bath with her clothes on (*sacelasnāna*) should be understood; thus says Jātukarṇi.
A Brāhmaṇī, a Kṣatriyā, or a Vaiśyā who has been bitten by a dog or even by wild beasts, become pure by bathing with their clothes on; of this there is no doubt.
Thus [ends the verse]. 23.8.

For one bitten by the aforementioned beasts of prey and the like, the expiation consists of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśana*). Manu, however, states:

"One bitten by dogs, jackals, donkeys, or even by domestic carnivorous animals, as well as by humans, horses, camels, and boars, becomes pure through breath control" (MDh 11.199). Regarding the case of a Brāhmaṇa, there is a specific rule from Vasiṣṭha.

"A Brāhmaṇa who has been bitten by a dog becomes purified by going to a river that flows into the ocean, performing one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), and consuming clarified butter. [VaDh 23.31]. Jātūkarṇya says:
"A Brāhmaṇa woman, a Kṣatriya woman, or a Vaiśya woman [who has been bitten] by a dog or even by wild beasts..."
Having bathed with one's clothes on after being bitten, one becomes pure; of this there is no doubt.
Thus [ends the section]. 23.7.
One who has violated the Guru’s bed shall lie upon a heated iron bed. 23.9 — 23.8.
One who has sexual intercourse with the wife of his teacher shall lie down upon a red-hot iron bed glowing like fire.

"In this context, 'guru' means father: 'He who performs the rites beginning with the *niṣeka* according to rule, and supports [the child] by other means, that Brahmin is called a guru'—thus says Manu (MDh 2.142). The mention of the 'Brahmin' (*vipra*) is an indicative mark for all social classes (*varṇa*). By the word *talpa*, which denotes a bed, the wife is indicated; therein, both the mother and her co-wife are included. One who approaches her is a *gurutalpagāmī*. On a bed made of heated black iron, he shall lie down in such a way that death indeed occurs. [23.8]
Or he might embrace a blazing iron image. || 23.10 || — || 23.9 ||

H reads "vā śliṣyej," meaning he should embrace or clasp a glowing *sūrmi*—an iron image of a woman that is hollow inside; others say it is a piece of wood that is hollow inside. He should embrace or hug it while it is burning. 23.10.
A female form made of iron is a *sūrmī*; one should embrace it while it is blazing, glowing like fire, and heated, until the separation of life. 23.9.

Or, having cut off his penis together with the testicles and holding them in his cupped hands, he should walk straight toward the southwest until his body collapses; when dead, he shall be purified. (23.11)
Or, having cut off his penis together with the testicles and holding them in his cupped hands, he should walk straight toward the southwest until he collapses from exhaustion.

Having cut off the male organ—the characteristic mark of a man—along with the seed and the root, and having placed it in both hands, he should go straight toward the southwest (the direction of Nirṛti), avoiding wells and the like, until his body falls, that is, until death. Upon dying, he becomes pure. And this [penance] applies as a general rule for all [cases], because it ends only with death. Thus, when these options are established, the mention of "either" (*vā*) is for the purpose of providing a systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*). Consequently, there is the first [penance] in the case of a voluntary union between those two; the second, when one is incited by her; and the third, when she has been incited by the man himself. This also applies to a Brāhmaṇa’s intentional, single instance of intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa woman. However, in the case of an unintentional, single instance of intercourse, that which was stated by Manu should be observed.
Carrying a skull-topped staff, clad in rags, or with a beard, he dwells in a solitary forest.

“One should perform the *prājāpatya* penance for one year with a concentrated mind. (MDh 11.105) This also applies when there is a union through the mutual desire of both. When she has incited him and he has acted upon her who was incited by him, the rule of Śukra (*auśanasa*) should be observed: “One who violates the Guru’s bed shall perform the vow for killing a Brahmin for one year, or the *taptakṛcchra* for six months. Thus, in the case of approaching a Brāhmaṇa woman, if it is intentional and occurs once, or if it is unintentional but repeated, the penance ends only in death. In the case of approaching a Kṣatriya woman, that which was stated by Vyāghra should be observed.
"A Brahmin who has approached his teacher's wife shall perform the *kṛcchra*, the *atikṛcchra*, and likewise the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* for three months.

In that case as well, if the act is intentional and occurs once, and both parties have acted out of mutual desire, it is an *atikṛcchra*. For one who was incited by her, it is a *kṛcchra*; for one who incited her himself, it is a *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*. Furthermore, if it is intentional and repeated, the penance ends only with death. As Kavaṣa said:
"Having intentionally approached the wife of his guru, who is the daughter of a Kṣatriya, the twice-born man should cut off his penis along with the testicles and die; thus he becomes pure.
This [penance] prescribed by Kaṇva should be understood to apply to a single instance of unintentional intercourse.

"A twice-born man who, through ignorance, has once approached the wife of his guru who is a Kṣatriya woman, shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa, the Taptakṛcchra, and likewise the Atikṛcchra. In that case as well, if the act proceeds from the mutual desire of both, it is the Taptakṛcchra; if he was incited by her, it is the Atikṛcchra; and if she was incited by him, it is the Cāndrāyaṇa. However, in the case of repetition—having again approached the wife of his guru, who is a daughter of a Kṣatriya, unintentionally... [the penance is as follows].
Having cut off only the testicles, he shall be purified whether he remains alive or dies.

Thus it should be understood as stated by Jātūkarṇya. Regarding intentional intercourse with a Vaiśya woman once, Kavaṣa says: "Having intentionally approached his teacher’s Vaiśya wife once, a twice-born man should perform for one month the Taptakṛcchra, the Parāka, and likewise the Sāntapana penances. In that case as well, if the act proceeds from the mutual desire of both, the penance is the Taptakṛcchra; if he was incited by her, the Sāntapana; if she was incited by him, the Parāka. In the case of repetition, the tip of the penis must be cut off. As Lokākṣi says:

"Having gone again to the wife of his guru, and having gone there repeatedly, he shall cut off the tip of his penis; then he shall be purified from that sin. From this very indicative text, it should be understood that the penance prescribed for violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*) applies even when the act is repeated many times. Regarding unintentional, single instances of such intercourse, Prajāpati says:
"He shall not eat for five nights, or likewise for seven or eight."

"Having approached the Vaiśya wife of his guru even once through ignorance, a twice-born man [must perform penance]. Regarding that, if the act was undertaken by mutual desire, the penance lasts seven nights; if he was incited by her, five nights; if she was incited by him, eight nights. However, in the case of repetition, one must maintain celibacy until death. Thus says Hārīta:

"A Brahmin who, deluded by ignorance, repeatedly approaches the Vaiśya wife of his guru, shall practice celibacy with its six ancillaries for as long as he lives. Regarding intentional intercourse with a Śūdra woman, Jābāli says:

"A Brahmin who intentionally approaches the Śūdra wife of his guru once must then perform the *atikṛcchra*, the *taptakṛcchra*, and likewise the *parāka* penances. In this case as well, it should be understood that if the act proceeds from the mutual desire of both, the *taptakṛcchra* is prescribed; if he was incited by her, the *atikṛcchra*; and if she was incited by him, the *parāka*. However, in the case of repetition, the observance of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for twelve years must be performed. As Upamanyu says:
"If a Brahmin, being composed, again intentionally approaches the Śūdra wife of his guru..."

"One of uncorrupted soul should practice celibacy for twelve years. Regarding ignorance, Dīrghatapas says: "Having once approached a Śūdra woman of his Guru, a Brāhmaṇa, being composed, should perform the Prājāpatya, the Sāntapana, or a fast for seven nights. Here too, if the act proceeds from the desire of both, it is a Sāntapana; if he was incited by her, it is a Prājāpatya; and if she was incited by him, it is a fast for seven nights. However, in the case of repetition, that which was stated by Manu should be observed.

"Or, with his senses restrained, he should practice the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance for three months, subsisting on sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) or barley-gruel (*yavāgū*), in order to remove the sin of violating the Guru’s bed. (MDh 11.106) There is no fault of violating the Guru’s bed regarding women who are common property, according to the statement of Vyāghra:
"That which is declared as a crime against another's wife by birth, as well as the defilement of a maiden..."
"And there is no status of violating the Guru's bed (*gurutalpatva*) in the case of a common woman.

Thus, with the exception of the *ācārya*, fathers and others are "Gurus"; for Vasiṣṭha, by means of the extended application (*atideśa*) in the rule "and likewise in the case of the son, pupil, and wife of the *ācārya*" (VaDh 20.15), establishes this regarding the wives of the *ācārya* and others. 23.11.

Having uprooted the *liṅga* with seed by cutting it off with a razor or similar tool, and having placed it in his joined palms, he should walk straight toward the southwest (nairṛtī) direction until his body collapses. "Without avoiding pits and the like, he should remain right where he is struck down until the dissolution of the world," says Vasiṣṭha (VaDh 20.13).
One who has died shall become pure. || 23.11 ||

This is a general rule: among the modes previously mentioned, only by one of them can a violator of the Guru’s bed be purified upon death, and not otherwise. All three of these [penances] apply to approaching one’s mother with the notion that she is one’s own wife and so forth, or unintentionally approaching her co-wife; as well as to intentional intercourse with a woman of the same caste. "But he who, having recognized her as his father's wife, approaches a woman of the same caste, or approaches his mother without recognizing her, is not purified unless he dies."

Thus it is seen in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*. Regarding intentional intercourse with one’s mother, the *Vasiṣṭha-smṛti* states: “Having been shaved clean and smeared with ghee, he should burn himself from the feet upward by means of a fire of cow-dung” (*VaDh* 20.42). The same applies even to repeated unintentional practice. However, regarding the repeated unintentional approach of a mother’s co-wife who is of the same caste or of a higher caste, that which was declared by Śaṅkha applies:
“Sleeping on the ground, wearing matted hair, subsisting on leaves, roots, and fruits, eating only once a day—for when twelve years have passed... (*Śaṅkha-smṛti*).
"The stealer of gold, the drinker of spirituous liquor, the slayer of a Brahmin, and the violator of the Guru's bed—
these perpetrators of mortal sins (mahāpātakin) are purified by this vow.
Regarding the case of a single act of intercourse where both parties proceed out of mutual desire, [one should follow] the rule of Manu.
Carrying a skull-topped staff and clad in rags, he dwelt with his mother-in-law in a lonely forest.

"One should perform the *prājāpatya* penance for one year with a concentrated mind" (MDh 11.105). When she has incited him, or when he has incited her, the two penances prescribed by Auśanas should be applied in sequence: "One who violates the Guru's bed shall observe the vow of a student (*brahmacarya*) for one year and the *taptakṛcchra* for six months. In this manner, regarding subsequent penances as well, it should be understood that the heavier penance applies when he has incited her himself, the lighter when she has incited him, and the intermediate one when both have proceeded by mutual desire. On this point, Vyāghra says:

"A Brahmin who has approached his teacher's wife should perform the Kṛcchra, the Atikṛcchra, and likewise the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra for three months. This [penance] applies to an unintentional single instance of approaching her; for intentional and repeated practice, it lasts for one year.

"Having approached his teacher’s wife, the daughter of a Kṣatriya, with a deliberate intent, the twice-born man cut off his own penis, deprived of its testicles; having done so, he died and became pure. Thus says Kaṇva.

"A twice-born man who, out of ignorance, has once approached the wife of his guru who is a Kṣatriya woman, [shall perform] the Cāndrāyaṇa, the Taptakṛcchra, and likewise the Atikṛcchra. Thus says Jātūkarṇya:
"Having again approached, unintentionally, the wife of his guru who is the daughter of a Kṣatriya..."
"Having cut off only the testicles, he is purified whether he lives or dies. Thus says Kaṇva:
"The *taptakṛcchra*, the *parāka*, and likewise the *sāntapana* [are prescribed] for the teacher..."

"Having approached a Vaiśya wife [of his teacher] even once intentionally, a twice-born man should perform penance for one month. Thus says Laugākṣi: "Having approached the teacher’s Vaiśya wife—whether once or repeatedly—one becomes purified from that sin only after having the tip of the penis cut off. Thus says Prajāpati.
"A twice-born man who, out of ignorance, has once approached his guru’s Vaiśya wife, shall not eat for five nights, or likewise for seven or eight. Thus says Hārīta:
"A Brahmin, deluded by ignorance, having repeatedly practiced [intercourse] with the guru’s Vaiśya wife..."

"He should practice celibacy with its six ancillaries for as long as he lives. Thus says Jābāli: "Having intentionally approached his teacher’s Śūdra wife even once, a Brāhmaṇa should then perform the Atikṛcchra, the Taptakṛcchra, and likewise the Parāka penances. Thus says Upamanyu.
"Furthermore, having intentionally approached a Śūdra woman, a composed Brāhmaṇa of uncorrupted soul shall observe the vow of celibacy for twelve years. Thus says Dīrghatapas:
"The Prājāpatya, the Sāntapana, and fasting for seven nights..."
"Having approached the Śūdra wife of his guru even once, a person should perform [penance] out of ignorance.
In that same context, regarding repeated practice, the rule of Manu should be observed:
"Or, with his senses restrained, he should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for three months."
"By means of sacrificial food (haviṣya) or barley-gruel (yavāgū), one may expiate the violation of the Guru’s bed. [MDh 11.106] Regarding this, Vyāghra states:
"Adultery as defined by caste, the violation of the Guru’s bed itself, intercourse with a common woman, and the defilement of a maiden—[these do not incur the same penance]."
Thus [ends the section]. 23.11.
In the case of a female friend, a woman born of the same womb, a woman of the same lineage, the wife of a pupil, a daughter-in-law, or a cow, the penance is equal to that for violating one's own bed.

H reads "gurutalpasamaḥ. A *sakhī* is a female friend; a *sayoni* is a sister; a *sagotrā* is one who belongs to the same ancestral lineage (*ekārṣeyā*). When sexual intercourse is practiced with these women—namely, the wife of a pupil, the wife of a son, and so forth—the expiation is equal to that for violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*). The compound is irregularly formed (*visamāsa*) in order to include the wives of friends and others. Thus says Manu:
"One should perform the vow for violating the Guru’s bed after having shed semen upon women of the same womb (*sayoni*)."
"Among the wives of a friend, of a son, of maiden girls, and of women of the lowest castes.
[MDh 11.170] The word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of including the wives of dependents and others. Thus Vyāghra says:
"Even for one who is dependent, for a learned man, for one who maintains the sacred fires, and for a yogin..."
Likewise, the wife of a teacher or of a king who has gone forth into homelessness.
Having approached a nurse, a daughter, a granddaughter, a mother’s female friend, or likewise a father’s female friend, one should practice the penance prescribed for violating the Guru's bed.
Thus [ends the section]. 23.12.

A *sakhī* is a female friend; a *sayoni* is a sister; a *sagotrā* is one of the same lineage; and a *snuṣā* is a daughter-in-law, that is, the wife of one's son. In having sexual intercourse with these women, as well as with a female disciple or a cow, the fault is equal to that of violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*). Yājñavalkya states:

"Sexual intercourse with the wives of friends, virgins, women of one's own womb, women of the lowest castes (*antyajā*), women of the same lineage, and the wives of sons is declared to be equal to violating the Guru’s bed."
The father’s sister, the mother’s sister, the maternal uncle’s wife, a daughter-in-law,
a mother’s co-wife, a sister, and likewise the teacher’s daughter;

"But one who approaches the wife of his teacher or his own daughter is a violator of the guru's bed; having had his penis cut off, he shall be executed, as shall the woman if she was willing. Thus [says Yājñavalkya, 3.231–233]. Nārada says:
"The mother, the mother’s sister, the mother-in-law, the maternal uncle’s wife, and the father’s sister..."
The wife of a paternal uncle, a female friend, a female disciple, a sister, her friend, and a daughter-in-law.
A daughter, a teacher’s wife, one of the same lineage, one who has sought refuge,
a queen, one who has gone forth, a nurse, a virtuous woman, and one of the highest caste.

"Going to any one of these [women] is called violating the Guru’s bed; for that offense, no punishment other than the excision of the penis is ordained. Thus [says Nārada, NSm 12.72–74]. Kātyāyana says:
"And likewise with respect to one's mother, sister, and daughter..."
And the act of approaching one's daughter-in-law should be known as an extreme sin (atipātaka).
But those who have committed heinous crimes (atipātakin) should enter the fire.
Bṛhadyama states: "Having emitted semen into virgins, women of one's own kin, women of the lowest castes,
female sapindas, or the wives of others, the abandonment of life is prescribed."
He himself [should approach]: a Cāṇḍālī, a Pulkasī, a Mlecchī, a daughter-in-law, a sister, a female friend,
the sister of his mother or father, one who has been entrusted to him, and one who has come for refuge.
"And having approached a maternal aunt who has gone forth, a woman of the same lineage, a king's wife, a disciple’s wife, or a teacher’s wife, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (23.12)
Some say it is on a heap of refuse. 23.13.

Some, however, maintain that the vow of the *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow of celibacy) must be performed, but not the vow for violating the Guru’s bed. The particle *iti* is intended to exclude doubt. If it were stated simply as "the *avakara* is one," there might arise the apprehension that even for the *avakīrṇin*, the offense is equal to that of violating the Guru’s bed. This alternative view is to be understood with regard to intention (*abhisaṃdhi*). In the case of intentional [action], it is equal to violating the Guru’s bed; but in the case of unintentional [action], it is the vow of the *avakīrṇin*. Thus, in this context, it should be understood that after performing the *kṛcchra* penance caused by adultery, one must further perform the vow of the *avakīrṇin*. So says Jātūkarṇi.

"But regarding the wives of a teacher and others, one should perform the vow for violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa-vrata*); thereafter, being composed, one should also perform the vow of the *avakīrṇin*. Thus, even in the case of an offense equal to violating the Guru’s bed, it should be determined as greater than adultery (*pāradārya*) but less than violating the Guru’s bed. That too should be regarded as a penance for another's wife, greater than the *cāndrāyaṇa*. And for the *cāndrāyaṇa*, a reduction by a quarter should be made according to the order of the social classes (*varṇa*). And so says Prajāpati:"

"But regarding the wives of a teacher, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow; it is decreed that for the castes, it is reduced by a quarter in successive order. Thus it is established. The penance for an *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow of celibacy) is also stated in secret: "Regarding this, they say, 'How many kinds of *avakīrṇins* are there? and so forth, as he will state later. And likewise, Prajāpati says:

But regarding sexual intercourse with the wives of a teacher (*ācārya*) and others, having completed the section on adultery, one who has spilled his seed (*avakīrṇin*) shall offer oblations of clarified butter into the fire for one month, a fortnight, ten days, seven days, or five days, respectively according to the order of the castes, using the two [mantras]: “I am one who has spilled his seed through desire; O Desire, to Desire, svāhā! I am one who has been overcome by desire; I am one who has been overcome; O Desire, to Desire, svāhā! They teach that for approaching the wife of a *śrotriya*, one should perform this oblation twice as much, and if the approach was with her consent, half as much. Thus it is said.

Regarding the statement that "in all matters concerning equalization, the universal expiation alone should be observed," this is to be understood as applying when no other specific expiation is available. 23.13.

Some maintain that the fault in approaching a female friend or others is a *avakīrṇin* offense; in this case, the penance is the vow of an *avakīrṇin*, not the vow for violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*). Regarding those penances enumerated for approaching a female friend and so forth, those ending in death apply to cases of intentional, continuous, and extreme repetition. Those, however, which are extremely light apply to cases where one has acted with the notion that she was one's own wife, but having realized the truth midway, desists before the emission of semen. For intermediate cases, intermediate penances are to be prescribed.

"One should never kill a Brāhmaṇa, even if he is established in all manner of sins"—this statement from the *Mānava* (Manu-smṛti) refers to cases other than those involving mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*) and the like that would otherwise merit the death penalty. 23.13.

In this context, it has been stated that a woman incurs loss of caste (*pātitya*) by approaching a man of inferior caste. Since the general penance for an outcaste would thus apply to her, the author says:
In this regard, he states the punishment for women who do not perform penance when they have had intercourse with a man of lower caste:
"The king shall cause the woman to be devoured by dogs in public. (23.14)
H reads "ādayet" (should cause to be devoured).

The term "low-caste" (*hīnavarṇa*) has been explained in the context of [the verse]: "In the case of killing an embryo and in serving a low-caste man" (GDh 21.9). Upon having intercourse with such a man, the king should have her devoured by dogs publicly, in the presence of the people. Thus says Manu:
"But that woman of high birth who, arrogant because of her caste and her qualities, transgresses against her husband..."

"The king should have her devoured by dogs at a public execution ground crowded with people" (MDh 8.371). This royal punishment applies when the act was unintentional; in the case of intentional action, that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha should be observed.

If a Śūdra approaches a Brāhmaṇī woman, one should wrap the Śūdra in *vīraṇa* grass and cast him into the fire; having caused the Brāhmaṇī’s head to be shaved and having anointed her with clarified butter, she should be paraded naked on a black donkey along the high road. It is declared that she becomes purified. If a Vaiśya approaches a Brāhmaṇī woman, one should wrap the Vaiśya in red *darbha* grass and cast him into the fire; having caused the Brāhmaṇī’s head to be shaved and having anointed her with clarified butter, she should be paraded naked on a white donkey along the high road. It is declared that she becomes purified. If a Kṣatriya approaches a Brāhmaṇī woman, one should wrap the Kṣatriya in *śara* reeds and cast him into the fire; having caused the Brāhmaṇī’s head to be shaved and having anointed her with clarified butter, she should be paraded naked on a white donkey along the high road. It is declared that she becomes purified. In the same manner, a Vaiśya [is dealt with] for approaching a Kṣatriya woman, and a Śūdra for approaching a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya woman. [VaDh 21.1–5]

Since it has been stated that [this applies to] "approaching one of inferior caste," this [penance] should be prescribed for a Brāhmaṇī who intentionally approaches a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya. As Manu says:
"But she who serves a man of lower rank, even if she remains self-controlled, should be kept confined in the house."

"But one of lower status who has intercourse with a woman of higher status deserves death. (MDh 8.366) This same rule should be understood to apply to approaching a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya woman as well, because it was stated in general terms. And likewise, this punishment for one of "lower caste" is also common to women of the twice-born castes, precisely because it was stated in general terms. However, regarding union in the direct order of castes (*anuloma*), Vyāghra says: "When those of the direct order of castes have sexual intercourse with one another out of sequence, the king should then have the woman devoured by monkeys."
"If a man intentionally kills jackals, he deserves death;
this same rule applies even to those born in the inverse order (pratiloma) when they deviate from their own caste.
This statement by Manu regarding union with those born in the inverse order should be understood as applying both to intentional and unintentional acts.
"In the case of the inverse order, there shall be execution for men and the cutting off of the nose and other features for women.
But is it not said:
"One should apply this very same rule even to women who have fallen from their status"? (MDh 11.188)

And since it has been established that "whatever [penance] applies to a man regarding another's wife, he who causes her to practice that vow [should undergo it]" (MDh 11.176), this rule for punishment would be redundant.

To this it is replied: for her who approaches the king of her own accord, there is only punishment; for her who is brought by force, there is both punishment and penance (*prāyaścitta*); and for her who neither approaches of her own accord nor is brought by force, there is only penance. This same principle is to be observed everywhere regarding punishment and penance. In this context, regarding those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*) who have deviated from their own caste, since there is an absence of penance—based on the rule, "But one born in the inverse order is devoid of dharma" (GDh 4.25)—punishment must be prescribed for others in order to avoid the fault of *saṃkara* (intermixture). And thus:

"In the case of the inverse order, there shall be death for men and the cutting off of the nose and so forth for women"—this should also be understood to apply to them. Likewise, regarding the major and minor sins (*pātaka* and *upapātaka*), that punishment which has been declared for a Brāhmaṇī who has intercourse with a man of the next lower caste (*anuloma*) should be understood to apply [with increasing severity] to those two degrees further removed, as well as to those separated by one or two intervening castes. Why? Because it is said:
"One must never study in the vicinity of a Caṇḍāla."
Likewise, even for the Pāraśava, he is remembered as being half of a Caṇḍāla.
Thus, because of the characteristic mark of the nature of a tiger. 23.14.

If a woman engages in sexual intercourse with one of inferior caste, the king, standing in the midst of the assembly while everyone looks on, shall have her devoured by dogs; he shall have her eaten. On this point, Manu says:

"But a woman of noble birth who, proud of her caste and virtues, violates her husband—the king, standing in the court surrounded by many, shall have her devoured by dogs" (MDh 8.371). Vasiṣṭha, however, states a distinction based on the specific caste:

If a Śūdra should have intercourse with a Brāhmaṇī woman, one should wrap the Śūdra in grass, cast him into the fire, cause the Brāhmaṇī’s head to be shaved, anoint her with clarified butter, place her naked upon a donkey, and cause her to be paraded along the high road; thus she becomes purified—so it is known. If a Vaiśya should have intercourse with a Brāhmaṇī woman, one should wrap the Vaiśya in red Darbha grass and cast him into the fire; having caused the Brāhmaṇī’s head to be shaved, anointed her with clarified butter, placed her naked upon a donkey, and caused her to be paraded along the high road, she becomes purified—so it is known. If a Kṣatriya should have intercourse with a Brāhmaṇī woman, one should wrap the Kṣatriya in reed-leaves and cast him into the fire; having caused the Brāhmaṇī’s head to be shaved, anointed her with clarified butter, placed her naked upon a donkey, and caused her to be paraded along the high road, she becomes purified—so it is known. In this same manner, a Vaiśya [is dealt with] for intercourse with a Kṣatriya woman, and a Śūdra for intercourse with a Kṣatriya or Vaiśya woman. [VaDh 21.1–5]
As they were proceeding in reverse order, the tiger said:
"When those of the same caste intermarry in the natural order,
but then [the woman] proceeds in the inverse order, the king shall therefore have that woman devoured by monkeys."
If a man is intentionally killed by jackals, he deserves death;
this same rule applies to those of lower castes when they transgress against their own kind.
Thus [ends the section]. 23.14.
One should cause a man to be executed. || 23.15 ||

The term "publicly" (*prakāśam*) is understood to carry over [from the preceding verse]. Furthermore, the methods of execution should be understood as those stated by Vasiṣṭha, especially since they have been cited specifically. Whether the act is intentional or unintentional, whether it occurs once or repeatedly, and because there are no other specific statements to the contrary, in all such cases, execution alone is to be understood. Likewise, in the case of the castes—whether in the direct order (*anuloma*) or the inverse order (*pratiloma*)—whether within their own group or across different groups, execution alone is to be understood. To this effect, the statements of other *smṛti* texts have also been cited. And thus, it should be understood that for women as well, whether the offense occurs once or repeatedly, the punishment is exactly as previously stated. (23.15)

In the matter just mentioned, the man who travels [with the woman] shall be executed by the king; and the manner of execution has been shown immediately following by the words of Vasiṣṭha. || 23.15 ||
Or as it has been stated: || 23.16 ||

The passage beginning with "the extraction of the *liṅga*" and so forth should be understood as applying to a Śūdra as previously stated; therein, it should be understood that what was previously stated applies to a virtuous Śūdra (*sacchūdra*), while this [present rule] applies to another. || 23.16 ||

The "extraction of the mark" (liṅgoddhāra) and so forth, or the infliction of punishment as previously described, should be carried out; this alternative depends on whether there was trust or lack of trust, and whether the act was habitual or not. || 23.16 ||
One who has committed the avakīrṇa offense should sacrifice a donkey to Nirṛti at a crossroads.

An *avakīrṇin* is a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) who has violated his vow of celibacy. As Jātukarṇi said: "The wise call him an *avakīrṇin* who, while observing the vow of a student, emits semen through intentional emission."

However, where no other expiation exists—as in the case of taking a *putrikā* (appointed daughter) and so forth—this expiation should be observed. In this way, there is the establishment of two expiations together with the expiation for approaching a maiden and other such acts elsewhere. With a donkey (*gardabha*), that is, a *khara*, which is one-eyed and dedicated to the deity Nirṛti, the *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow of celibacy) shall sacrifice at a crossroads in the forest itself, not everywhere, in a common (*laukika*) fire. As Vasiṣṭha says: “If a student (*brahmacārī*) should approach a woman, he should sacrifice a donkey as an animal dedicated to the Rakṣases at a crossroads in the forest using a common fire, or he should offer a *caru* oblation dedicated to Nirṛti” [VaDh 23.1–2]. In this regard, it should be understood that the donkey is for one who is not a learned scholar (*aśrotriya*), while the *caru* is for one who is a learned scholar (*śrotriya*). He should sacrifice and offer oblations according to the rules for a *sthālīpāka*. This must be done only at night, not by day, as Manu says: [Manu 11.118–120] "He should sacrifice a donkey to Nirṛti at a crossroads outside the village; having sacrificed, he should proceed in a southerly direction, wearing the skin of that [donkey], with his hair disheveled. He should live for six months subsisting on almsfood, eating only once a day at night, and wearing the skin of that [donkey]. [Manu 11.124] "Or, having confessed his sin to the king, he may, with the king’s permission, perform a horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) or a *sarvamedha* sacrifice. [Manu 11.125] "Alternatively, he may perform a *cāndrāyaṇa* penance for twelve months, or he may offer a *vaiśvānara-īṣṭi* for the sake of purifying his sin. [Manu 11.126] "A student who has broken his vow of chastity becomes pure by offering an oblation of clarified butter to Prajāpati according to the rules for a *sthālīpāka*. [Manu 11.127] "One who has committed a minor offense (*upapātakin*) should perform a *kṛcchra* penance for one month, or a *sāntapana*, or a *parāka*, or a *taptakṛcchra*. [Manu 11.128] "By performing these penances, a man is purified from all minor sins (*upapātaka*s), as well as from the four types of secret sins. [Manu 11.129] "But for a student who has approached a woman through lust, the sages prescribe the same penance as for a student who has broken his vow of chastity. [Manu 11.130] "If a student should intentionally discharge semen anywhere else than during sexual intercourse, he must bathe, touch water, and again touch water, reciting the *samyu* hymn. [Manu 11.131] "If a student should discharge semen during sleep, he must, after bathing, worship the sun with the *sūryāṇi* verses and recite the *samyu* hymn three times. [Manu 11.132] "If a student should eat honey or meat, he must fast for three days, reciting the *punarmṛtyu* hymn. [Manu 11.133] "If a student should drink liquor, he must perform the *prājāpatya* penance, and then undergo initiation again, even though he has already been initiated. [Manu 11.134] "If a student should touch liquor, he must drink boiling water for three days, or milk, or clarified butter, or air, or eat barley-grains for a month, in order to purify himself. [Manu 11.135] "If a student should speak untruthfully, he must fast for one day; if he should touch anything impure, he must bathe; and if he should eat the food of a Śūdra, he must fast for three days. [Manu 11.136] "If a student should step on the shadow of a teacher, of a cow, or of a king, he must immediately bathe, touching water and reciting the *samyu* hymn. [Manu 11.137] "If a student should see an impure thing, he must look at the sun after bathing; if he should hear an impure sound, he must likewise look at the sun after bathing. [Manu 11.138] "If a student should step on the footprint of a dog, of a crow, or of a donkey, or on blood, excrement, or urine, he must bathe, touching water and reciting the *samyu* hymn. [Manu 11.139] "If a student should step on a corpse, or on someone who has touched a corpse, or on a woman in her courses, or on one who has touched such a woman, he must bathe, touching water and reciting the *samyu* hymn. [Manu 11.140] "If a student should step on a bone to which fat adheres, he must bathe, touching water and reciting the *samyu* hymn; if he steps on something else, he must merely touch water. [Manu 11.141] "If a student should eat the food of someone for whom he performs sacrifices, or the food of a harlot, or the food of a thief, or the food of a person who has been initiated for a sacrifice, he must fast for three days. [Manu 11.142] "If a student should eat the food of a Śūdra, he must fast for seven nights; if he should eat the food of a person who sells Soma, of a carpenter, or of an oil-presser, he must fast for three days. [Manu 11.143] "If a student should eat the food of a physician, of a usurer, of a liar, or of a person who eats the food of others, he must fast for three days. [Manu 11.144] "If a student should eat the food of a person who sells weapons, of a person who sells meat, of a person who sells milk, or of a person who sells eggs, he must fast for three days. [Manu 11.145] "If a student should eat the food of a person who sells soma, of a person who sells lac, of a person who sells salt, or of a person who sells human beings, he must fast for three days. [Manu 11.146] "If a student should eat the food of a person who sells horses, of a person who sells wool, of a person who sells milk, or of a person who sells perfumes, he must fast for three days. [Manu 11.147] "If a student should eat the food of a person who sells grain, of a person who sells cooked food, of a person who sells spirituous liquor, or of a person who sells poison, he must fast for three days. [Manu 11.148] "If a student should eat the food of a person who sells ivory, of a person who sells hides, of a person who sells cane, or of a person who sells carts, he must fast for three days. [Manu 11.149] "If a student should eat the food of a person who sells dyed cloth, of a person who sells thread, of a person who sells grass, or of a person who sells wood, he must fast for three days. [Manu 11.150] "If a student should eat the food of a person who sells stones, of a person who sells salt, of a person who sells molasses, or of a person who sells curdled milk, he must fast for three days. [Manu 11.151] "If a student should eat the food of a person who sells cotton, of a person who sells birds, of a person who sells leather, or of a person who sells milk products, he must fast for three days. [Manu 11.152] "If a student should eat the food of a person who sells iron, of a person who sells lead, of a person who sells
But the student who has broken his vow of chastity shall, at a crossroads, [sacrifice] a one-eyed donkey.

“One should sacrifice to Nirṛti at night according to the procedure for the *sthālīpāka*. (MDh 11.118) In this regard, the following rule for the oblation (*homa*) is to be understood: having performed the oblation according to the *sthālīpāka* procedure up until the principal sacrifice, one should offer the animal meat with the mantras prescribed by Vasiṣṭha; for it is stated therein, “One should offer that” (VaDh 23.3). The offerings there are four: “To Kāma, svāhā! To Kāmakāma, svāhā! To Nirṛti, svāhā! To the deities of the Rākṣasas, svāhā! (VaDh 23.3). Because this is an offering of the omentum (*vapā*), there is no *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, as it is established in Jaimini’s Gṛhyasūtra: “The *sviṣṭakṛt* occurs elsewhere than in the offering of the omentum and the offering of clarified butter (*ājya*). Having thus offered the sacrificial food (*havis*), one should again offer clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*) to Vāyu and the others with the mantra beginning, “May they sprinkle me” (*saṃ mā siñcantu*). As Manu has said:

"Having offered oblations into the fire according to the rule, and finally with the verse beginning with *sam*, one should offer oblations of clarified butter to Vāyu, Indra, the Guru (Bṛhaspati), and Agni. [MDh 11.119] Having thus offered, one should again pour out the remainder of the oblation according to the procedure for the *sthālīpāka*. The repetition of the oblation should be understood from this specific instruction; as Kaṇva says:
"On the first night, the *avakīrṇin* [one who has broken his vow of celibacy] [should sacrifice] with a donkey..."

"One should sacrifice in this manner according to one's practice; he becomes purified in a single year. Thus, in this practice, there is only a repetition of the oblation, not a repetition of the time period. 23.17.

"A student who has gone to a woman becomes an *avakīrṇin*," says Yājñavalkya (YDh 3.280). He shall sacrifice to Nirṛti at a crossroads with a donkey as the victim. Regarding this, there is a specific rule from Manu:
"But an *avakīrṇin* [shall sacrifice] at a crossroads with a one-eyed donkey."
"One should sacrifice to Nirṛti in the southwestern direction according to the procedure for *pākayajña* offerings. [MDh 11.118] Vasiṣṭha, however, states:

"If a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) should approach a woman, he should sacrifice a donkey as an animal dedicated to the Rakṣas at a worldly fire in a forest or at a crossroads; or he should offer a *caru* oblation to Nirṛti. He should offer from it [saying]: 'To Kāma, svāhā! To Kāmakāma, svāhā! To Nirṛti, svāhā! To the deities who are Rakṣases, svāhā! [VaDh 23.1–3]
Thus [ends the section]. 23.17.
Having put on its skin with the hair facing upwards, carrying a red bowl, he should go for alms to seven houses while proclaiming his deed.

The skin of that donkey is its hide (*ajinam*). Although this is already established by the context, the specific mention of "his" is for the purpose of restriction: namely, that it must be the hide of the very donkey used for the sacrifice, and not that of another. That too, along with its parts, has its hair pointing upwards and its fur on the outside; having put that on, he should carry a red vessel—either made of copper or of a red color—and beg for alms every day at only seven houses, proclaiming his deed: "Give alms to an *avakīrṇin*," thus announcing, "I am an *avakīrṇin*. Furthermore, the wearing of the hide occurs only at the time of begging alms, and not even at the time of the fire-oblation (*homa*). And so Manu will also state [this] only after the oblation.

"When this offense has been committed, having worn the skin of a donkey, he shall go for alms to seven houses, proclaiming his own deed" (MDh 11.122). Even the eating is to be done only once a day, as Manu says:
"Subsisting on the alms obtained from them, he shall eat only one meal a day."
By touching water at the three daily libations for one year, he becomes pure.
Thus [ends the citation from] MDh 11.123. || 23.18 ||

Having thus sacrificed with a donkey, he should put on the skin of that very donkey with its hair standing erect, carry a red vessel in his hand—meaning a red earthenware vessel—and, announcing his deed while saying, "Give alms to one who has broken his vow of chastity," he should beg for food at seven houses. In those seven houses, he shall eat only as much as is obtained; if nothing is obtained, he shall fast. 23.18.
He shall be purified after one year. || 23.19 ||

By practicing in this manner for one year, he becomes purified. Since no distinction is made, this should be understood to apply to all twice-born (*dvija*) castes. Accordingly, Manu has used the term "twice-born": "The knowers of Dharma, the exponents of the Veda, declare that for a twice-born man established in a vow who intentionally emits semen, there is a transgression of his vow" (MDh 11.120). And thus, the principle that "for a Brāhmaṇa it is half [the penance], for a Kṣatriya [it is three-quarters]" does not apply here. As Śāṇḍilya has also said:

“A twice-born man who has spilled his seed, as well as a king or a Vaiśya, becomes pure after one year by performing the sacrifice with a donkey, eating only alms-food constantly, and remaining self-controlled. In this context, even when there is an emission of semen without sexual intercourse with a woman, only the *homa* (oblation) is to be understood; as Vasiṣṭha says: “This very same [penance applies] also to the intentional emission of semen” (VaDh 23.4). Likewise, it applies also to sexual intercourse with a male. Thus says Kāśyapa:
“Having indulged in intercourse with a male, and likewise having performed an intentional emission...”

"A celibate student (brahmacārī), having likewise practiced [the penance], should bathe and then perform a sacrifice with clarified butter. This same penance, augmented by a *kṛcchra*, is to be understood as applicable to forest-dwellers (*vānaprasthas*) and others. As Vasiṣṭha says: "A forest-dweller, upon a breach of his initiation (*dīkṣā*), having performed a *kṛcchra* for twelve nights, should increase the great thicket [of grass]; a mendicant (*bhikṣu*) should act like a forest-dweller, except for the increase of the *soma* [observances]. Here, the mention of "twelve nights" is intended to include the three *parāka* penances. As Śāṇḍilya says: "When a breach occurs intentionally, both the forest-dweller and the ascetic..."

"One should perform the vow of the *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow of celibacy) conjoined with three *parāka* penances. Even for those who have performed the penance, association must not be maintained; as Kauśika says:
"Of lifelong students (*naiṣṭhika*), forest-dwellers (*vanastha*), ascetics (*yati*), and those who have broken their vow (*avakīrṇin*)."

"Even for those who are pure in this world, there is no recovery [from such a lapse]. Regarding the abandonment of effort by ascetics (*yatins*) and forest-dwellers (*vanasthas*), one should look to what was stated by Kaṇva:
"Having abandoned his effort, a householder should perform ablutions with the *vāruṇī* verses;
but both a forest-dweller and an ascetic should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* vow."
"One should sip water three times with the domestic mantras, namely the three: *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*.
An ascetic (*yati*) and a forest-dweller (*vanastha*) should further recite the sixteen [verses] beginning with *punar mām*.
This also applies except in the case of sleep. Regarding sleep as well, Kāśyapa said:

"Having performed three salutations to the Sun in a dream, a householder should perform [the penance]; likewise, an ascetic and a forest-dweller should perform the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite three times. Regarding sexual intercourse with a male for a householder, that which was stated by Manu is to be observed:
"But having engaged in sexual intercourse with a male or again with a female..."
"One should perform a bath with one's clothes on while traveling, in water, and during the day.

And thus, the penance for acts causing loss of caste (*jātibhraṃśakara*) should be understood from sources other than this. [This applies] only in the case of one's own wife, and specifically regarding sexual intercourse during her fertile period (*ṛtu*). So said Aṅgiras:
"But because there is a suspicion of pregnancy during the fertile period, a bath is prescribed for the couple who have united."
"But when one approaches [a woman] outside the proper season, purification is like that for voiding urine or feces.
Regarding sexual intercourse during the day, one should perform cleansing with the Vāruṇī verses. As Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha says:
"Having engaged in sexual intercourse on the eighth, the fourteenth, or on a festival day (parvan)..."
Having bathed with his clothes on during the day, he should purify himself with the Vāruṇī hymns.
"One should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow during the impurity caused by a corpse, as well as during a Śrāddha ceremony;

and on the occasion of a solar or lunar transit (saṃkrānti) or an eclipse, one should perform the Taptakṛcchra penance. Regarding sexual intercourse with a male, that which was spoken by Kaṇva should be observed for both the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) and the wandering mendicant (parivrājaka):
"Having indulged in sexual intercourse with a male, a forest-dweller and likewise an ascetic..."
"By performing the Kṛcchra and the Cāndrāyaṇa penances, he shall be purified from that sin. (23.19)
One should observe this vow for one year; thus one becomes pure. Regarding this, Manu says:
"Subsisting on alms obtained from them, eating only once a day..."

“By touching water at the three daily libations for one year, he becomes pure. (MDh 11.123) This one-year penance is to be understood as applying to a *śrotriya* Brahmin who has had sexual intercourse with the wife of a Vaiśya. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “One who has spilled his seed (*avakīrṇin*) upon a protected Vaiśya woman shall perform the rite at the three daily libations for one year; for a Kṣatriya woman, two years; for a Brāhmaṇa woman, three years. “Protected” means if she possesses qualities such as being the wife of a *śrotriya*. Aṅgiras states:
“On account of the offense of spilling seed, however, he should perform the vow prescribed for the murder of a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmahatyā-vrata*).”

"But one wearing rags [as clothing] shall likewise be freed from the sin after six months. This [rule] of Gautama refers to unintentional [offenses], whereas that of Śaṅkha and Likhita pertains to intentional ones. Furthermore, Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

One who has discharged semen in a wanton *vṛṣalī* woman shall bathe with his clothes on and give a water-pot to a Brāhmaṇa. In the case of a Vaiśya woman, he shall eat only at every fourth mealtime, feed Brāhmaṇas, and give a load of barley to cows. In the case of a Kṣatriya woman, having fasted for three nights, he shall give a vessel of clarified butter. In the case of a Brāhmaṇa woman, having fasted for six nights, he shall give a cow. One who has discharged semen among cows shall perform the *prājāpatya* penance. One who has discharged semen in a eunuch shall give a load of straw and a māṣaka of lead. Thus it is said.
And this penance for one who has broken his vow of chastity (*avakīrṇa-prāyaścitta*) is common to all *brahmacārins* of the three twice-born castes. Thus says Śāṇḍilya:
"A twice-born man, a king, or even a Vaiśya who has broken his vow becomes pure after a year, provided he remains concentrated, eats only alms-food, and performs the sacrifice with a donkey. (23.19)
Enough with this digression; now the subject at hand is commenced.

If there is an emission of semen when there is no fear, no disease, and no dream, one must, for seven nights, refrain from kindling the fire and begging for alms; then an oblation of clarified butter or two fuel-sticks dedicated to Retas should be performed. (23.20)

In the event of the emission of semen, fear, illness, or dreaming, one should perform the kindling of fire, the gathering of alms, and the offering of oblations of clarified butter for seven nights, or the offering of fuel-sticks with the two *retasyā* verses.

This refers to an unintentional case, since it was previously stated that this applies to what is done intentionally. Regarding the "spilling of semen" (*retaḥskande*), that is, when there is an emission of semen, one who is not ill shall remain without fear, without disease, and without sleep for seven nights, refraining from kindling the fire, offering fuel, and begging for alms. Thus says Manu: "Without having performed the begging of alms... (MDh 2.187), and so forth. Alternatively, an oblation (*homa*) of clarified butter or fuel-sticks may be offered with the two *ṛc* verses beginning with "May my [seed] return to me" (*punar mām aitu*) and "May my mind return" (*punar manaḥ*). There is an option between the fuel-sticks and the clarified butter depending on what is available. However, in the case of an emission during sleep, the rule stated by Manu should be observed.
"A twice-born student who has unintentionally emitted semen in a dream shall bathe, worship the sun, and recite three times the verse beginning with 'punar mām'. (MDh 2.181).
This same rule should be understood to apply even when emission occurs due to fear or disease.
If one unintentionally emits semen during fear, illness, or in a dream,
one should worship the Sun and then mutter the verse beginning with "punar mām."

This is because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of Prajāpati’s dharma. And thus, whatever has been stated regarding the emission of semen in a dream for the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) and the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*), that same rule should be understood to apply even in the case of fear or illness. For the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*), however, whatever has been stated for the [ordinary] celibate student (*brahmacārin*) should be understood to be doubled. As Hārīta says: "Whatever the *upakurvāṇa* student might do, whether intentionally or unintentionally, the lifelong student and the celibate student must perform that very same act twice over."

Others, however, explain it as: "except when there is emission of semen in a dream, or in cases of fear or disease"; for them, an option identical to that stated by Manu should be observed. In cases other than dreams, the appropriate penance must be sought. (23.20)

If the semen of a celibate student (*brahmacārin*) should be discharged due to fear, disease, or in a dream, then an oblation of clarified butter (*ājya-homa*) must be performed with the two *retasyā* verses, or else fuel-sticks (*samidh*) may be offered. The word "oblation" (*homa*) is understood as being connected to all these cases. However, this rule regarding fear, disease, and so forth applies even to those other than the celibate student. Likewise, if one fails for seven nights to perform the kindling of the fire, the placing of fuel-sticks, and the begging of alms, an oblation must be performed as before. The two *retasyā* verses are: "May my virility return to me," and "May my mind return, may my self return to me"—though some say only the latter. According to Āśvalāyana, however, they are: "May my virility return to me," and "These which are the supports for Agni."

"Having involuntarily emitted semen during fear, illness, or in a dream, one should worship the Sun and then mutter the verse beginning with *punar mām*. This *prājāpatya* penance applies to the case of a single emission; the rule of Gautama applies to cases of repeated practice. Thus says Hārīta.

"Whether intentionally or unintentionally, he who commits [an offense] while still a student (upakurvāṇa) must perform that very same penance doubled; but a lifelong student (naiṣṭhika) must do so likewise. On this point, Vasiṣṭha says: "This same [penance applies] to the intentional emission of semen during the day, in dreams, and during other vows. The context here is: "One should sacrifice a donkey as an animal, or offer a sacrificial pap (caru) dedicated to Nirṛti.
For a forest-dweller (vānaprastha) and an ascetic (yati), when such a breach occurs intentionally, [the penance is as follows]:
One who has spilled his semen should perform the penance of Avakīrṇin, conjoined with three *parāka* fasts.
Thus says Śāṇḍilya:
Having engaged in sexual intercourse with a man and having made a deliberate effort to discharge semen,
a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) should bathe according to his practice and then perform a sacrifice with an oblation.

"Having engaged in sexual intercourse with a man, a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) or likewise an ascetic (*yati*), becomes purified from that taint by performing both the *kṛcchra* and the *cāndrāyaṇa* penances; thus says Kaṇva.
A householder, having emitted semen during sleep, should perform three prostrations to the Sun."
"A renunciant (*yati*) and one who dwells in the forest (*vanastha*) shall perform the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite three times"—thus says Kāśyapa.

"But having engaged in sexual intercourse with a man or a woman, or while riding in a vehicle drawn by cattle, or sleeping in water, or during the day, one should perform a bath"—this is the rule of Manu [MDh 11.174]. As for the householder (*gṛhastha*)—

During the fertile period, bathing is prescribed for one who has engaged in sexual intercourse due to the suspicion of conception; however, when one approaches his wife outside the fertile period, the purification is the same as that for voiding urine or excrement.
Thus says Aṅgiras. Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says:
But he who commits sexual intercourse with her after she has been taken by the hand (in marriage), his semen remains [within her] for that month, and during that time his ancestors lie there.
Thus [ends the section]. 23.20.

A student who has fallen asleep after sunrise shall remain standing for the day without eating, and one who has fallen asleep after sunset shall remain reciting the Sāvitrī mantra throughout the night.

“Upon whom the sun has risen” means that the sun rises while he is still lying down. Although the mention of the *brahmacārin* (celibate student) is already implied by the context, it is stated explicitly so that there might not be an assumption—based on the rule “and for the others, this is non-contradictory” (GDh 3.10)—that a different penance applies to householders and the like. Regarding the householder, one should consult the opinion of certain authorities as stated by Āpastamba: “Some say he should restrain his breath until he faints” (ĀpDh 2.12.15). For the ascetic (*yati*) and the forest-dweller (*vanastha*), the penance is fasting accompanied by the *brahmakūrca* rite. As Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha says:

"If a forest-dweller (*vanastha*) and a renunciant (*yati*) are both overtaken by the rising sun, they should subsist on *brahmakūrca* and recite the *praṇava* throughout the day. The procedure for the *brahmakūrca* is also to be understood from another *smṛti*, as Prajāpati says:
"A vessel made of *pālāśa* wood, a lotus leaf, copper, or even gold..."
Having taken [the materials] and having set them down, one should then commence the ritual action.
Taking cow urine with the Gāyatrī mantra, cow dung with "gandhadvārā," milk with "āpyāyasva," and curd with "dadhikrāvṇo."
With the mantra "Thou art semen, thou art splendor," he takes clarified butter; with "By the impulse of the god," he takes water from *kuśa* grass.
Having fasted on the fourteenth day, he should perform the rite on the full moon day.
One should give twice as much urine as cow dung, and four times as much clarified butter;
one should give eight times as much milk, and likewise five times as much curd.
Then, having placed it upon *darbha* grass with *pālāśa* leaves,
one should lift it up and offer it to the deities in the proper sequence.
Having likewise offered oblations to Agni, Soma, and Savitṛ with the Praṇava, he should likewise perform the Sviṣṭakṛt offering.
Having offered thus, one who is composed should then meditate upon the remaining sin; having stirred it with the *praṇava* alone, one should churn it out with the *praṇava*.
Having extracted [the blades] with the *praṇava* alone, he should drink [the water] with the *praṇava* as well;
performing this "Brahma-kūrca" rite month after month, the twice-born man [attains purity].
"His self liberated from all sins, he goes to the heavenly world;
even if the sin of embodied beings remains in their bodies, embedded in the very bones, the Brahmakūrca burns it all away like a blazing fire consumes fuel. Thus it is said.

One should stand day after day without eating; one should remain standing during the day, but must eat at night. For one who has practiced this—standing while performing the *saṃdhyā* worship—if the sun sets upon him, he too shall not eat during that night. This practice is to be understood from the indicative mark (liṅga) in the rule: "He should stand during the day and sit during the night" (GDh 26.6). In both cases, he should recite the *Sāvitrī*. Thus says Manu:
"If the sun should rise while he is lying down out of deliberate intent..."

"Or if he should set [the sun] while reciting [the *japa*], he should fast for the day out of ignorance. (MDh 2.220). This same [penance applies] whether done intentionally or unintentionally, because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the phrase "or if he should set [the sun] out of ignorance. In this case, bathing with one's clothes on (*sacelasnāna*) is to be understood, based on the statement of Śaṅkha: "One who has been overtaken by the rising or setting of the sun shall bathe with his clothes on and recite the *Sāvitrī* accompanied by the *savana*s. Here too, the words "if he is not in a state of fear or illness" (*abhaye aroge*) carry over, intended to show that there is no fault in those cases. Thus says Jābāli: "One who is overtaken by the rising sun while in a state of fear or illness becomes subject to penance. In this context, it should be understood that half [of the penance] applies to a Brāhmaṇa and [half] to a Kṣatriya. 23.21.

But as for the student who goes to sleep while the sun is rising, he is a *brahmacārin* "overcome by the rising sun" (*sūryābhyudita*); he should remain standing for the entire day without eating. And one who has gone to sleep while the sun has set should remain seated for the entire night; for this is seen in the rule for the *kṛcchra* penance: "He should stand during the day and sit during the night" (GDh 26.6). The injunction "reciting the *Sāvitrī*" applies equally in both cases. Because of the specific mention of the "student," there is another penance for householders and others. Regarding the householder, the rule of Āpastamba is: "Some say he should restrain his breath until sunset" (ĀpDh 2.12.15). Vasiṣṭha says:

"If a forest-dweller or an ascetic is overtaken by the rising sun, they shall subsist on the *brahmakūrca* and recite the *drupadā* mantra for a day. This same rule applies even if they are overtaken by the setting sun. Prajāpati said:
"A vessel made of *pālāśa* wood, or a lotus leaf, or copper, or even gold..."
Having taken it up and placed it down, one should then begin with the *kūrca*.
Taking cow’s urine with the *gāyatrī* mantra, cow dung with the verse beginning "gandhadvārā," milk with "āpyāyasva," and curd with "dadhikrāvṇo."
With the mantra "The seed is light," one takes clarified butter; with "Of the god," one takes water from *kuśa* grass.
Having fasted on the fourteenth day, one should then perform the rite on the full moon day.
One should give twice as much urine as cow dung, and four times as much clarified butter;
one should give eight times as much milk, and likewise five times as much curd.
Then, having placed [the food] upon *darbha* grass with *pālāśa* leaves,
one should lift it up and offer it to the deities in the proper sequence.
Having offered oblations to Agni, Soma, and Savitṛ with their respective mantras, as well as with the Praṇava, one should likewise perform the Sviṣṭakṛt offering with the Praṇava.
This is the *kūrca* made by Brahmā, and likewise the *pavitra*;
having offered these in this manner, one should then, with a concentrated mind, meditate upon the remaining sin.
Having stirred it with the *praṇava* alone, having churned it with the *praṇava*,
having drawn it up with the *praṇava* alone, one should drink it with the *praṇava*.
A twice-born man should perform this *kūrca* rite, ordained by Brahmā, month after month;
with his soul purified of all sins, he goes to the heavenly world.

"Whatever sin resides in the bodies of embodied beings, reaching even to the skin and bones, the *brahmakūrca* burns it all away, like a blazing fire consumes fuel. This [penance] applies equally to both intentional and unintentional acts; and so says Manu:

"If the sun should rise upon one who is sleeping out of his own volition, or should set while he is still unaware, he shall fast for the day while reciting [prayers]" (MDh 2.220). The word "day" is an elliptical expression; in the case of the sun setting, one should fast for the night. According to the statement of Jābāli, "for one who is free from fear and disease," there is no penance in cases of fear or illness. 23.21.
Having seen something impure, one should look at the sun after performing breath control (prāṇāyāma).

Upon seeing an impure person, such as a *caṇḍāla* or the like, one should perform one breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and look at the sun. Because of the context, this applies to a student (*brahmacārin*) during his period of observances; for lifelong celibates (*naiṣṭhika*) and others, that which was stated by Manu should be observed:
"Having sipped water and being purified, one should always mutter [mantras] upon seeing the impure."

"Mantras dedicated to Sūrya according to one's enthusiasm, and Pāvamānī verses according to one's ability" (MDh 5.86). For the householder, the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) is to be understood [as the means of purification], because of the observation in the Jābāli-Gṛhya-sūtra: "Upon seeing something impure, a twice-born man should mutter the *praṇava*. For all [castes], except during the time of religious observances (*niyamakāla*), there is merely the requirement to look at the sun, based on the statement of Auśanas: "Upon seeing something impure, one should look at the sun, or at a Brāhmaṇa, or at cows, or at fire. Furthermore, because of the mention of the "twice-born" (*dvija*) in the Jābāli-Gṛhya, this is a general rule for the twice-born castes; for a Śūdra, there is neither a mandatory injunction nor a prohibition. 23.22.

An impure person refers to a Caṇḍāla or the like. Upon seeing such a person, one should perform one breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and gaze at the sun; this rule applies to the student (brahmacārin) during the time of recitation and other observances.
Having sipped water and being purified, one should always mutter [mantras] upon seeing something impure.

"Mantras dedicated to Sūrya according to one's enthusiasm, and Pāvamānī verses according to one's ability" (MDh 5.86)—this rule from the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra] applies to those who have taken lifelong vows (*naiṣṭhika*) and others. "Upon seeing something impure, a twice-born man should mutter the *praṇava*"—this statement from the *Jābāli-gṛhya-sūtra* concerns the householder. "Upon seeing something impure, one should look at the sun, or a Brāhmaṇa, or cows, or fire"—this rule from the *Auśanasa* applies except during the time of fixed observances. Because the term "twice-born" is used in the *Jābāli-gṛhya*, there is neither a mandatory injunction nor a prohibition for a Śūdra.
In the case of eating what is unfit to be eaten, there is the state of being devoid of excrement.
In the case of eating what is unfit to be eaten, or consuming impure substances, purification is achieved by becoming free of excrement.
In the case of eating garlic or other such forbidden foods, one must achieve a state of being free from fecal matter through emesis or purgation. Thus says Manu:
"One who desires his own purity must not eat food that is unfit for consumption;
if it was eaten unknowingly, it should be vomited up or quickly purified by means of cleansing agents. (MDh 11.160)
Because of its antiquity, if the time for expiation has passed and vomiting or purging is no longer possible, one should look to what is stated in another Smṛti. As Prajāpati says:
"Having consumed food that should not be eaten, one should give the value of that food to a Brāhmaṇa."

"One should remain with wet clothes for a day, or else provide a cow's daily ration [to a Brahmin]. This refers to the case of eating food that is defiled by its source of acquisition (*parigraha-dūṣita*): one should give the value of that food to a Brahmin according to its usual price; if that is impossible, one should give a cow's daily ration; and if even that is impossible, having eaten sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) once, one should stand with clothes wet from water for as many days and nights as the number of days the offense was committed. This is the sequence therein. Regarding those things defiled by time, place, or nature, the rule stated by Vyāghra is to be observed:
"Having consumed food that should not be eaten, one should practice eating only at night."
Or he should eat food that is free from pungent substances and salt, day after day.
One should drink the milk of a tawny cow that has been milked, while it is still warm from the flow.

"This penance prescribed for eating tiger-killed meat would purify even a dog-eater. Here too, in the case of food defiled by time, the penance is eating only at night; in the case of food defiled by its source, it is eating food free from pungent salts and salt; and in the case of food defiled by its inherent nature, it is drinking the milk of a tawny cow. The phrase "day after day" applies to all these cases; the meaning is that the penance lasts for as many days as the forbidden food was consumed. Furthermore, regarding eating once a day, among the items mentioned in the preceding verse—such as the giving of wealth and so forth—one should understand that only a corresponding portion is to be given. Wearing wet clothes also lasts for only one day. In the verse concerning eating at night as well, if one eats once, the full meal is permitted; if one eats twice, only half a meal. Regarding the consumption of forbidden food by Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, the principle stated by Kaṣaṣa applies: namely, half and a quarter [of the penance] respectively. This being the case, half and half again should be calculated for those items mentioned in the verse on the giving of wealth. In the verse on eating at night, it should be understood that for a Brāhmaṇa the food is devoid of flavorful substances, for a Kṣatriya it contains some flavorful substances, and for a Vaiśya it contains a greater amount of them. In the verse on drinking milk, it should be understood that for a Kṣatriya there is drinking twice [a day], and for a Vaiśya drinking thrice [a day].
