Thus, when one has unknowingly eaten any of the four kinds of forbidden food, one should perform emetics and purgatives, provide the gift of wealth, and then observe the penance to be described hereafter, beginning with "fasting for at least three nights" (GDh 23.24). When the act is intentional, the penance should be performed after providing the gift of wealth and so forth, because there is no distinction made in the verse on the gift of wealth; and because regarding emetics and purgatives, it has been stated that "what is known is burnt away" (GDh 23.25). 23.23.

Beginning with the rule, “That which is constantly unfit for consumption is that into which hair or insects have fallen” (GDh 17.8–9), various things unfit for consumption have been described. These are of many kinds: those corrupted by their very nature (*jāti-duṣṭa*), such as garlic and the like; those corrupted by time (*kāla-duṣṭa*), such as food that has stood overnight; those corrupted by ownership (*parigraha-duṣṭa*), such as the food of those who have renounced worldly ties; those corrupted by contact (*saṃsarga-duṣṭa*), such as food defiled by hair or insects; and those corrupted by ritual action (*kriyā-duṣṭa*), such as food over which one has sipped water or risen from one’s seat. Regarding the eating of these unfit foods, and regarding the consumption of impure (*amedhya*) and unclean substances—where *medhya* means pure and *amedhya* means impure due to the place, the vessel, the cooking, the touch, or the giver—one must effect the state of being "devoid of excrement" (*niṣpurīṣībhāva*). One should act in such a way that the stomach becomes free of fecal matter. 23.23.
Now he states the expiation:
How is that?
"Abstaining from food for at least three nights. (23.24)

Since the [Gautama Dharma Sūtra 23.27], beginning with “prior to the five-toed animals,” will describe those things that are defiled by their source, their acceptance, time, or circumstance, this present rule should be understood as referring to those things that are defiled by their very nature (*svabhāva*). Among those, since garlic and the like, as well as certain animals, will be described by the two sūtras beginning with “for seven nights, or those that have fallen off naturally” (GDh 23.25–26), this present rule should be understood as referring to others besides those. Furthermore, regarding intentional eating even once, this [penance] applies; however, for unintentional eating even once, one should look to what was stated by Manu: “In the case of the remaining [forbidden foods], one should fast for a day” (MDh 5.20). Even here, for the intentional eating once of birds such as the *baka* crane and others, one should look to what is stated in another Smṛti. As Śaṅkha says: “Upon eating the flesh of the *baka*, *balākā*, *cakravāka*, *haṃsa*, *plava*, *khañjarīṭa*, *kāraṇḍava*, *vavaṭa*, *hāra*, *caṭaka*, domestic pigeon, parrot, *śārika*, *kiraka*, *sārasa*, *ṭiṭṭibha*, owl, *kapota*, red-footed bird, web-footed bird, *cāṣa*, *bhāsa*, *madgu*, *bhañji*, porpoise, crocodile, *makara*, *timi*, *timiṅgila*, ant-hill lizard, or *labhi*, one should abstain from food for twelve nights, or drink barley-gruel mixed with cow’s urine. For unintentional eating, Uśanas says: “Upon eating the flesh of the *balākā*, *plava*, *haṃsa*, *kāraṇḍava*, *cakravāka*, *khañjarīṭa*, domestic pigeon, *vaṭahāra*, *vīṭaka*, red-footed bird, owl, parrot, *sārasa*, *ṭiṭṭibha*, *bhāsa*, *madgu*, great *ṭiṭṭibha*, *cāṣa*, *bhāsa*, web-footed bird, crocodile, *kulika*, or carnivorous fish and the like, one should drink the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) for three nights. Because [the penance] is the minimum for merely threatening [to eat], the duration of three or five nights should be understood as depending on the capacity [of the offender]. (23.24)

For three nights, one should eat nothing, chew nothing, and drink nothing. In this way, the state of being free from feces (*niṣpurīṣībhāva*) is attained. Because of the mention of "at least" (*avara*), there is also the possibility (attainment) of four nights and so forth. At most, it is seven nights. And thus says Āpastamba: "Having eaten what is unfit to be eaten, that state of being free from feces is attained in seven nights" (ĀpDh 1.27.3–4). 23.24.
Or for seven nights. || 23.25 ||
Or, for seven nights, he may subsist on fruits that have fallen of their own accord, provided he does not overstep this limit.
This refers to the subject of garlic and similar items. As Manu has said:
"Having intentionally eaten a mushroom, a village pig, garlic, a village cock, an onion, or a leek, a twice-born man shall fall [from his caste]."

"Having unintentionally eaten these six, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance. [MDh 5.19] And thus, regarding the Sāntapana, no option is to be seen; for unintentional consumption, there is both the Sāntapana and a seven-night fast. 23.25.

The word "is purified" is to be supplied. Alternatively, he need not fast; rather, by eating fruits that have become withered or fallen of their own accord, without transgressing [the rule], and without going out to seek other sweet fruits when unpalatable ones are found—doing this for seven nights, he is purified. 23.25.
Using fruits that have fallen of their own accord, he did not overstep his bounds.

The word *vā* (or) is supplied [from the previous context]. The term *śudhyet* (he is purified) is to be supplied here. "Fruits" refers to those that have fallen of their own accord and have not been pecked open by crows or other such animals. The inclusion of the phrase "fallen of their own accord" is for the purpose of prohibiting injury to stationary beings (*sthāvara-hiṃsā*). The intention is that one who uses these [fruits] does so without transgression, meaning without performing an examination of their qualities or defects. This refers to the removal of hunger. The meaning is that he is purified in the amount of time required for this state to be accomplished. Regarding the unintentional consumption of animals such as the single-hoofed ones that are otherwise unfit to be eaten, the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance mentioned by Manu should be understood to apply.

"Having eaten dried meat and mushrooms growing from the earth, as well as anything unknown that has been situated in a slaughterhouse, one should perform this very penance. (MDh 11.155) In the case of intentional consumption, a Cāndrāyaṇa accompanied by a Taptakṛcchra should be understood [as the penance]. Thus said Śāṇḍilya:
"When a Brahmin intentionally eats the forbidden flesh of animals..."
One should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow accompanied by the Taptakṛcchra penance.
Thus [ends the section]. 23.26.
Before the five-toed animals, there shall be emetics and the consumption of clarified butter. 23.27–23.26.

Regarding that which was declared as unfit for consumption prior to the five-clawed animals (*pañcanakha*), the penance for ingesting it is emesis and the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśana*); there is no other separate penance as in the previous cases. Although the state of being "devoid of feces" (*niṣpurīṣībhāva*) already establishes this, by the force of the initial statement and the use of the word *ca* ("and"), in some instances fasting (*upavāsa*) is also required. The lack of compound formation is intended to indicate that the actions may be performed either individually or collectively, depending on the gravity of the offense. Among these, prior to those listed starting with the "accused" (*abhiśasta*), there is only the consumption of clarified butter. Furthermore, during the consumption of clarified butter, the intake of other food is prohibited; and that consumption should be of such a quantity as merely to fill the body. Prior to those starting with the "unfit for the company" (*apāṅktya*), there is emesis and the consumption of clarified butter; prior to cow's milk and the like, there is one night of fasting; and prior to the five-clawed animals, there is emesis alone—thus it should be understood. However, regarding non-five-clawed animals, it has been stated: "And of the limbs of beasts of prey, camels, and donkeys" (GDh 23.5). This applies to eating once unintentionally. If done intentionally, the *taptakṛcchra* penance mentioned by Manu should be observed.
"Having eaten the food of any one of these [others], however, if unintentionally, he should fast for three days;

but having eaten it intentionally, or semen, feces, or urine, he should perform the Kṛcchra penance. [MDh 4.222] In this regard, when the act is not preceded by conscious intent and vomiting is impossible, a three-day fast is to be observed. Regarding the repeated intentional consumption of these four types of food mentioned above—excluding that of cattle, dogs, and the like, as well as that of those born of inverse unions (pratiloma), the fallen (patita), and the impurities of birth and death (sūtaka-śāva)—one should observe what was stated by Manu:
"But having eaten the food of those whose food is unfit to be eaten, or even the leavings of women or Śūdras... [MDh 4.223]
"Having eaten forbidden meat and other things unfit for consumption, one should drink barley-gruel for seven nights. [MDh 11.152] Or as stated by Aṅgiras:
"In the case of consuming things that are unfit to be eaten, drunk, or licked, what is the expiation for semen, urine, and excrement?"
Having drunk the water of these— lotus, udumbara, bilva, kuśa, aśvattha, and palāśa— one becomes pure after seven nights.

Thus concludes the penance for eating forbidden food (*abhakṣyabhakṣaṇa*). For one who is capable, a *kṛcchra* penance is to be observed. As Vasiṣṭha says: "In the case of eating what has been licked by a dog or a crow, or the leavings of a Śūdra, an *atikṛcchra* is required; in other cases, a *kṛcchra*" [VaDh 14.33]. Regarding the repeated consumption of garlic and similar items, the *yaticāndrāyaṇa* prescribed by Manu is to be observed: "Or even the *yaticāndrāyaṇa*; in the case of the remaining [forbidden foods], one should fast for a day" [MDh 5.20]. In the case of repeated consumption of meat, three *cāndrāyaṇas* are to be observed. As Prajāpati says:
"One should perform three *cāndrāyaṇa* penances for eating forbidden food or meat;
however, having done so even once, one should perform only one—so says Prajāpati.
There are two kinds of outcasts (*patita*): the outcast and the great outcast (*mahāpatita*). The great outcast is one who has committed a mortal sin (*mahāpātakin*). As Manu said:
Killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, and violating the teacher's wife;

"They call the great sins (mahāpātakas), as well as association with those who commit them, [sins]. [MDh 11.53] One who is other than these is a *patita* (outcaste); his *pātitya* is the loss of the duties of the twice-born (*dvijāti*). In that regard, the *patita* is enumerated among those whose food is not to be eaten (*abhojyānna*), because for others, [the status of being untouchable] is already established by that very fact. And thus, the *patita* does not become untouchable [in the same sense]. As Uśanas says: "The *patita* and the one who commits minor sins (*upapātaka*) have food that is not to be eaten; the one who commits a great sin (*mahāpātaka*) is also untouchable. And so, since the perpetrator of a great sin is enumerated among those whose food is not to be eaten, another penance (*prāyaścitta*) must be observed. In that context, if one eats the food of a *pratiloma* or a perpetrator of a great sin once unintentionally, an *atikṛcchra* penance is to be observed. As Hārīta says:
The food of one born of a Śūdra from a woman of higher caste who has transgressed the natural order,
the food of a perpetrator of a mortal sin (mahāpātakin), and the food of an unchaste woman and an ingrate— [these are forbidden].
It is likewise for one who has fallen after having ascended [to a higher order], for the husband of a woman of the same lineage,
for those who have resorted to heretical sects, and for an ascetic as well.
If a Brahmin eats [forbidden food] once through negligence, he should perform the *atikṛcchra* penance;
if he does so intentionally, he should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa*; and if it is raw food, he should perform half of that.
"In the case of eating [forbidden food], it is half; in eating together [with such a person], threefold;

in eating his leavings, fourfold; and in drinking his water, half of that again. Thus, "if it is raw grain, it is half," and so forth, should be understood to apply everywhere. It is likewise heard in the case of repeated unintentional practice: "In the case of repeated eating of leavings through ignorance, one should perform a quarter of the Kṛcchra penance for a year."

"In the case of intentional repetition, the best of the twice-born shall perform thirty *kṛcchra* penances. In that regard, for the intentional repetition of [intercourse with] *caṇḍālas* and others, one should observe exactly the same [penance]. As Manu says: "Having approached women of the *caṇḍāla* or lowest castes," and so forth. Even concerning the subject of mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*), that which was stated by Āpastamba should be observed:

"Covering himself from below the navel to above the knees, bathing at the three times of day, and eating food that is not pungent or salty, he shall not enter a house for twelve years; then there is success, then there is union with the noble ones—this same rule applies to others who have committed acts causing loss of caste. [ĀpDh 1.28.11–14] In all matters concerning those born in the inverse (pratiloma) and natural (anuloma) orders, a penance must be determined. For those born in the inverse order from Śūdras, and for those born in the natural order from Śūdras or women of the twice-born castes, it should be regarded as being like the eating of a Śūdra’s food. As Śāṇḍilya said:

"Even for one born of a Śūdra from a Śūdra woman through transgression of the order of castes, they have prescribed that food is equal to that of the twice-born, even when produced by the women of those [lower castes]. Regarding the eating of a Śūdra’s food, Prajāpati said:
The food of a Śūdra is declared to be unfit for a Brāhmaṇa to eat;
if he eats it once through ignorance, he should drink the Brahmakūrca mixture once.

"But in the case of repeated practice, one should practice that very [penance]; for eating unforbidden raw food intentionally, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance for three nights, and if it is done habitually, one should perform the *abhyāsa-kṛcchra*. Regarding the eating of food during periods of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) or death-impurity (*śāva*), one should also observe what is stated in other *smṛtis*. As Garga says:
"Having eaten intentionally during a period of death-impurity or birth-impurity, one should perform the *aindava* (cāndrāyaṇa) penance."
Then, upon the practice of meditation, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance followed by the Cāndrāyaṇa.

"But for three days one should perform [the penance] unintentionally, and in the case of repetition, indeed the Kṛcchra. This also applies to a Brāhmaṇa during the impurity of another Brāhmaṇa; however, regarding the impurity of Kṣatriyas and others, it has been stated therein:
"Twofold, threefold, and even fourfold."
"Thus it is proclaimed regarding the period of impurity for those of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes.

In this regard, whatever penance has been prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa during the impurity of another Brāhmaṇa, that very same [penance] should be understood to apply to the Kṣatriyas and others as well. However, in the case of lower castes, it should be seen as increased in the sequence of double and triple; in the case of higher castes, it is decreased according to that same sequence. Thus it is stated in that very same [text]: "For all those of the same caste, the expiation is recorded as being like that of a Brāhmaṇa."

"Increasing in degree and decreasing in degree, even among those of lower and higher castes. Thus, it should be understood that in all cases, the penance (*prāyaścitta*) is to be performed only after the period of impurity (*āśauca*) has elapsed, based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the verse:

"He who eats their food becomes pure after ten days" (MDh 5.102). In that regard, for one who has eaten due to a formal appointment (*niyoga*), the rule stated by Vasiṣṭha is to be observed: "But he who has eaten during the impurity of a Śūdra, or during a birth-impurity (*sūtaka*)," and so forth.
Having become worms, he subsists upon that very excrement at the end of his own body.
And if a twice-born man, by appointment, has eaten at a funeral feast held within ten days of the death;

"He shall go to a terrible hell or be born among the wombs of animals" (VaDh 4.31–32). "It is known from tradition that by fasting for twelve months or six months while studying the *Saṃhitā*, one becomes purified" (VaDh 4.33). In this regard, the following should be understood: for one who has eaten during the period of impurity (*aśauca*) of a Śūdra, the penance lasts twelve months; for a Vaiśya, ten months; for a Kṣatriya, eight months; and for a Brāhmaṇa, six months. Likewise, since garlic and similar items are mentioned separately, the drinking of barley-gruel (*yavāgū*) for seven nights prescribed by Manu should be understood as applying only to those [impurities] excluding such items. Furthermore, its inclusion among the minor offenses (*upapātaka*) is likewise intended for the purpose of social exclusion (*asaṃvyavahāra*), not for inclusion within the category of penances like the case of the *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow of celibacy), nor for inclusion in the rite of pacifying waters (*śāntyudaka*). In the case of intentional repetition, the penance should be regarded as equal to that for drinking liquor (*surāpāna*).
"Consuming forbidden food and drink are six acts equal to drinking liquor," according to the statement of Manu (MDh 11.56). That [penance] is likewise two *cāndrāyaṇas*. As Garga says:

"When the intentional eating of things that should not be eaten or consumed has been performed, one should perform two *cāndrāyaṇas*, for that is indeed equal to drinking liquor. It should be understood that for the one who causes another to eat [such things], the penance is double, because Kātyāyana stated: "The punishment for the one who causes another to eat is double. 23.27.

In that same section on forbidden food (*abhojya-prakaraṇa*), among those foods declared inedible by the eight sūtras beginning with "and five-toed animals such as the porcupine" (*pañcanakhāś ca śalyaketyādibhiḥ*), there are certain foods declared inedible by the nineteen sūtras beginning with "always inedible" (*nityam abhojyam*, GDh 17.8). If one has eaten these, one becomes pure by vomiting and consuming clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Thus, the two preceding penances apply specifically to naturally impure things such as five-toed animals and the like. Regarding this, Viṣṇu states: "Upon consuming any of the impurities or intoxicants, one should perform the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance; and upon eating garlic, onion, leek, the meat of village pigs, village cocks, or human flesh—one of these, or all of them—the penance for the twice-born is re-initiation (*punaḥ-saṃskāra*). Bṛhaspati says:
For consuming things that should not be licked, drunk, or eaten—
including semen, urine, and feces— purification is declared to be the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Aṅgiras:
For consuming things that should not be licked, drunk, or eaten,
as well as semen, urine, and feces, the Ṛṣikṛcchra is the means of purification.
Having drunk water from these— lotus, udumbara, bilva, kuśa, and palāśa— one is purified by that very same [act] even if it is hot.

Kāśyapa: In the case of eating garlic, onions, leeks, or chicken; drinking fat or semen; officiating at a sacrifice for one for whom it should not be performed; eating what is unfit to be eaten; or having sexual intercourse with a woman who should not be approached—the penance is as follows: having informed the Brāhmaṇas, having fasted for six nights, and at the conclusion of that observance, having gone toward the eastern or northern direction to a place where the sound of domestic animals is not heard, having kindled a fire in that region and spread out a seat for the Brahman (brahmāsana), he deserves to undergo the rite of re-consecration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*) according to the procedure prescribed therein.
Sumantu:

Upon eating garlic, onions, or leeks; at a *vīraśrāddha*; upon eating food from a woman who has recently given birth; or upon consuming honey, meat, urine, semen, or other impure, forbidden foods—one should pour eight thousand oblations of water mixed with the *Sāvitrī* mantra over one’s head. These same acts are not prohibited for a sick person when performed as part of medical treatment. There is likewise no fault in other similar cases. As for those others of this kind, there is no transgression. Regarding onions, garlic, leeks, and mushrooms: having unknowingly eaten these four, a twice-born man should perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance. Manu, however, says:
Having intentionally eaten mushrooms, village pigs, garlic, village cocks,
onions, and leeks, a twice-born man shall fall [from his caste].
Having unknowingly eaten these six, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra or the Yati-Cāndrāyaṇa; for the remaining [forbidden foods], one should fast for a day.

The best of the twice-born should perform even a single *kṛcchra* penance for the sake of purifying food eaten unknowingly; but for food eaten knowingly, he must perform it specifically. [MDh 5.19–21]

Śātātapa says: “For eating garlic, onions, leeks, safflower, mushrooms, or impure substances, one must perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance. Viṣṇu says: “For eating eggplants or mushrooms, one must perform the *sāntapana* penance” [ViDh 51.34]. Paiṭhīnasi says: “For eating garlic, onions, or leeks, one must perform the *prājāpatya* penance. Devala says: “For eating what is unfit to be eaten, one must perform the *kṛcchra* penance. Paiṭhīnasi says: “For eating what is unfit to be eaten, one must perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance. Saṃvarta says:
“Having consumed food that should not be eaten, a group consisting of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, or Vaiśyas becomes pure after seven nights of subsisting on cow’s urine and barley-gruel (*yāvaka*).”
Bṛhaspati says:
Having drunk white decoctions and having eaten food that is censured, a Brahmin becomes impure; his ritual action shall lead to a downward course.
Viṣṇu: “Having consumed all white substances here, with the exception of curd, one should fast. This is the subject under discussion. Śaṅkha:
Having eaten red exudations from trees, as well as those produced by cutting, and having eaten what is cooked in a frying pan (*ṛbīsa*), one who observes the vow must remain so for three nights.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "In the case of all [animals] with two teats, regarding the consumption of their milk, this same [penance] applies with the exception of the goat. In this regard, there is fasting for six nights and the Cāndrāyaṇa penance"—this is the established rule. Upon consuming the milk of a cow that has not passed ten days since calving, one must fast for that day and perform a bath with one's clothes on. Śātātapa says: "The milk of a camel, the milk of a sheep, food during a death or birth impurity..."

Having eaten the food of a thief or having consumed food at a *navashrāddha* (a funeral rite on the ninth day), one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance. Paiṭhīnasi states: "Upon consuming the milk of a sheep, a donkey, a camel, or a human, there must be a second initiation (*punar-upanayana*) and the *prājāpatya* penance. Baudhāyana says: "For drinking the milk of a sheep, the *kṛcchra* penance is required, except in the case of cow's milk; for cow's milk, there is a fast for three nights" [BDh 1.12.12–13]. Śaṅkha states: "Having drunk the milk of a cow within ten days of calving, or the milk of a goat, a buffalo, or a cow whose calf has been taken away, one should observe the vow for a fortnight (*pakṣavrata*)."
A wise person who eats the products of those milks that are unfit for drinking should perform the vow prescribed here for seven nights.

Sumantu states: “Upon consuming the milk of a one-hoofed animal, a camel, or a female ass; or upon consuming the milk of cows, buffaloes, or goats within ten days of calving, one must subsist on barley-gruel for three nights and perform the triple ablution (triṣavaṇa). Viṣṇu says: “With the exception of the milk of cows, goats, sheep, and buffaloes, one should fast after consuming the milk of all other animals, as well as the milk of those within ten days of calving, of a cow that is discharging milk spontaneously (syandinī), of a cow in heat (sandhinī), of a cow whose calf has died (vivatsā), or the milk of an animal that eats impure things. This is the context. Hārīta says: “For eating animals not specifically mentioned, the atikṛcchra penance is prescribed; for domestic animals, the cāndrāyaṇa. Yama says:
The boar, single-hoofed animals, as well as the crow and the cock,
all carnivorous creatures, and those that have been declared inedible— [these are forbidden].
Having consumed meat, urine, feces, or even beef,
as well as the flesh of dogs, jackals, and monkeys, the *taptakṛcchra* penance is the means of purification.
Or, having fasted for twelve days, one should offer clarified butter with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras.

Vasiṣṭha: "Upon eating the flesh of a dog, a cock, a village pig, a crow, a vulture, a bearded vulture, a crow, a pigeon, a human, a raven, or an owl, one must fast for seven nights, become free of feces, consume clarified butter, and undergo a purificatory rite again" (VaDh 23.30).
"And having eaten the leavings of a cat, a crow, or a mouse, or those of a mongoose, or food contaminated by hair or insects, one should drink *brahmasuvarcalā*. (MDh 11.159)
Food contaminated by hair or insects, as well as that tasted by women,
or touched by a dog or a menstruating woman, is purified by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Yama states:
Having eaten honey, molasses, vegetables, cow's milk products, salt, or ghee that have been offered directly by hand, one should perform the Sāntapana penance.
Śaṅkha says:
"He who offers unequally to those seated in a single row,
and he who eats [the food so offered]— all such persons must perform the penance prescribed for a slayer of a Brahmin."
Yama states: For Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras eating together,
the penances are respectively the Prājāpatya, the Taptakṛcchra, and likewise the Atikṛcchra.
The penance known as Cāndrāyaṇa is thus declared in its proper sequence.
Śātātapa says: He who considers himself a householder without having taken the marriage fire—
his food must not be eaten, for he is remembered as one who cooks in vain.
Having eaten the food of one who cooks for himself in vain, a twice-born man should perform an expiation;
by practicing three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and consuming clarified butter (ghṛta), he becomes purified.
Aṅgiras says: For those who maintain the sacred fires (agnihotrin), there is no fault in eating the food of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, or Vaiśyas during the period of impurity caused by birth or death,
provided it is after the collection of the bones.
The Cāṇḍāla, the Śvapaca, the Kṣattṛ, the Sūta, the Vaidehaka,
as well as the Māgadha and the Āyogava— these seven are the Antyāvasāyins.
He who, out of desire, eats the food of those who dwell at the very lowest level of society,
shall perform either the Cāndrāyaṇa penance or the Taptakṛcchra.

Yama says: A Śūdra who gives food to Brāhmaṇas, and a Brāhmaṇa who gives food to Śūdras—both of these are persons whose food should not be eaten; having eaten it, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (23.26)
Enough with excessive talkativeness; we shall now explain the subject at hand.
For verbal abuse, falsehood, and violence, the penance lasts for a maximum of three nights. (23.28) — (23.27)
H reads “trirātraṃ paramam.”

Regarding verbal abuse (*ākrośa*), this applies except in cases involving mortal sins (*pātaka*) or minor sins (*upapātaka*). Regarding falsehood (*anṛta*), it refers to lying after having promised to bear witness, or in matters such as the non-payment of debts. Regarding injury (*hiṃsā*), it concerns stationary beings (*sthāvara*), since injury to mobile beings has already been mentioned. "Three nights at most" means for all [offenses] lasting many nights; therefore, one should calculate it as one night, two nights, or three nights. "Austerity" (*tapas*) refers to what has been stated, such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*); that constitutes the penance (*prāyaścitta*). In that regard, for abusing a Brāhmaṇa it is three nights, for abusing a Kṣatriya it is two nights, for abusing a Vaiśya it is one night, and for abusing a Śūdra it is one day. Thus it should be understood regarding the subject of verbal abuse. Regarding falsehood as well, it should be understood according to the sequence starting with the Brāhmaṇa and so forth. And regarding injury, for a fruit-bearing tree it is two nights, for a shade-tree that provides livelihood it is one night, and for such things as these it is one day. This also applies when the act was performed for some other purpose, without the permission of the owner.

Others explain it as follows: when one is accused by someone else in one's presence through mere abusive sound; however, in the case of being accused in person, that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha should be observed: "Having falsely accused a Brāhmaṇa," and so forth. In that regard, for a sound indicating a mortal sin (*pātaka*), the penance lasts three nights; for that equal to a mortal sin, two nights; for a minor sin (*upapātaka*), one night; and in other cases, merely a day. Furthermore, by the word *hiṃsā* (violence), those who have made a resolve to commit violence are meant. And so says Vasiṣṭha.

One who voluntarily abandons his life while still living shall perform the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights and fast for three nights; constantly wearing a smooth garment and restraining his vital breaths within himself, he should recite the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn three times. Furthermore, according to this same procedure, he may recite the *gāyatrī*, or else, having kindled the fire, he should offer clarified butter with the *kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras.

Thus [VaDh 23.19–21]. In that regard, for a Brāhmaṇa and others, having caused a wound or similar injury with a weapon or the like while the person remains alive: if done intentionally (*buddhimātre*), there is a three-night fast; if done unintentionally, a mere *kṛcchra* penance. For a Kṣatriya, having caused a wound or similar injury while he remains alive: wearing wet clothes for three nights, the recitation of the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn, or the chanting of the *Gāyatrī*; if intentional, a mere penance (*tapomātra*) for three nights. For a Vaiśya, having caused a wound or similar injury while he remains alive: wearing wet clothes, eating sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), and constantly performing oblations (*homa*) with the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras three times each day; if intentional, this same mere penance for three nights. For a Śūdra, having caused a wound or similar injury while he remains alive: a fast of one day and night; if intentional, a mere fast for one day. This should be understood accordingly. The meaning of the word "falsehood" (*anṛta*) applies to these cases as well.
Others explain that by the word "abuse" (ākrośa), physical violence (daṇḍapāruṣya) is meant.

That is incorrect. First of all, regarding a Brāhmaṇa, an expiation for verbal assault against a Brāhmaṇa has been stated: “Threatening while enraged,” and so forth [GDh 21.20]. By that very rule, it is possible to determine the penalty for all castes through the principle that “for a Kṣatriya, it is half of what it is for a Brāhmaṇa. Therefore, this [present rule] pertains specifically to the subject of verbal assault (*vākpāruṣya*). Even within that, this applies to the case of a learned Brāhmaṇa (*śrotriya*) reviling one who is not learned (*aśrotriya*). However, when one who is not learned reviles a learned Brāhmaṇa, a penalty corresponding to the offense must be determined according to such rules as: “A Kṣatriya [shall pay] a hundred [paṇas] for reviling a Brāhmaṇa” [GDh 12.8]. For Kṣatriyas and others, even when reviling their own caste, a penalty corresponding to the offense must be determined. As for the specific fines, they have been stated by Manu.
In the case of an offense against a woman of a different caste by the twice-born, the fine shall be exactly twelve [paṇas].

"In cases where no specific [punishment] has been stated, that very [penance] shall be doubled. [MDh 8.269] Thus, even for a *śrotriya*, a punishment proportionate to the penance must be determined. Where only the penance is prescribed and no punishment is mentioned, there the determination of punishment [must be made]; however, where only the punishment is mentioned and no penance, there the determination of penance must be performed. In this way, penance is established even in cases where no specific [punishment] has been stated. Even "that which is not to be spoken of" (*avacanīya*) refers to false accusation regarding many [diseases] such as leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), and does not concern mortal sins (*pātaka*) or minor sins (*upapātaka*), because in those cases a greater severity of penance is observed. Furthermore, this penance for the fault of lying applies specifically to the case of one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) regarding material wealth. Thus says Prajāpati:

"If one who drinks Soma should speak untruth, he should perform the supreme penance for three nights, or he should offer seven full oblations of clarified butter with the mantra 'svāhā'. Regarding matters concerning what is not beneficial, one should refer to what will be stated later: "In the case of a lapse of speech or mind, there are the five Vyāhṛtis" (GDh 25.12). If it is argued that this refers to secret (rahasya) offenses, we say no; for since it has been stated, "The expiation is the same because there is no distinction" (GDh 25.9), it does not mean that the rule applies only to secret acts and not to public ones. In the case of what is harmful, there is the touching of the right ear. As Vyāghra says:

"One should touch the right ear upon speaking untruth, spitting, touching the teeth, sneezing, and likewise upon conversing with those who have fallen from their caste. However, in the capacity of a witness, speaking untruth constitutes an offense equal to a *pātaka* (mortal sin) for both those who maintain the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) and others; as it is said: "False testimony," and so forth [GDh 21.10]. Regarding the speaking of untruth after having made a promise, Hārīta says:
"One might speak untruth after having promised, whether falsely or even truthfully."
"He shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow together with the Taptakṛcchra. A specific rule for the religious student (brahmacārin) should also be observed, as Garga says:
"A religious student shall observe [the penance] for three nights or one night in the case of untruth."

"For eating honey or meat, as well as for carrying out a corpse, one must perform a *kṛcchra* penance. In that regard, the penance lasts three nights for the former case, and one night for the latter. However, upon consuming forbidden meat, this following *taptakṛcchra* must be performed. If the act was unintentional, it is like the penance for a *avakīrṇin*; but if intentional, there must be a re-initiation (*punaḥsaṃskāra*) as well. Thus says Prajāpati: "A student who has eaten meat should undergo re-initiation; in the case of repetition, he should perform the *aindava* penance, and a lifelong celibate (*naiṣṭhika*) should perform double [the penance]."

"One living in the forest should perform it threefold, and an ascetic (yati) should perform it fourfold; likewise in the case of eating meat, speaking untruth, and carrying out a corpse. As for the carrying out of a corpse, this refers to those other than the preceptor (upādhyāya) and so forth who are still students (brahmacārins). As Manu has said:

"Having carried out the funeral rites for one's own *ācārya*, *upādhyāya*, father, mother, or guru, the one observing a vow (*vratī*) is not deprived of his vow. [MDh 5.91] Regarding this, it has been stated that the word "own" (*sva*) is connected with each term individually; therefore, it refers to one's own *ācārya* specifically, and not the *ācārya* of one's *ācārya*, and so on in every case.

"In the presence of the teacher's teacher, conduct toward him is desired to be the same as toward the teacher" (MDh 2.205). This is stated so that such [a lapse] might not occur; consequently, if one fails to remove [the bone], a breach of the vow (*vrata-viyoga*) certainly occurs. In that case, it should be understood that after performing a *kṛcchra* penance, there must be a re-consecration (*punaḥ-saṃskāra*). Since there is no breach of the vow in the case of the preceptor (*ācārya*) and others, the absence of impurity (*āśauca*) is also established by the statement: "Impurity due to death (*śāvam āśaucam*) lasts ten nights for those who are not officiating priests, not initiated for sacrifice, and not celibate students, among the *sapiṇḍas*" (GDh 14.1). Even before the end of the ten days, one becomes impure at the time of offering the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa-nirvāpaṇa*). Thus says Śāṇḍilya.

"When a celibate student performs the removal of the funeral cake for his father, he shall remain impure for that many units of time; thereafter, having bathed, he becomes pure. Thus it is said. Regarding eating without having bathed after offering the funeral cake, the penance prescribed by Prajāpati should be observed:
"When one who observes the vow eats without even bathing after giving the cake to his father..."
Having touched a corpse, a woman in her courses, a Caṇḍāla, or likewise a woman who has recently given birth;

"If [the act] was unintentional, it shall last for three nights; if done intentionally, one should perform the Sāntapana penance. Furthermore, regarding householders and others touching or eating [food] from those who have recently given birth (sūtaka), the rules stated in other Smṛtis should be observed. As Vyāghra says: "When a householder eats after having touched someone who is untouchable (aspṛśya), it shall be for three nights if unintentional, and he should perform it for six nights if intentional."

"A renunciant (yati) and one dwelling in the forest (vanastha) should perform that very same [penance]. Where, however, there is no specific distinction for the student (brahmacārī) and the others, it should be understood that the rule is the same for all. As Uśanas says:

"Having touched a Caṇḍāla or a Śvapaca, or indeed feces, urine, or the remnants of food, purification occurs after three nights; having eaten the remnants of another's meal, one should perform [the penance] for six [days]. Likewise, Vyāghra also says:

"If one is touched by a Caṇḍāla or a woman in her courses, one should perform a bath alone; if touched by him while he is impure from food remnants, one should observe a three-night penance. Likewise, Yama also says:
"He who, being thirsty, drinks water from the water-vessels of a Caṇḍāla..."
But he who casts it away at that very moment should perform the Prājāpatya penance.

"If one does not pour water [over the body], yet the food is digested within his body, the Prājāpatya penance need not be given; he should instead perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra. Likewise, Vyāsa also says:
"If one should drink water touched by a vessel belonging to a Caṇḍāla unintentionally..."
Having fasted for a day and night and bathed, one becomes pure by means of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
"Therefore, having bathed, one should act accordingly; out of desire, one should perform the *sāntapana* penance.
Regarding those [cases] involving a tank or a well, it has been stated by the wise in the same way. Thus also says Vyāghra:

"Having consumed water from a well containing feces, urine, or food remnants, twice-born men are purified by a three-night fast; for [drinking] from a jar, the Sāntapana penance is prescribed. Likewise, Śātātapa also says:
"A twice-born man who, having voided urine or excrement, fails to perform his own purification..."

"Having eaten out of delusion, one should perform the *sāntapana* penance for three nights; however, if one eats while seated in the same row, provided one does not touch the other. Thus also says Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha:
"If one who is seated in the same row eats, provided he does not touch the other..."

"One whose boundary is marked by ashes does not incur fault in that [lineage]. Likewise, Śaṅkha says: "If one voids urine or feces within the water, there must be a bath with one's clothes on and an oblation with the Mahāvyāhṛtis. Similarly, in that same [text] another rule is given: "Having discharged semen, urine, or feces into the water, one should fast for three nights and mutter the mantra: 'O Waters, carry away this [sin]' (RV 10.9.1). In that very same [text]: "Upon seeing a bad dream or an ill omen, one should give ghee and gold. Other Smṛti texts should be consulted in the same manner. 23.28.

In cases other than those involving major or minor sins (*mahāpātaka* and *upapātaka*), when there is verbal abuse—whether true or false—or harsh speech based on a fault; in falsehoods other than those concerning witness testimony and the like, as that has already been addressed there; and in acts of violence against things other than living beings, as that has already been addressed regarding living beings—in these circumstances, "supreme austerity" (*paramaṃ tapaḥ*) must be performed, which consists of fasting for three nights (*trirātra*) with celibacy (*brahmacarya*). By the inclusion of the word "supreme," a period of one night and so forth may also be obtained. In that regard, the rule is: three nights for abusing a Brāhmaṇa, two nights for a Kṣatriya, one night for a Vaiśya, and one day for a Śūdra.

The same applies even in the case of falsehood. Likewise, in the case of injuring trees and the like belonging to Brāhmaṇas and others, depending on whether they bear fruit or not, the same penance applies. On this point, Prajāpati says: "For a Soma-drinker who has spoken a lie, one should perform the supreme austerity for three nights;
or one should offer a full oblation with the verse, 'Seven are thy [fires], O Agni'."
Thus it is said:

"Upon speaking an untruth, upon spitting, upon touching the teeth, and upon conversing with those who have fallen [from their caste], one should touch the right ear. This refers to the case of untruth spoken for purposes such as jesting. Hārīta says:
If one should speak a falsehood after having promised, whether it be a lie or even a truth,
he shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow together with the Taptakṛcchra penance.
Having eaten meat, a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) must undergo the purificatory rite (saṃskāra) again;
in case of repetition, he must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, and one who is a lifelong student (naiṣṭhika) shall perform it twice.
"One who dwells in the forest should perform it threefold, and an ascetic (yati) should perform it fourfold, in the case of eating meat, speaking untruth, or likewise carrying out a corpse. [23.27]
Regarding verbal abuse, there is a distinction: if one has spoken the truth, the oblation should be performed with the Vāruṇī and Mānavī verses. 23.29.
When the speech is truthful, there is an oblation with the Vāruṇī and Mānavī verses. 23.28.

But if he has been provoked by a truthful statement, or reviles him with truth—by implication, it is understood that previously he was provoked by untruth—then an oblation (*homa*) must be performed with clarified butter using the *vāruṇī*, *mānavī*, and those addressed to Prajāpati; or else the previously mentioned three-night rite should be performed. Since no specific distinction is made, the oblation is performed only once. It is performed with the three *vāruṇī* verses and likewise with the *mānavī* verses. Because of the use of the plural number, they may be used either optionally or collectively. In this regard, it should be understood that if a non-Vedic scholar (*aśrotriya*) reviles a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), the verses are used collectively; in the opposite case, they are used optionally. (23.29)

When verbal abuse occurs, or when a true statement is made [in anger], an oblation of clarified butter (*ājya*) should be performed with the Vāruṇī and Mānavī verses. The maximum duration is three nights. The Vāruṇī verses are: “*yat kiṃcedam*,” “*imaṃ me varuṇa*,” “*tat tvā yāmi*,” and “*avate heḍa*. The Mānavī verses consist of fifty-nine *ṛcs* beginning with “*agnir ukthe purohita*” and extending to the end of the chapter; these were seen by Manu. Among them, the last four—beginning with “*makṣū devavata*”—are employed as *dhāyyā* verses in the *Saumāraudra* sacrifice according to the *Taittirīyaka*: “In this section, one should use two Mānavī *ṛcs* as *dhāyyās*. The author of the Sūtras also says: “One should use two of these as *dhāyyā* verses, namely the Mānavī *ṛcs* beginning with ‘*makṣū devavata*’. Regarding this, some hold that the oblation should be performed with these last four verses, while others maintain it should be performed with all the verses recited in the Ṛgveda. (23.28)
Some say there is no fault in speaking untruth in the context of marriage, sexual intercourse, jesting, or when one's life is at stake. (23.30) — (23.29)

The intention is that at the time of marriage, when inauspicious signs appear among the bride or the groom, there is no fault in speaking untruth for the sake of declaring auspiciousness; likewise in sexual intercourse, such as when one’s lineage (*gotra*) is accidentally mispronounced; and in jest, which is playful mockery; and in a situation involving one who is afflicted or suffering, where what is spoken is for the purpose of alleviating that suffering—in these circumstances, some hold the view that there is no penance for speaking untruth because there is no fault. Gautama, however, maintains that there is indeed a fault even in these cases. In this regard, Gautama’s opinion should be understood to apply to one who is bound by religious observances (*niyamastha*), while the other view represents the opinion of some. (23.30)

At the time of marriage, there is no fault in speaking of virtues that do not exist, or in promising "I will give this to you" and then failing to give it; likewise, in the context of sexual union, having said "I will give this to you," there is no fault even if it is not given after the union has occurred. In jest—that is, in the context of playful mockery—there is no fault in speaking untruths. For example, when a brother-in-law or similar person comes to a house desiring to eat, one might say to him: "Come, my friend, you shall eat rice," even though it has already been eaten by the guests; such instances are of this nature. In the context of distress—that is, in speaking an untruth for the sake of alleviating the suffering of one who is afflicted—there is no fault. Therefore, regarding untruths spoken under these specific circumstances, there is no need for expiation. (23.29)
But indeed not for the sake of one's teachers. 23.31 — 23.30.

One should not speak untruth even for the sake of a guru, even in matters such as marriage and the like. The particle *khalu* is used for emphasis; [it means] never, even according to a single opinion. The word *tu* (but/rather) serves to specify. One should not speak it even for the sake of gurus such as a maternal uncle, and especially so for the sake of the teacher (*ācārya*). (23.31)
Even for the sake of a guru’s purposes, such as marriage and the like, one must not speak untruth. || 23.30 ||
What, then, is the reason for that? It is this very one.
Why? Because:
"One who speaks a falsehood to a guru, even in thought, regarding trifling matters, destroys seven generations of men both before and after him."
Even regarding objects. || 23.32 || — 23.31 ||

It destroys and afflicts—joining them with sin—the seven who come after, such as sons and others, as well as those who have passed away before, such as fathers and others. This applies even to one who merely thinks of a falsehood for the sake of a teacher, let alone one who speaks it; this holds true even for minor purposes, much more so for great ones. (23.32)

The word "hither" (itaḥ) refers to oneself. Starting from oneself, one strikes—that is, afflicts and joins with evil—seven generations of descendants, such as sons and grandsons, and seven generations of ancestors, such as fathers and grandfathers. If one commits falsehood even by thinking it in the mind for the sake of minor purposes, how much more so when speaking it aloud, especially for great ones?
For sexual intercourse with an outcaste woman (antāvasāyinī), the penance is a Kṛcchra for one year. 23.33. — 23.32.

The woman of the lowest caste (antāvasāyinī) has been explained in the passage: "And he who would lie with those of the lowest castes" (GDh 20.1). If sexual intercourse is committed with her, for a single act of going, there is a year-long Kṛcchra penance; that is to say, one must remain for a year following the Prājāpatya rule. || 23.33 ||

For approaching women of the lowest caste (antyāvasāyinī) and engaging in sexual intercourse with them, the penance is a year-long *kṛcchra*: remaining for one year according to the rules of the *prājāpatya* penance. This applies when the act is intentional. 23.32.
For ministers, it is twelve nights. || 23.34 || — || 23.33 ||

And thus it is understood that [the penance] previously mentioned was performed intentionally. Although it should have been called simply "kṛcchra," the mention of "twelve nights" (dvādaśarātra) is for the purpose of including the *parāka* penance. Thus Aṅgiras said:
"In the case of approaching, eating with, or killing those born of the lowest castes (*antyaja*)," [and so forth].

"Purification may be achieved by the *parāka* penance; so said the Lord Aṅgiras. This also applies only to one who has desisted before the emission of semen. Why? Because of the traditional rule (*smṛti*) regarding an action performed at a prior time: "Having emitted semen into his own wombs" (MDh 11.170). Therefore, it is understood that there is a lightness of the penance. And in this way, even in cases such as sexual intercourse with an unmarried girl (*kumārī*), a penance of half the prescribed fine should be observed. But when the act of intercourse has been completed, that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha should be observed: "One should subsist on water for twelve nights, or fast for twelve nights; or one should go to the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of an Aśvamedha sacrifice. By this, sexual intercourse with a Caṇḍāla woman is explained" (VaDh 23.38, 40–41). In the case of intentional repetition, the penance for violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*) should be observed. Even there, because of the employment of the word "equal" (*sama*), that which was stated by Manu should be observed: "But [the fine for] an Antyaja woman is a thousand" (MDh 8.385). Since the penalty is a thousand, and because of the equality of the penance to that fine, three *Cāndrāyaṇas* should be observed. In that regard, for a second act committed unintentionally, the penance should be observed only to the extent required until conception occurs; there is no assumption of a greater amount. Why?

"Double the fine is for a wicked man accused after a year, as well as for cohabiting with a *vrātyā* woman or a *caṇḍālī* woman"—this is the indication from the text. Alternatively, the *kūśmāṇḍa* oblation should be observed, as Prajāpati said:
"O best of the twice-born, [this applies to] the union with or sexual intercourse with all women."

"One who is dissatisfied with [ordinary] expiation (prāyaścitta) should offer clarified butter with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras. Thus it is said. However, when a conception has actually occurred, there is no expiation. As Śāṇḍilya states:
"For a twice-born man who has fathered a child upon women of the lowest castes, even if unintentionally, no atonement is prescribed; by his very birth, he is indeed a Caṇḍāla. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, there is no expiation for intentional and habitual practice.

This is based on the statement of Manu: "Having approached women of the Caṇḍāla or other lowest castes, having eaten their food, and having accepted gifts from them, a Brahmin falls [from his caste] through ignorance; through knowledge, he becomes equal [to them]. (MDh 11.175). In this regard, whatever expiation has been prescribed for eating their food, half of that should be applied to accepting gifts as well. Why?
"Of the cooked, the uncooked shall be half; whatever else has come for consumption, this other substance is declared to be half of that," according to the statement of Vyāghra (23.34).

When *kṛcchra* is the subject under discussion, the mention of "twelve nights" is for the purpose of including the *parāka* penance. And so it is said: "In the case of approaching, eating with, or killing those of the lowest castes (*antyaja*), one becomes purified by the *parāka*; thus spoke the venerable Aṅgiras. This also applies only to one who has desisted before the emission of semen. But after that, the rule of Vasiṣṭha applies: "One should subsist on water for twelve nights, fast for twelve nights, or go to the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of an Aśvamedha sacrifice. By this, sexual intercourse with a Cāṇḍāla woman is explained. (VaDh 23.38, 40–41)
Thus [ends the verse]. 23.33.
In approaching a woman in her courses, there is a three-night penance; a three-night [penance]. 23.35 — 23.34.

In approaching a woman during her menstrual period, there shall be fasting for three nights. Although the context already concerns "approaching," the repetition of the word "approaching" is intended to include cases other than one's own wife, as well as excessive frequency even with one's own wife; this is how it should be understood. In that regard, for a single instance of unintentional approach, the rule stated by Śātātapa should be observed: "Upon handling urine or feces without water, upon touching a dog or a crow, and upon approaching a woman in her menses, one should bathe with one's clothes on and perform the *mahāvyāhṛti* oblation. For repeated unintentional acts, the rule stated by Vasiṣṭha should be observed: "For approaching a woman in her menses, one should give a white bull with black genitalia. However, for a single intentional act, this [present] rule applies. For repeated intentional acts, the rule stated by Manu should be observed.

"Having emitted semen in non-human females—with the exception of cows—into a woman in her courses, into those who are not the proper womb, or into water, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance. (MDh 11.173). In this regard, it should be understood that for a Kṣatriya woman the penance is double, and for a Vaiśya woman it is triple. Likewise, it should be known that for a Kṣatriya it is half of what is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa, and so forth. Regarding sexual intercourse, the *Kūśmāṇḍa* oblation should also be observed. The repetition [of the concluding verse] is for the purpose of marking the end of the chapter. 23.35.

When one has sexual intercourse with a woman in her courses, a three-night period must be passed as penance by means of celibacy and fasting; this applies when the act is intentional and occurs once. In the case of repetition, the penance prescribed by Manu applies. This same rule holds for intercourse with non-human females—with the exception of cows—as well as with a woman in her courses or in non-vaginal orifices.

"Having discharged semen even into water, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance. [MDh 11.173] Regarding a single unintentional emission, that which was stated by Śātātapa is as follows: "In the case of voiding urine or feces where there is no water, or upon touching a crow, one should bathe with one's clothes on and perform a fire-oblation (homa) with the Mahāvyāhṛtis; the same applies to approaching a woman during her menses. Regarding repeated practice, the Vasiṣṭha-smṛti states: "Upon approaching a woman during her menses, one should give a white bull with reddish-brown markings. [The repetition of the meaning has already been explained. 23.33.
Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter.
The expiation for those who have confessed their sins has been stated; however, the expiation for those whose sins have not been confessed must now be declared, and therefore he says:
"The secret expiation shall be explained."
Secret expiation is for a fault that has not been made public. 24.1.

The secret [atonement] is to be kept undisclosed so that it is not known by others. The undertaking of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is for the purpose that even through a small [act], there may be atonement for a great sin. "Of one whose fault is unproclaimed" means of one whose transgression is unknown to the world. By "through another means," it is meant that it cannot be accomplished otherwise; thus, the sense is "of one whose transgression is unknown to others. In cases such as adultery or association with outcasts, it is impossible for there to be knowledge [of the act] by the perpetrator alone. But how can there be a state of "small fault" in a hidden sin? Is it not rather of a uniform nature, like the consumption of poison? No logical justification need be sought here, because this is understood from the scriptural statement itself, just as in the distinction between intentional and unintentional acts. Alternatively, this is stated because [atonement] must necessarily be performed. For he who commits a public sin proceeds without regard for either world; his intention (*saṃkalpa*) is greater, and consequently his fault is more abundant, and he becomes a cause for the engagement of others, since people generally follow the path of those who have gone before. Therefore, in the case of a public act, both the removal of public censure and the expiation must be performed; in the other case, however, there is merely the destruction of the sin. (24.1)

For that sin whose fault is not made known by others, there is a secret expiation; that is to say, it must be performed in such a way that it is not known by others. What is prohibited here is being known by anyone other than those without whom it would be impossible to commit that particular transgression. Therefore, even if adultery or association with outcasts becomes known to them, the expiation to be described below still applies. 24.1.
One who desires to accept something that should not be accepted, or who has already accepted it, should mutter over water the four-verse hymn beginning with "taratsamandī" (RV 10.178). 24.2.

One should mutter these four verses beginning with “tarat sa mandī dhāvati” in the waters in the form of the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite; otherwise, one would be recognized by others. This muttering is to be understood as lasting for three nights. Thus says Manu:
“Having accepted what should not be accepted, or having eaten food that is censured...”

"A man who recites the *Taratsamandī* while fasting is purified in three days" (MDh 11.253). This should also be understood in the context of eating forbidden food (*haviṣya-bhojana*). Regarding the phrase "desiring to accept" (*pratijighṛkṣan*), it means wishing to take possession of that substance which belongs to one whose gifts should not be accepted due to the corruption of their birth or conduct. By speaking thus, he shows that even for a sin committed intentionally (*kāmakāra-kṛta*), there is a secret penance; and that even by the mere desire [to accept], there is fault in accepting what should not be accepted. This should be seen as applying to cases other than what will be stated later: "Or [there is penance] for the transgression of speech and mind regarding what is prohibited" (GDh 25.12). Or, having accepted [such a gift], one should perform this very rite. From the word "or" (*vā*), it follows that this also applies after eating forbidden food. In that regard, when one did not previously know that "this person's gifts should not be accepted," then one should recite [the mantra] after having accepted it; otherwise, it should be understood that one should do so beforehand. Here, in the case of eating forbidden food, it should be understood as excluding the consumption of urine and such, because Śaṅkha has stated: "Upon consuming semen, urine, or feces, one should drink water consecrated with the syllable *Oṃ*. Where no specific recitation is mentioned, the *Ekādaśāvara* [formula] should be understood. In that regard, the distinction between intentional and unintentional acts is this: it should be performed after forming a resolution (*saṃkalpa*) such as, "I have committed a transgression intentionally; let this be the expiation for it. By that much, the penance becomes more severe. Thus says Āpastamba: "He who kills [an animal] through negligence incurs the fruit of the fault along with the [weight of his] intention, even more so" (ĀpDh 1.29.2–3). But in the case of an unintentional act, the mere expiation should be performed without a formal resolution. Likewise, Vasiṣṭha also shows the severity of the expiation based on the mental contemplation of the sin: "Having mentally contemplated a sin, one should recite the *Vyāhṛtis* preceded by *Oṃ*, or the *Aghamarṣaṇa* verse, three times" (VaDh 23.23). Consequently, the determination of the expiation depends on the distinction between intentional and unintentional acts. Even in the case of repetition, one should repeat that same [penance].
The best of the twice-born, whose fault is well known, should perform the fulfillment of his recitations and other rites;
likewise, for a sin committed in secret, he should practice that very same penance.
Thus, because of the statement of Prajāpati. 24.2.

The black antelope skin and other such items belonging to a person who is corrupt by birth or corrupt by his actions are inherently impure and must not be accepted. Desiring to accept them—that is, wishing to take them—one should mutter the four-verse hymn beginning with *taratsamandī dhāvati* while standing in water reaching up to the navel, according to some; others say while submerged. Or one may mutter it after having accepted them, or even after the act of acceptance. Thus, there is an equal option. Others hold that if it is known before the acceptance that the object is unfit to be received, the muttering should be done beforehand; if it is known afterwards, the muttering should be done afterwards. On this point, Manu says:
"Having accepted what should not be accepted, or having eaten censured food, a man is released from that sin after three days by reciting the *Taratsamandīya* hymn. [MDh 11.253] Prajāpati says:
"An excellent twice-born man whose fault is publicly known should perform the fulfillment of his recitation and other rites."
"In the same way, one should practice that very thing for a fault committed in secret.
This refers to the subject of repeated practice. 24.2.
Desiring to eat what is unfit for consumption, one would as well sow it upon the earth. || 24.3 ||

The four kinds of forbidden food have been mentioned previously. "Desiring to eat" means wishing to consume it. The mention of "desiring to eat" is intended to indicate a state of distress; therefore, it should be understood that if survival is not possible without consuming it, [then one may do so]. "He should sow in the earth" means he should cast it into the ground.
Others, however, read "āvaped pṛthivyām" (he should sow on the earth) and explain it as "he should cast it upon the earth.
That is incorrect, for if that were the case, it would be understood differently by others.
Thus [ends the section]. 24.3.

It has been stated: “That which is constantly defiled by hair or insects is unfit for consumption” (GDh 17.8–9). If, due to the absence of any other way, one desires to eat that very food, then one should scatter it upon the earth—that is, throw dirt over it—and thereafter eat.
Some say that for one who has sexual intercourse during another season, purification occurs by touching water. 24.4.

The second case ending is used for the purpose of connecting with the word *eka* (one). "In the midst of the season" (*ṛtumadhye*) means during sexual intercourse or approaching a woman. Some say that purification is achieved by touching water—that is, by bathing with one's clothes on. Gautama, however, desires that after bathing with one's clothes on, one should also perform the ritual wiping (*apāmārjana*) with water-mantras (*ābliṅga*) and mantras addressed to Varuṇa (*vāruṇī*). And so he will state later: "Deceit, calumny," and so forth [GDh 25.10]. Since "sexual intercourse" (*āramaṇa*) has been mentioned, this refers specifically to one's own wife. In the case of another's wife, this additional penance for violating another's wife (*paradāra-prāyaścitta*) is to be observed. That too he will state: "Regarding this they ask: 'In how many ways does the *avakīrṇin* enter [the state of impurity]? and so forth" [GDh 25.1]. 24.4.

Some say that during the menstrual period, if one has sexual intercourse with a woman in her courses, purification occurs by touching water followed by a bath with one's clothes on. The rule, "In the case of approaching a woman in her courses, there is a three-night penance" (GDh 23.33), refers to cases where the act is public. The inclusion of the word "some" (eke) applies to the following rules as well. 24.4.
Some say: "In women. (24.5)
Regarding women: 24.5.

Some maintain that after engaging in sexual intercourse with female animals such as mares—with the exception of cows—one should perform this very same ritual bathing in water. Gautama, however, will state [in GDh 25.10] regarding "dishonesty" (*anārjava*) and so forth. Regarding the cow, one should look to what was stated by Manu: "He who, being self-controlled, fasts for three days while entering the water three times a day, is released from all sins after reciting the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn three times" (MDh 11.259).
Some describe it thus: "This very same penance applies even when women are unchaste.
That is incorrect;
for a woman is not defiled by her paramour, nor is a Brahmin by his Vedic ritual.

For it has been stated by Vasiṣṭha: "Water is not defiled by urine or feces, nor fire by the act of burning. (VaDh 28.1). Likewise, in times of distress, it should be understood that there is no fault even for a Brahmin who is defiled by Vedic ritual action. 24.5.

Some consider that for [intercourse with] one's own wives, purification is by touching water, whereas in other cases it is three nights; others say that regarding women—even those such as mares—with the exception of cows, some consider purification through the performance of sexual intercourse to be by touching water. 24.5.
Now he speaks regarding the secret penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa:
"Next, the secret penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa:
[the offender] shall subsist on milk for ten nights, on clarified butter for the second [period], and on water for the third. (24.6)

Or, observing the vow of milk for ten nights, the second with ghee, and the third with water; eating a single meal during the day and so forth, with clothes moistened by water, [one performs] the oblations of hair, nails, skin, flesh, blood, sinew, bone, and marrow, ending each with "I offer myself into the mouth of Death. This is the atonement for all [sins], including the killing of an embryo. 24.6.

One who observes the milk-vow subsists on milk; likewise for the first ten nights, the second with clarified butter, and the third with water. According to the word "or" (vā), one may instead eat sacrificial food (haviṣya) throughout these thirty nights. The option is to be understood according to one's capacity. 24.6.

Feticide and the killing of a Brahmin—this expiation for that is now stated: for the first ten nights, one should subsist on milk alone; for the second ten nights, one should live on clarified butter; for the third, on water. Or, according to the word "or" (*vā*), one may eat sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) according to one's capacity; there is an option based on ability. During these days, eating only once a day, one should consume any of the aforementioned items, such as milk and so forth, only once [per meal]. When? During the morning and other [specified] times, not in the evening nor at midday. On these days, one should wear wet clothes, remaining in moist garments. Likewise, eight oblations (*homāḥ*) must be performed daily with clarified butter. The mantras therein are: "hair, nails, skin, flesh, blood, sinews, bone, marrow"—at the end of each, one should apply: "all these of myself I offer into the mouth of Death, *svāhā*. This is because of the rule that the injunction to offer (*juhoti*) involves the presentation with the utterance of *svāhā*. Thus: "Hair of myself I offer into the mouth of Death, *svāhā*; nails of myself I offer into the mouth of Death, *svāhā*"—such are the oblations. (24.6)
He states the prescription of its qualities:
"In the [periods] beginning with the day, one should eat only one meal, wearing clothes moistened with water. (24.7)

"During the first parts of the day" means eating only once during the forenoons; by the use of the plural, this refers to the milk-vow (*payovrata*) option during three ten-night periods. Consequently, eating twice while consuming sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) is not contradictory. "With clothes wet with water" means he should wear damp garments. This also should be understood as not applying to cases such as "only that vow" (GDh 24.12), so that he does not become conspicuous. 24.7.
The expiation for the killing of an embryo. 24.9.

This is the expiation for killing an embryo as previously described. The repetition of the word "expiation" (*prāyaścitta*) in this section on expiations is for the sake of an unseen spiritual purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), and not for a visible worldly purpose. Although one could have specified the person by saying "the killer of an embryo" (*bhrūṇagha*), the reference is made to the sin itself in order to indicate that this applies only to a single performance of the act; however, in the case of repetition, a more severe penance must be devised, as stated by Manu: "Desiring to remove even gross and subtle sins, one should mutter for a year the verse beginning with *ava* and the verse beginning with *yat kiṃcedam*" (MDh 11.252). // 24.9 //
Now, another expiation for the killing of an embryo is stated.
Now, as for the other [expiation], the rule has already been declared. 24.10.
The rule has been stated. 24.7.

Now another expiation will be stated; the previous one was optional. This is distinct from the previous expiation for the killing of a learned Brahmin (*bhrūṇahatyā*). The rule has been stated [in GDh 24.6]: "Or he may subsist on milk," and so forth; now, however, specific provisions are being enjoined. 24.10.
The phrase beginning with “or one whose vow is milk” (GDh 24.6) should be understood as applicable even to what will be stated hereafter. || 24.7 ||
With the [mantra] "O Agni, do thou carry us across" and with the Mahāvyāhṛtis, he should offer oblations of clarified butter; and likewise with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras. 24.11 — 24.8.

With the mantra beginning “O Agni, do thou carry us across” (RV 1.189.2), with the Great Utterances (mahāvyāhṛtis) such as *bhūḥ* and the others, with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras, and with those beginning “Whatever offense, O God, against the gods” (GDh 27.7), one should offer clarified butter (*ājya*) once daily in sequence. The mention of *ājya* (clarified butter) should be applied to the preceding [rules] as well, according to the maxim of the lion’s glance (*siṃhāvalokita-nyāya*). Some hold that wherever there is no specific mention of a substance, clarified butter is to be used in all such cases. By the use of the word “and” (*ca*), it is also implied that the offering is made with the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*). 24.11.

With the verse, "O Agni, do thou ferry us across" (RV 1.189.2), with the Great Utterances beginning with *bhūḥ*, with the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* formulas, and with the hymns beginning with "Whatever offense against the gods we have committed" (VS 20.14), he should offer clarified butter once each in due order. || 24.8 ||

Or, remaining under that very vow, one who is exhausted by breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) for the [sins of] killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, or violating the Guru’s bed should mutter the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn; this is equal to the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) of a horse sacrifice.

Or, while remaining under that very vow, one who is exhausted by breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) for the [sins of] killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, or violating the Guru’s bed, and who mutters the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn, attains equality with the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse-sacrifice; and this is the expiation (*prāyaścitta*). 24.9.

By that very statement beginning with "or one who observes the vow of milk" (GDh 24.6), one should perform penance for the four sins beginning with the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*). Here, "theft" refers specifically to the theft of gold, due to its association with the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, and violating the Guru's bed. One who is exhausted and weary from *prāṇāyāmas* should mutter the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn, beginning with "Ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ ca. This is equal to—that is, equivalent to—the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of the Aśvamedha sacrifice. By this, he shows that for the drinking of liquor and other such sins, bathing at the Aśvamedha’s *avabhṛtha* is the cause of purification. By the logic of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpika*), the Aśvamedha itself should also be understood [as a means of purification]. As Manu has said:
"Just as the Aśvamedha, the king of sacrifices, is the dispeller of all sins, so too is the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn the destroyer of all sins. [MDh 11.260] Thus [it is said]. 24.12.

Or else, observing that very vow—endowed with the vow prescribed by him [Gautama Dharmasūtra 24.6] beginning with "or one who subsists on milk"—he shall perform the penance for the four sins such as the killing of a Brahmin. Exhausted by breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), that is, until he becomes weary by so many breath-restraints, he shall recite the *aghamarṣaṇa*. The *aghamarṣaṇa* is that which was seen by the seer Aghamarṣaṇa, beginning with "Righteousness and Truth" (*ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ ca*). And that is equal to the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice. By the use of the present participle "reciting," it is indicated that he should observe the vow every day for thirty nights. On this point, Manu says:
Just as the horse-sacrifice, the king of rituals, is the destroyer of all sins, so too is the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn the destroyer of all sins. [MDh 11.260] || 24.9 ||
Or he should repeat the Sāvitrī a thousand times; he indeed purifies his own self. || 24.13 || — || 23.10 ||
H reads "āvartayan" (repeating).

By virtue of the context, this means that for these very same sins, one attains purification quickly by practicing the *sāvitrī* many times for a month while observing that specific vow. The particle "ha" is used to indicate that this is a Vedic teaching. The word "eva" (only) serves to emphasize restriction. The word "vā" (or) is intended to show that the practice of the *sāvitrī* is a cause of purification even for other sins as well. Thus says Vasiṣṭha:
"The divine [Gāyatrī] has a maximum of a thousand repetitions, a middle of a hundred, and a minimum of ten."

"One who desires purification, even while situated amidst all sins, should employ [this]. (VaDh 26.15) This restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) should be understood as being for the purpose of demonstrating its status as the most purifying. As Vyāghra says:
"There is no recitation equal to the *Sāvitrī*, no oblation equal to the *Vyāhṛtis*, no gift equal to food and water, and no austerity equal to non-violence (*ahiṃsā*)."
Thus [ends the verse]. 24.13.

The phrase "observing that very vow" (tadvrata eva) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], as is the phrase "exhausted by breath-restraints" (prāṇāyāmais tāntaḥ). In the case of "repeating the Sāvitrī one thousand times," only the quantity of the recitation differs; everything else is the same. Acting in this manner, he purifies himself—that is, he cleanses himself from the four [sins] beginning with the killing of a Brāhmaṇa. The word *ha* indicates well-known fact; *eva* is used for emphasis. Consequently, even for other sins, the practice of the Sāvitrī is a cause of purification. And so Vasiṣṭha says:
"The goddess [Sāvitrī] has a maximum of one thousand [repetitions], a middle of one hundred, and a minimum of ten."
"One who desires purification should employ this, even if situated amidst all sins" (VaDh 26.15). Vyāghra also said:
"There is no recitation equal to the Sāvitrī, no oblation equal to the Vyāhṛtis, no gift equal to food and water, and no austerity equal to non-violence. (24.10)
He states another expiation:
"Or, by reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times while submerged in water, one is released from all sins; one is released. (24.14)

Remaining under that very vow, by practicing the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times within the water for thirty nights, one is released from all evil committed whether knowingly or unknowingly; the meaning is that one becomes purified. || 24.14 ||

Remaining under that very vow, submerged within water, by practicing the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times for thirty nights, one is released from all sin, whether committed intentionally or unintentionally; and the repetition [of the rule] has already been explained. 24.11.

Now begins the twenty-fifth chapter. The secret expiations for the great sins (*mahāpātaka*) have been stated; now those for the minor sins (*upapātaka*) must be declared. Among these, the expiation for one who has broken his vow of celibacy (*avakīrṇin*) is stated first, because he is guilty of a minor sin and because his expiation is extended [from other cases]. In this regard, a Vedic text is cited to demonstrate the extreme reprehensibility [of the act]. The secret expiations for the great sins have been stated. Now, about to speak regarding the minor sins, he first cites a Vedic text to show the extreme reprehensibility of the expiation for one who has broken his vow of celibacy.
Regarding this, they ask: "In how many ways does one who has broken his vow of chastity enter [into penance]? 25.1.

Seeing the gravity of this fault, the distinguished ones have said: "In how many ways?"—for the word *avakīrṇin* denotes one who has violated [his vow], that is to say, one who is stained (*raktasya*). By this, the intention is: "Where does his vital breath and so forth go? (25.1)

Through the fivefold vital breath (*prāṇa*), he enters the Maruts, the winds; through strength, he enters Indra; through the excellence of his conduct and Vedic study, he enters Bṛhaspati; and through all other faculties, such as sight and the rest, he enters Agni alone.
