Thus, being short-lived, lacking energy, devoid of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), and lacking sight and the other senses, he becomes one who has violated his vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*). Therefore, an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must be performed. 25.2.
Having thus raised a doubt, he himself states the answer: "In this regard, the answer is:
by means of breath he [attained] Maruts, by strength Indra, by spiritual luster Bṛhaspati, and by the remainder Agni."
"By all means," [it is said]. 25.2.
The Maruts [consecrated him] with breath, Indra with power, Bṛhaspati with the splendor of sacred knowledge, and Agni with all the rest. || 25.2 ||

One enters the Maruts—the winds—by means of the fivefold vital breath (*prāṇa*); Indra by means of strength, that is, the power of enthusiasm; Bṛhaspati by means of splendor (*tejas*) born from the study of the revealed scriptures (*śruti*) and so forth; and Agni by means of the other [breaths]. By the use of the word "only" (*eva*), it is indicated that there is no entry into others such as the mind (*manas*). By the inclusion of the term "all," it includes the eyes, ears, and so on. One becomes undisciplined, empty, short-lived, lacking enthusiasm, devoid of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), and deficient in the eyes and other senses. This scriptural passage has been cited for the purpose of producing a sense of urgency or for the occasion of prescribing expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*). (25.2)

Through the fivefold vital breath (*prāṇa*), he enters the Maruts, the winds; through strength, he enters Indra; through the excellence of his conduct and Vedic study, he enters Bṛhaspati; and through all other faculties, such as sight and the rest, he enters Agni alone. Thus, he becomes short-lived, lacking energy, devoid of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), and deficient in sight and other senses—an *avakīrṇin*. Therefore, an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must be performed. 25.2.
Now he states the expiation;
he says regarding that time: "On the night of the new moon, having established the fire, he offers oblations of clarified butter as expiations. (25.3)

If it is argued that the word "he" (*sa*) is redundant because the subject "the *avakīrṇin*" has already been introduced, [we reply: it is for the purpose of referring specifically to one who has broken his vow in secret; otherwise, since a Vedic citation is provided, there might be the suspicion that this expiation applies to all celibate students (*brahmacārin*). It should be understood that "on the new moon day" (*amāvāsyāyām*) means at night, specifically at midnight; otherwise, it would be public. "Having established the fire" (*agnim upasamādhāya*) means having produced fire by friction from some piece of wood; otherwise, since the fire is already established by the very mention of the oblation (*juhoti*), this statement would be superfluous. The inclusion of the term "expiation" (*prāyaścitta*) is for the purpose of making known that the performance of the rite must follow immediately after the transgression, or it serves to include what is stated in other Smṛtis.

[This is] for the purpose of establishing the general rule for expiation, beginning with: "And one should daily recite the Sāvitrī and purificatory texts according to one's ability" (MDh 11.225). Furthermore, the mention of *ājya* (clarified butter) is for the sake of restriction. Thus says the Gṛhyasmṛti: "There are four sources of *ājya*: that from the udder, or forest produce, curds, or milk. The mention of an oblation (*āhuti*) is for the purpose of performing the fire-sacrifice (*homa*) with focused attention. 25.3.

Having spilled [the oblation], he—on the night of the new moon, at midnight—having established the fire according to the procedure prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras and having kindled it, offers oblations of clarified butter as expiations at the conclusion of the *ājyabhāga* offerings. 25.3.
In that regard, there are two mantras:
"I am besprinkled by desire, I am besprinkled; O Desire, to Desire, svāhā! I am oppressed by desire, I am oppressed; O Desire, to Desire, svāhā! || 25.4 ||

"I am besprinkled by desire; I am besprinkled, O Desire! To Desire, svāhā! I am milked over by desire; I am milked over, O Desire! To Desire, svāhā! Having thus offered a fuel-stick, sprinkled water around the fire, and performed the ritual of the sacrificial site, he should rise and worship three times with this verse: "May he pour together. 25.4.
The entire recitation of the mantra is [authoritative], because it is found to be so in the direct revelation (pratyakṣa-śruti). || 25.4 ||

At the conclusion of the *homa*, having silently placed one fuel-stick (*samidh*) into the fire, he sprinkles water around the fire while reciting the formulas beginning with "O Aditi, you have given your consent" (*adite 'nvamaṃsthāḥ*). Thereafter, he performs the ritual for the sacrificial site (*yajñavāstu*). Regarding this, it is stated in the *Gṛhya-sūtra* of the Chandogas immediately after the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering: "Having placed a fuel-stick into the fire, and having thrice dipped blades of *darbha* grass and the sacrificial oblations into the clarified butter, he should sprinkle the tips, middles, and roots [of the grass] while reciting, 'Licking what is smeared, let the birds disperse' (*aktaṃ rihāṇā vi yantu vayaḥ*), and then cast them into the fire with the formula: 'May Rudra, the lord of beings, who moves along the threads and is the bull, not harm our cattle; may this be an offering for you, Svāhā! One should perform this ritual for the sacrificial site everywhere. Having performed this ritual for the sacrificial site, he should rise, stand near the fire, and worship the fire three times with the verse, "May he pour together" (*samāsiñcatu*). 25.4.
Having placed a fuel-stick on the fire, sprinkled water around it, and prepared the sacrificial site, he should rise and worship [the fire] three times with the verse, "May they sprinkle me. (25.5)

At the conclusion of the oblation of the two mantras, having offered one fuel-stick silently, he then sprinkles water around [the fire] with the formulas beginning, "O Aditi, you have granted your consent. Then, having performed the consecration of the sacrificial site as prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtra of the Chandogas, he should rise behind the fire and worship the established fire three times with the verse, "May they sprinkle me.
He states a Vedic explanatory passage (arthavāda) for the purpose of praising the attendance upon the fires. This is the explanatory passage regarding the threefold attendance:
"For these worlds are three; [it is] for the conquest and the overcoming of these worlds. (25.6)—(25.5)

H reads: "These three"—namely, these three worlds known as Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar. Their "conquest" (*abhijitiḥ*) means non-falling away; "advancement" (*abhikrāntiḥ*) means rebirth right there. By stating both "by conquest" and "by advancement," [the text] shows that for one who has spilled his seed and has not performed expiation, there is no place even in the three worlds. The word *vai* is meaningless, because it has been said that "Vedic syllables may be meaningless. The direct designation "these worlds" is for the sake of emphasis. 25.6.

For there are three worlds: Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar. Their conquest (*abhijiti*) is the attainment of fitness for enjoyment; their mastery (*abhikrānti*) is the state of remaining presiding over them with sovereignty. The connection is that one should act in this manner for that very purpose. 25.5.
Regarding this very matter, some [teachers] say that one who might be as if purified should sacrifice in this manner and consecrate with these mantras. 25.7.

Regarding this very matter concerning ritual action, some maintain that for one who might be as if impure, he should offer the oblation in this manner and recite the mantra in this manner, with a choice gift as the sacrificial fee; this is the expiation because no specific distinction is made. 25.6.

This refers specifically to that ritual action; the meaning is "having performed it. According to the opinion of some, he who might consider himself as if purified—even when a secret expiation (*rahasyaprāyaścitta*) has been performed according to the [general] rule—he should offer this very oblation and likewise worship the fire in this manner. (25.7)

He who is as if impure, or even another who considers himself as if impure—not only one who has violated the vow of chastity—should, with reference to this very rite, offer oblations in this manner and recite the mantras in this manner; he should thus perform the oblation and the ritual attendance. A *vara* (choice gift) is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Indeed, a cow is the *vara*, because of the specific scriptural statement that "she is to be given to the Brahman priest" due to the act being performed by oneself. According to the opinion of some, this expiation applies without distinction to all those who have committed minor offenses (*upapātakin*). 25.6.
"The bridegroom is the sacrificial fee. || 25.8 ||

It should be given before the performance of the rite; because it is to be performed by oneself, it must be given to another Brahmin. Due to its gravity, this should be understood as referring to the case of a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*). According to Gautama, however, there is a repetition of that very same penance. 25.8.
The expiation is [the same] because there is no distinction. 25.9.

The common expiation for all those who have committed minor offenses (*upapātakin*) has already been stated. Some explain this as a supplement to the subsequent sūtras—namely, that the expiation which is about to be described applies without distinction to both secret and public offenses. In that regard, it should be described as supplementary to those [penances] prescribed for public offenses, whereas for secret offenses, it stands independently. The mention of "expiation" implies that one should not show disregard even in the case of a minor offense. (25.9)

Having committed acts of dishonesty, calumny, or forbidden conduct, having consumed forbidden food, or having emitted semen in a Śūdra woman, in a non-vaginal opening, or during a blameworthy act—even if done intentionally—one should touch water with verses addressed to Varuṇa that contain the word "water" (ab-liṅga). 25.10.

Having committed acts of dishonesty, calumny, or forbidden conduct; having consumed forbidden food; having discharged semen into a Śūdra woman or into a non-vaginal opening; or having performed a blameworthy act intentionally—even in these cases—one should touch water with verses addressed to the Apsarases (Abliṅga), or with verses addressed to Varuṇa (Vāruṇī), or with other purificatory texts. 25.7.

Deceit (*anārjava*) is mental action consisting of crookedness or guile (*śāṭhya*). Slander (*paiśuna*) is verbal action consisting of speaking ill of others. Violation of a rule (*niyamalopa*) is physical action consisting of engaging in prohibited conduct. Consuming what is not fit for food (*anādya*) refers to the eating of various kinds of unfit food. Sexual intercourse (*maithuna*) refers to the emission of semen into a *śūdra* woman; the separate mention of this case is intended to indicate that this applies even when she is married. Although the penance for this is indeed the same as that for a minor offense (*upapātaka*), nevertheless, because it is specifically taught here, it should be understood as being this very one. Having thus considered the relationship between the general and the particular, a determination must be made in all cases. The word "and" (*ca*) is for the purpose of including a woman in her menses. "In a non-vagina" (*ayoni*) means in the mouth and so forth. From the word "and," it includes the voiding of excrement with effort. "In a faulty act" (*doṣavati karmaṇi*) means when an act has been committed that causes pain to another. From the word "and," it includes the non-performance of what is enjoined. The phrase "even if intentional" (*abhisaṃdhipūrve*) means even if it was undertaken for that specific purpose. Although the consumption of unfit food and so forth are instances of practicing what is prohibited, they are taught separately for the purpose of emphasizing their avoidance with great care, or for the purpose of indicating the severity of the penance. Consequently, purification should be understood as being performed many times. Some say that "faulty act" refers to theft; in that case, it should be understood as theft other than that of gold, since the latter is mentioned under the heading of "killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor," etc. Others say it refers to violence (*hiṃsā*); in that case too, it should be understood as excluding mortal sins (*pātaka*) and minor offenses (*upapātaka*), since those two have already been mentioned. Regarding the word "even" (*api*) in "even if intentional," some explain it to mean "even in the case of repetition. That is incorrect, because it has already been stated that the penance is repeated for each repetition. It is included there so that the penance may not be considered light even in the case of unintentional acts. With the *abliṅga* verses—those addressed to the deity Water beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, etc.—the plural number indicates at least three. With the *vāruṇī* verses—those addressed to the deity Varuṇa beginning with *imaṃ me varuṇa*, etc.—having first bathed, he should pour water over his head. The irregular grammatical construction (using the locative *visame*) is for the sake of indicating an option. Therefore, it should be understood as "either with the *abliṅga* verses or with the *vāruṇī* verses. || 25.10 ||

Crookedness is deceit. Backbiting is the pointing out of another's faults. Prohibited conduct is the performance of forbidden acts. Eating what should not be eaten is the consumption of forbidden food. Having spilled semen upon these—upon a Śūdra woman, or having spilled it in a non-vaginal opening such as the mouth, or having performed a faulty act consisting of causing pain to others or theft, whether premeditated and intentional, or by implication, unintentional—one should touch water with the *ṛg* verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ" (RV 10.9.1), the three verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ" (TS 5.6.1.1), the Vāruṇī verses beginning with "yat kiṃcedam," "imaṃ me varuṇa," "tat tvā yāmi," and "ava te heḍaḥ" (RV 7.89.5; RV 1.24.11; RV 1.24.14), or with other purificatory (*pavitra*) hymns such as "pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ. Having first bathed, one should afterwards pour water over the head with joined palms while reciting these mantras. Although eating what is unfit for consumption is also a form of prohibited conduct, nevertheless, because it is mentioned separately, it should be understood that among those [other acts], purification is performed with many [verses], whereas in the case of eating what is unfit, it is according to the circumstances. 25.7.
Or with other purifying substances. || 25.11 ||

The mention of "purifiers" (*pavitra*) is so that the inclusion may be understood as referring exclusively to purifiers such as the *aghamarṣaṇa* and others; there is an option [between them] according to what is possible.
If there is a transgression of speech or mind that has been forbidden, the five vyāhṛtis are to be recited.
If there is a transgression of speech or mind regarding what has been forbidden, the five vyāhṛtis ending with "satya" [should be recited]. 25.8.

In the case of transgressing what is forbidden, or in the case of transgression of speech and mind, there is the previously mentioned expiation. This is stated for the sake of specification: the five *vyāhṛtis*, beginning with *bhūḥ* and ending with *puruṣa-satya*, should be recited eleven times in the form of an adoration of the Sun (*ādityopasthāna*), accompanied by water-mantras (*abliṅga*), immediately after the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*). 25.12.

Regarding that misconduct of speech and mind—which is a reprehensible engagement with prohibited objects—the five *vyāhṛtis*, beginning with *bhūḥ* and ending with *satya*, are to be muttered; these were taught in the first chapter. We do not favor the reading "of speech and mind" (*vāṅmanasoḥ*), because it would entail the application of the rule for forming compound endings such as *acatura-* (Pāṇini 5.4.77), and because the inclusion of the term "prohibited" (*pratiṣiddha-*) would be difficult to construe [with the rest of the sentence]. 25.8.
In all cases, he should sip water while reciting: "May the day and the sun purify me," in the evening. 25.13.
In all [the sips], he should sip water with the formula: "May the day and the sun purify me," in the morning; "May the night and Varuṇa purify me," in the evening. 25.9.

"In all actions" means in actions such as dishonesty and the like. Some maintain that there should be a sipping of water (*ācamana*) for each of the *vyāhṛtis*; however, that is incorrect, because it would lead to the undesirable consequence [of requiring a sip] for all [the syllables] together. The inclusion of the word "all" is intended to ensure that this does not apply only to the three immediately preceding [syllables]. The mention of "water" is for the purpose of excluding alkaline substances and the like. Thus, having consecrated [the water] every evening and morning, one should sip water for each sin. This is an option depending on the circumstances. (25.13)

For all evil deeds, such as dishonesty and the like, one should sip water after consecrating it with these two mantras; one should drink it in the morning with the words "And the day," and in the evening with the words "And the night. (25.9)
Or he should offer eight fuel-sticks; having offered with the mantra "devakṛtasya... (RV X.164.3), he is released from every sin—yes, he is released. 25.14 — 25.10.

Or one should offer eight fuel-sticks with these mantras: "Thou art the expiation for sin committed against the gods, svāhā! Thou art the expiation for sin committed against men, svāhā! Thou art the expiation for sin committed against the ancestors, svāhā! Thou art the expiation for sin committed by oneself, svāhā! Thou art the expiation for sin committed by others, svāhā! For whatever sin we have committed by day or by night, thou art its expiation, svāhā! For every sin, thou art the expiation, svāhā! The meaning is that one should perform this very act and nothing else. The particle *eva* (only) is used to emphasize its primacy; therefore, when possible, this alone should be performed. One is liberated from all sin—not only from dishonesty and the like, but even from sins such as officiating at sacrifices for those for whom one should not sacrifice. (25.14)

Alternatively, one should offer eight fuel-sticks (*samidh*) by means of the mantras beginning with “*devakṛtasya*” [VS 8.13]. By offering these alone, one is released from all sin—not only from dishonesty and the like, but even from the sin of officiating at sacrifices for those who should not be sacrificed for. The particle *eva* (“only”) is used to demonstrate the primacy of this oblation; that is, “having offered this alone, and having done nothing else. Therefore, when possible, this is the superior course. The eight mantras are: “*devakṛtasyainaso ‘vayajanam asi svāhā*,” and so forth. (The repetition of the meaning has been stated. 25.10.
Now begins the twenty-sixth chapter.

It has been stated that the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* and the *cāndrāyaṇa* constitute the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*). Here, for the purpose of defining the nature of the *kṛcchra*, he says this. It was stated:
"the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* and the *cāndrāyaṇa*. In that regard, he states the nature of the *kṛcchra* and the others in their proper order.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the Kṛcchra penances. 26.1.

The word *atha* (now/then) has the sense of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) and serves to exclude the previously mentioned inauspicious recitation. In this way, these [words] also serve the purposes of religious merit (*dharma*) and worldly benefit (*artha*). Thus says Śaṅkha: "One should purify the body according to one's ability through restraints (*yama*), observances (*niyama*), mantras, vows (*vrata*), and so forth. Here, by the word *vrata*, the *kṛcchra* penances are intended. The word *ataḥ* (therefore) indicates the reason: because these [penances] also serve the purpose of auspiciousness, we shall therefore explain them. The mention of *kṛcchra* is for the sake of providing a technical name (*saṃjñā*). This is an etymological name (*anvarthasaṃjñā*), as it means "that which liberates (*mocayati*) from suffering (*kṛcchra*) or sin (*pāpa*). (26.1)

The word *atha* (now) has the sense of introducing a topic (*adhikāra*). The word *ataḥ* (hence) indicates a reason (*hetu*). Since these [penances] that have been mentioned cannot be performed [in their entirety], we shall therefore explain the *kṛcchra* penances. 26.1.
Having eaten sacrificial food for breakfast, he shall not eat for three nights. || 26.2 ||

He should consume morning meals consisting of pure sacrificial foods (*haviṣya*) prepared from rice and other grains, mixed with ghee and similar substances, and free from alkaline salts and salt. By using the term "meals" (*āśān*), he indicates that one should not eat to excessive fullness. Having consumed these for three days, he should then not eat at all for three nights in that same place.

Now, one might object: since eating in the evening and morning is already established by custom, does not the prohibition of eating at night follow as a matter of course simply from the injunction regarding the morning meal?

It is said: because of the specific commencement with the term "sacrificial foods" (*haviṣyān*), there might arise the suspicion that the morning meal consists of sacrificial foods while the evening meal is whatever is available; therefore, this statement is made to prohibit even whatever is available at night. (26.2)

Having eaten the morning meals—prepared with sacrificial grains other than *varaka* and the like, mixed with clarified butter and such, and devoid of alkaline substances and salt—the morsels (*āśāḥ*) being those things to be consumed; that is, having eaten the morsels to be enjoyed during the day, one should fast for three nights. Since it will be stated later [GDh 26.3], "Then for another three days," it is understood here as well that this refers to a period of three days. The prohibition against eating at night during those three days is formulated in accordance with the Vedic text: "One should not eat for three nights. Furthermore, this must be stated: "Twice-born men have eating in the evening and in the morning as enjoined by the Śruti."

Thus, because of this restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyāna*), eating is established as occurring only twice. In that context, when it is said "having eaten the morning meal," the cessation of eating at night is established by virtue of that restriction, just as the cessation of eating during the day is established later on.
Then, for another three days, he should eat only at night.

Immediately thereafter, there is another three-day period; by the inclusion of the word "another," it is established that the previous [three days] are also accomplished. One should eat ordinary sacrificial food (haviṣya) only at night, as before. 26.3.
Having thus spent three days eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) during the day, he should thereafter eat only at night for three days; [the food must be] sacrificial food indeed. 26.3.
Then, for another three days, he should not beg from anyone at all. || 26.4 ||

The word *atha* (now) serves the purpose of introducing the topic. There is no specific restriction on the time for eating once [a meal] obtained without asking; however, the mention of "another" (*apara*) is intended to establish a similarity with the preceding three-day period. Consequently, the requirement that the food be fit for sacrifice (*haviṣya*) and the prohibition against overeating (*atisauhitya*) should also be understood to apply here. One should not request anything from even a kinsman. And thus, there is no prohibition regarding what is obtained without being asked.

Some say: "If, when food is being offered, one should say, 'I will not eat non-sacrificial food (ahaviṣya),' then by implication a request for sacrificial food (haviṣya) has been made; therefore, there is no restrictive rule regarding the eating of sacrificial food in this case."

But others say: "By this, receiving gifts is prohibited; since the prohibition against eating sacrificial offerings (*haviṣya*) pertains to the acceptance of what has not already been accepted through a request for sacrifice, it is not a prohibition of eating such food. Thus, there is no prohibition regarding one's own [food]. Since the injunction 'one should not beg' would have been established [by the previous rule], the specific statement 'not anyone at all'—by the force of its commencement—implies that even begging for the sake of attendants and the like must not be performed. (26.4)

Now, after the three days of eating only at night, for the next three days he should not ask for anything from even a relative; this is a prohibition against begging. However, there is no prohibition regarding his own property or what is obtained unasked. If this were the case, the restriction to sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) would not apply, and because no specific time is mentioned, eating twice a day would also follow. In the phrase "he shall not ask," the term "sacrificial foods" (*haviṣyān*) likewise carries over. Even when obtained unasked, it is established that he should eat only once. Why? Because the statement "then another [period]" has the same meaning as the preceding one. Others, however, citing the view of Āpastamba—"for three days he observes the vow of not begging" (ĀpDh 1.27.7)—maintain that his subsistence during those three days must be solely by means of what is obtained unasked, neither by his own property nor by what is obtained through begging; they explain it thus. The practice should indeed be performed in this manner. 26.4.
Then he should fast for another three days. 26.5.

The word *atha* has the meaning already stated. Immediately thereafter, one should remain without food for three days. Here, the inclusion of the word *apara* (another) is for the purpose of establishing the performance of the three-day rite by way of another method as well. As Vasiṣṭha says:
"One day [eating] in the morning, one day at night, one day eating what is unasked for, and one day the *parāka* penance; in that very manner, there are two further sets of four days."

"For the sake of favoring the Brahmins, Manu, the best among the upholders of dharma, has indeed prescribed the *śiśukṛcchra* for children, the elderly, and the sick. [VaDh 23.43] For one who is unable to perform a fast, that which was spoken by Bhāradvāja should be observed:
"If a Brahmin performing the *prājāpatya* penance is unable [to fast] day after day..."
"One should properly feed five pure Brahmins, having honored them well. (26.5)
This is clear. Thus is this *kṛcchra* penance accomplished in twelve days. Vasiṣṭha has also shown another method:
"One day in the morning, one day at night, one day eating only what is unasked for, and one day fasting;
in this way, there are two further sets of four days."

"For the sake of favoring the Brahmins, Manu, the best among the upholders of dharma, indeed declared the *śiśukṛcchra* for children, the elderly, and the sick. Thus [says VaDh 23.43]. Bharadvāja says:

"If a Brahmin performing the *prājāpatya* penance is unable [to do so] day by day, he should properly feed five pure Brahmins at a minimum, having honored them well. This applies on the day he is unable; on other days, it is as before. If he is unable even then, or if he is unable on the days of fasting, he should give a meal to a Brahmin and then eat sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) himself properly. (26.5)
Now he states the rule for the qualities [of the penance]:
"Next is the rule for the qualities of the *kṛcchra*:
one who desires speed should stand during the day and sit during the night. (26.6)

During times not incompatible with eating and other such activities, he should remain standing during the day and sit during the night. In this way, since sleep is inevitable, it should be understood that he should resort to sleep only while remaining seated. Both by day and by night, he should be one who desires speed; "kāma" here means resolve. The meaning is that he should destroy even any experience that has arisen in every respect [as being unreal]. Alternatively, he should constantly maintain the thought: "By every effort, may I quickly become pure."

Some explain: for one who desires purification quickly, he should stand during the day and sit at night; however, there is no fixed rule for one whose intention is, "I shall perform purification gradually according to my capacity. Thus, due to the abundance of auxiliary elements (*guṇa*), the severity of the penance (*prāyaścitta*) is inferred. Accordingly, this [penance] prescribed by Gautama should be understood as a *prājāpatya* accompanied by the full procedure (*itikartavyatā*), serving as the substitute for two *prājāpatyas*. In cases where there is merely the status of a *prājāpatya*, it is without the procedure. As Vasiṣṭha says: "Eating in the morning for three days, likewise in the evening, and eating food obtained unasked for three days—this is the *parāka* penance" (VaDh 24.2).

Others say: for those such as women and *śūdras* who do not have the entitlement (*adhikāra*) to [Vedic] mantras, they should perform the rite without mantras according to the method taught by Vasiṣṭha and others; whereas for those who do have that entitlement, this [present rule applies]. Still others read "one desiring speed" (*akṣiprakāmaḥ*) and explain it thus: "One desiring speed should perform the *prājāpatya* penance, but one desiring quick results should perform that which was taught by Vasiṣṭha. And so he says: "Now, if he wishes to perform it quickly, he should subsist on air for a day."
Standing in water throughout the night until dawn is equal to the Prājāpatya penance.
Having performed the recitation of the Sāvitrī mantra eight thousand times when the sun has risen, one is released from all sins, provided that one is not a killer of an embryo. (VaDh 27.17–18) 26.6.

He who desires, "May I be purified quickly," should spend the day standing, provided it does not conflict with eating and other necessary activities; at night he should remain seated, and even his sleep should be while remaining seated. Vasiṣṭha, however, mentions another method for one desiring speed: "If he hastens to perform [the penance], he should subsist on air during the day and remain standing in water at night; that is equal to a Prājāpatya."

Having performed the recitation of the Sāvitrī mantra eight thousand times when the sun has risen, one is liberated from all sins, provided that one is not a killer of an embryo. [VaDh 27.17–18] || 26.6 ||
One should speak the truth. 26.7.

One should speak truthfully, exactly as it is. The intention is that even in matters such as marriage and the like, one must not speak untruth by taking the side of any particular party. And thus, it is understood that even through truthful speech, there occurs the destruction of evil. 26.7
Truth is that which is seen as it truly is. Even in matters such as marriage and the like, one should speak only the truth. (26.7)
One should not converse with those who are ignoble. || 26.8 ||

The non-noble ones (anārya) are those castes other than the twice-born, as well as those who are outcasts from the castes; this is due to the use of the plural number, which includes females, males, and neuters. 26.8.
Since gender is not intended to be significant for those other than the twice-born, he should not converse with their women either. 26.8.
One should always employ [the hymns] Raurava and Yodhāji. || 26.9 ||
One should always employ the Raurava and Yaudhājaya [Sāmans]. || 26.9 ||

The *raurava* and *yodhājaya* *sāmans* are sung upon this *ṛc*: “O Soma, being purified, flow forth in a stream. The word “constantly” (*nityam*) should be understood as applying everywhere, as in the rule “he should stand during the day” (GDh 26.6), because the use of the term “should employ” (*prayuñjīta*) is employed where one might have expected “should recite” (*japet*). Some say that because of the word “constantly,” it should be connected with the form of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*). Others say it means “repeatedly” or “many times. (26.9)

The *raurava* and *yaudhājaya* *sāmans* are sung upon this verse: "O Soma, being purified, flow with thy stream" (*punānaḥ soma dhāraya*, RV 9.63.28). One should employ them—that is, chant them—daily, every day. Another says: "One should employ them again daily. (26.9)

At each pressing, he should perform the ritual touching of water and purify himself with the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," which contain the word "pavitra," and with the eight verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ. (26.10)

At each libation, he should perform the ritual touching of water and purify himself with the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," which contain the word *pavitra*, and with the eight verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ. (26.10)

At each *anusavana*—that is, during the forenoon, midday, and afternoon—the ritual bathing (*snāna*) consists of touching water (*udakopasparśana*), because of the use of the prefix *upa*. One should perform the sprinkling (*mārjana*) with the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, which contain the word *pavitra*; with the four verses beginning with *pavitraṃ te vitataṃ*; and with the eight verses beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ*. Since no specific number is mentioned for these latter ones, and since the plural number would otherwise remain unfulfilled without the inclusion of the triad [of *āpo hi ṣṭhā*], one should sprinkle the water after consecrating it with mantras and pour it upon the head. Others explain that the bathing itself is performed with these very verses, because they are indicated by the instrumental case; furthermore, because the word *mārjana* is taught in the middle [of the sequence], it implies that the sprinkling is also done with other purifying verses (*pavitra*). (26.10)

Sprinkling with water (*udakopasparśana*) constitutes bathing; that should be performed at the three daily sessions (*savana*). Immediately thereafter, the ritual purification (*mārjana*) is performed with the verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā. Those verses found in the section of the *Anuvāka* titled "Pavamāna suvarjanaḥ" are called *pavitravatyaḥ* because of their association with the characteristic mark (*liṅga*). In the fifth book (*kāṇḍa*), sixth chapter (*praśna*) of the Taittirīya, the verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ" are recited; these number ten. Among them, [the rite is performed] with eight. However, if in another Vedic branch (*śākhā*) only eight are recited, then those alone are to be taken. (26.10)
Now follows the libation with water. || 26.11 ||

Immediately thereafter, its inclusion is for the purpose of ensuring that [the rite] is performed at each of the three daily libations (*anusavana*). And thus it is understood that water-libation (*udakatarpaṇa*) exists even in the case of occasional (*naimittika*) baths. So says Bhṛgu:
"Bathing is said to be of three kinds: obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*).
This same rule always applies to the water-libation for all three of these."

Regarding the phrase "touching water" (*udakopasparśanam*): where there is already a context concerning water, the repetition of the word "water" is for the purpose of ensuring that the libation (*tarpaṇa*) is performed even by one who is standing in water. Thus, after stating a contradiction in another *smṛti*, it is further justified as follows: "Water that is not offered upon the ground does not reach [the ancestors], whether it is in [other] waters, in vessels, when one is angry, or when offered with only one hand."
Likewise: "One should never offer water to the ancestors while standing in water;
rather, having emerged from the water, one should perform the libation of water in a clean place."
Having spoken thus, it was said:
"All the hosts of gods are water, and the hosts of ancestors are remembered as water.
Therefore, water should be given in water; what is given to the ancestors becomes inexhaustible."
Likewise:
One should offer handfuls of water for the deities and the ancestors in the water;
one should offer handfuls of water for those who have died without the proper rites on dry land.
Thus [ends the section]. 26.11.
Now, immediately after the purification, the satiation with water must be performed.
Furthermore, from whom and how [does this arise]? To this he says:
"In that regard, the mantras."

Homage to Hamāya, Mohamāya, Maṃhamāya, to the Shaker, to the Ascetic, to Punarvasu, homage! Homage to Mauñjyāya, Ūrmyāya, Vasuvindāya, Sarvavindāya, homage! Homage to Pārāya, Supārāya, Mahāpārāya, Pāradāya, Pārayiṣṇave, homage! Homage to Rudra, Paśupati, the Great God, Tryambaka, the Solitary Walker, the Overlord, to Hara, Śarva, Īśāna, Ugra, the Wielder of the Thunderbolt, the Compassionate One, Karpadī, homage! Homage to Sūrya, to Āditya, homage! Homage to Nīlagrīva, to Śitikaṇṭha, homage! Homage to Kṛṣṇa, to Piṅgala, homage! Homage to Jyeṣṭha, Śreṣṭha, Vṛddha, Indra, Harikeśa, to the One with Upward-Spreading Vital Energy, homage! Homage to Satya, to Pāvaka, to the One of Purifying Color, to Kāma, to the One who Takes Any Form at Will, homage! Homage to Dīpta, to the One of Radiant Form, homage! Homage to Tīkṣṇa, to the One of Sharp Form, homage! Homage to Saumya, to the Excellent Being, to the Great Being, to the Intermediate Being, to the Supreme Being, to the Vow-Observer, homage! Homage to the One with the Moon on His Forehead, to the One Clothed in a Skin, homage! (26.12)

Homage to Ahamāya, Mohamāya, Maṃhamāya, to the Shaker, to the Ascetic, to Punarvasu; homage! Homage to Mauñjyāyu, to Urvyāya, to Vasuvinda, to Sārvavinda; homage! Homage to Pāra, to Supāra, to Mahāpāra, to Vārayiṣṇu; homage! Homage to Rudra, to Paśupati, to the Great God, to Tryambaka, to the Solitary Wanderer, to the Overlord, to Hara, to Śarva, to Īśāna, to Ugra, to the Wielder of the Thunderbolt, to the Compassionate One, to the One with Matted Hair; homage! Homage to Sūrya, to Āditya; homage! Homage to the Blue-necked One, to the White-throated One; homage! Homage to the Black One, to the Tawny One; homage! Homage to the Eldest, to the Best, to the Ancient, to Indra, to the Golden-haired One, to the One with Upward Vital Energy; homage! Homage to the Truthful One, to the Purifier, to the One of Purifying Color, to Kāma, to the One who takes Form at Will; homage! Homage to the Radiant One, to the One of Radiant Form; homage! Homage to the Sharp One, to the One of Sharp Form; homage! Homage to the Auspicious One, to the Excellent Person, to the Great Person, to the Middle Person, to the Supreme Person, to the Student of Sacred Knowledge; homage! Homage to the Moon-browed One, to the One Clothed in a Skin; homage! 26.12

This is not a single mantra; for there is an indication by means of the plural number, stating that "these are the offerings of clarified butter. What then? These thirteen mantras, beginning with the salutation (*namaskāra*) and ending with the salutation, are to be understood as such, because the Vedic text is seen to be recited in that very manner. Consequently, the water-libation (*udakatarpaṇa*) is to be performed with these mantras ending in salutations.

Others, however, say: "These mantras are fifty-six in number, ending in the dative case of the recipient. Still others say: "They begin with the salutation but do not end with the salutation," because the text is seen to be recited in that way. || 26.12 ||

This is not a single mantra, because of the use of the plural number in the expression "these oblations of clarified butter" (*etāś cājyāhutayaḥ*). What then? There are thirteen mantras. All of them begin with a salutation and end with a salutation. Among them, in the first [mantra], there are six names of the God ending in the dative case; in the second, four; likewise in the third; and in the fourth, thirteen. In the fifth, the term *mahādeva* itself is stated in its expanded form as *mahate devāya*. In the three beginning with the fifth, there are two [names each]. In the eighth, there are six. In the ninth, five. In the tenth, two; likewise in the eleventh. In the twelfth, six. Thus, there are fifty-six names of the God. With these mantras, one should perform the libation at each pressing of the Soma. (26.12)
This indeed is the worship of the sun. 26.13.
This very *yajus* is the worship (*upasthāna*) of Āditya.

Now, since the word "worship" denotes an action, its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "yajus" is untenable; therefore, it must be stated that "the worship of Āditya is performed by means of these [verses]."

This is not a fault. Since "upasthāna" (worship) is defined as that by which one approaches (*upatiṣṭhate*), it is simply the *yajus* formula itself that is being designated; thus, there is no fault. Consequently, "the worship of the Sun" (*ādityopasthāna*) implies, by its very meaning, an injunction for an action. The word "eva" (only/just) is intended to indicate that this same mantra is to be used even for the water-libation (*udakatarpaṇa*). Otherwise, if it were merely stated that "this is the worship of the Sun," one might mistakenly assume that the water-libation should be performed with the mantra prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*. Furthermore, this should be understood as something additional to the obligatory rites, or rather, for the purpose of performing them exactly as they are recited in the tradition. From this, it is understood that the water-libation and other such acts are to be performed differently. If it is argued that praising the Sun with a mantra dedicated to Rudra is inappropriate, this is not a fault. For there is no such thing as an excessive burden for a scriptural injunction, and because the Sun is a portion (*aṃśa*) of Rudra. Thus it is said in the Purāṇa: "The eight forms of the Lord Śarva are known as Earth, Water, Wind, Fire, Sacrificer, Ether, Moon, and Sun. If it is argued that this is contradictory, since the Sun is seen there to be Viṣṇu, there is no fault, because the two are non-different. Accordingly, it is said in the Bhagavadgītā: "Among the Rudras, I am Śaṅkara" (BhG 10.23). Because the instruction follows immediately after the water-libation, the worship of the Sun should be understood as occurring three times at each of the three daily libations (*anusavana*).

Others explain: since the separate formulation of the rule was made when it could have simply been stated as "then the water libation and the worship of the Sun," this implies that the worship of the Sun is to be performed only once every day.

Others hold that the separate formulation is for the purpose of including it even outside of the context of expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*). There is no contradiction, even though the plurality [of days] has already been mentioned, because the singular number is used here just as it is used in the scriptural injunctions. || 26.13 ||

That by which the Āditya is worshipped is the "worship of the Āditya. This means that the Āditya is to be worshipped with this entire mantra; this too is to be performed at each pressing (anusavana) every day. Others say it is to be done once [daily], because of the separate formulation of the rule (yoga). Otherwise, he would have composed a single rule as follows: "The libation of water (udakatarpaṇa) and the worship of the Āditya. 26.13.
These indeed are the offerings of clarified butter. || 26.14 ||

Although it would have been sufficient to say "and the oblations of clarified butter (*ājyāhutayaḥ*)," the specific expression "these very ones" (*etā eva*) is intended to preclude the notion of a plurality of oblations. Therefore, these thirteen oblations of clarified butter are to be understood. The particle *eva* (only/very) is used here for the same purpose as in the previous enumeration, namely to restrict the application to the traditional sequence. Consequently, the mantras beginning with the salutation (*namaskāra*) and ending with the exclamation *svāhā* are to be understood [as constituting the oblations]. Why? Because of the force of the mention of "oblations" (*āhuti*). Although the mantras are masculine in gender, they are referred to here in the feminine as "these" (*etāḥ*) because of their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "oblation."

Some explain: "These are the fifty-six oblations of clarified butter (ājyāhuti) consisting of the dative case-endings; the use of the feminine gender is for the purpose of referring to the dative case-endings. This too should be understood as occurring at each pressing (anusavana), like the worship of the Sun (ādityopasthāna), performed once each time, because there is no mention of immediate succession. Thus one should proceed for twelve nights. 26.14.

The word *etāḥ* (these) also refers to the mantra; its feminine gender arises from its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the oblation (*āhuti*). It is thereby stated that the clarified butter (*ājya*) must also be offered with these very thirteen mantras. In this regard, since "an injunction to offer (*juhoti-codanā*) involves the utterance of *svāhā*," the oblation with them, accompanied by the *svāhā* formula, should be performed once every day. 26.14.
At the end of twelve nights, having cooked a sacrificial oblation (caru), he should offer it to these deities.

At the end of twelve nights—not every day—but on the thirteenth day, because of the mention of the ordinal number *ṣaṣṭhī*. Although it would have been sufficient simply to say "he should offer with the *caru*," the inclusion of the words "having cooked" (*śrapayitvā*) is for the purpose of indicating the sequence: having purified [the grain], having cooked it, having sprinkled clarified butter over it, and having removed it from the fire. The word "he should offer" (*juhuyāt*) is intended to prescribe the act of oblation. In this matter, one should follow the procedure for the *sthālīpāka* as prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*. If it is argued that the phrase "to these deities" need not be stated because it is already established by what is about to be said later, there is no fault; the instruction is given for the purpose of ensuring that the offering is preceded by meditative visualization (*dhyāna*). (26.15)

Having spent twelve nights in the manner thus described, on the thirteenth day at its conclusion, he should cook a sacrificial oblation (caru) according to the procedure prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras and offer it to the deities who are about to be mentioned.
She said:
"To Agni, svāhā! To Soma, svāhā! To Agni and Soma, to Indra and Agni, to Indra, to the All-gods, to Brahman, to Prajāpati, to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt."
Thus [ends the section]. 26.16.
"To Agni, Svāhā! To Soma, Svāhā! To Agni and Soma, to Indra and Agni, to the Viśvedevas, to Brahman, to Prajāpati, and to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. || 26.16 ||

The double recitation of the word *svāhā* is for the purpose of its application (*anuṣaṅga*) everywhere. The particle *iti* is used for the purpose of indicating the inclusion of the specific form. Therefore, in cases such as "to Indra," one should not append "to the much-invoked" (*puruhūta*) and so forth; rather, only that [specific name] itself [is to be used].

There are nine oblations together with the *sviṣṭakṛt*. The twofold recitation of the word *svāhā* is for the purpose of showing the manner of the syntactic connection (*anuṣaṅga*); that is to say, all [the mantras] end with *svāhā*. (26.16)
Then follows the gratification of the Brahmins. || 26.17 ||

After the fire-oblation, on the following day, one should perform the satiation of Brahmins according to one's ability; it should be understood that even in that case, one should feed at least three. 26.17.

Then, immediately after the fire-oblation, the Brahmins are to be gratified with food and other offerings. Āpastamba states: "In all ritual acts, one should feed those who are pure and learned in the mantras" (ĀpDh 2.15.11). 26.17.
By this very [rule], the Atikṛcchra penance is explained. || 26.18 ||

By this very same procedure for the *prājāpatya*, the *atikṛcchra*—which produces even greater suffering—is also explained. If it is argued that this is already established by the use of the plural form "kṛcchrān" (the kṛcchras), it is replied: the explicit mention is intended to indicate that the first [the *prājāpatya*] serves as the archetype (*prakṛti*), just as in the case of the *agniṣṭoma*. Therefore, even in the case of the *sāntapana* and other such penances, one must formulate the application of rules such as "he should stand during the day" [GDh 26.6] so as not to contradict them. Their specific nature, however, is to be understood from other *smṛtis*. Thus says Baudhāyana: "For twelve days, one who is self-controlled and vigilant shall abstain from food."
This penance called Parāka is the destroyer of all sins.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, ghee, and water infused with *kuśa* grass,
followed by a fast for one night, is known as the *sāntapana* penance.
Cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, and likewise ghee—
one whose food consists of these for five nights is purified by the *pañcagavya*.
Those who expound the Veda declare that the Mahāsāntapana penance consists of practicing each of the [five] substances, beginning with cow’s urine, three times for seven days each.
Subsisting on grain-particles, oil-cakes, and buttermilk, or likewise eating only raw grain and air,
this Tulāpuruṣa rite destroys sin after one, three, five, or seven days.
Barley-gruel for seven nights destroys the sins of embodied beings, or fasting for seven nights does so; this has been observed by the wise.

A twice-born man who observes the three bright fortnights of the months of Pauṣa, Bhādrapada, and Jyeṣṭha— devoting himself to the constellations Ārdrā, the sky (the full moon), and sunlight— is liberated from sin, with the exception of those sins that cause loss of caste.
By fasting on the new moon day and eating sesame seeds on the full moon day,
one is liberated from the sins committed during the bright and dark fortnights throughout the year by means of these sacred festivals.
One who subsists on almsfood becomes pure in one month from those who maintain the *agnihotra* fire;
from those who follow the *yāyāvara* mode of life or dwell in the forest, one becomes pure in ten or seven days respectively.
A twice-born man who subsists on the gleaning of grains is purified by eating food from a wealthy person for one day;
having drunk water [from such a source], he is purified after one day.
By reciting the *Ṛgveda*, the *Yajurveda*, the *Sāmaveda*, or any other Veda three times through to completion while fasting, one is liberated from sin.
He who gives food, speaks the truth, and is non-violent toward all beings surpasses all those previously mentioned as purified by mantras.
The *trimadhu*, the *chandasa*, the *rudra*, the *gāyatrī* accompanied by the *praṇava*,
and the seven *vyāhṛtis*— the recitation of these is the destroyer of sin.
The Mṛgāreṣṭi, the Pavitreṣṭi, and also the Pāvamānī sacrifices—
these, when combined with the Vaiśvānarī, are destroyers of sin.
And listen now to this other secret being told:
one is liberated from all sins, except for the most grievous crimes.
Performing the sprinkling with purificatory blades (pavitra), reciting the eleven Rudra hymns,
offering oblations of clarified butter with the Vyāhṛtis, and bestowing gold, cows, and sesame seeds;
One should eat boiled barley-gruel with cow’s urine and the liquid of cow dung, along with curd, milk, and ghee; such a person is instantly liberated from sin.
He who has procreated a son upon a Śūdra woman, and he by whom an unapproachable woman has been violated—
both of them are liberated from that sin after seven nights by this rite.

For consuming semen, urine, or feces; for eating food that should not be eaten; for performing the *paryādhāna* rite; for sacrificing when one is entitled to the *parivitti* status; and for being a *parivitti*—this [rite] is the remedy.
"Even after committing many deeds here that are not sins,
one is released from all evils"— this is the teaching of the virtuous.
The authority of the path of mantra and its ritual procedure have been proclaimed—
that by which Bharadvāja and others attained identity with Brahman.
With a serene heart, the brahmin, having consumed milk and curd through this rite,
attains those various desires that reside within his heart.
O Brahmins, for one who has turned away from all evils and engaged in meritorious deeds,
his ritual actions succeed even without effort.
Therefore, those brahmins who are upright, purified, and whose actions are straight, quickly attain whatever they desire with their minds.
Thus, these yogic exercises (yantras) should be performed by the wise man for as long as it takes for the impurity of the self's body to depart.
Purified by these mantras, having fasted for three nights and being pure, one whose self is cleansed should undertake that rite by which they desire to attain supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).
The *kṣāpavitra*, the *sahasrākṣa*, the *mṛgāra*, the two *aṃhomuc* hymns,
the *pāvamānī* verses, the *kūśmāṇḍa* verses, and those verses addressed to Vaiśvānara.
Offering oblations of rice cooked with ghee three times a day for seven days,
maintaining silence, subsisting on sacrificial food, and restraining the activities of his senses;
If one gazes upon a lion in a water-pot filled with water at a crossroads,
saying "ma," one is released from all sins, even from a great heinous crime.
One is liberated even from that accumulation of evil deeds committed in old age, youth, or childhood, or those produced in previous births.

"Having fed the twice-born with milk-rice mixed with ghee, one should cause cows, land, sesame seeds, and gold to be given to those who have eaten. Thus it is said, and so forth. Enough of this digression; that which is relevant is now being stated. 26.18.
This is clear. 26.18
But its specific distinction is now stated;
he declares that specific distinction:
one should eat only as much as one might take up in a single mouthful. 26.19.

One should eat only as much of the sacrificial food (haviṣya) as can be taken up at once with a single hand during those very days. This is an injunction regarding the size of the mouthful (grāsa). Thus says Manu: "One should eat one mouthful each for three three-day periods, as previously described."

"He should fast for three days; that is called the *atikṛcchra*. [MDh 11.213] The third [type] consists of subsisting on water; that is the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*. At the very same time for eating that was previously mentioned, he should drink only water. Such is the nature of the third *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*. The mention of "third" is intended to indicate that sequence, even though it is stated simply as "the last" (*antya*). Thus, the author will later say: "Having performed the first," [GDh 26.20], and so forth. Although one could have said "the third by means of water" (*adbhis tṛtīyaḥ*), the inclusion of the word *bhakṣa* (subsistence) is intended to show that water performs the function of food. Consequently, there is no drinking of water outside of the prescribed time. The assignment of a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is for the sake of common usage. 26.19.

One should eat only as much as can be taken up with a single hand at once. The specific rules remain the same: sacrificial food (haviṣya) by day and by night, unasked for, and fasting. Regarding this, Manu says: "One should eat a single morsel for three periods of three days each, as before; and one should fast for the final three days—this is called the Kṛcchra. (MDh 11.213) 26.19.
Subsisting on water for three days constitutes the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*. || 26.20 ||

During the very same meal-times mentioned previously, one should drink water alone; this is to be known as the third penance, called the *Kṛcchrātikṛcchra*. On the days of fasting here, even the drinking of water is not permitted, with the exception of sipping water for ritual purification (*ācamana*). These three types of *kṛcchra* have thus been described. (26.20)
Now he states the fruit of these:
"Having first practiced those, one becomes pure, purified, and fit for action. (26.20–26.21)

Having first performed the Prājāpatya penance, one becomes pure, free from the fault caused by the non-performance of prescribed duties, cleansed, and with the demerit produced by the practice of forbidden acts destroyed; thus one becomes fit for action—that is, capable of engaging in both optional and obligatory rites.

But is this not redundant? For its purpose is already established by the very injunction for expiation (*prāyaścitta*), since in the rule "one should perform [it]," it has been demonstrated that [the rite] is the cause for the destruction of sin. Furthermore, since that is also established by the word "from the first" alone, the inclusion of the term "having performed" (*caritvā*) is likewise redundant. Likewise, the mention of the specific sub-divisions of unrighteousness (*adharma*) through the words "pure" (*śuci*) and "purified" (*pūta*) yields little fruit, since both are established by the word "purified" alone. The same applies to the term "fit for action" (*karmaṇya*). If the intention is that one becomes eligible for ritual action simply by being free from unrighteousness, then it need not be stated, as it is already established by implication. If, on the other hand, the intention is the attainment of a more distinguished result, that too is incorrect; for whatever the fruit of a particular action may be, that alone it shall be, and no further excellence of fruit arises.

To this it is replied: This undertaking is for the purpose of making known that these two types of dharma performed in another body are the means for their exhaustion. The inclusion of the word *caritvā* (having performed) is for the purpose of making known that [expiation] occurs through a single performance, because later on [the text] states, "whatever other [sins there are] besides the great crimes" (GDh 26.21), and because the prescription of expiation generally applies only to the practice of what is prohibited. Furthermore, since the word *pūta* (purified) might give rise to the suspicion that it refers only to prohibited matters, the word *śuci* (pure/clean) is used. And it should be understood that this refers to [dharma] that is known (*jñāta*), because it has been stated [elsewhere] that for those [sins] not mentioned in the Veda, [expiation applies to] the unknown (*ajñāta*).

[Objection: But surely this too is established by the mention of the "universal expiation" (*sarvaprāyaścitta*), since that applies generally to acts committed both intentionally and unintentionally. [Reply: It is said: this [expiation] has a specified scope, whereas that [universal expiation] has an unspecified scope. The same should be understood regarding prohibited objects. Furthermore, the phrase "in ritual action" (*karmaṇya*) is intended to make known the fact that when there is a connection with unrighteousness (*adharma*), there occurs an obstruction to the fruit of the ritual action. (26.20)

Having first performed the *prājāpatya* penance, he becomes pure. For one who neglects the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*) is perpetually impure and unfit for all rites; thus, he is free from the defect caused by the non-performance of prescribed duties. Being "purified" (*pūta*), he is devoid of the demerit (*adharma*) arising from the practice of forbidden acts. He is "fit for action" (*karmaṇya*), meaning he is capable of performing rites. By the use of the term "fit for action," it is made known that even one whose fault was previously unknown becomes fit for desired rites through the performance of the *kṛcchra* penance. (26.21)
Having performed it a second time, he is liberated from whatever other sin he commits that is not among the great sins (mahāpātaka). || 26.21–26.22 ||

H reads: "By performing any other *atikṛcchra* penance whatsoever, one becomes liberated from sins other than the *mahāpātaka*s. Thus, while the destruction of the sin arising from the violation of *yama* and *niyama* is effected by the former [penance], this [latter] effects the exhaustion of the sin committed as a *upapātaka*. Furthermore, because it is stated that this is a universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) when combined with the former, it should be understood that it also exhausts even a *mahāpātaka* committed unintentionally. (26.21)
Having performed the second *atikṛcchra* penance, one is liberated from sins other than the *mahāpātaka*s (great crimes). || 26.22 ||
Having performed it for a third time, one removes all sin. || 26.22 ||
Having performed it for a third time, one is released from all sin. || 26.23 ||

Having performed the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*, one destroys even a great sin (*mahāpātaka*) committed unintentionally. Why? Because this [penance] is equal to the two preceding ones, and because the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*), when accompanied by the *cāndrāyaṇa*, is the cause for destroying a great sin committed intentionally. Thus, this too should be performed in place of the two preceding ones. The statement beginning with "the second" and so forth should also be understood as referring to that same context. This instruction is given so that there may not be a total combination of all [penances] in the case of the universal expiation. (26.22)

Having performed the third penance, the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra, one is released from all sin, even from the great mortal transgressions (mahāpātaka), provided they were committed unintentionally. || 26.23 ||
Having thus stated the fruit of these [penances] individually, he now speaks of them collectively:
"Now, having performed these three *kṛcchra* penances, one becomes bathed in all the Vedas; one becomes known by all the gods—both he who knows this, and he who knows this. (26.23)
Then, having performed these three kṛcchra penances, one becomes as if bathed in all the Vedas and becomes known by all the gods. || 26.24 ||

Now, immediately after this, one should perform these three [penances] themselves without interval—not the *taptakṛcchra* and so forth. The term "kṛcchras" is used for the purpose of performing them with extreme rigor; in the same way, the *ārdravastra* and others are also to be understood, as well as the recitations (*japa*), fire-oblations (*homa*), and so on. The phrase beginning with "sarveṣu" is stated with the intention that one becomes connected to a fruit equal to that which belongs to one who has bathed after studying all the Vedas. "He is known by all the gods" means he is capable of going to their world. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to conjoin this with what precedes: the previously mentioned fruit belongs to one who has performed [the penance] after knowing [this], not merely through the performance of the act or through knowledge alone. Thus, the fruit should be seen as corresponding to each individual factor.

Some maintain that even each [of these] individually [achieves this]; that is incorrect, because the destruction of evil occurs through practice alone, and not through mere knowledge. And so Manu says:
"Even though the fruit of the *kataka* tree is a clarifier of water..."
The water does not become clear merely by uttering his name. [MDh 6.67] || 26.23 ||

He who performs these three *kṛcchra* penances without interruption obtains a fruit equal to that of one who has bathed after completing the study of all the Vedas; by him, the worlds of all the gods have been conquered. 26.24.
Now, the praise of the wise one:
"And he who knows thus, and he who knows thus. 26.25.

And whoever understands these [sacrifices] according to their essential nature, their procedure, and their fruit, he too becomes one who has bathed in all the Vedas; he becomes known by all the gods. The meaning is that what is thus understood is praiseworthy. [The repetition of the sense already stated serves to conclude the section. 26.25
Now begins the twenty-seventh chapter.

It has been stated that there are the *kṛcchra*, the *atikṛcchra*, and the *cāndrāyaṇa*. Among these, the rule for the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* has been declared. Now, with the intention of explaining the rule for the *cāndrāyaṇa*, he says:
"Now, therefore, the *cāndrāyaṇa*. (27.1)

The word "we shall explain" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. The word *atha* (now/then) indicates the commencement of a new topic (*adhikāra*). Because its fruit is equal to that of the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra*, it does not follow immediately after them. Alternatively, the word *atha* signifies a reason (*hetu*), because this [penance] is connected with such a fruit. *Cāndrāyaṇa* is the name [of the rite]; it is so called because it conforms to the movement of the moon (*anvarthatvāt*). The singular number is used because it refers to the genus (*jāti*). And thus, it makes known that the *yaticāndrāyaṇa* and others mentioned in other *smṛtis* constitute a universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*). Manu says accordingly: "When midday has arrived, one should eat eight morsels (*piṇḍas*)."
With self-restraint, one should perform the Yati-cāndrāyaṇa using sacrificial food.
Having performed his daily rites, a twice-born man should eat four morsels in the morning;
he should eat four when the sun has set—thus he should perform the Śiśu-cāndrāyaṇa penance.
If one who is concentrated eats eighty-three morsels of sacrificial food (haviṣya) in some manner or other for a month, he attains the same world as the Moon.
And so forth. 27.1.
This is to be explained as before. *Cāndrāyaṇa* is the ritual action that serves as the cause for attaining the moon; thus, he will state at the end: "He attains the same world as the moon. (27.1)
The rule for that has been stated in the section on the Kṛcchra penance.

Of that [penance] of every kind—because of the employment of the word "that"—the rule (vidhi) and the procedure (itikartavyatā) have been stated, beginning with "In the first *kṛcchra*, he should stand during the day" [GDh 26.6], and so forth. || 27.2 ||
The rule beginning with "He should remain standing during the day" (GDh 26.6), which prescribes the *kṛcchra* penance, is to be understood as applying to the *cāndrāyaṇa* as well. || 27.2 ||
But that which is the distinction here is now stated: shaving and the observance of vows. || 27.3 ||

If it is a *vrata* (vow), then shaving—the removal of hair and so forth—must be performed; this constitutes its purpose if it is for the sake of expiation (*prāyaścitta*). For by the word *vrata*, expiation is indicated in another *smṛti*; as Manu says: "By these vows, the twice-born who have made their sins public are to be purified" (MDh 11.226). And thus, it is made known that if it is for the sake of an unseen spiritual result (*adṛṣṭārtha*), then that vow occurs even without shaving.

Others, however, say that this refers to the vow of a religious student (*brahmacārin*), because such is seen in passages like, "There are four types of those under vows" (MDh 11.121). According to this view, it applies to a householder even in the absence of such a vow. This same principle should be understood to apply to the *kṛcchra* penance and others as well. || 27.3 ||
He says that "vow" (vrata) refers to expiation (prāyaścitta).

"By these vows, the twice-born who have manifested their sins are to be purified" (MDh 11.226); because of such statements as these, if the Cāndrāyaṇa is performed for the purpose of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), then shaving (*vapana*) must also be performed. Even though no distinction is made, this applies only to men; for there is the traditional teaching of Baudhāyana: "That same [penance] applies to women, with the exception of shaving the hair" (BDh 2.2.45). Since shaving is prescribed specifically for the Cāndrāyaṇa, it does not take place in the *Kṛcchra* even when performed for expiation. Because of the injunction "one should observe the vow," there is no shaving in the Cāndrāyaṇa when it is performed for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*) or for the sake of fitness for ritual action (*karmayogyatārtha*). 27.3.
To state its own nature, he says:
"One should fast on the day when the full moon has occurred. (27.4)
Fasting is the renunciation of food; the meaning is that one should perform this on the fourteenth day. || 27.4 ||
Having understood that "the full moon will be tomorrow," one should fast on the preceding day, the fourteenth. Fasting (upavāsa) is the abstention from eating. || 27.4 ||
The satiation, the oblation of clarified butter, and the consecration of the sacrificial food are performed with these [verses]: "Swell up," "May your milks," and "New, new. || 27.5 ||

The satiation is performed with these [verses]: "Swell up" (*ā pyāyasva*), "May thy milks" (*saṃ te payāṃsi*), and "New, new" (*navo nava*); there is also an oblation of clarified butter and the recitation over the sacrificial food, as well as the worship of the moon. 27.5.

With these three verses—“Swell up! Let [the waters] meet thee; let thy milks meet; let thy strengths meet; ever new he becomes as he is born”—one should perform the water-satiation (*udakatarpaṇa*), the oblation of clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and the consecration (*anumantraṇa*) of the sacrificial food (*havis*) that is about to be described.

Regarding this, some say: since it is accepted that an increase in the number of constituent parts results in an increase in the fruit, and because of the extension (*atideśa*) of the rules for the *kṛcchra* penance, those rites such as the water-satiation which are taught in the *raudra-kṛcchra* are to be combined (*samuccīyante*) with these.

That is incorrect. For, according to the maxim that "that which is obtained through extended application (*atideśa*) is set aside by what is directly heard in scripture (*pratyakṣa-śruta*)," cessation [of the former] alone is logical. Now, should each [rite] be performed individually according to their respective order, or everything collectively? Others say: because of the singular number in the expression "ājyahoma" (ghee-oblation), one should perform them individually; for if they were combined, there would be a multiplicity of rites due to the multiplicity of mantras, and the plural number would consequently follow in the case of separate oblations. 27.5.

The four rites beginning with the libation (*tarpaṇa*) are to be performed with the mantras beginning with "āpyāyasva" and so forth. Due to the disparity in number, they do not correspond respectively. In this regard, the libation and the fire-oblation (*homa*) are performed for each individual mantra; the recitation (*anumantraṇa*) and the worship (*upasthāna*) are to be combined. Some say that because of the extension (*atideśa*) of the rules for the *kṛcchra* penance, those rites such as the water-libation which are obtained through the *raudra* [mantra] are also to be combined. Others say that the prescribed rites supersede those obtained by extension. (27.5)
And the attendance upon the moon. || 27.6 ||

By virtue of the word "and" (ca), these [rites] themselves must be performed. If that [deity] is not seen, then the rite for the Sun (āditya) is to be performed, because of the observation of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the mantra: "Suṣumna, the ray of the Sun. Here, because the purpose is different, the worship of the Sun—which would have been obtained through the extension (*atideśa*) of the rule for *kṛcchra* penance—is set aside. 27.6.
And one should offer oblations with the four verses beginning with "yad devā devaheḍanam. || 27.7 || — || 27.6 ||

With the *ṛc*s beginning with “*yad devā devaheḍanam*,” one should offer clarified butter (*ājya*) because no other [substance] has been prescribed. The mention of the feminine gender and number refers to the meaning of the *ṛc*s; this is for the purpose of excluding those *yajus* formulas of a similar nature that are recited in the *Yajurveda*. Thus, together with the preceding [formula], there are five or seven oblations of clarified butter.

In the section beginning with "yad devā devaheḍanam" [VS 20.14], one should offer clarified butter (ājya) with the first four verses; since no specific instruction is given, one should also include the preceding three, making seven oblations of clarified butter. || 27.6 ||
And at the end, with the words "devakṛtasya," [he offers] with fuel-sticks. || 27.8 || — || 27.7 ||

The [mantras] beginning with "devakṛtasya" have been stated [GDh 25.14]. With those mantras, one should perform eight oblations of fuel-sticks (samidh). At the end—that is, at the conclusion of the Cāndrāyaṇa—and because of the word "ca" (and), also at the beginning. 27.8.

At the conclusion of the *ājya* oblations, an oblation with fuel-sticks (*samidh*) must be performed using the eight previously mentioned mantras beginning with "devakṛtasya" (VS 8.13). Although this is established by the very sequence of the instruction, the inclusion of the word "end" (*anta*) is a restatement of what has already been reached. Others, however, explain it as being at the end of the *cāndrāyaṇa*; for them, the word "and" (*ca*) would not be appropriate. || 27.7 ||
"Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, tapas, satyam, yaśas, śrīs, ūrj, iḍ, ojas, tejas, puruṣa, dharma, śiva"—with these [words] the consecration of the morsels is performed. 27.9.

"Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, tapas, satyam, yaśas, śrīs, ūrg, iḍ, ojas, tejas, varcas, puruṣas, dharmas, śivas"—with these [mantras], one should perform the consecration of the morsels mentally with each individual mantra. 27.8.

These fifteen mantras, beginning with the *praṇava*, are to be used for the consecration (*anumantraṇa*) of each mouthful in their proper sequence. Previously, the consecration of the sacrificial food (*havis*) was mentioned; however, when the final morsel is set aside, the final mantra is also [to be applied], so that the end of the mantras is thus observed. || 27.9 ||

There are fifteen mantras beginning with *praṇava*; one should perform the mental consecration (*anumantraṇa*) of each morsel with each individual mantra. Eating is to be done according to the sequence of these consecrations. However, when there are fewer morsels, then as many mantras as there are morsels should be taken from the beginning; those at the end are omitted. Because of the statement "consecration of the morsels," these are not mantras for the act of eating itself. Consequently, there is no cessation of the mantras for the *prāṇāhuti* offerings. When there are four morsels, then two [mantras] are used first; when three, then the first two [are used], and the next two; when two, then the first two and the last one with three [mantras]; when one, then with all [fifteen]. Regarding the previously mentioned "consecration of the sacrificial food" (*haviṣaḥ*), that applies here, but since it is now "consecration of the morsels," the *prāṇāhuti* mantras remain in force. The practical application (*prayoga*) therein is as follows: having placed all the food in a vessel and consecrated it with the mantras beginning with *āpyāyasva*, having divided it into morsels, and having consecrated the morsels in order with the mantras beginning with *praṇava*, one should eat after performing the *prāṇāhuti* offerings. (27.8)
Or he may offer all of them with the thought "namas" or "svāhā" for each mantra.
Or he may offer to all [the deities] with "namaḥ" and "svāhā. 27.9.

Having performed a prostration or an utterance of *svāhā* for each individual mantra at the end, one should mentally consecrate all morsels with the mantras. There is an option according to one’s preference; because of the word "all," the consecration applies to morsels that have been separated, but not to those that have not been separated. Furthermore, these are consecration-mantras (*anumantraṇa-mantra*), not consumption-mantras (*bhakṣaṇa-mantra*). Therefore, having thus consecrated the food, one should eat it. 27.10

Alternatively, one should consecrate all morsels with the formula "namaḥ svāhā. There is an option between these two, "namaḥ" and "svāhā," or others maintain that the two together constitute a single mantra. 27.9.
The measure of a mouthful is that which can be taken without distorting the mouth. 27.11 — 27.10.
The measure [of the mouth] should be just that much by which the mouth is not distorted—that is to say, not opened too wide. || 27.11 ||
The measure of a morsel is such that when it is being swallowed, the mouth remains undistorted. 27.10.

Caru, alms-food, barley-meal, grain-particles, barley-gruel, vegetables, milk, curd, ghee, roots, fruits, and water—these sacrificial offerings are increasingly praised in the sequence mentioned. || 27.12 || — || 27.11 ||

These are the twelve substances. Among these sacrificial substances (*havirdravya*), each subsequent one is more excellent than each preceding one, because it causes less physical distress. *Caru* is a sacrificial food that must be cooked by oneself; *bhaikṣa* (alms) is that which is obtained by a religious student (*brahmacārin*) or brought to him by others. The remaining items are well known. The mention of "sacrificial" (*havis*) is for the purpose of indicating that they are to be prepared like a sacrificial offering; from this, the exclusion of salt, molasses, and similar items is established. In that regard, the morsels of the substances are to be measured using a small leaf-cup (*puṭikā*), and the measurement should be performed according to the principle: "For heavy foods, the portions are large" (GDh 19.19). || 27.12 ||

The *caru* is rice that has been prepared with sacrificial offerings (*haviṣya*), freshly boiled, pure, and fully cooked. Alms (*bhaikṣa*) refers to what has been personally brought by a student (*brahmacārin*), a disciple, or others, since for a householder the practice of wandering for alms is forbidden. *Cūrṇīkṛtā lājāḥ* are parched grain reduced to flour; *saktavaḥ* are groats. *Kaṇāḥ* are the husks of grain. *Yāvaka* has been mentioned previously. The other items are well known. These are the twelve sacrificial foods (*havīṃṣi*). Among them, each subsequent one is more meritorious than the preceding one. In that regard, for liquid substances, the portioning into mouthfuls is done using leaf-cups or similar vessels. And as for penances, they are heavy when the sins are heavy, and light when the sins are light. (27.11)
Having eaten fifteen morsels on the full moon day, one should eat during the waning fortnight by decreasing the amount by one morsel each day. 27.13—27.12.

Having observed a fast on the fourteenth day and having consumed fifteen morsels of one of these sacrificial foods on the fifteenth day, one should then eat [only] one morsel per day starting from the first day of the dark fortnight (pratipad) until the end of the dark fortnight.
