The mention of the "latter fortnight" (aparapakṣa) is for the sake of completeness; it means that one should complete the entire fortnight in this manner, rather than filling the required number of days irregularly. Or, the repetition is intended to indicate that this applies even to one who is traveling for the purpose of eating only once a day. 27.13.

Having thus fasted on the fourteenth day, one should eat fifteen morsels on the following day, the fifteenth. Thereafter, by decreasing by one at each subsequent utterance, the meaning becomes clear: that there is a reduction of one morsel every day. One should eat in this manner throughout the entire dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*). When a decrease in lunar days (*tithi*) occurs, such that the meal on the ninth day is reached according to the sequence, and when the ninth day lasts for five *nāḍīs* in the morning while the tenth day does not exist on the following day, then one should eat nine morsels on the ninth day itself which arrived on the previous day, and on the following day, one should eat eleven morsels upon the arrival of the eleventh day. This constitutes the omission of the ten morsels that would have been consumed upon the arrival of the tenth day. Likewise, when there is an increase in lunar days and the meal on the eleventh day is reached, if the tenth day lasts twenty-six *nāḍikās* during the day and the eleventh day lasts four [during the day], and if some portion of the eleventh day also exists on the following night, then one should eat eleven morsels on the eleventh day which has entered the previous day, and on the following day as well, one should eat those same eleven. On the day after that, the practice is to eat twelve.

"In whatever manner one may eat two hundred and forty morsels of sacrificial food (haviṣya) with a concentrated mind during a month, one attains the same world as the Moon"—thus another form of Cāndrāyaṇa is prescribed in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra]. However, this is not a restriction on the number of morsels for the Cāndrāyaṇa already described in terms of its increase and decrease. And so it has been clearly stated by Yājñavalkya:
"In whatever manner one may [eat] two hundred and forty morsels..."
"Or else, one may perform another Cāndrāyaṇa penance by eating for one month. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.324) || 27.12 ||
Having fasted on the new moon day, he should pass the waxing fortnight by increasing [the number of morsels] by one each day.
Having fasted on the new moon day, he should pass the fortnight of the waxing moon by increasing [the number of morsels] by one each day.

Then, having observed a fast on the new moon day, one should eat during the bright fortnight by increasing the intake by one morsel starting from the first day. Thus, on the full moon day there are fifteen morsels. Because it is thin in the middle, this is called the "ant-middled" (pipīlikāmadhya) fast. 27.14.

In this manner, as he consumes [the food] by decreasing it by one [mouthful] each day, on the fourteenth day there is one mouthful. On the new moon day (amāvāsya), there is a fast. Having fasted on the new moon day, on the first day of the waxing fortnight (pūrvapakṣa) he eats one mouthful; then, by increasing one mouthful at a time, he should eat throughout the entire waxing fortnight. On the full moon day (paurṇamāsī), there are fifteen mouthfuls. Because it is thin in the middle, this is the "ant-waisted" (pipīlikāmadhya) Cāndrāyaṇa. || 27.13 ||
For some, it is the opposite. 27.15 — 27.14.

According to the opinion of some teachers, this very [practice] is reversed: having observed a fast on the fourteenth day, one should eat a single morsel on the new moon day (amāvāsyā). Then, beginning from the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad), one should eat during the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa) by increasing the amount by one morsel each day; thus, on the fourteenth day, there are fifteen morsels. Then, there is a fast on the full moon day (paurṇamāsī); on the first day of the next fortnight, there are fifteen morsels. From there, one should eat during the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa) by decreasing by one morsel each day.

Others, however, explain it otherwise and in a contrary manner: having fasted on the full moon day, one should eat during the dark fortnight starting from the first day (pratipad) by decreasing the amount by one morsel each day; then, starting from the new moon day, one should eat during the bright fortnight by increasing the amount by one morsel each day. Because it is broad in the middle, this is called "barley-shaped" (yavamadhya). Therefore, the previously mentioned one is "ant-shaped" (pipīlikāmadhya). || 27.15 ||

According to the opinion of some teachers, this very procedure is reversed: having fasted on the new moon day and eaten during the bright fortnight by increasing [the number of mouthfuls] by one each day, one should eat during the dark fortnight starting from the first day of the waning moon by decreasing [the number of mouthfuls] by one each day, so that there is one mouthful on the fourteenth day. There is a fast on the new moon day. Because it is thick in the middle, this is the barley-middled (yavamadhyama) Cāndrāyaṇa. || 27.14 ||
And this is the Cāndrāyaṇa month. 27.16 — 27.15.
That by which the moon is followed through its waning and waxing is the *cāndrāyaṇa*; the month associated with that is also called *cāndrāyaṇa*. || 27.16 ||

Thus, the *cāndrāyaṇa* is accomplished in a month; because of that connection, this month is called *cāndrāyaṇa*. Even though, according to the methods described, there are thirty-two days in the "ant-waist" (*pipīlikāmadhya*) and thirty-one in the "barley-waist" (*yavamadhya*), it is nevertheless called "this month" by the maxim that "one [is not excluded] by even a single syllable. (27.15)
Having attained this, one who is free from evil and free from sin destroys all transgression. 27.17 ||
Having thus obtained [this], he becomes free from evil and sinless; he destroys all transgression. || 27.16 ||

Having performed this Cāndrāyaṇa of such a kind, one becomes free from sin (*vipāpa*) through the destruction of the transgression caused by the non-performance of prescribed duties; one becomes free from evil (*vipāpman*) through the eradication of the defilement caused by the performance of prohibited acts. It destroys every other form of sin as well, even that which has entered into another body. And thus it is indicated that the Cāndrāyaṇa must be performed both for the non-performance of prescribed duties and when there is affliction by leprosy and other diseases. (27.17)

In this very manner, having completed such a Cāndrāyaṇa for a month—having performed this vow which is accomplished in a month—one becomes free from sin, devoid of the impurity arising from the non-performance of prescribed duties. Being "free from sin" (vipāpmā), one is also devoid of the sin resulting from the performance of prohibited acts. He destroys every transgression; he destroys even all other subtle sins accumulated in previous births. || 27.16 ||
Having attained the second [birth], he purifies ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself as the twenty-first, as well as his entire lineage. || 27.18 || — || 27.17 ||
The sūtra is explained by its very wording. || 27.18 ||

Regarding the statement "having attained two," the expression "the second" is used for the sake of continuity, meaning "having attained the second month continuously. But how is such continuity possible? For it has been stated that one should fast on the full moon day (paurṇamāsī) occurring after the "ant-hill" [period], and that on the full moon day one should eat fifteen morsels; likewise, having fasted on the new moon day (amāvāsyā), one should eat during the waxing fortnight by increasing the morsels by one each day. Thus, that performance ends with the second full moon day. Immediately following that, at the commencement of the second [Cāndrāyaṇa], there would be a fast on the fourteenth day, and eating fifteen morsels on the fifteenth day—which is not tenable. Therefore, it should be stated here as follows: there is no injunction for two Cāndrāyaṇas here. What then? There is one Cāndrāyaṇa to be accomplished over two months. This is the injunction regarding its fruit. At its beginning, there is a fast on the fourteenth day, and the performance ends on the third full moon day. In the middle, it is as previously described. And the second full moon day serves both as the end of the first and the beginning of the second through the principle of *tantra* (common application). Similarly, in the "barley-shaped" (*yavamadhya*) version, the second new moon day serves both purposes. By this, the rule "or having attained a year" is also explained. (27.17)
But having reached a full year, he attains the same world as the moon; he attains it. 27.19.
Having attained this for a year, one becomes equal to the moon and attains the same world; one attains the same world. || 27.18 ||
The word "tu" (but) has the sense of immediate succession. He goes to *salokatām*, which means *sālokya* (the state of being in the same world). || 27.19 ||

But he who performs the Cāndrāyaṇa vow without interruption for one year attains the same world as the Moon (candramasaḥ sālokya). The repetition [of the concluding phrase] has been explained. On this point, Manu says: "Restraining his self, one performing the Yati-cāndrāyaṇa should eat eight morsels of sacrificial food when the sun is at its zenith."

“A twice-born man, being composed, should eat four morsels in the morning and four when the sun has set, while performing the *śiśu-cāndrāyaṇa*,” [MDh 11.218–219], and also: “in whatever manner [he obtains] the morsels,” [MDh 11.220]. || 27.18 ||

Now begins the twenty-eighth chapter. Herein, he explains the partition of inheritance, which was indicated by the sūtras: "The owner [is one who acquires property] through inheritance, purchase... (GDh 10.38), and "The heirs to the estate [must pay] the debt" (GDh 12.37).
Now follows the partition of inheritance.
After the father's death, the sons shall divide the inheritance. 28.1.

Now, why is there no mention [of this] before the penance (*prāyaścitta*), as in other cases? On this point, some say: "If sons forcibly compel their father to divide the estate, or if the father—despite the sons' eligibility for ritual duties (*karmādhikāra*)—does not perform the division as it has accrued, then there is no penance for these two; it is for this purpose [that it is mentioned here]. However, this is not to be considered as implying that a lack of penance is intended in the case of no transgression whatsoever. Therefore, the mention is made in this way solely for the sake of emphasizing the gravity of the penance.

Now the Sūtra is explained: "after the father's death" means when he has passed away; and a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one term) should be understood, as in the rule "the father [is mentioned] with the mother. Thus Manu says:
"After both the father and the mother have died, the brothers, having come together..."

“They shall divide the paternal inheritance, for they have no authority while [the parents] are alive. (MDh 9.104) Because the word *pitṛ* (father/paternal) is a relative term, the inclusion of the sons (*putra*)—though already implied—is explicitly stated for the purpose of indicating that the partition applies specifically to males. Accordingly, regarding women, it is heard in the Taittirīya Śruti: “Therefore women are without power and without inheritance” (TaitS 6.5.8.10). Likewise, regarding eunuchs, Vasiṣṭha says: “But those who have entered another stage of life, as well as the impotent, the insane, and the outcastes, are non-sharers” (VaDh 17.52). Although the phrase “after [the father] has died” is already understood from the statement “or when he is living and desires [to divide]” (GDh 28.2), it is explicitly mentioned here to establish that the partition occurs after the performance of the *ekoddiṣṭa* and other funeral rites. *Riktha* refers to the paternal property, such as land acquired through agriculture and so forth; this is a conventional usage.
"They shall divide. Here it is considered: does ownership exist prior to division, or does ownership arise upon division?
On this point, some say that it exists upon division.

That is incorrect, because it would follow that all [sons] must divide [the estate]. If it is argued that by the scriptural statement, the rule applies only to sons, we reply: this is known from the indicative mark (liṅga) in the verse, “They have no power over the two while they live” (MDh 9.104). Why? Because since the absence of division prior [to death] is already established by the very restriction, “after the father and the mother,” the fact that the text merely prohibits ownership (*īśatva*) indicates the continued existence of property-ownership (*svatva*). Otherwise, the prohibition would be meaningless, as there would be no possibility for it to apply. Therefore, division occurs only when property-ownership exists. If it is then argued that, in the case of one who has begotten a son, since the property has been transferred to the son, the taking of another’s property would result, we reply: there is no fault, because the term "son" applies to both [the father and the son] just like the word "birth. Furthermore, due to the prohibition of ownership, the non-gifting of the sons is established as a matter of course. 28.1.

After the father has died, his heirs—his wealth consisting of house, field, slaves, cattle, horses, gold, and so forth—shall be divided by the sons; the sons are the sharers therein. This means that the sons possess ownership over those assets. Because of the statement "after the father," the sons do not have ownership over them while he is alive. And thus says Manu:
"After both the father and the mother [have died], the brothers, having come together, [shall divide the estate]."

“They shall divide the paternal inheritance; for they have no authority while [the parents] are living. (MDh 9.104) Since the word *pitṛ* (father) is a relative term, the inclusion of the word *putra* (son) is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*). Consequently, the collection of statements such as “when dividing after the father’s death, the mother also shall take an equal share” is not the intention of the Teacher (Ācārya). He considers that the sons alone, having taken all the wealth and so forth, should protect the mother properly. And it is heard in scripture: “Therefore women are powerless and non-inheritors. Manu also says:
"The father protects her in childhood, the husband protects her in youth, and the sons protect her in old age; a woman does not deserve independence. [MDh 9.3] || 28.1 ||
When the mother's menstrual flow has ceased, or when she is alive and desires it. || 28.2 ||

H reads "cecchati" [meaning]: "Or, when the mother's passions have subsided, even while she is living, there is partition with the father's permission; and this desire belongs to the father, not to the sons, because of the grammatical coreferentiality with the word 'living'. This partition is to be understood as referring to the sons' eligibility for ritual duties. 28.2.

Alternatively, even while the father is living, the sons may divide the inheritance—provided he so desires; that is to say, with his permission. The time for this is: "when the mother’s menses have ceased. This means when she has ceased to menstruate and her capacity for procreation has ended. (28.2)
Or the eldest may maintain all the others like a father. (28.3)

Or rather, the eldest alone, having taken all the wealth, should maintain and support the other younger brothers; the meaning is that he should not effect a partition. He should act like a father, just as a father maintains [his children]. This rule is to be understood as applying when the eldest brother adopts the conduct of an elder toward the younger ones, provided they lack the capacity to perform their religious duties. 28.3.
The eldest alone, having taken possession of all the wealth and having received it, should maintain the other younger brothers; they too should live with him as sons. 28.3.
But upon partition, there is an increase in merit. 28.4.

The word *tu* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*). Since the increase of merit (*dharma*) occurs through the performance of acts such as giving to guests by each individual, therefore partition alone is more appropriate. This instruction is for the purpose of showing that partition must be made even during childhood, provided there is a difference in intellect. Furthermore, by the mention of "increase," it makes known that there is indeed merit even for the one who provides the shares. (28.4)

The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position. It is not the case that "the eldest alone should maintain [the family]. For it has been stated that partition itself is superior, since through it there is an increase in dharma. As Bṛhaspati said:

"For those living together under a single cooking fire, the worship of the ancestors, the gods, and the twice-born shall be one; for those who are divided, that same worship shall be performed in each individual household. (28.4)
Now, as to how [the estate] is to be divided, he says:
"Now, after the father's death, while he is still living, he states the manner of division: a twentieth part for the eldest, a pair [of animals], a chariot yoked on both sides, and a bull. (28.5)

From the entire paternal estate, the twentieth part belongs to the eldest. A "pair" refers to a well-known pair of cattle. "Animals with two rows of teeth" refers to horses, mules, and donkeys; a chariot yoked with any one of these as available. A "bull" is well known. This preferential share (*uddhāra*) belongs to the eldest when it is possible [to provide it]. (28.5)

From the entire paternal estate, the twentieth part [is the preferential share]; "pair" refers to a pair of female and male animals, such as cows and so forth; "with a team of draught animals" means a chariot yoked with either one of these—horses, mules, or donkeys that have tusks; and a "bull" is a prime male ox. This is the preferential share for the eldest son. (28.5)
One-eyed, lame, humpbacked, or with a withered arm; there are many such [defects] for the middle [finger].

H reads *vaṇeṭā*; "one-eyed" (*kāṇaḥ*) is well known. "Khora" means old. However, if the reading is *khoṭa*, it means one who is deficient in his feet. "Kūṭa" means one who is deficient in horns. "Vaṇṭa" means one whose tail has been cut off. Since they are not specifically qualified, this should be understood as applying to all [animals], such as cows, horses, and so forth, according to what is possible. This is the share for the middle-ranking [son], provided that they are many; the meaning is that there are shares for the others as well. (28.6)

"One-eyed" (kāṇa) means having one eye; that is to say, having a defective limb. "Khora" means old. In the reading "khoṭa," it means having defective feet. "Kūṭa" means hornless. "Vaṇeṭa" means having a defective tail. Among cattle, horses, and so forth, whatever is of such a nature is the share for the middle-ranking person, provided that such a one-eyed animal and the rest are more than one. For there is an injunction regarding the others as well. (28.6)
A ram, an iron vessel, a house, and one draft-ox from among the quadrupeds—each of these belongs to the youngest brother. || 28.7 ||

*Aviḥ* is well known [as a sheep]. Because it is in the singular number, there is one; *dhānyaṃ* refers to grain such as rice and the like; *ayaḥ* is iron. The dual number is used for the sake of allotting grain and iron in accordance with their respective proportions. And thus, one should not take everything. One house equipped with a cart, and one each of the four-footed animals such as cows and so forth, the younger ones—the youngest (*yavīyasaḥ*)—should take separately and individually in accordance with their proportion. This is the special share for the youngest (*kaniṣṭhoddhāraḥ*). (28.7)

*Aviḥ* means woolly; it is used in the singular because it refers to the species. This is established by the rule that "as many sheep as there are, [the eldest takes] one from each of the four-footed animals. Another says: although there is only one sheep for the father, it still belongs to the youngest; however, the rule "one from each of the four-footed animals" applies to a large number of cases. *Dhānya* refers to rice and other grains. *Aya* refers to iron, such as a sickle and so forth. *Dhānyāyasī* means grain and iron. Whatever of these two is in the house—where one resides—is included. *Anaḥ* means a cart yoked with draft animals. From among the four-footed animals, such as cows and others, he should take one desired animal. This is the preferential share (*uddhāra*) for the youngest son. And this applies to the absolute youngest. As for the preferential shares of the others, they belong to the middle son. (28.7)
Everything other than that is concentration (samādhi). 28.8
And everything else is included within concentration. 28.8
Thus, what remains after the preferential shares have been set aside is to be divided equally.

Now, one might object: since equal division applies to everything by default, and since the preferential share has already been mentioned in the rule, it follows that the remainder must also be divided equally; therefore, this sūtra is unnecessary.
This is not a fault, for if the father himself performs the partition, this [sūtra] serves to prohibit the preferential share.

Others, however, say that this [verse] is intended to prohibit the father’s preferential share (*uddhāra*). And this method is to be understood as applying when both the eldest and the youngest are virtuous. (28.8)

All the rest, that which remains after being set aside, they should all take in equal shares. "Equally" is the meaning. The suffix *dhā* is employed as seen in such expressions as *dvidhā* (twofold) and *bahudhā* (manifold). || 28.8 ||
Or the first-born may receive two shares. || 28.9 ||
"Two parts" means two shares; that which belongs to him is "two-share-possessing" (*dvyaṃśī*), meaning that two portions constitute the special allotment (*uddhāra*) for the eldest son. || 28.9 ||
Each one [is the cause] of the others. || 28.10 ||

Each person should take one intended category of property in order of seniority; in that case, the taking of a specific desired object itself constitutes the preferential share (*uddhāra*). This rule should also be understood to apply if all [the brothers] are virtuous. (28.11)
Or, each desirable object of wealth shall be obtained by each person in order, starting from the first. || 28.11 || — || 28.9 ||

H reads "labhate. Each person should take their intended share of wealth in order of seniority; in this case, the taking of the specific intended object itself constitutes the *uddhāra* (preferential share). This rule should also be understood to apply if all [the brothers] are virtuous. || 28.11 ||

In many other [types of] divisions, they should each take one item from among the fields and so forth according to the order of seniority; or, whatever is desired by each, that he may take. Among all [possessions], what is desired belongs to the eldest; in the absence of such, what is desired belongs to the next [in seniority]. This is the preferential share (*uddhāra*) for all. (28.9)
Furthermore, there is a specific rule regarding the sacrificial animals (paśu) in this very context: ten animals [are required]. 28.12 — 28.10.

By the phrase "in the form of wealth," since there would otherwise be the possibility of taking only a single animal for the sake of a desired result, this statement—"ten animals are to be taken"—is intended to establish a restriction on the number. (28.12)
That which has ten parts is a "tenfold" (daśaka). Among cattle such as cows and the like, he receives ten at a time, one after another, but not all at once. || 28.10 ||
In that case as well, there is this exception:
"Not [the meat] of one-hoofed animals or bipeds. (28.13)
Nor [the meat] of animals with uncloven hoofs or those that have two feet. || 28.11 ||

The meaning is that ten items each from among horses and so forth, and women and so forth, are not to be taken [as a preferential share]. If all are devoid of special qualities (*nirguṇa*), then the division must be seen as equal; for no distinction is mentioned here, and because of the repetition in another *Smṛti*, that is the purpose of the former rule. As Vasiṣṭha says: "Now follows the division of inheritance among brothers" (VaDh 17.40). When some are endowed with qualities and others are devoid of them, then the eldest, having taken a tenth part as a preferential share (*uddhāra*), shall divide the remainder equally. As Uśanas says: "A tenth part is the preferential share for the eldest; the intended share belongs to the youngest. In this region, this very division is to be observed, due to established custom. 28.13.

They should not take a tenth part from single-hoofed animals such as horses, nor from bipeds such as female slaves; rather, they should take only one share each as previously stated. In the reading "dvipādānām" (of bipeds), the word *pada* has the same meaning as the word *pāda*. Thus, the division with the preferential share (*uddhāra*) for those born of the same mother has been described. (28.11)
The partition for those of the same caste who have a single mother has been stated. Now, he speaks in order to describe the case of those who, although of the same caste, have multiple mothers;
thus he says: "Now he speaks of those with multiple mothers:
'The bull is the additional share for the eldest. (28.14) — [End of] 28.12.
For the eldest son of the youngest [wife], the *ṛṣabha* (an extra share) is the preferential portion (*uddhāra*); the remainder is to be divided equally. 28.14.

Because of the statement "of the son of the eldest" (*jyaiṣṭhineyasya*) in the subsequent sūtra, this [term] refers to the eldest son born of the youngest wife. If he is the son of the youngest wife, then his special share (*uddhāra*) is a bull; the rest is equal. 28.12.
The Ṛṣabha-ṣoḍaśa [is the chant] of the son of the eldest wife. 28.15 — 28.13.
One born of the eldest wife is called a *jyaiṣṭhineya*. His special share (*uddhāra*) consists of fifteen cows and one bull; the remainder is to be divided equally. 28.15.

The term "of the eldest" continues [to apply]. And the son who belongs to the eldest [wife] is the one who belongs to the eldest [husband]; his special share (*uddhāra*) consists of fifteen cows and one bull. The remainder is divided equally. 28.13.

Now, the rule that "the bull is the additional share for the eldest" is an exception [to the general rule]. The younger brothers shall receive equal shares with the son of the appointed daughter (*aiṣṭineya*). (28.16) — || 28.14 ||

H reads "yavīyasām," [explaining that] this division remains equal: between the eldest son born of the youngest wife by means of the *ajyaiṣṭhineya* rite and the younger son, the son of the eldest wife; for one, seniority is based on the mother, while for the other, it is based on birth. This case also should be understood as referring to those who possess virtuous qualities. (28.16)

The word *jyeṣṭhasya* is supplied [from the previous rule]. And because it stands in grammatical apposition with *ajyaiṣṭhineyena*, it becomes a word ending in the third case. By means of the *ajyaiṣṭhineya*—that is, by the eldest son born of a junior wife—the division of the younger *jyaiṣṭhineya* brothers shall be equal. For one possesses seniority by birth, while for the others it is by virtue of their mother. (28.14)
Or, according to each mother, there shall be a specific share for those belonging to her own group. 28.17–28.15.
H reads "svasvavarge.

However, when there are many wives of the same caste who have offspring by different husbands, then, because a division based on the sons would be difficult to carry out, the inheritance is divided according to the mothers alone. Furthermore, the specific share for each within their own respective group should be observed; that has been stated in the passage beginning with, "The eldest receives one-twentieth," [GDh 24.5]. 28.17.

The specific allotment of shares that was stated, beginning with "one-twentieth for the eldest," should be applied according to each mother within their respective groups. This is what is meant: when the wealth is divided among as many mothers as have sons, one should combine the shares belonging to however many sons each mother has; then, within each such group, the specific allotment—beginning with "one-twentieth for the eldest"—is to be assigned to whichever son is the eldest in that group. Thus, the division for those who have sons has been explained. (28.15)
This applies only to those who have sons;
however, for one who has no son, it is said:
"A man without offspring, having sacrificed to Agni and Prajāpati, may designate a daughter as his son (putrikā) for our sake."
Having thus conversed. 28.18 — 28.16.
The father, but not even the mother, should relinquish [him]—that is, hand him over—and not merely give him away, because by the sacred law he is [already] a son.

Because it has been stated: "The mantras for taking the hand are established only in the case of maiden daughters" (MDh 8.226). Regarding the *putrikā*, that is, the daughter: "one who is childless," meaning one who has no son. It should be understood that if he has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), he should perform the *Āgneyī* and *Prājāpatyā* sacrifices according to the procedure for the *sthālīpāka* and offer two oblations. Then, at the time of the gift, having entered into an agreement with the groom, saying, "Whatever offspring shall be born of her shall be for our sake," the son born of her when she has thus been bestowed becomes the son of the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*), and not of the progenitor—this is the intended meaning. || 28.18 ||

The father should release her—that is, he should give her away. This is an indication by means of a future designation, as in the expression "he cuts the sacrificial post" (*yūpaṃ chinatti*). Being childless—meaning having no son—he should sacrifice to Agni and Prajāpati; immediately after the *ājyabhāga* offerings, having offered clarified butter into the *aupāsana* fire with the formulas "Svāhā to Agni! and "Svāhā to Prajāpati!", and having made an agreement that "the offspring shall be for our sake," he should cause an agreement to be made with the one to whom he gives her. Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha has shown the procedure: "I shall give to you an unbrothered maiden, adorned."

"In her a son shall be born; may he be my son"—thus given away, she is a *putrikā* (appointed daughter). A son born of her belongs only to the maternal grandfather, not to the biological progenitor. Therefore, Manu says:
"The son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāsuta*) should first offer the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) to his mother."

"The second [son] belongs to her father, but the third belongs to her father's father. [MDh 9.140] Thus, all such offspring—even this appointed daughter (*putrikā*)—is a substitute for a son of the [maternal] father. The suffix *kan* is applied here in the sense of "likeness" (*iva*) when forming a name, according to Pāṇini 5.3.96. She alone is the heir to the inheritance. And so says Manu:
"But if, after an appointed daughter has been designated, a son is subsequently born..."

"In that case, there shall be an equal division; for a woman has no right of primogeniture" (MDh 9.134). Her lineage (*gotra*) is also that of her father alone. As for her husband, she is his companion in religious duties and the source of the fruit of sexual pleasure. However, for the sake of obtaining a son, another marriage must be performed for the purpose of continuing one's own family line; otherwise, there is fault. (28.16)
According to some, she is called "Putrikā" merely by virtue of the [father's] intention. 28.19. — 28.17.

But when it is impossible to carry out the previous injunction—namely, that one makes the formal resolution (*saṃkalpa*) before the gift by means of choosing [the bride] and so forth, thinking, "Whatever offspring shall be born of her, let that be mine"—some maintain that sonship is established by this very act alone. This alternative should be understood as dependent upon the possibility [of the circumstances]. (28.19)

Some maintain that at the time of giving her away, if the father has the intention, "This girl of mine shall be a *putrikā*," she becomes a *putrikā* by that alone, without depending on the fire-oblation (*homa*), the formal agreement (*saṃvādana*), or other such rites. (28.17)
And therefore:
"One should not marry a woman who has no brother, because of the doubt regarding her [legitimacy]. (28.20) — [End of] 28.18.

Out of apprehension regarding that, one should not take all the daughters of anyone who is childless. Why? Because, although it should have been said "her" (*tām*), the text begins with the phrase "one who has no brother" (*abhrātṛkām*). (29.20)
This is due to doubt regarding him, doubt regarding his intention, or doubt regarding her being an appointed daughter (*putrikā*). Manu also said:
"A wise man should not marry a girl whose brother does not exist or whose father is not known, for fear that she might be an appointed daughter according to the law" (MDh 3.11). 28.18.
Those who are connected by the offering of funeral cakes, by lineage, or by ancestral sages shall divide the inheritance.
Those related by funeral offerings, lineage, or ancestral sages, or a wife, shall inherit the estate of one who dies without offspring.

Those connected by the *piṇḍa* (ancestral offerings) are the *sapiṇḍas*; in their absence, those connected by the *gotra* (lineage) are the *sagotras*; in their absence, those connected by the *ṛṣis* (ancestral sages) are the *samānārṣeyas*. Thus, in the absence of one who is proximate, a more distant relative shall be the recipient of that property. || 28.21 ||

He who has no offspring, not even in the form of a daughter, is childless (*anapatya*). His inheritance shall be divided among those related by the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and so forth, or by the wife. Those related by the *piṇḍa* are the *sapiṇḍas*; those related by lineage (*gotra*) are the *sagotras*, as in the case of "Hārīta" for one belonging to the Hārīta clan. Those related by a sage (*ṛṣi*) are those with common *pravara*s, such as Harita, Kutsa, Piśaṅga, Śaṅkha, Darbha, and Haimagava, who are mutually related in this way, and so too elsewhere. Among them, the *sapiṇḍas* and others shall take the property according to the order of proximity. Thus says Āpastamba: "In the absence of a son, whoever is the nearest *sapiṇḍa*" [ĀpDh 2.14.2]. For example: father, mother, uterine brothers, their sons, half-brothers, their sons, paternal uncles, and so forth. In the absence of *sapiṇḍas*, the *sagotras* take; in their absence, those with common *pravara*s. The wife, however, is included together with all these, beginning with the *sagotra*s. When the *sapiṇḍas* and others take the estate, the wife shall also receive one share along with them. Thus it is said:

"When dividing after the father's death, the mother shall also receive an equal share. [YDh 2.123] For this very reason, the woman is mentioned separately from the *sapiṇḍas* and others, who are grouped together by the common term. However, according to the view of the Teacher (Ācārya), the wife does not receive a share of the inheritance. Manu also says: "Women are eternally devoid of power and incapable of inheriting; such is the settled rule. [MDh 9.18] Regarding the absence of *sapiṇḍas* and others, Bṛhaspati states:
"Except in the case of a Brāhmaṇa, however, the King devoted to dharma [shall take the property]."
He shall provide that as the livelihood for the women; this is declared to be the rule for inheritance.
For the sake of food, one prastha of rice with fuel should be given in the afternoon;
and one garment purchased for three paṇas should be given every three months.
"Only this much is enjoined by the rule for virtuous women as the means of their maintenance.

Thus, Manu and Bṛhaspati have stated that there is an absolute absence of a wife's inheritance. However, Yājñavalkya has stated that wife's inheritance in the passage beginning with "The wife and the daughters... (YDh 2.135). Regarding this, Vyāsa says:
"A share of two thousand paṇas of wealth should be given to the wife."

"And whatever wealth was given by the husband, she shall receive that according to her desire. However, the Teacher has stated that the *sapiṇḍas* and others should take equal shares. In that case, the primary rule (*mukhya-kalpa*) is that the *sapiṇḍas* and others, having taken all the wealth, should protect the women for as long as they live. In the absence of that possibility, they should set aside sufficient wealth, fields, and so forth, calculated as a share for food and clothing, and take the remainder. And likewise, Bṛhaspati, after prohibiting the wife's inheritance, stated at the end: "Of clothing, of food, and likewise of silver..."
Having set aside these three, he should assign what remains to the heirs.
"Previously, she calculated the expenses for smoke-offering materials, her companions, as well as food and clothing;
thus, she died while [still] possessing wealth."
And [the inheritance goes to] the wife of one who has no offspring. 28.22.

This [rule] also applies in the absence of a son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*). Why? Because of the repeated mention of "one without offspring" (*anapatya*) in the section concerning those without offspring, namely: "An appointed daughter who is without offspring... [GDh 28.18]. When they—[the sons of the appointed daughter]—should divide the estate upon the cessation of their connection to the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and so forth, then the woman also shall receive a share. By virtue of the word "and" (*ca*), the teacher (*ācārya*) and the pupil (*śiṣya*) [are included], as is evident from the context, in the event of the total absence [of other heirs]. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "In the absence of those, the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) and the teacher (*ācārya*). (28.22)
Or he should seek to obtain seeds. 28.23 — 28.20.
Or rather—the meaning is that one should desire seed from a sapinda relative or others, that is, one should procreate offspring; this may be by choice or by obligation.

Alternatively, it may be that a woman should seek seed from her sapinda relatives and others; the meaning is that she should produce offspring. In this case, however, the sapindas and others shall not take the property, but shall preserve it for the sake of the offspring. (28.20)
In this view, there is a distinction:
that which is born of another [man] in Devaravatī is without a share. (28.24) — (28.21)
When a husband is present, offspring produced by another is not entitled to a share, because it is born of lust; this is an exception to the rule concerning the *kṣetraja* son.

If, while the husband's brother is present, she should seek offspring from another, then the child born of her is "without a share," meaning devoid of a portion; he has no right to the inheritance. But if the husband's brother is absent, even a child born from another is indeed "with a share. (28.21)
The property of a woman belongs to her daughters who are unmarried and not established in life. 28.25. — 28.22.

Woman’s property (*strīdhana*) is of six kinds, as Manu has stated: "What is received before the fire, what is received at the wedding procession, what is given as a token of affection, and what is inherited from the mother, the brother, or the father—this is declared to be the sixfold woman’s property" (MDh 9.194). Furthermore, whatever else she has acquired through her own labor belongs to her daughters alone when she has died, provided they are unmarried and without offspring.

Others say: "of sons who are unsettled," meaning those who have not yet been married; others say: "of those who are destitute. Because of the word "and" (*ca*), this also includes the husband. Here, the sequence should be understood as follows: in the absence of unmarried daughters, the sons who are destitute shall take [the property]; in their absence, those who are unmarried; in their absence, childless women; and in the absence of all these, the husband. (28.25)
That which is given by a father, mother, son, or brother, and that which is received in the presence of the sacred fire;

"And the *ādhivedanika* (gift for supersession) and so forth are declared to be woman’s property (*strīdhana*)," says Yājñavalkya (YDh 2.143). When that woman has died, that woman’s property belongs to her unmarried daughters. If all are married, it belongs to those who are unsettled (*apratiṣṭhitā*). Among the married, some are settled and some are unsettled; when there is a combination of both married and unmarried daughters, the unmarried one takes it. When there is a combination of both settled and unsettled daughters, the unsettled one takes it. When it is property such as that obtained from offspring (*prasūta*), then it belongs to all of them. This is the rule for the woman’s property acquired from the father’s family after the mother's death while she was still living. And likewise Manu:

"That which may be the mother's separate property (yautaka) is indeed the portion for the unmarried daughter. And Vasiṣṭha says: "The women shall divide the mother's dowry (pāriṇeya). As for what was stated by Śākala and Khāṇḍika—namely, "All uterine brothers and the daughters, both married and unmarried, are entitled to an equal share of the mother's property"—that refers to [property] obtained from the husband's family in the case of daughters who have been given away in marriage. Regarding that matter concerning married daughters, the extensive rule of Manu applies: "But when the mother has passed away, all the uterine brothers [shall divide it] equally."
The mother's property shall be divided among the uterine sisters as well.

"But whatever daughters they may have, to them also something should be given from the maternal grandmother's wealth, according to their merit and with affection. (MDh 9.192–193). On that same point, regarding small amounts of wealth, there is the teaching of Bṛhaspati:
"That woman’s property belongs to her offspring; in her absence, it belongs to her daughters."
"If she is unmarried but has been betrothed, she shall receive her share together with her mother."
The sister’s dowry belongs to the uterine brothers after the mother [has passed away]. 28.26. — || 28.23 ||

The property obtained on account of giving away a sister in the *ārṣa* and *āsura* forms of marriage belongs to the uterine brothers after the mother; that is to say, when she has died. And thus it is stated that, in the absence of the father, the mother alone is intended as its owner. (28.2)

Regarding the property taken by the father on account of giving away his daughter in the *āsura* or *ārṣa* forms of marriage: when he has died, that belongs to her uterine brothers alone. Furthermore, while the mother is still living after his death, it belongs to her alone, and not to the deceased father as his own property. In this regard, those brothers who are born of different mothers, as well as the stepmother, shall all not receive a share. As for the ornaments, fields, and so forth given to the sister or others by the family of the husband and so on at the time of marriage, those belong to her alone. And regarding her when she has died childless, Yājñavalkya has stated:
Likewise, the property given by a kinsman, the nuptial fee,
and even the after-acquired property shall be taken by the relatives when she has died childless.
"By whomsoever that which was given, by him shall it be obtained"; but when there is offspring, that very offspring shall take it. || 28.23 ||
And some [hold that it occurs] previously. 28.27–28.24.

Some maintain that even before the mother’s death, the sister’s dowry belongs to the uterine brothers. This alternative should be understood as depending on her conduct. Alternatively, regarding what was stated previously—that "the woman’s property belongs to the daughters" (GDh 28.25)—some maintain that this occurs only after the mother's death and not while she is living. The scope of the subject has been explained. 28.27.
Some maintain that even before the mother's death, the sister’s dowry belongs to the uterine brothers; the alternative depends on her conduct.
The division of inheritance among those who have not lived together belongs to the eldest of the deceased. 28.28 — 28.25.

When brothers who are ununited and separated carry on their affairs individually, if one among them dies childless, [the question arises: from where [does his share come]? Because the context concerns those who are childless, that share belongs only to his own respective eldest brother and not to all; he is equal to a father. As for those born of two mothers—whether of the same caste or of different castes—and those whose mothers are not distinct, the share belongs only to the eldest of each respective group. 28.28.

"Those who are not reunited" refers to brothers who have been divided. "Partition" (*vibhāga*) means that which is to be partitioned. "The partition of those not reunited" (*asaṃsṛṣṭivibhāga*) is the partition belonging to those who were not reunited. The term "of the deceased" (*pretānām*) is an adjective qualifying even those "not reunited" who have become subordinate [to the compound]. The phrase "and of one who is childless" (*anapatyasya ca*) also applies here. The teacher’s position is as follows: the partition—that is, the property and so forth to be divided—belonging to brothers who were not reunited, who had been divided, who are deceased, and who are childless, goes to the eldest brother alone; it does not belong to the other brothers, nor to the wife, nor to the parents. And thus Śaṅkha, Likhita, and Paiṭhīnasi state: "The wealth of one who has died without a son goes to his brothers; in their absence, the mother and father shall take it, or the eldest wife; or [it goes to] a fellow-student (*sagotra*) or a celibate student (*brahmacārin*). But Manu says:
"The father shall take the inheritance of one who has no son, as shall the brothers. (Manu Dharma Śāstra 9.185). And Devala says:
"Then the uterine brothers, the paternal kinsmen, the daughter, or even the father, if he be living, shall divide the estate of one who has no son."
When a *saṃsṛṣṭin* has died, the *saṃsṛṣṭin* is the heir to the inheritance. (28.29) — (28.26)

But he who, even though partitioned, is reunited again by reason of necessity, becomes a sharer in that portion. The repetition of the word "again" (punaḥ) is for the sake of including uterine brothers; for others, it remains as previously established. || 28.29 ||
One who has reunited wealth with his brothers and others is a *saṃsṛṣṭin*, one who possesses common property; he is either unpartitioned or one who, having been partitioned, has reunited.
Furthermore, he who, having been partitioned, should live again in one place with his father, brother, or paternal uncle out of affection, is called *saṃsṛṣṭa* (reunited).

This is because of the view expressed in the *Bārhaspatya*: "The term 'one who has no offspring' (*anapatya*) carries over. When one who was reunited (*saṃsṛṣṭin*) dies without offspring, his heir shall take that property. Even there, when he is reunited with both uterine and non-uterine brothers, the uterine brother shall take it—based on the observation of Yājñavalkya: 'But for a uterine brother, [the share goes to] a uterine brother' (YDh 2.138). Thus, when a divided brother dies without offspring, his wealth belongs to the eldest; if there is no eldest, it belongs to the other brothers. But when he dies undivided, his share belongs to all the brothers. (28.26)
That which is born of a divided estate belongs exclusively to the father. 28.30 — 28.27.

By the rule, “When the mother’s menses have ceased,” [GDh 28.2], if a son is subsequently born after the sons have already divided the inheritance and performed the marriage rites, he shall receive only the paternal share. Thus, in the case of partition during the father’s lifetime, the father’s entitlement to a share is established by implication; even then, two shares for the father are to be understood from another Smṛti text stating, “Two shares for the father.

However, a son born after partition, whether from that [same] wife or another wife, shall receive only the paternal estate. He shall share whatever was acquired by the father after partition, or whatever was taken at the time of partition, whether it be small or large. On this point, Bṛhaspati says:
"Whatever was acquired by the father himself after he had been divided from his sons..."

"Regarding all that, the ancestors who were born before [the partition] are traditionally held to have no authority. However, when the father possesses nothing at all, then the rule of Viṣṇu applies: "Those separated from their father shall give a share to one born after the partition. Yājñavalkya also says: "A son born after the partition from a wife of the same caste is entitled to a share;
or his share may be determined from what is visible, after deducting income and expenses. On this point, Manu and Nārada state:
"But one born after the partition shall take the paternal wealth alone;
or, those who were reunited with him shall divide it together with them. (MDh 9.216) || 28.27 ||
A physician should not, at his own will, give what he has earned himself to those who are unlearned. (28.31) — (28.28)

H reads "arjitam": however, that property of the father which has been acquired by oneself without depleting [the paternal estate], whether through medical practice or by means of receiving gifts and so forth—that one may, at will, according to one's desire, not give to the others. As Manu says:
"That which a son acquires by his own labor without depleting the father’s property..."
That which is obtained through one's own effort, he ought not to refuse to give if he so desires.
"But whatever constitutes the wealth of knowledge belongs to that person alone as his own wealth," and so forth. [MDh 9.206, 208] || 28.31 ||

One who has studied knowledge is called a "learned man" (*vaidya*). He may, at his pleasure, not give what he has earned by himself to brothers who are devoid of learning; for there is no fault in not giving, whereas in giving, there is spiritual merit. || 28.28 ||
Those who are unlearned shall divide [the estate] equally. 28.32–28.29.

However, whatever the fools might earn through agriculture and other such means, they should divide that equally. Thus it is said: "But if all those who are unlearned should acquire wealth through their own efforts, the division there shall be equal; for it is the settled rule that such wealth is not ancestral. (MDh 9.205). Although this is already established by the sense of the matter, it is stated here for the sake of a restrictive rule. Consequently, even if the learned man does not give an unequal share, if the wealth was acquired by the unlearned, the learned man must also give an equal share. (28.32)

But when all the brothers are unlearned, they should divide equally whatever they acquire through agriculture and other such means. Even that which is acquired by a physician through agriculture and the like—provided it was not obtained through his learning and does not conflict with the paternal estate—is subject to equal division. In this regard, both of these two sūtras refer specifically to the case of brothers. However, while the father is alive, whatever is acquired by one who is undivided—whether learned or unlearned—belongs to the father alone.
"The wife, the son, and the slave—these three are declared to be without property."
"What they acquire belongs to him to whom they belong"—thus says Manu (MDh 8.416). 28.29.
Because of the statement, "Sons shall divide the inheritance" (GDh 28.1), one might think that this traditional rule applies only to *aurasa* (legitimate) sons; therefore, he says:
since the teacher stated that "sons shall divide the inheritance," he adds [this clarification] so that there may be no misconception that only *aurasa* sons are meant by "sons.
[The term "sons"] refers to the *aurasa*, *kṣetraja*, *dattaka*, *kṛtrima*, *gūḍhotpanna*, and *apaviddha* [sons].
The heirs to the inheritance. || 28.33 || — || 28.30 ||
The *aurasa* (legitimate son) is one who is procreated by oneself upon one’s own wife. Thus Manu says:

"That son whom one procreates oneself in one’s own consecrated field (*kṣetra*), one should know as the *aurasa*, the first-enumerated son" (MDh 9.166). The *kṣetraja* (son born of the wife) is one who is procreated through the rite of *niyoga*. As Manu says:

"He who is born on the bed of one who has died, is impotent, or is diseased—being begotten according to his own law upon a wife duly appointed—is known as the *kṣetraja* son. [MDh 9.167] The *datta* (given) son is one obtained from another through formal acceptance; as Manu says:
"The mother or the father may give him away with water in times of distress..."

"One who is similar [in status] and endowed with affection is to be known as an adopted son (dattrima). [MDh 9.168] An adopted son (*kṛtrima*) is one who is made [one's own] by saying, "You are my son. As Manu says: "But he whom one should make similar, free from defects and endowed with the qualities of a son, he is to be known as an adopted son (*kṛtrima*). [MDh 9.169] A son born in secret (*gūḍhotpanna*) is one produced in concealment; since the progenitor is not known, he belongs to the caste of the mother due to the lack of knowledge regarding the progenitor. The same applies to the son born of a pregnant bride (*sahoḍha*) and the son of an unmarried girl (*kānīna*).

"He who is born in a house but whose father is not known—he is one born secretly in the house; he belongs to him from whose wife he was born" (MDh 9.170). An *apaviddha* is one who, having been abandoned by another, is taken up through recognition, as it is said:
"One who has been cast off by both parents, or by either of them..."
"The son whom one may adopt is called an *apaviddha* (cast-off). [MDh 9.171]. These are the heirs to the inheritance. 28.33.
The *aurasa* (legitimate son) is one born of a lawful wife. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states:
"A son begotten through *niyoga* by a man without a son upon the field of another..."

"By law, he is the heir and the offerer of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) for both. [YDh 2.127] This [status] belongs only to the progenitor and not to the biological father (*bījin*). Regarding the subject of an adopted son (*datta*), Vasiṣṭha states: "One should neither give nor receive an eldest son; for he is for the sake of the lineage of the ancestors. A woman should neither give nor receive a son without the permission of her husband. One intending to adopt a son, having summoned his kinsmen and announced it to the king, and having offered oblations with the *vyāhṛti* mantras in the middle of the house, should adopt one who is not far removed and is closely related by kinship. [VaDh 15.3–6] That is the adopted son (*datta*). Regarding the subject of a made son (*kṛtrima*), Manu says:
But he whom one may make similar to oneself, free from [the father's] faults and endowed with the virtues of a son, is to be known as the *kṛtrima* (adopted) son.
He who is born in a man's house, yet it is not known whose he is—
He who is born secretly in the house shall belong to him whose wife gave birth to him.

"He whom one may adopt as a son after he has been abandoned by both his parents or by either of them is known as the *apaviddha* (cast-off). Thus [it is said in MDh 9.169–171]. These six sons are heirs to the estate.

The son of an unmarried girl, the son received with a pregnant bride, the son of a remarried woman, the son of an appointed daughter, the self-given son, and the purchased son are entitled to share the family lineage. 28.34. — 28.31.
The *kānīna* is one born of an unmarried girl (*kanyā*); he belongs to him who marries her. Thus it is said:
"But the son whom an unmarried girl may secretly bear in her father’s house, one should call him by the name *kānīna*, for he originates from the maiden and belongs to the husband" (MDh 9.172).
The *sahoḍha* is born when the woman is married while she is pregnant. As Manu says:

"If a woman who is already pregnant—whether her condition be known or unknown—is married, the child in her womb belongs to the one who marries her; he is called *sahoḍha* in this world" (MDh 9.173). The *paunarbhava* is the son of an unchaste woman; he belongs to him who, having remarried her, procreates a son upon her. As Manu says: [MDh 9.174].
She who, having been abandoned by her husband or even becoming a widow by her own will,
bears a son after marrying again, is called *paunarbhava*.

"If she be one whose virginity is intact, or even one who has returned after having gone away, she deserves to undergo the sacramental rite again with a husband taken from a second marriage. [MDh 9.175–76] The son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*) has been mentioned previously. The "self-given" (*svayamdatta*) is one who offers himself of his own accord. As it is said: "One who is deprived of mother and father, or one who has been abandoned without cause..."
"He whom one should touch as one's own is known as *svayaṃdatta* (self-given). [MDh 9.177] "Purchased" means acquired through wealth. As Manu said:
"He whom one might purchase from his mother and father for the sake of offspring..."

"That adopted son (krītaka) of his may be either similar or dissimilar [to him]. [MDh 9.174] The meaning is that these [other sons] share the lineage (*gotra*) and perform the offering of water and other rites for the sake of being sons. And thus, these do not share in the inheritance; however, the preceding ones [the legitimate sons] both share in the inheritance and share in the lineage. Why is this so? Because they are mentioned together with the legitimate son (*aurasa*), and because of another Smṛti text: "The legitimate son, the son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*), the given son (*datta*), and the made son (*kṛtrima*)."

"The *gūḍhotpanna* (secretly born), the *apaviddha* (cast off), and the six heirs and kinsmen. [MDh 9.159] "Kinsmen" (*bāndhavāḥ*) means those who share the lineage (*gotra*). Since the right to share the lineage follows from their status as sons, that specific mention here is for the purpose of prohibiting their right to inherit property. Furthermore, because their right to inherit is prohibited when a legitimate son (*aurasa*) and the others exist, and since these others are entitled to mere food and clothing due to their status as sons, it is as he said:
"But it is right for the wise man to give to all of them according to his ability."

"For one who has fallen [from caste], failing to provide food and clothing to the utmost degree, would indeed incur sin. (MDh 9.202) However, in the absence of such [provision], he certainly becomes an heir to the estate, because he serves as a substitute for a son. As it is said:
"These eleven sons, beginning with the *kṣetraja*, have been declared as above..."

"The wise call these substitutes for a son [means of preventing] the omission of ritual duties" (MDh 9.180). Furthermore, a substitute yields the complete result when the primary substance is absent, just as *pūtīka* plants do in the absence of *soma*. The mention of the daughter’s son here is for the purpose of establishing his right to the family lineage (*gotra*). However, his right to the inheritance (*riktha*) certainly remains even when a legitimate son (*aurasa*) exists. As Manu says: "But if, after a daughter has been appointed, a son is subsequently born..."

"In that case, there shall be an equal division; for there is no primogeniture for a woman. (MDh 9.134) The son of a Śūdra wife is not mentioned here either because he is not a legitimate son of the body (*aurasa*) or because he does not share in the inheritance. Thus it is said:
"The son of a Śūdra wife of Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya castes does not share in the inheritance;
whatever his father may give him, that alone shall be his wealth. (MDh 9.155) || 28.34 ||

"A daughter who bears a son here in her father's house—one born from a maiden—should be called by the name *kānīna* (maiden-born), not [the son] of the husband. Thus [says Manu, MDh 9.172]. On this point, Vasiṣṭha says:

"He whose unmarried daughter should obtain a son by [marrying] one of equal status, through that grandson the maternal grandfather shall offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) and inherit the wealth. [VaDh 17.23] Yājñavalkya says:

"The *kānīna* is born of an unmarried girl; he is the son of the maternal grandfather. [YDh 2.129] In this regard, if she dies while still unmarried, the son or grandson belongs to the maternal grandfather; if she is married, he belongs to the husband. On this point, Manu says:
If a woman who is pregnant is married, whether her condition be known or unknown, the child belongs to the one who marries her;
such a son is called *sahoḍha* (one taken with the bride).

"One who, having been abandoned by her husband or being a widow, produces offspring by her own will after becoming a *punarbhū* (a remarried woman), is called *paunarbhava*. The son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*) has already been mentioned previously. Manu says:
"One who is deprived of both mother and father, or has been abandoned without cause..."
He to whom one transfers oneself is known as a *svayaṃdatta* (self-given) son.

"He who, for the sake of offspring, purchases [a son] from his mother and father—that is his *krītaka* (bought) son, whether he be similar or dissimilar [in caste]. [MDh 9.177, 174] These [sons], however, are "sharers of the lineage" (*gotrabhāj*); they share only the lineage, not the inheritance. The former [sons], on the other hand, are "sharers of the inheritance" (*rikthabhāj*) as well as "sharers of the lineage," because they are mentioned together with the *aurasa* (legitimate) son. And all these [sons] belong to the same caste, according to the statement of Yājñavalkya: "This rule has been declared by me regarding sons of the same caste. [YDh 2.133] || 28.31 ||
In the absence of a legitimate son and others, [the estate] belongs to those entitled to a fourth share.
Those entitled to a fourth part [receive it] in the absence of a legitimate son (*aurasa*) and the others.

In the absence of the six [sons] beginning with the legitimate son of the body (*aurasa*), the sons born of an unmarried girl (*kānīna*) and the others are entitled to a fourth share, or they may take the entire inheritance; this is indicated by the word "or" (*vā*). Thus says Śaṅkha: "The property acquired goes to the eldest; in his absence, to the *kṣetraja* and the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*); in their absence as well, to the other three; and in their absence, to the six [remaining categories]. Others, however, maintain that the phrase "in the absence of the legitimate son of the body and the rest" refers to the meaning of the subsequent sūtra. Consequently, the *kānīna* and the others are entitled to a fourth part, or they are merely entitled to subsistence. (28.35)

Alternatively, these—the son of an unmarried girl (*kānīna*) and the others—are neither excluded from inheritance nor are they mere non-heirs; rather, they are entitled to a fourth share. They shall take a fourth part of the father’s estate in the absence of the six previously mentioned sons, beginning with the legitimate son (*aurasa*). However, if those [six] exist, they themselves shall take the inheritance. As for the property remaining beyond the fourth share, the *sapiṇḍas* shall take it. Regarding the fact that here the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā-putra*) is stated to be entitled to a fourth share even in the absence of the *aurasa* and other sons, this refers to the case of an inferior son of an appointed daughter. The meaning is that this applies to the son of one who makes a daughter an appointed daughter through a mere agreement with a wife of a lower caste. On this point, Manu says:

"But if a son is born after a daughter has been appointed as an heir (putrikā), the division of the property shall be equal; for there is no right of primogeniture for a woman. [MDh 9.134] And one should give a sixth share of the paternal wealth to the *kṣetraja* son.
The legitimate son, when dividing the paternal inheritance, shall receive exactly one-fifth.
"The two sons, the *aurasa* (body-born) and the *kṣetraja* (field-born), are entitled to shares of the father's inheritance;

but ten others, in their respective order, are entitled to shares of the family name and the inheritance" (MDh 9.164–165). Regarding this, after mentioning the *dattaputra* (given son), Vasiṣṭha states: "If a *aurasa* son is born after one has been adopted, the latter shall be entitled to a fourth share. On this point, Kātyāyana says:
"But when a *aurasa* son is born, the other sons are entitled to a third share."
"But those of the same caste and those of a different caste shall share in food and clothing.
On this point, Bṛhaspati says:
"The legitimate son alone is declared to be the sole owner of the paternal wealth."
The son of an appointed daughter (putrikā-putra) is equal to him; others are recorded as being entitled to maintenance.

"But other sons, such as the *kṣetraja* and the rest, are entitled to five, six, seven, or eight shares. Hārīta says: "When about to divide the estate, one should give twenty-one parts to the *kānīna*, twenty to the *paunarbhava*, nineteen to the *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa*, eighteen to the *kṣetraja*, seventeen to the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*), and the remainder to the legitimate son (*aurasa*). Yājñavalkya, having enumerated the twelve types of sons, states:
"Among these, each subsequent one offers the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) and inherits the share in the absence of each preceding one. Manu also says: [The text continues with the citation from Manu.]
"In the absence of each superior [heir], the next junior one is entitled to the inheritance. [Manu Dharmaśāstra 9.184]. Nārada also says:
"These [heirs] succeed to the father's wealth in order when he has died."

"In the absence of each preceding one, the succeeding one shall obtain that [inheritance]. Vasiṣṭha also states: "If among these there is no heir for the ancestors, these [others] shall take his inheritance" (VaDh 17.39). Here, Devala, having enumerated the sons in order—the legitimate son (aurasa), the son of an appointed daughter (putrikāputra), the son begotten on the wife (kṣetraja), the maiden-born son (kānīna), the secretly born son (guḍhotpanna), the cast-off son (apaviddha), the son received with a bride (sahoḍha), the son of a remarried woman (paunarbhava), the adopted son (datta), the son who comes of his own accord (svayamupāgata), the made son (kṛtaka), and the bought son (krīta)—says:
"These twelve sons have been declared for the sake of continuity."
Those born of oneself, those born of others, and likewise those obtained by chance.
Of these, six are kinsmen and heirs, as were previously mentioned in relation to the father alone;
furthermore, among sons, the distinction is determined by their specific order of precedence.
All these sons of one who has no legitimate son (aurasa) are declared to be heirs;
however, when a legitimate son is subsequently born, they no longer possess the status of primogeniture.
"Those sons of theirs who are of the same caste (savarṇa) shall share a third part;
those of lower caste shall subsist [upon the estate], provided with food and clothing.

Regarding the term *bandhudāyādāḥ*, these [sons] may inherit the property of their paternal kinsmen (*bandhu*), that is, their *sapiṇḍas* as well, and not only that of the father; whereas others [the sons of lower caste] inherit from the father alone. This is precisely the meaning of the term *bandhudāyāda* in other Smṛtis as well. Thus it is:

The legitimate son (aurasa), the son of an appointed daughter (putrikā), the sons of the seed-owner and the field-owner (bījikṣetriṇau), the son of an appointed daughter (putrikāsuta), the son of a remarried woman (paunarbhava), the maiden-born son (kānīna), the son received with a wife (sahoḍha), and the son born in secret (gūḍhasambhava).
The son given, the son bought, the son self-given, the adopted son, the son cast off,
and the son begotten on a woman by one other than her husband— these are the fifteen known as sons.

"In this very sequence, in the absence of each preceding one, each subsequent person is the giver of the funeral cake (piṇḍa) and the taker of the share; thus is established the order according to their qualities."
The division of property for sons born of wives of the same caste has been stated. Now he states the specific rule regarding sons born of wives of different castes.

The division for sons of the same caste has been declared; now he states the distinction concerning sons of different castes born of marriages in the prescribed order. "The son of a Brāhmaṇa by a Kṣatriya wife, if he is the eldest and endowed with good qualities, shall receive an equal share. (28.36) — [End of] 28.33.
The son of a Brāhmaṇa born of a Kṣatriya woman, if he is the eldest and endowed with good qualities, shares an equal portion with the younger son of the Brāhmaṇa wife.

If a son born of a Brāhmaṇa father and a Kṣatriya mother is endowed with good qualities and is the eldest, then he shares equally [in the inheritance] with the younger son of the Brāhmaṇa wife; for one has seniority by age, while the other has it by birth. (28.33)
The other [portion] is diminished by the share of the eldest. 28.37 — 28.34.

The "extra share" (*uddhāra*) for the eldest, previously mentioned in the passage beginning with "the twentieth part belongs to the eldest" (GDh 28.5), is excluded; he shall receive the other property equally. The meaning is that there is no preferential share. Although the reference is primarily to the property itself, nevertheless, by the force of the initial statement, what is intended here is merely the prohibition of the extra share for the eldest. Otherwise, it would have been necessary to say, "one endowed with qualities receives the share of the eldest"; thus, one devoid of qualities does not receive an equal share. In this regard, the statement of Manu should be consulted.
A Brahmin son shall take four shares, and the son of a Kṣatriya mother three shares.

"The son of a Vaiśya wife shall take two shares; the son of a Śūdra wife shall take one share" (MDh 9.153). If it is argued that this constitutes a prohibition regarding the son of a Śūdra wife, it is replied: the prohibition applies to one born of a woman whose virginity has been violated (*kṣatayoni*). One born of a woman whose virginity is intact (*akṣatayoni*) is entitled to a share. Furthermore, through the status of being "born again" (*paunarbhava*) and so forth, it is indeed possible for a son to be born even of a woman whose virginity has been violated. The phrase "in the absence of sons of the *aurasa* type and others" is the understood remainder. Those who explain that he is entitled to an equal share when such sons (*aurasa*, etc. are absent, should be understood to mean that when they are present, the rule stated in another *Smṛti* must be observed. Thus Vasiṣṭha says: "The son of a Brāhmaṇī wife shall take three shares; the son of a Rājanyā wife shall take two shares; the others shall divide the remainder equally" (VaDh 17.48–50). An alternative application of the subject matter should be understood according to the conduct of the individuals involved. (28.37)

It is understood from the context that one should divide what remains after excluding that "extra portion" (*uddhāra*) previously mentioned, such as "a twentieth part for the eldest," and so forth. Regarding an eldest son who is devoid of good qualities or is the son of a *rājanya* (Kṣatriya) mother, the law of Manu applies: "Or, having divided the entire collection of inheritance here into ten parts, one who knows the Dharma should make a righteous division according to the rule."
"A Brāhmaṇa son shall take four shares; the son of a Kṣatriya woman, three shares;
the son of a Vaiśya woman shall take two shares; and the son of a Śūdra woman shall take one share. (MDh 9.152–153) || 28.34 ||
In a case where there is a gathering of sons born of a Kṣatriya woman and a Vaiśya woman, [the inheritance] is according to the same rule as that for the son of a Brāhmaṇa woman. 28.38. — 28.35.

When the son of the Vaiśya woman is the eldest and endowed with good qualities, while the son of the Kṣatriya woman is younger and the son of the Brāhmaṇī woman does not exist at all, then just as that son of the Kṣatriya woman shares equally with the son of the Brāhmaṇī woman, so too the son of the Vaiśya woman shares equally with the son of the Kṣatriya woman, being deprived of the additional share due to seniority. And thus, in this case, it is made known that there exists an additional share for the eldest son of the Kṣatriya woman. (28.38)

When the son of the Brāhmaṇī is not present, then the son of the Rājanyā shares equally with the son of the Brāhmaṇī; likewise, the son of the Vaiśyā shares equally with the son of the Kṣatriyā. || 28.35 ||
If [the woman] is a Kṣatriya... [28.39] — ...[28.36]

"The eldest son of a Vaiśya who is endowed with good qualities shall have an equal share"—this is how the text proceeds. The meaning is that even from a Kṣatriya, if the son of a Vaiśya is the eldest, he receives an equal share with the younger son of a Kṣatriya. Some maintain that this same principle should be understood to apply to the son of a Śūdra born of a Vaiśya; however, that is incorrect because it has been stated by Manu. (28.39)

The word *ca* has the sense of *ca* (and). When there is a concurrence of two sons born of a Kṣatriya woman, the son of the Vaiśya woman who is senior and endowed with good qualities shares equally with the younger son of the Kṣatriya woman. Some maintain that this same principle should be seen to apply to the son of a Śūdra woman born of a Vaiśya father; others say "no," because it has not been so stated. (28.36)
Even the son of a Śūdra woman, if he is obedient, may receive a means of subsistence from a childless [father] according to the rule for a pupil (antevāsī). || 28.40 || — || 28.37 ||

Even for a Brāhmaṇa who has no son of the twice-born caste, one born from a Śūdra womb shall receive only so much as is necessary for him to be capable of performing tasks such as agriculture, provided he is intent on service like a pupil. The meaning is that he should follow his brother and his brother’s wife as he would a guru, because the rule regarding the *antevāsin* (resident pupil) is characterized by specific forms of service. As for the statement "in the fourth part [of the estate], his offspring [shall have] a livelihood," and so forth—why is this? If it is argued that it is because of the mention of "one whose womb was violated" (*kṣatayoni*), [the answer is: because of the word *api* (even), which implies reproach, he is entitled to a share in this case as well. (28.40)

The term "of the Brāhmaṇa" continues [from the previous rule]. Even the son of a Śūdra woman from a Brāhmaṇa who is childless—that is, one who has no son of the twice-born caste—shall obtain the means of subsistence. He shall obtain as much as he is capable of performing work such as agriculture and so forth, provided that he serves according to the rules for a resident pupil (*antevāsin*); that is, provided he serves just as a student serves his teacher. In this same manner, even the son of a Śūdra woman from a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya shall obtain the means of subsistence. (28.37)
According to some, even the son of a woman of all castes (sarvarṇā), if he behaves unjustly, would not obtain [the inheritance]. 28.41. — 28.38.

H reads "anyāyyavṛttaḥ" (one who behaves improperly). This means that even a son born of a woman of the same caste falls [from his share], and by the use of the word "api" (even), it is implied that even an eldest son falls if he is ill-behaved. Some maintain that he would not receive [a share]. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "Those who have entered another stage of life, as well as the impotent, the insane, and the outcastes, do not receive a share" [VaDh 17.52–53]. The Teacher [Bhāruci] maintains that he *would* receive [a share]. The option [between receiving or not receiving] depends on whether the person can be reformed. 28.41.

However, some hold the opinion that one who behaves unjustly and acquires property through unrighteous means, or bestows it upon courtesans and the like—even if he is the son of a wife of the same caste (*savarṇā*), and even if he is the eldest—shall not receive his inheritance. Thus says Āpastamba: "But one who acquires property through unrighteousness, even if he is the eldest, they shall exclude him from a share" (ĀpDh 2.14.15). || 28.38 ||
The Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*) shall divide the inheritance of a childless Brāhmaṇa. (28.42) — (28.39)

“Learned in the Vedas” (*śrotriyāḥ*) means those who are advanced in the knowledge of the three Vedas, not merely those who have studied the *Chandoga* [Sāmaveda]. Thus Manu says: “Those learned in the three Vedas, pure and self-controlled,” and so forth (MDh 9.188). “Heirs of one without offspring” means heirs of one for whom no son exists. They shall divide the inheritance with the king’s permission, as the mention of the king occurs later in the text. (28.42)

The mention of "offspring" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), the lineage (gotra), the ancestral sages (ṛṣi), and other such connections. For the property of a Brāhmaṇa who is childless and possesses no wealth shall indeed be divided among those learned in the Vedas (śrotriya). 28.39.
For others than the king. || 28.43 || — || 28.40 ||
In the absence of all these, the king alone shall take [the property] from the Kṣatriyas and others.
The king shall take the inheritance of other [classes], such as Kṣatriyas and the rest, who die without offspring. || 28.40 ||
The dull-witted and the impotent must be maintained [by others]. 28.44 — 28.41.

The *jaḍa* is one whose mind is impaired; the *klība* is one of the third gender (*tṛtīyā-prakṛti*). These two must be maintained by means of food and clothing. This also serves as an illustration for those who are mute and so forth. Thus Manu says:

"Those who are impotent (*klība*) or outcastes (*patita*), those blind from birth, deaf, as well as the insane, the mentally dull (*jaḍa*), the mute, and whoever are devoid of sense organs—these do not receive a share. (MDh 9.201) || 28.44 ||
The "jaḍa" is one whose mind is impaired; the "klība" is a person of the third gender. These two must be maintained by providing food and clothing. Manu, however, states:

"The impotent, the outcast, those blind from birth, the deaf, as well as the insane, the mentally deficient, the mute, and whoever lacks their faculties, do not receive a share. (MDh 9.201) || 28.41 ||
The offspring of a fool is entitled to a share. 28.45 — 28.42.
