The offspring of one who is mentally deficient (jaḍa) is worthy of a share. Because of the inclusion of the term "worthy" (arha), it is only if he is capable that he receives a share, and not merely by virtue of being the offspring of a deficient person. Although one might have expected the expression "the offspring of a deficient person" (*jaḍāpatyam*) to be used, this irregular compound (*visamāsa*) is intended to include the offspring born of the wives of eunuchs and others. Thus Manu says:
"If, in any way, there should be a desire for wives on the part of eunuchs and the like..."

"The offspring of those who have produced [such] offspring is entitled to a share. [MDh 9.203] From this very indicative mark (liṅga), one may infer the performance of sacramental rites for them as far as possible. Otherwise, since they are fallen from the Sāvitrī, their offspring would indeed be utterly unworthy. Or rather, it should be understood as referring to one who has performed penance (prāyaścitta). And thus, even that which was previously permitted for an outcaste should be understood as referring to one who has performed penance. By speaking thus, he makes known this: that even after the time of partition, a share must be given to that offspring. 28.45.
If, however, a son is born to one who is impotent (*jaḍa*), then he is entitled to a share; that share should be given to him by his father. On this point, Manu says:

"But if, for some reason, there should be a desire for wives on the part of those who are impotent and so forth, their offspring, having continued the lineage, deserves the inheritance" (MDh 9.203). 28.42.
As in the case of the son of a Śūdra woman, so it is with those born of women in the inverse order of castes. 28.46. — 28.43.

H reads "pratilomās tu," meaning that even for those born of women in the inverse order (pratiloma), if they are intent on service, the means of subsistence should be given just as to the son of a Śūdra; however, since service is possible for Caṇḍālas and others, it should be understood that a lower amount should be given. Thus, it should be understood that this same duty applies to those born in the inverse order as well. (28.46)

Even for those born in the inverse order, such as the Sūta and others, if they are distinguished by superior qualities, the means of subsistence should be provided just as it is for the son of a Śūdra.
There is no division regarding food prepared for the security and well-being [of the household], such as water. 28.47–28.44.
Water refers to wells and the like. *Yoga* is what is desired (*iṣṭa*), and *kṣema* is what is performed for public welfare (*pūrta*). Thus says Lokākṣi:
"Those who perceive reality declare that *kṣema* is *pūrta* and *yoga* is *iṣṭa*; these two are said to be indivisible, as are beds and food."

When cooked food has been prepared for the sake of a festival, there is no fault in [giving it] because of the mention of "prepared" [food]; thus, there is no restriction regarding rice and other such items. Regarding these, there is no division. In that regard, some maintain that like the bed, the rice and other items should be given to one person alone; others desire them for the eldest or the youngest. It should be understood that other items are to be set aside for the group as a whole. (28.47)
Water refers to wells and the like. *Yogakṣema* refers to *iṣṭāpūrta* (sacrificial rites and charitable works). Thus says Laugākṣi:
"Those who perceive the truth declare that *yoga* is *pūrta* and *kṣema* is *iṣṭā*; these two are said to be indivisible, as are the bed and food."

But regarding cooked food prepared for festivals and the like, even if it is abundant, no division should be made among these [co-residents]. They shall enjoy it exactly as it stands, according to their respective shares. (28.44)
And [the same applies] to women who are married. 28.48 — 28.45.

And as for those women who have been taken by fathers—who are free from fear of the next world—for the purpose of sexual enjoyment, one might ask: "Why is their fault not accepted? If this is asked, it is because an expiation is heard in the rule: "For men, there is death in the case of an inverse [union]" (GDh 28.46). Furthermore, there is no partition of property with them by the sons. The intention is that food and clothing must be provided for them when they are old, and intercourse should be had with other women. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), other things also [are included], which, due to their unity, are impossible [to divide]; as Manu has said:
"Garments, vehicles, ornaments, prepared food, water, women, security of possession (yogakṣema), and pasture land are declared to be indivisible. [MDh 9.219] || 28.48 ||

As for those women who are female slaves and have been united with someone among the brothers and others, and are taken as objects of enjoyment, they belong to that person alone. If there are other [wives], then they are the share of the others elsewhere; if there are none, then they must be made equal by means of wealth. Furthermore, when there is only one female slave and she is united [with him], then let her perform work in turn. 28.45.
Regarding that which is not yet known, an action should be performed as recommended by at least ten learned men who possess the capacity for deliberation and are free from greed. (28.49) — (28.46)

"Known" means understood; its opposite is "unknown. Regarding that which has not been correctly understood or is doubted, [the rule applies] with at least ten people—meaning the absolute minimum. They must be "learned," meaning those who have understood the meaning of the Vedas. As Manu says:
"Those by whom the Veda, along with its supplements, has been mastered in accordance with dharma..."

"Those remaining Brahmins are to be known as those for whom the Vedas are the basis of direct perception. (MDh 12.109) "Possessing *ūha*" means being capable of reasoning through inclusion and exclusion (*ūhāpoha*), that is, having their intellects refined by the study of the Mīmāṃsā and other treatises. "Not greedy" means free from craving. "Praised" means commended, in the sense that "this is appropriate here. "That should be done" means it is to be performed; the intention is that it must be carried out in their presence. || 28.49 ||

That which is known as if it were unknown is "anājñāta" (the unacknowledged). The opposite of that is [not so]. When a matter has not been understood as it truly is, or is doubtful, regarding that "anājñāta" case, [the decision] is made by at least ten learned men (*śiṣṭa*), no fewer than ten—those by whom the Veda, along with its supplements (*paribṛṃhaṇa*), has been mastered according to the Law (*dharma*).

"Those remaining Brāhmaṇas are to be known as those whose authority is based on the revealed scripture (śruti) and direct perception," as stated by Manu [MDh 12.109]. By such Brāhmaṇas—those who know the *ūha* (logical reasoning), who are skilled in *ūhāpoha* (the process of inclusion and exclusion), and who are free from greed, having no desire for bribes or the like—it is proper to perform that which they have praised, commended, or declared to be appropriate and fit for this occasion. 28.46.
Who, then, are those ten at minimum? He says:

four who have mastered the four Vedas, including the ancillary sciences; three belonging to the [first] stages of life (*āśrama*), each separately knowing the Dharma; and three others. These ten at minimum are called an assembly (*pariṣad*). (28.50) — || 28.47 ||
H reads "prāg uttamāt" (before the last).

Only Brāhmaṇas, because they alone have the authority (*adhikāra*) for the proclamation of Dharma. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "A Brāhmaṇa should proclaim the Dharmas" (VaDh 1.40). There must be four, not just one, even if he is a knower of the four Vedas (*caturveda*). They are those who have mastered the four Vedas along with their secret portions (*rahasya*), that is, those who have studied the Vedas together with their auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga*). The three highest stages of life (*āśrama*) were mentioned in the third chapter; the mention of "stages of life" is made so that the term "Brāhmaṇas" alone might not be understood [to exclude others]. These too are accepted only as those who know the meaning of the Vedas, since those who do not know it lack the authority. However, this was stated with reference to the performance of their own specific duties (*svadharma*). There are three who separately know the *Dharmaśāstra*, not just one, even if he knows all Dharmas. And these are mentioned separately by taking into account their status as knowers of the Vedas and their status as being in the stages of life. The learned call such a group of ten or more a "pariṣad" (assembly). This is also for the sake of providing consistency with other Smṛtis. Furthermore, that [other rule] is for the purpose of including groups of three or more in the event that these [ten] are unavailable. And so says Manu:

"Whatever legal principle (*dharma*) an assembly (*pariṣad*) of at least ten members may determine, or even one of three who are established in virtuous conduct (*vṛtta*), that *dharma* shall not be overturned. Thus [says Manu, MDh 12.110]. Likewise, Vasiṣṭha also says:
"Whatever four or even three who have mastered the Vedas (*vedapāraga*) might declare..."

"That alone is to be known as the Dharma, and not that of thousands of others"—thus [it is said in VaDh 3.7]. In this regard, it should be understood that when a great number is impossible, only a small portion is to be accepted. 28.50.

Those who have mastered the four Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), as well as those who know their meaning—four such persons constitute a *cāturvidya*, not one alone. Regarding the stages of life (*āśrama*), three were mentioned in the third chapter: the student (*brahmacārin*), the householder (*gṛhastha*), and the mendicant (*bhikṣu*); the forest-dweller (*vāikhānasa*) is also included among them. Among these, the three stages preceding the highest, the forest-dweller, are each experts in the treatises on Dharma. They are mentioned separately so that there might be no confusion regarding the inclusion of three individuals who each know a single treatise on Dharma. Those who know the Dharma call this assembly of at least ten persons a "pariṣad. (28.47)
But in the absence of these, that which a learned man versed in the Vedas and disciplined says when there is a conflict of opinions [is authoritative]. (28.51) — (28.48)

"That [is] the task," is the ellipsis. The word *tu* (but) is used for emphasis. It means that these [qualities] must be present together; it does not mean that even a few of them may be absent as long as some are possible. Since the use of the word *vā* (or) in the phrase "or one who is not a *śrotriya*" already establishes the alternative of absence, this instruction implies that [the assembly is valid] only when all those previously mentioned qualities are impossible, and not merely when there is an impossibility of having ten members. A *śrotriya* is one who has mastered the entirety of the Vedas, not merely one who studies the mantras and brāhmaṇas mentioned in other smṛtis, because extensive recitation is what is intended here. In the context of defining him, he is a knower of the Veda and a knower of its meaning. The term *śrotriya* is employed because we observe that knowledge of the meaning exists even without excellence in the textual recitation. A *śiṣṭa* is one who remains established in his own dharma. Even a single such person is an authority (*pramāṇa*) in the event of a conflict or difference of opinion. (28.51)

In the absence of many such persons, whether individually or collectively, there may be a *śrotriya*—one who has studied the Veda together with its auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*), a knower of the Veda (*vedavit*) who understands its meaning, and a refined person (*śiṣṭa*) devoted to his own duty. Even if such a person is alone, whatever he declares regarding a point of dispute—that "this is appropriate" or "this must be done"—that is what should be performed. Thus says Manu:

"Even a single person who knows the Veda, being composed in mind, shall determine a duty; that is to be known as the supreme duty, not that which is proclaimed by thousands of ignorant men. (MDh 12.113) || 28.48 ||
Regarding this, he states the reason:
Why, then, must the word of even a single learned person—a Vedic scholar who is disciplined—be followed? To this he says: "Because they are the source of Yama for all beings. (28.52)
For this one is powerless regarding the acts of harming or favoring living beings. || 28.49 ||

Because from the Veda arise both [the cessation of transmigratory existence and its engagement]; by the word *yama* (restraint) the cessation of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāranivṛtti*) is denoted, and by the word *prabhava* (origin) the engagement (*pravṛtti*) in that very same [existence] is denoted; and the comprehension of the means for both is attained from the Veda. Therefore, the Veda is the authoritative means (*pramāṇa*) in cases of conflicting opinions. As Manu has said:

"The four castes, the three worlds, and the four stages of life separately—the past, the present, and the future—all these have attained their established proof from the Veda" (MDh 12.97). Furthermore, the mention of *yama* at the beginning is for the purpose of making known that the cessation of transmigratory existence is the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*).

"Origin" (*prabhava*) means a cause (*kāraṇa*), because things originate from it. That which lacks such a [cause] is "without origin" (*aprabhava*). Since he is not perceived to have any other cause for his engagement in the harming or favoring of living beings—such as punishment or penance—but has the scripture alone as his eye, therefore even the word of a single person is to be followed. Another says: "Origin" (*prabhava*) means arising (*prabhavana*), that is, sovereignty (*prabhutva*). He who does not possess that is "without origin" (*aprabhava*). For he does not, independent of scripture and acting on his own authority, favor or harm anyone. Therefore, his word is to be followed. (28.49)
Furthermore: "In matters of harming or favoring [others]," || 28.53 ||

"The Veda alone is the authority"—this is the completion of the sentence. Regarding the connection with violence—in the case of "these animals and so forth are to be sacrificed in the sacrifice"—and regarding the application of favor—in the case of "all [classes], beginning with Brāhmaṇas, are to be favored"—the Veda alone is the authority. And by means of that, the intended meaning is "one who knows the Veda.
Now he states the fruit of one who knows the Dharma. He says that one who practices after having understood [the Dharma] is superior to those who merely practice the Dharma;
specifically, the knower of the Dharma attains the heavenly world.
By means of knowledge and attachment. || 28.54 || — || 28.50 ||

The *dharmī* is one who possesses only the *dharma*; the intention is that he does so specifically until the dissolution of the world (*pralaya*). A *dharmavit* is one who, having known, practices it. Why? Because of the mention of "knowledge" (*jñāna*). "Adherence" (*abhiniveśa*) means the performance of that practice. And thus Vasiṣṭha says: "One who is righteous" (*dhārmika*), and so forth. (28.54)

Those who possess the attributes (*dharma*) of the subject (*dharmin*) are the righteous (*dhārmika*). Among them, he who knows the *dharma*—having studied the *Dharmaśāstra* according to its full meaning—is one who understands the *dharma* in its true essence. [This occurs] through both knowledge (*jñāna*) and application (*abhiniveśa*). Knowledge is a competent understanding; application is the performance [of duty] with total devotion. Through both knowledge and application, he attains the heavenly world (*svargaloka*) more excellently than those who merely perform [the rites]. (28.50)
Thus, this is the Dharma, the Dharma. 28.55 — 28.51.
The supplementary statement is that from the beginning with "The Veda is the root of Dharma" (GDh 1.1) up to this point, the designation "Dharma" belongs to Gautama. 28.55.

Thus, beginning from the outset with "The Veda is the root of Dharma" (GDh 1.1), this Dharma has been declared up to this point. The repetition [of the concluding statement] is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the treatise. 28.51.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter in the *Purāṇamaskarīya* commentary on the *Gautama-dharma-sūtra*.
And thus is completed this *Nibandhana* of Gautama, the commentary (*bhāṣya*) by Maskarī.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the third book of the *Mitākṣarā*, the commentary on the *Śrī-Gautamīya* composed by Haradatta.
This treatise is completed.
